case_title: M/s. Freshlee Retail Pvt. Ltd. vs. Anil Kumar Jain, Resolution Professional M/s. MSX Mall Pvt. Ltd.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1528 of 2023 & I.A. No. 5497 of 2023
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is M/s Freshlee Retail Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent is Anil Kumar Jain, Resolution Professional (later representing the Liquidator) of Corporate Debtor M/s MSX Mall Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 3] 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Commercial lease and occupation of premises in MSX Mall giving rise to operational dues demanded by the Resolution Professional via I.A. No. 3362 of 2020[cite: 3]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Direction issued by the lower tribunal against the Appellant to contribute and deposit unpaid outstanding dues of Rs. 74,48,820/- (noted as Rs. 74,48,828/-)[cite: 3]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Adjudicating Authority passed an ex-parte order on 20.03.2023; Respondent issued a demand letter on 03.04.2023 (received on 03.04.2023); Appellant filed recall application I.A. No. 2337 of 2023 on 19.04.2023 (dismissed for non-prosecution on 28.04.2023); Appellant filed second recall application I.A. No. 3270 of 2023 on 10.05.2023 (dismissed as withdrawn on 16.06.2023); Company Appeal was e-filed on 02.07.2023 with an alleged delay of 74 days[cite: 3]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Demand letter dated 03.04.2023, orders of dismissal for non-prosecution dated 28.04.2023 and withdrawal dated 16.06.2023, and ex-parte order dated 20.03.2023[cite: 3]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench (Court-II) in CP (IB)-334(ND)/2018 allowed I.A. No. 3362 of 2020 ex-parte on 20.03.2023; Appellant approached NCLAT with I.A. No. 5497 of 2023 seeking condonation of 74 days delay under Section 14 of the Limitation Act[cite: 3].
legal_issues: 1. Whether an appellant can claim the benefit of Section 14 of the Limitation Act, 1963 to exclude time spent pursuing recall applications that were dismissed for non-prosecution or voluntarily withdrawn before the Adjudicating Authority[cite: 3]. 2. Whether the voluntary withdrawal of a maintainable recall application satisfies the statutory condition of failing from 'defect of jurisdiction or other cause of a like nature' under Section 14[cite: 3]. 3. Whether the Appellate Tribunal has jurisdiction to condone delay beyond the 15-day period stipulated in the proviso to Section 61(2) of the IBC[cite: 3].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 14 of the Limitation Act cannot be invoked to exclude time spent prosecuting an earlier proceeding before the same forum when such proceeding was maintainable on merits and failed solely due to non-prosecution or voluntary withdrawal, as voluntary abandonment does not constitute a defect of jurisdiction or other cause of like nature[cite: 3]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The phrase 'defect of jurisdiction or other cause of a like nature' in Section 14(1) and 14(2) requires a jurisdictional or near-jurisdictional impediment that disables the court from determining the dispute on merits; furthermore, while Section 5 principles apply via Section 238A, the statutory jurisdiction under the proviso to Section 61(2) of the IBC is strictly capped at 15 days[cite: 3]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal applied the five mandatory conditions established in Consolidated Engineering Enterprises and Roshanlal Kuthalia, finding the third condition unfulfilled because the NCLT had full jurisdiction under Rule 49 and Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 to entertain the recall petition[cite: 3]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because Section 14 was inapplicable, the 74-day delay could not be excluded, and since the Tribunal lacks statutory power under the proviso to Section 61(2) to condone delays exceeding 15 days, the appeal was time-barred[cite: 3].
operative_order: I.A. No. 5497 of 2023 for condonation of 74 days delay is dismissed, and consequently, the Memo of Appeal in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1528 of 2023 is rejected[cite: 3].
summary: Freshlee Retail Pvt. Ltd. filed an appeal before the NCLAT challenging an ex-parte order of NCLT New Delhi directing payment of Rs. 74,48,828/- to the Corporate Debtor, MSX Mall Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 3] The appeal was delayed by 74 days, and the appellant sought exclusion of time under Section 14 of the Limitation Act, 1963, citing pendency of recall applications that were dismissed for non-prosecution and voluntary withdrawal[cite: 3]. The NCLAT held that voluntary withdrawal of a maintainable application does not constitute a defect of jurisdiction or cause of like nature under Section 14[cite: 3]. Consequently, the delay could not be excluded, exceeding the non-extendable 15-day statutory condonation period under Section 61(2) of the IBC, resulting in rejection of the appeal[cite: 3].

case_title: Gloster Cables Ltd. vs. Fort Gloster Industries Ltd. & Ors.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Gloster Cables Ltd. (formerly Crest Cables Pvt. Ltd.); Respondent No. 1 is Fort Gloster Industries Ltd. (Corporate Debtor / CD); Respondent No. 2 is Gloster Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant / SRA); Respondent No. 3 is Bijay Murmuria (Resolution Professional / RP)[cite: 4]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Technical collaboration agreements were executed on 02.05.1995 and 02.05.2003 granting the Appellant trademark usage rights for 'GLOSTER' against royalties[cite: 4]; a 33-year exclusive trademark license agreement was executed on 29.07.2004 for Rs. 3 Crores fee plus Rs. 2 Lakhs annual royalty[cite: 4]; a loan agreement dated 10.11.2006 for Rs. 10 Crores (Rs. 5,68,05,114/- disbursed) was secured by hypothecation of the trademark on 31.01.2008[cite: 4]; a supplemental agreement was executed on 15.07.2008 assigning the trademark to the Appellant for Rs. 10 Lakhs, effective upon discharge of BIFR proceedings[cite: 4]; and a formal assignment deed was executed on 20.09.2017 for recordal before the Trademark Registry[cite: 4]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Section 9 application [CP (IB) 61/KB/2018] was initiated by former employee Jayant Panja for unpaid operational dues against the Corporate Debtor[cite: 4]; the underlying dispute concerned whether the trademark assigned for Rs. 10 Lakhs constituted CD's asset[cite: 4]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: BIFR stayed disposal of CD's assets on 10.09.2001 under SICA[cite: 4]; SICA was repealed on 01.12.2016 with the 180-day transition expiring on 29.05.2017[cite: 4]; Section 9 CIRP was admitted on 09.08.2018[cite: 4]; Appellant applied for trademark assignment recordal on 25.08.2018[cite: 4]; Registrar of Trademarks registered Appellant as proprietor on 17.09.2018[cite: 4]; CoC approved SRA's plan on 24.04.2019[cite: 4]; Appellant filed CA (IB) 713/KB/2019 on 30.05.2019[cite: 4]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Supplemental trademark agreement dated 15.07.2008[cite: 4], deed of assignment dated 20.09.2017[cite: 4], trademark registration certificate dated 17.09.2018[cite: 4], CD's 2017-18 balance sheet showing trademark hypothecation and royalty receipts[cite: 4], and 5th CoC meeting minutes recording a forensic audit report confirming no preferential or undervalued transactions[cite: 4]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed CA (IB) 713/KB/2019 in CP (IB) 61/KB/2018 before NCLT Kolkata Bench seeking exclusion of the 'GLOSTER' trademark from CD's assets and the resolution plan[cite: 4]; NCLT dismissed it on 27.09.2019 holding the assignment void under BIFR stay, hit by moratorium under Section 14, and undervalued/preferential under Sections 43 and 45[cite: 4]; Appellant filed this appeal under Section 61 of the IBC[cite: 4].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Adjudicating Authority has jurisdiction under Section 60(5)(c) of the IBC to decide title over a registered trademark or whether such jurisdiction vests exclusively in the District Court under Section 134(1)(b) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999[cite: 4]. 2. Whether an assignment of trademark executed during the operation of a BIFR stay under Section 22A of SICA is void ab initio or becomes effective upon repeal of SICA[cite: 4]. 3. Whether title to a trademark vests in the assignee upon execution of the assignment deed under Sections 37 and 38 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, or only upon registration under Section 45, and whether registration obtained after the imposition of moratorium violates Section 14 of the IBC[cite: 4]. 4. Whether the Adjudicating Authority possesses jurisdiction to suo motu declare a transaction preferential or undervalued under Sections 43 and 45 of the IBC without an application by the Resolution Professional or Liquidator[cite: 4].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 60(5)(c) of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority possesses statutory jurisdiction to adjudicate disputes regarding title to assets claimed by or against a corporate debtor if they directly relate to the corporate insolvency resolution process[cite: 4]. An assignment of an intangible asset executed subject to the vacation of a statutory stay becomes fully operative upon the abatement/repeal of the underlying statutory framework, vesting title in the assignee[cite: 4]. Furthermore, the Adjudicating Authority cannot suo motu avoid transactions under Sections 43 and 45 without an application filed by the Resolution Professional or Liquidator[cite: 4]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 37, 38, and 45(1) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 establish that title in a trademark vests in the assignee immediately upon execution of a written agreement between the parties; subsequent registration under Section 45 is merely procedural recognition of pre-existing title and does not constitute a creation or transfer of interest in violation of Section 14 of the IBC[cite: 4]. Sections 43(1) and 45(1) of the IBC require the RP or Liquidator to form an opinion or make an examination and submit an avoidance application, making an application an indispensable jurisdictional condition precedent[cite: 4]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying the doctrine from Thomson Press and Anuj Jain, transfers made during an operative interim injunction are not void ab initio between the contracting parties[cite: 4]. For proving undervaluation, a variance between a prior hypothecation amount and subsequent assignment consideration does not satisfy the evidentiary test in the absence of independent valuation evidence and specific pleadings by the RP[cite: 4]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The trademark 'GLOSTER' validly vested in the Appellant upon execution of the 2008 agreement and the repeal of SICA on 01.12.2016, prior to CIRP commencement; its subsequent registration did not breach Section 14, and the NCLT lacked statutory authority to declare the transaction undervalued suo motu[cite: 4]. Consequently, the trademark is not an asset of the Corporate Debtor and must be excluded from the resolution plan[cite: 4].
operative_order: The NCLAT allowed the appeal and set aside the impugned order dated 27.09.2019 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Kolkata Bench), holding that the trademark 'GLOSTER' belongs to the Appellant and does not form part of the assets of the Corporate Debtor, with no order as to costs[cite: 4].
summary: Gloster Cables Limited appealed an NCLT Kolkata order holding that the registered trademark 'GLOSTER' was an asset of the Corporate Debtor, Fort Gloster Industries Limited, and dismissing the appellant's application to exclude it from the resolution plan[cite: 4]. The NCLT had held that the assignment was void due to a BIFR stay, hit by moratorium under Section 14, and undervalued under Sections 43 and 45 of the IBC[cite: 4]. The NCLAT Principal Bench allowed the appeal, ruling that trademark title vested in the appellant upon execution of the assignment agreement and repeal of SICA[cite: 4]. It held that post-CIRP registration was merely procedural and the NCLT lacked jurisdiction to avoid transactions suo motu without an application by the Resolution Professional[cite: 4].

case_title: Sudhir Gupta vs. JM Financial Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. & Ors.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Corporate Debtor is Asian Hotels (West) Ltd. (operating Hyatt Regency, Mumbai); Original Financial Creditor was Yes Bank Ltd., whose debt was assigned to JM Financial Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. and subsequently to UV Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. (UVARCL, holding 98.84% voting share in CoC) and PTC India Financial Services Ltd. (1.16%); Appellants are Sandeep Gupta and Sudhir Gupta (Suspended Directors/Promoters) and Asian Hotels (East) Ltd. / Robust Hotels Ltd. / Saraf Group (shareholders holding ~88% equity)[cite: 5]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed credit facilities from Yes Bank on 21.04.2016 comprising a Term Loan of Rs. 180 Crores, subsequent term tranches totaling Rs. 200 Crores, an Overdraft facility of Rs. 27 Crores, and FITL facilities on 01.09.2020; an additional Rs. 40 Crores facility sanctioned under ECLGS 2.0 was not disbursed by the bank[cite: 5]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Defaults occurred between April 2021 and August 2021 due to pandemic lockdowns; Section 7 petition claimed default of Rs. 264,07,35,129/- as of 13.08.2021; total admitted dues computed by the RP under the Section 12A proposal stood at Rs. 361,69,75,766/- (principal plus accrued interest up to 30.09.2023) alongside balance CIRP costs of Rs. 2,80,43,124/-[cite: 5]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan recall notice and Section 13(2) SARFAESI notice issued on 30.07.2021; Section 7 petition filed on 19.08.2021; asset possession taken under SARFAESI on 21.08.2021; debt assigned to JM Financial on 21.06.2022; NCLT admitted Section 7 on 16.09.2022; debt assigned to UVARCL on 30.11.2022; initial 12A proposal submitted on 11.08.2023; revised proposal submitted on 04.10.2023; CoC voted to reject the proposal on 13.10.2023[cite: 5]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank Guarantee of Rs. 40 Crores submitted to and verified by the RP; two FDRs totaling Rs. 331 Crores (Rs. 316 Crores from Kotak Mahindra Bank and Rs. 15 Crores from IDBI Bank) deposited with lien marked in favor of Registrar, NCLAT; minutes of the 13th to 16th CoC meetings reflecting shifting requirements from the CoC[cite: 5]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-IV admitted Section 7 application [CP (IB) No. 571/PB/2021] on 16.09.2022 and allowed substitution of JM Financial; Suspended Directors and Shareholders appealed to NCLAT; during appeal, Appellants tendered 100% payoff under Section 12A which was rejected by CoC, leading to challenge against CoC's decision[cite: 5].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the decision of the Committee of Creditors (holding 98.84% voting share) to reject a Section 12A withdrawal proposal that offers 100% repayment of all admitted claims of financial and operational creditors along with interest and CIRP costs is arbitrary and subject to judicial review under Section 60 of the IBC[cite: 5]. 2. Whether promoters or suspended directors are disqualified by virtue of Section 29A of the IBC from submitting a settlement or withdrawal proposal under Section 12A[cite: 5]. 3. Whether a Section 12A withdrawal proposal funded with the assistance of majority shareholders or related corporate entities is invalid or barred as third-party participation[cite: 5]. 4. Whether prospective resolution applicants possess any vested legal right to compel evaluation of resolution plans over a complete 100% debt liquidation proposal under Section 12A[cite: 5].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in voting on a Section 12A withdrawal proposal is not absolute or immune from judicial review; where a CoC arbitrarily rejects a just settlement offering 100% payment of all admitted debts of all classes of creditors along with complete insolvency resolution costs, the Adjudicating Authority and Appellate Tribunal possess statutory jurisdiction under Section 60 of the IBC to set aside such arbitrary refusal and terminate the CIRP[cite: 5]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12A and Section 29A operate in mutually distinct statutory domains; Section 29A prescribes disqualification criteria exclusively for resolution applicants seeking to submit a resolution plan, whereas Section 12A is an exit mechanism restoring the corporate debtor to its pre-admission status upon full settlement, meaning Section 29A restrictions cannot be read into Section 12A[cite: 5]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying the standard laid down in Swiss Ribbons v. Union of India, the Tribunal evaluated whether the CoC acted arbitrarily; the uncontradicted physical deposit of FDRs marking lien to the Tribunal covering 100% of admitted claims, interest, and CIRP costs conclusively proved bona fide capacity, exposing the CoC's abrupt reversal and voting dissent as an arbitrary attempt to capture corporate assets[cite: 5]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Prospective resolution applicants hold no vested right to have their plans approved when the corporate debtor's debts are fully liquidated; because all creditors were receiving 100% of their claims without haircut, the CoC's rejection was legally unsustainable, warranting the setting aside of the Section 7 admission order and closure of CIRP[cite: 5].
operative_order: The NCLAT allowed the appeals, set aside the order dated 16.09.2022 admitting Section 7 application, closed the CIRP of Asian Hotels (West) Ltd., and accepted the Section 12A proposal dated 11.08.2023 as revised on 04.10.2023[cite: 5]; directed the Registrar, NCLAT to discharge the lien on FDRs deposited with Kotak Mahindra Bank and IDBI Bank and remit the proceeds to the Resolution Professional within one week[cite: 5]; authorized the RP to invoke the Rs. 40 Crore Bank Guarantee and distribute 100% dues to all creditors within three weeks thereafter[cite: 5]; dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1271 of 2022 as infructuous, with parties bearing their own costs[cite: 5].
summary: Suspended directors and majority shareholders of Asian Hotels (West) Ltd. appealed an NCLT order admitting the company into CIRP under Section 7 on an application initiated by Yes Bank (subsequently assigned to UVARCL)[cite: 5]. During the appeal, the appellants submitted a Section 12A proposal offering 100% repayment of all admitted dues of financial, operational, and other creditors with interest and CIRP costs, depositing Rs. 331 crores in FDRs and a Rs. 40 crore bank guarantee[cite: 5]. The CoC arbitrarily rejected the proposal[cite: 5]. The NCLAT held that the CoC cannot arbitrarily refuse a 100% debt settlement and that Section 29A does not bar promoters under Section 12A, set aside the admission order, and closed the CIRP[cite: 5].

case_title: Authum Investment and Infrastructure Ltd. vs. Rajneesh Sharma, Administrator of SREI Equipment Finance Ltd. & Ors.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Authum Investment and Infrastructure Ltd. (unsuccessful Prospective Resolution Applicant); Respondent No. 1 is Rajneesh Sharma, Administrator of Corporate Debtors SREI Equipment Finance Ltd. (SEFL) and SREI Infrastructure Finance Ltd. (SIFL); Respondent No. 2 is National Asset Reconstruction Company Limited (NARCL, Successful Resolution Applicant); other parties include the Consolidated Committee of Creditors (CoC) and Reserve Bank of India (RBI)[cite: 7]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 227 of the IBC for twin financial service providers (SIFL and SEFL), governed by a consolidated CIRP and a Challenge Process mechanism designed to evaluate competing resolution proposals comprising upfront cash, security receipts, debentures, and equity allotments[cite: 7]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose in large-scale financial service liabilities following RBI's supersession of boards on 04.10.2021; NARCL proposed a Total Resolution Amount of Rs. 14,867.50 Crores (including Rs. 3,180 Crores upfront cash recovery and Rs. 1,800 Crores in security receipts backed by committed NCDs), resulting in a evaluated NPV of Rs. 5,555.58 Crores compared to Authum’s NPV of Rs. 5,526 Crores[cite: 7]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: RBI superseded boards on 04.10.2021; NCLT admitted CIRP on 08.10.2021; CIRP consolidated on 14.02.2022; Challenge Process conducted on 03.01.2023 across five rounds; final resolution plans submitted on 18.01.2023; CoC voting concluded on 15.02.2023 approving NARCL's plan by 84.86% majority; NCLT approved the plan on 11.08.2023[cite: 7]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Challenge Process Note dated 27.12.2022, Evaluation Matrix, NARCL clarification email dated 03.01.2023 sent at 12:49 PM, minutes of 30th and 32nd CoC meetings, and SBI Capital Markets evaluation report (Process Advisors)[cite: 7]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Authum filed IA No. 413/KB/2023 (alleging wrongful denial of 5 marks for equity allotment) and IA No. 557/KB/2023 (challenging NPV calculation and failure to apply a 60% discount rate to NARCL's security receipts); NCLT Kolkata Bench rejected both IAs and approved NARCL's plan on 11.08.2023; Authum appealed under Section 61 of the IBC[cite: 7].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal has jurisdiction to review and modify the commercial evaluation, scoring matrix, and Net Present Value (NPV) computation determined by the Committee of Creditors and its expert financial advisors[cite: 7]. 2. Whether security receipts backed by committed Non-Convertible Debentures (NCDs) with a fixed repayment schedule offered by NARCL were required to be discounted at 60% under the Evaluation Matrix[cite: 7]. 3. Whether an unsuccessful resolution applicant is entitled to claim marks for an optional equity allotment introduced after the conclusion of the Challenge Process[cite: 7].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The scoring, quantitative assessment, and Net Present Value (NPV) calculation of resolution plans under an evaluation matrix fall within the exclusive, non-justiciable commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors and its financial experts, and unsuccessful resolution applicants hold no statutory right to challenge the scores or methodology absent a breach of Section 30(2) of the IBC[cite: 7]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The author of a tender document or Request for Resolution Plan (RFRP) is the best judge of its interpretation; where the process document empowers the CoC to determine binding NPV calculations and reserves the right to approve any plan irrespective of whether it scored the highest NPV, judicial interference under Section 31 or Section 61(3) is impermissible[cite: 7]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Relying on K. Sashidhar, Essar Steel, and Silppi Constructions, courts exercise judicial restraint in business decisions; the evaluation by SBI Capital Markets treating instruments backed by committed NCDs as committed repayment instruments rather than uncommitted vanilla security receipts was neither arbitrary nor perverse[cite: 7]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant was rightly denied marks for equity because its conditional option was submitted after the challenge process freeze date and failed the minimum Rs. 250 Crore threshold; the NPV computation for NARCL complied with the Process Document, rendering the CoC's 84.86% approval lawful and conclusive[cite: 7].
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1072 of 2023, affirming the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 11.08.2023 which rejected IA No. 413/KB/2023 and IA No. 557/KB/2023 and approved the Resolution Plan of NARCL, with no order as to costs[cite: 7].
summary: Authum Investment and Infrastructure Ltd., an unsuccessful resolution applicant, appealed against the NCLT Kolkata Bench order approving the resolution plan submitted by National Asset Reconstruction Company Limited (NARCL) for SREI Equipment Finance Ltd. and SREI Infrastructure Finance Ltd. Authum contended that the Committee of Creditors wrongfully denied it five marks for equity allotment and improperly calculated NARCL’s Net Present Value by not applying a 60% discount rate to its security receipts[cite: 7]. The NCLAT Principal Bench dismissed the appeal, ruling that plan evaluation, scoring matrix interpretation, and NPV computations fall squarely within the non-justiciable commercial wisdom of the CoC and its financial advisors, finding no violation of Section 30(2) of the IBC[cite: 7].

case_title: M/s Earthin Projects Limited vs. Indu Projects Limited & Ors.
bench: Chennai Bench
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is M/s Earthin Projects Limited (in consortium with K. Ramachandra Rao Transmission & Projects Pvt. Ltd., the defaulted Successful Resolution Applicant); Respondent No. 1 is Indu Projects Limited (Corporate Debtor / CD); Respondent No. 2 is Anup Kumar Singh (Resolution Professional / RP); Respondent No. 3 is Consortium of B. Subba Reddy and C. Venkateswara Reddy (subsequent Successful Resolution Applicant); Respondent No. 4 is the Committee of Creditors (CoC). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Bank of India initiated Section 7 CIRP against Indu Projects Limited; Appellant submitted a Resolution Plan proposing Rs. 501 Crores towards settling admitted creditor claims of Rs. 4,138.5 Crores plus Rs. 40 Crores working capital infusion (total Rs. 541 Crores), with mandatory full payment within 90 days from the effective approval date. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant failed to pay the balance settlement amount within 90 days of approval (due by 23.01.2022); deposited only around Rs. 60 Crores (broadly 10%), defaulting on approximately 90% of its financial commitments despite interest accrual provisions at 8% per annum. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 CIRP admitted on 25.02.2019; NCLT approved Appellant's plan on 01.10.2021 (uploaded 25.10.2021); NCLT dismissed 60-day extension application (I.A. No. 77 of 2022) on 01.02.2022; NCLAT granted 3 months extension on 13.04.2022 expiring on 12.07.2022; Supreme Court dismissed creditor appeal as infructuous on 29.08.2022 noting non-payment; NCLT allowed RP's I.A. No. 283 of 2022 on 05.09.2022 granting 60 days to conduct CIRP afresh; NCLAT dismissed challenge on 25.11.2022; Supreme Court appeal (Civil Appeal No. 1133 of 2023) dismissed as withdrawn on 04.12.2023; CoC approved Respondent No. 3's plan on 03.02.2023; NCLT approved it on 05.07.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Terms of approved Resolution Plan defining effective date as 01.10.2021; Bank Guarantee No. 52760IGL0003421 for Rs. 56 Crores issued by Union Bank of India; banking records confirming default on 90% of funds; minutes of 100% CoC vote approving Respondent No. 3's resolution plan and upfront remittance of Rs. 40 Crores by Respondent No. 3. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad Bench-II approved Respondent No. 3's Resolution Plan in I.A. No. 305 of 2023 on 05.07.2023 and dismissed Appellant's recall petition I.A. No. 1031 of 2023; Appellant appealed to NCLAT Chennai under Section 61 claiming the first approval order was never formally set aside and that fresh CIRP without re-imposing moratorium was void.
legal_issues: 1. Whether a Successful Resolution Applicant who defaulted on its financial commitments and failed to adhere to statutory and judicially extended timelines retains locus standi under Section 31(1) and Section 61(1) of the IBC to challenge the approval of a subsequent resolution plan. 2. Whether the direction to conduct CIRP afresh upon the failure of an approved resolution plan requires a fresh, independent order declaring a moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC. 3. Whether an earlier order approving a resolution plan must be formally recalled or set aside by a judicial order before the Adjudicating Authority can approve a subsequent resolution plan. 4. Whether the legal challenges against conducting fresh CIRP are barred by constructive res judicata under Explanation IV of Section 11 of the CPC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A successful resolution applicant that defaults on its binding financial commitments under an approved resolution plan and exhausts all statutory and judicially granted extension periods forfeits its status as a resolution applicant and stakeholder under Section 31(1) of the IBC, thereby lacking locus standi under Section 61(1) to assail the approval or implementation of a subsequent resolution plan. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Conducting CIRP afresh following the failure of an approved resolution plan constitutes a continuation of the original insolvency proceedings initiated under Section 7; it does not require a de novo declaration of moratorium under Section 14, as the statutory moratorium imposed at inception automatically revives upon the collapse of the initial plan. Furthermore, failure to satisfy mandatory payment timelines renders the prior plan approval automatically inexecutable and terminated by operation of law. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal applied the principles of commercial wisdom of the CoC (under K. Shashidhar and Essar Steel) and constructive res judicata under Explanation IV of Section 11 of the CPC, holding that the applicant’s failure to deposit 90% of funds within judicially extended deadlines and the unconditional withdrawal of its appeal before the Supreme Court extinguished all enforceable rights. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant ceased to be an aggrieved person or stakeholder possessing locus standi to obstruct resolution; the fresh CIRP and subsequent approval of Respondent No. 3's plan by 100% CoC voting share were lawful, valid, and conclusive.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 201 of 2023 is dismissed as devoid of any merit without any order as to costs, and all connected pending Interlocutory Applications are closed.
summary: Bank of India initiated CIRP against Indu Projects Limited, where the NCLT approved a resolution plan submitted by Earthin Projects Limited offering Rs. 541 crores[cite: 8]. After Earthin failed to remit approximately 90% of the resolution fund within extended deadlines, the NCLT authorized the Resolution Professional to conduct the CIRP afresh[cite: 8]. Consequently, the CoC approved a subsequent resolution plan submitted by a consortium of B. Subba Reddy and C. Venkateswara Reddy with 100% voting share[cite: 8]. Earthin appealed against the approval order, alleging procedural defects regarding moratorium revival[cite: 8]. The NCLAT Chennai Bench dismissed the appeal, holding that a defaulting resolution applicant forfeits locus standi under Section 31(1) of the IBC once timelines expire, thereby upholding the CoC's commercial wisdom[cite: 8].

case_title: M/s. Kineta Global Limited vs. IDBI Bank Limited & Ors.
bench: Chennai Bench
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is M/s Kineta Global Limited (in consortium with Power Mech Projects Limited, designated H1 bidder for a compromise scheme); Respondents 1 to 6 are secured financial creditors led by IDBI Bank Limited (holding 98.68% voting share); Respondent No. 7 is S. Harikarthik, Liquidator of Corporate Debtor M/s The Jeypore Sugar Company Limited; Respondents 8 and 9 are prospective scheme proponents (M/s Aaria Projects Ltd. and M/s Synergy Holdings)[cite: 9]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Following liquidation of the Corporate Debtor on 29.05.2020, the Liquidator invited expressions of interest to formulate a compromise or arrangement scheme under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with the IBC Liquidation Process Regulations[cite: 9]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Admitted claims of secured financial creditors in liquidation stood at Rs. 571.50 Crores (consortium debt of Rs. 567.59 Crores); the initial liquidation value of Rs. 332.52 Crores (including Rayagada land valued at Rs. 1,087.98 Crores) dropped to Rs. 223.21 Crores after Rayagada land was re-valued at 'Zero' based on an advocate's legal opinion; Appellant tendered a scheme offer of Rs. 207 Crores[cite: 9]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidation was ordered on 29.05.2020; Section 230 EOI was issued on 03.07.2020; revised valuations were conducted on 30.09.2020 and 01.11.2020; secured creditors filed IA No. 255/IB/2021 challenging the valuation; NCLT Chennai allowed the application on 17.11.2021; Orissa High Court recognized compensation rights over 506.690 acres of Rayagada surplus land on 16.03.2022 in WP(C) No. 4490/2015[cite: 9]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Initial valuation report dated 25.09.2019 valuing Rayagada assets at Rs. 1,087.98 Crores; legal opinion dated 28.10.2019 advising that land was embroiled in ceiling litigation under the Orissa Land Reforms Act; Asset Memorandum dated 21.09.2020 excluding Rayagada assets with realisable value recorded at Rs. 217.52 Crores; and Liquidator's email dated 16.03.2022 acknowledging 281 unencumbered acres worth over Rs. 1,000 Crores[cite: 9]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Secured creditors filed IA No. 255/IB/2021 in CP/1307/IB/2018 before NCLT Chennai Bench; on 17.11.2021, NCLT set aside the revised valuation reports, ordered fresh valuation of all assets including Rayagada land under Regulation 35, and directed fresh Section 230 compromise schemes; Appellant appealed to NCLAT Chennai under Section 61[cite: 9].
legal_issues: 1. Whether a bidder or prospective scheme proponent under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 has locus standi as an 'aggrieved person' under Section 61(1) of the IBC to challenge an order of the Adjudicating Authority setting aside a flawed valuation and ordering a fresh valuation and bidding process[cite: 9]. 2. Whether immovable properties of a Corporate Debtor embroiled in title or land ceiling litigation before statutory or constitutional courts can be assigned a 'Zero' valuation and excluded from the Liquidation Estate under Section 36(3)(e) of the IBC and Asset Memorandum under Regulation 34[cite: 9]. 3. Whether the Liquidator violated the mandatory dual-valuation procedure under Regulation 35 of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 and confidentiality obligations under Regulation 34(5) and IP Regulations by obtaining single, piecemeal valuations and leaking draft reports to prospective bidders[cite: 9]. 4. Whether a compromise scheme under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 can override or bypass the mandatory 75% voting approval of secured creditors and valuation provisions under the IBC[cite: 9].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A prospective bidder or compromise proponent participating in a Section 230 process during corporate liquidation has no vested or fundamental right to have its scheme accepted or approved; consequently, such a bidder lacks locus standi as an 'aggrieved person' under Section 61(1) of the IBC to challenge an Adjudicating Authority order directing a fresh valuation and re-invitation of schemes to achieve asset value maximization[cite: 9]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 36(3)(e) of the IBC explicitly mandates that assets subject to determination of ownership by a court or authority form part of the liquidation estate; therefore, a liquidator cannot ascribe 'Zero' value to or exclude properties simply because they are subject to pending litigation or lack clear marketable title[cite: 9]. Furthermore, Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 must operate harmoniously with the IBC, requiring strict compliance with mandatory valuation rules under Regulation 35 and 75% creditor approval under Section 230(2)(c)[cite: 9]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying the standards in Periasamy Palani Gounder and ArcelorMittal, valuation reports must be comprehensive, simultaneous, and independent; procuring separate single reports for distinct asset classes without holistic dual independent valuations under Regulation 35(3), combined with unauthorized circulation of draft valuations in breach of statutory confidentiality, vitiates the integrity of the valuation exercise[cite: 9]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The revised valuation assigning zero value to the Rayagada property was fundamentally flawed and contrary to Section 36(3)(e); the Appellant suffered no legal injury and holds no locus standi; and the NCLT's directions ordering a fresh valuation under Regulation 35 and fresh invitation of Section 230 schemes were lawful, proper, and valid[cite: 9].
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 302 of 2021 without costs, vacated all interim stay orders granted earlier, and closed all connected pending Interlocutory Applications, thereby affirming the NCLT order dated 17.11.2021 directing fresh valuation of all assets including the Rayagada property and fresh invitation of schemes under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 9].
summary: In liquidation proceedings of The Jeypore Sugar Company Limited, the Liquidator invited compromise schemes under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 9]. In a revised valuation, 784 acres of prime Rayagada land was ascribed zero value due to pending ceiling litigation, reducing total liquidation value by nearly Rs. 100 Crores[cite: 9]. Consequently, Appellant Kineta Global Limited was declared H1 bidder for Rs. 207 Crores[cite: 9]. Secured creditors holding 98.68% voting share challenged the process[cite: 9]. NCLT Chennai set aside the valuation and directed fresh valuation and re-tendering[cite: 9]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT Chennai held that litigated assets form part of the liquidation estate under Section 36(3)(e) and cannot be valued at zero, ruling that a bidder lacks locus standi to challenge fresh valuation orders[cite: 9].

case_title: UV Asset Reconstruction Company Limited vs. Electrosteel Castings Limited
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is UV Asset Reconstruction Company Limited (Assignee / Financial Creditor); Respondent is Electrosteel Castings Limited (ECL / Promoter-Obligor); Principal Borrower is Electrosteel Steels Limited (ESL); Original Lender is SREI Infrastructure Finance Limited (SREI); Successful Resolution Applicant for ESL is Vedanta Limited[cite: 10]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: SREI sanctioned a Rupee Loan facility of Rs. 500 Crores to ESL on 26.07.2011; Promoter ECL (holding 34.40% in ESL) executed a Deed of Undertaking, Warranty and Indemnity on 27.07.2011 agreeing under Clause 2.2 to arrange for the infusion of funds into ESL to meet financial covenants upon breach; and on 21.11.2011 executed a Supplementary Agreement creating an exclusive mortgage over factory land in Elavur Village, Ponneri Taluk, Tamil Nadu[cite: 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: ESL defaulted in 2013; in ESL's CIRP, SREI filed an admitted financial claim of Rs. 577.90 Crores; under Vedanta's approved plan, SREI received upfront cash of Rs. 241.71 Crores for sustainable debt and 67,23,710 equity shares of ESL (face value Rs. 10/- reduced to Rs. 0.20) for unsustainable debt; SREI assigned remaining rights to UVARCL on 30.06.2018 claiming unpaid default from ECL[cite: 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 CIRP admitted against ESL on 21.07.2017; Vedanta's plan approved on 17.04.2018; SREI issued NOC on 25.06.2018; debt assigned to UVARCL on 30.06.2018; SARFAESI notices issued on 27.12.2018 and 19.06.2019; Madras High Court suit leave dismissed on 20.09.2019 and appeal dismissed on 13.08.2021; Supreme Court dismissed appeal on 26.11.2021; Section 7 petition [C.P. (IB) No. 16/CB/2021] filed against ECL on 24.04.2021; DRT Chennai dismissed Section 17 challenge on 08.04.2022; NCLT Cuttack rejected Section 7 on 24.06.2022[cite: 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Rupee Loan Agreement dated 26.07.2011; Deed of Undertaking dated 27.07.2011; Supplementary Agreement dated 21.11.2011; SREI letter dated 26.07.2011 confirming no corporate guarantee was required from ECL; Assignment Deed dated 30.06.2018 recording 'Nil' under guarantor details in Schedule 1; ESL Information Memorandum omitting guarantee details; and Clause 3.2(ix) of Vedanta's resolution plan[cite: 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: UVARCL filed a Section 7 petition against ECL before NCLT Cuttack Bench; on 24.06.2022, NCLT rejected the petition holding ECL was not a guarantor and that approval of ESL's resolution plan extinguished the debt; UVARCL appealed to NCLAT[cite: 10].
legal_issues: 1. Whether an undertaking given by a promoter (ECL) to arrange for the infusion of funds into the principal borrower (ESL) upon a breach of financial covenants constitutes a contract of guarantee under Section 126 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, rendering ECL liable for a financial debt under Section 7 of the IBC[cite: 10]. 2. Whether the approval of a corporate debtor's resolution plan under the IBC operates to extinguish and efface the surviving liabilities of third-party guarantors and security providers where the resolution plan contains an express reservation of rights[cite: 10].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A contractual covenant executed by a promoter or sponsor obligating it merely to arrange for the infusion of funds into a borrower to enable the borrower to meet financial covenants does not constitute a contract of guarantee under Section 126 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, absent an express undertaking to directly perform the promise or discharge the debt liability of the borrower upon default; however, approval of a resolution plan does not ipso facto efface surviving claims against third-party guarantors or mortgagors where rights are expressly preserved in the plan[cite: 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 126 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 requires a clear and unambiguous promise by the surety to answer for the debt or default of the principal debtor directly to the creditor[cite: 10]. A covenant to arrange funds into the borrower creates no creditor-surety privity and cannot be construed as a financial debt under Section 5(8) or Section 7 of the IBC[cite: 10]. Under the doctrine in Lalit Kumar Jain, approval of a plan discharges the principal debtor but does not extinguish third-party liabilities if saved by plan provisions[cite: 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying the contractual interpretation principle from Silppi Constructions (that the author of a document is its best judge), the bench evaluated the text of the undertaking, the lender's contemporaneous letter expressly disclaiming any corporate guarantee requirement, and the assignment deed indicating 'Nil' under guarantor schedules[cite: 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: ECL was an obligor and third-party mortgagor rather than a corporate guarantor; therefore, no financial debt was owed by ECL to sustain a Section 7 insolvency petition, justifying rejection of the application while clarifying that debt effacement under the resolution plan operated strictly qua ESL only[cite: 10].
operative_order: The NCLAT upheld the order dated 24.06.2022 of the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Cuttack Bench) rejecting the Section 7 Application against ECL, while clarifying that the finding in paragraph 15 regarding the extinguishment and effacement of the entire debt of ESL upon resolution plan approval is strictly confined qua the Corporate Debtor (ESL) only and does not extinguish surviving claims or remedies against third parties, with parties bearing their own costs[cite: 10].
summary: UV Asset Reconstruction Company Limited appealed an NCLT Cuttack Bench order rejecting its Section 7 IBC application against Electrosteel Castings Limited (ECL), promoter of principal borrower Electrosteel Steels Limited (ESL)[cite: 10]. SREI had extended loan facilities to ESL, where ECL executed a deed of undertaking to arrange fund infusions upon covenant breach and created a mortgage[cite: 10]. SREI assigned the debt to UVARCL following ESL's resolution under Vedanta[cite: 10]. The NCLAT Principal Bench upheld the rejection, ruling that an agreement merely to infuse funds into a borrower does not constitute a contract of guarantee under Section 126 of the Contract Act, meaning no financial debt was owed by ECL[cite: 10]. However, the Tribunal clarified that plan approval does not automatically extinguish third-party security liabilities[cite: 10].

case_title: Jeevagan Narayana Swami Nadar (Suspended Director of Sinnar Thermal Power Ltd.) vs. Shapoorji Pallonji & Co. Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor is Shapoorji Pallonji & Co. Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 1); Corporate Debtor is Sinnar Thermal Power Ltd.; Appellant is Jeevagan Narayana Swami Nadar (substituted for original appellant Chandan Mishra, deceased Suspended Director); Respondent No. 2 is Adarsh Sharma, Interim Resolution Professional (IRP)[cite: 11]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor awarded civil and structural construction contracts for Boiler Turbine Generator (BTG) on 28.05.2010 (Rs. 180 Crores, enhanced to Rs. 224.13 Crores) and Offsite Boiler Turbine Generator (OBTG) work order on 22.11.2012 (Rs. 12.56 Crores) for its 1350 MW Thermal Power Project at Sinnar SEZ, Nashik[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor raised 77 Running Account Bills (RABs) for BTG and 19 RABs for OBTG totaling executed work of Rs. 208.33 Crores, against which the Corporate Debtor paid Rs. 146.14 Crores, leaving an outstanding unpaid default balance of Rs. 62.19 Crores[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Operational Creditor issued Section 8 demand notice on 16.08.2019; Corporate Debtor replied on 29.08.2019 alleging slow progress; Operational Creditor filed Section 9 petition under Arbitration Act on 16.08.2019 to protect its performance bank guarantee (stay granted on 20.08.2019); Section 21 arbitration was invoked on 23.09.2019 (culminating in an arbitral award of Rs. 62.19 Crores in favor of R1 on 22.04.2022, challenged under Section 34); Section 9 IBC petition [C.P. (IB) No. 2561/(ND)/2019] was admitted on 19.09.2022[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Unqualified Work Completion Certificate dated 09.05.2019 issued by the Corporate Debtor confirming satisfactory execution as of 31.03.2018; expiration of the 12-month Defect Liability Period on 31.03.2019 without dispute; withdrawal of previous contract termination; and failure by Corporate Debtor to refer disputes to the contractually designated Engineer-in-Charge[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-IV admitted Section 9 application on 19.09.2022 holding that operational debt exceeded statutory threshold and no genuine pre-existing dispute existed prior to demand notice; Suspended Director appealed to NCLAT under Section 61[cite: 11].
legal_issues: 1. Whether there existed any genuine pre-existing dispute within the meaning of Section 5(6) and Section 8 of the IBC prior to the issuance of the demand notice dated 16.08.2019[cite: 11]. 2. Whether the invocation and pendency of post-demand notice arbitration proceedings and a Section 34 challenge against an arbitral award bar an application under Section 9 of the IBC filed independently on unpaid invoices[cite: 11]. 3. Whether an unqualified and unconditional Work Completion Certificate issued by the Corporate Debtor estops it from setting up a defense of deficient workmanship or delay[cite: 11].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 9 of the IBC, a defense of pre-existing dispute must be supported by credible contemporaneous evidence existing prior to the issuance of the Section 8 demand notice; disputes raised belatedly in reply to the demand notice or subsequent arbitration proceedings initiated post-demand notice do not constitute a valid pre-existing dispute when the underlying claim is independently founded on unpaid invoices substantiated by an unqualified completion certificate[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9(5)(a) mandates that the Adjudicating Authority 'shall' admit an application if it is complete and no notice of a pre-existing dispute under Section 8(2) or prior suit/arbitration was received before the demand notice, leaving no statutory discretion unlike the word 'may' in Section 7(5)(a)[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying the Mobilox Innovations standard, the defense raised by the Corporate Debtor was illusory and spurious; the issuance of an unqualified Work Completion Certificate after the expiry of the 12-month Defect Liability Period and the failure to refer issues to the contractual Engineer-in-Charge conclusively rebutted allegations of defective execution or delay[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because no genuine pre-existing dispute existed prior to 16.08.2019 and default exceeding Rs. 1 Lakh occurred on valid operational debt, the Adjudicating Authority's order admitting the Corporate Debtor into CIRP was legally sound and unassailable[cite: 11].
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1185 of 2022 as devoid of merit, affirming the order dated 19.09.2022 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench-IV in C.P. (IB) No. 2561/(ND)/2019, and closed all connected interlocutory applications with no order as to costs[cite: 11].
summary: Shapoorji Pallonji & Co. Pvt. Ltd. filed a Section 9 application under the IBC against Sinnar Thermal Power Ltd. for unpaid operational debt of Rs. 62.19 crores arising from BTG and OBTG civil construction contracts for a thermal power plant in Nashik[cite: 11]. The NCLT admitted the Corporate Debtor into CIRP, rejecting claims of pre-existing disputes[cite: 11]. The suspended director appealed, arguing that project delays, pending arbitration proceedings, and a Section 34 challenge precluded Section 9 admission[cite: 11]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the Corporate Debtor issued an unqualified work completion certificate after the defect liability period and raised no disputes before the contractually designated engineer-in-charge prior to the Section 8 demand notice[cite: 11]. Consequently, the alleged disputes were illusory, justifying CIRP[cite: 11].

case_title: Punjab National Bank vs. Sandwoods Infratech Projects (P) Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1527 of 2023 & IA No. 5383 of 2023
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Punjab National Bank (dissenting/abstaining secured Financial Creditor holding 17.80% voting share); Corporate Debtor is M/s Sandwoods Infratech Projects (P) Ltd.; Respondent No. 1/3 is Ravinder Kumar Goel (Resolution Professional / RP); Respondent No. 2 is M/s Balaji Durobuild (P) Ltd. / D. Konda (Successful Resolution Applicant / SRA); other CoC members include Homebuyers as Financial Creditors in class (71.75% voting share) and State Bank of India (10.45% voting share)[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Real estate development of group housing projects at Mohali and Kasauli, funded by credit facilities from financial creditors (PNB and SBI) and advances received from homebuyers[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by Corporate Debtor resulted in initiation of CIRP; Successful Resolution Applicant D. Konda submitted a resolution plan to complete both housing projects within 9 months utilizing receivables from homebuyers and sale proceeds of unsold flat inventories without cost escalation[cite: 12]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 25.10.2021; Form G published pursuant to 3rd CoC meeting dated 01.01.2022; resolution plan submitted by SRA on 12.03.2022; minor plan adjustments communicated on 21.04.2022; CIRP period extended by 90 days on 24.05.2022; 6th CoC meeting held on 04.05.2022; e-voting conducted from 08.05.2022 to 11.05.2022 approving the plan by 71.75% majority; NCLT dismissed PNB's recall application (IA No. 2304/2022) on 12.07.2023; NCLT approved the plan in IA No. 2414/2022 on 10.08.2023[cite: 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Minutes of the 5th and 6th CoC meetings; emails dated 02.05.2022 and 04.05.2022 from PNB seeking additional data; transaction auditor's report confirming no transactions under Sections 43, 45, 50, and 66; Section 29A eligibility affidavit; and Clause 6.5(c)(ii) & (vii) of the Resolution Plan stipulating that all securities (primary, secondary, and collateral) and guarantees provided by third parties shall stand unconditionally released, vacated, and transferred to the Corporate Debtor/SRA[cite: 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench (Court-III) in CP (IB) No. 292(ND)/2021 dismissed PNB's recall petition on 12.07.2023 and allowed RP's application IA No. 2414 of 2022 on 10.08.2023 approving D. Konda's resolution plan; PNB appealed to NCLAT under Section 61[cite: 12].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Resolution Professional and the majority Committee of Creditors committed a material irregularity or breach of natural justice by refusing the dissenting financial creditor's request for additional time to analyze modifications to the resolution plan and proceeding with e-voting[cite: 12]. 2. Whether a resolution plan can lawfully provide under Regulation 37 of the CIRP Regulations, 2016 for the unconditional release, vacation, and assignment of securities, third-party collaterals, and personal/corporate guarantees held by secured financial creditors without violating Section 30(2)(e) of the IBC or Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872[cite: 12]. 3. Whether a dissenting secured financial creditor is entitled to challenge an approved resolution plan based on the higher value of its security interest over the allocation determined in the commercial wisdom of the CoC under Section 30(2)(b)[cite: 12].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Regulation 37 of the CIRP Regulations, 2016 read with Sections 30 and 31 of the IBC, the Committee of Creditors in the exercise of its commercial wisdom has the statutory competence to approve a resolution plan providing for the transfer, vacation, modification, or satisfaction of security interests and guarantees held by secured creditors; dissenting financial creditors cannot leverage the value of their underlying security interests to seek a higher payout or disrupt an approved plan[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 37(b) and 37(d) expressly allow a resolution plan to provide for the sale or transfer of assets whether subject to security interest or not and for the satisfaction or modification of any security interest[cite: 12]. The entitlement of a dissenting financial creditor is circumscribed strictly by Section 30(2)(b) of the IBC, which operates independently of the value of security interest held[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying the binding doctrines of K. Sashidhar, Essar Steel, and India Resurgence ARC, the Tribunal held that judicial review cannot evaluate the commercial merits of a plan approved by over 66% voting share[cite: 12]. The record established that required audit and valuation reports were available 20 days prior, and the minor modifications (reducing BSP by Rs. 80,000/- and excluding wooden flooring) affected only homebuyers, who voted 71.75% in favor[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC committed no illegality in denying further extensions given the strict time-bound nature of CIRP and the rights of homebuyers[cite: 12]. The release and transfer of securities under Clause 6.5 complied fully with Regulation 37 and Section 30(2), rendering the plan approval valid and binding[cite: 12].
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1527 of 2023 along with IA No. 5383 of 2023 without costs, affirming the order dated 10.08.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT New Delhi Bench-III) in IA No. 2414 of 2022 approving the resolution plan[cite: 12].
summary: Punjab National Bank, a dissenting financial creditor holding 17.80% voting share, appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order approving a resolution plan submitted by D. Konda for Sandwoods Infratech Projects (P) Ltd., approved by a 71.75% CoC majority led by homebuyers[cite: 12]. The appellant contended that the Resolution Professional conducted e-voting without granting adequate time to analyze plan modifications and that provisions releasing and assigning third-party securities and guarantees violated Section 128 of the Contract Act and Section 30(2)(e) of the IBC[cite: 12]. The NCLAT Principal Bench dismissed the appeal, ruling that under Regulation 37 of the CIRP Regulations, the CoC in its commercial wisdom can lawfully extinguish security interests, and dissenting creditors cannot claim higher distribution based on security value[cite: 12].

case_title: SREI Equipment Finance Ltd. vs. Uday Narayan Mitra, Interim Resolution Professional of ARSS Infrastructure Projects Ltd.
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 770 of 2023 & I.A. No. 2694 of 2023
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is SREI Equipment Finance Ltd. (Financial Creditor); Corporate Debtor is ARSS Infrastructure Projects Ltd. (under CIRP); Respondent is Uday Narayan Mitra, Resolution Professional (RP)[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed financial assistance under three loan contracts: Contract No. 50430 dated 03.09.2013 (Rs. 138,51,01,300/-), Contract No. 92744 dated 22.09.2015 (Rs. 20,00,00,000/-), and Contract No. 94261 dated 22.09.2015 (Rs. 64,30,00,000/-), totaling Rs. 222,81,01,300/-, secured by hypothecation of movable plant, machinery, spares, personal guarantees, and registered RoC charges under Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 14]. On 29.03.2017, parties executed a Deed of Assignment where CD assigned arbitration receivables of Rs. 1071.22 Crores represented as unencumbered to settle Rs. 240.30 Crores of dues, subject to an automatic revival clause of original loan contracts upon default[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted on loan repayments; SREI submitted Form C claim for Rs. 919,78,94,038/- (principal plus accrued contractual interest) during CIRP, which the RP rejected in full[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: On 08.06.2017, State Bank of India informed SREI that assigned receivables were already encumbered in favor of consortium lenders[cite: 14]; SREI issued rectification notice on 17.06.2017[cite: 14]; SREI terminated assignment agreement on 15.06.2019 and issued recall/demand notice on 15.07.2019[cite: 14]; CIRP admitted against CD on 30.11.2021[cite: 14]; SREI filed Form C claim; RP rejected claim on 28.01.2022 as time-barred[cite: 14]; NCLT dismissed IA 64/CB/2022 on 10.05.2022[cite: 14]; NCLAT allowed appeal on 30.08.2022 holding claim within limitation[cite: 14]; NCLAT issued clarification on 18.10.2022 directing RP to verify claim on merits by 31.10.2022[cite: 14]; RP rejected claim again on 01.11.2022[cite: 14]; NCLT dismissed IA 11/CB/2023 on 18.04.2023[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Three Loan Contracts and Hypothecation Deeds dated 03.09.2013 and 22.09.2015[cite: 14]; balance sheet entries for FY 2015-16 reflecting long-term borrowings from NBFCs of Rs. 196,07,50,906/-[cite: 14]; Assignment Deed dated 29.03.2017 containing automatic revival Clause 7.2.1(ii)[cite: 14]; SBI letter dated 08.06.2017 establishing prior encumbrance[cite: 14]; and termination communication dated 15.06.2019[cite: 14]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: SREI filed IA (IB) No. 11/CB/2023 under Section 60(5) of the IBC before NCLT Cuttack Bench challenging RP's rejection email dated 01.11.2022[cite: 14]; NCLT dismissed it on 18.04.2023 holding that unilateral termination of the assignment deed was invalid without approaching civil court and that an arbitration dispute was pending under Section 21 of the Arbitration Act[cite: 14]; SREI appealed to NCLAT under Section 61[cite: 14].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Resolution Professional possesses quasi-judicial or adjudicatory jurisdiction under Section 18(1)(b) of the IBC and Regulation 8 of the CIRP Regulations to determine the legal validity of a contractual termination or reject a financial claim supported by loan contracts[cite: 14]. 2. Whether a contractual deed of assignment containing an express automatic revival clause upon an event of default revives the underlying financial contracts automatically without requiring an antecedent decree of rescission from a civil court[cite: 14]. 3. Whether the mere issuance of a notice invoking arbitration under Section 21 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, without the appointment of an arbitrator or pendency of proceedings under Section 11, justifies rejection of a financial creditor's claim[cite: 14].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under the IBC, a Resolution Professional is an administrative facilitator obligated to receive, collate, and verify claims under Section 18(1)(b) based on financial contracts and accounting records, and possesses no adjudicatory authority to determine the legal validity of a contract termination, declare a rescission invalid, or reject a claim on contested contractual defenses[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The terms 'claim' under Section 3(6) and 'debt' under Section 3(11) of the IBC are expansive and include rights to payment whether disputed or undisputed[cite: 14]; where an assignment agreement explicitly stipulates that existing finance agreements and obligations 'shall automatically revive' upon an event of default, the occurrence of default restores the original financial debt by operation of contract without requiring a civil court decree[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated the original loan contracts, registered RoC charges, balance sheet admissions, and the unambiguous wording of Clause 7.2.1 of the Assignment Deed alongside SBI’s encumbrance letter, holding that these established a revived, enforceable financial debt under Regulation 8(2)(b)(i) of the CIRP Regulations[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor committed misrepresentation regarding encumbrances, triggering automatic revival of the original loan contracts[cite: 14]; as no arbitral tribunal was ever constituted under Section 11 of the Arbitration Act, the RP and NCLT committed a material error in rejecting the claim[cite: 14].
operative_order: The NCLAT allowed Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 770 of 2023, set aside the impugned order dated 18.04.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Cuttack Bench) in I.A (IB) No. 11/CB/2023, and held that the Resolution Professional committed an error in rejecting the Appellant's financial claim, with no order as to costs[cite: 14].
summary: SREI Equipment Finance Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Cuttack Bench order dismissing its application against the Resolution Professional of ARSS Infrastructure Projects Ltd., who rejected SREI's financial claim of Rs. 919.78 crores[cite: 14]. SREI had granted term loans of Rs. 222.81 crores, which were temporarily substituted by an assignment of receivables[cite: 14]. Upon discovering the receivables were already encumbered with SBI, SREI terminated the assignment, invoking an automatic revival clause for original loan agreements[cite: 14]. The NCLAT held that under the assignment deed, the original debt automatically revived upon default without requiring civil court rescission[cite: 14]. It ruled that the RP lacks adjudicatory powers to determine contractual validity, setting aside the rejection[cite: 14].

case_title: Sivagnanagovindasamy Nambi vs. The Registrar of Companies, Chennai
bench: Chennai Bench
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Sivagnanagovindasamy Nambi, Shareholder cum Director of Manasanthi Mental Health Care Private Limited; Respondent is the Registrar of Companies (RoC), Chennai[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Incorporation and operation of Manasanthi Mental Health Care Private Limited to provide mental healthcare services to society and establish a psychiatric hospital, having infused additional capital of Rs. 19 Lakhs during 2011-2012 and carrying active liabilities and loans[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Failure to file statutory Annual Returns and Financial Statements with the RoC for seven consecutive financial years, namely FY 2010-11, 2011-12, 2012-13, 2013-14, 2014-15, 2015-16, and 2016-17[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: RoC struck off the company's name under Section 248(5) on 29.06.2017 and published Form STK-7 in the Gazette of India on 05.07.2017 (Gazette dated 15-21 July 2017, S.No. 1516)[cite: 15]; MCA launched Condonation of Delay Scheme (CODS) on 29.12.2017[cite: 15]; Madras High Court issued interim orders in WP No. 8590/2018 on 26.03.2018/12.04.2018 regarding director disqualification[cite: 15]; NCLT Chennai dismissed the restoration application on 12.01.2022[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Audited balance sheets demonstrating capital infusion of Rs. 19 Lakhs, project records for setting up a mental health hospital, active loans and creditors reflected in accounts, and RoC report dated 16.12.2020 citing non-compliance under Sections 92 and 137[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed CA/558/2020 under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 before NCLT Chennai Bench-I seeking revival of the company's name; NCLT dismissed it on 12.01.2022 holding the company non-operational at the time of striking off; Appellant appealed to NCLAT under Section 421[cite: 15].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Condonation of Delay Scheme (CODS), 2018 operates as a substitute or alternative remedy to statutory restoration under Section 252 of the Companies Act, 2013 for a company whose name was already struck off by the Registrar of Companies under Section 248[cite: 15]. 2. Whether the disqualification of directors under Section 164(2)(a) is legally distinct from the striking off and removal of a company under Section 248 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 15]. 3. Whether it is 'just' under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 to order the restoration of a company providing essential mental healthcare services with active creditors and loans, upon undertaking to regularize statutory filing defaults and pay penal costs[cite: 15].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory disqualification of directors under Section 164(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 is legally distinct from the striking off of a corporate entity under Section 248; administrative schemes designed to relieve disqualified directors do not displace the statutory procedure for judicial revival under Section 252, but where a struck-off entity is engaged in vital public-welfare services with active creditor liabilities, it is 'just' under Section 252(3) to restore its corporate status subject to appropriate penal costs and full regularisation of overdue statutory filings[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 252(3) confers wide equitable discretion upon the Tribunal to restore a company's name not only where it was carrying on business or in operation, but also if it is otherwise 'just' to do so; this statutory discretion must be exercised pragmatically taking into account the social utility of the enterprise and creditor interests[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying the 'concept of justness' from established appellate precedents, the Tribunal evaluated whether the company had bona fide operational existence, active balance sheet liabilities, and demonstrated genuine readiness to cure filing defaults and pay statutory late fees and costs[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in rigidly dismissing the restoration application; because the company provided essential mental healthcare services and had outstanding creditors, ordering restoration to the RoC Register upon payment of Rs. 1 Lakh cost was equitable, proper, and legally warranted[cite: 15].
operative_order: The NCLAT allowed Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 32 of 2022 and set aside the impugned order dated 12.01.2022 passed by NCLT Chennai Bench-I with the following directions: (a) Appellant shall pay a cost of Rs. 1 Lakh to the RoC, Chennai within four weeks[cite: 15]; (b) upon restoration of the company's name in the Register, the company shall file all overdue Annual Returns and Balance Sheets and pay all applicable fees and late charges within four weeks thereafter[cite: 15]; (c) RoC remains free to initiate punitive steps under the Companies Act, 2013 for late filing or non-filing of statutory documents[cite: 15].
summary: Sivagnanagovindasamy Nambi, director of Manasanthi Mental Health Care Private Limited, appealed an NCLT Chennai order dismissing an application under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 to restore the company's name[cite: 15]. The Registrar of Companies struck off the company under Section 248 for failing to file returns from FY 2010-11 to FY 2016-17[cite: 15]. The appellant contended that the company was active, constructing a mental health hospital with outstanding creditors, and complied with the Condonation of Delay Scheme 2018[cite: 15]. The NCLAT Chennai Bench allowed the appeal, ruling that while CODS does not supplant Section 252, the company's public healthcare purpose rendered restoration just under Section 252(3), conditional upon paying Rs. 1 lakh costs and submitting overdue filings with statutory fees[cite: 15].

case_title: Rajiv Kumar Agarwalla vs. Rajesh Kumar Kejriwal & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 284 of 2020 & Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 285 of 2020
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor is Olympia Credit and Mercantile Private Ltd.; Corporate Debtor is Prithvi Finvest Company Private Limited; Appellant is Rajiv Kumar Agarwalla (Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor); Respondents are Rajesh Kumar Kejriwal (Interim Resolution Professional / IRP) and Jitendra Lohia (Liquidator)[cite: 16]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial facility of Rs. 25 Lakhs availed by the Corporate Debtor from Olympia Credit and Mercantile Private Ltd.; Corporate Debtor is an RBI-registered Non-Banking Financial Company (NBFC) engaged in financial services without accepting public deposits[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed default amount was Rs. 25 Lakhs under Section 7 of the IBC; the audited balance sheet of the Corporate Debtor as of 31.03.2017 showed total assets (current and non-current) amounting to Rs. 4,17,86,35,943/- (approx. Rs. 41.78 Crores), well below the Rs. 500 Crores statutory threshold[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application [CP (IB) No. 695/KB/2017] was admitted on 15.01.2018; initial appeal [Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 65/2018] was dismissed on 22.02.2018; Section 227 of IBC was notified on 01.05.2018; MCA issued FSP Rules on 15.11.2019 and notification on 18.11.2019 bringing NBFCs with assets of Rs. 500 Crore or more under IBC; NCLT dismissed recall application (CA No. 642/2018) on 02.01.2020; NCLAT final order passed on 31.01.2024[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Certificate of Registration issued by RBI Department of Non-Banking Supervision, Kolkata Regional Office[cite: 16]; RBI NBFC list confirming status as a non-deposit taking NBFC[cite: 16]; Balance Sheet as of 31.03.2017 showing asset size under Rs. 500 Crores[cite: 16]; and MCA Notifications dated 15.11.2019 and 18.11.2019[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench admitted Section 7 application on 15.01.2018 and subsequently passed a liquidation order[cite: 16]; Appellant filed CA No. 642/2018 under Section 60(5) read with Rule 11 seeking recall of the admission order for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction[cite: 16]; NCLT dismissed it on 02.01.2020 holding it could not review its order[cite: 16]; Appellant filed Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 284 & 285 of 2020 before NCLAT[cite: 16].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Corporate Debtor, being a Non-Banking Financial Company (NBFC) with an asset size below Rs. 500 Crores, is excluded from the definition of a 'corporate person' under Section 3(7) and exempt from insolvency resolution proceedings under Section 7 of the IBC[cite: 16]. 2. Whether an objection regarding inherent lack of subject-matter jurisdiction can be raised at any subsequent stage of proceedings, including through an application for recall under Section 60(5) read with Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016, notwithstanding the dismissal of an earlier appeal against the admission order[cite: 16]. 3. Whether an order admitting an application under Section 7 and subsequent liquidation orders passed without subject-matter jurisdiction are void ab initio, non-est, and a nullity[cite: 16].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A decree or order passed by an Adjudicating Authority lacking subject-matter jurisdiction is coram non judice, non-est, and a complete nullity; such an invalidity goes to the root of the matter and can be raised at any stage of proceedings, including in collateral proceedings or recall applications, and cannot be cured by consent, waiver, acquiescence, estoppel, or res judicata[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(7) of the IBC excludes financial service providers from the definition of a corporate person[cite: 16]; under Section 227 read with MCA Notification dated 18.11.2019, only NBFCs having an asset size of Rs. 500 Crores or more are subject to insolvency and liquidation proceedings under the Code[cite: 16]. An NBFC with assets below Rs. 500 Crores falls wholly outside the subject-matter jurisdiction of the Adjudicating Authority under Section 7[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying the jurisdictional doctrines in Harshad Chiman Lal Modi, Jagmittar Sain Bhagat, and Isabella Johnson, subject-matter jurisdiction is a pure question of law[cite: 16]. Official registration certificates from the Reserve Bank of India and audited financial statements establishing asset size below the statutory threshold operate as jurisdictional facts demonstrating total absence of authority[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor was an NBFC with an asset size below Rs. 500 Crores, depriving the NCLT of subject-matter jurisdiction; the Section 7 admission order dated 15.01.2018 and all consequential orders, including the liquidation order, were non-est and void ab initio[cite: 16].
operative_order: The NCLAT allowed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 284 & 285 of 2020, set aside the impugned orders dated 02.01.2020 and the liquidation order, declared the Section 7 admission order dated 15.01.2018 and all consequential proceedings to be non-est in law, and granted liberty to the Liquidator to apply to the NCLT within one month for recovery of fees[cite: 16].
summary: Rajiv Kumar Agarwalla, suspended director of Prithvi Finvest Company Pvt. Ltd., appealed an NCLT Kolkata order dismissing an application to recall the Section 7 admission order dated 15.01.2018 and challenging the subsequent liquidation order[cite: 16]. The appellant established that the corporate debtor was an RBI-registered Non-Banking Financial Company (NBFC) with an asset size of less than Rs. 500 crores[cite: 16]. The NCLAT Principal Bench allowed the appeals, ruling that under Section 3(7) and Section 227 of the IBC read with MCA notification dated 18.11.2019, NBFCs below Rs. 500 crores are excluded from CIRP[cite: 16]. Lack of subject-matter jurisdiction renders the initial admission and consequential liquidation non-est, which can be raised at any stage[cite: 16].

case_title: Kesoram Industries Limited vs. Pratim Bayal, Resolution Professional of Birla Tyres Limited
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Kesoram Industries Limited (demerged parent entity / claimant); Corporate Debtor is Birla Tyres Limited (under CIRP); Respondent is Pratim Bayal, Resolution Professional (RP) who replaced erstwhile IRP Mr. Seikh Abdul Salam[cite: 18]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was carved out and demerged from the Appellant under a Scheme of Arrangement under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013, approved by NCLT Kolkata on 08.11.2019; Appellant claimed to have funded loan repayments, interest, devolved letters of credit, bank guarantees, and operational losses of the demerged tyre division during transition[cite: 18]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant submitted Form C claiming a financial debt of Rs. 518,28,98,356/- (comprising Principal: Rs. 424,25,19,253/-, Interest: Rs. 92,13,86,995/-, and TDS Recoverable: Rs. 1,89,92,111/-), describing the transaction as an 'Inter Company Loan given from time to time along with accrued interest thereon'[cite: 18]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 9 CIRP was admitted against the Corporate Debtor on 05.05.2022; Appellant filed Form C on 16.05.2022; erstwhile IRP collated the claim at Rs. 516,81,01,037/-; NCLT substituted the IRP with the Respondent on 31.10.2022; Respondent sought loan documents on 23.12.2022 and 27.12.2022; Appellant refused on 27.12.2022 and 28.12.2022 contending the RP lacks power to re-verify; Respondent formally rejected the claim on 19.04.2023; NCLT dismissed IA No. 957/KB/2023 on 18.10.2023[cite: 18]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: A balance confirmation letter dated 02.05.2022 signed by the Corporate Debtor's Accounting Controller (obtained 3 days prior to CIRP admission); Audited Financial Statements of the Corporate Debtor for FY 2021-22 recording Rs. 52,119.06 Lakhs under 'Note 14: Other Financial Liabilities - Payable to Demerged Company' (rather than under Note 13: Borrowings); and Appellant's written email admission that no formal loan agreement or bank disbursement occurred because the CD was its internal business division[cite: 18]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA (IBC) No. 957/KB/2023 under Section 60(5) of the IBC before NCLT Kolkata Bench challenging the RP's rejection email dated 19.04.2023; NCLT dismissed the application on 18.10.2023 holding that disbursement against time value of money was unproven; Appellant appealed to NCLAT under Section 61[cite: 18].
legal_issues: 1. Whether an inter-company liability arising out of a corporate demerger and recorded in the balance sheet under 'Other Financial Liabilities' constitutes a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC in the absence of actual monetary disbursement against consideration for the time value of money[cite: 18]. 2. Whether a successor Resolution Professional is empowered under the IBC and CIRP Regulations to call for supporting documentation, re-examine, and reject a financial claim that was previously admitted by an erstwhile Interim Resolution Professional[cite: 18]. 3. Whether the Adjudicating Authority possesses statutory jurisdiction under Section 60(5) of the IBC to adjudicate the substantive validity and merits of a creditor's rejected claim[cite: 18].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 5(8) of the IBC, the requirement of an actual disbursal of funds against the consideration for the time value of money is an indispensable condition precedent for establishing a financial debt; mere accounting balances, demerger liabilities, or balance confirmations lacking underlying financial contracts and bank transfer records cannot convert an operational or restructuring adjustment into a financial debt[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) must be strictly interpreted such that the core element of disbursal for time value of money permeates all sub-clauses; a Resolution Professional is statutorily empowered under Section 25(2)(e) and Regulation 10 of the CIRP Regulations to maintain an updated list of claims and demand verification documents, and the Adjudicating Authority holds plenary jurisdiction under Section 60(5) to decide all questions of law and fact regarding rejected claims[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying the fundamental principles in Anuj Jain v.
