Axis Bank Limited, the claimant must prove actual money flow through banking channels; balance sheet reflections under 'Other Financial Liabilities' (signed by common board leadership) and balance confirmation letters executed on the eve of CIRP without primary loan agreements or disbursement proof fail the evidentiary threshold[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant admitted that no loan agreements existed and no funds were disbursed; therefore, the essential genesis of a financial debt was completely absent, and the RP and Adjudicating Authority acted in accordance with law in rejecting the claim[cite: 18].
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1467 of 2023 without costs, affirming the order dated 18.10.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Kolkata Bench-II) in IA (IBC) No. 957/KB/2023 which upheld the Resolution Professional's decision rejecting the Appellant's claim as a Financial Creditor[cite: 18].
summary: Kesoram Industries Limited appealed an NCLT Kolkata Bench order rejecting its application to restore its admitted financial debt claim of Rs. 518.28 crores against Corporate Debtor Birla Tyres Limited[cite: 18]. The Corporate Debtor had been carved out of Kesoram under a demerger scheme[cite: 18]. Although the erstwhile IRP initially admitted the claim, the successor Resolution Professional re-verified it and rejected it due to the absence of loan agreements or bank disbursement records[cite: 18]. The NCLAT Principal Bench dismissed the appeal, ruling that under Section 5(8) of the IBC, disbursal of funds against the consideration for the time value of money is indispensable; accounting entries under 'other financial liabilities' without actual disbursement do not constitute a financial debt[cite: 18].

case_title: Mr. Narendrabhai S/O Kantibhai Patel vs. PNB Housing Finance Ltd. & Another
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor is PNB Housing Finance Ltd. (Respondent No. 1); Corporate Debtor is M/s Nakoda Fruit Products Pvt. Ltd.; Appellant is Narendrabhai (Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 2 is Varun Vashisht, Interim Resolution Professional (IRP)[cite: 19]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan facility sanctioned by PNB Housing Finance Ltd. on 29.09.2018 for an amount of Rs. 10.52 Crores for a tenure of 144 months with floating interest, repayable in monthly installments (EMIs) of Rs. 13,03,220/-, secured by mortgage of immovable property and Fixed Deposit Receipts (FDRs/DSRA)[cite: 19]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose in 2019; the account was classified as NPA on 14.12.2019; total claimed default in Part IV of Section 7 petition was Rs. 15.18 Crores (with Rs. 10.95 Crores outstanding at loan recall) with date of default indicated as 14.12.2019 (reckoned 90 days prior as 13.09.2019)[cite: 19]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan recall cum arbitration notice issued on 26.12.2019; Section 13(2) SARFAESI notice issued on 15.01.2020; physical possession taken under SARFAESI on 16.09.2021; Corporate Debtor submitted written OTS proposals on 24.08.2020, 11.11.2022, and 27.07.2023; Section 7 petition [CP (IB) No. 264/MB/IV/2023] was filed on 24.01.2023[cite: 19]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Sanction letter dated 29.09.2018; FDR ledger records showing partial liquidation of Rs. 50 Lakhs from pledged FDRs/DSRA without borrower replenishment; demand email dated 07.01.2020 directing restoration of the reserve; and written One-Time Settlement (OTS) letters dated 24.08.2020 and 11.11.2022 acknowledging loan debt and NPA conversion[cite: 19]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV admitted Section 7 application on 13.10.2023 holding that default exceeded Rs. 1 Crore and OTS letters constituted valid limitation acknowledgments under Section 18; Suspended Director appealed to NCLAT under Section 61[cite: 19].
legal_issues: 1. Whether written One-Time Settlement (OTS) and restructuring proposals submitted by a corporate debtor, even if made on a 'without prejudice' basis, constitute valid acknowledgments of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 to extend limitation for Section 7 IBC applications[cite: 19]. 2. Whether unilateral adjustment of EMIs from pledged Fixed Deposit Receipts (Debt Service Reserve Account) regularizes an NPA loan account or negates the existence of default when the borrower fails to replenish the security[cite: 19]. 3. Whether Section 10A of the IBC bars initiation of CIRP when the underlying financial default and NPA classification occurred prior to 25.03.2020 and continued into the Section 10A period[cite: 19].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Written One-Time Settlement (OTS) proposals submitted by a corporate debtor prior to the expiration of the three-year limitation period—irrespective of whether they are marked 'without prejudice'—operate as valid acknowledgments of liability under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963, renewing the limitation period for an application under Section 7 of the IBC; furthermore, Section 10A does not immunize continuing defaults that originated prior to 25.03.2020[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applying the Supreme Court doctrine in Laxmi Pat Surana and Dena Bank, Section 18 of the Limitation Act applies directly to Section 7 IBC proceedings, whereby successive written acknowledgments trigger fresh three-year limitation windows[cite: 19]. Section 10A must be interpreted strictly to bar only defaults that arose between 25.03.2020 and 24.03.2021, and does not apply to defaults committed prior to 25.03.2020[cite: 19]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under the Innoventive Industries standard, the Adjudicating Authority is required only to ascertain the existence of a financial debt and default exceeding the statutory threshold[cite: 19]. Pledged FDRs serving as a Debt Service Reserve Account (DSRA) are security instruments; their appropriation by the lender without replenishment by the debtor does not regularize an NPA account, and multiple OTS letters constitute conclusive evidence of admitted debt and default[cite: 19]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The default occurred in 2019 prior to the Section 10A period, and the OTS letters dated 24.08.2020 and 11.11.2022 renewed limitation up to the filing in January 2023; because debt and default exceeding Rs. 1 Crore were established, the admission of CIRP was lawful and justified[cite: 19].
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1461 of 2023 without costs, affirming the order dated 13.10.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV) in CP (IB) No. 264/MB/IV/2023 admitting the Section 7 application and initiating CIRP against M/s Nakoda Fruit Products Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 19]
summary: Narendrabhai, suspended director of Nakoda Fruit Products Pvt. Ltd., appealed an NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 7 IBC application filed by PNB Housing Finance Ltd. for defaulting on a Rs. 10.52 crore loan facility, claiming Rs. 15.18 crores[cite: 19]. The appellant contended that EMIs were adjusted from fixed deposits, the application was barred by limitation, and default during COVID-19 was protected under Section 10A[cite: 19]. The NCLAT Principal Bench dismissed the appeal, holding that adjusting pledged deposits without replenishment does not regularize default[cite: 19]. The Tribunal affirmed that successive OTS proposals constituted written acknowledgments extending limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, and Section 10A does not bar antecedent defaults originating prior to 25.03.2020[cite: 19].

case_title: Africa Power Company CC vs. Jyoti Structures Limited & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Africa Power Company CC (lessor/claimant based in South Africa); Respondent No. 1 is Jyoti Structures Limited (Corporate Debtor, operating under new management post-resolution); Respondent No. 2 is Ms. Vandana Garg (Erstwhile Resolution Professional)[cite: 20]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Alleged equipment rental contracts entered into in October 2017 and January 2018 (purportedly extended to May and August 2018) between the Appellant and one Mr. Sudeep Sharma on behalf of the Corporate Debtor (Africa Branch) for execution of turnkey transmission works at Masa Ngwedi C&D sites in South Africa[cite: 20]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed unpaid lease rental dues and replacement value for unreturned equipment aggregating to ZAR 1,17,81,893.174 (specifically ZAR 90,53,355.58 with 2% monthly compounded interest from 15.06.2020 and ZAR 40,66,000 with 10% annual interest from 14.07.2020)[cite: 20]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced against the Corporate Debtor on 04.07.2017; Adjudicating Authority approved the Resolution Plan on 27.03.2019; High Court of South Africa (Gauteng Local Division, Johannesburg) passed an ex-parte default judgment against Corporate Debtor on 06.10.2020; Appellant first issued a settlement demand to the RP on 07.05.2021; control transferred to the new management on 09.11.2021; Appellant filed IA No. 1020 of 2023 before NCLT Mumbai in early 2023, which was dismissed on 06.07.2023[cite: 20]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Rental agreements executed during CIRP without the RP's signature or knowledge; ex-parte default judgment dated 06.10.2020 from the High Court of South Africa; Approved Resolution Plan containing Clauses VII(K) and (L) providing for complete extinguishment of all unadmitted and excluded pre-approval claims; and RP's records establishing that the alleged liabilities were never approved or accounted for as CIRP costs[cite: 20]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 1020 of 2023 under Section 60(5) of the IBC before NCLT Mumbai Bench seeking recovery of outstanding rental dues; NCLT dismissed the application on 06.07.2023 under the Ghanashyam Mishra doctrine holding that unadmitted claims stand extinguished upon plan approval; Appellant appealed to NCLAT under Section 61[cite: 20].
legal_issues: 1. Whether claims arising out of alleged contractual transactions executed during the CIRP period without the authorization, consent, or knowledge of the Resolution Professional can be categorized as CIRP costs or enforced against the reorganized Corporate Debtor post-approval of the Resolution Plan[cite: 20]. 2. Whether the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal possesses jurisdiction under Section 60(5) of the IBC to enforce or execute a foreign default money judgment against a Corporate Debtor[cite: 20]. 3. Whether all unadmitted and undisclosed claims stand permanently extinguished under the 'clean slate' doctrine upon approval and implementation of a Resolution Plan[cite: 20].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 31 of the IBC and the 'clean slate' doctrine, approval and implementation of a resolution plan permanently extinguishes all claims, liabilities, and proceedings that were not submitted, admitted, or incorporated as insolvency resolution process costs; neither the NCLT nor the NCLAT possesses jurisdiction under Section 60(5) to act as an execution forum for enforcing foreign money decrees against a restructured corporate debtor[cite: 20]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(5) of the IBC confers jurisdiction strictly over questions of law or fact arising out of or in relation to pending insolvency resolution or liquidation proceedings, and does not encompass powers under Section 44A or Section 13 of the CPC to recognize or execute foreign decrees[cite: 20]. Furthermore, under Section 5(13) read with Section 23(1), operational expenses cannot be classified as CIRP costs unless expressly incurred or authorized by the Resolution Professional managing the corporate debtor[cite: 20]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying the Supreme Court doctrine in Committee of Creditors of Essar Steel and Ghanashyam Mishra & Sons, a successful resolution applicant acquires the corporate debtor on a clean slate and cannot be ambushed by undecided, unverified, or post-approval claims; an ex-parte foreign default decree obtained without the RP's privity cannot circumvent statutory insolvency mechanisms[cite: 20]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the alleged contracts were never authorized by the Resolution Professional, never formed part of verified CIRP costs, and were never submitted prior to the approval of the resolution plan on 27.03.2019, the claims stood legally extinguished, rendering the Section 60(5) application fundamentally non-maintainable[cite: 20].
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1084 of 2023 with no order as to costs, affirming the order dated 06.07.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai Bench) in IA No. 1020 of 2023 in CP (IB) No. 1137 of 2017[cite: 20].
summary: Africa Power Company CC appealed an NCLT Mumbai order dismissing its application under Section 60(5) of the IBC seeking payment of ZAR 1.17 crore from Jyoti Structures Limited for equipment leased during CIRP[cite: 20]. The appellant relied on a default judgment from the High Court of South Africa[cite: 20]. The NCLAT Principal Bench dismissed the appeal, holding that the alleged lease agreements were never authorized by the Resolution Professional nor accounted for as CIRP costs[cite: 20]. Relying on the Supreme Court doctrines in Essar Steel and Ghanashyam Mishra, the Tribunal ruled that all undecided claims outside the approved Resolution Plan stand extinguished, and Section 60(5) confers no jurisdiction to execute foreign decrees in India[cite: 20].

case_title: Santosh Kumar vs. ASK Trusteeship Services Private Limited & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor is ASK Trusteeship Services Private Limited (through ASK Property Investment Advisory Private Limited, R1); Corporate Debtor is Nobility Estates P. Ltd. (R2); Appellant is Santosh Kumar (Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 2 is represented through IRP Hitesh Goel[cite: 21]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor issued unlisted Optionally Convertible Cumulatively Secured Debentures (OCDs) aggregating to Rs. 125,00,00,000/- (Rs. 125 Crores) subscribed by the Financial Creditor under a Debenture Subscription Agreement (DSA), secured by a Debenture Trust Deed, memorandum of entry for equitable mortgage, and personal guarantees[cite: 21]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Redemption was originally due on 06.10.2020, extended at Corporate Debtor's request to 31.07.2021; Corporate Debtor failed to redeem; total claimed default in Part IV of Section 7 petition as of 24.05.2023 was Rs. 687,50,00,000/- (Rs. 687.50 Crores, principal plus redemption premium and accrued coupons), with date of default designated as 06.05.2022 (following default notice dated 05.02.2022 claiming Rs. 504.50 Crores)[cite: 21]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CD requested extension on 03.10.2020; FC agreed on 05.10.2020; modification agreement executed on 16.06.2021 fixing redemption to 31.07.2021; default occurred on 31.07.2021; recall notice issued on 05.02.2022; CD replied on 30.03.2022 admitting liability; Section 7 petition [C.P. (IB) No. 390(PB)/2023] was filed on 24.05.2023; NCLT admitted CIRP on 24.11.2023[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Debenture Subscription Agreement, Debenture Trust Deed, Modification Agreement dated 16.06.2021, NeSL Record of Default dated 05.07.2023, and Corporate Debtor's reply email dated 30.03.2022 and written reply in Section 7 admitting failure to redeem OCDs due to COVID-19 pandemic distress[cite: 21]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi admitted Section 7 application on 24.11.2023 holding that OCDs constitute financial debt and default was admitted; Suspended Director appealed to NCLAT under Section 61[cite: 21].
legal_issues: 1. Whether funds raised through unlisted Optionally Convertible Debentures (OCDs) constitute a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8)(c) of the IBC or are in the nature of equity investments under the IFCI Ltd. v. Sutanu Sinha doctrine[cite: 21]. 2. Whether the Adjudicating Authority violated principles of natural justice by considering a rejoinder affidavit or admitting Section 7 proceedings based on instruments alleged to be insufficiently stamped[cite: 21]. 3. Whether the Adjudicating Authority has discretion under Section 7(5)(a) of the IBC to refuse or defer admission of an insolvency petition solely because the Corporate Debtor is an ongoing solvent concern[cite: 21].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Monies disbursed against Optionally Convertible Debentures (OCDs) carrying a defined redemption timeline and yield constitute a financial debt under Section 5(8)(c) of the IBC, as they are disbursed against consideration for the time value of money; they are legally distinct from Compulsorily Convertible Debentures (CCDs), which represent equity investments[cite: 21]. Once the twin criteria of financial debt and default exceeding the statutory threshold are established, admission of a Section 7 petition is mandatory, and the corporate debtor cannot avert CIRP merely by asserting that it is an ongoing concern[cite: 21]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8)(c) of the IBC explicitly includes within 'financial debt' any amount raised pursuant to note purchase facilities or the issuance of bonds, notes, debentures, loan stock, or similar instruments[cite: 21]. Unlike CCDs which mandate equity conversion, OCDs grant an option for repayment/redemption of principal, retaining the character of a debt obligation[cite: 21]. Under Section 7(5)(a) read with Section 3(12), the Adjudicating Authority possesses no discretion to refuse admission where debt and default are undisputed[cite: 21]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying the binding doctrines from Innoventive Industries, E.S. Krishnamurthy, and M. Suresh Kumar Reddy, as well as NCLAT precedent in MAIF Investments, the bench evaluated NeSL default certificates, the DSA and DTD contracts, and written admissions in the debtor's correspondence admitting non-redemption of OCDs[cite: 21]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The OCDs represented an enforceable financial debt and default was established by written admission and NeSL records; the Supreme Court ruling in IFCI Ltd. (applicable strictly to CCDs) was distinguished; objections regarding stamp duty and natural justice were rejected, rendering the CIRP admission order lawful and unassailable[cite: 21].
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1575 of 2023 without costs, affirming the order dated 24.11.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi) in C.P. (IB) No. 390(PB)/2023 admitting the Section 7 application against Nobility Estates P. Ltd.[cite: 21]
summary: Santosh Kumar, suspended director of Nobility Estates P. Ltd., appealed an NCLT Principal Bench order admitting a Section 7 IBC application filed by ASK Trusteeship Services Private Limited for default on Optionally Convertible Debentures (OCDs) amounting to Rs. 687.50 crores[cite: 21]. The appellant contended that OCDs are in the nature of equity investment (relying on IFCI Ltd. v. Sutanu Sinha), the transaction documents were insufficiently stamped, and the corporate debtor was a solvent going concern[cite: 21]. The NCLAT Principal Bench dismissed the appeal, holding that unlike Compulsorily Convertible Debentures, OCDs carry a redemption obligation and qualify as financial debt under Section 5(8)(c) of the IBC[cite: 21]. Given the corporate debtor's written admissions of default and NeSL records, admission of CIRP was mandatory[cite: 21].

case_title: Sainik Industries Private Limited vs. Ritesh Raghunath Mahajan, RP, Indian Sugar Manufacturing Company Limited
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Sainik Industries Private Limited (sugar purchaser/claimant); Corporate Debtor is M/s Indian Sugar Manufacturing Company Limited (sugar manufacturer); Respondent is Ritesh Raghunath Mahajan, Resolution Professional (RP) of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 22]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Parties entered into an agreement dated 28.07.2016 (titled 'Supply Agreement/Loan Agreement-1' / White Sugar Supply Agreement) for the sale and delivery of 5,200 MT of white crystal sugar at a fixed price of Rs. 3,215/- per quintal against an advance payment of Rs. 10 Crores paid by the Appellant, with clauses providing for delivery default penalties, interest on unadjusted advance, two security cheques of Rs. 5 Crores each, and a pledge of 10% equity shares[cite: 22]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor failed to supply sugar or refund the advance; Appellant claimed a total debt of Rs. 34,65,36,490/- (principal advance of Rs. 10 Crores plus interest and damages) in Form C, which the RP reclassified from a financial debt to an operational debt[cite: 22]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Agreement executed on 28.07.2016; Legal notice issued on 31.01.2017; Section 138 NI Act proceedings initiated after security cheques were dishonoured; Commercial Suit No. 474 of 2019 resulted in summary judgment for Rs. 3,75,35,765/- on 12.01.2023; Appellant filed Section 9 CIRP petition (CP No. 469 of 2020) on 29.01.2020; Section 7 CIRP initiated against CD by a third party on 23.03.2023; Appellant submitted Form C on 01.06.2023; RP rejected financial debt status on 05.06.2023; Section 9 petition dismissed as infructuous on 28.08.2023; NCLT dismissed IA No. 2909 of 2023 on 17.10.2023[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: White Sugar Supply Agreement dated 28.07.2016, Sale Order dated 27.07.2016, dishonoured security cheques, and prior Section 9 petition filed by the Appellant acknowledging the debt as operational[cite: 22]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 2909 of 2023 in CP (IB) No. 162/MB/2023 before NCLT Mumbai Bench-I seeking direction to the RP to admit its claim of Rs. 34.65 Crores as a financial debt; NCLT dismissed the application on 17.10.2023; Appellant appealed to NCLAT under Section 61[cite: 22].
legal_issues: 1. Whether an advance payment made for the supply and purchase of commercial goods under a supply contract containing default interest, penal damages, and security instruments constitutes a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) or an 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) of the IBC[cite: 22]. 2. Whether the inclusion of security cheques, penal interest, or share pledge covenants converts an advance payment for goods into a transaction having the commercial effect of a borrowing under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC[cite: 22]. 3. Whether a creditor who previously instituted Section 9 insolvency proceedings on the basis of an operational debt can subsequently claim the status of a financial creditor in CIRP[cite: 22].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An advance payment made by a buyer to a seller pursuant to an agreement for the procurement and delivery of goods bears a direct nexus with the provision of goods and constitutes an operational debt under Section 5(21) of the IBC; contractual covenants providing for default penalties, interest on unadjusted advance funds, or collateral securities such as security cheques and share pledges do not alter the foundational character of a sale transaction into a financial borrowing or disbursement for the time value of money under Section 5(8)[cite: 22]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(21) of the IBC encompasses claims 'in respect of' the provision of goods and services broadly to include both suppliers and recipients of goods who make advance payments, as established by the Supreme Court in Consolidated Construction Consortium Ltd.; conversely, Section 5(8) mandates a disbursement against consideration for the time value of money, which cannot be inferred from commercial trade advances[cite: 22]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying the standards in Consolidated Construction Consortium Ltd. and Pioneer Urban Land, the Tribunal examined the underlying recitals of the White Sugar Supply Agreement, the transaction's commercial purpose (delivery of 5,200 MT sugar), and the Appellant's prior conduct in initiating Section 9 proceedings, concluding that security and interest clauses were merely standard protective mechanisms to ensure supply performance rather than commercial borrowings[cite: 22]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The transaction was an advance for the procurement of goods rather than a financial borrowing; the Resolution Professional correctly categorized the claim as an operational debt, and the Adjudicating Authority's dismissal of the application was lawful and affirmed[cite: 22].
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1614 of 2023 without costs, affirming the order dated 17.10.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai Bench-I) in IA No. 2909 of 2023 upholding the classification of the Appellant's claim as an operational debt[cite: 22].
summary: Sainik Industries Private Limited appealed against an order of NCLT Mumbai Bench-I rejecting its application to classify an advance of Rs. 10 crores, along with interest and damages totaling Rs. 34.65 crores, as a financial debt in the CIRP of Indian Sugar Manufacturing Company Limited[cite: 22]. The appellant contended that contractual penalty clauses, default interest, security cheques, and share pledge provisions gave the advance the commercial effect of a borrowing[cite: 22]. The NCLAT Principal Bench dismissed the appeal, holding under the Supreme Court doctrine in Consolidated Construction Consortium Ltd. that advance payments for the supply of goods constitute an operational debt under Section 5(21) of the IBC[cite: 22]. Ancillary security terms do not convert a commercial supply contract into a financial debt[cite: 22].

case_title: Standard Chartered Bank vs. Satish Kumar Gupta, R.P. of Essar Steel Ltd. & Ors. (In re: SREI Infrastructure Finance Ltd. & Anr.)
appeal_number: I.A. No. 2853 & 2854 of 2023 in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 242 of 2019
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Corporate Debtor is Essar Steel India Ltd. (ESIL); original petitioner under Section 7 is Standard Chartered Bank; Resolution Professional is Satish Kumar Gupta; Successful Resolution Applicant is ArcelorMittal India Pvt. Ltd. (AMIPL); Applicants in I.A. Nos. 2853 & 2854 of 2023 are SREI Infrastructure Finance Ltd. (SIFL, financial creditor/CoC member under an RBI-appointed Administrator) acting through individual shareholder Ms. Limalemla Longkumer, and Ms. Limalemla Longkumer personally[cite: 20]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Multi-crore CIRP of Essar Steel India Ltd. under Section 7 of the IBC, leading to the approval of AMIPL's Resolution Plan by NCLT Ahmedabad on 08.03.2019, modifications by NCLAT on 04.07.2019, and final affirmation and implementation following the Supreme Court's judgment on 15.11.2019[cite: 20]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by Corporate Debtor on substantial consortium credit facilities; the underlying interlocutory applications sought to reopen and recall the final approval and implementation of the Resolution Plan after more than three and a half years[cite: 20]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT approved AMIPL's resolution plan on 08.03.2019[cite: 20]; NCLAT disposed of appeals on 04.07.2019[cite: 20]; Supreme Court upheld the plan on 15.11.2019[cite: 20]; Applicants filed IA No. 647 of 2023 on 13.02.2023 seeking recall of the 04.07.2019 order[cite: 20]; NCLAT dismissed IA 647 of 2023 on 31.03.2023[cite: 20]; Applicants filed IA No. 2854 of 2023 on 29.05.2023 seeking recall of the 31.03.2023 dismissal order[cite: 20]; final order passed on 16.01.2024[cite: 20]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Order of NCLT Kolkata placing SIFL under the control of an RBI-appointed Administrator[cite: 20]; NCLAT order dated 31.03.2023 running into 42 pages dismissing IA 647 of 2023 on maintainability and lack of locus[cite: 20]; 5-Judge Bench judgment dated 25.05.2023 in Union Bank of India v. Dinkar T. Venkatasubramanian[cite: 20]; and pleadings alleging fraud and misapplication of Kunhayammed and A.V. Papayya Sastry precedents[cite: 20]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Applicants filed IA No. 647 of 2023 in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 242 of 2019 seeking recall of the 04.07.2019 NCLAT order; NCLT dismissed it on 31.03.2023 for lack of locus and application of the doctrine of merger[cite: 20]; Applicants then filed IA No. 2854 of 2023 seeking recall of the 31.03.2023 dismissal order along with IA No. 2853 of 2023 for amendment[cite: 20].
legal_issues: 1. Whether an application under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 for recall of an earlier order dismissing a recall application can be entertained to re-adjudicate questions of locus standi and doctrine of merger, or whether such an application constitutes an impermissible review in disguise[cite: 20]. 2. Whether the doubting or overruling of legal precedents relied upon in an earlier decision renders that decision void ab initio or provides a valid legal ground to recall the judgment under inherent powers[cite: 20]. 3. Whether an individual shareholder of a financial creditor company under the management of an RBI-appointed Administrator possesses the derivative standing to seek recall of a resolution plan approval order that has merged with a Supreme Court judgment[cite: 20].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While the Appellate Tribunal possesses inherent jurisdiction under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 to recall a judgment on narrow, established grounds (such as patent lack of jurisdiction, fraud practiced upon the court, or procedural failure of justice ex debito justitiae), it has no statutory power of review; consequently, an application that seeks to re-argue points of law, re-examine findings on locus standi, or challenge the application of the doctrine of merger after a full hearing constitutes an impermissible application for review disguised as a recall[cite: 20]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 11 preserves the inherent powers of the Tribunal but cannot be used to confer substantive appellate or review jurisdiction where none is provided by the IBC[cite: 20]; once an order of the Appellate Tribunal merges with the final judgment of the Supreme Court, the subordinate appellate tribunal cannot disturb the merged decree absent demonstrable procedural fraud practiced directly upon the court[cite: 20]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying the 5-judge bench standard in Union Bank of India v. Dinkar T. Venkatasubramanian and Supreme Court precedents in Budhia Swain and A.R. Antulay, the bench examined whether the applicants were denied a hearing or if fraud was practiced in procuring the order dated 31.03.2023[cite: 20]; finding that the applicants were fully heard and that the allegations amounted only to legal disagreements with judicial conclusions, the evidentiary threshold for recall was not met[cite: 20]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: There was no fraud practiced upon the Tribunal and no procedural defect occurred in delivering the order dated 31.03.2023; the applicants were attempting to secure an impermissible second hearing to review decided issues, warranting the rejection of both applications[cite: 20].
operative_order: The NCLAT rejected and dismissed I.A. No. 2854 of 2023 seeking recall of the judgment dated 31.03.2023, and consequently rejected I.A. No. 2853 of 2023 seeking amendment, in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 242 of 2019, with no order as to costs[cite: 20].
summary: Applicants SREI Infrastructure Finance Ltd. and its shareholder filed applications seeking recall of an NCLAT order dated 31.03.2023, which had dismissed their earlier recall application (I.A. No. 647 of 2023) challenging the Essar Steel resolution plan approval order dated 04.07.2019 on grounds of lack of locus and the doctrine of merger[cite: 20]. The applicants alleged the 31.03.2023 order was a nullity and obtained by fraud through misapplication of judicial precedent[cite: 20]. The NCLAT Principal Bench dismissed the applications, holding that while inherent powers under Rule 11 permit recall for patent lack of jurisdiction, fraud, or procedural failure, they do not confer review powers[cite: 20]. Since the applicants were heard extensively and failed to prove fraud, seeking a review disguised as recall was impermissible[cite: 20].

case_title: Mudraksh Investfin Pvt. Ltd. vs. Brijesh Singh Bhadauriya, RP of RCI Industries and Technologies Ltd.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Mudraksh Investfin Pvt. Ltd. (RBI-registered NBFC / Assignee); Corporate Debtor is M/s RCI Industries and Technologies Limited; Respondent is Brijesh Singh Bhadauriya, Resolution Professional (RP); Original Financers/Assignors are SBI Global Factors Ltd. and DBS Bank India Ltd. (alongside Lakshmi Vilas Bank); Supplier is BC Power Controls Ltd.; Platform Facilitator is Mynd Solutions Pvt. Ltd. (operating M1 Exchange)[cite: 21]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor purchased ferrous and non-ferrous products from supplier BC Power Controls Ltd. and, due to liquidity constraints, availed invoice discounting and factoring services under the Factoring Regulation Act, 2011 via the M1 Exchange platform hosted by Mynd Solutions Pvt. Ltd. pursuant to Master Financer and Master Buyer Agreements, where financers discounted sales invoices and remitted funds directly to the supplier on a non-recourse basis[cite: 21]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted on its trade payables owed to the financers; Appellant submitted Form C in CIRP claiming a financial debt of Rs. 7,05,91,531.39 pursuant to assignment of the receivables, which the RP reclassified as an operational debt[cite: 21]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Master Financer Agreement executed on 28.04.2017; Master Buyer Agreement on 21.12.2018; trade invoices discounted between 13.06.2019 and 27.06.2019; legal notice issued on 01.10.2019; debts assigned to Appellant on 23.06.2022 and 08.08.2022; CIRP commenced against Corporate Debtor on 25.11.2022 on an application by Standard Chartered Bank Singapore; Appellant filed Form C on 13.12.2022; RP rejected financial creditor status on 21.12.2022; NCLT dismissed IA No. 1990/2023 on 10.11.2023[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Master Financer Agreement dated 28.04.2017 (specifically Clause 5.1.5.1 stipulating non-recourse discounting); Master Buyer Agreement dated 21.12.2018 (Clause 4.3.7.1); Assignment Agreements dated 23.06.2022 and 08.08.2022; and underlying commercial trade invoices for the supply of goods[cite: 21]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 1990 of 2023 in IB-2688(ND)/2019 before NCLT New Delhi Court-III seeking admission as a Financial Creditor; NCLT dismissed the application on 10.11.2023 holding the debt arose from purchase of goods; Appellant appealed to NCLAT under Section 61[cite: 21].
legal_issues: 1. Whether trade receivables discounted by financers on an electronic factoring platform (M1 Exchange) on a non-recourse basis constitute a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8)(e) or Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC, or an 'operational debt' under Section 5(21)[cite: 21]. 2. Whether the assignment of discounted trade payables by original financers to a third-party NBFC transforms the character of an operational debt into a financial debt under Section 21(5) of the IBC[cite: 21]. 3. Whether reverse factoring arrangements have the commercial effect of a borrowing under Section 5(8)(f) when there is no direct monetary disbursal to the corporate debtor against consideration for the time value of money[cite: 21].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 5(8) of the IBC, the disbursement of money against consideration for the time value of money is an indispensable condition precedent of a financial debt; invoice discounting of trade payables executed on a non-recourse basis falls under Section 5(8)(e) (which expressly excludes non-recourse receivables from financial debt), meaning that financers and their assignees merely step into the shoes of the original trade suppliers as operational creditors under Section 5(20) and Section 21(5)[cite: 21]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8)(e) specifically governs receivables sold or discounted; therefore, non-recourse invoice discounting cannot be brought under the residuary sweep of Section 5(8)(f)[cite: 21]. Furthermore, Section 21(5) of the IBC expressly provides that where an operational debt is assigned or legally transferred to a financial creditor, the transferee shall continue to be considered an operational creditor to the extent of such transfer[cite: 21]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Following the precedent in Minions Ventures Pvt. Ltd. v. TDT Copper Ltd., the Tribunal scrutinized the Master Agreements, noting that Clause 5.1.5.1 explicitly specified that discounting was without recourse to the supplier, and funds were paid directly to the supplier for the supply of goods without any direct loan disbursement to the Corporate Debtor[cite: 21]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The underlying liability arose strictly from commercial purchase of goods in the ordinary course of business; subsequent assignments did not alter the nature of the transaction, and the claim was properly categorized as an operational debt[cite: 21].
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1671 of 2023 without costs, affirming the order dated 10.11.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT New Delhi Bench Court-III) in IA No. 1990 of 2023 upholding the Resolution Professional's classification of the Appellant as an Operational Creditor[cite: 21].
summary: Mudraksh Investfin Pvt. Ltd., an NBFC assignee of debts from SBI Global Factors and DBS Bank, appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order dismissing its application to be categorized as a financial creditor of RCI Industries and Technologies Ltd[cite: 21]. The Corporate Debtor had purchased goods from a supplier and discounted the trade invoices on the M1 Exchange factoring platform, where the financers settled dues directly with the supplier without recourse[cite: 21]. The NCLAT Principal Bench dismissed the appeal, holding that under Section 5(8)(e) and Section 21(5) of the IBC, discounting of trade receivables on a non-recourse basis does not constitute a financial debt[cite: 21]. The financers and subsequent assignees stepped into the supplier's shoes as operational creditors[cite: 21].

case_title: In Style Fashion vs. Aditya Birla Fashion and Retail Limited
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1679 of 2023 & I.A. No. 6046 of 2023
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is In Style Fashion (partnership firm acting as franchisee and commission agent / Operational Creditor); Respondent is Aditya Birla Fashion and Retail Limited (retail apparel company / Corporate Debtor)[cite: 22]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Parties entered into commercial Agency Agreements dated 08.07.2011 ('Planet Fashion Agreement') and 20.12.2011 ('Allen Solly Agreement') for operating retail brand showrooms on a commission basis, with interior fit-out costs borne by the agent and depreciating over five years[cite: 22]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Following showroom closures on 02.02.2016, Appellant raised invoices on 18.11.2016 for salvageable assets (Rs. 15.26 Lakhs) and non-salvageable assets (Rs. 4.28 Lakhs), alongside unpaid commission of Rs. 86.34 Lakhs, totaling Rs. 1.05 Crores; Corporate Debtor made a part-payment of Rs. 51,283.28 on 28.04.2017[cite: 22]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Agency agreements signed on 08.07.2011 and 20.12.2011; meeting regarding revised commission held on 28.08.2012; showrooms closed/terminated on 02.02.2016; invoices raised on 18.11.2016; part-payment made on 28.04.2017; Section 8 demand notice issued on 07.08.2019; reply sent on 21.08.2019; Section 9 petition [CP (IB) No. 4099/MB/VI/2019] filed on 01.10.2019; NCLT rejected petition on 11.10.2023[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Planet Fashion and Allen Solly Agency Agreements (specifically interior investment Clauses 1.11, 5.1, 6.10, and termination reconciliation Clause 10.3(iv)); Minutes of Meeting dated 28.08.2012 signed by Nitesh Agrawal agreeing to a variable commission matrix; email dated 09.12.2013 from Nitesh Agrawal admitting excess payment of Rs. 14.51 Lakhs; and bank statement verifying part-payment of Rs. 51,283.28 on 28.04.2017[cite: 22]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed CP (IB) No. 4099/MB/VI/2019 under Section 9 before NCLT Mumbai Bench-VI; NCLT dismissed the application on 11.10.2023 on grounds of limitation (calculating from 27.08.2016 stated in Section 8 notice) and pre-existing dispute regarding commission computation; Appellant appealed to NCLAT under Section 61[cite: 22].
legal_issues: 1. Whether a Section 9 application is barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963 when the date of default mentioned in the Section 8 demand notice was erroneously stated as 27.08.2016, but an intervening part-payment was received on 28.04.2017[cite: 22]. 2. Whether an email from a corporate debtor seeking information on asset lists for account reconciliation pursuant to contract termination clauses constitutes an unequivocal admission of debt and liability[cite: 22]. 3. Whether a dispute regarding the computation of agency commission based on minutes of meeting signed by an authorized representative constitutes a bona fide pre-existing dispute under Section 5(6) and Section 8 of the IBC under the Mobilox Innovations standard[cite: 22]. 4. Whether allegations of unauthorized signatures or forgery of minutes of meeting can be adjudicated in summary proceedings under Section 9 of the IBC[cite: 22].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 9 of the IBC, where the defense raised by a corporate debtor demonstrates a plausible, bona fide pre-existing dispute regarding the computation and entitlement of operational debt that is neither spurious nor hypothetical, the Adjudicating Authority exercising summary insolvency jurisdiction must dismiss the application; however, part-payment of debt during the subsistence of the limitation period starts a fresh period of limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963[cite: 22]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The provisions of the Limitation Act, 1963 apply equally to applications under Section 7 and Section 9 of the IBC as affirmed in B.K. Educational Services; an inadvertent typographical error in specifying the date of default in a Section 8 notice does not render an application time-barred if the actual default and subsequent part-payments within three years of filing are established by bank records[cite: 22]. Under Section 5(6) read with Section 9(5)(ii)(d), operational debt must be free from pre-existing controversies[cite: 22]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying the Mobilox Innovations (P) Ltd. test, the Tribunal determined whether the defense raised a plausible contention requiring further trial[cite: 22]. Contemporaneous minutes of meeting dated 28.08.2012 altering commission slabs, supported by subsequent email correspondence by the same representative admitting excess payments, established a genuine pre-existing dispute[cite: 22]. Asset reconciliation correspondence post-termination did not constitute an admission of liability, and claims of forgery cannot be tried summarily[cite: 22]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: While the NCLT erred in finding the application time-barred, its rejection of the Section 9 petition was legally sound and justified due to substantial, pre-existing disputes over commission computation and interior renovation liability[cite: 22].
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1679 of 2023 along with I.A. No. 6046 of 2023 without costs, affirming the order dated 11.10.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai Bench-VI) rejecting the Section 9 application on the ground of pre-existing dispute, while granting liberty to the Appellant to pursue inter se contractual remedies before an appropriate competent forum[cite: 22].
summary: In Style Fashion appealed an NCLT Mumbai order rejecting its Section 9 application against Aditya Birla Fashion and Retail Ltd. for alleged operational dues of Rs. 1.05 crores arising from showroom franchise agreements[cite: 22]. The NCLT rejected the petition on limitation grounds and the existence of pre-existing disputes over commission computation and interior renovation expenses[cite: 22]. The NCLAT Principal Bench clarified that the application was within limitation since part-payment on 28.04.2017 renewed the three-year period under the Limitation Act[cite: 22]. However, applying the Mobilox Innovations test, the Tribunal affirmed the dismissal on merits, holding that bona fide pre-existing disputes existed regarding variable commission arrangements and reconciliation of accounts, which cannot be adjudicated in summary insolvency proceedings[cite: 22].

case_title: D. Srinivasa Rao vs. Stressed Assets Stabilization Fund & Anr.
appeal_number: IA No. 1014 of 2023 in Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS.) No. 159 of 2023
bench: Chennai Bench
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Applicant/Appellant is D. Srinivasa Rao (Promoter and Suspended Vice Chairman & Director of Corporate Debtor M/s Priyaranjani Fiber Ltd.); Respondent No. 1 is Stressed Assets Stabilisation Fund (SASF / Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is M/s Priyaranjani Fiber Ltd. (Corporate Debtor represented by IRP Raghu Babu Gunturu); related management faction is K. Sivananda Reddy Group[cite: 23]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed financial assistance from IDBI Bank (assigned to SASF), with debt recovery and revival proceedings subsequently taken before the Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR) under SICA[cite: 23]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in repayment of credit facilities led SASF to file a Section 7 application under the IBC; the core dispute concerned whether the claim was barred by limitation since 01.04.2000 or kept alive through a continuous series of One-Time Settlement (OTS) proposals[cite: 23]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: BIFR directed the Sivananda Reddy Group to manage the company on 22.11.2011 (stayed by AIFR on 21.02.2012)[cite: 23]; NCLT Hyderabad ruled in favor of the Applicant on 15.05.2017[cite: 23]; extensive OTS proposals were submitted between 2008 and 2022 (including 22.11.2008, 15.11.2012, 03.07.2017, 06.04.2019, 26.08.2019, and multiple proposals post-filing up to 27.08.2022)[cite: 23]; NCLAT dismissed the main appeal on 21.09.2023[cite: 23]; Applicant filed IA No. 1014/2023 for recall on 29.09.2023[cite: 23]; Applicant filed Civil Appeal No. 7831/2023 before the Supreme Court on 02.11.2023 without disclosing it to NCLAT[cite: 23]; NCLAT dismissed the recall application on 18.01.2024[cite: 23]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Letter dated 15.11.2012 signed by the Applicant confirming acceptance of OTS terms and acknowledging payments made by K. Sivananda Reddy on behalf of the company[cite: 23]; BIFR order dated 22.11.2011[cite: 23]; letter dated 16.02.2010 by authorized signatory K. Ranganathan[cite: 23]; and written OTS proposals across multiple years[cite: 23]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT admitted the Section 7 petition; Appellant appealed to NCLAT in Comp. App (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 159/2023, which was dismissed on 21.09.2023 holding debt within limitation[cite: 23]; Appellant filed IA No. 1014 of 2023 under Rule 11 seeking recall of the dismissal order alleging fraud, lack of jural relationship, and limitation expiry[cite: 23]; NCLAT Chennai heard the parties and dismissed the application on 18.01.2024[cite: 23].
legal_issues: 1. Whether an application under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 for recall of an appellate judgment can be invoked to re-examine decided questions on limitation, acknowledgement of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and jural relationship of persons offering OTS proposals[cite: 23]. 2. Whether One-Time Settlement proposals submitted by a management group managing the corporate debtor pursuant to BIFR directions constitute valid acknowledgments of debt or establish fraud practiced upon the Tribunal[cite: 23]. 3. Whether non-disclosure of a pending civil appeal before the Supreme Court challenging the substantive judgment affects the maintainability of a recall application before the Appellate Tribunal[cite: 23].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The inherent jurisdiction of the Appellate Tribunal to recall a judgment under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 is restricted strictly to procedural errors, patent lack of jurisdiction, or fraud practiced directly upon the court, and cannot be utilized as a tool for rehearing or reviewing a judgment on its merits[cite: 23]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Following the Full Bench decision in Union Bank of India v. Dinkar T. Venkatasubramanian and the Supreme Court rulings in Budhia Swain and A.R. Antulay, the Tribunal has no power of review; questions regarding Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963, conditional acknowledgments, and jural relationships are matters of substantive adjudication that cannot be re-opened in a recall petition[cite: 23]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To establish fraud sufficient to recall a final judgment, the applicant must demonstrate intentional deception or false representation[cite: 23]; where the applicant was himself a party to BIFR proceedings and had admitted in writing (letter dated 15.11.2012) the OTS terms and payments made by the management group, no fraud is established[cite: 23]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Applicant was fully heard on merits in the main appeal and actively concealed the pendency of his appeal before the Supreme Court; the recall application was a disguised attempt to re-argue concluded findings, warranting dismissal[cite: 23].
operative_order: I.A. No. 1014 of 2023 in Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS.) No. 159 of 2023 seeking recall of the order dated 21.09.2023 passed by the Appellate Tribunal is dismissed, with no order as to costs[cite: 23].
summary: The suspended director of Priyaranjani Fiber Ltd. filed an application under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 seeking recall of the NCLAT Chennai Bench order dated 21.09.2023, which had dismissed his appeal against an order admitting Section 7 CIRP initiated by Stressed Assets Stabilisation Fund[cite: 23]. The applicant argued that the financial creditor played fraud, the debt was time-barred, and OTS letters submitted by a rival management group lacked jural relationship[cite: 23]. Dismissing the recall application, the NCLAT held that inherent powers under Rule 11 are limited to procedural errors, patent lack of jurisdiction, or fraud, and cannot be used to review or re-argue merits regarding Section 18 limitation acknowledgments[cite: 23].

case_title: Glamour India Private Limited vs. Canara Bank & Anr.
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 443 of 2023 & I.A. No. 1464 of 2023
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Glamour India Private Limited (unsecured Financial Creditor / Section 7 applicant); Respondent No. 1 is Canara Bank (sole secured Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is Vishnukant Kabra, Resolution Professional (RP) of Shree Sai OTO Tube Mills Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Canara Bank sanctioned multiple credit facilities totaling Rs. 64 Crores between 2010 and 2013 to the Corporate Debtor, secured by equitable mortgages over land, buildings, plant, and machinery, and personal guarantees of ex-directors; on 17.08.2021, Canara Bank sanctioned a One-Time Settlement (OTS) for Rs. 25 Crores requiring Rs. 3.75 Crores upfront and balance Rs. 21.25 Crores on or before 16.11.2021[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted under the OTS as its initial upfront cheque bounced and only Rs. 3.20 Crores was paid, leaving an upfront shortfall of Rs. 55 Lakhs and complete non-payment of the Rs. 21.25 Crores balance; following CIRP admission, Canara Bank submitted a claim in Form C for Rs. 105.53 Crores, subsequently revised to Rs. 130.59 Crores (calculated up to 10.05.2022); the RP arbitrarily admitted only Rs. 22.62 Crores while admitting Appellant's claim of Rs. 155.09 Crores in full[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: OTS sanctioned on 17.08.2021; payment deadline under OTS expired on 16.11.2021; CIRP admitted against Corporate Debtor on 08.04.2022; Canara Bank issued formal OTS cancellation letter on 25.05.2022; RP communicated restricted admission on 30.06.2022; NCLT allowed Canara Bank's IA No. 1961/2022 on 02.03.2023; NCLAT dismissed appeal on 09.01.2024[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: OTS sanction letter dated 17.08.2021 (specifically Clause 7 providing that non-compliance causes the OTS sanction to stand automatically withdrawn without assigning reasons and reserves full legal recovery rights); dishonoured cheque intimation dated 28.08.2021; reminder emails dated 18.10.2021, 20.12.2021, 03.03.2022, and 25.05.2022; Form C claim with statement of accounts; and Corporate Debtor's audited books of accounts reflecting the original outstanding debt[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Canara Bank filed IA No. 1961/2022 in CP 289/I&B/MB/2022 before NCLT Mumbai Bench challenging the RP's decision restricting its claim; NCLT allowed the application on 02.03.2023 directing the RP to admit Canara Bank's full original claim of Rs. 130.59 Crores as per its claim form and books of accounts; Appellant appealed to NCLAT under Section 61[cite: 24].
legal_issues: 1. Whether a Resolution Professional has the adjudicatory power under the IBC to unilaterally restrict a secured financial creditor's claim to a compromised OTS amount when the corporate debtor committed default under the OTS terms prior to the initiation of CIRP[cite: 24]. 2. Whether the automatic cancellation of a conditional OTS upon pre-CIRP default violates the moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC, or whether the issuance of a formal cancellation letter post-admission bars the creditor from claiming its full contractual debt[cite: 24]. 3. Whether a defaulting borrower or a competing financial creditor can enforce the terms of a lapsed OTS against a bank to reduce admitted financial liabilities in CIRP[cite: 24].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Resolution Professional is an administrative facilitator tasked with collating and verifying claims under Section 18 and Regulation 8, and possesses no judicial or adjudicatory authority to rewrite contractual debts or restrict a financial creditor's claim to a compromised OTS figure that was breached and automatically cancelled prior to the insolvency commencement date[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A One-Time Settlement is a conditional concession, not an absolute contract, which ceases to exist automatically upon failure of the borrower to comply with mandatory payment timelines; the automatic termination of an OTS before CIRP admission does not constitute an 'action or proceeding' hit by the moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC, and the creditor's full pre-settlement debt stands fully revived[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examined Clause 7 of the OTS sanction letter dated 17.08.2021, establishing that default on or before 16.11.2021 operated to cancel the settlement automatically without notice; because default occurred months before CIRP initiation on 08.04.2022, the subsequent formal revocation letter was merely technical and did not diminish the creditor's right to claim the entire outstanding balance reflected in the debtor's books[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The RP exceeded his jurisdiction in acting as an Adjudicating Authority to cap Canara Bank's claim; the NCLT correctly directed the admission of Canara Bank's full original claim of Rs. 130.59 Crores as substantiated by loan records and the Corporate Debtor's books of accounts[cite: 24].
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 443 of 2023 along with I.A. No. 1464 of 2023 without costs, affirming the order dated 02.03.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai Bench) in I.A. 1961/2022 in C.P. 289/I&B/MB/2022 directing the Resolution Professional to admit the full original claim of Canara Bank as per its claim form and the books of accounts of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 24].
summary: Glamour India Private Limited, a financial creditor, appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order directing the Resolution Professional of Shree Sai OTO Tube Mills Ltd. to admit Canara Bank's full financial claim of Rs. 130.59 crores instead of restricting it to a defaulted One-Time Settlement (OTS) amount of Rs. 22.62 crores[cite: 24]. The appellant argued that the OTS subsisted on the CIRP commencement date and formal withdrawal post-admission breached the Section 14 moratorium[cite: 24]. The NCLAT Principal Bench dismissed the appeal, ruling that under the explicit terms of the sanction letter, the OTS stood automatically cancelled upon non-payment on 16.11.2021, months prior to CIRP[cite: 24]. Consequently, the RP exceeded his administrative collation jurisdiction, and Canara Bank was entitled to its full claim[cite: 24].

case_title: Rajeev Kumar Jain vs. M/s Uno Minda Limited & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 947 of 2022 & I.A. No. 2682, 2683 of 2022 & 1652 of 2023
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Rajeev Kumar Jain (Ex-Director and Shareholder of Corporate Debtor); Corporate Debtor is M/s Unicast Autotech Private Limited (aluminium die-cast manufacturer); Respondent No. 1 is M/s Uno Minda Limited (formerly M/s Minda Industries Limited, automotive solution provider / Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is Corporate Debtor represented through its IRP[cite: 25]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Proposed acquisition of 100% equity in Corporate Debtor by Respondent No. 1 pursuant to Non-Binding Offers dated 15.02.2021 and 15.04.2021; parties executed a Business Support Agreement (BSA) on 17.04.2021 wherein R1 agreed to provide raw material funding and critical working capital support to CD, categorized under Clause 2.4 as unsecured debt to CD; further secured by Share Pledge Agreement dated 12.05.2021 / 14.05.2021 and Deed of Guarantee dated 14.05.2021 creating joint and several liability[cite: 25]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: R1 disbursed Rs. 1.15 Crores directly to raw material suppliers at the instruction and for the benefit of the Corporate Debtor between April and May 2021; following termination of BSA, R1 demanded Rs. 1.43 Crores with 18% per annum interest; CD repaid Rs. 24 Lakhs, leaving an outstanding default of Rs. 1,28,94,205/- claimed in Section 7[cite: 25]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: BSA executed on 17.04.2021; SPA and Deed of Guarantee executed on 12.05.2021 and 14.05.2021; R1 issued termination notice demanding repayment under Clause 2.5; CD made part payment of Rs. 24 Lakhs on 10.06.2021/2022; R1 issued guarantee invocation notice on 08.10.2021; R1 filed Section 7 petition [IB-763/(ND)/2021] on 06.12.2021; NCLT New Delhi admitted Section 7 on 08.07.2022; NCLAT final judgment delivered on 02.01.2024[cite: 25]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Business Support Agreement dated 17.04.2021 (Recital D, Clauses 2.4, 2.5, 3.2); Deed of Pledge dated 14.05.2021 (Recital A, Clauses 1.1, 2, 18.7); Deed of Guarantee dated 14.05.2021; bank payment records showing direct disbursements to vendors for raw materials; and termination/demand notices[cite: 25]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 1 filed Section 7 application IB-763/(ND)/2021 before NCLT New Delhi Bench-VI; NCLT admitted the petition on 08.07.2022 holding that the working capital support constituted financial debt and default was undisputed; Appellant appealed to NCLAT under Section 61[cite: 25].
legal_issues: 1. Whether funds disbursed by a financier directly to third-party suppliers to meet the critical working capital and raw material requirements of a corporate debtor, pursuant to a business support agreement, constitute a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC or an 'operational debt' under Section 5(21)[cite: 25]. 2. Whether the definition of 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) mandates direct disbursement into the corporate debtor's bank account, or whether disbursement to third parties on behalf of and at the instruction of the corporate debtor satisfies the statutory requirement[cite: 25]. 3. Whether the corporate debtor is jointly and severally liable as a primary borrower where the business support agreement and security documents are executed jointly by the corporate debtor and its promoters[cite: 25].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 5(8) of the IBC, 'financial debt' encompasses any financial accommodation or working capital assistance provided against consideration for the time value of money, wherein interest is not a sine qua non; the statutory definition does not require that disbursements must be deposited directly into the bank account of the corporate debtor, and third-party disbursements made to trade suppliers at the instructions and for the business benefit of the corporate debtor constitute valid financial debt disbursals[cite: 25]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) uses the phrase 'debt alongwith interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money', indicating that interest is not an indispensable prerequisite; furthermore, financing the procurement of raw materials for working capital needs is legally distinguishable from supplying goods as an operational vendor, establishing that an entity providing working capital funding acts as a financial creditor under Section 5(7)[cite: 25]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized Recital D and Clause 2.4 of the Business Support Agreement, which explicitly stipulated that all amounts spent by the financier shall be deemed unsecured debt extended to the corporate debtor, alongside Clause 2.5 providing 18% interest on termination, and Clause 18.7 of the pledge agreement establishing joint and several liability[cite: 25]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The financial accommodation provided by Respondent No. 1 for raw material procurement constituted a financial debt; because the Corporate Debtor was a party to the agreements and committed an undisputed default exceeding the statutory threshold, the NCLT's admission order under Section 7 was lawful and valid[cite: 25].
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 947 of 2022 as devoid of merit without costs, affirming the order dated 08.07.2022 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT New Delhi Bench-VI) in IB-763/(ND)/2021 admitting the Section 7 petition and initiating CIRP against M/s Unicast Autotech Private Limited, and closed all pending interlocutory applications[cite: 25].
summary: Rajeev Kumar Jain, ex-director of Unicast Autotech Private Limited, appealed an NCLT New Delhi order admitting a Section 7 IBC application filed by Uno Minda Limited for defaulting on a debt of Rs. 1.28 crores[cite: 25]. Under a Business Support Agreement, Uno Minda had disbursed Rs. 1.15 crores directly to raw material suppliers to support the corporate debtor's critical working capital[cite: 25]. The appellant contended this constituted operational debt rather than financial debt because funds were not disbursed directly to the debtor's account and lacked time value of money[cite: 25]. The NCLAT Principal Bench dismissed the appeal, holding that Section 5(8) does not mandate direct deposit into the debtor's account, interest is not sine qua non, and third-party disbursements for working capital at the debtor's instruction constitute financial debt[cite: 25].

case_title: Jindal Power Limited vs. Dhiren Shantilal Shah & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Jindal Power Limited (JPL / unsolicited resolution applicant); Respondent No. 1 is Dhiren Shantilal Shah, Resolution Professional (RP) of Corporate Debtor Tuticorin Coal Terminal Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent No. 2 is the Committee of Creditors (CoC); Intervenor is M/s SEAPOL Ports Pvt. Ltd. (sole Prospective Resolution Applicant in the final list)[cite: 26]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor is an SPV developing North Cargo Berth II for bulk cargo handling at Tuticorin Port on a Design, Build, Finance, Operate and Transfer (DBFOT) basis, financed by credit facilities from a consortium led by Bank of India[cite: 26]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by Corporate Debtor resulted in admission under Section 7 of the IBC; during CIRP, Form G was issued resulting in a final list of 6 PRAs; only two PRAs submitted plans which the CoC rejected; RP filed liquidation application IA No. 836 of 2022 on 20.08.2021; subsequently, NCLT permitted SEAPOL (a listed PRA) on 09.01.2023 to submit a plan and dismissed liquidation as withdrawn; SEAPOL submitted a plan on 18.02.2023 (revised multiple times up to 22.08.2023)[cite: 26]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 CIRP admitted on 20.02.2020; Form G issued on 08.09.2020; final list of PRAs published on 31.10.2020 under Regulation 36A(12); liquidation application filed on 20.08.2021 and withdrawn on 09.01.2023; Appellant submitted an unsolicited EOI to the RP on 12.07.2023 (nearly three years after PRA finalization); NCLT granted conditional opportunity in IA No. 3223/2023 on 27.07.2023; RP sought clarification in IA No. 3699/2023; NCLT held Appellant ineligible on 22.08.2023; NCLAT final order passed on 08.01.2024[cite: 26]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Final list of PRAs dated 31.10.2020 (omitting JPL); revised sealed resolution plan of SEAPOL dated 22.08.2023; minutes of 45th and 46th CoC meetings; and IBBI Discussion Paper dated 27.08.2021 addressing delays caused by unsolicited late bids[cite: 26]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 3223 of 2023 seeking leave to submit a resolution plan; NCLT allowed it on 27.07.2023 subject to compliance with Regulation 39(1B) read with Regulation 36B(7); on clarification sought by RP in IA No. 3699 of 2023, NCLT on 22.08.2023 ruled that Regulation 39(1B) imposes an absolute statutory bar on applicants not in the final PRA list; Appellant appealed both orders under Section 61[cite: 26].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Committee of Creditors or the Adjudicating Authority can permit an entity whose name does not appear in the final list of prospective resolution applicants (PRAs) under Regulation 36A(12) to submit a resolution plan under the guise of asset value maximization[cite: 26]. 2. Whether Regulation 39(1B) read with Regulation 36B(7) of the CIRP Regulations, 2016 constitutes a mandatory statutory bar prohibiting the CoC from considering unsolicited resolution plans received from persons outside the final PRA list[cite: 26]. 3. Whether the commercial wisdom of the CoC can override express regulatory prohibitions and procedural timelines governing the submission of resolution plans[cite: 26].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The principle of asset value maximization and the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors cannot be exercised in contravention of express statutory regulations; Regulation 39(1B) of the CIRP Regulations, 2016 imposes an absolute statutory bar prohibiting the CoC from considering any resolution plan submitted by an entity that does not appear in the final list of prospective resolution applicants published by the Resolution Professional under Regulation 36A(12)[cite: 26]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 39(1B) contains an explicit negative mandate stating that the Committee 'shall not consider any resolution plan' received after specified timelines or from a person not in the final list of PRAs[cite: 26]. Inserted pursuant to the IBBI Discussion Paper of August 2021, this regulation was intentionally framed to prevent unending delays, unsolicited midway proposals, and subversion of time-bound resolution[cite: 26]. Under Regulation 36B(7), the CoC's sole permissible route when plans are unsatisfactory is to re-issue the RFRP to PRAs in the final list or restart the CIRP lawfully[cite: 26]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying the judicial precedents in Kalpraj Dharamshi, Vistra ITCL, and Ramneek Goel, the Tribunal tested whether CoC discretion could permit mid-stream entries[cite: 26]. Because the Appellant submitted its EOI nearly three years after the PRA list was finalized and while active negotiations with sole eligible PRA SEAPOL were nearing conclusion, permitting unsolicited participation would completely vitiate the integrity of the CIRP framework[cite: 26]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Appellant JPL was not part of the final PRA list; hence, the statutory bar under Regulation 39(1B) applied strictly, rendering the Appellant legally ineligible to submit a plan and validating the Adjudicating Authority's clarificatory order[cite: 26].
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1166-1167 of 2023 without costs, held all connected interlocutory applications infructuous, and directed the Resolution Professional and Committee of Creditors to proceed with the CIRP and decide upon the resolution plan currently available before them in accordance with law[cite: 26].
summary: Jindal Power Limited (JPL) appealed against orders of the NCLT Mumbai Bench holding it ineligible to submit a resolution plan for Tuticorin Coal Terminal Pvt. Ltd[cite: 26]. JPL sought to submit a late bid on grounds of asset value maximization, supported by the RP and CoC, despite not appearing in the final list of prospective resolution applicants (PRAs) issued in October 2020[cite: 26]. The NCLAT Principal Bench dismissed the appeal, holding that Regulation 39(1B) read with Regulation 36B(7) of the CIRP Regulations imposes an absolute statutory bar against entertaining resolution plans from entities not on the final PRA list[cite: 26]. The Tribunal affirmed that the CoC's commercial wisdom and value maximization cannot override mandatory regulations designed to ensure time-bound resolution[cite: 26].

case_title: Mr. A Rajendra vs. Mr. Gonugunta Madhusudhan Rao & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins.) No. 364 of 2023 & Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins.) No. 365 of 2023
bench: Chennai Bench
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Mr. A Rajendra (Ex-Shareholder and Suspended Managing Director of Corporate Debtor Dharti Dredging & Infrastructure Ltd.); Respondent No. 1 is Mr. Gonugunta Madhusudhan Rao (Resolution Professional / RP); Respondents 2 to 4 are members of the Committee of Creditors (CoC); Respondent No. 5 is the Consortium of Yogayatan Ports Pvt. Ltd. and Dr. Rajendra Raja Bali Singh (Successful Resolution Applicant / SRA)[cite: 27]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Dharti Dredging & Infrastructure Ltd. under Section 7 in CP (IB) No. 329/7/HDB/2020, wherein the CoC approved a resolution plan dated 10.01.2023 submitted by the SRA, while the Appellant sought consideration of a competing promoter resolution plan[cite: 27]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Adjudicating Authority passed two orders on 20.07.2023: dismissing Appellant's IA No. 407 of 2023 seeking to place his plan before the CoC, and allowing RP's IA No. 385 of 2023 approving the SRA's resolution plan[cite: 27]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned orders were pronounced on 20.07.2023; the 30-day statutory limitation under Section 61(2) expired on 19.08.2023; both appeals were e-filed on 28.08.2023 (on the 40th day); Appellant filed applications for condonation of delay (IA Nos. 1315 & 1316 of 2023) on 06.12.2023 seeking condonation of 10 days' delay[cite: 27]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appeal memorandum containing a declaration in Para 6 that the appeal was within limitation, and Para 17 stating that a certified copy was applied for on 01.08.2023 and received on 10.08.2023 to claim 10 days' exclusion under Section 12(3) of the Limitation Act[cite: 27]; free certified copy made available on 01.08.2023 (used in Appeal 364); unofficial copy shared by RP on 07.08.2023 (used in Appeal 365); IA No. 1118 of 2023 falsely pleading that the certified copy was lost in transit; and Appellant's subsequent admission that no paid certified copy was ever applied for[cite: 27]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad Bench passed orders in IA No. 407 of 2023 and IA No. 385 of 2023 on 20.07.2023; Appellant filed CA (AT) (CH) (Ins) Nos. 364 & 365 of 2023 before NCLAT Chennai Bench on 28.08.2023; Respondents contested limitation; Appellant filed IA Nos. 1315 & 1316 of 2023 for condonation of delay on 06.12.2023[cite: 27].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the limitation period of 30 days for preferring an appeal under Section 61(2) of the IBC commences from the date of pronouncement of the order or from the date a free certified copy or shared copy is made available to the appellant[cite: 27]. 2. Whether an appellant who never applied for a certified copy under Rule 22(2) of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 can claim exclusion of time under Section 12(3) of the Limitation Act, 1963[cite: 27]. 3. Whether an appellant who makes false averments and verified declarations regarding the date of applying for and receiving a certified copy (suppressio veri and suggestio falsi) is entitled to discretionary condonation of delay under the proviso to Section 61(2) of the IBC[cite: 27]. 4. What constitutes 'sufficient cause' to justify condonation of delay up to 15 days under the proviso to Section 61(2) of the IBC[cite: 27].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Limitation for filing an appeal under Section 61(2) of the IBC runs strictly from the date of pronouncement of the order by the Adjudicating Authority; exclusion of time under Section 12 of the Limitation Act, 1963 can only be claimed for the period requisite to obtain a certified copy when a paid application has actually been made with due diligence; an appellant who makes false statements in verified pleadings is guilty of suppressio veri and suggestio falsi, disentitling them to discretionary condonation of delay under the proviso to Section 61(2)[cite: 27]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Compliance with Rule 22(2) of the NCLAT Rules, 2016, which requires an appeal to be accompanied by a certified copy, is mandatory as settled in V. Nagarajan v. SKS Ispat; the statutory clock under Section 61(2) begins upon pronouncement and cannot be suspended pending the receipt of a free certified copy or copies shared informally by the RP[cite: 27]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying the binding principles in V. Nagarajan and Sanjay Pandurang Kalate, the court evaluated the verified averments in the appeal memo[cite: 27]. The assertion in Para 17 that a certified copy was applied for on 01.08.2023 and received on 10.08.2023 was contradicted by the Appellant's admission that no application was ever submitted, proving an intentional attempt to mislead the court and precluding any finding of 'sufficient cause'[cite: 27]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeals filed on the 40th day without applying for a certified copy were barred by limitation; the Appellant failed to establish sufficient cause and approached the court with unclean hands, warranting dismissal of the delay condonation applications and the appeals[cite: 27].
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed I.A. Nos. 1315 & 1316 of 2023 (applications for condonation of delay) and consequently dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins.) Nos. 364 & 365 of 2023 as not duly constituted, with no order as to costs[cite: 27].
summary: A. Rajendra, suspended director of Dharti Dredging & Infrastructure Ltd., appealed NCLT Hyderabad orders dated 20.07.2023 rejecting his resolution plan and approving the plan of Yogayatan Ports consortium[cite: 27]. The appeals were filed on 28.08.2023, beyond the 30-day limitation period under Section 61(2) of the IBC, with applications seeking condonation of a 10-day delay[cite: 27]. The appellant falsely declared in his appeal petition that he had applied for a certified copy to claim exclusion under Section 12 of the Limitation Act, whereas no copy was ever applied for[cite: 27]. Relying on V. Nagarajan and Sanjay Pandurang Kalate, the NCLAT Chennai Bench held that limitation commences from pronouncement[cite: 27]. Finding false statements and no sufficient cause, the Tribunal dismissed the condonation applications and appeals[cite: 27].

case_title: Abhiyan Developers Private Limited vs. Shreepati Build Infra Investment Limited
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Abhiyan Developers Private Limited (real estate flat purchaser / allottee claiming status of Financial Creditor); Respondent is Shreepati Build Infra Investment Limited (Corporate Debtor / developer)[cite: 28]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant entered into a flat purchase agreement dated 15.02.2011 to acquire Flat Nos. 4201 and 4202 on the 42nd Floor of 'Shreepati Estate', Mumbai, paying an advance booking deposit of Rs. 3,50,00,000/- (Rs. 3.50 Crores); when the project stalled due to lack of municipal and jail authority approvals, Corporate Debtor issued letters dated 31.03.2015 and 31.03.2018 temporarily transferring the deposit into a loan account while expressly retaining the Appellant's permanent right to flat allotment upon completion[cite: 28]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor failed to commence construction, hand over possession, or refund the deposit; Appellant filed Section 7 petition claiming a financial debt of Rs. 3,50,00,000/- along with 15% cumulative interest[cite: 28]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Flat purchase agreement executed on 15.02.2011[cite: 28]; temporary loan account letters issued on 31.03.2015 and 31.03.2018[cite: 28]; Section 7 petition [CP (IB) 4149(MB)/2018] filed in 2018[cite: 28]; IBC Amendment Act, 2020 enforced w.e.f. 28.12.2019 inserting provisos to Section 7(1)[cite: 28]; NCLT admitted Section 7 on 29.10.2021[cite: 28]; NCLAT set aside admission and remanded matter on 07.03.2022 in Comp. App. (AT) Ins. No. 939 of 2021[cite: 28]; Supreme Court dismissed appeal against remand as withdrawn on 05.09.2022[cite: 28]; NCLT dismissed Section 7 petition on remand on 28.07.2023[cite: 28]; NCLAT final order pronounced on 10.01.2024[cite: 28]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Purchase agreement dated 15.02.2011[cite: 28]; letters dated 31.03.2015 and 31.03.2018 confirming temporary parking of booking advance without relinquishment of allotment rights[cite: 28]; Corporate Debtor's ledger accounts demonstrating zero interest accrual or payment[cite: 28]; and petition records establishing that Appellant filed as a single allottee without meeting statutory numerical thresholds[cite: 28]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai admitted Section 7 petition on 29.10.2021[cite: 28]; NCLAT remanded on 07.03.2022 to examine compliance with the third proviso to Section 7(1)[cite: 28]; on remand, NCLT Mumbai Bench-II dismissed the petition on 28.07.2023 as non-maintainable and deemed withdrawn[cite: 28]; Appellant appealed to NCLAT under Section 61[cite: 28].
legal_issues: 1. Whether an advance payment made for the booking and purchase of flats under a real estate contract loses its foundational character as an allottee transaction and converts into a pure financial loan/debt by virtue of a builder's unilateral letter temporarily parking the funds in a loan account pending regulatory approvals[cite: 28]. 2.
