Whether an application filed under Section 7 of the IBC by a single real estate allottee prior to the 2020 Amendment is deemed withdrawn before admission under the third proviso to Section 7(1) if the applicant fails to join the statutory minimum threshold of 100 allottees or 10% of total allottees within 30 days[cite: 28]. 3. Whether the findings regarding allottee status rendered in an earlier appellate remand order operate conclusively to bar re-litigation of the nature of the debt[cite: 28].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The substantive commercial character of a transaction originating as a real estate advance payment for the purchase of flats cannot be altered into a simple financial loan or commercial borrowing merely through accounting adjustments or unilateral letters parking the advance in a loan account, particularly where the investor retains the right to permanent flat allotment; such a creditor remains an allottee under Section 2(d) of RERA and is strictly bound by the minimum threshold requirements under the second and third provisos to Section 7(1) of the IBC[cite: 28]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under the second proviso to Section 7(1) of the IBC, real estate allottees can only initiate CIRP jointly with not less than 100 allottees or 10% of total allottees in the project[cite: 28]; the third proviso creates a mandatory statutory fiction whereby any application pending prior to the 2020 Amendment (effective 28.12.2019) that is not modified within 30 days to satisfy the requisite threshold is deemed to be withdrawn before admission[cite: 28]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Scrutinizing the agreement dated 15.02.2011 and letters dated 31.03.2015, the Tribunal observed that the arrangement expressly retained the Appellant's right to take permanent possession of the flats at the agreed rate upon project completion, and no interest was ever recorded or paid in the Corporate Debtor's financial statements, demonstrating that the funds were merely parked temporarily to avert regulatory defaults[cite: 28]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant retained the character of a real estate allottee governed by Section 5(8)(f); because it proceeded as a single allottee and failed to comply with the threshold mandated by the third proviso to Section 7(1), the application was deemed withdrawn and rightly dismissed as non-maintainable[cite: 28].
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1694 of 2023 without costs, affirming the order dated 28.07.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai Bench-II) in IA/739/2022 in C.P. (IB) -4149 (MB)/2018 which rejected the Section 7 application as non-maintainable[cite: 28].
summary: Abhiyan Developers Private Limited appealed an NCLT Mumbai order rejecting its Section 7 application against Shreepati Build Infra Investment Limited as non-maintainable[cite: 28]. The appellant booked two flats in 2011, advancing Rs. 3.5 crores[cite: 28]. Due to delayed approvals, the corporate debtor temporarily parked the advance in a loan account while preserving the appellant's permanent flat allotment rights[cite: 28]. The appellant claimed this transformed the transaction into a pure financial debt exempt from allottee thresholds[cite: 28]. The NCLAT Principal Bench dismissed the appeal, holding that unilateral accounting reclassifications cannot alter the substantive nature of a real estate booking[cite: 28]. A single allottee who fails to join 100 allottees or 10% under the third proviso to Section 7(1) cannot maintain a Section 7 petition[cite: 28].

case_title: Jaiprakash Associates Limited vs. Jaypee Infratech Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 548 of 2023 & Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 559 of 2023
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Corporate Debtor is Jaypee Infratech Limited (JIL). Jaiprakash Associates Limited (JAL) is the holding company, erstwhile promoter, and corporate guarantor. Manoj Gaur is the erstwhile Managing Director and personal guarantor. IDBI Bank is the financial creditor leading the consortium of lenders. The Yamuna Expressway Industrial Development Authority (YEIDA) and the Income Tax Department are statutory/operational creditors. The Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA) is the Consortium of M/s Suraksha Realty Limited and M/s Lakshdeep Investment and Finance Private Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: On 07.02.2003, Taj Expressway Industrial Development Authority executed a Concession Agreement with JAL to construct the Yamuna Expressway with toll collection rights for 36 years and development rights over 6,177 acres. On 19.10.2007, JIL was incorporated as a special purpose vehicle (SPV) and assigned all concession rights. Consortium bank financing was secured by mortgaging project lands and personal/corporate guarantees from JAL and Manoj Gaur. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: JIL defaulted on debt servicing under credit facilities extended by IDBI Bank and consortium lenders. Creditor claims included institutional financial debt, YEIDA's claim of Rs. 6,111.60 Crores (including Rs. 1,689 Crores Additional Farmers' Compensation), and Income Tax claims (Rs. 3,334 Crores assessed and Rs. 33,000 Crores potential future liability). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: IDBI Bank filed an application under Section 7 of the IBC, which was admitted by NCLT Allahabad on 09.08.2017. Following repeated rounds before the Supreme Court under Article 142 (Chitra Sharma on 09.08.2018, IDBI Bank on 06.11.2019, and Jaypee Kensington on 24.03.2021), the SRA submitted its resolution plan on 07.06.2021 with an addendum on 09.06.2021. The CoC approved it on 23.06.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Evidence included: (i) Supreme Court judgment in Anuj Jain (26.02.2020) releasing 758 acres from preferential mortgages under Section 43 back to JIL; (ii) CoC minutes of the 17th and 18th meetings proving the 758 acres were accounted for in liquidation value; (iii) Clause 34.50 of the Resolution Plan expressly terminating guarantors' subrogation rights; (iv) Clause 12 of the Plan stating the SRA would implement the plan irrespective of whether reliefs and concessions were granted; and (v) NCLAT judgment dated 26.09.2023 in CA (AT) (Ins) No. 549 of 2023 settling the Income Tax Department's operational claim. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The IRP filed IA No. 2836 of 2021 for plan approval on 07.07.2021. JAL and Manoj Gaur filed objections on 30.07.2021. By order dated 07.03.2023, the NCLT Special Bench New Delhi approved Suraksha Realty's resolution plan with 98.66% CoC approval and granted 8 out of 38 sought concessions, dismissing the promoters' objections. JAL and Manoj Gaur appealed the approval under Section 61.
legal_issues: (i) Whether erstwhile promoters and directors have locus standi under Section 61 to challenge an approved resolution plan; (ii) Whether the treatment of Income Tax Department claims as operational debt receiving Rs. 10 Lakhs violates Section 30(2); (iii) Whether treating YEIDA's claims for additional farmers' compensation as operational debt violates Section 30(2); (iv) Whether YEIDA is a secured creditor under the UP Industrial Area Development Act, 1976; (v) Whether Clause 34.50 of the resolution plan violates Section 30(2)(e) of the IBC by extinguishing the corporate and personal guarantors' rights of subrogation under Sections 135, 140, and 141 of the Indian Contract Act; (vi) Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in approving the plan instead of remanding it to the CoC after denying several non-severable reliefs and concessions; (vii) Whether the Adjudicating Authority exceeded its jurisdiction in issuing directions to statutory authorities to facilitate plan implementation; (viii) Whether the resolution plan failed to incorporate 758 acres of land recovered via avoidance applications pursuant to Supreme Court orders; (ix) Whether homebuyer intervenors who failed to submit timely claims during CIRP are entitled to independent relief.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 31(1) of the IBC, an approved resolution plan is statutory and binding upon all stakeholders, including personal and corporate guarantors. The commercial terms of a resolution plan approved by the requisite majority of the CoC may lawfully extinguish a guarantor's right of subrogation against the corporate debtor while preserving the creditors' independent rights to enforce guarantees. Further, the non-grant or refusal of discretionary reliefs and concessions by the adjudicating authority does not render a resolution plan non-compliant with Section 30(2) where the resolution applicant has furnished an unconditional undertaking to implement the plan regardless of such concessions. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31(1) overrides common law and statutory surety protections under Sections 133, 134, 135, 140, and 141 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. A discharge of the principal debtor through an involuntary statutory insolvency process does not absolve personal or corporate guarantors of their independent contractual liabilities. To facilitate the clean slate doctrine and prevent hydra-headed claims from destabilizing the corporate debtor post-resolution, rights of subrogation under Section 140 can be expressly extinguished by the resolution plan. Judicial review under Section 30(2) read with Section 61(3) is confined to verifying strict statutory compliance and cannot encroach upon the commercial wisdom of the CoC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated whether the plan breached any statutory mandates under Section 30(2). It examined CoC valuation records and unrefuted pleadings establishing that the 758 acres retrieved under Section 43 were factored into the liquidation metrics and resolution plan. Regarding third-party claims (YEIDA and Income Tax), the Tribunal evaluated whether the suspended management had standing to litigate issues that were either concluded in separate appeals or pending determination in the claimant's own substantive appeal. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that while erstwhile directors have limited locus to argue Section 30(2) non-compliance, all raised objections failed on merits. The extinguishment of subrogation rights was valid, Income Tax claims were conclusively settled, YEIDA's objections were sub judice in YEIDA's independent appeal, the 758 acres were accounted for, and the plan remained workable and binding despite the partial refusal of concessions.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 548 of 2023 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 559 of 2023 are dismissed, confirming the NCLT order dated 07.03.2023 approving the Resolution Plan of the Consortium of Suraksha Realty Limited and Lakshdeep Investment and Finance Private Limited. All pending interlocutory applications filed by homebuyers seeking fresh claim consideration (IA No. 2643 of 2023 and IA No. 3701 of 2023) are rejected. IA No. 3218 of 2023 is disposed of with liberty granted to approach the Implementation and Monitoring Committee. IA No. 3702 of 2023 seeking intervention is disposed of. Parties are directed to bear their own costs.
summary: Jaiprakash Associates Limited and its promoter Manoj Gaur challenged the NCLT order dated March 7, 2023, approving Suraksha Realty Consortium's resolution plan for corporate debtor Jaypee Infratech Limited. The appellants contested the extinguishment of personal and corporate guarantors' rights of subrogation, the treatment of statutory dues owed to the Income Tax Department and YEIDA, the partial grant of concessions, and the valuation of 758 unencumbered acres. Dismissing both appeals, NCLAT held that under Section 31(1) of the IBC, approved resolution plans can validly extinguish guarantors' subrogation rights while preserving their independent liability. Incidental concessions did not undermine commercial wisdom, nor did third-party claims vitiate the plan, affirming NCLT's approval.

case_title: Mr. Sethuraman Mahadevan & Ors vs. M/s Ozone Urbana Infra Developers Pvt. Ltd.
bench: Chennai Bench
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Financial Creditors are 184 homebuyers and allottees of the residential real estate project Ozone Urbana (originally 169 flat buyers, joined by 15 allottees impleaded via IA No. 128/2022), represented by lead petitioners Mr. Sethuraman Mahadevan and Mr. Bipul Bhattacharya. The Corporate Debtor is M/s Ozone Urbana Infra Developers Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The allottees entered into agreements for sale and construction agreements with the Corporate Debtor for the purchase and delivery of residential units in the under-construction project Ozone Urbana in Bangalore, Karnataka, with financing facilitated through home loans, bank tripartite arrangements, and buy-back schemes. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The total financial debt paid by the allottees was Rs. 1,27,05,10,277, and the aggregate claimed default amount stood at Rs. 191,65,13,949. Default commenced in 2016, which was the contractual timeline for delivery of possession, and was continuous due to incomplete project construction and failure to hand over units. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 7 company petition CP(IB) No. 119/BB/2021 was originally filed by 169 flat buyers before the NCLT Bengaluru Bench. On 24.05.2022, 15 additional homebuyers were impleaded vide IA No. 128/2022. The NCLT dismissed the petition on 24.06.2022, and the present appeal was filed under Section 61 in July 2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Evidence included the Form 1 Section 7 petition; registered sale and construction agreements with 2016 possession deadlines; individual affidavits and signed vakalatnama executed solely by Petitioners Nos. 1 and 2; and informal authorization letters executed by Petitioners Nos. 3 to 184 authorizing Petitioners Nos. 1 and 2 to institute the petition. The Corporate Debtor produced objections asserting that the authorization letters lacked advocate or notarial attestation, failed to comply with foreign country execution laws and stamping under Section 18 of the Indian Stamp Act, omitted co-owners of joint allotments, and alleged that several applicants were speculative investors under buy-back schemes. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The original Section 7 petition was filed before NCLT Bengaluru Bench. On 24.06.2022, the NCLT dismissed the petition on the threshold ground that because authorization letters of Petitioners Nos. 3 to 184 were unattested, un-notarized, and legally defective, the petition was deemed filed by Petitioners Nos. 1 and 2 alone, failing the mandatory threshold of 100 allottees or 10% under Section 7(1). The allottees appealed to the NCLAT Chennai Bench.
legal_issues: (i) Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in summarily dismissing the Section 7 petition for failure to meet the numerical threshold under Section 7(1) of the IBC by discarding informal authorization letters of 182 co-petitioners without framing issues or granting opportunity to cure defects; (ii) Whether letters of authorization executed by allottees residing in India and abroad have the trappings of a power of attorney requiring notarial authentication under Section 85 of the Indian Evidence Act and stamping/adjudication under Section 18 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899; (iii) Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in failing to frame and determine the substantive issue of whether the applicant homebuyers were bona fide allottees or speculative investors excluded under Explanation (i) to Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When an application under Section 7 of the IBC is instituted by a class of financial creditors through authorized representatives, the Adjudicating Authority cannot summarily discard authorization letters and dismiss the petition for want of threshold without properly framing the contested legal and factual issues, evaluating whether procedural defects in representation are curable, and affording the parties an adequate opportunity of hearing in accordance with principles of natural justice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7(1) mandates satisfaction of the numerical threshold (100 allottees or 10%) by genuine allottees, whereas Explanation (i) to Section 5(8)(f) distinguishes bona fide allottees from speculative investors. Procedural defects regarding authorization instruments, the applicability of the Powers of Attorney Act, 1882, the necessity of stamping under Sections 17 and 18 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, and the presumption under Section 85 of the Indian Evidence Act are mixed questions of law and fact. There is no estoppel against statute preventing parties from advancing legal and factual pleas to establish the validity of their representation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated whether the Adjudicating Authority followed procedural fairness and fair play. The lower tribunal committed a procedural error by bypassing the core dispute regarding the applicants' status under Section 5(8)(f) and summarily rejecting the petition on technical flaws in the authorization letters without framing specific issues or conducting an inquiry on the merits. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: In the interest of fair play and good conscience, the dismissal order could not be sustained; the matter was remitted back to the Adjudicating Authority for a de novo enquiry to frame all relevant legal and factual issues, hear both sides, and render a reasoned speaking order in accordance with law.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 330 of 2022 is disposed of without costs. The matter in CP(IB) No. 119/BB/2021 is remitted back to the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, Bengaluru Bench) for conducting a de novo enquiry, directing it to frame and adjudicate all legal and factual issues—including threshold compliance, the validity of authorization letters under the Powers of Attorney Act and Stamp Act, and the status of applicants as allottees or speculative investors under Section 5(8)(f)—by providing a fair hearing to both parties in adherence to principles of natural justice and passing a reasoned speaking order. All connected interlocutory applications are closed.
summary: Homebuyers of the 'Ozone Urbana' project appealed an NCLT Bengaluru Bench order dismissing their Section 7 IBC application against corporate debtor Ozone Urbana Infra Developers Pvt. Ltd. The NCLT had rejected the petition for failing the minimum threshold of 100 allottees or 10%, treating it as filed by only two applicants after discarding authorization letters of 182 co-allottees as un-notarized, unstamped, and lacking co-purchaser signatures. The NCLAT Chennai Bench held that the Adjudicating Authority failed to frame and decide substantive legal and factual controversies, including whether the applicants were bona fide allottees or speculative investors under Section 5(8)(f), and the validity of their authorisations. Consequently, NCLAT remitted the petition for a comprehensive de novo inquiry.

case_title: State Bank of India vs. Darwin Platform Infrastructure Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1354 of 2023 & I.A. No. 5067 of 2023
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is State Bank of India (SBI), a public sector bank and Financial Creditor of the Corporate Debtor. The Respondent No. 1 is M/s Darwin Platform Infrastructure Ltd., the Successful Resolution Applicant. Respondent No. 2 is the Resolution Professional of the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: SBI extended credit facilities to the Corporate Debtor. Upon default, CIRP was initiated against the Corporate Debtor under the IBC, culminating in the submission and approval of a resolution plan by Darwin Platform Infrastructure Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose from unpaid financial debt owed to SBI. The present proceedings arose from SBI's grievance regarding the treatment and allocation of its claims under the resolution plan approved by the Adjudicating Authority, specifically reconsidered following legal opinions regarding the Supreme Court's ruling in Rainbow Papers. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT Mumbai Bench delivered the impugned order approving the resolution plan on 21.07.2023 (a Friday). SBI applied for a certified copy on the next working day, 24.07.2023, which was delivered on 25.07.2023. SBI e-filed the appeal on 07.09.2023 alongside IA No. 5067 of 2023 seeking condonation of delay. The Appellate Tribunal was closed from 07.09.2023 to 10.09.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Relevant record evidence included the certified copy application dated 24.07.2023; the certified copy delivery endorsement dated 25.07.2023 (establishing 2 days requisite under Section 12(2) of the Limitation Act); the NCLAT e-filing portal timestamp dated 07.09.2023; the official tribunal holiday calendar showing closure from 07.09.2023 to 10.09.2023; and SBI's delay condonation application citing internal legal consultations regarding review petitions in the Rainbow Papers case. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: By order dated 21.07.2023 in IA No. 1007/2023, the NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-II approved the resolution plan for the Corporate Debtor. SBI filed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1354 of 2023 under Section 61 with IA No. 5067 of 2023 before the NCLAT Principal Bench seeking condonation of 14/15 days delay.
legal_issues: (i) Whether the appeal was filed on the 15th day of the condonable period or on the 46th day after the delivery of the impugned order; (ii) Whether the benefit of Section 4 of the Limitation Act, 1963 or Section 10 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 is available when the discretionary 15-day condonable period under the proviso to Section 61(2) of the IBC expires on a court holiday.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 61(2) of the IBC read with Section 2(j) of the Limitation Act, 1963, the 'prescribed period' of limitation for filing an appeal is strictly thirty days. The discretionary period of up to fifteen days that may be condoned under the proviso to Section 61(2) does not constitute the 'prescribed period' of limitation. Consequently, the benefit of Section 4 of the Limitation Act—permitting institution on the next court reopening day when the prescribed period expires on a holiday—applies solely to the statutory 30-day limitation period and cannot be extended to cover the discretionary 15-day condonable period. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238A of the IBC makes the Limitation Act, 1963 applicable to proceedings and appeals under the Code. By virtue of the proviso to Section 10(1) of the General Clauses Act, 1897, Section 10 is inapplicable to proceedings governed by the Limitation Act, 1963. Under Section 12(2) of the Limitation Act, limitation commences the day after the order is delivered; intervening non-working days prior to applying for a certified copy cannot stall the commencement of limitation. The maximum condonable window under the proviso to Section 61(2) is capped at 15 days, beyond which the appellate tribunal possesses no jurisdiction to condone delay. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal performed an objective mathematical computation: excluding the pronouncement date (21.07.2023) and 2 days requisite for obtaining the certified copy (24.07.2023 to 25.07.2023), the 30-day prescribed period expired on 22.08.2023. The subsequent 15-day discretionary period expired on 06.09.2023 (a working day). E-filing on 07.09.2023 constituted filing on the 46th day. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal was filed beyond the total permissible 45 days (30 days limitation + 15 days condonable). Because Section 4 of the Limitation Act does not apply to discretionary condonation periods and Section 10 of the General Clauses Act is excluded, the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to condone the delay.
operative_order: The Delay Condonation Application (I.A. No. 5067 of 2023) is dismissed. Consequently, the Memo of Appeal in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1354 of 2023 is rejected.
summary: The State Bank of India appealed an NCLT Mumbai Bench order dated July 21, 2023, which approved the resolution plan submitted by Darwin Platform Infrastructure Ltd. for the corporate debtor. SBI sought condonation of delay for filing the appeal on September 7, 2023, arguing that the tribunal was closed on that day and invoking Section 4 of the Limitation Act and Section 10 of the General Clauses Act. Rejecting the application, NCLAT held that the 'prescribed period' under Section 61(2) is strictly 30 days, while the additional 15-day discretionary period is not a prescribed period. Since the 45-day outer limit expired on September 6, 2023, Section 4 was inapplicable, and the tribunal lacked jurisdiction to condone delay beyond 15 days.

case_title: PLBB Products Pvt. Ltd. vs. Madhulika Periwal & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 525 of 2022 (with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 947 & 1001 of 2021, 499, 526 & 612 of 2022)
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is PLBB Products Pvt. Ltd., the Successful Resolution Applicant under the second EOI. The Corporate Debtor is National Plywood Industries Ltd. (NPIL), an MSME unit. The Principal Borrower is National Boards Limited (NBL). The Financial Creditor is IDBI Bank, which assigned its facility to Stressed Assets Stabilization Fund (SASF). The Suspended Promoter/Director was Piyush Periwal (substituted upon death by Madhulika Periwal, Director and 40.43% shareholder). The Resolution Professionals are Sandeep Khaitan (erstwhile RP) and Amit Pareek (newly appointed RP). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: On 27.03.1997, IDBI sanctioned a loan facility of Rs. 320 lakhs to NBL (which availed Rs. 307.71 lakhs). NPIL executed a corporate guarantee dated 16.07.1997 along with two personal guarantors. Upon NBL's default, IDBI recalled the loan facility on 09.11.2001 and invoked NPIL's corporate guarantee on 03.12.2001, demanding Rs. 5,42,94,868. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose upon invocation of the guarantee on 03.12.2001. IDBI obtained a DRT decree on 03.01.2005 against NBL for Rs. 5,42,94,868 with 12% interest. On 30.04.2005, SASF and NBL executed a Negotiated Settlement for Rs. 215.89 lakhs, against which NBL paid Rs. 92.24 lakhs from asset sales, leaving a balance of Rs. 123.65 lakhs. In Section 7 proceedings, SASF claimed an inflated debt of Rs. 133.55 Crores, and subsequently lodged a Form-C claim of Rs. 16,12,23,209.72 (including Rs. 11,61,52,341.72 charged as 18 years of 12% interest). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The corporate guarantee was invoked on 03.12.2001. NPIL was under BIFR from 2003 to 30.11.2016. SASF filed Section 7 CP (IB) No. 09/GB/2019 on 12.03.2019, which was admitted by NCLT Guwahati on 26.08.2019. The first Form-G was published on 07.11.2019, and the second Form-G was published on 27.06.2020. PLBB submitted its resolution plan on 05.09.2020, which the CoC approved on 06.11.2020 and 01.06.2021. The promoter filed IA No. 43 of 2021 seeking removal of the RP and cancellation of CIRP actions. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Relevant evidence included: (i) Publication records establishing that the second Form-G was published solely in local Assam newspapers (The Assam Rising and Dainandin Barta, circulation 28,000) despite the CD having corporate offices and units across Assam, Tamil Nadu, and West Bengal; (ii) MCA incorporation records showing that PLBB was formally incorporated on 20.07.2020, eight days after submitting its EOI on 12.07.2020; (iii) CoC voting records showing SASF was improperly allocated an 87.76% majority based on an inflated claim; (iv) Audited financial statements showing the CD was an operational, profit-making MSME post-BIFR from FY 2016-17 to 2018-19 before operations ceased during CIRP; and (v) MSME Udyog Aadhaar registration [Aadhaar Redacted] of the Corporate Debtor. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Guwahati admitted Section 7 on 26.08.2019. In IA No. 43 of 2021 filed by the promoter, NCLT Guwahati by order dated 08.04.2022 terminated the CIRP from the second EOI stage, set aside the resolution process that approved PLBB's plan, and replaced RP Sandeep Khaitan with Amit Pareek due to lack of transparency, conflict of interest, and flawed CoC voting structure. PLBB appealed to the NCLAT Principal Bench.
legal_issues: (i) Whether the Adjudicating Authority possesses inherent jurisdiction under the IBC to terminate the CIRP from the stage of the second Expression of Interest and replace the Resolution Professional for lack of transparency and statutory infractions without a prior CoC resolution under Section 27; (ii) Whether the approval of PLBB's resolution plan by a Committee of Creditors dominated by a financial creditor holding an 87.76% voting share derived from an inflated and improperly admitted claim is protected under the commercial wisdom of the CoC; (iii) Whether entertaining an Expression of Interest from an entity not in existence at the time of submission and publishing Form-G in newspapers with inadequate circulation vitiates the resolution process.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When a corporate insolvency resolution process is fundamentally tainted from a specific procedural stage—due to restricted and non-compliant publication of invitations for expression of interest, entertainment of bids from entities not yet legally in existence, and control of the Committee of Creditors by a single creditor exercising an artificial voting majority founded upon an inflated and improperly admitted claim—the Adjudicating Authority possesses inherent jurisdiction to terminate the process from the flawed stage and replace the Resolution Professional, and such tainted proceedings cannot be shielded or validated under the doctrine of commercial wisdom of the CoC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 27 of the IBC prescribes the procedure for replacement of a Resolution Professional by a vote of the CoC, but it is not exhaustive and does not denude the Adjudicating Authority, as the appointing authority, of its inherent jurisdiction to replace an RP when conflict of interest, lack of transparency, or failure to discharge statutory duties compromises the CIRP. Section 21(2) mandates accurate determination and collation of financial debts; an illegally constituted CoC holding an artificial majority vitiates all consequential resolutions. The commercial wisdom of the CoC cannot override foundational compliance with the IBC and CIRP Regulations. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated whether the procedural irregularities—specifically publishing the second Form-G solely in regional newspapers with minimal circulation (28,000 copies) rather than national papers across all locations where the CD operated, entertaining an EOI from an entity prior to its formal incorporation, and ascribing an 87.76% voting share based on an unsustainable claim calculation that charged 18 years of 12% interest—demonstrated a tainted process that undermined value maximization. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that the Adjudicating Authority was fully justified in setting aside the proceedings from the second EOI stage, rejecting PLBB's selection as resolution applicant, and replacing the Resolution Professional to ensure a fair, transparent, and competitive resolution process.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 525 of 2022 is dismissed, confirming the NCLT Guwahati Bench order dated 08.04.2022 in IA No. 43 of 2021 to the extent that it terminated the CIRP from the stage of the second EOI and replaced Resolution Professional Sandeep Khaitan with Amit Pareek. The newly appointed Resolution Professional is directed to conclude the entire CIRP afresh within 90 days from the date of the order under the supervision and control of the properly constituted Committee of Creditors. Adverse observations against counsel are deleted, and observations regarding the erstwhile RP are clarified not to constitute a finding against his professional integrity. Parties shall bear their own costs.
summary: PLBB Products Pvt. Ltd., the successful resolution applicant, appealed against the NCLT Guwahati Bench order terminating the corporate insolvency resolution process of National Plywood Industries Limited from the second Expression of Interest stage and replacing the Resolution Professional. The promoter had challenged the resolution process, alleging that the Resolution Professional admitted an inflated claim of Rs. 16.12 Crores for Stressed Assets Stabilization Fund, granting it an improper 87.76% voting majority, and improperly entertained PLBB's bid prior to its formal incorporation. Upholding the NCLT's decision, the NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority possesses inherent powers to replace a Resolution Professional and roll back a tainted CIRP where procedural improprieties compromise statutory integrity, commercial wisdom notwithstanding.

case_title: E.M. Najeeb Ellias Mohammed vs. Union Bank of India
bench: Chennai Bench
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Financial Creditor is Union Bank of India (Respondent)[cite: 7]. The Corporate Debtor / Corporate Guarantor is M/s Air Travel Enterprises India Ltd. (represented by Appellant E.M. Najeeb Ellias Mohammed, Promoter/Director)[cite: 7]. The Principal Borrower is M/s Green Gateway Leisure Ltd. (GGL)[cite: 7]. The Interim Resolution Professional appointed is Mr. Raj Mohan R[cite: 7]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Union Bank of India sanctioned a term loan facility of Rs. 24.86 Crores (approved up to Rs. 25 Crores) to GGL for developing a beach resort on 55.42 acres of leasehold land at Bekel, Kerala, vide sanction letter dated 12.06.2010 (renewed/restructured on 29.09.2012, 24.02.2014, 12.01.2015, and 01.07.2016)[cite: 7]. The Corporate Debtor executed corporate guarantee agreements dated 02.07.2010, 29.09.2012, 24.02.2014, and 12.01.2015, alongside demand promissory notes, hypothecation of movables, and equitable mortgage to secure repayment[cite: 7]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: GGL defaulted in debt servicing, leading to account classification as NPA on 30.09.2015[cite: 7]. As of 04.07.2023, the gross default stood at Rs. 66,48,11,742 (Principal: Rs. 24,85,00,000; Interest: Rs. 40,72,84,195; Penal interest: Rs. 9,98,915; Other charges: Rs. 80,28,632)[cite: 7]. After accounting for recoveries of Rs. 23,60,84,594, the net outstanding claimed default was Rs. 42,87,27,148[cite: 7]. The default date was crystallised as 09.03.2022 upon failure to settle within the 6-month window granted in prior proceedings[cite: 7]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Guarantee invoked via demand notice under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002 on 29.12.2017 (received 03.01.2018; reply dated 27.02.2018)[cite: 7]. An initial Section 7 petition against GGL (IBA/01/KOB/2020) was admitted on 15.10.2020, but NCLAT disposed of the appeal on 09.09.2021 granting GGL 6 months to settle[cite: 7]. Upon GGL's failure to settle, a fresh Section 7 petition against GGL (CP(IBC)/46/KOB/2022) was admitted on 25.01.2023, culminating in a liquidation order against GGL on 24.11.2023[cite: 7]. Section 7 petition CP(IBC)/33/KOB/2023 was filed against the Corporate Guarantor on 18.07.2023[cite: 7]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreements, sanction letters, and guarantee deeds[cite: 7]; guarantee covenants stipulating that written admissions or acknowledgments by the Principal Borrower bind the guarantor as its authorized agent under the Limitation Act, 1963[cite: 7]; repeated written OTS proposals by GGL dated 12.11.2019, 27.11.2019, 05.10.2021, 14.01.2022, 04.02.2022, 19.03.2022, 21.11.2022, 13.02.2023, 10.08.2023, 18.09.2023, and 05.10.2023 (accompanied by an upfront deposit of Rs. 1.10 Crore)[cite: 7]; and GGL's audited financial statements for FY 2016-17 to FY 2021-22 reflecting continuous debt acknowledgment[cite: 7]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Union Bank of India filed CP(IBC)/33/KOB/2023 under Section 7 on 18.07.2023 before NCLT Kochi Bench[cite: 7]. On 22.12.2023, NCLT Kochi admitted the petition, held the debt, default, and creditor-debtor relationship established, rejected the plea of limitation in light of continuous acknowledgments, initiated CIRP, and declared a moratorium[cite: 7]. The Promoter appealed under Section 61 before NCLAT Chennai[cite: 7].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the Section 7 petition filed against the Corporate Guarantor on 18.07.2023 was barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, given that the account was classified as NPA on 30.09.2015 and guarantee was invoked under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act on 29.12.2017; (ii) Whether written acknowledgments of debt and One Time Settlement (OTS) proposals made solely by the Principal Borrower renew limitation against the Corporate Guarantor under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and the terms of the guarantee deed; (iii) Whether non-mentioning or alteration of the default date in Part-IV of Form-1 vitiates the maintainability of a Section 7 application under the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the liability of a guarantor is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor unless contractually modified[cite: 7]. Where the deed of guarantee explicitly provides that any admission or acknowledgment of indebtedness in writing by the principal debtor binds the guarantor as an authorized agent for the purposes of the Limitation Act, 1963, valid acknowledgments of debt and OTS proposals executed by the principal borrower within the limitation period trigger Section 18 of the Limitation Act, renewing limitation against both the principal borrower and the guarantor[cite: 7]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 applies to Section 7 proceedings under the IBC[cite: 7]. An acknowledgment of debt does not create a new contract but renews the existing liability and commences a fresh period of limitation from the date of acknowledgment[cite: 7]. By operation of law and contractual incorporation, the principal borrower's acknowledgment acts as an acknowledgment on behalf of the guarantor[cite: 7]. Additionally, technical discrepancies or omission of the exact date of default in Part-IV of Form-1 are directory and curable under Section 7(5), not fatal defects that invalidate an otherwise complete petition where debt and default are undisputed[cite: 7]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized whether the series of written OTS letters (2019 to 2023), audited balance sheets of the borrower from FY 2016-17 through FY 2021-22, and the upfront deposit of Rs. 1.10 Crore constituted an unbroken chain of written admissions of jural relationship and existing liability prior to the expiration of the three-year limitation window[cite: 7]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that default by the principal borrower was conclusively established through confirmed CIRP and liquidation orders, and the continuous written acknowledgments by the borrower legally bound the guarantor[cite: 7]. The Section 7 petition was filed well within limitation, and NCLT Kochi committed no error in initiating CIRP against the Corporate Guarantor[cite: 7].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins.) No. 08 of 2024 is dismissed without costs, affirming the order dated 22.12.2023 passed by the NCLT Kochi Bench admitting CP(IBC)/33/KOB/2023 and initiating CIRP against M/s Air Travel Enterprises India Ltd. Moratorium and appointment of the Interim Resolution Professional are upheld. All connected pending interlocutory applications are closed.
summary: The promoter of corporate guarantor Air Travel Enterprises India Ltd. appealed an NCLT Kochi Bench order admitting Union Bank of India's Section 7 IBC application[cite: 7]. The appellant contended that the petition was barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, as the borrower's account became NPA in 2015 and the guarantee was invoked via SARFAESI notice in 2017 without acknowledgment by the guarantor[cite: 7]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Chennai Bench held that under Section 128 of the Contract Act and express guarantee terms, the guarantor's liability is co-extensive with the principal borrower[cite: 7]. Continuous OTS proposals and balance sheet acknowledgments by the borrower extended limitation under Section 18, rendering the Section 7 petition timely and maintainable[cite: 7].

case_title: Leka Consulting Services Pvt. Ltd. vs. The Registrar Of Companies, Odisha
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Leka Consulting Services Private Limited, an incorporated private limited company whose name was struck off from the Register of Companies[cite: 8]. The Respondent is the Registrar of Companies (ROC), Odisha, Ministry of Corporate Affairs[cite: 8]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant company was incorporated under the Companies Act and acquired substantial immovable properties comprising land parcels via nine sale deeds executed between 2007 and 2013 funded through promoter loans, intended for subsequent business activities and loan repayments[cite: 8, 8]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose from non-filing of statutory annual returns and balance sheets for Financial Years 2016-17 and 2017-18[cite: 8, 8]. The company generated nil operational revenue after 31.03.2017, maintained no employees on its rolls, and recorded continuous financial losses[cite: 8, 8]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The ROC issued a show-cause notice in Form STK-1 under Section 248(1)(c), published gazette notice Form STK-5/5A, and issued a strike-off notice Form STK-7 dated 23.10.2019, published in the Official Gazette on 02.11.2019, dissolving the company w.e.f. 24.10.2019[cite: 8, 8]. The company filed revival petition CP No. 69/CB/2020 on 26.02.2020 (dismissed 21.08.2020)[cite: 8, 8]. The High Court of Orissa disposed of WP(C) No. 35437 of 2020 on 23.12.2021 granting liberty to approach NCLT for amendment[cite: 8, 8]. Appellant filed CA No. 15/CB/2023 on 16.12.2022[cite: 8, 8]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Documentary evidence included: (i) nine registered sale deeds executed between 2007 and 2013 alongside encumbrance certificates evidencing immovable property ownership[cite: 8]; (ii) audited profit and loss accounts demonstrating zero revenue from operations and continuous losses[cite: 8]; (iii) bank account statements and income tax returns[cite: 8]; and (iv) ROC report dated 16.03.2020 requiring strict proof of active operations at the time of striking off[cite: 8, 8]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Cuttack Bench dismissed CP No. 69/CB/2020 on 21.08.2020, holding the company was not a going concern[cite: 8, 8]. On 23.12.2021, the Orissa High Court in WP(C) No. 35437 of 2020 permitted the appellant to approach NCLT to seek amendment of the order under Section 420[cite: 8, 8]. Appellant filed CA No. 15/CB/2023 seeking to produce additional documents and reconsider revival[cite: 8]. By order dated 08.08.2023, NCLT Cuttack dismissed CA No. 15/CB/2023 as time-barred under Section 420(2) and beyond the scope of an amendment[cite: 8]. Appellant appealed to NCLAT[cite: 8].
legal_issues: (i) Whether Company Application No. 15/CB/2023 was barred by limitation under Section 420(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, having been filed more than two years after the dismissal order dated 21.08.2020[cite: 8]; (ii) Whether an application praying to place additional documents on record to reconsider the revival of a struck-off company falls within the statutory scope of rectifying a mistake apparent from the record under Section 420(2) read with Rule 154 of the NCLT Rules, 2016, or amounts to an impermissible review[cite: 8]; (iii) Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in misinterpreting the liberty granted by the High Court of Orissa to file an amendment application[cite: 8].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory power of rectification under Section 420(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Rule 154 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 is strictly circumscribed to rectifying patent errors or mistakes apparent on the face of the record without disturbing finality[cite: 8]. It cannot be utilized as a device to introduce fresh or additional evidence, fill evidentiary lacunae, or seek substantive rehearing and review of an order passed on merits[cite: 8]. Moreover, any application under Section 420(2) must strictly adhere to the mandatory two-year limitation period from the date of the original order[cite: 8]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 420(2) confers limited jurisdiction to amend an order only when a patent, self-evident error is apparent from the record, and expressly establishes an outer limit of two years[cite: 8]. An error apparent on the face of the record must be manifest and cannot be established through elaborate argument, elucidation, or introduction of new documents[cite: 8]. Section 420 does not confer an inherent or plenary power of review upon the Tribunal[cite: 8]. Where an application to introduce additional evidence is filed after two years from the final dismissal order, it is time-barred and outside the scope of Section 420(2)[cite: 8]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized whether the appellant's application sought to rectify a patent clerical/arithmetical error or sought to overturn a substantive finding of dormancy[cite: 8]. The Tribunal evaluated the nine historical sale deeds (2007-2013) and determined that an applicant cannot claim a right to introduce additional documents at a belated stage to fill gaps in proof without establishing due diligence or showing that the evidence was previously unavailable[cite: 8]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that CA No. 15/CB/2023 was instituted on 16.12.2022, beyond the two-year limitation period from the order dated 21.08.2020[cite: 8]. Furthermore, the prayer to admit additional evidence and grant substantive revival exceeded both the liberty granted by the High Court and the statutory ambit of Section 420(2), warranting dismissal of the appeal[cite: 8].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 227 of 2023 is dismissed without costs[cite: 8]. The impugned order dated 08.08.2023 passed by the National Company Law Tribunal, Cuttack Bench in C.A. (Companies Act) No. 15/CB/2023 in CP No. 69/CB/2020 is affirmed[cite: 8]. Connected pending interlocutory application IA No. 5615/2023 for stay and all other pending IAs are closed[cite: 8].
summary: Leka Consulting Services Private Limited appealed against an NCLT Cuttack Bench order dismissing its application filed under Section 420(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, which sought to introduce additional documents and reconsider the revival of the company struck off by the Registrar of Companies, Odisha[cite: 8]. The company’s earlier revival petition under Section 252(3) had been dismissed on August 21, 2020[cite: 8]. Affirming the dismissal, NCLAT held that the application was filed on December 16, 2022, beyond the mandatory two-year limitation under Section 420(2)[cite: 8]. Furthermore, introducing additional evidence to seek a substantive rehearing exceeded the narrow statutory scope of rectifying mistakes apparent on the face of the record, rendering the appeal devoid of merit[cite: 8].

case_title: Bhavesh Harkishandas Mehta vs. Kookmin Bank & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 75 of 2024, Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 77 of 2024 & Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1341 of 2023
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Personal Guarantors: Bhavesh Harkishandas Mehta (CA No. 75 of 2024) and Atul Harkishan Das Mehta (CA No. 77 of 2024) for Corporate Debtor Compuage Infocom Limited[cite: 9]; and Saranga A. Aggarwal (CA No. 1341 of 2023) for Corporate Debtor AA Estates Private Limited[cite: 9]. The Financial Creditors are Kookmin Bank and State Bank of India (SBI)[cite: 9]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Bhavesh Mehta and Atul Mehta executed Deeds of Personal Guarantee dated 24.11.2022 in favor of Kookmin Bank to secure credit facilities granted to Compuage Infocom Limited[cite: 9]. Saranga A. Aggarwal executed a personal guarantee in favor of SBI securing financial credit facilities extended to AA Estates Private Limited[cite: 9]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Defaults occurred upon failure by the corporate debtors and personal guarantors to repay credit facilities[cite: 9]. Kookmin Bank issued demand notices to Bhavesh Mehta and Atul Mehta on 29.03.2023[cite: 9]. SBI demanded repayment from Saranga A. Aggarwal leading to personal insolvency proceedings[cite: 9]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: In Compuage Infocom Ltd., another financial creditor (Plus Unified Engaugement Services Pvt. Ltd.) initiated Section 7 proceedings in NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-V, which admitted CIRP on 02.11.2023[cite: 9]. Prior to that, Kookmin Bank filed Section 95 applications against the guarantors on 31.10.2023 (CP(IB)-1165 & 1164/2023)[cite: 9]. In AA Estates Pvt. Ltd., SBI filed a Section 95 petition against Saranga Aggarwal on 20.01.2022 in Court-I (notice issued 20.06.2022)[cite: 9], while Section 7 CIRP against the CD commenced in Court-V on 06.12.2022[cite: 9]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Relevant documentary evidence comprised: (i) Deeds of Personal Guarantee dated 24.11.2022[cite: 9]; (ii) Section 95 applications filed by Kookmin Bank and SBI[cite: 9]; (iii) Section 7 admission orders passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-V dated 02.11.2023 and 06.12.2022[cite: 9]; (iv) Central Government Notification dated 01.06.2016 issued under Section 419(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 establishing the NCLT Mumbai Bench as a single territorial entity[cite: 9]; and (v) administrative roster orders of the President of NCLT under Rule 16 of NCLT Rules, 2016[cite: 9]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-III by orders dated 18.12.2023 appointed a Resolution Professional under Section 97 and directed a report under Section 99(1) regarding Bhavesh Mehta and Atul Mehta[cite: 9]. NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-I by order dated 17.08.2023 appointed a Resolution Professional regarding Saranga Aggarwal[cite: 9]. The personal guarantors appealed to NCLAT under Section 61, contending that under Section 60(2) of the IBC, their Section 95 petitions could only be heard by Court-V where the Section 7 CIRP petitions against the Corporate Debtors were pending[cite: 9].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an order passed under Section 95 appointing a Resolution Professional by a courtroom of an NCLT Bench different from the courtroom of the same Bench where the Corporate Debtor's insolvency resolution process is pending is without jurisdiction[cite: 9]; (ii) Whether the mandate of Section 60(2) of the IBC requiring an application relating to a personal guarantor to be filed before 'such National Company Law Tribunal' refers to the institutional territorial Bench of the NCLT or mandates filing and hearing in the identical courtroom of that Bench[cite: 9]; (iii) Whether the coordinate bench decision of NCLAT in Monica Jajoo vs. PHL Fininvest Pvt. Ltd. laid down the correct law regarding courtroom-level transfer under Section 60(2)[cite: 9].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 60(2) of the IBC read with Section 419 of the Companies Act, 2013 and Rule 2(7) of the NCLT Rules, 2016, the statutory expression 'National Company Law Tribunal' denotes the Tribunal or its notified territorial Bench as a single institutional unit[cite: 9]. Section 60(2) does not mandate filing or hearing before an identical courtroom or combination of members within that Bench[cite: 9]. The distribution, assignment, and listing of cases among multiple courtrooms of a single Bench fall exclusively within the administrative superintendence and master-of-the-roster powers of the President of NCLT under Rule 16 of the NCLT Rules, 2016[cite: 9]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(2) uses the words 'a' and 'such' NCLT to ensure that both the corporate insolvency process of the corporate debtor and the insolvency resolution of its personal guarantor are initiated within the same territorial Bench, preventing concurrent proceedings across disparate territorial jurisdictions or between the NCLT and the Debts Recovery Tribunal (DRT)[cite: 9]. It does not dictate intra-bench courtroom allocation[cite: 9]. An individual litigant has no vested legal right to demand hearing by a particular courtroom[cite: 9]. The prior contrary ruling of the two-member bench in Monica Jajoo vs. PHL Fininvest Pvt. Ltd. misapplied precedent and is not good law[cite: 9]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified whether both the Section 7 CIRP proceedings against the Corporate Debtors and the Section 95 applications against the Personal Guarantors were filed within the territorial jurisdiction of the NCLT Mumbai Bench as notified by Central Government Notification dated 01.06.2016[cite: 9]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because all relevant matters were properly filed and pending before the NCLT Mumbai Bench, the assignment of Section 95 petitions to Court-I and Court-III pursuant to administrative roster directions was valid and within jurisdiction; neither court lacked jurisdiction to appoint a Resolution Professional under Section 97 and direct a report under Section 99(1)[cite: 9].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 75 of 2024, 77 of 2024, and 1341 of 2023 are dismissed[cite: 9]. The impugned orders dated 18.12.2023 (passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-III) and dated 17.08.2023 (passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-I) appointing Resolution Professionals and directing reports under Section 99(1) of the IBC are affirmed[cite: 9]. It is clarified that the Appellate Tribunal has not examined the merits of the Section 95 applications, leaving it to the respective courts of the Adjudicating Authority to proceed and decide in accordance with law[cite: 9].
summary: Personal guarantors Bhavesh Harkishandas Mehta, Atul Harkishan Das Mehta, and Saranga A. Aggarwal appealed NCLT Mumbai Bench orders appointing Resolution Professionals under Section 95 of the IBC[cite: 9]. The appellants contended that under Section 60(2), the applications were without jurisdiction because corporate insolvency proceedings against their respective corporate debtors were pending before Court-V, whereas their personal insolvency applications were heard by Court-III and Court-I[cite: 9]. Dismissing the appeals, NCLAT held that Section 60(2) mandates filing before the same territorial Bench of the NCLT, not the identical courtroom[cite: 9]. Internal listing among courtrooms falls within the administrative roster powers of the President of NCLT[cite: 9]. Overruling Monica Jajoo, NCLAT affirmed the orders[cite: 9].

case_title: Saranga A. Aggarwal vs. State Bank of India & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1341 of 2023 (with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 75 & 77 of 2024)
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Saranga A. Aggarwal, personal guarantor to Corporate Debtor AA Estates Private Limited[cite: 10]. The Respondent No. 1 is State Bank of India (SBI), Financial Creditor[cite: 10]. Respondent No. 2 is the Resolution Professional appointed under Section 97[cite: 10]. (Decided alongside connected appeals involving personal guarantors Bhavesh Harkishandas Mehta and Atul Harkishan Das Mehta and creditor Kookmin Bank)[cite: 10]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: SBI extended financial credit facilities to corporate debtor AA Estates Private Limited, which were secured by a personal guarantee executed by Saranga A. Aggarwal in favor of the lender[cite: 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred upon failure of AA Estates Private Limited to repay outstanding credit facilities, triggering enforcement of the personal guarantee by SBI against Saranga Aggarwal[cite: 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: SBI filed an application under Section 95 against personal guarantor Saranga Aggarwal on 20.01.2022 before NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-I[cite: 10]. Court-I issued notice on 20.06.2022[cite: 10]. Insolvency proceedings under Section 7 against corporate debtor AA Estates Private Limited commenced before NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-V on 06.12.2022[cite: 10]. NCLT Court-I passed the impugned order appointing a Resolution Professional on 17.08.2023[cite: 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Relevant documentary record comprised: (i) Personal Guarantee Deed executed by Saranga Aggarwal[cite: 10]; (ii) Section 95 application CP (IB) 452(MB)/2022 filed by SBI[cite: 10]; (iii) Section 7 CIRP admission order dated 06.12.2022 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-V against AA Estates Private Limited[cite: 10]; (iv) Central Government Notification S.O. 1935(E) dated 01.06.2016 issued under Section 419(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 establishing the territorial jurisdiction of NCLT Mumbai Bench[cite: 10]; and (v) Roster and administrative assignment orders of the President of NCLT issued under Rule 16 of NCLT Rules, 2016[cite: 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: SBI filed CP (IB) 452(MB)/2022 under Section 95 against Saranga Aggarwal before NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-I[cite: 10]. On 17.08.2023, NCLT Court-I appointed a Resolution Professional and directed a report under Section 99(1)[cite: 10]. Saranga Aggarwal appealed to the NCLAT Principal Bench under Section 61, contending that because CIRP against the corporate debtor was pending before Court-V, Court-I lacked jurisdiction under Section 60(2) of the IBC[cite: 10].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an order appointing a Resolution Professional under Section 95 passed by a courtroom of an NCLT Bench different from the courtroom of the same Bench where the Corporate Debtor's CIRP is pending is null and void for want of jurisdiction[cite: 10]; (ii) Whether Section 60(2) of the IBC mandates that personal insolvency applications under Section 95 must be filed in and adjudicated by the exact identical courtroom where the Corporate Debtor's insolvency proceedings are pending[cite: 10]; (iii) Whether the coordinate bench ruling in Monica Jajoo vs. PHL Fininvest Pvt. Ltd. laid down the correct legal interpretation of Section 60(2)[cite: 10].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 60(2) of the IBC read with Section 419 of the Companies Act, 2013 and Rule 2(7) of the NCLT Rules, 2016, the statutory reference to 'National Company Law Tribunal' designates the institutional territorial Bench of the NCLT as a composite adjudicatory unit[cite: 10]. Section 60(2) does not mandate filing or hearing before the identical courtroom or division of that Bench[cite: 10]. The internal listing, distribution, and assignment of matters across multiple courtrooms of a single Bench fall exclusively within the administrative superintendence and master-of-the-roster powers of the President of NCLT under Rule 16 of the NCLT Rules, 2016[cite: 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(2) employs the words 'a' and 'such' NCLT to ensure that insolvency proceedings against both the principal corporate debtor and its personal guarantor are centralized within the same territorial Bench rather than distributed across different geographical Benches or between the NCLT and the DRT[cite: 10]. The provision does not regulate intra-bench courtroom allocation[cite: 10]. Litigants possess no legal entitlement to demand adjudication by a particular courtroom[cite: 10]. The coordinate bench decision in Monica Jajoo vs. PHL Fininvest Pvt. Ltd. misconstrued precedent and does not lay down correct law[cite: 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examined whether both the CIRP proceedings against AA Estates Private Limited and the Section 95 petition against Saranga Aggarwal were instituted within the territorial jurisdiction of the NCLT Mumbai Bench under Central Government Notification dated 01.06.2016[cite: 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because both matters were situated within the NCLT Mumbai Bench, Court-I possessed full and lawful jurisdiction to entertain SBI's Section 95 application and appoint a Resolution Professional pursuant to administrative roster orders[cite: 10].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1341 of 2023 is dismissed along with connected appeals[cite: 10]. The impugned order dated 17.08.2023 passed by the National Company Law Tribunal, Mumbai Bench, Court-I in C.P. (IB) 452(MB)/2022 appointing a Resolution Professional is affirmed[cite: 10]. The Appellate Tribunal clarified that it did not consider the substantive merits of the Section 95 application, leaving it to the Adjudicating Authority to proceed and decide in accordance with law[cite: 10]. Parties shall bear their own costs[cite: 10].
summary: Saranga A. Aggarwal, personal guarantor of corporate debtor AA Estates Private Limited, appealed an NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-I order appointing a Resolution Professional under Section 95 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code[cite: 10]. The appellant contended that under Section 60(2) of the Code, Court-I lacked jurisdiction because the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process against the corporate debtor was pending before Court-V of the same Mumbai Bench[cite: 10]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that Section 60(2) mandates filing before the same territorial Bench of the NCLT and does not require proceedings to be heard by the identical courtroom[cite: 10]. Case allocation among courtrooms is governed by the administrative roster powers of the President under Rule 16[cite: 10].

case_title: Mayur Ratilal Suchak & Anr. vs. Mr. Birendra Kumar Agarwal
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 25 of 2024 & I.A. No. 85 of 2024
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Mayur Ratilal Suchak & Anr., promoters/applicants seeking MSME registration for the Corporate Debtor[cite: 11]. The Respondent is Mr. Birendra Kumar Agarwal, Resolution Professional of the Corporate Debtor in CP(IB)/979(MB)/2022[cite: 11]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) was pending against the Corporate Debtor before NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-V under CP(IB)/979(MB)/2022[cite: 11]. The Appellants instituted interlocutory application IA No. 3445 of 2023 seeking directions to register the Corporate Debtor as a Micro, Small and Medium Enterprise (MSME) to enable participation in the resolution process under the IBC[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose in the principal debt servicing of the Corporate Debtor leading to CIRP[cite: 11]. The interlocutory dispute involved the dismissal of the Appellants' application for MSME registration on 09.11.2023, which the Appellants sought to challenge on appeal[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-V) heard and dictated the order dismissing IA No. 3445 of 2023 in open court on 09.11.2023 in the presence of counsel[cite: 11]. Deepawali vacation followed from 11.11.2023 to 19.11.2023[cite: 11]. The order was uploaded on the NCLT portal on 22.11.2023[cite: 11]. Appellants applied for a certified copy on 22.11.2023 and received it on 23.11.2023[cite: 11]. Appellants e-filed the appeal before NCLAT on 27.12.2023 alongside IA No. 85 of 2024 seeking condonation of delay[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Documentary evidence comprised: (i) the report of the Court Officer/Assistant Registrar of NCLT Mumbai Bench dated 16.02.2024 certifying that the order dated 09.11.2023 in IA/3445/2023 was dictated on board in open court to the knowledge of counsel and uploaded on 22.11.2023[cite: 11]; (ii) the cause list for 09.11.2023; (iii) the application for certified copy dated 22.11.2023 and receipt endorsement dated 23.11.2023[cite: 11]; and (iv) NCLAT e-filing portal timestamp dated 27.12.2023[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-V dismissed IA No. 3445 of 2023 on 09.11.2023[cite: 11]. The Appellants filed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 25 of 2024 with IA No. 85 of 2024 before the NCLAT Principal Bench on 27.12.2023 praying for condonation of delay, claiming limitation commenced on 22.11.2023 upon uploading of the order[cite: 11].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the 30-day period of limitation for filing an appeal under Section 61(2) of the IBC commences from the date the order is pronounced/dictated in open court in the presence of counsel or from the date the order is uploaded on the tribunal website[cite: 11]; (ii) Whether the Appellate Tribunal has jurisdiction under the proviso to Section 61(2) of the IBC to condone delay when an appeal is e-filed beyond the statutory 30-day limitation period plus the maximum permissible 15-day discretionary condonation window[cite: 11].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 61(2) of the IBC, the prescribed period of thirty days for filing an appeal commences from the date the order is pronounced or dictated in open court in the presence of counsel, rather than the date on which the order is uploaded on the tribunal's website[cite: 11]. A party represented in court when an order is dictated is imputed with constructive knowledge of the order, creating an immediate obligation to exercise due diligence and apply for a certified copy[cite: 11]. The appellate tribunal possesses no statutory power or jurisdiction under the proviso to Section 61(2) to condone any delay exceeding the outer limit of fifteen days[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Unlike Section 421(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, Section 61(2) of the IBC deliberately omits language computing limitation from when the order is 'made available'[cite: 11]. Pronouncement or dictation in open court triggers the running of limitation[cite: 11]. Under Section 12(2) of the Limitation Act, 1963, exclusion is restricted strictly to the time requisite for obtaining a certified copy once applied for; delayed application for a copy or awaiting website upload cannot halt or defer the commencement of limitation[cite: 11]. The strict statutory cap of 15 days under the proviso to Section 61(2) overrides general condonation principles under Section 5 of the Limitation Act[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the official report forwarded by the Registrar of NCLT Mumbai establishing that the order was dictated on board in open court on 09.11.2023 in the presence of the appellant's counsel[cite: 11]. Computing limitation from 10.11.2023 (excluding the pronouncement date under Section 12(1)), the statutory 30-day period expired on 09.12.2023, and the additional 15-day condonable period expired on 24.12.2023[cite: 11]. E-filing on 27.12.2023 fell on the 48th day[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal was filed beyond the 15-day condonable period under the proviso to Section 61(2)[cite: 11]. The Appellate Tribunal lacked jurisdiction to condone the delay, requiring dismissal of the condonation application and rejection of the memo of appeal[cite: 11].
operative_order: I.A. No. 85 of 2024 praying for condonation of delay is dismissed[cite: 11]. Consequently, the Memo of Appeal in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 25 of 2024 is rejected[cite: 11].
summary: Appellants Mayur Ratilal Suchak and another appealed an order of NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-V dismissing IA No. 3445 of 2023, which sought directions to register the corporate debtor as an MSME during CIRP[cite: 11]. The appellants sought condonation of delay, contending that the thirty-day limitation under Section 61(2) of the IBC commenced only upon uploading the order on November 22, 2023[cite: 11]. Rejecting the application, NCLAT held that limitation begins running when an order is dictated in open court in counsel's presence, constructively communicating the decision[cite: 11]. Because the appeal was e-filed on December 27, 2023, which was beyond the maximum fifteen-day condonable period, the appellate tribunal lacked jurisdiction to condone the delay, resulting in rejection of the appeal[cite: 11].

case_title: M/s. Rare Asset Reconstruction Ltd. vs. Sh. Avishek Gupta
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Corporate Debtor is Sarga Hotel Private Limited (SHPL), a subsidiary of Shristi Infrastructure Development Corporation Limited (SIDCL), controlled by the Kanoria Foundation[cite: 12]. The Appellant is M/s. Rare Asset Reconstruction Ltd. (Rare ARC), acting as trustee of Rare ARC 051 Trust[cite: 12]. The Assignor is Srei Equipment Finance Limited (SEFL), a subsidiary of Srei Infrastructure Finance Limited (SIFL), also controlled by the Kanoria Foundation[cite: 12]. The Respondent is Sh. Avishek Gupta, Resolution Professional (RP) of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 12]. Intervenors include JC Flowers ARC, SRA Shri Ram Multicom Pvt. Ltd., and NARCL[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: On 29.08.2018, SIFL sanctioned a Rupee Term Loan of Rs. 300 Crores to SHPL[cite: 12]. In 2019, SIFL transferred its lending portfolio, including the SHPL loan, to SEFL via a Business Transfer Agreement[cite: 12]. On 09.09.2020, SEFL executed an Assignment Agreement assigning the loan facility and security interests to Rare ARC as trustee of Rare ARC 051 Trust for an upfront cash consideration of Rs. 43.85 Crores in exchange for 15% security receipts, while SEFL retained 85% of the security receipts and beneficial interest[cite: 12, 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose from unpaid financial debt under the credit facility[cite: 12]. Rare ARC lodged a Form C claim on 24.02.2022 claiming Rs. 393.46 Crores (Rs. 393,46,52,000 as of 31.01.2022 plus contractual interest and charges)[cite: 12]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: On 12.08.2020, NCLT admitted a Section 9 petition against SHPL (Universal International Creation Ltd.)[cite: 12]. On 09.09.2020, the Assignment Agreement was executed with a retrospective cut-off date of 12.08.2020, and Rare ARC filed its claim the same day[cite: 12]. On 27.08.2021, NCLAT set aside the first CIRP as collusive[cite: 12]. On 11.02.2022, NCLT admitted Yes Bank's Section 7 petition against SHPL[cite: 12]. Rare ARC filed its Form C claim on 24.02.2022[cite: 12]. On 30.04.2022, the RP admitted the claim as financial debt but excluded Rare ARC from the CoC as an assignee akin to a related party[cite: 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Relevant evidence comprised: (i) Assignment Agreement dated 09.09.2020 defining the cut-off date as 12.08.2020[cite: 12]; (ii) Rare ARC 051 Trust Deed showing SEFL held 85% beneficial interest[cite: 12]; (iii) MCA records and Significant Beneficial Owner (SBO) filings under Section 90 of the Companies Act establishing common ultimate ownership and control of both SEFL and SHPL by Hari Prasad Kanoria / Kanoria Foundation[cite: 12]; (iv) Share Subscription and Shareholders Agreement dated 07.08.2008 and Addendum dated 31.08.2009 identifying SIFL facilities as connected party transactions[cite: 12]; (v) Avoidance Application (IA No. 744/2022 in CP(IB) No. 294/2021) filed by the Administrator of SIFL/SEFL under Section 66 alleging the loan was fraudulent and that consideration funds of Rs. 25 Crores to Rs. 44 Crores were round-tripped from SEFL to Rare ARC via shell entities (Predicate Consultants and Ambrelo Ventures)[cite: 12]; and (vi) Rare ARC's failure to disclose independent source of funding[cite: 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Rare ARC filed IA(IB) No. 822/(KB)/2022 before NCLT Kolkata Bench Court-II challenging the RP's decision dated 30.04.2022 and seeking voting rights in the CoC[cite: 12]. On 13.09.2023, NCLT dismissed the application, holding Rare ARC was an assignee of a related party brought in to circumvent Section 21(2)[cite: 12]. Rare ARC appealed to NCLAT under Section 61[cite: 12].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an assignee of a related party financial creditor can be disqualified and excluded from participating, voting, or being represented in the Committee of Creditors under the first proviso to Section 21(2) of the IBC[cite: 12]; (ii) Whether the related-party disqualification under the first proviso to Section 21(2) applies strictly in praesenti or extends to an assignee where the assignment is undertaken in bad faith or as a contrivance to circumvent statutory disability[cite: 12]; (iii) Whether the Resolution Professional and Adjudicating Authority are precluded by the rule in Mohinder Singh Gill from considering supplementary affidavits, subsequent transaction audit disclosures, and pending Section 66 avoidance applications regarding round-tripping of funds to sustain the exclusion decision[cite: 12].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under the first proviso to Section 21(2) of the IBC, where a related party financial creditor assigns its debt to a third party in bad faith, under suspicious circumstances, or as a commercial contrivance to shed its related-party label and secure backdoor entry into the Committee of Creditors, the assignee must be treated as akin to a related party financial creditor and disqualified from participating, voting, or being represented in the CoC[cite: 12]. The statutory exclusion cannot be defeated by interposing an assignee while the assignor retains substantial economic interest or beneficial ownership in the debt[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While the baseline rule under the first proviso to Section 21(2) of the IBC debars financial creditors who are related parties in praesenti, this rule prevents abuse: a related party creditor that divests itself of formal status or assigns debt to circumvent the statutory disability remains barred, as established in Phoenix ARC and the 2020 Insolvency Law Committee Report[cite: 12]. Furthermore, because the Resolution Professional performs administrative and collation duties rather than judicial functions, the rule in Mohinder Singh Gill does not apply to administrative claim verification[cite: 12]. The Adjudicating Authority exercising adjudicatory powers under Section 60(5) is fully entitled to receive and consider supplementary affidavits, subsequent evidence, and transaction audit records to ascertain the bona fides of the assignment[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examined the objective indicia of bad faith: (a) assignment executed during an active CIRP with an artificial retrospective cut-off date matching the insolvency commencement date[cite: 12]; (b) claim filed on the exact day of the assignment agreement[cite: 12]; (c) retention of an 85% beneficial interest by the related party assignor via security receipts[cite: 12]; (d) corporate filings establishing common beneficial control under Kanoria Foundation[cite: 12]; and (e) failure of the assignee to produce evidence of an independent funding source against specific pleadings of round-tripping through connected intermediaries[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The assignment was a collusive contrivance devised by SEFL to indirectly dominate the CoC through an assignee; consequently, Rare ARC was rightly treated as akin to a related party and excluded from the CoC, warranting dismissal of the appeal[cite: 12].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1304 of 2023 is dismissed on its merits without costs, affirming the order dated 13.09.2023 passed by the National Company Law Tribunal, Kolkata Bench (Court-II) in IA(IB) No. 822/(KB)/2022[cite: 12]. Pending Interlocutory Application I.A. No. 5357 of 2023 and all other connected applications are disposed of[cite: 12].
summary: Appellant M/s Rare Asset Reconstruction Limited challenged the NCLT Kolkata Bench order dated September 13, 2023, which upheld the Resolution Professional's decision excluding the appellant from the Committee of Creditors of Sarga Hotel Private Limited[cite: 12]. The appellant claimed voting rights as an assignee of a Rupee Term Loan from Srei Equipment Finance Limited[cite: 12]. The Resolution Professional disqualified the appellant under the first proviso to Section 21(2) of the IBC, citing common control under Kanoria Foundation, assignor's 85% economic interest via security receipts, and suspicious assignment timing[cite: 12]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that assignments executed in bad faith to circumvent statutory related-party disabilities treat the assignee akin to a related party, barring CoC participation[cite: 12].

case_title: Rosario D'Souza vs. Mahesh Chand Gupta & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 111 of 2022 & Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 233 of 2023
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Corporate Debtor is Dolphin Marine Foods and Processors (India) Private Limited, an MSME engaged in fish processing and export[cite: 13]. The Appellant is Rosario D'Souza, a member of the Suspended Board of Directors and promoter/shareholder[cite: 13]. The Financial Creditor is Union Bank of India, the sole member of the Committee of Creditors (CoC)[cite: 13]. Respondent No. 1 is Mr. Mahesh Chand Gupta, erstwhile Resolution Professional[cite: 13]. Respondent No. 3 is Mrs. Lalita S Powle in consortium with Suyog Agro & Poultry Products Pvt. Ltd., the Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA)[cite: 13]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Between August 2008 and July 2017, Union Bank of India sanctioned, enhanced, and renewed credit facilities (including cash credit, FDBP/FUDBP, and Term Loan) up to a sanctioned limit of Rs. 11 Crores (last sanction letter dated 30.03.2017), secured by personal guarantees, hypothecation of goods and book debts, and mortgages[cite: 13, 13]. In FY 2017-18, the Corporate Debtor faced financial distress following a closure notice issued by the Maharashtra Pollution Control Board, which halted processing plant operations[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtor failed to service its debt facilities, leading to its loan account being classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 30.04.2018 in terms of RBI Prudential Norms[cite: 13, 13]. The aggregate outstanding default claimed in the Section 7 petition stood at Rs. 12,38,92,192 (comprising principal of Rs. 8.77 Crores and interest of Rs. 3.61 Crores), exceeding the Section 4 threshold of Rs. 1 Crore[cite: 13]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Union Bank of India issued a demand notice under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002 on 19.06.2018 for Rs. 13,26,33,585.12[cite: 13]. The bank subsequently permitted 'Holding on Operations' with 15%, 25%, and 30% cut-backs between 31.10.2018 and 30.09.2019[cite: 13]. Upon failure to regularize, a Loan Recall Notice was issued on 03.07.2019, and symbolic possession was taken under Section 13(4) on 06.01.2020[cite: 13]. The bank filed Section 7 CP No. 1352/(IB)-MB-V/2020, which NCLT Mumbai admitted on 03.08.2021[cite: 13]. Form G was published on 04.10.2021; the CoC approved the SRA's revised resolution plan on 13.04.2022; and the RP filed IA No. 1736 of 2022 for plan approval under Section 31[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Documentary evidence comprised: (i) sanction letters, loan agreements, and guarantee documents[cite: 13]; (ii) computerized bank account statements establishing principal and interest default of Rs. 12.38 Crores[cite: 13]; (iii) RBI Prudential Norms Circular dated 01.07.2015 governing NPA classification[cite: 13]; (iv) 'Holding on Operations' sanction letters and recall notices[cite: 13]; (v) approved Resolution Plan of Rs. 25,39,57,466.47 providing 100% payment to CIRP costs, operational creditors, workmen/employees, and the secured financial creditor, along with Rs. 1 Crore upfront post-CIRP accrued interest to Union Bank of India and Rs. 2 Crores redeemable preference shares to existing promoters[cite: 13]; and (vi) absence of claims filed by other creditors under Regulation 9A (Form F)[cite: 13]. 6.
