PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-V admitted the Section 7 petition on 03.08.2021[cite: 13]. Appellant challenged admission in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 111 of 2022[cite: 13]. On 19.01.2023, NCLT Mumbai approved the SRA's resolution plan in IA No. 1736 of 2022[cite: 13]. Appellant filed Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 233 of 2023 challenging plan approval, specifically disputing the additional Rs. 1 Crore payment of accrued interest to Union Bank of India[cite: 13]. Both appeals were heard together by NCLAT Principal Bench[cite: 13].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in admitting the Section 7 application despite the Corporate Debtor operating under 'Holding on Operation' arrangements and alleging lack of default or erroneous calculation of interest[cite: 13]; (ii) Whether the provision in the approved Resolution Plan for payment of Rs. 1 Crore as upfront accrued interest from the CIRP commencement date to the sole secured financial creditor over and above its admitted claim violates Section 30(2) of the IBC or the rights of existing shareholders[cite: 13]; (iii) Whether the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in approving the distribution of amounts and allocation of post-commencement interest in a resolution plan is subject to judicial review by the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal[cite: 13].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in evaluating, accepting, and approving the financial terms, distribution of funds, and commercial payoffs in a resolution plan—including the commercial decision to allocate post-CIRP accrued interest to a secured financial creditor—is paramount and non-justiciable[cite: 13]. The scope of judicial review exercisable by the Adjudicating Authority under Section 31(1) and the Appellate Tribunal under Section 61(3) is strictly circumscribed to the limited parameters enumerated under Section 30(2) of the IBC[cite: 13]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2) and Section 30(4) of the IBC read with CIRP Regulations entrust the determination of feasibility, viability, and distribution of funds exclusively to the commercial discretion of the CoC[cite: 13]. Financial debt carries time value, and no provision in the Code prohibits a resolution applicant from proposing, or the CoC from approving, an upfront payment towards accrued interest arising after the insolvency commencement date to a secured financial creditor[cite: 13]. Furthermore, temporary permissions granted by a lender to conduct 'Holding on Operations' with cut-backs constitute standard banking accommodation and do not extinguish an antecedent default or bar the financial creditor from invoking Section 7 once the statutory threshold is crossed[cite: 13]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified the computerized bank account statements and security documents establishing that the total financial debt and default of Rs. 12.38 Crores far exceeded the Section 4 threshold of Rs. 1 Crore and conformed with RBI prudential norms[cite: 13]. With respect to the resolution plan, the Tribunal examined the allocation breakdown showing 100% satisfaction of CIRP costs, operational debts, workmen/employee dues, and secured financial debt, alongside an allotment of Rs. 2 Crores in redeemable preference shares to existing promoters, confirming compliance with Section 30(2)[cite: 13]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority correctly admitted the Section 7 application as both debt and default were conclusively established[cite: 13]. Furthermore, the approval of the resolution plan granting an additional Rs. 1 Crore accrued interest to the secured lender was a valid exercise of commercial wisdom, devoid of any statutory violation or arbitrariness, warranting dismissal of both appeals[cite: 13].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 111 of 2022 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 233 of 2023 are dismissed without costs[cite: 13]. The orders dated 03.08.2021 (initiating CIRP) and dated 19.01.2023 (approving the Resolution Plan) passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-V in C.P. No. 1352/(IB)-MB-V/2020 and IA No. 1736 of 2022 are affirmed[cite: 13]. All connected pending interlocutory applications (including IA Nos. 830, 831, and 832 of 2023) are closed[cite: 13].
summary: Rosario D'Souza, suspended director of corporate debtor Dolphin Marine Foods and Processors (India) Private Limited, appealed against two NCLT Mumbai Bench orders: admitting Union Bank of India's Section 7 IBC petition and approving a resolution plan submitted by Mrs. Lalita S Powle and Suyog Agro & Poultry Products Pvt. Ltd[cite: 13]. The appellant disputed the default, cited 'Holding on Operation' accommodations, and challenged paying Rs. 1 Crore in post-CIRP accrued interest to the sole financial creditor[cite: 13]. Dismissing both appeals, NCLAT held that default exceeding the statutory threshold was conclusively established[cite: 13]. Furthermore, allocating post-commencement interest falls squarely within the Committee of Creditors' non-justiciable commercial wisdom under Section 30(4), violating no provision of Section 30(2)[cite: 13].

case_title: Mr. Nandkishor Vishnupant Deshpande vs. Central Bank of India & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1672-1673 of 2023 & Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 163-164 of 2024
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Corporate Debtor is ETCO Denim Private Limited[cite: 14]. The Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA) is Ramesh Shah (ex-promoter of the Corporate Debtor) in consortium with Masitia Capital Services Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 14]. The Resolution Professional is Nandkishor Vishnupant Deshpande[cite: 14]. The Committee of Creditors (CoC) comprises Union Bank of India (66.91%), Central Bank of India (dissenting financial creditor, 22.44%), Corporation Bank, and Andhra Bank[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: ETCO Denim Private Limited availed multiple credit facilities from a consortium of commercial lenders led by Union Bank of India and Central Bank of India[cite: 14]. Following operational distress, an operational creditor initiated insolvency proceedings against the Corporate Debtor under Section 9 of the IBC[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose from unpaid operational and financial debt servicing leading to CIRP admission[cite: 14]. The SRA's resolution plan proposed total settlement consideration of Rs. 66.60 Crores payable over two years, contemplating a 71.90% haircut against admitted financial creditor claims[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP was initiated upon admission of the Section 9 petition[cite: 14]. Ministry of MSME notifications revising enterprise classification criteria were issued on 01.06.2020 (S.O. 1702(E)) and 26.06.2020[cite: 14]. Form-G was published on 10.08.2020 (last date 30.10.2020) and a second Form-G on 05.05.2021 (last date 22.06.2021)[cite: 14]. MSME Udyam Registration Certificate (UDYAM-MH-18-0020176) was issued to the Corporate Debtor on 23.10.2020[cite: 14]. The SRA submitted its resolution plan on 30.10.2020[cite: 14]. The CoC approved the plan in its 26th meeting with a 77.56% majority[cite: 14]. The RP filed plan approval application IA No. 2895/2021[cite: 14]. Central Bank of India filed IA No. 317/2022 challenging SRA eligibility[cite: 14]. NCLT passed impugned orders on 08.12.2023[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Documentary evidence comprised: (i) Udyam Registration Certificate dated 23.10.2020 issued by the competent authority[cite: 14]; (ii) Chartered Engineer valuation reports dated 01.08.2021 and 31.08.2021 certifying the Written Down Value (WDV) of plant and machinery at Rs. 29.27 Crores and Rs. 24.88 Crores[cite: 14]; (iii) court-directed Chartered Accountant valuation certificate dated 25.10.2023 assessing WDV at Rs. 37.57 Crores[cite: 14]; and (iv) minutes of the 4th, 5th, 11th, 20th, 21st, and 22nd CoC meetings demonstrating consistent deliberation and acknowledgment of MSME status and Section 240A eligibility[cite: 14]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-III passed two orders on 08.12.2023: allowing IA No. 317/2022 (holding the SRA ineligible under Section 29A read with Section 240A because MSME registration occurred post-CIRP commencement and recalculating WDV above Rs. 50 Crores), and rejecting IA No. 2895/2021 for plan approval[cite: 14]. The SRA and the RP appealed both orders to the NCLAT Principal Bench under Section 61[cite: 14].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the ex-promoter of a Corporate Debtor that obtained MSME registration after the commencement of CIRP but prior to the submission of the resolution plan is eligible to submit a resolution plan under Section 240A of the IBC[cite: 14]; (ii) Whether the Adjudicating Authority exercising summary jurisdiction under the IBC possesses statutory authority to investigate accounts, recalculate the Written Down Value of assets, and unilaterally revoke or disregard an MSME registration certificate issued by the competent authority under the MSMED Act, 2006[cite: 14]; (iii) Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in rejecting a resolution plan approved by a 77.56% CoC majority by impermissibly substituting its judgment for the commercial wisdom of the CoC on the objection of a dissenting minority financial creditor[cite: 14].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 240A of the IBC, the relevant cut-off date for determining whether a corporate debtor qualifies as an MSME to exempt an ex-promoter from disqualification under Section 29A(c) and (h) is the date of submission of the resolution plan, not the date of insolvency commencement[cite: 14]. Furthermore, the Adjudicating Authority exercising summary jurisdiction under the IBC has no statutory jurisdiction to enquire into accounts, re-evaluate asset calculations, or revoke an MSME registration certificate validly issued by the competent statutory authority under the MSMED Act, 2006[cite: 14]. Once an MSME certificate is granted and subsisting, and a resolution plan is approved by the requisite statutory majority of the CoC, its commercial wisdom is sacrosanct and non-justiciable under Sections 30(2) and 31(1)[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 240A contains a non-obstante clause designed to protect and revive micro, small, and medium enterprises by exempting promoters from Section 29A restrictions[cite: 14]. Following the Supreme Court ruling in Hari Babu Thota, post-CIRP MSME registration obtained prior to plan submission validly attracts Section 240A[cite: 14]. Redressal of discrepancies or cancellation of Udyam registration falls exclusively within the statutory mechanism under Clause 9(4) of the MSME Notification dated 26.06.2020 through District Industries Centres and State Government authorities, and the NCLT cannot arrogate regulatory powers to invalidate certificates[cite: 14]. Under Sections 30(4) and 31(1), a dissenting financial creditor holding a minority voting share must abide by the commercial decision of the majority creditors[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the MSME certificate was obtained on 23.10.2020, prior to plan submission on 30.10.2020[cite: 14]. It scrutinized CoC records confirming full creditor apprisedness across multiple meetings, and evaluated valuation certificates from Chartered Engineers and an independent Chartered Accountant assessing plant and machinery WDV between Rs. 24.88 Crores and Rs. 37.57 Crores, well within the Rs. 50 Crore ceiling[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that the SRA was fully eligible under Section 240A to submit the resolution plan as an MSME, the MSME certificate could not be unilaterally disregarded by the NCLT, and the plan received valid approval with a 77.56% voting majority, requiring both orders to be set aside and the matter remanded to NCLT to pass fresh approval orders within three months[cite: 14].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1672-1673 of 2023 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 163-164 of 2024 are allowed without costs[cite: 14]. The impugned orders dated 08.12.2023 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-III in IA No. 317/2022 and IA No. 2895/2021 are set aside[cite: 14]. The Successful Resolution Applicant is held eligible under Section 240A to submit a resolution plan as an MSME[cite: 14]. The Adjudicating Authority is directed to pass a fresh order in IA No. 2895/2021 filed by the Resolution Professional for approval of the resolution plan along with necessary directions, endeavouring to do so within a period of three months from the date of receipt of the order[cite: 14].
summary: Appeals were preferred by successful resolution applicant Ramesh Shah (consortium with Masitia Capital Services) and Resolution Professional Nandkishor Deshpande challenging NCLT Mumbai Bench orders that held the ex-promoter ineligible under Section 29A read with Section 240A of the IBC and rejected the CoC-approved resolution plan for ETCO Denim Private Limited[cite: 14]. Dissenting creditor Central Bank of India had contested the Corporate Debtor's MSME status obtained post-CIRP commencement[cite: 14]. Allowing the appeals, NCLAT held that under the Supreme Court's Hari Babu Thota ruling, MSME status acquired prior to plan submission validly confers Section 240A benefits[cite: 14]. Furthermore, NCLT lacks jurisdiction to unilaterally recalculate asset valuations or revoke an MSME certificate, remanding the plan approval application to NCLT for fresh orders within three months[cite: 14].

App. (AT) (Ins) No. 233 of 2023 challenging plan approval, specifically disputing the additional Rs. 1 Crore payment of accrued interest to Union Bank of India[cite: 15]. Both appeals were heard together by NCLAT Principal Bench[cite: 15].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in admitting the Section 7 application despite the Corporate Debtor operating under 'Holding on Operation' arrangements and alleging lack of default or erroneous calculation of interest[cite: 15]; (ii) Whether the provision in the approved Resolution Plan for payment of Rs. 1 Crore as upfront accrued interest from the CIRP commencement date to the sole secured financial creditor over and above its admitted claim violates Section 30(2) of the IBC or the rights of existing shareholders[cite: 15]; (iii) Whether the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in approving the distribution of amounts and allocation of post-commencement interest in a resolution plan is subject to judicial review by the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal[cite: 15].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in evaluating, accepting, and approving the financial terms, distribution of funds, and commercial payoffs in a resolution plan—including the commercial decision to allocate post-CIRP accrued interest to a secured financial creditor—is paramount and non-justiciable[cite: 15]. The scope of judicial review exercisable by the Adjudicating Authority under Section 31(1) and the Appellate Tribunal under Section 61(3) is strictly circumscribed to the limited parameters enumerated under Section 30(2) of the IBC[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2) and Section 30(4) of the IBC read with CIRP Regulations entrust the determination of feasibility, viability, and distribution of funds exclusively to the commercial discretion of the CoC[cite: 15]. Financial debt carries time value, and no provision in the Code prohibits a resolution applicant from proposing, or the CoC from approving, an upfront payment towards accrued interest arising after the insolvency commencement date to a secured financial creditor[cite: 15]. Furthermore, temporary permissions granted by a lender to conduct 'Holding on Operations' with cut-backs constitute standard banking accommodation and do not extinguish an antecedent default or bar the financial creditor from invoking Section 7 once the statutory threshold is crossed[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified the computerized bank account statements and security documents establishing that the total financial debt and default of Rs. 12.38 Crores far exceeded the Section 4 threshold of Rs. 1 Crore and conformed with RBI prudential norms[cite: 15]. With respect to the resolution plan, the Tribunal examined the allocation breakdown showing 100% satisfaction of CIRP costs, operational debts, workmen/employee dues, and secured financial debt, alongside an allotment of Rs. 2 Crores in redeemable preference shares to existing promoters, confirming compliance with Section 30(2)[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority correctly admitted the Section 7 application as both debt and default were conclusively established[cite: 15]. Furthermore, the approval of the resolution plan granting an additional Rs. 1 Crore accrued interest to the secured lender was a valid exercise of commercial wisdom, devoid of any statutory violation or arbitrariness, warranting dismissal of both appeals[cite: 15].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 111 of 2022 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 233 of 2023 are dismissed without costs[cite: 15]. The orders dated 03.08.2021 (initiating CIRP) and dated 19.01.2023 (approving the Resolution Plan) passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-V in C.P. No. 1352/(IB)-MB-V/2020 and IA No. 1736 of 2022 are affirmed[cite: 15]. All connected pending interlocutory applications (including IA Nos. 830, 831, and 832 of 2023) are closed[cite: 15].
summary: Rosario D'Souza, suspended director of corporate debtor Dolphin Marine Foods and Processors (India) Private Limited, appealed two orders of NCLT Mumbai Bench: admitting Union Bank of India's Section 7 IBC application and approving a resolution plan submitted by Lalita Powle in consortium with Suyog Agro & Poultry Products[cite: 15]. The appellant contested the default metrics, cited 'Holding on Operation' accommodations, and challenged the resolution plan's allocation of Rs. 1 Crore in post-CIRP accrued interest to the sole financial creditor[cite: 15]. Dismissing both appeals, NCLAT held that default exceeding the statutory threshold was conclusively established[cite: 15]. Furthermore, allocating post-commencement interest falls within the Committee of Creditors' non-justiciable commercial wisdom under Section 30(4), violating no statutory provision under Section 30(2)[cite: 15].

case_title: Mr. Nandkishor Vishnupant Deshpande vs. Central Bank of India & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1672-1673 of 2023 & Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 163-164 of 2024
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Corporate Debtor is ETCO Denim Private Limited[cite: 16]. The Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA) is Ramesh Shah (ex-promoter of the Corporate Debtor) in consortium with Masitia Capital Services Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 16]. The Resolution Professional is Nandkishor Vishnupant Deshpande[cite: 16]. The Committee of Creditors (CoC) comprises Union Bank of India (66.91%), Central Bank of India (dissenting financial creditor, 22.44%), Corporation Bank, and Andhra Bank[cite: 16]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: ETCO Denim Private Limited availed multiple credit facilities from a consortium of commercial lenders led by Union Bank of India and Central Bank of India[cite: 16]. Following operational distress, an operational creditor initiated insolvency proceedings against the Corporate Debtor under Section 9 of the IBC[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose from unpaid operational and financial debt servicing leading to CIRP admission[cite: 16]. The SRA's resolution plan proposed total settlement consideration of Rs. 66.60 Crores payable over two years, contemplating a 71.90% haircut against admitted financial creditor claims[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP was initiated upon admission of the Section 9 petition[cite: 16]. Ministry of MSME notifications revising enterprise classification criteria were issued on 01.06.2020 (S.O. 1702(E)) and 26.06.2020[cite: 16]. Form-G was published on 10.08.2020 (last date 30.10.2020) and a second Form-G on 05.05.2021 (last date 22.06.2021)[cite: 16]. MSME Udyam Registration Certificate (UDYAM-MH-18-0020176) was issued to the Corporate Debtor on 23.10.2020[cite: 16]. The SRA submitted its resolution plan on 30.10.2020[cite: 16]. The CoC approved the plan in its 26th meeting with a 77.56% majority[cite: 16]. The RP filed plan approval application IA No. 2895/2021[cite: 16]. Central Bank of India filed IA No. 317/2022 challenging SRA eligibility[cite: 16]. NCLT passed impugned orders on 08.12.2023[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Documentary evidence comprised: (i) Udyam Registration Certificate dated 23.10.2020 issued by the competent authority[cite: 16]; (ii) Chartered Engineer valuation reports dated 01.08.2021 and 31.08.2021 certifying the Written Down Value (WDV) of plant and machinery at Rs. 29.27 Crores and Rs. 24.88 Crores[cite: 16]; (iii) court-directed Chartered Accountant valuation certificate dated 25.10.2023 assessing WDV at Rs. 37.57 Crores[cite: 16]; and (iv) minutes of the 4th, 5th, 11th, 20th, 21st, and 22nd CoC meetings demonstrating consistent deliberation and acknowledgment of MSME status and Section 240A eligibility[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-III passed two orders on 08.12.2023: allowing IA No. 317/2022 (holding the SRA ineligible under Section 29A read with Section 240A because MSME registration occurred post-CIRP commencement and recalculating WDV above Rs. 50 Crores), and rejecting IA No. 2895/2021 for plan approval[cite: 16]. The SRA and the RP appealed both orders to the NCLAT Principal Bench under Section 61[cite: 16].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the ex-promoter of a Corporate Debtor that obtained MSME registration after the commencement of CIRP but prior to the submission of the resolution plan is eligible to submit a resolution plan under Section 240A of the IBC[cite: 16]; (ii) Whether the Adjudicating Authority exercising summary jurisdiction under the IBC possesses statutory authority to investigate accounts, recalculate the Written Down Value of assets, and unilaterally revoke or disregard an MSME registration certificate issued by the competent authority under the MSMED Act, 2006[cite: 16]; (iii) Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in rejecting a resolution plan approved by a 77.56% CoC majority by impermissibly substituting its judgment for the commercial wisdom of the CoC on the objection of a dissenting minority financial creditor[cite: 16].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 240A of the IBC, the relevant cut-off date for determining whether a corporate debtor qualifies as an MSME to exempt an ex-promoter from disqualification under Section 29A(c) and (h) is the date of submission of the resolution plan, not the date of insolvency commencement[cite: 16]. Furthermore, the Adjudicating Authority exercising summary jurisdiction under the IBC has no statutory jurisdiction to enquire into accounts, re-evaluate asset calculations, or revoke an MSME registration certificate validly issued by the competent statutory authority under the MSMED Act, 2006[cite: 16]. Once an MSME certificate is granted and subsisting, and a resolution plan is approved by the requisite statutory majority of the CoC, its commercial wisdom is sacrosanct and non-justiciable under Sections 30(2) and 31(1)[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 240A contains a non-obstante clause designed to protect and revive micro, small, and medium enterprises by exempting promoters from Section 29A restrictions[cite: 16]. Following the Supreme Court ruling in Hari Babu Thota, post-CIRP MSME registration obtained prior to plan submission validly attracts Section 240A[cite: 16]. Redressal of discrepancies or cancellation of Udyam registration falls exclusively within the statutory mechanism under Clause 9(4) of the MSME Notification dated 26.06.2020 through District Industries Centres and State Government authorities, and the NCLT cannot arrogate regulatory powers to invalidate certificates[cite: 16]. Under Sections 30(4) and 31(1), a dissenting financial creditor holding a minority voting share must abide by the commercial decision of the majority creditors[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the MSME certificate was obtained on 23.10.2020, prior to plan submission on 30.10.2020[cite: 16]. It scrutinized CoC records confirming full creditor apprisedness across multiple meetings, and evaluated valuation certificates from Chartered Engineers and an independent Chartered Accountant assessing plant and machinery WDV between Rs. 24.88 Crores and Rs. 37.57 Crores, well within the Rs. 50 Crore ceiling[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that the SRA was fully eligible under Section 240A to submit the resolution plan as an MSME, the MSME certificate could not be unilaterally disregarded by the NCLT, and the plan received valid approval with a 77.56% voting majority, requiring both orders to be set aside and the matter remanded to NCLT to pass fresh approval orders within three months[cite: 16].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1672-1673 of 2023 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 163-164 of 2024 are allowed without costs[cite: 16]. The impugned orders dated 08.12.2023 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-III in IA No. 317/2022 and IA No. 2895/2021 are set aside[cite: 16]. The Successful Resolution Applicant is held eligible under Section 240A to submit a resolution plan as an MSME[cite: 16]. The Adjudicating Authority is directed to pass a fresh order in IA No. 2895/2021 filed by the Resolution Professional for approval of the resolution plan along with necessary directions, endeavouring to do so within a period of three months from the date when a copy of the order is produced before it[cite: 16].
summary: Appeals were preferred by successful resolution applicant Ramesh Shah (consortium with Masitia Capital Services) and Resolution Professional Nandkishor Deshpande challenging NCLT Mumbai Bench orders that held the ex-promoter ineligible under Section 29A read with Section 240A of the IBC and rejected the CoC-approved resolution plan for ETCO Denim Private Limited[cite: 16]. Dissenting creditor Central Bank of India had contested the Corporate Debtor's MSME status obtained post-CIRP commencement[cite: 16]. Allowing the appeals, NCLAT held that under the Supreme Court's Hari Babu Thota ruling, MSME status acquired prior to plan submission validly confers Section 240A benefits[cite: 16]. Furthermore, NCLT lacks jurisdiction to unilaterally recalculate asset valuations or revoke an MSME certificate, remanding the plan approval application to NCLT for fresh orders within three months[cite: 16].

case_title: Mr. Rakshit Dhirajlal Doshi & Anr. vs. Sumedha Management Solutions Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Corporate Debtor is M/s Doshion Private Limited (DPL), an EPC company claiming MSME status[cite: 17]. The Appellants are Mr. Rakshit Dhirajlal Doshi and Mr. Ashit Doshi, Suspended Directors of DPL[cite: 17]. Respondent No. 1 is Sumedha Management Solutions Pvt. Ltd., Liquidator of DPL[cite: 17]. Respondent No. 2 is the Committee of Creditors (CoC) represented by lead member IDBI Bank Ltd., comprising five banks, one ARC, and one NBFC[cite: 17]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: IDBI Bank originally sanctioned financial credit assistance of Rs. 32.7 Crores to DPL, which was subsequently restructured in 2014 under consortium finance with an enhanced aggregate credit limit of Rs. 93.48 Crores to support DPL's EPC operations[cite: 17]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred upon failure to service the consortium credit facilities, culminating in total financial creditor claims aggregating to approximately Rs. 1,288 Crores filed by seven financial creditors[cite: 17]. The estimated liquidation value of the CD was roughly Rs. 15 Crores, which the suspended directors informally offered to pay as an OTS/resolution amount[cite: 17]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: IDBI Bank filed Section 7 CP(IB) No. 59 of 2019 on 19.12.2018[cite: 17]. NCLT Ahmedabad admitted the petition on 30.01.2021[cite: 17]. Public announcement was made on 12.09.2021; the CoC was constituted on 04.10.2021; and the first CoC meeting convened on 08.10.2021[cite: 17]. The CoC concluded e-voting on 02.11.2021 unanimously approving liquidation under Section 33(2)[cite: 17]. The RP filed liquidation application IA No. 769(AHM)2021 on 10.11.2021[cite: 17]. NCLT ordered liquidation on 03.10.2023[cite: 17]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Documentary record comprised: (i) Minutes of the 1st CoC meeting dated 08.10.2021 recording that DPL had ceased business and manufacturing operations since 2016, that pending EPC contracts lacked proprietary technology or licenses and required fresh capital, and that group entities had received zero bids[cite: 17]; (ii) 100% affirmative e-voting results dated 02.11.2021 resolving to liquidate DPL and sell assets as a going concern under Regulation 39C[cite: 17]; (iii) Form H certifying the lapse of the statutory CIRP period[cite: 17]; and (iv) Gujarat High Court orders concerning the suspended directors' challenges to wilful defaulter classifications[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench admitted Section 7 on 30.01.2021[cite: 17]. In the first CoC meeting, the CoC decided not to issue Form-G and instead resolved to liquidate the CD[cite: 17]. In IA No. 769(AHM)2021, NCLT Ahmedabad Bench on 03.10.2023 ordered the liquidation of DPL under Section 33(2)[cite: 17]. Suspended directors appealed to NCLAT under Section 61, alleging material irregularity and arbitrariness[cite: 17].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the Committee of Creditors' decision to liquidate the Corporate Debtor in its first meeting without publishing an Expression of Interest (Form-G) or appointing registered valuers was tainted with material irregularity and arbitrariness[cite: 17]; (ii) Whether the decision of the Adjudicating Authority ordering liquidation under Section 33(2) of the IBC based on the unanimous commercial wisdom of the CoC is amenable to judicial review under Sections 30(2) and 61(3)[cite: 17]; (iii) Whether the appellants' alleged ineligibility under Section 29A(b) of the IBC as wilful defaulters affects the validity of the CoC's liquidation decision[cite: 17].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 33(2) of the IBC read with its Explanation, the Committee of Creditors is empowered with wide statutory authority to resolve to liquidate a corporate debtor at any time after its constitution under Section 21(1) and before the confirmation of a resolution plan, including at its very first meeting and prior to the preparation of an information memorandum, valuation of assets, or issuance of an Expression of Interest (Form-G)[cite: 17]. The commercial wisdom of the CoC exercised with the requisite statutory majority (at least 66%) to liquidate a defunct and unviable corporate debtor is non-justiciable and cannot be subjected to judicial review by the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal absent patent material irregularity under Section 61(3)[cite: 17]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The Explanation to Section 33(2), inserted by Act 26 of 2019, codifies the legislative intent that the CoC is not mandated to undergo the entire resolution process or issue invitations for expression of interest where it concludes that revival is commercially unfeasible[cite: 17]. When the Resolution Professional intimates a liquidation decision approved by the requisite majority, Section 33(2) mandates that the Adjudicating Authority 'shall' pass a liquidation order[cite: 17]. Subjective hesitation or procedural notes expressed by the Interim Resolution Professional cannot override the supremacy of the CoC's collective commercial decision[cite: 17]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed the minutes and deliberations of the 1st CoC meeting, verifying that the corporate debtor had been completely non-functional since 2016, possessed no proprietary technology or active revenue-generating contracts, faced massive financial claims of Rs. 1,288 Crores against an estimated liquidation value of roughly Rs. 15 Crores, and that associated group companies had failed to attract any resolution applicants[cite: 17]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that the unanimous (100%) recommendation of the CoC to liquidate the Corporate Debtor was a lawful, bona fide exercise of commercial wisdom free from material irregularity or arbitrariness, and the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in passing the liquidation order under Section 33(2), warranting dismissal of the appeal[cite: 17].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 29 of 2024 is dismissed without costs[cite: 17]. The impugned order dated 03.10.2023 passed by the National Company Law Tribunal, Ahmedabad Bench in I.A. No. 769 (AHM) 2021 in Company Petition (IB) No. 59 of 2019 ordering the liquidation of M/s Doshion Private Limited is affirmed[cite: 17].
summary: Suspended directors of corporate debtor Doshion Private Limited appealed an NCLT Ahmedabad Bench order admitting the company into liquidation under Section 33(2) of the IBC[cite: 17]. The appellants contended that the Committee of Creditors acted arbitrarily by resolving to liquidate the company in its very first meeting without issuing an Expression of Interest, appointing valuers, or entertaining their MSME revival proposal[cite: 17]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that under Section 33(2) and its Explanation, the CoC possesses wide statutory discretion to resolve to liquidate a corporate debtor at any stage prior to plan approval[cite: 17]. Given the company's shutdown since 2016 and overwhelming debt, the unanimous liquidation decision reflected valid, non-justiciable commercial wisdom[cite: 17].

case_title: Gokul Kripa Colonizers and Developers Private Limited vs. Radiant Hotels Private Limited
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant/Applicant is Gokul Kripa Colonizers and Developers Private Limited (claiming status as Financial Creditor/Allottee)[cite: 18]. The Respondent/Corporate Debtor is Radiant Hotels Private Limited (Landowner/Promoter)[cite: 18]. A sister entity involved in development is Gokul Kripa Pvt. Buildtech[cite: 18]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Respondent owned land totaling 73,585 sq. m. in Village Sanganer and Khokhawas, Jaipur, earmarked by the Jaipur Development Authority (JDA) for group housing/plotting schemes[cite: 18]. On 28.02.2019, the parties entered into a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) wherein the Respondent agreed to sell 36,402 sq. m. at Rs. 21,000 per sq. yd. for a total consideration of Rs. 91,42,94,850/-, with an advance payment of Rs. 7.51 Crores[cite: 18, 18]. Following JDA layout map approval, the parties executed an Agreement to Sale dated 14.10.2019 for 36,399.38 sq. m. comprising the residential scheme 'The Royal Avenue' (155 residential plots measuring 19,397.53 sq. m. and 16 retail commercial shops measuring 148.80 sq. m.) for a revised sale consideration of Rs. 92,91,99,184/-, acknowledging Rs. 23,22,99,796/- (25%) received as security deposit[cite: 18, 18]. The contracts authorized the Appellant to market and book plots to prospective third-party buyers/nominees at any price, treating excess collections as Appellant's commission while adjusting deficits against the security deposit[cite: 18, 18]. A supplementary agreement was executed on 10.07.2020[cite: 18]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant claimed a default of Rs. 13,48,07,556/- in Part-IV of Form-1, alleging this was the balance excess amount collected by the Respondent (out of Rs. 33,96,45,071/- received from plot buyers, only Rs. 20,38,37,501/- was refunded or adjusted to the Appellant)[cite: 18, 18]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The MoU was signed on 28.02.2019; Agreement to Sale on 14.10.2019; and Supplementary Agreement on 10.07.2020[cite: 18]. The Appellant filed Section 7 application CP(IB)-849/MB/2019 on 29.07.2021 before NCLT Mumbai Bench[cite: 18]. NCLT dismissed the application on 21.04.2022[cite: 18]. The Appellant filed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 837 of 2022 under Section 61 before NCLAT[cite: 18]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Documentary records comprised: (i) MoU dated 28.02.2019 and Agreement to Sale dated 14.10.2019 containing clauses defining parties as seller and purchaser, stipulating plot booking rights, commission payouts, and 18% per annum delay interest[cite: 18, 18]; (ii) Supplementary Agreement dated 10.07.2020[cite: 18]; (iii) RERA registration certificates[cite: 18]; (iv) RERA Authority order dated 18.07.2022 (which was stayed by the Real Estate Appellate Tribunal on 02.09.2022)[cite: 18]; and (v) ledger accounts and banking transaction entries showing plot leases issued directly to third-party nominees rather than the Appellant[cite: 18]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench Court No. 5 dismissed CP(IB)-849/MB/2019 on 21.04.2022, holding that the arrangement was an ordinary commercial marketing and promoting agreement and that the payment obligations could not be construed as financial debt or allottee claims under Section 5(8)[cite: 18]. The Appellant appealed the dismissal order to the NCLAT Principal Bench[cite: 18].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a contractual arrangement for marketing, promoting, and booking plots under an agreement to sell, where collections exceeding an agreed base price are treated as commission, constitutes a 'financial debt' disbursed against consideration for the time value of money under Section 5(8) and Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC[cite: 18]; (ii) Whether the Appellant qualifies as an 'allottee' of a real estate project under Section 2(d) of RERA and Explanation (ii) to Section 5(8) of the IBC[cite: 18]; (iii) Whether an application under Section 7 of the IBC filed by a single real estate claimant without meeting the mandatory threshold of 100 allottees or 10% of total allottees under the second proviso to Section 7(1) is maintainable[cite: 18].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: To constitute a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC, a transaction must involve a disbursal of money against consideration for the time value of money[cite: 18]. A commercial transaction for the purchase, promotion, and marketing of real estate plots where the applicant acts as an intermediary procuring third-party buyers in exchange for commissions or price differentials does not constitute financial borrowing or financial debt[cite: 18]. Furthermore, any application under Section 7 of the IBC founded on real estate allottee status must strictly comply with the minimum numerical threshold under the second proviso to Section 7(1) by being filed jointly by not less than 100 allottees or 10% of the allottees in the project[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8)(f) read with Explanation (ii) adopts the definition of 'allottee' and 'real estate project' from Sections 2(d) and 2(zn) of the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016[cite: 18]. However, the second proviso to Section 7(1) of the IBC, introduced via Act 1 of 2020, establishes a mandatory statutory condition precedent: allottees can only initiate CIRP jointly with at least 100 allottees or 10% of total allottees in the project[cite: 18]. An individual commercial intermediary cannot circumvent Section 7(1) threshold restrictions by adopting an allottee label on appeal[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the terms of the MoU dated 28.02.2019 and Agreement to Sale dated 14.10.2019[cite: 18]. The clauses established that plots were not allotted to the Appellant for personal occupation or ownership; instead, allotments and leases were issued directly by the landowner to third-party purchasers nominated by the Appellant, with the Appellant receiving excess proceeds as sales commission and bearing deficits via deductions from security deposits[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The claimed debt of Rs. 13.48 Crores represented unrefunded excess sale realization and commission arising from a commercial sales arrangement rather than a financial borrowing[cite: 18]. Moreover, even if allottee status were assumed, the Section 7 petition was fundamentally non-maintainable for total non-compliance with the numerical threshold mandated under the second proviso to Section 7(1)[cite: 18].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 837 of 2022 is dismissed without costs, affirming the order dated 21.04.2022 passed by the National Company Law Tribunal, Court No. 5, Mumbai Bench in CP(IB)-849/MB/2019 rejecting the Section 7 application[cite: 18].
summary: Appellant Gokul Kripa Colonizers and Developers Private Limited appealed an NCLT Mumbai Bench order rejecting its Section 7 application against Radiant Hotels Private Limited[cite: 18]. The appellant claimed a financial debt of Rs. 13.48 Crores representing unrefunded excess sale consideration and commission under an agreement to market and sell plots in a residential scheme[cite: 18]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that the arrangement was essentially a commercial sale, promotion, and marketing contract, which lacked the essential element of disbursal against the time value of money under Section 5(8)(f)[cite: 18]. Furthermore, even if considered an allottee, the appellant failed to satisfy the mandatory threshold of 100 allottees or 10% under Section 7(1), rendering the petition non-maintainable[cite: 18].

case_title: M/s Laxmi Trading Corporation vs. M/s Hindustan Construction Company Limited
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Operational Creditor is M/s Laxmi Trading Corporation (LTC)[cite: 19]. The Corporate Debtor is M/s Hindustan Construction Company Limited (HCCL), an infrastructure, real estate, urban development, and construction enterprise[cite: 19]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: LTC supplied hardware tools, rubber goods, pipes, fittings, and related equipment to HCCL pursuant to multiple purchase orders issued between 2010 and 2019 across six distinct infrastructure projects: Kashang Hydro Electric Project, T-48 Ram Ban, Peerpanjal Tunnel VA Rail Project, Pipalkoti Project, Uri Project, and T-49A[cite: 19]. LTC raised 234 invoices totaling Rs. 3,71,55,764.80[cite: 19]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: HCCL made partial payments on running account and project-specific accounts amounting to Rs. 2,17,47,092.13, leaving an unpaid principal balance of Rs. 1,54,08,672.77[cite: 19]. In its Section 9 demand notice and petition, LTC claimed a total default of Rs. 3,73,32,239.30 (including 24% p.a. interest up to 29.02.2020)[cite: 19]. Out of 234 invoices, 224 invoices aggregating to Rs. 1,44,03,646 matured between 2012 and 2014, whereas only 10 invoices aggregating to Rs. 9,98,244 (pertaining to Pipalkoti Project) matured between 14.12.2017 and 10.04.2019[cite: 19]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: LTC sent payment demand emails on 14.07.2017, 07.01.2019, and 26.01.2019[cite: 19]. Partial payments of Rs. 3,00,000 and Rs. 2,00,000 were made on 30.10.2019 and 03.08.2021[cite: 19]. LTC issued a Section 8 demand notice under Rule 5 on 17.03.2020[cite: 19]. HCCL failed to reply[cite: 19]. LTC filed Company Petition (IB) No. 147/MB-IV/2021 under Section 9 on 25.02.2021[cite: 19]. NCLT Mumbai dismissed the petition on 25.08.2023[cite: 19]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Relevant documentary evidence comprised: (i) 234 project-specific purchase orders and invoices with 30-day payment stipulations[cite: 19]; (ii) project-wise ledger accounts maintained separately by LTC across pages 330–367[cite: 19]; (iii) email dated 13.08.2016 sharing a ledger showing Rs. 1,67,92,643 outstanding[cite: 19]; (iv) emails dated 14.07.2017, 10.11.2017, 07.01.2019, and 26.03.2019 demanding clearance[cite: 19]; and (v) bank transaction entries evidencing partial payments[cite: 19]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-IV dismissed Company Petition (IB) No. 147/MB-IV/2021 on 25.08.2023, ruling that 224 invoices were time-barred under Article 137 and the remaining 10 invoices (Rs. 9,98,244) failed to meet the Rs. 1 Crore threshold under Section 4[cite: 19]. LTC appealed to NCLAT Principal Bench under Section 61[cite: 19].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the period of limitation for initiating Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 9 of the IBC is governed by Article 1 of the Limitation Act, 1963 (mutual, open, and current running account) or Article 137 (residuary limitation running from the date default occurs on each invoice)[cite: 19]; (ii) Whether email exchanges and ledger transmissions sent after the expiration of the three-year limitation period constitute a valid acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963[cite: 19]; (iii) Whether a Section 9 application can be admitted when the legally enforceable claims within limitation fall below the Section 4 threshold of Rs. 1,00,00,000[cite: 19].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for initiation of Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 9 of the IBC is not a suit relating to accounts; therefore, Article 1 of the Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1963 is inapplicable, and the period of limitation is governed exclusively by Article 137[cite: 19]. The right to apply under Article 137 accrues on the date default occurs in respect of each individual invoice[cite: 19]. Furthermore, an acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act must be made in writing prior to the expiration of the prescribed three-year limitation period; an acknowledgment made after limitation has already expired cannot revive a time-barred debt[cite: 19]. Claims that are time-barred cannot be aggregated, and any legally subsisting balance within limitation must independently satisfy the statutory threshold of Rs. 1 Crore under Section 4 of the IBC[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238A of the IBC applies the provisions of the Limitation Act, 1963 to insolvency proceedings[cite: 19]. As affirmed in B.K. Educational Services and Babulal Vardharji Gurjar, the trigger for IBC proceedings is default, and the right to apply under Article 137 expires three years from the date the debt becomes due and payable[cite: 19]. Maintaining project-specific ledgers and allocating receipts to distinct projects precludes treating transactions as a consolidated running account under Article 1[cite: 19]. Section 18 operates only where an acknowledgment is made before limitation expires[cite: 19]. Section 4 establishes an absolute monetary jurisdictional threshold that must be met solely by legally enforceable, non-time-barred debts[cite: 19]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the 234 invoices across six different projects and the project-specific ledgers[cite: 19]. It found that for 224 invoices, payment was due within 30 days during 2012–2014, causing the three-year limitation period under Article 137 to expire by September 2018 at the latest[cite: 19]. The email exchanges relied upon by the appellant from July 2017, November 2017, and 2019 were transmitted long after limitation had expired for the respective project invoices, rendering Section 18 inapplicable[cite: 19]. Only 10 invoices totaling Rs. 9,98,244 were within limitation, falling well short of Rs. 1 Crore[cite: 19]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that 224 out of 234 invoices were ex-facie time-barred under Article 137, and the remaining 10 invoices within limitation were legally insufficient to satisfy the Section 4 threshold of Rs. 1 Crore, justifying dismissal of the Section 9 petition[cite: 19].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1476 of 2023 is dismissed without costs, affirming the order dated 25.08.2023 passed by the National Company Law Tribunal, Mumbai Bench in Company Petition (IB) No. 147/MB-IV/2021[cite: 19].
summary: M/s Laxmi Trading Corporation appealed an NCLT Mumbai Bench order dismissing its Section 9 IBC application against corporate debtor Hindustan Construction Company Limited[cite: 19]. The appellant claimed an operational debt of Rs. 1.54 Crores (plus interest) across 234 invoices for hardware goods supplied to six separate infrastructure projects, arguing the debt subsisted under a continuous running account governed by Article 1 of the Limitation Act, with limitation extended via emails[cite: 19]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that Section 9 applications are governed by Article 137, not Article 1, with limitation running from individual invoice default dates[cite: 19]. Because 224 invoices were time-barred and post-limitation emails failed Section 18, the remaining claims totaled only Rs. 9.98 Lakhs, failing Section 4’s one-crore threshold[cite: 19].

case_title: Amit Tyagi vs. M/s Indirapuram Habitat Centre Pvt. Ltd.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Amit Tyagi, an allottee of commercial space[cite: 20]. The Corporate Debtor is Indirapuram Habitat Centre Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 20]. The Respondent is Shri Narender Kumar Sharma, Resolution Professional (RP) of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 20]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor entered into Memorandums of Understanding (MoUs) with the Appellant (including MoU dated 08.06.2016) allotting commercial space, specifically Shop No. TW-14A (Ground Floor, Block A&B, super area 23.50 sq. m.)[cite: 20]. Under the MoU and its Annexure-A, the Corporate Debtor assured lease rent payouts to the Appellant until 27.01.2032[cite: 20]. The Appellant paid approximately 95% of the total unit cost prior to CIRP initiation[cite: 20]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by the Corporate Debtor occurred prior to CIRP when assured return/rent payouts ceased after June 2018 (over a year prior to CIRP commencement), prompting allottees to file cases under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act[cite: 20]. The Appellant sought release of pending and future monthly rent and execution of conveyance deeds upon payment of the remaining 5% balance[cite: 20]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced against the Corporate Debtor vide order dated 22.08.2019 in C.P. (IB) No. 1397/PB/2019[cite: 20]. Allottees filed IA Nos. 3492/2020 and 3314/2020 seeking registration of shops, which NCLT disposed of on 31.08.2020 directing verification of titles via forensic audit[cite: 20]. Appellant filed IA No. 4252/2020 and IA No. 4924/2021[cite: 20]. NCLT New Delhi Bench Court-II dismissed both IAs on 19.12.2023[cite: 20]. Appellant appealed to NCLAT under Section 61[cite: 20]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Documentary records comprised: (i) MoU dated 08.06.2016 with Annexure-A rental payout schedule[cite: 20]; (ii) proofs of payment establishing deposit of approximately 95% consideration[cite: 20]; (iii) forensic audit report commissioned by the RP to determine genuine ownership and title of commercial units[cite: 20]; (iv) NCLT order dated 31.08.2020[cite: 20]; and (v) bank records showing rental receipts collected from existing project lessees deposited into interest-bearing Fixed Deposit Receipts (FDRs) by the RP[cite: 20, 20]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench Court-II heard IA No. 4252/2020 and IA No. 4924/2021 filed by the Appellant and rejected both applications on 19.12.2023, refusing to direct execution of conveyance deeds during moratorium and holding that rental collections deposited in FDRs would be dealt with at the appropriate stage[cite: 20, 20]. The Appellant appealed the rejection to the NCLAT Principal Bench[cite: 20].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an allottee of a commercial unit who has paid 95% of consideration is entitled as a matter of right during CIRP to an order directing the Resolution Professional to execute a conveyance deed in respect of corporate debtor assets notwithstanding the statutory moratorium under Section 14(1)(b) of the IBC[cite: 20]; (ii) Whether the Resolution Professional is obligated during CIRP to honor pre-CIRP contractual assured return/lease rent arrangements and disburse ongoing rental collections directly to commercial space allottees rather than parking them in Fixed Deposit Receipts for collective resolution[cite: 20].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: During the subsistence of a Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process and the statutory moratorium imposed under Section 14(1)(b) of the IBC, allottees cannot claim mandatory execution of conveyance deeds or specific performance of pre-insolvency real estate contracts as an absolute legal right[cite: 20]. The Resolution Professional, vested with asset management and business powers under Sections 17, 18, and 25 of the IBC, retains exclusive administrative discretion over what contractual obligations can be executed while preserving the corporate debtor as a going concern[cite: 20]. Furthermore, pre-CIRP assured return or rental arrangements cannot be enforced against the RP during moratorium; parking third-party rental yields in interest-bearing fixed deposits pending final resolution fully protects stakeholder interests[cite: 20, 20]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(1)(b) prohibits transferring, encumbering, alienating, or disposing of any corporate debtor assets or legal/beneficial rights therein during CIRP[cite: 20]. A direction compelling an RP to execute a conveyance deed operates as an order for specific performance of contract, which encroaches on the statutory scheme of CIRP and the RP's custodial domain under Sections 18 and 25[cite: 20]. While homebuyer and allottee interests must be protected under the IBC, the manner and mode of protection are governed by the overall resolution framework and not by piecemeal property transfers or preferential cash outflows[cite: 20]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the prayers in IA No. 4252/2020 and IA No. 4924/2021, observing that conveyance deed execution was not specifically prayed for in the pleadings and that assured returns had already ceased since June 2018 prior to CIRP[cite: 20, 20]. It verified that current lessees occupied the premises at rates lower than the MoU figures and that the RP had safeguarded rental receipts in FDRs under tribunal oversight[cite: 20, 20]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in refusing to order execution of conveyance deeds during the Section 14 moratorium, and that parking rental proceeds in Fixed Deposit Receipts pending final CIRP adjudication adequately protected the Appellant's rights, warranting dismissal of the appeal[cite: 20].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 272 of 2024 is dismissed without costs, affirming the order dated 19.12.2023 passed by the National Company Law Tribunal, New Delhi Bench (Court-II) in IA No. 4252/2020 and IA No. 4924/2021[cite: 20].
summary: Appellant Amit Tyagi, a commercial space allottee in Indirapuram Habitat Centre Pvt. Ltd., appealed an NCLT New Delhi Bench order dismissing his applications seeking execution of a conveyance deed and release of monthly assured lease rentals under an MoU dated June 8, 2016[cite: 20]. The appellant contended that having paid 95% of the purchase price, he was entitled to registration of his unit and ongoing rent[cite: 20]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that allottees cannot enforce specific performance or demand execution of sale deeds during CIRP, as Section 14(1)(b) prohibits transferring corporate debtor assets[cite: 20]. Furthermore, the RP's action of depositing rental collections into fixed deposit accounts pending resolution adequately preserved stakeholder interests[cite: 20].

case_title: Piramal Capital & Housing Finance Ltd. vs. Hydric Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd.
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 851 of 2023 & Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 852 of 2023
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Financial Creditor/Appellant is Piramal Capital & Housing Finance Ltd. (merged into Dewan Housing Finance Corporation Limited [DHFL] pursuant to an approved resolution plan and subsequently renamed)[cite: 21]. The Corporate Debtor/Corporate Guarantor in the first appeal is Hydric Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 21], and in the second appeal is Hydric Town Planners Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 21]. The Principal Borrower is Crystal Facilities Management Pvt. Ltd. (CFMPL)[cite: 21]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Pursuant to a sanction letter dated 28.03.2018 and a Loan Agreement dated 29.03.2018 entered into between CFMPL and DHFL, a loan facility of Rs. 35 Crores was sanctioned and extended to CFMPL[cite: 21]. To secure repayment of the facility, the Corporate Debtors executed unconditional and irrevocable deeds of corporate guarantee on 29.03.2018 in favor of the lender[cite: 21]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: CFMPL and the Corporate Guarantors defaulted on their repayment obligations under the credit facility[cite: 21]. The alleged default amount claimed in the Section 7 application was Rs. 53,26,52,972/-[cite: 21]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Financial Creditor served a loan recall/demand notice on CFMPL and the corporate guarantors on 22.02.2020[cite: 21]. Failing payment, the Appellant filed a Section 7 application against the borrower CFMPL, which was admitted into CIRP on 19.01.2023 (and subsequently ordered into liquidation)[cite: 21]. Simultaneously, on 23.05.2022, the Appellant filed Section 7 applications against the corporate guarantors (IB-440/ND/2022 and IB-441/ND/2022)[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Documentary records included the sanction letter dated 28.03.2018, Loan Agreement dated 29.03.2018, unconditional and irrevocable corporate guarantee deeds dated 29.03.2018, default demand notices dated 22.02.2020, the NCLT Mumbai order dated 07.06.2021 approving Piramal's resolution plan for DHFL, and the RoC certificate of incorporation dated 03.11.2021 confirming the merger and name change[cite: 21]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT New Delhi Bench Court-IV dismissed the Section 7 applications against the corporate guarantors on 26.05.2023, relying on the NCLAT ruling in Dr. Vishnu Kumar Agarwal vs. Piramal Enterprises Ltd. to hold that an application cannot be maintained simultaneously against both the principal borrower and corporate guarantor for the same debt[cite: 21]. The Financial Creditor appealed both orders to the NCLAT Principal Bench under Section 61[cite: 21].
legal_issues: Whether an application filed by a Financial Creditor under Section 7 of the IBC is maintainable simultaneously against both the Principal Borrower and the Corporate Guarantor on the exact same set of debt and default[cite: 21].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A financial creditor is fully entitled to initiate and maintain Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) under Section 7 of the IBC simultaneously against both the principal borrower and the corporate guarantor for the same set of debt and default[cite: 21]. The statutory scheme of the IBC imposes no bar against concurrent or parallel proceedings against a borrower and a corporate guarantor[cite: 21]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the liability of a guarantor is co-extensive and co-terminous with that of the principal debtor[cite: 21]. When the principal borrower defaults, the guarantor incurs independent liability, and the default triggers the creditor's right of action under Section 3(8) and Section 3(12) of the IBC[cite: 21]. The earlier contrary interpretation in Dr. Vishnu Kumar Agarwal vs. Piramal Enterprises Ltd. has been superseded and is no longer good law in light of the Supreme Court's ruling in Laxmi Pat Surana vs. Union Bank of India and subsequent NCLAT rulings in State Bank of India vs. Athena Energy Ventures Pvt. Ltd. and Naresh Kumar Aggarwal vs. CFM Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 21]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified whether the Section 7 applications arose out of an invoked unconditional corporate guarantee where default occurred on the part of the principal borrower and whether the Adjudicating Authority dismissed the petitions solely on the invalid premise of bar against simultaneous filing[cite: 21]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that the dismissal of the Section 7 petitions against the corporate guarantors was patently illegal, as simultaneous CIRP proceedings against both principal borrower and corporate guarantor are maintainable on the same debt, warranting setting aside the impugned orders and remanding the applications for fresh adjudication[cite: 21].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 851 of 2023 and Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 852 of 2023 are allowed, and the impugned dismissal orders are set aside[cite: 21]. Original company petitions IB-440/ND/2022 and IB-441/ND/2022 are restored to the file of the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT New Delhi Bench) and remanded back to be decided afresh in accordance with law[cite: 21]. The parties are directed to appear before the Tribunal on 12.02.2024[cite: 21]. All pending interlocutory applications are disposed of[cite: 21].
summary: Piramal Capital & Housing Finance Ltd. appealed NCLT New Delhi Bench orders dismissing its Section 7 IBC applications against corporate guarantors Hydric Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. and Hydric Town Planners Pvt. Ltd. for a default of Rs. 53.26 Crores[cite: 21]. The NCLT had dismissed the petitions relying on Dr. Vishnu Kumar Agarwal, holding that simultaneous proceedings cannot lie against both the principal borrower and the corporate guarantor for the same debt[cite: 21]. Setting aside the dismissal, NCLAT held that following the Supreme Court's binding ruling in Laxmi Pat Surana, a financial creditor is entitled to proceed simultaneously against the principal borrower and corporate guarantors under Section 7[cite: 21]. The applications were restored and remanded for fresh adjudication[cite: 21].

case_title: Paradise Consumer Products Ltd. vs. J. Maheshkumar Petrochemicals Pvt. Ltd.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 901 of 2020 & Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 219 of 2022
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Corporate Debtor is Paradise Consumer Products Ltd. (Appellant in CA No. 901 of 2020, with Dr. Anjali Patil as Appellant in CA No. 219 of 2022)[cite: 22]. The Operational Creditor is J. Maheshkumar Petrochemicals Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent), acting as a Del Credere Agent of Reliance Industries Limited[cite: 22]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Reliance Industries Limited supplied goods to the Corporate Debtor through the Operational Creditor acting as Del Credere Agent[cite: 22]. The Operational Creditor made payments directly to Reliance Industries Limited in 2015 and sought to recover the corresponding sums from the Corporate Debtor against 10 specific invoices issued between 22.07.2014 and 09.09.2014[cite: 22]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The claimed default amount totaled Rs. 81,37,643.77 (comprising principal of Rs. 52,94,356 and interest of Rs. 28,43,287.77)[cite: 22]. The due dates for the 10 invoices spanned from 02.08.2014 to 20.09.2014, with the corresponding dates of default stated as 01.08.2014 to 19.09.2014[cite: 22]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Operational Creditor issued a Section 8 demand notice on 06.11.2018, to which the Corporate Debtor replied on 27.11.2018[cite: 22]. The Section 9 application, C.P. (IB) No. 476/MB.IV/2018, was filed on 13.12.2018[cite: 22]. NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV admitted the petition on 23.09.2020[cite: 22]. Corporate Debtor appealed under Section 61[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Relevant documentary evidence comprised: (i) 10 commercial invoices with payment due dates ending 20.09.2014[cite: 22]; (ii) a cheque dated 10.11.2015 for Rs. 65,54,884.87 issued by the Corporate Debtor[cite: 22]; (iii) cheque dishonour memo dated 18.12.2015[cite: 22]; (iv) judgment of the Metropolitan Magistrate, 33rd Court, Ballard Pier, Mumbai dismissing Section 138 NI Act complaint CC No. 1815/SS/2016 on grounds of forgery and fabrication (presently under appeal)[cite: 22]; and (v) ledger receipts showing payments made by the Operational Creditor to Reliance Industries Limited in 2015[cite: 22]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV admitted the Section 9 application on 23.09.2020 without limitation being contested by the Corporate Debtor in its reply[cite: 22]. The Corporate Debtor and its director appealed to NCLAT Principal Bench, raising the bar of limitation under Article 137 for the first time[cite: 22].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a plea of limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963 can be raised for the first time before the Appellate Tribunal under Section 61 of the IBC if it was omitted from the reply to the demand notice and the reply to the Section 9 application[cite: 22]; (ii) Whether an application under Section 9 filed on 13.12.2018 founded on invoices defaulting in August–September 2014 is barred by limitation, or whether payments to a third-party supplier in 2015 and a dishonoured cheque memo dated 18.12.2015 constitute mixed questions of fact and law requiring remand for trial and evidence[cite: 22].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 3 of the Limitation Act, 1963, a court or tribunal is bound to examine whether an action is instituted within the prescribed period of limitation even if limitation has not been set up as a defence in the pleadings, and such a plea can be validly raised for the first time at the appellate stage[cite: 22]. However, where determining whether the claim is barred by limitation involves mixed questions of fact and law—such as whether third-party payments or cheque dishonour memos renew or extend the cause of action—the matter cannot be summarily decided on appeal without providing both parties an opportunity to lead evidence before the adjudicating authority[cite: 22]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3 of the Limitation Act imposes a mandatory statutory duty that overrides procedural waiver, allowing a party to plead limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963 in an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC[cite: 22]. An application under Section 9 must be filed within three years from the date default occurred[cite: 22]. However, whether events such as del credere payments in 2015 or a cheque memo dated 18.12.2015 trigger Section 18 acknowledgments or alter the accrual of the right to apply constitutes a mixed question of fact and law[cite: 22]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed the default dates across the 10 invoices (ending 19.09.2014) against the petition filing date (13.12.2018)[cite: 22]. It considered the respondent's potential evidentiary grounds (cheque dated 10.11.2015, dishonour memo dated 18.12.2015, and payments made to Reliance Industries Limited in 2015) and noted that because limitation was not pleaded below, the creditor was deprived of the opportunity to produce necessary rebuttal documents and records[cite: 22]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that since limitation is a mixed question of fact and law requiring evidentiary substantiation, it was just and expedient to set aside the admission order and remand the proceedings to the Adjudicating Authority to decide limitation afresh after affording both parties full opportunity to lead evidence[cite: 22].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 901 of 2020 is allowed and the impugned admission order dated 23.09.2020 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV in C.P. (IB) No. 476/MB.IV/2018 is set aside[cite: 22]. The case is remanded back to the Tribunal to decide the question of limitation afresh by affording both parties an opportunity to lead evidence in support of their respective cases, directing the parties to appear before the Tribunal on 26.02.2024[cite: 22]. Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 219 of 2022 is dismissed as infructuous[cite: 22].
summary: Corporate debtor Paradise Consumer Products Ltd. appealed an NCLT Mumbai Bench order admitting an operational debt claim of Rs. 81.37 Lakhs filed by del credere agent J. Maheshkumar Petrochemicals Pvt. Ltd. under Section 9 of the IBC[cite: 22]. The appellant argued for the first time on appeal that the petition filed on 13.12.2018 was time-barred under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, as defaults on the 10 invoices occurred in August–September 2014[cite: 22]. Setting aside the admission order, NCLAT held that under Section 3 of the Limitation Act, limitation can be raised on appeal; however, because limitation involves mixed questions of fact and law concerning 2015 del credere payments and cheque dishonour records, the matter was remanded to NCLT for fresh evidentiary determination[cite: 22].

case_title: Mayank Goyal vs. G. Madhusudhan Rao & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 147 & 148 of 2024 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 182 of 2024
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Corporate Debtor is Bil Energy Systems Limited, formerly engaged in manufacturing transformers for electricity generation[cite: 24]. The Appellants are Mayuk Goyal, a Prospective Resolution Applicant (PRA) who submitted an Expression of Interest (CA No. 147-148 of 2024), and Suresh More (CA No. 182 of 2024)[cite: 24]. Respondent No. 1 is G. Madhusudhan Rao, Resolution Professional (RP)[cite: 24]. Respondent No. 2 is State Bank of India (SBI), the sole member of the Committee of Creditors (CoC) with 100% voting share[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: SBI extended credit facilities to the Corporate Debtor, secured by a mortgage over its manufacturing factory land and hypothecation of plant and machinery situated at Wada, Palghar, Maharashtra[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose from unpaid credit facilities owed to SBI, which prompted SBI to initiate Section 7 insolvency proceedings after unsuccessful attempts to recover possession of secured assets under the SARFAESI Act[cite: 24]. The Corporate Debtor had completely ceased business operations since 2020 (over three years prior to the insolvency commencement date) and had no active business, cash flows, or demarcated possession of factory premises[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: On 09.12.2022, NCLT Mumbai admitted SBI's Section 7 petition CP (IB) 4058 (MB) of 2019 against the Corporate Debtor[cite: 24]. The IRP was replaced by RP G. Madhusudhan Rao in the 3rd CoC meeting with 100% voting share[cite: 24]. Form-G was published on 23.03.2023, attracting three EOIs including from Mayank Goyal[cite: 24]. In its 5th meeting on 03.06.2023, the CoC resolved with 100% voting to liquidate the Corporate Debtor[cite: 24]. The RP filed liquidation application IA No. 2947 of 2023, while Mayank Goyal filed IA No. 2825 of 2023 to set aside the liquidation resolution[cite: 24]. NCLT allowed liquidation and dismissed the PRA's application on 04.12.2023[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Relevant documentary record comprised: (i) Minutes of the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, and 5th CoC meetings establishing that the Corporate Debtor was defunct for three years prior to CIRP, that its registered office operated from rented premises, that plant and machinery had been sold off by suspended management in 2015 without bank permission, that land at Wada lacked clear demarcation from adjoining entity Aesthetic Stampings and Laminations Ltd., and that neither SBI nor the RP obtained actual custody of physical assets[cite: 24]; (ii) BSE annual reports for FY 2020-21 showing abnormal asset write-offs[cite: 24]; (iii) 7/12 land revenue extracts[cite: 24]; (iv) Palghar District Magistrate SARFAESI possession order dated 19.08.2015[cite: 24]; and (v) 100% affirmative e-voting records approving liquidation under Section 33(2)[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-II by common order dated 04.12.2023 allowed IA No. 2947 of 2023 ordering liquidation under Section 33(2) and dismissed IA No. 2825 of 2023 filed by Mayank Goyal[cite: 24]. The Appellants appealed under Section 61, contending that the liquidation decision was arbitrary and taken in haste without issuing the Information Memorandum or evaluating resolution plans from PRAs[cite: 24].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the Committee of Creditors has statutory authority under Section 33(2) of the IBC read with its Explanation to resolve to liquidate a Corporate Debtor before issuing the Information Memorandum, Request for Resolution Plans (RFRP), or considering resolution plans from prospective resolution applicants[cite: 24]; (ii) Whether the commercial decision of the CoC to liquidate a corporate debtor that has been non-operational for three years and lacks custody or clear title of physical assets is tainted with material irregularity or arbitrariness amenable to judicial review[cite: 24]; (iii) Whether a Prospective Resolution Applicant has locus standi to assail the commercial wisdom of the CoC in approving liquidation under Section 61(4) of the IBC absent fraud or material irregularity[cite: 24].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 33(2) of the IBC read with the Explanation inserted by Act 26 of 2019, the Committee of Creditors is vested with wide statutory power to resolve to liquidate a corporate debtor at any time during the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process prior to the confirmation of a resolution plan, including before the preparation of the Information Memorandum, issuance of RFRP, or consideration of prospective resolution plans[cite: 24]. The commercial wisdom of the CoC in resolving to liquidate an unviable, non-operational corporate debtor possessing negligible traceable assets is non-justiciable, and an appeal under Section 61(4) against a liquidation order under Section 33 can be entertained solely on established grounds of fraud or material irregularity[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory expression 'any time' occurring in Section 33(2) and reiterated in its Explanation unambiguously establishes that the CoC is not statutorily mandated to complete the full resolution cycle or entertain resolution bids if it determines that revival is impossible[cite: 24]. Once the CoC approves liquidation by not less than sixty-six percent of voting share, Section 33(2) mandates that the Adjudicating Authority 'shall' pass a liquidation order[cite: 24]. Judicial review over such a decision is strictly limited; where a corporate debtor has ceased operations for years prior to insolvency and lacks physical custody of identifiable assets, prolonging the CIRP merely escalates administrative costs without corresponding benefit[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the minutes across five CoC meetings, verifying that the Corporate Debtor had been shut down since 2020, its registered office was situated on leased premises, its plant and machinery were alienated in 2015 without bank consent, its Wada property lacked demarcation and remained inaccessible, and suspended management failed to hand over physical assets or account books[cite: 24]. These unrefuted operational facts justified the CoC's business determination that the Corporate Debtor was incapable of revival[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that the unanimous (100%) recommendation of the sole-member CoC to liquidate the Corporate Debtor was a valid exercise of commercial wisdom, devoid of material irregularity, fraud, or statutory violation, and the Adjudicating Authority committed no legal error in passing the liquidation order under Section 33(2)[cite: 24].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 147 & 148 of 2024 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 182 of 2024 are dismissed on their merits without costs, affirming the common impugned order dated 04.12.2023 passed by the National Company Law Tribunal, Mumbai Bench (Court-II) in IA No. 2947 of 2023 and IA No. 2825 of 2023 in CP (IB) 4058 (MB) of 2019 ordering the liquidation of Bil Energy Systems Limited[cite: 24].
summary: Appellants Mayank Goyal (a Prospective Resolution Applicant) and Suresh More challenged an NCLT Mumbai Bench order allowing the Resolution Professional's application to liquidate Bil Energy Systems Limited under Section 33(2) of the IBC and dismissing the PRA's challenge to the CoC's liquidation decision[cite: 24]. The appellants contended that the decision to liquidate was premature and arbitrary as Form-G had been published and EOIs submitted[cite: 24]. Dismissing both appeals, NCLAT held that under Section 33(2) and its Explanation, the Committee of Creditors possesses unfettered authority to approve liquidation at any time prior to plan approval[cite: 24]. Given that the debtor had been non-functional for three years and lacked identifiable assets, the 100% CoC decision was a valid exercise of non-justiciable commercial wisdom[cite: 24].

case_title: Jaitnder Pal Singh Hanjra vs. Vivek Raheja, Resolution Professional & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1611 of 2023 & I.A. No. 171 of 2024
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Jaitnder Pal Singh Hanjra (Successful Resolution Applicant / Prospective Resolution Applicant), represented by Authorized Representative Ajay Nagpal[cite: 25]. Respondent No. 1 is Vivek Raheja, Resolution Professional (RP) of Corporate Debtor J.P. Engineers Private Limited[cite: 25]. Respondents No. 2 to 5 are Financial Creditors comprising Union Bank of India (84.90%), Axis Bank (6.48%), ICICI Bank (6.18%), and Yes Bank (2.44%)[cite: 25]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor J.P. Engineers Private Limited was admitted into CIRP on 26.02.2020 upon an application filed by an Operational Creditor under Section 9 of the IBC[cite: 25]. The RP issued Form-G on five separate occasions inviting Expressions of Interest (EOIs) for submission of resolution plans[cite: 25]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose from unpaid operational debts. Three resolution plans were received in response to earlier Form-G publications, but all were rejected by the Committee of Creditors (CoC) in its 20th and 21st meetings because their values fell below the liquidation value, prompting the RP to file a liquidation application (I.A. No. 3199 of 2022)[cite: 25]. The appellant subsequently submitted a resolution plan offering Rs. 19.50 Crores, which significantly exceeded the values offered by earlier prospective resolution applicants[cite: 25]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 26.02.2020[cite: 25]. The statutory 330-day CIRP period expired on 18.06.2022[cite: 25]. On 09.01.2023, the Appellant submitted an EOI, followed by I.A. No. 228 of 2023, which NCLT allowed on 16.01.2023 permitting plan submission[cite: 25]. NCLT recalled this order on 08.02.2023, but NCLAT set aside the recall on 25.04.2023 and permitted consideration of the Appellant's plan[cite: 25]. The CoC deliberated the plan in its 23rd meeting (12.05.2023) and 26th meeting (23.08.2023), passing a resolution with 97.56% majority seeking a 60-day CIRP extension (I.A. No. 3016 of 2023) and deciding against publishing a fresh Form-G[cite: 25]. NCLT passed the impugned order on 30.11.2023 extending CIRP by 60 days while suo motu directing fresh Form-G publication[cite: 25]. 5.
