FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Documentary records comprised: (i) NCLAT order dated 25.04.2023 allowing consideration of the Appellant's plan[cite: 25]; (ii) minutes of the 23rd (12.05.2023) and 26th (23.08.2023) CoC meetings recording 97.56% affirmative votes to extend CIRP by 60 days and expressly rejecting fresh Form-G publication as a time-consuming redundancy; (iii) comparative evaluation table showing the Appellant's plan value (Rs. 19.50 Crores) outperforming all prior PRAs (Pankaj Saraogi: Rs. 7.00 Cr; Anuj Goyal: Rs. 11.05 Cr; Vickey Gupta: Rs. 14.55 Cr; Ranjana Saraogi: Rs. 18.50 Cr)[cite: 25]; and (iv) CoC resolution withdrawing liquidation application I.A. No. 3199 of 2022[cite: 25]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench Court-II on 30.11.2023 disposed of I.A. No. 3016 of 2023 by granting a 60-day CIRP extension but suo motu ordering the RP to publish a fresh Form-G to invite competing EOIs[cite: 25]. The Appellant appealed the Form-G directive to NCLAT under Section 61[cite: 25].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority is justified in suo motu directing the issuance of a fresh Form-G to invite new Expressions of Interest while granting a 60-day CIRP extension, notwithstanding the conscious, reasoned business decision of the Committee of Creditors passed with a 97.56% majority not to issue fresh Form-G and to consider solely the resolution plan of the Appellant[cite: 25].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in deciding whether or not to re-run the CIRP process by publishing a fresh Form-G is paramount, non-justiciable, and entitled to absolute judicial deference, provided it aligns with the twin objectives of timely resolution and asset maximization[cite: 25]. Where the CoC has considered multiple rounds of Form-G, evaluated competing plans, and in its commercial wisdom explicitly resolved with an overwhelming majority (97.56%) against issuing a fresh Form-G so as to avoid endless delays and consider an enhanced resolution plan, the Adjudicating Authority cannot suo motu mandate the republication of Form-G[cite: 25]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The overarching objective of the IBC is to achieve time-bound insolvency resolution and asset maximization[cite: 25]. While asset maximization is vital, it must operate within strict statutory timelines and the collective commercial assessment of financial creditors[cite: 25]. The Adjudicating Authority's power to grant an extension of CIRP under Section 12 does not empower it to thrust procedural steps upon the CoC that the CoC has consciously and deliberately rejected in the exercise of its commercial wisdom[cite: 25]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that Form-G had already been issued on five prior occasions without yielding a viable plan, that the statutory 330-day timeline had expired, that the CoC deliberated upon and compared all available plan values across 23rd and 26th meetings, and that the CoC specifically recorded that publishing a fresh Form-G would consume at least three additional months, impair the corporate debtor's value, and risk the withdrawal of the higher-value plan submitted by the Appellant[cite: 25]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed a legal error by overriding the CoC's commercial decision against issuing fresh Form-G; consequently, the Form-G directive was set aside while the 60-day CIRP extension and direction to vote on the appellant's plan were affirmed[cite: 25].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1611 of 2023 is allowed[cite: 25]. That part of the impugned order dated 30.11.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority directing the Resolution Professional to issue a fresh Form-G is set aside[cite: 25]. That part of the impugned order granting a 60-day extension of the CIRP period is affirmed[cite: 25]. The Resolution Professional is directed to place the resolution plan of the Appellant before the Committee of Creditors for consideration and voting and to complete the CIRP within the extended period[cite: 25]. I.A. No. 171 of 2024 is disposed of accordingly[cite: 25]. Parties shall bear their own costs[cite: 25].
summary: PRA Jaitnder Pal Singh Hanjra appealed an NCLT New Delhi order granting a 60-day CIRP extension for J.P. Engineers Private Limited but suo motu directing the Resolution Professional to issue a fresh Form-G[cite: 25]. The appellant contended that the CoC had already considered five rounds of Form-G, rejected prior plans, and consciously resolved with a 97.56% majority not to publish fresh Form-G but to vote solely on the appellant's enhanced resolution plan of Rs. 19.50 Crores[cite: 25]. Allowing the appeal, NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority cannot override the commercial wisdom of the CoC by forcing a fresh Form-G rollout when the CoC has validly decided against it to prevent undue delay[cite: 25]. The Form-G directive was struck down, and the RP was directed to put the appellant's plan to vote within the extended timeframe[cite: 25].

case_title: Board of Trustees for Shyama Prasad Mookerjee Port, Kolkata vs. Sanjai Kumar Gupta & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is the Board of Trustees for Shyama Prasad Mookerjee Port, Kolkata (an Operational Creditor and landowner/lessor)[cite: 17]. Respondent No. 1 is Sanjai Kumar Gupta, erstwhile Resolution Professional of Stone India Limited[cite: 17]. Respondent No. 2 is Jupiter Wagons Limited, the Successful Resolution Applicant[cite: 17]. The Corporate Debtor is Stone India Limited[cite: 17]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant originally leased and licensed land parcels (Plate A, Plate B, and Plate C) between 1947 and 1987[cite: 17]. The Corporate Debtor (Stone India Ltd.) held leasehold and residuary interests in Plates A and B as an assignee and occupied Plate C under license[cite: 17]. Disputes arose regarding rent rates and eviction, leading to litigation before the Calcutta High Court and the Supreme Court[cite: 17]. The Supreme Court remanded the matter on 07.12.2009 (CA No. 5158 of 2005) directing the Corporate Debtor to pay Rs. 2 Lakhs per month, and the Calcutta High Court granted an interim stay against eviction on 11.12.2009, later revising the rent to Rs. 11,97,144/- per month on 19.07.2013[cite: 17]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) commenced against the Corporate Debtor on 09.11.2021[cite: 17]. The Appellant filed an operational claim of Rs. 98,39,70,929.51/- as occupational charges, out of which the RP partly admitted Rs. 12,86,73,543.20/-[cite: 17]. The approved resolution plan allocated Rs. 42,37,569/- to the Appellant[cite: 17]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 09.11.2021[cite: 17]. The Adjudicating Authority approved the resolution plan on 08.06.2023 via IA No. 1335/KB/2022[cite: 17]. The Appellant filed the present appeal under Section 61 of the IBC[cite: 17]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Relevant record evidence included lease and assignment deeds from 1947–1987; Supreme Court order dated 07.12.2009; Calcutta High Court interim orders and rent redetermination order dated 19.07.2013; and the resolution plan approved with 100% CoC vote share (comprising Indian Overseas Bank, ICICI Bank, and State Bank of India)[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Kolkata Bench Court-I approved the resolution plan on 08.06.2023[cite: 17]. The Appellant challenged the approval order before the NCLAT, raising issues regarding unauthorized occupation, pending eviction/title disputes, and the meagre payout under the plan[cite: 17].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in approving a resolution plan that allocated a meagre sum of Rs. 42.37 Lakhs to the Appellant operational creditor against its substantial admitted claim[cite: 17]; (ii) Whether land held under leasehold by the Corporate Debtor subject to pending eviction proceedings and title disputes before the High Court could lawfully be included in the CIRP asset pool[cite: 17].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 30(2) of the IBC, an operational creditor is entitled to receive an amount not less than the liquidation value[cite: 17]. The distribution of funds among creditors is a commercial decision falling squarely within the non-justiciable domain of the Committee of Creditors (CoC) commercial wisdom, and an operational creditor cannot challenge an approved resolution plan merely on the ground of receiving a smaller allocation relative to its total claim[cite: 17]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Approval of a resolution plan operates only to transfer the leasehold rights and existing interests actually possessed by the corporate debtor[cite: 17]. It does not adjudicate upon, extinguish, or prejudicially affect independent title, lease expiration, or eviction proceedings pending before competent courts or tribunals, leaving parties free to pursue their respective rights outside the CIRP framework[cite: 17]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the operational creditor's claim was verified and partly admitted by the RP based on rent redetermined by the High Court (Rs. 11,97,144 per month), that the payout exceeded the statutory liquidation floor under Section 30(2), and that the plan received 100% CoC approval[cite: 17]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that no statutory violation vitiated the plan approval, but clarified that the resolution plan's operation is strictly confined to the corporate debtor's existing leasehold rights, leaving all pending proceedings before the Calcutta High Court unaffected[cite: 17].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1009 of 2023 is dismissed, affirming the order dated 08.06.2023 passed by the NCLT Kolkata Bench in IA No. 1335/KB/2022 approving the Resolution Plan[cite: 17]. It is clarified that the approval of the resolution plan shall have no effect on the determination of rights pending before the Calcutta High Court and other forums, and parties shall abide by the final decisions in those proceedings[cite: 17].
summary: The Board of Trustees for Shyama Prasad Mookerjee Port, Kolkata, appealed an NCLT Kolkata Bench order approving the resolution plan for Stone India Limited[cite: 17]. The appellant, an operational creditor and lessor of land parcels Plate A and Plate B, contested the meagre allocation of Rs. 42.37 Lakhs against its operational claim and disputed the corporate debtor's continued possession amidst pending eviction litigation[cite: 17]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that financial allocations approved by a 100% CoC majority fall within non-justiciable commercial wisdom as long as Section 30(2) is satisfied[cite: 17]. NCLAT clarified that the resolution plan transfers only the corporate debtor's existing leasehold rights and does not prejudice ongoing title and eviction proceedings before the Calcutta High Court[cite: 17].

case_title: Veena Ramanathapura Sreenivasarangan & Anr. vs. Amruthamgamaya Nature Care and Leisure Private Limited & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 101 of 2022 & I.A. Nos. 854 of 2022 & 146, 1326 of 2023
bench: Chennai Bench (Appellate Jurisdiction)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants (Original Respondents in CP) are Veena Ramanathapura Sreenivasarangan (Appellant No. 1) and Iyer Sudhakar Jayaram (Appellant No. 2). Respondent No. 1 is Amruthamgamaya Nature Care and Leisure Private Limited. Respondents No. 2 and 3 (Ajith Nagappan Nair Radhamony and Gayatri Padmakumari Sukumaran) are the original petitioners before the NCLT. Respondent No. 6 is Ms. Sarah Judith Tamara Cohen (co-founder who brought foreign direct investment and transferred shares to appellants). Other respondents include company secretaries, chartered accountants, and former auditors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Respondent No. 1 Company was founded in 2006 by Ajith Nagappan Nair Radhamony and Sarah Judith Tamara Cohen, with R-6 bringing in FDI across tranches and later transferring her shares to the Appellants. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The dispute involved allegations of financial irregularities, accounting fraud, misstatement of accounts under Sections 129 and 134, and wrongful classification of funds as 'Loan from Directors' during the financial years 2015-16, 2016-17, and 2017-18. The original applicants held a 19.18% equity stake, satisfying the maintainability threshold under Section 241. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Ajith Nagappan Nair Radhamony and Gayatri Padmakumari Sukumaran filed CP/127(KOB)/2019 under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 before NCLT Kochi Bench[cite: 18]. NCLT Kochi passed the interim impugned order on 08.06.2022[cite: 18]. Appellants filed Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 101 of 2022 before NCLAT Chennai[cite: 18]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Documentary records comprised: (i) Audited Financial Statements and notes to Balance Sheets for FY 2015-16, 2016-17, and 2017-18 reflecting 'Loan from Directors'; (ii) company records showing FDI tranches brought in by foreign national Sarah Judith Tamara Cohen and subsequent share transfers; and (iii) pleadings detailing mutual allegations of fabrication, siphoning, and accounting errors. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kochi Bench held the company petition maintainable (19.18% shareholding) and on 08.06.2022 passed an interim order under Section 242(4) read with Rule 11, appointing Shri Rajmohan R as an Independent Auditor to conduct an investigative audit of accounts for FY 2015-16, 2016-17, and 2017-18[cite: 18]. Appellants challenged this interim order before NCLAT Chennai[cite: 18].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the National Company Law Tribunal has the power under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 or Section 242(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 to direct an independent investigative audit of company accounts without first recording a definitive finding of 'Oppression and Mismanagement' or fraud; (ii) Whether an interim order appointing an independent auditor amounts to an impermissible fishing and roving expedition.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Rule 11 of the National Company Law Tribunal Rules, 2016 read with Section 242(4) of the Companies Act, 2013, the Tribunal possesses wide inherent powers and discretionary jurisdiction to issue interim orders—including the appointment of an independent chartered accountant to conduct an investigative audit or forensic review of accounts—to regulate the conduct of a company's affairs, meet the ends of justice, and properly appreciate complex issues involving allegations of siphoning and accounting irregularities[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 11 and Section 242(4) do not establish any pre-conditions requiring the Tribunal to conclusively adjudicate the merits or record a final finding of fraud or oppression at the interlocutory stage before ordering an audit[cite: 18]. An independent audit is an investigative aid designed to assist the Tribunal in uncovering true financial facts, separating genuine accounting errors from manipulation, and ensuring a just resolution of disputes between contesting shareholders[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated the conflicting claims regarding amounts entered as 'Loan from Directors' in the balance sheets versus explanations of inadvertent clerical errors[cite: 18]. It determined that in the face of competing allegations of financial distortion, an independent audit report is a necessary mechanism to safeguard parties' rights and facilitate a fair adjudication under Sections 241 and 242[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that NCLT Kochi committed no legal error or procedural fault in directing an independent audit via an interim order, as such measures fall squarely within its inherent and statutory powers, requiring dismissal of the appeal[cite: 18].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 101 of 2022 is dismissed without costs[cite: 18]. The impugned interim order dated 08.06.2022 passed by the National Company Law Tribunal, Kochi Bench in CP/127/(KOB)/2019 is affirmed[cite: 18]. All connected pending Interlocutory Applications (I.A. Nos. 854 of 2022 & 146, 1326 of 2023) are closed[cite: 18].
summary: Appellants Veena Ramanathapura Sreenivasarangan and Iyer Sudhakar Jayaram appealed against an interim order of the NCLT Kochi Bench that appointed an independent auditor to investigate the accounts of Amruthamgamaya Nature Care and Leisure Private Limited for financial years 2015-16, 2016-17, and 2017-18[cite: 18]. The appellants contended that ordering an investigative audit without a definitive finding of oppression, mismanagement, or fraud amounted to an impermissible fishing expedition[cite: 18]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT Chennai held that under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 and Section 242(4) of the Companies Act, 2013, the Tribunal possesses inherent and discretionary powers to order audits or forensic examinations as interim measures to uncover facts and meet the ends of justice[cite: 18].

case_title: Kiran Martin Gulla vs. Sandeep
bench: Chennai Bench
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Kiran Martin Gulla (also referred to as Kiran Marin Golla), Resolution Professional (RP) / Interim Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor M/s Varadharaja Foods Pvt Ltd[cite: 19]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) was admitted against the Corporate Debtor M/s Varadharaja Foods Pvt Ltd on 19.11.2022 in CP (IB)/9(CHE)/2022[cite: 19]. The third Committee of Creditors (CoC) concluded on 17.04.2023 approved the publication of Expression of Interest (EoI) for submitting resolution plans[cite: 19]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose from unpaid debts owed by the Corporate Debtor, triggering CIRP admission[cite: 19]. The initial 180-day CIRP period was set to lapse on 10.05.2023[cite: 19]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 19.11.2022[cite: 19]. The sole CoC member passed a resolution on 21.04.2023 seeking a 90-day CIRP extension from 10.05.2023[cite: 19]. The RP filed IA (IBC)/1235(CHE)/2023 on 09.05.2023[cite: 19]. NCLT Chennai passed the impugned order allowing the 90-day extension retrospectively from 10.05.2023 on 27.07.2023[cite: 19]. The RP received the reporting email on 27.07.2023 and downloaded the uploaded order on 11.08.2023[cite: 19]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Documentary evidence comprised: (i) CoC resolution and voting records dated 21.04.2023 approving the 90-day extension[cite: 19]; (ii) Form-G timeline published with the last date for submission of resolution plans as 30.06.2023[cite: 19]; and (iii) application filing receipts and tribunal order logs establishing that IA (IBC)/1235(CHE)/2023 remained pending before NCLT Chennai from 09.05.2023 to 27.07.2023 (79 days)[cite: 19]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai Special Bench Court-I allowed IA (IBC)/1235(CHE)/2023 on 27.07.2023, granting a 90-day CIRP extension calculated retrospectively from 10.05.2023[cite: 19]. The Resolution Professional appealed the retrospective calculation under Section 61 before NCLAT Chennai[cite: 19].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in granting a 90-day CIRP extension calculated retrospectively from the original expiry date (10.05.2023) rather than prospectively from the date of disposal, and whether the period of pendency of the extension application before the tribunal should be excluded from the CIRP calculation[cite: 19].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When an Adjudicating Authority grants an extension of the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) under Section 12(2) of the IBC, the extended period must run prospectively from the date of disposal or approval of the application, rather than retrospectively from the original expiry date[cite: 19]. Furthermore, the period during which an extension application remains pending due to judicial proceedings before the tribunal must be excluded from the computation of the CIRP timeline, as no litigant should suffer prejudice from the delay of a judicial forum[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory concepts of 'extension' (stretching or elongating time) and 'exclusion' (keeping out or eliminating specific periods of judicial delay) operate distinctly under the IBC[cite: 19]. Relying on the Supreme Court's ruling in Essar Steel, time taken in legal proceedings and pendency before the NCLT or NCLAT cannot be counted against litigants who are not at fault[cite: 19]. Discretionary powers under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 and Regulation 40C of the IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016 empower tribunals to exclude judicial pendency to keep the corporate debtor a going concern[cite: 19]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified the timelines: the extension application was filed on 09.05.2023, disposed of on 27.07.2023, and the order was uploaded on 11.08.2023[cite: 19]. Calculating the 90-day extension retrospectively from 10.05.2023 rendered the relief infructuous because the pendency period consumed almost the entire extension window[cite: 19]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed an error by making the 90-day extension run retrospectively[cite: 19]. NCLAT set aside that part of the impugned order, ordered the exclusion of the entire pendency period of IA (IBC)/1235(CHE)/2023 (09.05.2023 to 27.07.2023) as well as the appeal proceedings, and directed that the 90-day CIRP extension shall run prospectively from the date of disposal of the appeal[cite: 19].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 450 of 2023 is allowed[cite: 19]. The direction in the NCLT Chennai impugned order dated 27.07.2023 in IA(IB)/1235(CHE)/2023 making the CIRP extension run retrospectively from 10.05.2023 is set aside[cite: 19]. It is ordered that the period of pendency of IA(IB)/1235(CHE)/2023 before the Adjudicating Authority (09.05.2023 to 27.07.2023) and the period of pendency of the appeal shall be excluded[cite: 19]. The 90-day CIRP extension under Section 12(2) of the IBC is granted to run prospectively from the date of disposal of the appeal (21.02.2024)[cite: 19]. No costs[cite: 19].
summary: Resolution Professional Kiran Martin Gulla appealed against an NCLT Chennai order granting a 90-day CIRP extension for Varadharaja Foods Pvt Ltd calculated retrospectively from May 10, 2023[cite: 19]. The appellant contended that because the extension application remained pending before the tribunal until July 27, 2023, retrospective calculation rendered the extension practically infructuous[cite: 19]. Allowing the appeal, NCLAT Chennai held that CIRP extensions must run prospectively from the date of disposal, and the entire period of judicial pendency must be excluded from the timeline to prevent prejudice to litigants[cite: 19].

case_title: Essel Finance Advisors and Managers LLP vs. Mr. Pankaj Srivastava
bench: Chennai Bench
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Essel Finance Advisors and Managers LLP, acting as Investment Manager for debenture holders[cite: 1]. Respondent No. 1 is Mr. Pankaj Srivastava, Liquidator of M/s. Samruddhi Realty Limited[cite: 1]. Respondent No. 2 is Assets Care and Reconstruction Enterprise Ltd. (ACRE)[cite: 1]. Respondent No. 3 is Phoenix ARC Private Limited[cite: 1]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant entered into Debenture Subscription Agreements dated 30.09.2016 with the Corporate Debtor for subscribing to 7,500 senior, secured, unlisted, redeemable, non-convertible debentures aggregating to Rs. 75 Crores, with investors investing up to Rs. 55 Crores through 5,500 debentures[cite: 1]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtor defaulted on its financial obligations, leading to the admission of the insolvency petition on 16.04.2019[cite: 1]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The maximum CIRP period expired on 17.02.2020; liquidation was ordered on 13.03.2020; public announcement was issued on 17.03.2020 with claims due by 17.04.2020; the impugned order was passed on 25.05.2023[cite: 1]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant filed its claim in Form D on 17.04.2020, choosing to stand outside the liquidation estate to realize its security interest under Section 52 of the IBC, and subsequently refused to pay upfront liquidation costs demanded by the Liquidator[cite: 1]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Liquidator filed IA No. 399/BB/2020 in CP (IB) No. 189/BB/2018 before the NCLT Bengaluru Bench seeking directions for the respondents to defray liquidation process costs, which was allowed by the Adjudicating Authority on 25.05.2023, leading to the present appeal under Section 61 of the IBC[cite: 1].
legal_issues: Whether a secured financial creditor / investment manager opting out of the liquidation process to realize its security interest under Section 52 of the IBC is exempted from contributing towards liquidation process costs under Regulation 2A of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016, and whether the Appellant and its represented debenture holders qualify as 'Financial Institutions' under Section 3(14) of the IBC and Section 45-I of the RBI Act, 1934[cite: 1].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A secured creditor who chooses to realize its security interest outside the liquidation estate remains statutorily liable to pay its proportional share of liquidation process costs and fees as mandated by Regulation 2A and Regulation 21A of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016[cite: 1]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The definition of a financial institution under Section 3(14)(b) of the IBC incorporates entities engaging in financing and acquisition of debentures/securities under Section 45-I of the RBI Act, making institutional subscribers and financial creditors liable for these costs[cite: 1]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Perusal of the relationship notes and claim submissions established that the Appellant invested substantial funds by subscribing to redeemable secured non-convertible debentures, bringing them squarely within the applicable financial framework[cite: 1]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the Impugned Order directing the respondents to defray their portion of liquidation process costs is free from legal infirmity and dismissed the appeal[cite: 1].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 332 of 2023 is dismissed with no orders as to costs, and all pending interlocutory applications are closed[cite: 1].
summary: Essel Finance Advisors and Managers LLP appealed against an NCLT order directing it to contribute towards liquidation process costs after opting out of the liquidation process to realize its security interest in M/s. Samruddhi Realty Limited[cite: 1]. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal held that secured creditors realizing security interests independently are still obligated to pay liquidation costs and fees under Regulation 2A and Regulation 21A of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations[cite: 1]. The appellate tribunal found no legal infirmity in the Adjudicating Authority's directions and consequently dismissed the appeal along with pending interlocutory applications, upholding the requirement for proportional cost contribution[cite: 1].

case_title: Adv. (CA) V. Venkata Sivakumar vs. Hari S. Hari Karthik & Ors.
appeal_number: Review Application No. 3 of 2024 in Comp. App. (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 8 of 2022
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Member M. Venugopal, Judicial Member Sharad Kumar Sharma, and Technical Member Jatindranath Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Review Petitioner is Adv. (CA) V. Venkata Sivakumar (Erstwhile Liquidator of M/s. The Jeypore Sugar Co. Ltd.) appearing in person[cite: 2]. Respondent No. 1 is Hari S. Hari Karthik (New Liquidator of M/s. The Jeypore Sugar Company Ltd.)[cite: 2]. Respondents No. 2 to 7 are financial creditors including IDBI Bank Limited, Bank of India, Pridhvi Asset Reconstruction, Bank of Baroda, Indian Overseas Bank, and The District Cooperative Central Bank[cite: 2]. Respondents No. 8 to 10 are corporate entities (Kineta Global Limited, Aaria Projects Limited, and Synergy Holdings)[cite: 2]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate insolvency resolution process (CIRP) and subsequent liquidation proceedings were initiated against the Corporate Debtor, M/s. The Jeypore Sugar Co. Ltd., under Section 7 of the IBC[cite: 2]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid financial debts owed by the Corporate Debtor to institutional lenders triggered the insolvency and liquidation process[cite: 2]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Adjudicating Authority approved liquidation on 29.05.2020 and appointed the Review Petitioner as liquidator[cite: 2]. On 01.07.2022, the Adjudicating Authority allowed IA No. 815/2020 replacing the Review Petitioner with a new liquidator[cite: 2]. NCLAT dismissed the Review Petitioner's challenge to his removal on 20.12.2022 in Comp. App. (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 269/2022[cite: 2]. On 05.01.2024, NCLAT permitted the New Liquidator to withdraw Comp. App. (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 8/2022, which was formally dismissed as withdrawn[cite: 2]. The Review Petitioner filed Review Application No. 3/2024 on an unspecified date prior to 22.03.2024[cite: 2]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Documentary records included the NCLT order dated 01.07.2022 removing the erstwhile liquidator, the NCLAT appellate judgment dated 20.12.2022 upholding the removal, the new liquidator's memo and application to withdraw Comp. App. (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 8/2022, and the withdrawal order dated 05.01.2024[cite: 2]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Erstwhile Liquidator filed Review Application No. 3 of 2024 under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 seeking to recall the NCLAT order dated 05.01.2024 that permitted the withdrawal of Comp. App. (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 8/2022 and to expunge adverse remarks, which the Chennai Bench dismissed on 22.03.2024[cite: 2].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an erstwhile liquidator removed by a judicial order has the locus standi and vested right in a personal capacity to seek a review or recall of an order permitting the withdrawal of an appeal filed in the official capacity of the liquidator[cite: 2]; (ii) Whether the New Liquidator, acting as dominus litis under Section 35(1)(k) of the IBC, is legally competent to withdraw an ongoing appeal filed on behalf of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 2].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An erstwhile liquidator who has been legally replaced by a new liquidator pursuant to an order of the Adjudicating Authority—affirmed on appeal—ceases to represent the corporate debtor and possesses neither locus standi nor a vested right to challenge, review, or recall procedural decisions or withdrawals made by the new liquidator in their official capacity[cite: 2]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 35(1)(k) of the IBC, the power and duty to institute, continue, or withdraw any suit, prosecution, or legal proceedings on behalf of the corporate debtor vests exclusively in the incumbent liquidator, who acts as dominus litis[cite: 2]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the Review Petitioner was validly removed as liquidator vide order dated 01.07.2022 (upheld on 20.12.2022), that the appeal in question was instituted in an official capacity rather than a personal one, and that the new liquidator filed a formal memo on 08.01.2024 seeking withdrawal of the appeal in the interest of stakeholders[cite: 2]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Tribunal concluded that the review application was ex-facie non-maintainable in the absence of a statutory review power, that the power of recall cannot be invoked as a substitute for an appeal or re-hearing by a non-party, and that the application was devoid of merits[cite: 2].
operative_order: Review Application No. 3 of 2024 filed by the Review Petitioner / Erstwhile Liquidator in person is dismissed with no orders as to costs[cite: 2].
summary: Adv. (CA) V. Venkata Sivakumar, the erstwhile liquidator of M/s. The Jeypore Sugar Co. Ltd., filed Review Application No. 3 of 2024 seeking to recall an NCLAT order dated January 5, 2024, which had permitted the new liquidator, Hari S. Hari Karthik, to withdraw Comp. App. (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 8 of 2022[cite: 2]. The applicant alleged fraud, collusion, and suppression of facts by IDBI Bank and the new liquidator[cite: 2]. Dismissing the review application, the NCLAT Chennai Bench held that because the applicant was legally removed as liquidator and his removal was upheld on appeal, he lacked locus standi and any personal vested right to maintain a review against an official action[cite: 2]. The Tribunal ruled that the new liquidator, as dominus litis under Section 35(1)(k) of the IBC, is fully competent to decide whether to prosecute or withdraw legal proceedings[cite: 2].

case_title: Canara Bank vs. Mr. S. Rajendran, Liquidator of M/s. Cape Engineers Pvt. Ltd.
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Member M. Venugopal, Judicial Member Sharad Kumar Sharma, and Technical Member Jatindranath Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Canara Bank (Secured Financial Creditor). The Respondent is Mr. S. Rajendran, Liquidator of M/s. Cape Engineers Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Guarantor). The principal borrower is M/s. Sree Ganesh EPC P. Ltd[cite: 3]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: M/s. Sree Ganesh EPC P. Ltd. availed credit facilities of Rs. 23 crores from the Appellant bank, for which the Corporate Guarantor M/s. Cape Engineers Pvt. Ltd. offered its immovable property as collateral security and executed a Corporate Guarantee Agreement alongside a Memorandum of Deposit of Title Deeds (MODTD) registered on 07.07.2015 as document No. 747/2015/SRO Thovalai[cite: 3]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred on the credit facilities, and the corporate guarantor's total claim submitted by the bank amounted to Rs. 34,78,78,231/-[cite: 3]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The corporate guarantor was admitted into CIRP under Section 10 on 06.09.2019[cite: 3]. Liquidation was ordered on 25.04.2022, appointing the Respondent as Liquidator[cite: 3]. The Appellant filed Form D on 20.05.2022, expressing its desire to stand outside liquidation under Section 52[cite: 3]. The Liquidator issued email notices on 27.05.2022 and 01.07.2022 classifying the bank as an unsecured financial creditor due to non-registration of charge under Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 3]. The Appellant registered the charge with CERSAI on 05.06.2022 and filed IA (IBC)/887(CHE)/2022, which was dismissed by the NCLT Chennai on 14.06.2023[cite: 3]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Relevant records included the registered MODTD dated 07.05.2015 at SRO Thovalai, Form D claim filings, the Liquidator's claim determination note dated 03.06.2022, CERSAI registration certificate dated 05.06.2022, and SARFAESI notices[cite: 3]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed IA (IBC)/887(CHE)/2022 under Section 60(5) of the IBC read with Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules before NCLT Chennai Division Bench II to quash the Liquidator's communications treating it as an unsecured creditor[cite: 3]. The Adjudicating Authority dismissed the application on 14.06.2023, prompting the bank to file Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 277 of 2023[cite: 3].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a financial creditor holding a registered mortgage under Section 58(f) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 can be classified as an unsecured financial creditor solely on the ground that the charge was not registered with the Registrar of Companies under Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 3]; (ii) Whether non-registration under Section 77(3) overrides pre-existing statutory mortgage rights and bars the creditor from standing outside the liquidation process under Section 52 of the IBC[cite: 3].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The right to recover money lent by enforcing a mortgage is a substantive right to enforce an interest in property under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, and a valid mortgage created by act of parties cannot be completely negated or stripped of its character as a security interest merely due to the absence of registration of charge under Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013, particularly when the mortgage was duly registered before a public sub-registrar office[cite: 3]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Provisions of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 and pre-existing property rights are not automatically diluted or overridden by Regulation 21 of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 or Section 77(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, in the absence of explicit retrospective application, and public registration at an SRO provides adequate notice of encumbrance[cite: 3]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the MODTD was duly registered at the Sub-Registrar Office, Thovalai in 2015 (prior to the IBC), that CERSAI registration was completed on 05.06.2022 before the final classification notice, and that the bank held a 95.76% voting share based on valid collateral documents[cite: 3]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that classifying the Appellant bank as an unsecured financial creditor was illegal and invalid, and that the bank must be treated as a secured creditor entitled to exercise its rights under Section 52 of the IBC and the SARFAESI Act[cite: 3].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 277 of 2023 is allowed without costs[cite: 3]. The impugned order dated 14.06.2023 passed by NCLT Chennai in IA(IBC)/887(CHE)/2022 is set aside, and the appellant's application is allowed, declaring the bank to be a secured creditor[cite: 3].
summary: Canara Bank challenged an NCLT Chennai order upholding the Liquidator's decision to treat the bank as an unsecured financial creditor of M/s. Cape Engineers Pvt. Ltd. because the mortgage charge was not registered under Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 3]. The NCLAT allowed the appeal, holding that a registered mortgage created under Section 58(f) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, and registered at the Sub-Registrar Office constitutes a valid security interest[cite: 3]. The Appellate Tribunal ruled that non-registration under Section 77 does not strip a valid mortgagee of its status as a secured creditor in liquidation, enabling the bank to stand outside the liquidation process under Section 52 of the IBC[cite: 3].

case_title: Sumit Singh Basisth & Anr. / Sunny Kr. Singh vs. Sare Gurugram Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 138 of 2024 & Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 367 of 2024
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan, Judicial/Technical Members Barun Mitra and Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Sumit Singh Basisth, Poonam Shatrughan Singh, and Sunny Kr. Singh (Homebuyers/Allottees/NRIs). The Respondent is Sare Gurugram Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) represented through the Monitoring Committee[cite: 4]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Allottees purchased commercial spaces or residential apartments in the project developed by the Corporate Debtor, Sare Gurugram Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 4]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) commenced against the Corporate Debtor on 09.03.2021, and the resolution plan was approved by the Committee of Creditors (CoC) with a 100% vote on 17.12.2021[cite: 4]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, Principal Bench, New Delhi) approved the Resolution Plan via an order dated 24.04.2023 in I.A. No. 702/PB/2022[cite: 4]. The Appellants claimed they only discovered the CIRP and the approval order in October/November 2023 through a WhatsApp group and emails[cite: 4]. Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 138 of 2024 was e-filed on 25.01.2024 (with a delay of 223 days), and Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 367 of 2024 was e-filed on 09.01.2024 (with a delay of 230 days)[cite: 4]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The record showed that public announcements were made by the IRP/RP under standard regulations, but the Appellants failed to file claims during the CIRP and later sought condonation of over 200 days of delay based on lack of knowledge[cite: 4]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellants filed applications (I.A. No. 808 of 2024 and I.A. No. 1251 of 2024) seeking condonation of delay under Section 61(2) of the IBC, which were contested by the respondents and heard by the NCLAT Principal Bench[cite: 4].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the period of limitation for filing an appeal under Section 61(2) of the IBC commences from the date of the order or from the date of knowledge of the order[cite: 4]; (ii) Whether this Tribunal has the jurisdiction to condone a delay exceeding the statutory 15-day grace period stipulated under the proviso to Section 61(2) of the IBC[cite: 4].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 61(2) of the IBC, the limitation period commences from the date of pronouncement of the order, and the NCLAT does not have the power or jurisdiction to condone a delay exceeding 15 days beyond the initial 30-day statutory limitation period[cite: 4]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The IBC deliberately omits phrases like 'from the date on which a copy of the order is made available' (which were present in the Companies Act), indicating that limitation is strict, objective, and does not start from the date of a party's knowledge or receipt of the order[cite: 4]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the impugned order was pronounced on 24.04.2023, while the appeals were filed with delays of 223 and 230 days respectively—vastly exceeding the maximum condonable limit of 15 days under Section 61(2)[cite: 4]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Ignorance of the CIRP proceedings or later discovery of the order cannot extend the strict statutory limitation framework of the IBC, rendering the delay un-condonable and the appeals liable to be dismissed[cite: 4].
operative_order: I.A. No. 808 of 2024 and I.A. No. 1251 of 2024 (Delay Condonation Applications) are dismissed, and consequently, the respective Memo of Appeals in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 138 and 367 of 2024 are rejected[cite: 4].
summary: Appellants Sumit Singh Basisth and Sunny Kr. Singh filed appeals against the NCLT order dated April 24, 2023, which approved the resolution plan for Sare Gurugram Pvt. Ltd., along with applications seeking condonation of delays of 223 and 230 days respectively[cite: 4]. The appellants argued they were unaware of the CIRP until late 2023 and that limitation should run from the date of knowledge[cite: 4]. Relying on Supreme Court precedents including V. Nagarajan and Safire Technologies, the NCLAT Principal Bench dismissed both delay condonation applications[cite: 4]. The Tribunal reaffirmed that limitation under Section 61(2) of the IBC begins upon order pronouncement, ignorance of proceedings does not extend limitation, and the appellate tribunal cannot condone delays beyond the statutory 15-day ceiling[cite: 4].

case_title: Sanjay Goyal & Anr. vs. M/S Soni Realtors Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Rakesh Kumar Jain and Technical Member Naresh Salecha)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Corporate Debtor is Soni Realtors Pvt. Ltd., which was developing a residential township named 'Palm City' in Karnal, Haryana[cite: 6]. The Financial Creditor is SE Investment Limited (now Paisalo Digital Ltd.), and the Resolution Professional (RP) is Manoj Kulshreshta[cite: 6]. The appellants comprise various home buyers, allottees, and other entities challenging the plan approval[cite: 6]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Soni Realtors Pvt. Ltd. developed 'Palm City' involving 377 plots, a nursing home, nursery school, and commercial land[cite: 6]. A Section 7 application was admitted against the Corporate Debtor on 27.02.2018[cite: 6]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Defaults by the Corporate Debtor led to the initiation of CIRP under Section 7 of the IBC[cite: 6]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Adjudicating Authority approved the resolution plan submitted by Srijan Infra LLP vide order dated 10.06.2022[cite: 6]. A batch of thirteen appeals was subsequently filed before the NCLAT[cite: 6]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The RP raised preliminary objections pointing out that multiple appeals were filed without annexing certified copies of the impugned order, and that certified copies were applied for long after the expiry of the 30-day and 45-day limitation periods[cite: 6]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The RP filed objections regarding maintainability across a batch of 13 appeals, leading the NCLAT to consider whether appeals filed without certified copies or with delayed certified copy applications are maintainable under the NCLAT Rules and the IBC[cite: 6].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an appeal filed under Section 61 of the IBC without a certified copy of the impugned order is maintainable when accompanied by an interlocutory application seeking exemption from filing a certified copy under Rule 14 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016[cite: 6]; (ii) Whether failure to apply for a certified copy within the limitation period renders an appeal non-maintainable pursuant to the ruling in V. Nagarajan[cite: 6].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While Rule 22(2) of the NCLAT Rules mandates that every appeal be accompanied by a certified copy of the impugned order, Rule 14 grants the Appellate Tribunal explicit discretionary power to exempt parties from compliance with any rule upon showing sufficient cause and upon a formal application being moved[cite: 6]. However, where an appellant fails to file any application seeking exemption from filing a certified copy, the appeal is not maintainable[cite: 6]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The procedural requirement to annex a certified copy is a handmaid of justice, and the Tribunal possesses inherent and explicit powers under Rules 11 and 14 to excuse compliance or extend time to place certified copies on record when proper applications are filed[cite: 6]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examined the record of all 13 appeals and verified which appellants had filed formal interlocutory applications for exemption from filing certified copies under Rule 14, distinguishing them from those who completely omitted filing such exemption applications[cite: 6]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Appeals where formal exemption applications were filed are maintainable subject to subsequent consideration of delay condonation applications, whereas appeals filed without certified copies and without any exemption applications (specifically CA (AT) (Ins) Nos. 1135 of 2022, 1136 of 2022, and 270 of 2023) are not maintainable and stand dismissed[cite: 6].
operative_order: Interlocutory applications seeking exemption from filing certified copies in ten appeals (CA (AT) (Ins) Nos. 691 of 2023, 1076 of 2022, 1085 of 2022, 757 & 758 of 2022, 964 & 965 of 2022, 1015 of 2022, 1122 of 2022, 1143 of 2022, 1174 of 2022, and 1079 of 2023) are allowed, and appellants are directed to file certified copies within 30 days; applications for condonation of delay will be considered individually with the main appeals[cite: 6]. Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) Nos. 1135 of 2022, 1136 of 2022, and 270 of 2023 are dismissed as not maintainable due to the total absence of exemption applications[cite: 6].
summary: The NCLAT adjudicated upon preliminary objections regarding maintainability raised against a batch of thirteen appeals challenging the NCLT order dated June 10, 2022, which approved the resolution plan for Soni Realtors Pvt. Ltd[cite: 6]. The Resolution Professional argued that the appeals were defective and time-barred because they lacked certified copies applied for within the limitation period[cite: 6]. Delivering the judgment, the Appellate Tribunal held that under Rule 14 of the NCLAT Rules, it possesses the discretionary power to exempt parties from filing certified copies if sufficient cause is shown via a formal application[cite: 6]. Consequently, the Tribunal allowed the exemption applications for ten appeals while directing appellants to submit certified copies, but dismissed three appeals (Nos. 1135 of 2022, 1136 of 2022, and 270 of 2023) that were filed without any exemption applications[cite: 6].

case_title: Mr. Vikas Aggarwal & Ors. vs. Asian Colour Coated Ispat Limited & Ors.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Rakesh Kumar Jain and Technical Member Naresh Salecha)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Vikas Aggarwal, Sapna Aggarwal, Archana Aggarwal, and Kamlesh Devo Aggarwal (Personal Guarantors of the Corporate Debtor)[cite: 8]. Respondent No. 1 is Asian Colour Coated Ispat Limited (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 8]. Respondent No. 2 is JSW Steel Coated Products Limited (Successful Resolution Applicant / SRA)[cite: 8]. Respondent No. 3 is the Committee of Creditors (CoC)[cite: 8]. Respondent No. 4 is Kuldeep Kumar Bassi (Resolution Professional)[cite: 8]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor underwent Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) admitted on 28.07.2018 under CP No. (IB) 50(PB)/2018[cite: 8]. The SRA submitted a resolution plan providing for the assignment of debt to a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) named Hasaud Steels Limited, incorporating the concept of 'Excluded Rights' to reserve financial creditors' recourses against personal guarantors[cite: 8]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Admitted financial debt of the corporate debtor totaled approximately Rs. 7,801 Crores, while the SRA's proposed resolution plan payment was Rs. 1,550 Crores (representing an 80.13% haircut for creditors)[cite: 8]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The CoC approved the resolution plan with a 79.3% voting share, and the Adjudicating Authority approved it on 26.10.2020 in CA No. 1393(PB)/2019[cite: 8]. The personal guarantors appealed the order under Section 61 of the IBC[cite: 8]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record included the final resolution plan dated 06.05.2019 along with addendum dated 17.06.2019 defining 'Remaining Debt' and 'Excluded Rights', the assignment deed dated 27.10.2020, and 'no due' certificates issued to the corporate debtor[cite: 8]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellants filed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) Nos. 1104, 1105, 1107, and 1108 of 2020 before NCLAT Principal Bench, challenging the plan's survival of personal guarantees and 'Excluded Rights' after debt assignment[cite: 8].
legal_issues: (i) Whether financial creditors can retain 'Excluded Rights' to pursue legal remedies and recover unpaid dues against personal guarantors of the corporate debtor after assigning the financial debt to an SPV under an approved resolution plan[cite: 8]; (ii) Whether the approval of a resolution plan extinguishes a guarantor's right of subrogation under Sections 140 and 141 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872[cite: 8]; (iii) Whether reserving rights against personal guarantors violates Section 6(e) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 prohibiting the transfer of a 'mere right to sue'[cite: 8].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The approval of a resolution plan under the IBC does not ipso facto discharge a personal guarantor of a corporate debtor from liabilities under an independent contract of guarantee, and financial creditors can validly carve out 'Excluded Rights' in a resolution plan to independently pursue legal remedies against personal guarantors for unfulfilled debt obligations[cite: 8]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238 of the IBC grants overriding effect over inconsistent provisions in other enactments, including the Indian Contract Act, 1872 and the Transfer of Property Act, 1882; consequently, a guarantor's right of subrogation against the corporate debtor stands extinguished upon plan approval to implement the clean slate theory for the revived corporate entity[cite: 8]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the resolution plan and addendum explicitly defined 'Remaining Debt' (assigned to the SRA's SPV) while expressly carving out 'Excluded Rights' (retained by financial creditors to proceed against personal guarantors), a structure approved by the CoC in its collective commercial wisdom[cite: 8]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that resolution of corporate debt does not equate to full satisfaction of liabilities payable by guarantors, and upholding 'Excluded Rights' does not transfer a 'mere right to sue' under Section 6(e), rendering the appeals completely meritless[cite: 8].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1104, 1105, 1107, and 1108 of 2020 are dismissed with no orders as to costs, and all pending interlocutory applications are closed[cite: 8].
summary: Personal guarantors Vikas, Sapna, Archana, and Kamlesh Devo Aggarwal appealed against the NCLT order approving the resolution plan for Asian Colour Coated Ispat Limited, arguing that the assignment of the corporate debtor's total debt to an SPV extinguished all liabilities and left financial creditors with no right to pursue personal guarantees[cite: 8]. Dismissing all four appeals, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that the commercial wisdom of the CoC can validly incorporate 'Excluded Rights' into a resolution plan, allowing financial creditors to independently pursue legal remedies against personal guarantors for unpaid portions of debt[cite: 8]. The Tribunal further reaffirmed that a guarantor's right of subrogation stands extinguished under the clean slate doctrine, and Section 238 of the IBC overrides contract and property law limitations[cite: 8].

DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Appeals where formal exemption applications were filed are maintainable subject to subsequent consideration of delay condonation applications, whereas appeals filed without certified copies and without any exemption applications (specifically CA (AT) (Ins) Nos. 1135 of 2022, 1136 of 2022, and 270 of 2023) are not maintainable and stand dismissed[cite: 9].
operative_order: Interlocutory applications seeking exemption from filing certified copies in ten appeals (CA (AT) (Ins) Nos. 691 of 2023, 1076 of 2022, 1085 of 2022, 757 & 758 of 2022, 964 & 965 of 2022, 1015 of 2022, 1122 of 2022, 1143 of 2022, 1174 of 2022, and 1079 of 2023) are allowed, and appellants are directed to file certified copies within 30 days; applications for condonation of delay will be considered individually with the main appeals[cite: 9]. Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) Nos. 1135 of 2022, 1136 of 2022, and 270 of 2023 are dismissed as not maintainable due to the total absence of exemption applications[cite: 9].
summary: The NCLAT adjudicated upon preliminary objections regarding maintainability raised against a batch of thirteen appeals challenging the NCLT order dated June 10, 2022, which approved the resolution plan for Soni Realtors Pvt. Ltd[cite: 9]. The Resolution Professional argued that the appeals were defective and time-barred because they lacked certified copies applied for within the limitation period[cite: 9]. Delivering the judgment, the Appellate Tribunal held that under Rule 14 of the NCLAT Rules, it possesses the discretionary power to exempt parties from filing certified copies if sufficient cause is shown via a formal application[cite: 9]. Consequently, the Tribunal allowed the exemption applications for ten appeals while directing appellants to submit certified copies, but dismissed three appeals (Nos. 1135 of 2022, 1136 of 2022, and 270 of 2023) that were filed without any exemption applications[cite: 9].

case_title: Amit Tyagi vs. M/S Indirapuram Habitat Centre Pvt. Ltd.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan, Technical Members Barun Mitra and Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Amit Tyagi, an allottee of commercial space[cite: 10]. The Corporate Debtor is Indirapuram Habitat Centre Pvt. Ltd[cite: 10]. The Respondent is Shri Narender Kumar Sharma, Resolution Professional (RP) of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 10]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor entered into Memorandums of Understanding (MoUs) with the Appellant (including MoU dated 08.06.2016) allotting commercial space, specifically Shop No. TW-14A (Ground Floor, Block A&B, super area 23.50 sq. m.)[cite: 10]. Under the MoU and its Annexure-A, the Corporate Debtor assured lease rent payouts to the Appellant until 27.01.2032[cite: 10]. The Appellant paid approximately 95% of the total unit cost prior to CIRP initiation[cite: 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by the Corporate Debtor occurred prior to CIRP when assured return/rent payouts ceased after June 2018 (over a year prior to CIRP commencement), prompting allottees to file cases under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act[cite: 10]. The Appellant sought release of pending and future monthly rent and execution of conveyance deeds upon payment of the remaining 5% balance[cite: 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced against the Corporate Debtor vide order dated 22.08.2019 in C.P. (IB) No. 1397/PB/2019[cite: 10]. Allottees filed IA Nos. 3492/2020 and 3314/2020 seeking registration of shops, which NCLT disposed of on 31.08.2020 directing verification of titles via forensic audit[cite: 10]. Appellant filed IA No. 4252/2020 and IA No. 4924/2021[cite: 10]. NCLT New Delhi Bench Court-II dismissed both IAs on 19.12.2023[cite: 10]. Appellant appealed to NCLAT under Section 61[cite: 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Documentary records comprised: (i) MoU dated 08.06.2016 with Annexure-A rental payout schedule[cite: 10]; (ii) proofs of payment establishing deposit of approximately 95% consideration[cite: 10]; (iii) forensic audit report commissioned by the RP to determine genuine ownership and title of commercial units[cite: 10]; (iv) NCLT order dated 31.08.2020[cite: 10]; and (v) bank records showing rental receipts collected from existing project lessees deposited into interest-bearing Fixed Deposit Receipts (FDRs) by the RP[cite: 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench Court-II heard IA No. 4252/2020 and IA No. 4924/2021 filed by the Appellant and rejected both applications on 19.12.2023, refusing to direct execution of conveyance deeds during moratorium and holding that rental collections deposited in FDRs would be dealt with at the appropriate stage[cite: 10]. The Appellant appealed the rejection to the NCLAT Principal Bench[cite: 10].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an allottee of a commercial unit who has paid 95% of consideration is entitled as a matter of right during CIRP to an order directing the Resolution Professional to execute a conveyance deed in respect of corporate debtor assets notwithstanding the statutory moratorium under Section 14(1)(b) of the IBC[cite: 10]; (ii) Whether the Resolution Professional is obligated during CIRP to honor pre-CIRP contractual assured return/lease rent arrangements and disburse ongoing rental collections directly to commercial space allottees rather than parking them in Fixed Deposit Receipts for collective resolution[cite: 10].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: During the subsistence of a Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process and the statutory moratorium imposed under Section 14(1)(b) of the IBC, allottees cannot claim mandatory execution of conveyance deeds or specific performance of pre-insolvency real estate contracts as an absolute legal right[cite: 10]. The Resolution Professional, vested with asset management and business powers under Sections 17, 18, and 25 of the IBC, retains exclusive administrative discretion over what contractual obligations can be executed while preserving the corporate debtor as a going concern[cite: 10]. Furthermore, pre-CIRP assured return or rental arrangements cannot be enforced against the RP during moratorium; parking third-party rental yields in interest-bearing fixed deposits pending final resolution fully protects stakeholder interests[cite: 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(1)(b) prohibits transferring, encumbering, alienating, or disposing of any corporate debtor assets or legal/beneficial rights therein during CIRP[cite: 10]. A direction compelling an RP to execute a conveyance deed operates as an order for specific performance of contract, which encroaches on the statutory scheme of CIRP and the RP's custodial domain under Sections 18 and 25[cite: 10]. While homebuyer and allottee interests must be protected under the IBC, the manner and mode of protection are governed by the overall resolution framework and not by piecemeal property transfers or preferential cash outflows[cite: 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the prayers in IA No. 4252/2020 and IA No. 4924/2021, observing that conveyance deed execution was not specifically prayed for in the pleadings and that assured returns had already ceased since June 2018 prior to CIRP[cite: 10]. It verified that current lessees occupied the premises at rates lower than the MoU figures and that the RP had safeguarded rental receipts in FDRs under tribunal oversight[cite: 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in refusing to order execution of conveyance deeds during the Section 14 moratorium, and that parking rental proceeds in Fixed Deposit Receipts pending final CIRP adjudication adequately protected the Appellant's rights, warranting dismissal of the appeal[cite: 10].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 272 of 2024 is dismissed without costs, affirming the order dated 19.12.2023 passed by the National Company Law Tribunal, New Delhi Bench (Court-II) in IA No. 4252/2020 and IA No. 4924/2021[cite: 10].
summary: Appellant Amit Tyagi, a commercial space allottee in Indirapuram Habitat Centre Pvt. Ltd., appealed an NCLT New Delhi Bench order dismissing his applications seeking execution of a conveyance deed and release of monthly assured lease rentals under an MoU dated June 8, 2016[cite: 10]. The appellant contended that having paid 95% of the purchase price, he was entitled to registration of his unit and ongoing rent[cite: 10]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that allottees cannot enforce specific performance or demand execution of sale deeds during CIRP, as Section 14(1)(b) prohibits transferring corporate debtor assets[cite: 10]. Furthermore, the RP's action of depositing rental collections into fixed deposit accounts pending resolution adequately preserved stakeholder interests[cite: 10].

case_title: Garodia Chemicals Limited vs. Respondent
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Members Barun Mitra and Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Garodia Chemicals Limited (a registered Micro Enterprise under the MSME Development Act, 2006)[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The corporate debtor initiated steps for a Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (PPIRP) under Chapter III-A of the IBC, filing a Base Resolution Plan jointly with its financial creditor, M/s. WZ Enterprises Private Limited[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The corporate debtor experienced financial distress, reporting nil revenue for the financial years ending March 31, 2021, March 31, 2022, and March 31, 2023[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Board of Directors approved filing for PPIRP on 09.08.2021, an EGM passed a special resolution on 17.09.2021, and the application under Section 54C (CP(IBPP) No. 02 of 2023) was filed along with the Base Resolution Plan on 12.09.2023[cite: 15]. The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, Mumbai Bench-1) rejected the application on 08.11.2023[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record included the MSME registration certificate, special resolutions, directors' declarations, financial creditor approvals, the resolution professional's report under Section 54B(1)(a), audited financial statements, and the Base Resolution Plan[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority acknowledged that all statutory compliances under Sections 54A and 54C were fulfilled, but dismissed the application on merits regarding the appropriateness of the Base Resolution Plan and potential circumvention of SEBI Takeover Regulations, prompting the present appeal under Section 61[cite: 15].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the Adjudicating Authority is legally justified in entering into a comprehensive assessment and rejecting a pre-packaged insolvency application under Section 54C on the merits of the Base Resolution Plan at the admission stage[cite: 15]; (ii) Whether submitting a Base Resolution Plan jointly with a financial creditor who takes over control constitutes an attempt to circumvent SEBI Takeover Regulations precluding the admission of a Section 54C application[cite: 15].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: At the admission stage of an application under Section 54C for a Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process, the Adjudicating Authority is strictly confined to verifying whether the application is complete and whether the corporate debtor satisfies the eligibility criteria under Section 54A; it cannot delve into an exhaustive assessment or premature adjudication of the appropriateness of the Base Resolution Plan[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under the statutory scheme of Chapter III-A of the IBC, the consideration, evaluation, and approval of a Base Resolution Plan fall exclusively within the commercial domain of the Committee of Creditors (CoC) under Section 54K after the process has commenced, and a corporate applicant is legally permitted under Section 5(25) and Section 54K to submit a Base Resolution Plan individually or jointly with any other person[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Adjudicating Authority explicitly noted that the corporate debtor complied with all statutory requirements of Sections 54A, 54B, and 54C, but erred by prematurely evaluating the Base Resolution Plan's impact on SEBI regulations and corporate control[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that rejecting a Section 54C application by pre-judging the Base Resolution Plan violates the statutory scheme of Chapter III-A, warranting the setting aside of the impugned order and restoration of the petition for fresh consideration[cite: 15].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1682 of 2023 is allowed[cite: 15]. The order dated 08.11.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority is set aside, and CP(IBPP) No. 02 of 2023 is revived for fresh consideration and disposal under Section 54C(4) of the IBC expeditiously within a period of three months[cite: 15].
summary: Garodia Chemicals Limited appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order rejecting its application under Section 54C of the IBC to initiate a Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (PPIRP)[cite: 15]. Although the NCLT acknowledged that all statutory pre-conditions and documentation were complete, it dismissed the petition, holding that the joint Base Resolution Plan attempted to bypass SEBI Takeover Regulations. Allowing the appeal, the NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority cannot evaluate or reject a Base Resolution Plan at the Section 54C admission stage, as plan evaluation is exclusively a CoC function under Section 54K. The matter was remanded back to the Adjudicating Authority for a fresh decision within three months[cite: 15].

case_title: Anjani Kumar Prashar (Suspended Director of Grandstar Realty Pvt. Limited) vs. Manab Datta & Ors.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Anjani Kumar Prashar, Suspended Director of Grandstar Realty Pvt. Limited (Corporate Debtor / Auction Purchaser). The Respondents are Manab Datta & Other Homebuyers/Allottees. The original developer was Akme Projects Ltd. ("Akme")[cite: 17]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Land was originally purchased by M/s Subros Ltd., which sold it to Akme via a registered sale deed dated 23.01.2012. Akme entered into Builder Buyer Agreements (BBAs) with allottees between 2012 and 2015. Due to default by Akme to YES Bank, SARFAESI proceedings were initiated, and Grandstar Realty Pvt. Ltd. purchased the property as an auction purchaser for Rs. 40.75 Crores. Sale confirmation and sale certificate were issued on 17.06.2016 and 19.07.2016, explicitly noting that allotments to prospective buyers were encumbrances and that the auction purchaser was required to honour allotments and receive unpaid consideration[cite: 17]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose from failure to complete construction and deliver possession of units to the allottees within the stipulated timelines under the BBAs, leading to an application under Section 7 filed on 25.09.2020 for a default amount of INR 78,09,94,385.56/-[cite: 17]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Adjudicating Authority admitted the Section 7 application vide order dated 26.09.2023[cite: 17]. The suspended director appealed the admission order to NCLAT[cite: 17]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record included the SARFAESI sale notice, sale confirmation advice noting allottees' encumbrances and obligations to honour allotments, the sale certificate containing the list of 220 allottees, and subsequent Supreme Court clarification orders regarding land acquisition proceedings[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench, Court V admitted CP (IB) No. 995/PB/2020 on 26.09.2023, prompting the appellant to file Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1366 of 2023[cite: 17].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an auction purchaser of a real estate project under the SARFAESI Act, 2002 that takes over project assets subject to allottee encumbrances can be held to owe a financial debt to the home allottees, qualifying them as financial creditors under Section 5(7) and 5(8) of the IBC[cite: 17]; (ii) Whether interim orders or litigation concerning land acquisition (Rameshwar v. State of Haryana) constituted a valid legal impossibility preventing construction so as to negate the existence of default[cite: 17].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An auction purchaser who acquires a real estate project under the SARFAESI Act, 2002 burdened with existing allottee encumbrances and an explicit obligation to honour allotments and receive unpaid consideration steps into the shoes of the original developer, making the financial debt owed to homebuyers enforceable against the transferee corporate debtor under the IBC[cite: 17]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(7) of the IBC defines a financial creditor as any person to whom a financial debt is owed, which broadly encompasses situations where assets and corresponding liabilities/encumbrances vest in a successor or transferee entity, preventing such entities from escaping statutory rigours[cite: 17]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed the SARFAESI Sale Confirmation Advice and Sale Certificate, verifying that Grandstar acquired the land with notice of 220 allottees as encumbrances and undertook the liability to honour their allotments, while noting that no legal restraint prevented the appellant from initiating construction after the Supreme Court's final order in 2018[cite: 17]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that Grandstar Realty owed a financial debt to the allottees, that default was clearly established due to prolonged inaction and non-construction, and that the Section 7 application was rightly admitted[cite: 17].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1366 of 2023 is dismissed, affirming the order dated 26.09.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority admitting the Section 7 application[cite: 17].
summary: Anjani Kumar Prashar, the suspended director of Grandstar Realty Pvt. Ltd., appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order admitting a Section 7 insolvency petition filed by home allottees[cite: 17]. Grandstar had acquired the project land via a SARFAESI auction from YES Bank, taking it subject to allottee encumbrances[cite: 17]. The appellant argued there was no disbursal of money to Grandstar and that land acquisition litigation prevented construction[cite: 17]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT held that because Grandstar took over the project assets along with the obligation to honour existing allotments, a financial debt was owed to the homebuyers[cite: 17]. The Tribunal also found that the appellant failed to prove any legal restraint justifying years of complete inaction, thereby confirming the existence of default and upholding the initiation of CIRP[cite: 17].

case_title: M/s. SEL Manufacturing Company Limited vs. Punjab Small Industries & Export Corporation Limited
bench: New Delhi (Judicial Member Rakesh Kumar Jain and Technical Member Ajai Das Mehrotra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is M/s. SEL Manufacturing Company Limited (Corporate Debtor / Company undergoing insolvency). The Respondent is Punjab Small Industries & Export Corporation Limited (PSIEC), a public sector undertaking of the Government of Punjab and lessor of the land[cite: 18]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A lease deed dated 22.12.2008 was executed between the appellant and the respondent for Plot No. 256-57, Phase-VIII, Focal Point, Ludhiana for 99 years, containing clauses stating that the plot price is subject to variation and enhancement of land acquisition compensation[cite: 18]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Prior to CIRP, enhanced land cost demands were raised against the allottee and its predecessor, amounting to an unpaid enhanced demand which led to a demand notice of Rs. 1,12,97,128/- issued on 05.03.2021 and a subsequent revised demand of Rs. 2,17,74,283/-[cite: 18]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Insolvency proceedings against the appellant commenced on 11.04.2018[cite: 18]. The resolution plan submitted by the Consortium of Arr Ess Industries Private Limited and Leading Edge Commercial FZE was approved by the Adjudicating Authority on 10.02.2021[cite: 18]. The respondent issued demand notices on 05.03.2021 and 27.06.2022[cite: 18]. The appellant filed IA No. 598 of 2021, which was dismissed by NCLT Chandigarh on 03.06.2022[cite: 18]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record included the allotment letter dated 01.12.1995, lease deed dated 22.12.2008, demand notices for enhanced land costs based on high court and supreme court judgments, and pending civil litigation records before the Civil Judge, Ludhiana[cite: 18]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The appellant filed IA No. 598 of 2021 before NCLT Chandigarh seeking to quash the demand notice, which was dismissed on 03.06.2022[cite: 18]. The appellant subsequently filed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 881 of 2022 before the NCLAT[cite: 18].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the 'clean slate principle' under the IBC can extinguish prior statutory demands raised by a public sector land-development authority/lessor for enhanced land acquisition costs when such demands and related litigation were not disclosed to the IRP or CoC during CIRP[cite: 18]; (ii) Whether an allottee/lessee can claim unconditional ownership or transfer of leasehold rights from a statutory lessor without clearing defects in the title and complying with enhanced cost payment obligations under the lease deed[cite: 18].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The protective umbrella and 'clean slate principle' of the IBC do not extend to compel public sector land development authorities or statutory lessors to part with public assets or issue No Objection Certificates without full payment of enhanced land costs and complete compliance with the terms and conditions of the lease deed or transfer policy[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Provisions of Section 238 of the IBC cannot be invoked to override the public duties and ownership rights of statutory bodies over public properties when pre-existing demands for clearing title defects were concealed from the IRP and CoC during CIRP[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the lease clauses and discovered that the pending litigation and enhanced land cost liabilities before the Civil Judge, Ludhiana were never disclosed in the resolution plan's extensive litigation schedules, meaning the corporate debtor and its promoters failed to disclose vital encumbrances[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the demand for enhanced land cost was meant to clear defects in the title of the land, was independent of standard CIRP operational claims, and that the appellant could not benefit from the clean slate principle given the non-disclosure, warranting dismissal of the appeal[cite: 18].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 881 of 2022 is dismissed, and all pending interlocutory applications are closed with no orders as to costs[cite: 18].
summary: M/s. SEL Manufacturing Company Limited appealed against an NCLT Chandigarh order that dismissed its application to quash a demand notice for enhanced land acquisition costs issued by the Punjab Small Industries & Export Corporation Limited (PSIEC)[cite: 18]. The appellant argued that under the 'clean slate principle' and Section 31 of the IBC, all past un-filed operational claims stood extinguished upon the approval of its resolution plan[cite: 18]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT held that the 'clean slate principle' does not apply where a public sector land authority's pre-existing demand for enhanced land costs—meant to clear land title defects—was intentionally or defaultingly omitted from disclosure to the IRP and CoC during CIRP[cite: 18]. The Tribunal ruled that statutory lessors cannot be forced to surrender property rights without full compliance with lease obligations[cite: 18].

case_title: Munagala Roja Harsha Vardhini vs. Vardhansmart Private Limited
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 23 of 2024 & IA No. 83 of 2024
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Members M. Venugopal, Sharad Kumar Sharma, and Technical Member Jatindranath Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Munagala Roja Harsha Vardhini. The Respondent is Vardhansmart Private Limited[cite: 19]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate insolvency proceedings were initiated under Section 7 of the IBC via CP (IB) No. 45/7/AMR/2020 before the NCLT Amaravathi Bench[cite: 19]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Financial defaults by the corporate debtor led to company petition filings under the IBC[cite: 19]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Adjudicating Authority pronounced the impugned order dismissing the application on 24.11.2022[cite: 19]. A free copy of the order was prepared on 02.12.2022 and received by the appellant's counsel on 07.12.2022[cite: 19]. The appellant e-filed the appeal on 19.01.2023 along with a delay condonation application (IA No. 83 of 2024) claiming a delay of 12 days based on the date of receipt of the free copy[cite: 19]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Medical certificates showing the appellant's illness (enteric fever, hepatitis, and urinary tract infection) between 18.11.2022 and 06.01.2023 were submitted, alongside records showing the appellant never applied for a paid certified copy under Section 76 of the Indian Evidence Act[cite: 19]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The appellant filed IA No. 83 of 2024 in Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 23 of 2024 before the NCLAT Chennai Bench seeking condonation of delay, which was heard and dismissed on 15.03.2024[cite: 19].
