legal_issues: (i) Whether the period of limitation for filing an appeal under Section 61(2) of the IBC commences from the date of pronouncement of the order or from the date of receipt of the free-of-cost copy supplied by the registry under Rule 50 of the NCLT Rules, 2016[cite: 19]; (ii) Whether a litigant who fails to apply for a paid certified copy can exclude time under Section 12(2) of the Limitation Act, 1963 and whether the total delay exceeding the 45-day statutory outer limit can be condoned[cite: 19].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 61(2) of the IBC, limitation commences strictly from the date of pronouncement of the order, and receipt of a free-of-cost copy under Rule 50 of the NCLT Rules does not extend limitation or substitute the mandatory requirement of applying for a certified copy under Section 76 of the Indian Evidence Act[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12(2) of the Limitation Act allows exclusion of time requisite for obtaining a copy only if a formal application for a certified copy has been made within the limitation period; in the absence of such an application, no exclusion ensues, and the appellate tribunal cannot condone delays beyond the absolute 45-day outer limit (30 days plus 15 days grace) prescribed under Section 61(2) of the IBC[cite: 19]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the order was pronounced on 24.11.2022, that the appeal was filed on 19.01.2023 (the 56th day), resulting in an actual delay of 26 days beyond the 30-day period, and that the appellant never applied for a certified copy[cite: 19]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the delay condonation application was devoid of merits because the total delay exceeded the 45-day condonable limit under the IBC, leading to the rejection of both the delay application and the appeal[cite: 19].
operative_order: IA No. 83 of 2024 (Condone Delay Application) in Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 23 of 2024 is dismissed, and consequently, the appeal itself is rejected as barred by limitation with no orders as to costs[cite: 19].
summary: Munagala Roja Harsha Vardhini filed an appeal along with a delay condonation application (IA No. 83 of 2024) against an NCLT Amaravathi Bench order dated November 24, 2022[cite: 19]. The appellant argued that the delay was only 12 days if calculated from the date she received the free copy of the order, and cited medical grounds[cite: 19]. Dismissing the application and rejecting the appeal, the NCLAT Chennai Bench held that limitation under Section 61(2) of the IBC begins strictly from the date of order pronouncement, not from the receipt of the free copy[cite: 19]. The Tribunal reiterated that failing to apply for a certified copy disentitles an appellant from claiming time exclusions under Section 12 of the Limitation Act, and because the actual delay of 26 days exceeded the maximum statutory 45-day limit, the tribunal lacked the jurisdiction to condone it[cite: 19].

case_title: State Bank of India & Others vs. The Consortium of Mr. Murari Lal Jalan and Mr. Florian Fritsch
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are the Lenders in the Monitoring Committee (MC Lenders), namely State Bank of India, JC Flowers Asset Reconstruction Private Limited, and Punjab National Bank[cite: 20]. Respondent No. 1 is the Consortium of Mr. Murari Lal Jalan and Mr. Florian Fritsch (Successful Resolution Applicant / SRA)[cite: 20]. Respondent No. 2 is the Authorized Representative of the Monitoring Committee of Jet Airways (India) Limited[cite: 20]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Jet Airways Ltd. was admitted into Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) under Section 7 of the IBC on 20.06.2019[cite: 20]. The SRA submitted a resolution plan that was approved by the Committee of Creditors (CoC) with a 99.22% vote share and sanctioned by the Adjudicating Authority on 22.06.2021[cite: 20]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Jet Airways had grounded operations since April 2019[cite: 20]. The resolution plan required an upfront first tranche payment of INR 350 Crores and Performance Bank Guarantees (PBG) totaling INR 150 Crores[cite: 20]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) re-issued the Air Operation Certificate (AOC) to the corporate debtor on 20.05.2022[cite: 20]. Following disputes over the effective date, the SRA filed an Implementation Application (I.A. No. 3398 of 2022) and an Exclusion Application (I.A. No. 3508 of 2022) before the NCLT Mumbai Bench[cite: 20]. The Adjudicating Authority allowed both applications on 13.01.2023, holding that all conditions precedent under Clause 7.6.1 of the plan were fulfilled by 20.05.2022[cite: 20]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record included the approved resolution plan, the DGCA AOC re-issuance dated 20.05.2022, joint lender meeting minutes, performance bank guarantees, and subsequent SRA capital infusion records[cite: 20]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The MC Lenders challenged the NCLT order dated 13.01.2023 via Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 129 & 130 of 2023 before the NCLAT[cite: 20]. Concurrently, various appeals and interim orders were dealt with by the Supreme Court, culminating in the NCLAT's final judgment delivered on March 12, 2024[cite: 20].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the Successful Resolution Applicant completed all conditions precedent under Clause 7.6.1 of the resolution plan by May 20, 2022[cite: 20]; (ii) Whether the lapse of the initial Air Operation Certificate during the pendency of litigation renders the resolution plan unimplementable[cite: 20]; (iii) Whether failure to deposit INR 150 Crores by January 31, 2024 pursuant to Supreme Court timelines warrants mandatory liquidation under Section 33(3) of the IBC[cite: 20].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a resolution plan is approved and conditions precedent are substantially fulfilled within extended timelines, minor operational delays caused by lender obstructionism do not invalidate the plan, and the appellate tribunal must adopt a pragmatic, pro-revival approach to save the corporate debtor from liquidation[cite: 20]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory scheme of the IBC prioritizes corporate revival over creditor recovery; performance security guarantees and provisional timelines can be adjusted or extended by the tribunal via subsequent event analysis to ensure successful implementation[cite: 20]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the DGCA re-issued the AOC on 20.05.2022, that business plan approval is an implicit part of the AOC certification workflow (CAP 3100), that slot acquisitions exceeded business plan requirements, and that international traffic rights requirements were subject to fleet thresholds governed by national civil aviation policy[cite: 20]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the Adjudicating Authority correctly held that conditions precedent were fulfilled on May 20, 2022, and dismissed the lenders' appeals while issuing structured, time-bound directions for plan implementation and operational handover[cite: 20].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 129 & 130 of 2023 are dismissed, upholding the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 13.01.2023[cite: 20]. The Monitoring Committee, MC Lenders, and SRA are directed to complete Dubai property mortgage charges within 30 days, adjust the INR 150 Crores PBG towards the first tranche payment, execute share reconstitution, disburse payments to creditors and workmen within 60 days, apply for AOC re-issuance, and complete corporate debtor handover on the closing date set at 90 days from the judgment[cite: 20].
summary: State Bank of India and other lenders appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order ruling that the Successful Resolution Applicant (Consortium of Murari Lal Jalan and Florian Fritsch) had fulfilled all conditions precedent for the revival of Jet Airways (India) Limited by May 20, 2022[cite: 20]. Dismissing the appeals, the NCLAT Principal Bench affirmed that the SRA successfully achieved conditions precedent including AOC re-issuance, business plan submission, and slot allocations[cite: 20]. The Tribunal rejected the lenders' demands for liquidation, emphasizing that the primary object of the IBC is revival rather than recovery, and issued comprehensive timelines for capital infusion, security creation, and final operational handover to make India's first aviation insolvency resolution a success[cite: 20].

case_title: Regional Provident Fund Commissioner vs. Ms. Mamta Binani & Ors.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is the Regional Provident Fund Commissioner, EPFO, Jamshedpur. Respondent No. 1 is Ms. Mamta Binani, Resolution Professional. Respondent No. 2 is the Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA). Respondent No. 3 is the State of Jharkhand. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) commenced against R.D. Rubber Reclaim Limited (Corporate Debtor) on 25.10.2019[cite: 21]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant submitted a claim totaling Rs. 2,84,11,288/-, comprising Rs. 1,02,84,785/- under Section 7A, Rs. 75,62,576/- under Section 7Q, and Rs. 1,05,63,927/- under Section 14B of the EPF & MP Act, 1952[cite: 21]. The Resolution Professional admitted the entire claim[cite: 21]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The CoC approved the resolution plan with 100% vote share on 06.11.2020[cite: 21]. The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Kolkata Bench) approved the resolution plan on 11.05.2021, providing for 100% payment of the Section 7A claim but zero payment for the Section 7Q and Section 14B claims[cite: 21]. The RP submitted the implementation report to the CoC on 02.02.2022[cite: 21]. The Appellant filed the appeal on 21.02.2022[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record included the claim forms submitted under Sections 7A, 7Q, and 14B, the RP's admission letters, the approved resolution plan, and implementation reports[cite: 21]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 245 of 2022 challenging the NCLT order dated 11.05.2021 approving the plan without payment under Sections 7Q and 14B[cite: 21].
legal_issues: (i) Whether unpaid dues under Section 7Q (interest) and Section 14B (damages) of the EPF & MP Act, 1952 form part of provident fund dues that must be paid in full under an approved resolution plan[cite: 21]; (ii) Whether the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal can recommend or facilitate the waiver of 100% damages under Section 14B through the Central Board[cite: 21].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Dues claimed under Section 7Q (interest) and Section 14B (damages) of the EPF & MP Act, 1952 constitute integral parts of provident fund dues entitled to priority, but the power to waive 100% damages under Section 14B rests with the Central Board under paragraph 32B of the EPF Scheme, a recommendation for which can be made by the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal[cite: 21]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Full payment of statutory provident fund liabilities is mandatory under Section 30(2) of the IBC; however, statutory provisions allowing the waiver of penal damages by the Central Board continue to apply to resolution applicants under the insolvency regime[cite: 21]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the Section 7A principal claim was fully paid, the Section 7Q interest claim was admitted but unpaid under the plan, and the Section 14B damages claim remained outstanding following full plan implementation[cite: 21]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the SRA must pay the admitted interest under Section 7Q within two months, while granting the SRA liberty to apply to the Central Board for a 100% waiver of damages under Section 14B within 30 days[cite: 21].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 245 of 2022 is partly allowed; the SRA (Respondent No. 3) is directed to pay the admitted Section 7Q claim of Rs. 75,62,576/- within two months, and liberty is granted to the SRA to apply to the Central Board for 100% waiver of Section 14B damages within 30 days[cite: 21]. The NCLT order dated 11.05.2021 is affirmed subject to these directions[cite: 21].
summary: The Regional Provident Fund Commissioner appealed against an NCLT Kolkata Bench order approving the resolution plan for R.D. Rubber Reclaim Limited, which paid the principal EPF dues under Section 7A in full but omitted payments for interest under Section 7Q and damages under Section 14B[cite: 21]. The NCLAT partly allowed the appeal, holding that interest under Section 7Q forms part of PF dues and must be paid in full by the SRA within two months[cite: 21]. Regarding the damages under Section 14B, the Tribunal granted liberty to the SRA to petition the Central Board for a 100% waiver, following its established precedent[cite: 21].

case_title: Dipak Dahyalal vs. M/s Steel Resources and Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 300 of 2024 & I.A. No. 1009 of 2024
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan, Technical Members Barun Mitra and Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Deepak Dahyalal, Ex-Director of M/s Pritdip Impex (India) Private Limited (Corporate Debtor). Respondent No. 1 is M/s Steel Resources (Operational Creditor). Respondent No. 2 is Mr. Rajesh Ramesh Kamath (Interim Resolution Professional)[cite: 22]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Operational Creditor filed a Section 9 petition (CP (IB) No. 277/MB/2022) against the Corporate Debtor before NCLT Mumbai Bench-VI[cite: 22]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational default by the corporate debtor led to the initiation of insolvency proceedings[cite: 22]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Adjudicating Authority admitted the Section 9 petition via an ex-parte order dated 22.11.2023[cite: 22]. The NCLT Registry sent a free copy of the impugned order to the appellant by email on 29.11.2023[cite: 22]. The appellant claimed to have learned of the order from the IRP on 06.12.2023 and subsequently filed the appeal through e-filing on 01.02.2024[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record included emails from the NCLT Registry dated 29.11.2023, communications from the IRP, records showing the appellant attended the first CoC meeting on 28.12.2023, and delay condonation arguments citing winter/Christmas holidays, bereavement, and medical issues[cite: 22]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The appellant filed I.A. No. 1009 of 2024 seeking condonation of a 41-day delay under Section 61(2) of the IBC, which was opposed by Respondent No. 1 and decided by the NCLAT Principal Bench[cite: 22].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the period of limitation for filing an appeal under Section 61(2) of the IBC commences from the date of the order or from the date of the appellant's knowledge of the order[cite: 22]; (ii) Whether the NCLAT has the power to condone a delay beyond the maximum 15-day extended period prescribed under the proviso to Section 61(2) of the IBC[cite: 22].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The limitation period for filing an appeal under Section 61(2) of the IBC is 30 days from the date of the order and is extendable by a maximum of only 15 days upon showing sufficient cause; no appeal can be entertained after the expiry of this 45-day statutory outer limit, and limitation commences from the date of the order regardless of when a party claims knowledge[cite: 22]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Unlike Section 421(3) of the Companies Act, Section 61 of the IBC consciously omits the requirement of computing limitation from the date the order is made available, establishing that the IBC is a complete code whose strict timeframes cannot be extended via general procedural rules or external considerations[cite: 22]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal calculated that the 30-day limitation period expired on 22.12.2023 and the extended 15-day grace period expired on 07.01.2024, whereas the appeal was filed on 01.02.2024—well beyond the 45-day condonable limit[cite: 22]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the appellant's excuses regarding lack of early knowledge, winter holidays, and personal bereavement could not override the absolute statutory ceiling on limitation under the IBC, requiring the dismissal of the delay application and rejection of the memo of appeal[cite: 22].
operative_order: I.A. No. 1009 of 2024 (Delay Condonation Application) is dismissed, and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 300 of 2024 is rejected as time-barred[cite: 22].
summary: Deepak Dahyalal, the ex-director of Pritdip Impex (India) Pvt. Ltd., appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 9 petition filed by M/s Steel Resources[cite: 22]. The appellant sought condonation of a 41-day delay, arguing he had no prior knowledge of the ex-parte order until December 2023 and faced intervening Christmas holidays and family bereavement[cite: 22]. Dismissing the delay application, the NCLAT Principal Bench reiterated that under the strict statutory framework of the IBC, limitation starts from the date of the order and cannot be extended beyond the maximum condonable limit of 45 days (30 + 15 days)[cite: 22]. The Tribunal held that lack of knowledge and holiday closures do not extend the statutory limitation window, resulting in the rejection of the appeal[cite: 22].

case_title: DD Finance and Holdings Private Ltd vs. Registrar of Companies, NCT of Delhi & Haryana
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Yogesh Khanna and Technical Member Ajai Das Mehrotra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is DD Finance and Holdings Private Ltd, and the Respondent is the Registrar of Companies (ROC), NCT of Delhi & Haryana[cite: 23]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant company was incorporated in 1981 and purchased an immovable property (Bhakti Bhawan Estate, Kulri Mussoorie, Uttarakhand) in 1983[cite: 23]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The company defaulted on non-filing of financial statements and annual returns, leading the ROC to initiate striking off proceedings[cite: 23]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The ROC struck off the company's name from the register vide Dissolution Notice dated 30.06.2017 under Section 248(5)[cite: 23]. The appellant's company appeal (No. 137/252/ND/2021) was dismissed by NCLT Court III, New Delhi on 27.05.2022[cite: 23]. The appellant appealed to the NCLAT[cite: 23]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record included the 1983 sale deed for the Mussoorie property, financial statements and balance sheets for multiple years (2011 to 2020), water bills, electricity bills, rent receipts, and master data showing the last AGM was held on 30.09.2011[cite: 23]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT dismissed the restoration application under Section 252(3) on 27.05.2022 due to a lack of immediate operational revenue and rental proof, prompting the company to file Company Appeal (AT) No. 112 of 2022[cite: 23].
legal_issues: Whether the Tribunal can order the restoration of a struck-off company under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 on the ground that it is 'otherwise just' when the company holds substantial fixed assets and unfiled financial records despite having zero revenue from operations[cite: 23].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, the Tribunal may order the restoration of a struck-off company if it was carrying on business, in operation, or if it is 'otherwise just' to do so, particularly where the company owns substantial immovable assets and is not a shell company engaged in illegal siphoning or tax evasion[cite: 23]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The expression 'or otherwise it is just' is an enabling provision empowering the Tribunal to prevent deadlocks and wastage of valuable properties and assets when non-compliance with filing was inadvertent and non-deliberate[cite: 23]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the company held a valuable, unencumbered fixed asset (land in Mussoorie), that default in filing returns occurred due to severe illness and the passing of key directors/accountants, and that the company possessed physical utility records, distinguishing it from abusive shell entities[cite: 23]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that keeping the company struck-off would result in an irreparable loss and deadlocked assets contrary to public policy, warranting restoration subject to appropriate cost impositions and compliance filings[cite: 23].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 112 of 2022 is allowed, setting aside the NCLT order dated 27.05.2022, and directing the ROC, New Delhi to restore the name of DD Finance and Holdings Private Ltd to the Register of Companies, subject to the appellant paying costs of Rs. 2,00,000/- to the ROC within eight weeks and filing all annual returns and balance sheets within four weeks[cite: 23].
summary: DD Finance and Holdings Private Ltd appealed against an NCLT order dismissing its petition to restore its name to the ROC register after it was struck off under Section 248(5) in 2017[cite: 23]. The appellant explained that filing defaults occurred due to the ill health and death of its managing directors and chartered accountant, and emphasized that the company owned a valuable unencumbered property in Mussoorie[cite: 23]. Allowing the appeal, the NCLAT held that because the company holds substantial fixed assets and is not a fraudulent shell company, it is 'otherwise just' to restore its name under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, thereby avoiding property deadlock and waste, subject to statutory filing compliance and cost payments[cite: 23].

case_title: M/s. Murphy Steel vs. M/s. Gujarat Wedge Wire Screens Limited
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Members Barun Mitra and Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is M/s. Murphy Steel (Operational Creditor). The Respondent is M/s. Gujarat Wedge Wire Screens Limited (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The operational creditor supplied goods to the corporate debtor over a business relationship spanning more than three decades[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The operational creditor issued a Section 8 Demand Notice on 26.12.2019 claiming an amount of Rs. 1,57,06,741/- (comprising a principal of Rs. 60,79,306/- and interest of Rs. 96,27,435/- at 24% per annum)[cite: 24]. The last invoice was dated 07.01.2017 with a default date of 22.01.2017[cite: 24]. Out of 27 total invoices submitted, 26 pertained to the period between 25.03.2011 and 28.10.2016, while only one invoice dated 07.01.2017 amounted to Rs. 8,849/-[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The corporate debtor replied to the demand notice on 07.01.2020[cite: 24]. The Section 9 application was filed before the Adjudicating Authority on 08.09.2020[cite: 24]. The Adjudicating Authority dismissed the petition on 31.10.2023[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record included 27 invoices, the Section 8 demand notice, the corporate debtor's reply notice denying the debt, and the operational creditor's claim of a running account[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad dismissed CP(IB) No. 355/AHM/2020 on 31.10.2023 holding that the bulk of the claims were old and time-barred, prompting the operational creditor to file Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 171 of 2024[cite: 24].
legal_issues: (i) Whether invoices dating back more than three years from the date of filing the Section 9 petition are barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963[cite: 24]; (ii) Whether the existence of a 'running account' can save time-barred invoices from the bar of limitation in the absence of written acknowledgments or foundational documentation[cite: 24]; (iii) Whether a single surviving invoice amounting to Rs. 8,849/- satisfies the minimum statutory threshold of Rs. 1 lakh under Section 4 of the IBC[cite: 24].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The period of limitation for filing an application under Section 9 of the IBC is governed by Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, which is three years from the date when the right to apply accrues upon default; the IBC is not a money recovery legislation and cannot be used to give a new lease of life to time-barred debts[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Invoices older than three years cannot be swept under a 'running account' theory to cross the limitation barrier unless supported by explicit documentary evidence or written acknowledgments of liability by the corporate debtor[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that 26 out of 27 invoices were dated between 2011 and 2016—well over three years prior to the petition filing date of September 8, 2020—leaving only a single valid invoice of Rs. 8,849/-, which fell far short of the Rs. 1 lakh statutory threshold under Section 4[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in dismissing the Section 9 petition as time-barred, reserving liberty for the appellant to pursue other appropriate legal remedies for debt recovery[cite: 24].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 171 of 2024 is dismissed with no orders as to costs, granting the appellant liberty to approach the appropriate forum of law to seek remedial recovery actions permissible under law[cite: 24].
summary: M/s. Murphy Steel appealed against an NCLT Ahmedabad order dismissing its Section 9 insolvency petition against M/s. Gujarat Wedge Wire Screens Limited[cite: 24]. The operational creditor claimed Rs. 1.57 Crores based on a series of invoices, arguing they formed part of a running account[cite: 24]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that 26 out of 27 invoices were more than three years old and thus time-barred under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, since no evidence established a running account or a valid written acknowledgement of debt[cite: 24]. The sole surviving invoice of Rs. 8,849/- failed to meet the statutory threshold of Rs. 1 lakh required under Section 4 of the IBC, confirming that the insolvency framework cannot be used as a substitute for ordinary money recovery[cite: 24].

case_title: Mr. Pawan Vikram Sajhwani vs. Mr. Santanu T. Ray, Liquidator of Oneworld Industries Pvt Ltd
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan, Judicial Member Yogesh Khanna, and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Mr. Pawan Vikram Sajhwani (Licensee of the premises). The Respondent is Mr. Santanu T. Ray, Liquidator of Oneworld Industries Pvt Ltd (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 25]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor licensed certain premises to the Appellant prior to liquidation proceedings[cite: 25]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Following the failure of multiple auction attempts to sell the liquidation estate assets, the Liquidator filed an interlocutory application (I.A. No. 1160 of 2021) seeking the eviction of the licensee to facilitate the sale of the vacant property[cite: 25]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A liquidation order was passed against the corporate debtor on 15.11.2019[cite: 25]. The Small Causes Court granted an interim status quo order in favor of the appellant on 06.10.2021 (LD Suit No. 97 of 2021) restraining dispossession without due process[cite: 25]. The Adjudicating Authority passed the eviction order directing the appellant to hand over vacant possession within 15 days on 04.01.2024[cite: 25]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record included the lease/license arrangement, the Small Causes Court order dated 06.10.2021, and records showing five failed auction attempts due to the appellant's continued physical possession[cite: 25]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Mumbai Bench allowed I.A. No. 1160 of 2021 on 04.01.2024, prompting the appellant licensee to file Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 166 of 2024 before the NCLAT[cite: 25].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) possesses the residuary jurisdiction under Section 60(5)(c) of the IBC to entertain and pass eviction orders against a licensee occupying assets forming part of the liquidation estate, notwithstanding parallel proceedings or injunctions issued by a civil court/Small Causes Court[cite: 25]; (ii) Whether a civil suit instituted against the liquidator after the commencement of liquidation violates the bar under Section 33(5) and Section 63 of the IBC[cite: 25].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority possesses the necessary residuary jurisdiction under Section 60(5)(c) of the IBC to pass eviction orders against licensees occupying immovable properties that form part of the corporate debtor's liquidation estate, and the jurisdiction of civil courts is barred under Section 63 in respect of matters where the NCLT has jurisdiction[cite: 25]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 35(1)(b), 35(1)(d), and 36(3) of the IBC empower the liquidator to take custody and control of all assets of the corporate debtor—regardless of whether they are in physical possession—and Section 33(5) prohibits the institution of suits or legal proceedings against the corporate debtor or liquidator once liquidation has commenced without prior NCLT approval[cite: 25]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that five previous auction attempts failed due to the appellant's physical occupation, that the civil suit was instituted in 2021 after the 2019 liquidation order in contravention of Section 33(5), and that the liquidator invoked NCLT jurisdiction as the appropriate due process of law[cite: 25]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the NCLT acted completely within its statutory competence in ordering the eviction of the licensee to preserve and maximize the liquidation estate, warranting the dismissal of the appeal[cite: 25].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 166 of 2024 is dismissed, affirming the NCLT Mumbai order dated 04.01.2024 directing the appellant to hand over vacant and peaceful possession of the premises to the liquidator[cite: 25].
summary: Pawan Vikram Sajhwani, a licensee occupying premises owned by Oneworld Industries Pvt Ltd, appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order directing him to hand over vacant possession of the property to the liquidator within 15 days[cite: 25]. The appellant argued that eviction matters exclusively vest in the Small Causes Court under Section 41 of the Presidency Small Causes Courts Act, 1882, and cited a subsisting status quo order[cite: 25]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that the NCLT has full residuary jurisdiction under Section 60(5)(c) of the IBC to evict occupants from assets belonging to the liquidation estate[cite: 25]. The Tribunal ruled that the civil suit filed after the 2019 liquidation order violated Section 33(5) and Section 63 of the IBC, and that invoking NCLT jurisdiction satisfies the requirement of following 'due process of law'[cite: 25].

case_title: Yester Investment Private Limited vs. Manish Motilal Jaju & Ors.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Yester Investment Private Limited (Homebuyer/Allottee). Respondent No. 1 is Manish Motilal Jaju (Resolution Professional / Chairman of Monitoring Committee of Sivana Realty Private Limited). Respondent No. 3 is LIC Housing Finance Limited (LICHFL). Respondent No. 4 is Mr. Vithal M. Dahake (Authorized Representative of Homebuyers/Allottees). Respondent No. 5 is M/s. Kabra Estate and Investment Consultant (Successful Resolution Applicant / SRA)[cite: 26]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor (Sivana Realty Pvt. Ltd.) developed two real estate projects: Samridhi Gardens (Phase-1) and Oakwood Plaza (Phase-2). In 2015, the appellant advanced Rs. 7.50 Crores for six flats in Wing-D of Samridhi Gardens, initially executed via an unregistered agreement dated 10.07.2015 and later through a registered agreement dated 09.08.2018[cite: 26]. Meanwhile, the corporate debtor had executed a loan facility agreement with LICHFL on 15.09.2017 granting LICHFL a charge over the project[cite: 26]. The appellant's subsequent 2018 agreement was executed without obtaining a No Objection Certificate (NOC) from LICHFL[cite: 26]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The corporate debtor defaulted on financial obligations, resulting in the admission of CP (IB) No. 3169/MB/2019 on 11.08.2020[cite: 26]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The initial Phase-1 resolution plan submitted by Vira Realspace LLP was withdrawn by the CoC on 03.08.2021[cite: 26]. A fresh Form-G inviting holistic resolution for both phases was published on 08.08.2021[cite: 26]. The SRA (Kabra Group) submitted its EOI on 17.08.2021, and the CoC approved its resolution plan on 30.10.2021 with a 99.96% vote share[cite: 26]. The Adjudicating Authority approved the resolution plan and dismissed the appellant's objection on 19.07.2023[cite: 26]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record included the unregistered 2015 agreement, the registered 2018 agreement without LICHFL's NOC, CoC meeting minutes, EOI submissions, voting patterns within the homebuyer class, and previous NCLAT rulings upholding the plan's classification of homebuyers[cite: 26]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The appellant filed IA No. 368/2022 to object to the plan and IA No. 2981/2021 was filed by the RP for plan approval; both were dismissed/allowed respectively by NCLT Mumbai on 19.07.2023, leading to Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) Nos. 1286 and 1287 of 2023[cite: 26].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a homebuyer who purchased units without obtaining an NOC from the mortgagee financial institution (LICHFL) can challenge their classification as an 'affected homebuyer' under an approved resolution plan[cite: 26]; (ii) Whether the CoC acted illegally by withdrawing an earlier phase-1 plan and issuing a fresh Form-G for holistic project resolution[cite: 26].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Homebuyers within a class must sail with the collective decision of the majority, and minority or dissenting homebuyers cannot maintain independent objections against a resolution plan approved by an overwhelming majority of their class, nor can they challenge classifications that differentiate between units allotted with or without mortgagee NOCs[cite: 26]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The commercial wisdom of the CoC in restructuring real estate projects, consolidating phases, and categorizing allottees into 'affected' and 'unaffected' homebuyers based on valid mortgagee charges is non-justiciable under the IBC[cite: 26]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the appellant's 2018 agreement was executed without LICHFL's NOC post-dating the 2017 mortgage agreement, that 87.56% of unaffected and 57.63% of affected homebuyers voted in favor of the plan, and that the total CoC approval stood at 99.96%[cite: 26]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the appellant's categorization as an affected homebuyer was fully justified, that no material irregularity or back-door entry occurred during the fresh Form-G process, and that the appeals lacked merit[cite: 26].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1286 and 1287 of 2023 are dismissed, upholding the Adjudicating Authority's orders dated 19.07.2023 with no orders as to costs[cite: 26].
summary: Yester Investment Pvt. Ltd., an allottee of six flats in Sivana Realty's Samridhi Gardens project, appealed against NCLT Mumbai orders approving the resolution plan submitted by M/s. Kabra Estate and Investment Consultants and dismissing the appellant's objections[cite: 26]. The appellant argued that its 2015 advance payment predated LICHFL's mortgage agreement and that the SRA was given a back-door entry[cite: 26]. Dismissing the appeals, the NCLAT held that because the appellant's formal agreement was executed in 2018 without LICHFL's required NOC, its categorization as an 'affected homebuyer' was proper[cite: 26]. Citing the Supreme Court's ruling in Jaypee Kensington, the Tribunal emphasized that a minority homebuyer must abide by the commercial wisdom and majority vote of the homebuyer class (which approved the plan with 99.96% total CoC share), and found no procedural irregularity in the fresh Form-G issuance[cite: 26].

case_title: Prem Prakash vs. Competition Commission of India & Ors.
appeal_number: I.A. No. 758 of 2023 in Compensation Application No. 1 of 2023 in Competition Commission Case No. 50 of 2014
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice M. Venugopal and Technical Member Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Applicant is Prem Prakash, Sole Proprietor of Venus Testing and Research Laboratory. Respondent No. 1 is the Competition Commission of India (CCI). Respondent No. 2 is the Director General, CPWD. Respondent No. 3 is the Principal Secretary, Madhya Pradesh PWD[cite: 25]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The applicant filed compensation applications/appeals following CCI's order dated 17.03.2017 in Case No. 50 of 2014 concerning material testing accreditation requirements by MPPWD and CPWD[cite: 25]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The applicant sought compensation of Rs. 9 Crores against DG, CPWD and Rs. 30 Crores against Principal Secretary, MPPWD[cite: 25]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CCI passed its order on 17.03.2017. Compensation Application No. 01 of 2022 was dismissed as withdrawn with liberty to file a corrected application on 27.07.2022[cite: 25]. The applicant subsequently filed I.A. No. 758 of 2023 to waive re-filing fees[cite: 25]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record included previous NCLAT withdrawal orders, records regarding the applicant's unauthorized counsel (Mr. Sumit Jain), and Rule 4 of the Competition Appellate Tribunal Rules, 2009[cite: 25]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The applicant filed I.A. No. 758 of 2023 in Compensation Application No. 1 of 2023 seeking a waiver of the Rs. 3,00,000/- court fee for re-filing, which the NCLAT Principal Bench dismissed on 11.03.2024[cite: 25].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLAT can waive the statutory court fees for re-filing a compensation application under Rule 4(3) of the Competition Appellate Tribunal (Form and Fee for filing Competition Applications) Rules, 2009 due to alleged unauthorized withdrawal by a proxy counsel or on grounds of client suffering from counsel default[cite: 25].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Rule 4(3) of the Competition Appellate Tribunal Rules, 2009 restricts the waiver of fees strictly to circumstances involving the economic condition or indigent circumstances of the petitioner/appellant, or similar compelling reasons[cite: 25]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: General principles protecting clients from advocate default (such as in Rafiq v. Munshilal) do not apply to exempt statutory court fees when the counsel was actively present, participating, and acting on instructions during hearings, and when the applicant fails to demonstrate any indigent circumstances[cite: 25]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed the applicant's financial standing and submissions, finding no evidence of indigent circumstances or extreme economic hardship that would justify waiving the mandatory Rs. 3 lakhs fee[cite: 25]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the application for fee waiver lacked legal justification under the governing rules, resulting in the dismissal of the interlocutory application[cite: 25].
operative_order: I.A. No. 758 of 2023 in Compensation Application No. 1 of 2023 is dismissed[cite: 25].
summary: Prem Prakash, sole proprietor of Venus Testing and Research Laboratory, filed an interlocutory application (I.A. No. 758 of 2023) seeking a waiver of the Rs. 3,00,000/- court fee required to re-file a compensation application[cite: 25]. The applicant argued that his previous counsel had unauthorizedly withdrawn the initial application and that he should not suffer for counsel's default[cite: 25]. The CCI opposed the application, highlighting multiple litigations filed by the same proxy representative[cite: 25]. Dismissing the application, the NCLAT held that fee waivers under Rule 4(3) of the Competition Appellate Tribunal Rules, 2009 require proof of indigent circumstances or severe economic hardship, neither of which was demonstrated by the applicant[cite: 25].

case_title: CA Pranaav G. Ambekar vs. National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) & Ors.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Rakesh Kumar Jain and Technical Member Naresh Salecha)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is CA Pranaav G. Ambekar (ICAI Membership No. 240379, member of the engagement team for statutory audit of Coffee Day Global Limited). The Respondent is the National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) along with others. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: NFRA initiated investigations into statutory auditors following a SEBI report shared in April 2022 regarding the fraudulent diversion of Rs. 3,535 Crores from seven subsidiary companies of Coffee Day Enterprises Limited (CDEL) to Mysore Amalgamated Coffee Estate Limited (MACEL). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The statutory audit for the Financial Year 2018-19 failed to uncover material misstatements totaling Rs. 7,514.10 Crores, including fraudulent transactions with MACEL, un-reported understatements of loans, and lack of internal financial controls. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NFRA issued a show-cause notice to the appellant on 15.11.2022. The appellant sought an extension, which was granted until 29.01.2023. The auditing firm filed a detailed reply on 24.01.2023, and the appellant adopted the firm's reply as his own on 30.01.2023. NFRA passed the impugned order on 12.04.2023 holding the appellant guilty of professional misconduct, imposing a penalty of Rs. 5 Lacs, and debarring him for five years. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Audit files, DVDs containing audit papers, show-cause notices, and letters/emails exchanged between the appellant and NFRA, including the appellant's adoption letter dated 30.01.2023. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The appellant filed Comp. App. (AT) No. 89 of 2023 before the NCLAT challenging the NFRA order solely on grounds of violation of principles of natural justice due to allegedly missing annexures/documents with the show-cause notice.
legal_issues: Whether the failure to physically enclose documents listed in Annexure A with the show-cause notice vitiates the disciplinary proceedings under principles of natural justice when the appellant chose to adopt the detailed reply submitted by his audit firm instead of requesting the documents or filing an independent response.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A plea of violation of principles of natural justice due to non-supply of documents fails when an appellant demonstrates complete awareness of the charges, seeks and utilizes extended time to respond, and voluntarily adopts the comprehensive defense reply filed by their primary audit firm rather than requesting the specific documents during the pendency of proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 132(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 empowers NFRA to investigate and penalize chartered accountants for professional misconduct, and procedural compliance is satisfied if the noticee is afforded a reasonable opportunity to defend themselves. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the audit firm (ASRMP & Co.) had full access to the documents, submitted a detailed response on 24.01.2023, and that the appellant formally adopted that response on 30.01.2023 without ever requesting the missing DVD or raising a grievance regarding documents prior to the final order. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the appellant's belated grievance regarding natural justice was an afterthought, as he suffered no prejudice having consciously chosen to rely on the firm's reply, rendering the appeal meritless.
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) No. 89 of 2023 is dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: CA Pranaav G. Ambekar appealed against an NFRA order finding him guilty of professional misconduct during the statutory audit of Coffee Day Global Limited for FY 2018-19, which resulted in a five-year debarment and a Rs. 5 Lac penalty. The appellant argued a violation of natural justice, claiming that documents listed in Annexure A of the show-cause notice were not enclosed. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT held that the appellant suffered no prejudice because he consciously chose to adopt the detailed reply filed by his audit firm instead of asking for the documents during the extension period granted to him. The Tribunal found no procedural infirmity or violation of natural justice.

case_title: Supreme Construction Developers Pvt. Ltd. vs. Puranik Builders Ltd.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 215 of 2024 & I.A. No. 734 of 2024
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan, Judicial Member Yogesh Khanna, and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Supreme Construction Developers Pvt. Ltd. The Respondent is Puranik Builders Ltd.. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An interlocutory application (IA-5059(MB)2023) seeking recall of an order dated 09.10.2023 was filed before the Adjudicating Authority. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (procedural appeal regarding limitation and dismissal of recall application). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Adjudicating Authority passed the impugned order dismissing the recall application on 07.11.2023 in the presence of counsels for both parties. The order was uploaded on the NCLT website on 19.12.2023, and the appellant applied for a certified copy on 19.12.2023, receiving it on 20.12.2023. The appeal was e-filed on 06.01.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record included the NCLT order sheet dated 07.11.2023 noting counsel appearances, certified copy application records, and delay condonation pleadings. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The appellant filed I.A. No. 734 of 2024 for condonation of delay in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 215 of 2024, which was dismissed by the NCLAT Principal Bench on 01.03.2024.
legal_issues: (i) Whether the limitation period for filing an appeal under Section 61(2) of the IBC commences from the date of the order pronounced in the presence of the parties or from the date the order is uploaded on the website; (ii) Whether the NCLAT has the power to condone a delay beyond the maximum 15-day extended period under the proviso to Section 61(2) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When an order is passed by the Adjudicating Authority in the presence of both parties or their counsels, limitation commences from the date of the order, and the party cannot plead lack of knowledge or rely solely on the website uploading date to bypass statutory timelines. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) of the IBC prescribes a strict 30-day limitation period extendable by a maximum of only 15 days upon sufficient cause, forming an absolute 45-day outer ceiling which cannot be exceeded. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the order dated 07.11.2023 was passed in the presence of the appellant's counsel, that the certified copy was applied for well after 30 days (on 19.12.2023), and that the appeal filed on 06.01.2024 was well beyond the maximum condonable 45-day period. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the appellant's reliance on the uploading date was misplaced given their presence at the pronouncement, and because the delay exceeded the 15-day condonable grace period, the delay application must be dismissed.
operative_order: I.A. No. 734 of 2024 (Delay Condonation Application) is dismissed, and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 215 of 2024 is rejected.
summary: Supreme Construction Developers Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order dated November 7, 2023, which dismissed its recall application. The appellant filed an application to condone the delay, arguing that it only became aware of the order when it was uploaded on the website on December 19, 2023. Dismissing the delay application, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that limitation began on November 7, 2023, because the order was passed in the presence of the appellant's counsel. The Tribunal distinguished the Supreme Court's ruling in Sanjay Pandurang Kalate on grounds that no substantive order was pronounced in that case, whereas here the order was delivered in open court in the presence of both parties. Since the appeal was filed beyond the 45-day maximum statutory ceiling, the tribunal lacked jurisdiction to condone the delay.

case_title: Manacles Transformers Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs. Registrar of Companies, Delhi
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Yogesh Khanna and Technical Member Ajai Das Mehrotra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Manacles Transformers Pvt. Ltd. and another. The Respondent is the Registrar of Companies (RoC), Delhi. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The company was incorporated on 20.07.2012 and intended to establish business operations with M/s Diamond Power Infrastructure Limited (DPIL); however, DPIL went into insolvency liquidation in 2017, preventing the commencement of business activities. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The company filed financial statements and annual returns up to 2015-16 but failed to file them for subsequent years, leading the RoC to strike off its name under Section 248(5) on 29.10.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT, New Delhi dismissed the appellant's restoration appeal (Appeal No. 03/252/ND/2022) via an impugned order dated 22.08.2022, prompting the present appeal before the NCLAT. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Independent auditor reports for FY 2016-17 through 2020-21 reflecting substantial fixed assets (Rs. 56.32 crores), non-current assets (Rs. 6.23 crores), non-current liabilities (Rs. 7.36 crores), current liabilities (Rs. 88.00 crores), and loans & advances (Rs. 25.93 crores). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT rejected restoration due to 'NIL' revenue and unfiled returns for 2016-17 and 2017-18, leading to Comp. App. (AT) No. 175 of 2022. NCLAT heard the matter and disposed of the appeal on 15.03.2024.
legal_issues: Whether a struck-off company with substantial movable and immovable assets, which failed to file statutory returns due to operational disruptions caused by a business partner's insolvency, qualifies for name restoration under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 on the ground that it is 'otherwise just'.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, a company's name may be restored if it was carrying on business, in operation, or if it is 'otherwise just' to do so, particularly when the company holds substantial assets, is not a fraudulent shell company, and default in filings resulted from inadvertence or external business failures. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Nil revenue from operations cannot be the sole standalone criterion to refuse restoration if the company possesses genuine, massive infrastructure, tangible assets, and active liabilities, and is facing pending proceedings (such as with the Income Tax Department) requiring a functional corporate entity to protect stakeholders. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the independent auditor reports and verified that the company held over Rs. 56 crores in fixed assets and faced genuine setbacks because its primary business associate (DPIL) entered insolvency, establishing that the company was not an abusive shell entity. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that restoring the company name causes no prejudice to the RoC and promotes substantial justice, subject to the payment of costs and the immediate filing of pending financial returns.
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) No. 175 of 2022 is disposed of, setting aside the NCLT order dated 22.08.2022, and directing the RoC, New Delhi to restore the name of Manacles Transformers Private Limited to the Register of Companies, subject to the appellant paying costs of Rs. 2,00,000/- to the RoC within eight weeks and filing all annual returns and balance sheets within four weeks.
summary: Manacles Transformers Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT order refusing to restore its name to the RoC register after it was struck off in 2019 under Section 248(5). The appellant explained that its failure to file returns for 2016-17 and 2017-18 occurred because its shared chartered accountant defaulted while its intended business partner, DPIL, entered insolvency liquidation. Allowing the appeal, the NCLAT held that because the company holds substantial fixed assets (exceeding Rs. 56 crores), is not a fraudulent shell company, and is involved in pending tax proceedings, it is 'just and equitable' to restore its name under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, subject to compliance filings and cost payments.

case_title: Novho Careers Private Limited vs. Karvy Next Limited
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 393 of 2023 & IA No. 1205/2023 & IA No. 1206/2023
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Members M. Venugopal, Sharad Kumar Sharma, and Technical Member Jatindranath Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Novho Careers Private Limited (Operational Creditor). The Respondent is Karvy Next Limited (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate insolvency proceedings were initiated under Section 9 via CP(IB) No. 92/09/HDB/2022 before the NCLT Hyderabad Bench-II, which dismissed the main company petition[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (procedural appeal regarding limitation and delay condonation)[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Adjudicating Authority passed the impugned order on 18.07.2023[cite: 15]. The 30-day limitation period expired on 17.08.2023 (or 18.08.2023), and the extended 15-day grace period lapsed on 01.09.2023[cite: 15]. The appellant e-filed the appeal on 02.09.2023, resulting in an actual delay of 16 days beyond the initial 30 days[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record included appeal papers, IA No. 1205 of 2023 seeking delay condonation citing time spent in obtaining a web copy and legal opinions, and exemption applications[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The appellant filed an application for delay condonation (IA No. 1205 of 2023) in Comp. App. (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 393 of 2023 before the NCLAT Chennai Bench, which was heard and dismissed on 11.03.2024[cite: 15].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the period of limitation for filing an appeal under Section 61(2) of the IBC commences from the date of order pronouncement or from the date of obtaining a web copy/legal opinion[cite: 15]; (ii) Whether the NCLAT has the jurisdiction to condone a delay exceeding the maximum statutory outer limit of 45 days (30 + 15 days)[cite: 15].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The limitation period for filing an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC is 30 days from the date of the order, extendable by a maximum of 15 days upon showing sufficient cause; the tribunal is not empowered to condone delays exceeding this absolute 45-day statutory outer limit. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Limitation must be computed strictly from the date of pronouncement of the order rather than the date of knowledge or the date of obtaining legal opinions, and procedural rules cannot override the mandatory timeframe of the IBC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the impugned order was pronounced on 18.07.2023, that the 45-day condonable period expired on 01.09.2023, and that the appeal filed on 02.09.2023 exceeded the statutory threshold. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the delay condonation application lacked sufficient cause and exceeded the maximum condonable window, resulting in the dismissal of the delay application and rejection of the appeal.
operative_order: IA No. 1205 of 2023 (Condone Delay Application) in Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 393 of 2023 is dismissed, and consequently, the appeal itself is rejected with no orders as to costs[cite: 15].
summary: Novho Careers Private Limited filed an appeal along with a delay condonation application (IA No. 1205 of 2023) against an NCLT Hyderabad order dated July 18, 2023[cite: 15]. The appellant argued that the 16-day delay occurred because it had to obtain a web copy and seek legal opinions from Chennai counsel[cite: 15]. Dismissing the application and rejecting the appeal, the NCLAT Chennai Bench held that limitation begins strictly from the date of order pronouncement and that the tribunal lacks jurisdiction to condone delays exceeding the maximum 45-day statutory limit (30 days plus 15 days grace) under Section 61(2) of the IBC[cite: 15].

case_title: M/s. Bhagyanagar Hotels Private Limited vs. Mr. Krishna Mohan Gollamudi, Liquidator of Sainath Estates Pvt. Ltd.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 13 of 2024 & IA No. 199 of 2024
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Members M. Venugopal, Sharad Kumar Sharma, and Technical Member Jatindranath Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is M/s. Bhagyanagar Hotels Private Limited (Lessee/Occupant). The Respondent is Mr. Krishna Mohan Gollamudi, Liquidator of M/s. Sainath Estates Private Limited (Corporate Debtor). The Intervenor/Petitioner in IA No. 199/2024 is Canara Bank (Proposed Respondent No. 2/Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor acquired land admeasuring 15,092 sq. yards at Begumpet, Secunderabad in 1993, which was leased to the Appellant (operating Chiraan Fort Club & Hotels). The Appellant executed an unregistered MOU on 26.07.2012, followed by a formal registered Lease Deed dated 30.09.2017 for a 5-year period. Appellant obtained credit facilities of Rs. 31 Crores from Canara Bank to construct superstructures (Manasarovar Fern Building) backed by Corporate Debtor's guarantee and mortgage. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default on the Corporate Debtor's own loan facilities with Canara Bank totaled Rs. 34,31,36,384.64 (Principal: Rs. 6,34,06,773.66; Interest: Rs. 27,97,29,610.98), leading to recovery orders by DRT-II Hyderabad on 31.12.2019; Canara Bank also filed a Section 7 application against the Appellant for defaulting on its Rs. 31 Crore facility. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The registered lease expired on 30.09.2022 by efflux of time without renewal. The Appellant requested lease extension and rent waiver citing Covid-19 lockdowns on 04.10.2021, which the Liquidator refused via email on 17.12.2022 following a formal delivery demand letter dated 26.11.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record included the registered Lease Deed dated 30.09.2017 expiring on 30.09.2022, unregistered MOU dated 26.07.2012, Form D dated 06.08.2022 filed by Canara Bank admitting a pari passu charge and relinquishment to the liquidation estate, GHMC regularization proceedings dated 22.12.2010, and MCA master data establishing common suspended directors between Appellant and Corporate Debtor. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Corporate Debtor entered liquidation in CP (IB) No. 651/7/HDB/2018. The Liquidator filed IA (IBC) No. 265/2023 under Sections 60(5), 35, and 36 of the IBC. NCLT Hyderabad Bench-I allowed the application on 04.12.2023, holding the Appellant's post-expiry occupation unlawful and directing physical possession handover by 29.01.2024 with rent arrears, prompting the present appeal.
legal_issues: (i) Whether the Adjudicating Authority possesses summary jurisdiction under Section 60(5), Section 35, and Section 36 of the IBC to order the eviction of an erstwhile lessee whose registered lease has expired by efflux of time without requiring the Liquidator to file a civil suit; (ii) Whether a secured financial creditor holding a pari passu charge who has relinquished its security interest into the liquidation estate is a necessary or proper party to an eviction appeal concerning the Corporate Debtor's liquidation assets.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority exercising jurisdiction under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code possesses summary statutory jurisdiction to direct eviction and restore physical possession of an asset forming part of the liquidation estate from an occupant whose registered lease has expired by efflux of time, without relegating the liquidator to prolonged civil eviction suits. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(5)(c) confers wide residuary jurisdiction to adjudicate questions arising out of or in relation to the liquidation of a corporate debtor. Sections 35(1)(b) and 36, read with Regulation 9 of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, mandatorily obligate the liquidator to take custody and control of all assets in actual or constructive possession forming part of the liquidation estate; post-expiry retention of premises reduces the lessee to a tenant at sufferance whose unauthorized possession directly obstructs liquidation timelines. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under Section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act and Sections 17(d) and 49(a) of the Registration Act, an unregistered agreement cannot confer leasehold rights beyond the statutory period, and once a registered lease expires without extension or waiver, the occupant's possession becomes unlawful juridical sufferance with no defense to summary eviction. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The registered lease having determined on 30.09.2022 by efflux of time, the Appellant occupied the premises unlawfully; hence the Adjudicating Authority committed no legal error in ordering eviction and recovery of rent arrears under Section 60(5), while Canara Bank lacked standing as a necessary or proper party having relinquished its charge.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 13 of 2024 is dismissed with no order as to costs[cite: 1]. The Appellant is directed to vacate and handover vacant physical possession of premises bearing House Nos. 1-8-322 to 335, Begumpet, Secunderabad (15,092 sq. yards) to the Liquidator within one month from the date of pronouncement, along with arrears of rent[cite: 1]. IA No. 199 of 2024 (Impleadment Application by Canara Bank) is dismissed, and IA No. 52 of 2024 is closed[cite: 1].
summary: M/s. Bhagyanagar Hotels Private Limited appealed against an NCLT Hyderabad order directing it to vacate and handover 15,092 sq. yards of commercial premises in Secunderabad to the Liquidator of Sainath Estates Private Limited, along with payment of rent arrears[cite: 1]. The Appellant claimed ownership over the superstructures based on an unregistered 2012 MOU and asserted that the NCLT lacked jurisdiction to order eviction without a formal civil suit[cite: 1]. Canara Bank also sought impleadment as a charge-holder[cite: 1]. Dismissing both the appeal and the bank's impleadment application, the NCLAT Chennai Bench held that upon expiry of the registered lease by efflux of time on 30.09.2022, the Appellant became a tenant at sufferance in unlawful possession[cite: 1]. The Tribunal ruled that the NCLT has full summary jurisdiction under Section 60(5) and Sections 35/36 of the IBC to order eviction to facilitate liquidation without requiring a civil suit[cite: 1].

case_title: Pankaj Mehta vs. M/s. Ansal Hi-Tech Townships Limited
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice M. Venugopal and Technical Member Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Pankaj Mehta (Authorised Representative of 152 allottees/financial creditors). The Respondent is M/s. Ansal Hi-Tech Townships Limited (Corporate Debtor/Developer). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor was selected under the UP Hi-Tech Township Policy, 2003, to develop a large-scale township named 'Sushant Megapolis' across 2504 acres adjoining Greater Noida, UP, comprising plots, built-up units, and high-rise apartments, entering into Plot Allottee, Built-up Unit, and Apartment Allottee agreements with allottees between 2006 and 2011. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The total debt claimed in default across 107 units was Rs. 41,81,90,116/- as on 15.03.2021 along with interest @ 18% per annum; units were not delivered within the promised 36 to 42 months from layout sanction. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A legal demand notice was issued by Applicant No. 1 on 17.10.2019. An NCDRC class action complaint was allowed on 16.10.2020 ordering principal refund plus 8% interest per annum, followed by execution proceedings (EA No. 77 of 2021). The Section 7 company petition, CP (IB) No. 596 (PB)/2021, was filed before the NCLT Principal Bench and dismissed on 06.01.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record included 3 kinds of allotment agreements, payment receipts/ledger statements, environmental clearance letter dated 09.10.2009/07.10.2009 for the township, marketing brochures, letters dated 22.07.2011 and 10.08.2023, and records showing 25 separate standalone RERA registrations covering 9 project categories across the township with separate building sanction plans, as well as a list showing approximately 50 joint co-applicants/third applicants for single units. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi dismissed CP (IB) No. 596 (PB)/2021 on 06.01.2023 as not maintainable, holding that the allottees belonged to different RERA-registered projects and failed to satisfy the threshold of 100 allottees or 10% under the second proviso to Section 7(1) of the IBC, leading to Company Appeal (AT) (INS) No. 248 of 2023.
legal_issues: (i) Whether allottees holding contracts across multiple distinct, separately RERA-registered phases/sub-projects within an expansive township can pool together to fulfill the minimum threshold criteria of 100 allottees or 10% under the second proviso to Section 7(1) of the IBC by treating the entire township as a 'single real estate project'; (ii) Whether each phase/sub-project registered separately under Section 3 of RERA, 2016 constitutes an independent 'real estate project' for reckoning the critical mass under Section 7(1) of the IBC; (iii) Whether multiple joint applicants for a single unit can be counted as individual separate allottees to reach the statutory threshold of 100 allottees.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: For the purpose of satisfying the statutory threshold under the second proviso to Section 7(1) of the IBC, allottees must belong to the 'same real estate project'; separate phases or sub-projects independently registered under RERA with distinct sanctioned plans and schedules constitute standalone real estate projects, and allottees across such separate projects cannot club together to reach the critical mass of 100 allottees or 10%. Furthermore, joint allottees of a single unit count as only one allottee. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8)(f) Explanation (ii) of the IBC adopts the definitions of 'allottee' and 'real estate project' from Sections 2(d) and 2(zn) of RERA, 2016. Read with the Explanation to Section 3(1) of RERA, where a project is developed in phases or distinct categories, each phase/sub-project having independent RERA registration constitutes a separate real estate project. The second proviso to Section 7(1) deliberately restricts the filing to the same project to ensure an authentic critical mass and avoid dragging multi-project developers into insolvency at the behest of fragmented buyers across separate undertakings. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized RERA registration certificates and building sanction approvals, finding 25 distinct RERA-registered sub-projects within the 1500+ acre township across 9 categories; the 107 unitholders (inflated by joint applicants) were distributed across these separate projects, and in none of the individual RERA project categories did the applicants meet either 100 allottees or the 10% threshold. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 company petition was not maintainable in law as the applicants failed to satisfy the mandatory threshold under the second proviso to Section 7(1) within any single registered real estate project, and the NCLT committed no error in dismissing the petition.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (INS) No. 248 of 2023 is dismissed with no order as to costs. All connected pending Interlocutory Applications are closed.
summary: Homebuyers and allottees led by Pankaj Mehta appealed against an NCLT Principal Bench order dismissing their Section 7 CIRP application against M/s. Ansal Hi-Tech Townships Limited regarding the 'Sushant Megapolis' project. The appellants claimed that despite 25 separate RERA registrations, the entire 2504-acre township constituted a single integrated project based on pre-RERA agreements and common layout clearances. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC read with Section 2(zn) and Section 3(1) of RERA, each separately registered phase constitutes an independent real estate project. Because the 107 applicants were scattered across 9 different project categories and joint unitholders could only count as a single allottee, the applicants failed to meet the statutory threshold of 100 allottees or 10% from the same project under Section 7(1), rendering the petition non-maintainable.

case_title: Pawankumar Manguturam Bairagra vs. Encore Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 701 of 2023 & IA No. 5362 of 2023
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Pawankumar Manguturam Bairagra, Suspended Director of Bairagra Builders Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Guarantor/Mortgagor). Respondent No. 1 is Encore Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. (Financial Creditor/Assignee). Respondent No. 2 is Bairagra Builders Pvt. Ltd. through the IRP. The original lender was Kallappanna Awade Ichalkaranji Janata Sahakari Bank Ltd. (KAIJS Bank). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: KAIJS Bank sanctioned term loans of Rs. 10 Crore to Shri Tradco Deesan Pvt. Ltd. (Borrower No. 1) and Rs. 15 Crore to Shri Tradco India Pvt. Ltd. (Borrower No. 2) on 27.03.2019. The Corporate Debtor secured these loans by executing two registered simple mortgage deeds on 28.03.2019 and two deeds of guarantee on 29.03.2019, which were subsequently registered with the ROC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The primary borrowers' accounts were declared NPAs on 27.01.2020; Respondent No. 1 filed the Section 7 petition claiming an outstanding financial default of Rs. 31,47,14,883/- as on 31.07.2021 plus contractual interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The debts were assigned to Respondent No. 1 on 21.03.2020 under a registered assignment agreement dated 07.08.2020. Respondent No. 1 issued Section 13(2) SARFAESI notices on 04.05.2021 and formal guarantee invocation/demand notices under Section 7 on 20.05.2021. The Section 7 petition (CP (IB) No. 1225/MB-IV/2021) was filed on 08.09.2021 and admitted by NCLT Mumbai on 16.05.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record included sanction letters, loan agreements, registered mortgage deeds bearing Rs. 12.5 Lakhs stamp duty, guarantee bonds stamped at Rs. 100 each under Article 54 proviso, registered assignment deed dated 07.08.2020 bearing Rs. 1,01,500/- stamp duty pursuant to Maharashtra Government Notification dated 06.05.2002, ROC charge filings, and subsequent complaints lodged by Appellant before the Collector of Stamps in August 2023. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV admitted the Section 7 application on 16.05.2023 finding valid guarantee invocation and debt default exceeding Rs. 1 Crore. Appellant appealed and obtained conditional interim stays upon offering a Rs. 24.10 Crore settlement, but defaulted on all deposit undertakings, prompting hearing on merits.
legal_issues: (i) Whether an assignment agreement executed in favor of an Asset Reconstruction Company (ARC) that is registered and stamped under a State stamp duty remission notification can be rejected as inadmissible in Section 7 summary insolvency proceedings on grounds of alleged deficit stamping while stamp adjudication proceedings remain pending; (ii) Whether an ARC acquiring debt and underlying corporate guarantees under Section 5(1) of the SARFAESI Act is deemed a 'lender' under Section 5(2) legally entitled to trigger Section 7 CIRP as a Financial Creditor against a corporate guarantor.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Asset Reconstruction Company acquiring debts along with underlying security documents and corporate guarantees under Section 5(1) of the SARFAESI Act is deemed to be a lender for all purposes pursuant to the statutory legal fiction under Section 5(2), thereby possessing full standing as a Financial Creditor under Section 5(7) of the IBC; furthermore, a registered assignment agreement and underlying securities that carry a presumption of regularity cannot be discarded in summary Section 7 proceedings on unadjudicated allegations of insufficient stamping. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(1) of the SARFAESI Act contains an overriding non-obstante clause, and Section 5(2) operates as an express deeming fiction vesting all rights of the original assignor bank into the ARC as lender. Inadmissibility of an instrument under stamp legislation relates to evidentiary defects that are curable and does not render the underlying transaction void ab initio, especially where stamp duty was paid under an applicable state cap/remission notification (such as Maharashtra Notification dated 06.05.2002). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the assignment agreement was duly registered with stamp duty of Rs. 1,01,500/- paid, the mortgage deeds and corporate guarantees were executed and registered with ROC, no competent stamp authority had declared the documents invalid or insufficiently stamped, and the appellant admitted the debt liability by repeatedly offering to pay Rs. 24.10 Crores during appeal hearings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor executed binding deeds of guarantee which were duly invoked upon default, making Respondent No. 1 an entitled Financial Creditor; therefore, the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in admitting the Section 7 petition, and the subsequent stamp complaints could not halt insolvency resolution.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 701 of 2023 is dismissed, the interim stay orders restraining CIRP steps and CoC constitution are discharged, and IA No. 5362 of 2023 is closed.
summary: The Suspended Director of Bairagra Builders Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 7 CIRP petition filed by Encore Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. for default on credit facilities totaling over Rs. 31.47 Crores granted by KAIJS Bank and guaranteed by the Corporate Debtor[cite: 3]. The appellant challenged the admissibility of the registered assignment deed on grounds of deficit stamp duty under the Maharashtra Stamp Act and disputed financial creditor status[cite: 3]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that under Section 5(2) of the SARFAESI Act, an ARC acquiring debt is deemed to be a lender with full statutory entitlement to initiate Section 7 CIRP against the corporate guarantor[cite: 3]. The Tribunal affirmed that registered instruments carry a presumption of valid execution that cannot be derailed in summary insolvency proceedings by unadjudicated stamp complaints, especially after the appellant repeatedly conceded the debt by seeking settlement extensions[cite: 3].

case_title: Pooja Mehra vs. Nilesh Sharma & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Ms. Pooja Mehra (claiming to be an allottee/financial creditor along with her late father Sh. Tej Paul Verma)[cite: 4]. Respondent No. 1 is Mr. Nilesh Sharma (Resolution Professional of Dream Procon Pvt. Ltd., Corporate Debtor)[cite: 4]. Respondent No. 2 is Victory Ace Social Welfare Society (Successful Resolution Applicant / SRA, an association of over 200/220 homebuyers)[cite: 4]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was developing the real estate project 'Victory Ace' at GH-02, Sector 143, Noida[cite: 4]. Appellant claimed to have invested Rs. 50,00,000/- in cash for Unit No. D2-601 under an allotment letter dated 15.05.2016, executed alongside a Buy Back Agreement on the same date offering monthly assured returns of Rs. 60,000/- and Rs. 40,000/- with post-dated buyback cheques of Rs. 30 Lakhs and Rs. 20 Lakhs[cite: 4]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted on handing over possession (due within 30–36 months expiring 15.06.2019), failed to pay monthly assured returns of Rs. 18 Lakhs, and failed to refund the Rs. 50 Lakhs principal consideration along with claimed interest of Rs. 13,33,333/-[cite: 4]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Insolvency commenced against the Corporate Debtor on 06.09.2019[cite: 4]. Public announcement in Form A was published on 18.10.2019 fixing the claim submission deadline as 29.10.2019[cite: 4]. The 90-day extended claim window under Regulation 12(2) expired on 13.01.2020 / 15.01.2020[cite: 4]. The CoC approved the SRA's resolution plan with 90.66% voting share on 07.05.2021 (e-voting concluded 15.05.2021)[cite: 4]. The RP filed IA No. 3250/2021 for plan approval on 09.06.2021[cite: 4]. Appellant submitted her claim in Form C on 20.07.2021, incurring an admitted delay of 552 days from the 90-day outer deadline and over two months after CoC plan approval[cite: 4]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant produced an unnumbered cash receipt dated 15.05.2016 bearing no serial/diary number or official stamp, a buyback agreement signed by one suspended director without company witness, and post-dated cheques[cite: 4]. The allotment letter specified Unit D2-601, whereas the buyback agreement specified Unit D2-2002[cite: 4]. Corporate Debtor's CRM and tally data showed no entry of Rs. 50 Lakhs cash, while Unit D2-601 was already allotted to Mr. Ashok Kumar Sharma whose timely claim was admitted under first sale[cite: 4]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA (IBC) No. 3462/2021 before NCLT New Delhi Bench-III seeking condonation of delay and admission of her claim[cite: 4]. The Adjudicating Authority dismissed the application on 11.08.2023 on grounds of unexplained inordinate delay post-CoC plan approval and lack of verified proof in corporate debtor records, prompting Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1511 of 2023[cite: 4].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a belated claim submitted by a purported homebuyer after a delay of 552 days and subsequent to the approval of the resolution plan by the Committee of Creditors (CoC) can be directed to be entertained by the Resolution Professional merely because the plan remains pending approval before the Adjudicating Authority[cite: 4]; (ii) Whether unauthenticated, unnumbered cash receipts and contradictory allotment/buyback documents reflecting assured return arrangements, which are completely absent from the Corporate Debtor's audited financial books and CRM records, constitute credible evidentiary proof of debt disbursement under the IBC[cite: 4].
ratio_decidendi: 1.
