ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A resolution plan approved by the requisite majority of the Committee of Creditors in its commercial wisdom cannot be sent back and forth to entertain belated claims submitted long after the statutory claim deadlines; once the CoC has approved the plan, late claimants cannot unleash a hydra-headed monster of undecided claims on the Successful Resolution Applicant, irrespective of whether the plan is still awaiting formal approval before the Adjudicating Authority[cite: 4]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Timelines prescribed under Section 15 of the IBC and Regulation 12 of the IBBI (CIRP) Regulations are sacrosanct to guarantee a time-bound restructuring process[cite: 4]. The protection of Supreme Court limitation extensions due to Covid-19 applies strictly where the limitation period expired during the pandemic window, and does not revive claim periods that had already lapsed prior to 15.03.2020[cite: 4]. Furthermore, under Section 31(1), the NCLT exercises a statutorily bounded jurisdiction focused on Section 30(2) compliance and possesses no equity-based jurisdiction to alter the commercial terms of an approved plan or enforce unverified, belated claims[cite: 4]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Uncorroborated, unnumbered cash receipts lacking diary numbers, company seals, or bank-trail entries in the books of accounts/CRM data of the corporate debtor, combined with material discrepancies in unit numbers between allotment and buyback instruments, fail to establish genuine disbursal against the time value of money, disentitling the claimant from indoor management protections[cite: 4]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant failed to submit her claim within the 90-day statutory period, sleeping over her rights for over 540 days until after the CoC approved the resolution plan; combined with the absence of accounting entries and contradictory documents, the Adjudicating Authority rightly rejected the application for condonation and admission of the claim[cite: 4].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1511 of 2023 is dismissed with no order as to costs, affirming the order dated 11.08.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT New Delhi Bench-III) in I.A. (IBC) No. 3462/2021[cite: 4].
summary: Pooja Mehra appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order rejecting her application to condone a 552-day delay in submitting a Rs. 50 Lakh financial debt claim against Dream Procon Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 4]. The appellant claimed to have booked a unit under an assured-return buyback agreement in 2016, but lodged her claim two months after the CoC approved the resolution plan submitted by the homebuyers' association (Victory Ace Social Welfare Society)[cite: 4]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that CIRP is strictly time-bound and that prospective resolution applicants cannot be burdened with belated, undecided claims post-CoC approval, reiterating the Supreme Court rulings in Essar Steel and RPS Infrastructure[cite: 4]. The Tribunal further noted that the claim was backed only by suspicious, unnumbered cash receipts not reflected in the corporate debtor's books, with unit descriptions conflicting with existing admitted allotments[cite: 4].

case_title: Noil Christuraj vs. State Bank of India & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 284 of 2023 & IA No. 867/2023
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Member Justice M. Venugopal and Technical Member Jatindranath Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Noil Christuraj, Suspended Director of M/s. Fossil Logistics Private Limited (Corporate Debtor / Corporate Guarantor)[cite: 5]. Respondent No. 1 is State Bank of India (Financial Creditor / Lender Consortium Member)[cite: 5]. Respondent No. 2 is Radhakrishnan Dharmarajan (Interim Resolution Professional / Resolution Professional)[cite: 5]. The Principal Borrower is M/s. Coastal Energen Private Limited[cite: 5]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A consortium of lenders sanctioned credit facilities to the Principal Borrower, including an additional term loan of Rs. 1,139 Crores under a Third Amended and Restated Common Loan Agreement dated 05.07.2016[cite: 5]. To secure these facilities, the Corporate Debtor executed a Deed of Guarantee dated 05.07.2016 in favor of SBICAP Trustee Company Limited (acting for the lender consortium) and created simple registered mortgages over 500.52 acres of land in Tuticorin District, Tamil Nadu[cite: 5]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Principal Borrower's account was classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 31.03.2017[cite: 5]. The default date was specified as 27.09.2018, with the total default amount claimed as on 20.09.2018 being Rs. 2,932,69,53,916.57, which escalated to Rs. 3,292,35,84,386/- as on 31.08.2021 plus subsequent interest[cite: 5]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A loan recall notice was issued by SBI to both the Principal Borrower and the Corporate Debtor on 20.09.2018[cite: 5]. SBI initiated Section 7 CIRP against the Principal Borrower in IBA No. 757 of 2019, which was admitted by NCLT Chennai on 04.02.2022[cite: 5]. SBI subsequently filed Section 7 application CP/IB/140(CHE)2022 against the Corporate Debtor on 17.09.2021[cite: 5]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record included the Deed of Guarantee dated 05.07.2016 (specifically Clauses 3, 5, and 22), Registered Indentures of Simple Mortgage (Doc. Nos. 1819/2016 and 1820/2016 dated 11.08.2016), Form CHG-1 charge registration filings with ROC reflecting encumbrance for the whole debt, bank statement of accounts as of 31.08.2021, and the recall notice dated 20.09.2018[cite: 5]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Division Bench-II, Chennai admitted CP/IB/140(CHE)2022 under Section 7 on 15.06.2023, declaring a moratorium and appointing Respondent No. 2 as IRP[cite: 5]. The Appellant challenged this admission via Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 284 of 2023[cite: 5].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a Financial Creditor is barred from initiating or proceeding with Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) under Section 7 of the IBC against a Corporate Guarantor when a prior Section 7 CIRP application has already been admitted against the Principal Borrower for the same debt and default[cite: 5]; (ii) Whether the liability of a Corporate Guarantor under a continuing guarantee is limited solely to the value of mortgaged properties or whether it is co-extensive with the entire default of the Principal Borrower under Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872[cite: 5]; (iii) Whether a member bank of a lending consortium can independently maintain a Section 7 petition as a Financial Creditor where the guarantee was executed in favor of a Security Trustee[cite: 5].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under the IBC, there is no statutory bar prohibiting a Financial Creditor from initiating and maintaining simultaneous or independent Section 7 CIRP proceedings against both the Principal Borrower and the Corporate Guarantor for the same underlying financial debt and default, subject only to adjustments at the stage of distribution or receipt of funds[cite: 5]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 5(7) and 5(8)(i) read with Section 3(8), 3(11), and 3(12) of the IBC establish that upon default by the principal borrower, the corporate guarantor's status transforms into that of a Corporate Debtor whose liability is co-extensive and coterminous with that of the principal debtor under Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872[cite: 5]. The ratio of Dr. Vishnu Kumar Agarwal (Piramal Enterprises) is superseded by the Supreme Court's pronouncement in Laxmi Pat Surana, which affirmed that the creditor's cause of action against the principal borrower and the corporate guarantor operates in equal measure[cite: 5]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified the execution of the unconditional continuing guarantee and mortgage charges registered via Form CHG-1 with the ROC covering the entire debt, the issuance of the recall notice demanding repayment, and the unrefuted failure of the Corporate Debtor to discharge the debt, thereby satisfying the dual requirements of debt and default under Section 7(5)(a)[cite: 5]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt and default exceeded the statutory threshold of Rs. 1 Crore, the Corporate Debtor failed to satisfy the guarantee obligations upon demand, and the Adjudicating Authority committed no legal error in admitting the Corporate Guarantor to CIRP despite preexisting CIRP against the Principal Borrower[cite: 5].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS.) No. 284 of 2023 is dismissed with no orders as to costs[cite: 5]. The impugned order dated 15.06.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Division Bench-II, Chennai) in CP/IB/140(CHE)2022 admitting the Corporate Debtor to CIRP is affirmed, and connected pending Interlocutory Application IA No. 867/2023 is closed[cite: 5].
summary: Noil Christuraj, Suspended Director of Fossil Logistics Private Limited (Corporate Guarantor), appealed against an NCLT Chennai order admitting a Section 7 CIRP application filed by State Bank of India for a default exceeding Rs. 3,292 Crores[cite: 5]. The appellant contended that CIRP could not be initiated against the Corporate Guarantor because CIRP had already been admitted against the Principal Borrower (M/s. Coastal Energen Pvt. Ltd.) for the exact same debt, relying on the NCLAT ruling in Piramal Enterprises[cite: 5]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Chennai Bench held that under the Supreme Court's binding precedents in Laxmi Pat Surana and subsequent NCLAT rulings, the liability of a corporate guarantor is co-extensive under Section 128 of the Contract Act and there is no legal bar preventing simultaneous or independent Section 7 proceedings against both the principal borrower and the corporate guarantor[cite: 5].

case_title: The Indian Performing Right Society Ltd. vs. Novi Digital Entertainment Private Limited & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice M. Venugopal and Technical Member Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is The Indian Performing Right Society Ltd. (IPRS - a registered copyright society under Section 33 of the Copyright Act, 1957)[cite: 6]. Respondent No. 1 is Novi Digital Entertainment Private Limited (Transferor Company operating 'Disney+Hotstar')[cite: 6]. Respondent No. 2 is Star India Private Limited (Transferee Company)[cite: 6]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A Scheme of Amalgamation was proposed between Novi Digital Entertainment Private Limited and Star India Private Limited[cite: 6]. Star India made royalty payments in June 2018 for the period 21.06.2012 to 31.03.2018 under a without-prejudice letter agreement, but no subsequent written license agreement under Section 30/30A of the Copyright Act was executed[cite: 6]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant asserted statutory royalty claims of Rs. 44.44 Crores against Respondent No. 1 and Rs. 254,19,44,137/- (following an earlier notice of Rs. 128,22,92,877/-) against Respondent No. 2 for the period 01.04.2018 to 31.03.2023, and filed Section 9 IBC applications (CP (IB) Nos. 1100/2023 and 1102/2023)[cite: 6]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Scheme application CA (CAA) No. 48/MB/2023 was filed by Respondents[cite: 6]. The Tribunal admitted the petition on 08.09.2023 directing publication of the scheme hearing advertisement under Rule 16 of the CAA Rules, 2016. The Appellant filed C.A. No. 320/2023 in CP No. 200/2023 seeking scheme documents and 4 weeks' time to file objections[cite: 6]. The NCLT dismissed C.A. 320/2023 on 09.02.2024[cite: 6]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Audited financial statements and statutory auditor-authenticated unsecured creditor lists produced by Respondents showing 194 unsecured creditors of Novi and 1,215 unsecured creditors of Star, which excluded the Appellant[cite: 6]; letter agreement of June 2018[cite: 6]; Star's reply letter dated 25.06.2022 agreeing to discuss royalties for reality shows; and Clause 4.2.15 of the Scheme transferring all debts, liabilities, and obligations to Star India. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Court No. V, Mumbai Bench dismissed C.A. No. 320/2023 on 09.02.2024, holding that IPRS was neither a creditor nor a shareholder in the audited financial statements and lacked locus to inspect documents or object to the scheme[cite: 6]. The Appellant challenged this dismissal in Company Appeal (AT) No. 59 of 2024 before NCLAT Principal Bench[cite: 6].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an entity claiming unadjudicated, disputed statutory royalties under the Copyright Act, 1957 qualifies as a 'creditor' having the locus standi under Section 230(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 to receive scheme documents and maintain objections against a Scheme of Amalgamation when its name does not appear in the audited financial statements or the statutory auditor's list of creditors of the amalgamating companies[cite: 6]; (ii) Whether a public hearing advertisement of a merger petition under Rule 16 of the CAA Rules, 2016 confers an enforceable right on any member of the public to demand confidential scheme documents and inspect company records in the absence of established creditor or shareholder credentials[cite: 6].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An entity whose pecuniary claim is unliquidated, disputed, and not admitted or recorded in the audited financial statements or verified creditor lists of amalgamating companies lacks locus standi as a creditor under Section 230(4) of the Companies Act, 2013, and cannot halt or intervene in a scheme of amalgamation or demand internal scheme documents as a matter of right[cite: 6]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 230(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 restricts the right to object to a compromise or arrangement exclusively to creditors holding not less than 5% of the total outstanding debt or persons holding not less than 10% shareholding as per the latest audited financial statements. The public advertisement mandated under Rule 16 of the Companies (CAA) Rules, 2016 does not enlarge the definition of an objector into an open public right for third parties possessing disputed unadjudicated claims, particularly when the scheme incorporates explicit covenants transferring all existing and contingent liabilities to a financially solvent transferee entity[cite: 6]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the Appellant did not feature as an unsecured creditor in the verified books of account or statutory auditor lists (194 creditors of Novi and 1,215 of Star), that no written license agreement under Sections 30 and 30A of the Copyright Act existed to crystallize an undisputed debt, that past payments made under a 2018 letter agreement constituted no binding precedent for future debts, and that Clause 4.2.15 of the Scheme provided full continuity and protection for any liability that might legally crystallize in the future[cite: 6]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Appellant was neither a shareholder nor an authenticated creditor as per the latest audited financial statements, it possessed no legal locus to intervene, demand scheme records, or stall the merger; hence, the NCLT committed no error in dismissing the application[cite: 6].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 59 of 2024 is dismissed, affirming the NCLT Mumbai Bench order dated 09.02.2024 in C.A. No. 320/2023 in CP No. 200/2023, and all connected pending Interlocutory Applications (including IA No. 1269/2024) are closed[cite: 6].
summary: The Indian Performing Right Society Ltd. (IPRS) appealed against an NCLT Mumbai Bench order dismissing its application (C.A. No. 320/2023) seeking copies of the Scheme of Amalgamation between Novi Digital Entertainment Pvt. Ltd. and Star India Pvt. Ltd., as well as time to file objections[cite: 6]. IPRS asserted that as a registered copyright society claiming statutory royalties, it qualified as a creditor and member of the public entitled to scheme documents under Sections 230–232 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 6]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that under Section 230(4) of the Act, only creditors recorded in the latest audited financial statements possessing 5% of debt have locus to object to a scheme[cite: 6]. Uncrystallized, disputed claims do not confer creditor status or entitle an entity to inspect scheme filings or halt a bona fide corporate amalgamation[cite: 6].

case_title: Gupta Textiles vs. Darshan Patel & Ors.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan, Technical Members Barun Mitra and Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Gupta Textiles (Operational Creditor)[cite: 7]. Respondent No. 1 is Darshan Patel (Resolution Professional of Television Home Shopping Network Limited, Corporate Debtor)[cite: 7]. Respondent No. 2 is Goblin India Limited jointly with M/s Khandwala Finstock Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicants / SRA)[cite: 7]. Respondent No. 3 is the Committee of Creditors of Television Home Shopping Network Ltd., through its sole 100% voting member, Centre for Economic & Social Inclusion Pvt. Ltd. (Secured Financial Creditor)[cite: 7]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Television Home Shopping Network Limited underwent Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP)[cite: 7]. Appellant supplied textile goods to the Corporate Debtor and lodged operational debt claims[cite: 7]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted on operational dues; Appellant filed Form-B claim for Rs. 1,41,16,647/-, out of which the RP admitted Rs. 1,24,73,281/-[cite: 7]. Total admitted claims of Operational Creditors (non-government/workmen) stood at Rs. 16,36,64,956/-; Secured Financial Creditor claim was admitted at Rs. 19,65,908/-; and statutory contingent claims of government departments stood at Rs. 377,37,53,914/- (admitted at notional Rs. 1/- each, totaling Rs. 4/-)[cite: 7]. The Corporate Debtor had a liquidation value of only Rs. 5,74,822/- (Rs. 5.74 Lakhs)[cite: 7]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 03.03.2023[cite: 7]. Appellant filed claim on 25.04.2023[cite: 7]. The sole CoC member approved the SRA's resolution plan with 100% voting share on 06.08.2023[cite: 7]. The RP filed IA No. 3908/2023 for plan approval, which NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-IV approved on 09.11.2023[cite: 7]. Appellant filed the instant appeal challenging the distribution[cite: 7]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resolution plan providing total plan value of Rs. 9.05 Crores, comprising Rs. 35 Lakhs CIRP costs, Rs. 19,65,908/- (100%) to Secured Financial Creditor, Rs. 15 Lakhs upfront to Government Departments, but only Rs. 35,34,092/- upfront cash (2.16%) to Operational Creditors plus an option of 1,60,00,000 partly paid (Rs. 5/- paid) redeemable preference shares worth Rs. 8 Crores liable to forfeiture on failure of call money payment[cite: 7]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai approved the resolution plan via IA No. 3908/2023 on 09.11.2023[cite: 7]. The Operational Creditor appealed to the NCLAT contending violation of Section 30(2)(b)(ii)[cite: 7].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a resolution plan offering only 2.16% upfront cash to Operational Creditors and proposing to satisfy the remainder through optional partly-paid redeemable preference shares complies with the mandatory priority payment requirements under Section 30(2)(b)(ii) read with Section 53(1) of the IBC[cite: 7]; (ii) Whether the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal can modify the distribution mechanism of an approved resolution plan to enforce statutory compliance under Section 30(2)(b) while affirming the plan in its entirety[cite: 7].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 30(2)(b) of the IBC, Operational Creditors are entitled to receive an amount which shall not be less than the amount payable under Section 53(1) in liquidation or the amount that would have been paid if the resolution plan distribution had followed the order of priority under Section 53(1), whichever is higher; such mandatory payments must be discharged strictly in money/cash in priority over financial creditors, and cannot be substituted or diluted by issuing equity, partly-paid shares, or preference shares. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2)(b)(ii) as amended by Act 26 of 2019 mandatorily entitles Operational Creditors to participate in the higher resolution plan value based on the waterfall mechanism of Section 53(1)[cite: 7]. Following the Supreme Court ruling in Jaypee Kensington, payment of debts to operational creditors must be by delivery of money alone, and offering equity or preference shares in successor entities keeping them glued to corporate liabilities is contrary to the statutory framework[cite: 7]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the total plan value was Rs. 9.05 Crores while the liquidation value was a meager Rs. 5.74 Lakhs, triggering the application of Section 30(2)(b)(ii)[cite: 7]. With the Secured Financial Creditor having an admitted claim of only Rs. 19.65 Lakhs and contingent government dues provided with Rs. 15 Lakhs, there were no unsecured financial creditors or secured operational creditors[cite: 7]; therefore, the remaining funds of the resolution plan were statutorily required to be distributed pro-rata in cash among the Operational Creditors in priority over the Financial Creditor under Section 53(1)[cite: 7]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The distribution mechanism approved by the Adjudicating Authority violated Section 30(2)(b)(ii)[cite: 7]. Rather than setting aside the entire revival scheme, justice required modifying the distribution mechanism to direct pro-rata cash payment of the balance resolution plan amount to Operational Creditors, failing which the plan would stand disapproved[cite: 7].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 408 of 2024 is disposed of with parties bearing their own costs[cite: 7]. The order of the Adjudicating Authority dated 09.11.2023 is modified to the extent of approving distribution to Operational Creditors (including the Appellant), while the rest of the approval order is affirmed[cite: 7]. The SRA is directed to distribute the balance Resolution Plan amount to Operational Creditors on a pro-rata cash basis in priority under Section 30(2)(b)(ii) read with Section 53(1), failing which the Resolution Plan shall be treated as disapproved[cite: 7].
summary: Gupta Textiles, an Operational Creditor of Television Home Shopping Network Limited with an admitted claim of Rs. 1.24 Crores, appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order approving the resolution plan submitted by Goblin India Limited and Khandwala Finstock Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 7]. The plan provided Rs. 9.05 Crores against a liquidation value of Rs. 5.74 Lakhs, but allocated only 2.16% (Rs. 35.34 Lakhs) upfront cash to Operational Creditors holding Rs. 16.36 Crores of debt, subsuming the rest in optional partly-paid redeemable preference shares[cite: 7]. Allowing the appeal in part, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that under Section 30(2)(b)(ii) and the Supreme Court precedent in Jaypee Kensington, Operational Creditors must be paid in cash in priority and are entitled to the higher amount calculated under Section 53(1) waterfall from the total plan consideration[cite: 7]. The Tribunal modified the approval order, directing the SRA to distribute the balance plan funds pro-rata in cash to Operational Creditors on pain of plan cancellation[cite: 7].

case_title: Shweta Sharma vs. SREI Equipment Finance Ltd. & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 370 of 2024 & I.A. No. 1260 of 2024
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan, Technical Members Barun Mitra and Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Shweta Sharma, Shareholder of Shweta Housing & Hospitality Private Limited (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 8]. Respondent No. 1 is SREI Equipment Finance Ltd. (Financial Creditor)[cite: 8]. Respondent No. 2 is the Corporate Debtor through the IRP[cite: 8]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Under a Loan Agreement dated 13.06.2017 (preceded by Offer Letter dated 09.06.2017), the Financial Creditor extended a term loan facility of Rs. 18,09,00,000/- at 14% interest per annum to the Corporate Debtor, repayable in 58 monthly installments commencing from 15.08.2017 till 15.05.2022, secured by deeds of guarantee and mortgage[cite: 8]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtor repaid only 3 installments totaling Rs. 40,00,000/- and defaulted on subsequent installments commencing 15.11.2017[cite: 8]. The loan recall and termination notice dated 24.01.2019 claimed Rs. 27,03,77,188/- as on 30.11.2018[cite: 8]. The Section 7 application claimed a total outstanding default of Rs. 35,90,58,448/- as on 01.12.2021 (comprising Rs. 27,02,74,828/- principal/award amount, Rs. 8,87,68,620/- interest, and Rs. 15,000/- costs) with default date indicated as 04.02.2020 (date of arbitral award)[cite: 8]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Financial Creditor issued loan recall and agreement termination notice on 24.01.2019[cite: 8]. An ex parte arbitral award was rendered on 04.02.2020[cite: 8]. Execution application was filed before Delhi High Court on 22.07.2021 (objections filed on 22.11.2021)[cite: 8]. Demand notice was issued on 01.12.2021[cite: 8]. The Financial Creditor filed the Section 7 petition (C.P. No. (IB) 132/MB/C-III/2022) on 31.01.2022[cite: 8]. NCLT Mumbai admitted the petition on 18.12.2023[cite: 8]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreement, deed of guarantee, and deed of mortgage dated 13.06.2017; CIBIL report dated 03.12.2021; default certificate dated 09.03.2022 issued by National E-Governance Services Limited (NeSL); loan recall notice dated 24.01.2019; and Corporate Debtor's reply admitting payment of only Rs. 40 Lakhs (3 installments)[cite: 8]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-III admitted the Section 7 petition on 18.12.2023, holding that debt and default were proven via NeSL certificate and default in 55 installments[cite: 8]. The shareholder filed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 370 of 2024 before the NCLAT challenging admission on grounds of limitation and reliance on a void unilateral arbitral award[cite: 8].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an application under Section 7 of the IBC filed on 31.01.2022 is barred by limitation when installments defaulted in late 2017 and a loan recall notice was issued on 24.01.2019, having regard to the Supreme Court's Covid-19 limitation exclusion orders[cite: 8]; (ii) Whether the pendency of execution proceedings and objections against an ex parte arbitral award bars the initiation or admission of a Section 7 CIRP application where debt and default are independently established through loan documents, admissions, and NeSL records[cite: 8]; (iii) What constitutes the scope of enquiry and discretion of the Adjudicating Authority under Section 7(5)(a) upon proof of debt and default[cite: 8].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In an application under Section 7 of the IBC, once the existence of a financial debt and default is established by independent documentary evidence, the Adjudicating Authority is statutorily bound to admit the petition; pending challenges, objections, or execution proceedings concerning an arbitral award between the parties do not preclude admission when default is independently proven on the basis of underlying loan agreements and statutory information utility records[cite: 8]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 7(5)(a) read with Section 3(12) of the IBC and the principles settled in Innoventive Industries and M. Suresh Kumar Reddy, the Adjudicating Authority's jurisdiction is limited to examining whether default has occurred (i.e., non-payment of debt due and payable); the tribunal lacks equitable discretion to refuse admission if debt and default exist[cite: 8]. Furthermore, under Section 3 of the Limitation Act, exclusion of the period from 15.03.2020 to 28.02.2022 under the Supreme Court's Suo Motu Cognizance for Extension of Limitation applies to save petitions where the cause of action accrued from loan acceleration or default within three years preceding that window[cite: 8]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified from the corporate debtor's written reply admitting payment of only Rs. 40 Lakhs across 58 agreed installments, the loan recall notice dated 24.01.2019 demanding Rs. 27.03 Crores, and the statutory NeSL certificate dated 09.03.2022 confirming default, thereby proving debt and default completely independent of the 04.02.2020 arbitral award[cite: 8]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 application was filed well within limitation (accounting for the Covid-19 exclusion period from the 2017 installment defaults and 2019 loan recall notice), and debt and default were conclusively demonstrated without reliance on the disputed arbitral award; hence, the NCLT committed no error in admitting the Corporate Debtor to CIRP[cite: 8].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 370 of 2024 is dismissed, affirming the order dated 18.12.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai Bench, Court-III) in C.P. No. (IB) 132/MB/C-III/2022[cite: 8]. Connected pending Interlocutory Application I.A. No. 1260 of 2024 is closed[cite: 8].
summary: A shareholder of Shweta Housing & Hospitality Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 7 CIRP application filed by SREI Equipment Finance Ltd. for default on an Rs. 18.09 Crore loan facility with outstanding dues of Rs. 35.90 Crores[cite: 8]. The appellant argued that the petition was time-barred and that the NCLT impermissibly relied on an ex parte, void arbitral award arising from a unilateral arbitrator appointment currently under challenge in the Delhi High Court[cite: 8]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that the application was well within limitation taking into account installment defaults since 2017, the 2019 recall notice, and Supreme Court Covid-19 exclusion orders[cite: 8]. The Tribunal held that debt and default were conclusively established independent of the arbitral award via the corporate debtor's admission of paying only three installments and the NeSL default certificate, making CIRP admission mandatory under Section 7[cite: 8].

case_title: Ashok Kumar Gulla vs. State Bank of India & Ors.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain and Technical Member Ajai Das Mehrotra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Ashok Kumar Gulla, Liquidator of M/s SRS Limited (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 10]. Respondent No. 1 is State Bank of India (Lead Secured Financial Creditor / SCC Member)[cite: 10]. Respondents Nos. 2 to 5 are Bank of India, Union Bank of India, Punjab National Bank, and Canara Bank (Secured Financial Creditors / SCC Members)[cite: 10]. Respondents Nos. 6 to 10 are representatives of deposit holders, operational creditors, and statutory authorities[cite: 10]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP was initiated against the Corporate Debtor by NCLT Chandigarh Bench on 21.08.2018[cite: 10]. CoC rejected the resolution plan on 16.05.2019, leading to the liquidation order on 15.10.2019[cite: 10]. Expressions of Interest for compromise/arrangement under Section 230 of Companies Act were issued on 13.12.2019, but going concern sale failed due to attachment of assets by the Enforcement Directorate (ED) on 08.01.2020 under PMLA and provisional attachment by the Income Tax Department (vacated on 12.01.2021)[cite: 10]. Cinema assets across 12 locations were auctioned between 15.01.2021 and 30.09.2021, generating proceeds from which liquidation costs and Rs. 2 Crores were distributed to stakeholders[cite: 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; dispute concerns fixation and recovery of liquidator's remuneration[cite: 10]. Appellant sought monthly fees of Rs. 4 Lakhs + GST from 29.01.2020 to 31.05.2022 and Rs. 2 Lakhs + GST per month from 01.06.2022 to 31.05.2024 (shared 25:75 with IPE), citing inability to sell major assets due to ED attachments[cite: 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 21.08.2018[cite: 10]. Liquidation commenced on 15.10.2019[cite: 10]. ED attached assets on 08.01.2020[cite: 10]. Adjudicating Authority directed SCC to consider fee proposals on 28.07.2022[cite: 10]. The 18th, 19th, and 20th SCC meetings were held in August-September 2022, culminating in unanimous rejection of monthly fees in the 20th meeting on 15.09.2022[cite: 10]. NCLT Chandigarh dismissed IA Nos. 307/2021 and 1260/2022 on 18.04.2023[cite: 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Minutes of 18th, 19th, and 20th SCC meetings showing Secured Financial Creditors (SBI, BOI, UBI, PNB) unanimously resolving that liquidator's fees are payable exclusively under Regulation 4(2)(b) as a percentage of realization and distribution; ED attachment orders dated 08.01.2020; and IBBI Circular No. IBBI/LIQ/61/2023 dated 28.09.2023 regarding exclusion of time periods stayed by court orders[cite: 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Liquidator filed IA No. 307/2021 and IA No. 1260/2022 under Section 60(5) seeking monthly remuneration[cite: 10]. NCLT Chandigarh Bench dismissed the applications on 18.04.2023, upholding the SCC's decision to pay solely under Regulation 4(2)(b)[cite: 10]. The liquidator appealed to the NCLAT via Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 786 of 2023[cite: 10].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal has the statutory jurisdiction under Section 60(5) of the IBC to fix and award monthly remuneration to a liquidator contrary to the scheme of Regulation 4(2)(b) of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016, where liquidation assets are under statutory attachment by investigative agencies like the ED[cite: 10]; (ii) Whether a liquidator whose fees were not determined by the CoC prior to liquidation can claim fixed monthly remuneration instead of the statutory percentage on realization and distribution under the regulations in force at the time of the liquidation order[cite: 10].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In the absence of fee fixation by the Committee of Creditors under Regulation 39D of the CIRP Regulations prior to the liquidation order, the remuneration payable to a liquidator is governed strictly by the statutory percentage schedule based on realization and distribution under Regulation 4(2)(b) of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016; tribunals cannot rewrite regulations or introduce monthly remuneration schemes merely because asset realization is stalled or delayed due to statutory attachments by enforcement authorities[cite: 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 4 of the Liquidation Process Regulations as it existed on the date of the liquidation order (15.10.2019) does not contemplate monthly remuneration if no fee was fixed by the CoC[cite: 10]. Where the statutory text is clear, judicial authorities cannot innovate or alter statutory provisions under Section 60(5) of the IBC[cite: 10]. While the liquidator may seek exclusion of time periods during which attachment prevented sale pursuant to administrative circulars, the method of remuneration remains tied exclusively to proceeds realized and distributed under Regulation 4(2)(b)[cite: 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that liquidation commenced on 15.10.2019, the CoC had not fixed any liquidation remuneration under Regulation 39D before the CIRP ended, and the Stakeholders' Consultation Committee in its 20th meeting held on 15.09.2022 explicitly voted that the liquidator must be remunerated solely as per the percentage formula of Regulation 4(2)(b)[cite: 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The liquidator is entitled to fee remuneration strictly on realization and distribution under Regulation 4(2)(b) of the Liquidation Process Regulations, and the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in declining to grant monthly remuneration[cite: 10].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 786 of 2023 is dismissed with no order as to costs, affirming the order dated 18.04.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Chandigarh Bench) in IA Nos. 307 of 2021 and 1260 of 2022 in CP (IB) No. 201/Chd/2018[cite: 10]. All pending Interlocutory Applications are closed[cite: 10].
summary: The Liquidator of SRS Limited appealed against an NCLT Chandigarh order dismissing his applications (IA Nos. 307/2021 and 1260/2022) seeking fixed monthly remuneration of Rs. 4 Lakhs and Rs. 2 Lakhs plus GST[cite: 10]. The liquidator argued that because major assets were attached by the Enforcement Directorate under PMLA, auctions were stalled, depriving him of percentage-based fees under Regulation 4(2)(b) of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 despite ongoing duties[cite: 10]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that under the statutory framework applicable at the date of liquidation (15.10.2019), when the CoC did not fix fees under Regulation 39D, the liquidator is entitled to fees solely as a percentage of realization and distribution under Regulation 4(2)(b)[cite: 10]. The Tribunal affirmed that courts cannot rewrite regulations to award monthly remuneration against the unanimous decision of the Stakeholders' Consultation Committee[cite: 10].

case_title: Unity Small Finance Bank Ltd. vs. Sripatham Venkatasubramanian Ramkumar & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Unity Small Finance Bank Ltd. (successor-in-interest to Punjab & Maharashtra Co-operative Bank Ltd. / PMC Bank via amalgamation)[cite: 11]. Respondent No. 1 is Sripatham Venkatasubramanian Ramkumar, Resolution Professional of Privilege Industries Limited (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 11]. Respondent No. 2 is the Committee of Creditors represented by Omkara Asset Reconstruction Company Limited[cite: 11]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: PMC Bank sanctioned mortgage overdraft facilities to the Corporate Debtor vide sanction letters dated 04.11.2011 (enhanced to Rs. 35 Crores) and 17.01.2013 (Rs. 10 Crores)[cite: 11]. Securities provided were registered mortgages over immovable lands situated at Ernakulam (standing in the name of Blue Star Realtors Pvt. Ltd.) and Vasai, Thane (standing in the name of personal guarantor Rakesh Kumar Wadhawan), alongside a general lien and set-off letter dated 04.11.2011[cite: 11]. No mortgage or charge was executed over the Corporate Debtor's own immovable assets[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted on the overdraft facilities, leading to NPA classification[cite: 11]. In CIRP, the Appellant filed a claim of Rs. 139,57,65,086/-, which the RP admitted as an unsecured financial debt, denying secured creditor status[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 15.02.2023[cite: 11]. The initial 180-day CIRP period expired on 13.08.2023[cite: 11]. In the 7th CoC meeting, CoC resolved to seek a 23-day exclusion, and an exclusion application was filed before NCLT on 11.08.2023[cite: 11]. CoC approved the Resolution Plan of SNJ Breweries Private Limited on 23.08.2023 with a 79.61% vote share[cite: 11]. The RP filed plan approval application IA No. 4004/2023 on 30.08.2023, which NCLT Mumbai approved on 23.02.2024[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Sanction letters dated 04.11.2011 and 17.01.2013; Corporate Debtor's lien and set-off letter dated 04.11.2011; Form CHG-1 belatedly attempted to be filed with ROC on 26.10.2023 post-CIRP initiation; CERSAI portal search results; and Form-H certifying fair value of Rs. 283 Crores and liquidation value of Rs. 213 Crores[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 3592/2023 challenging RP's classification; NCLT remanded for reconsideration on 08.01.2024, after which the RP reaffirmed unsecured status on 30.01.2024[cite: 11]. Appellant then filed IA No. 698/2024 (later IA No. 796/2024)[cite: 11]. NCLT Mumbai approved the resolution plan in IA No. 4004/2023 on 23.02.2024, treating Appellant as an unsecured creditor[cite: 11]. Appellant appealed to NCLAT[cite: 11].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a financial creditor who holds mortgages exclusively over the personal assets of third-party guarantors and a general lien/set-off letter qualifies as a 'secured creditor' under Section 3(30) and 3(31) of the IBC in respect of the Corporate Debtor's insolvency estate[cite: 11]; (ii) Whether the approval of a resolution plan by the CoC ten days after the expiry of the initial 180-day period is void when an exclusion application for 23 days was pending and subsequently subsumed in the approval order[cite: 11].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Sections 3(30) and 3(31) of the IBC, a creditor qualifies as a secured creditor of a corporate debtor only if a valid security interest (mortgage, charge, hypothecation, or encumbrance) is specifically created over the property and assets owned by the corporate debtor itself; mortgages created over properties belonging to third-party guarantors do not constitute security interest over the corporate debtor's estate[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(31) defines 'security interest' as a right, title, interest, or claim to property created by a transaction securing payment or performance[cite: 11]. Sanction letters referring to third-party assets and a standard banker's lien and set-off letter over bank balances do not create a proprietary charge or security interest over the corporate debtor's general assets or book debts[cite: 11]. Furthermore, where an application for exclusion of CIRP time was timely filed within the 180-day period on the instructions of the CoC, the formal approval of the resolution plan by the Adjudicating Authority after noting the exclusion application operates as an effective grant of exclusion, curing any procedural timing lapse[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the sanction letters dated 04.11.2011 and 17.01.2013, finding that all listed immovable mortgaged properties belonged exclusively to third parties (Blue Star Realtors and Rakesh Kumar Wadhawan)[cite: 11]. The lien and set-off letter lacked the character of a security creation transaction over the Corporate Debtor's assets, and the Appellant's post-CIRP attempts to register charges via Form CHG-1 in October 2023 confirmed the absence of any preexisting charge[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The RP committed no error in classifying the Appellant as an unsecured financial creditor for its Rs. 139.57 Crore claim, and the resolution plan was validly approved within an extended timeline deemed regularized by the 23-day exclusion[cite: 11].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 601 of 2024 is dismissed with no order as to costs, affirming the order dated 23.02.2024 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai Bench) in IA No. 4004 of 2023 approving the Resolution Plan[cite: 11].
summary: Unity Small Finance Bank Ltd. (as successor to PMC Bank) appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order approving the resolution plan of Privilege Industries Limited submitted by SNJ Breweries Pvt. Ltd., wherein the bank's Rs. 139.57 Crore claim was treated as unsecured[cite: 11]. The Appellant contended that it held secured status based on 2011 and 2013 overdraft sanction letters and a letter of lien/set-off, and argued the plan was approved after the 180-day CIRP period expired[cite: 11]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that securities furnished over properties of third-party guarantors do not constitute a security interest over the Corporate Debtor's assets under Section 3(30) and 3(31) of the IBC[cite: 11]. The Tribunal also held that the pendency and subsequent recognition of a 23-day exclusion application cured the timing of the plan's approval by the CoC[cite: 11].

case_title: Milind Kashiram Jadhav vs. State Bank of India & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan, Technical Members Barun Mitra and Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Milind Kashiram Jadhav, Suspended Director of Jabalpur MSW Private Limited (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 12]. Respondent No. 1 is State Bank of India (Financial Creditor)[cite: 12]. Respondent No. 2 is Mr. Sajjan Kumar Dokania (Interim Resolution Professional / Resolution Professional)[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Under a Sanction Letter dated 04.08.2014, the Financial Creditor sanctioned credit facilities of Rs. 54,00,00,000/- to the Corporate Debtor for part-financing a Municipal Solid Waste (MSW) treatment plant of 580 TPD capacity for Waste To Energy (WTE) conversion at Jabalpur on Design, Build, Own, Operate, and Transfer (DBOOT) basis[cite: 12]. Clause 16 provided events of default, cure periods, and remedies[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtor failed to pay the loan installment due on 30.06.2019[cite: 12]. Following 90 days of continuous non-payment, the loan accounts (Nos. 34331864441 and 61257831245) were classified as NPA on 27.09.2019[cite: 12]. As of 28.02.2021, the balance outstanding across both loan accounts (after adjusting subsequent partial repayments) stood at Rs. 46,79,88,297.64 (claimed as approx. Rs. 46.80 Crores in Form 1, Part IV)[cite: 12]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Installment default occurred on 30.06.2019[cite: 12]. The account was classified as NPA on 27.09.2019[cite: 12]. A loan recall notice was issued on 11.08.2020 calling for repayment of Rs. 47,32,54,888/- within 7 days (expiring 18.08.2020)[cite: 12]. Section 7 application [CP (IB) No. 417/ND/2021] was filed on 30.03.2021[cite: 12]. The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT New Delhi Bench-VI) admitted the petition on 14.09.2023[cite: 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Sanction letter dated 04.08.2014[cite: 12]; loan recall notice dated 11.08.2020[cite: 12]; bank statement of accounts showing partial interest payments post-NPA but no regularisation[cite: 12]; two failed OTS proposals submitted by the Corporate Debtor[cite: 12]; and NeSL Information Utility default certificates submitted on 09.03.2023[cite: 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-VI admitted SBI's Section 7 petition on 14.09.2023, fixing the date of default as 27.09.2019 (NPA date)[cite: 12]. The Suspended Director appealed to NCLAT via Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1589 of 2023 arguing the default occurred upon expiry of the loan recall notice on 18.08.2020, falling within the Section 10A bar period[cite: 12].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the date of Non-Performing Asset (NPA) classification (27.09.2019) or the date of expiry of the subsequent loan recall notice (18.08.2020) constitutes the 'date of default' under Section 3(12) of the IBC[cite: 12]; (ii) Whether subsequent partial interest payments made after an account is classified as an NPA cure the default or shift the default date into the period prohibited by Section 10A of the IBC[cite: 12]; (iii) Whether failure to serve a contractual 'cure period notice' under a pre-IBC sanction letter vitiates the statutory right of a Financial Creditor to initiate CIRP under Section 7 of the IBC[cite: 12].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 3(12) of the IBC, default occurs the moment whole or any part of a debt becomes due and payable and is not paid; the classification of a loan account as an NPA upon completion of 90 days of continuous default operates as a valid, definitive date of default for triggering Section 7 CIRP, and this date is not superseded or shifted by a subsequent loan recall notice or partial payments that fail to regularize the debt[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 10A of the IBC bars initiation of CIRP solely for defaults arising between 25.03.2020 and 24.03.2021[cite: 12]. A loan recall notice issued after NPA classification does not create a new or fresh default date to pull a preexisting 2019 default into the Section 10A window[cite: 12]. Contractual cure clauses in pre-IBC sanction agreements designed for civil recovery or SARFAESI remedies cannot override the statutory code or circumscribe the independent insolvency remedy under Section 7[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified from bank records and NeSL certificates that an installment default occurred on 30.06.2019, 90 days elapsed resulting in NPA classification on 27.09.2019, and the Corporate Debtor's subsequent partial payments were insufficient to clear or regularize the outstanding debt of over Rs. 46.79 Crores[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The default occurred and became complete on 27.09.2019, prior to the introduction of Section 10A; hence, the Section 7 petition was not barred by Section 10A, and the Adjudicating Authority acted correctly in admitting the Corporate Debtor into CIRP[cite: 12].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1589 of 2023 is dismissed with no order as to costs, upholding the order dated 14.09.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT New Delhi Bench-VI) admitting the Section 7 petition in CP (IB) No. 417/ND/2021[cite: 12].
summary: Milind Kashiram Jadhav, Suspended Director of Jabalpur MSW Private Limited, appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order admitting a Section 7 CIRP petition filed by State Bank of India for a default of Rs. 46.80 Crores[cite: 12]. The appellant argued that default only arose on 18.08.2020 upon expiry of a 7-day loan recall notice issued on 11.08.2020 without prior contractual cure notice, thereby falling squarely within the Section 10A bar period[cite: 12]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that under Section 3(12) of the IBC and Supreme Court precedents, the date of NPA declaration (27.09.2019) following 90 days of unpaid installments constitutes the true date of default[cite: 12]. The Tribunal ruled that the subsequent recall notice and partial payments did not wipe out the default or shift the default date into the Section 10A period[cite: 12].

case_title: Rahul Kumawat vs. Bank of India & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain, Technical Members Barun Mitra and Naresh Salecha)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Rahul Kumawat (Director/Shareholder of Corporate Debtor, M/s MP Agro BRK Energy Foods Limited)[cite: 14]. Respondent No. 1 is Bank of India (Financial Creditor)[cite: 14]. Respondent No. 2 is Ms. Chhaya Gupta (Interim Resolution Professional)[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Bank of India sanctioned multiple credit facilities to the Corporate Debtor since 2014, consisting of Working Capital Cash Credit-I of Rs. 1,00,00,000/-, Cash Credit-II of Rs. 7,00,00,000/-, and a Term Loan of Rs. 1,92,68,000/-, aggregating to an overall exposure of Rs. 9,92,68,000/-, secured by guarantees, third-party mortgages, and hypothecations[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Financial Creditor claimed an overdue amount of Rs. 13,20,491/- in the Term Loan account as of 01.09.2017, and an aggregate outstanding default of Rs. 11,57,89,697/- (Principal: Rs. 10,43,09,697/-; Interest: Rs. 1,14,80,000/-) as on the date of filing the Section 7 application, asserting the date of default to be 30.09.2017 (the date of NPA declaration)[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account was declared NPA on 30.09.2017[cite: 14]. Bank issued Section 13(2) SARFAESI notice on 06.11.2017 demanding Rs. 10.66 Crores (later withdrawn)[cite: 14]. RBI issued MSME relief circular on 07.02.2018[cite: 14]. Bank issued account operation certificate on 17.04.2018 certifying active operations[cite: 14]. Corporate Debtor's OTS proposal was rejected on 07.10.2019[cite: 14]. NCLT initially admitted Section 7 on 05.03.2020; NCLAT set aside that order and remanded on 14.11.2022[cite: 14]. On remand, NCLT Indore re-admitted the petition on 04.04.2024[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreements, sanction letters (2014-2017), ZLCC meeting minutes dated 13.09.2017 and bank communication dated 16.10.2017 recommending continuation of Rs. 955.42 Lakhs limits, bank certificate dated 17.04.2018 confirming active operations, bank statements showing Rs. 3.33 Crores credited into CC accounts between 01.09.2017 and 30.11.2018, and RBI MSME Circular dated 07.02.2018[cite: 14]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In the second round of litigation after an initial remand order dated 14.11.2022, NCLT Indore Bench admitted Bank of India's Section 7 petition on 04.04.2024[cite: 14]. The suspended management appealed to NCLAT via Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 720 of 2024, contending that the NCLT passed a cryptic order without recording reasoned findings on whether a default actually occurred or was artificially manufactured by the bank's refusal to auto-debit the active cash credit accounts[cite: 14].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the Adjudicating Authority satisfied its judicial obligation to record cogent and reasoned findings regarding the existence of debt and default under Section 7 of the IBC when it merely listed the documents without analyzing the disputed factual and legal contentions raised by the Corporate Debtor[cite: 14]; (ii) Whether an order of admission under Section 7 can withstand appellate judicial scrutiny if it fails to evaluate evidence showing continuous credit deposits in operating cash credit accounts and the applicability of the RBI MSME Circular dated 07.02.2018[cite: 14].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Recording cogent, speaking reasons is the indispensable heartbeat of judicial and quasi-judicial decision-making; an Adjudicating Authority adjudicating a Section 7 petition cannot merely summarize the rival contentions and enumerate the documents on record to pronounce an order of admission, but must conduct an active analytical evaluation and record specific findings demonstrating how the legal thresholds of financial debt and default are satisfied[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 requires the Adjudicating Authority to ascertain the existence of a default from the evidence before it[cite: 14]. While the inquiry is summary, it cannot be cryptic or devoid of factual reasoning, especially when substantial evidentiary challenges are raised concerning whether credit balances in linked accounts satisfied the debt or whether classification complied with governing regulatory circulars[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the impugned order and found that while the NCLT noted the Corporate Debtor's defenses (including the RBI MSME Circular dated 07.02.2018, the contemporaneous ZLCC approvals in late 2017 treating the account as standard, and substantial credits into the Cash Credit accounts), it failed to analyze how the default was established from those documents or reconcile conflicting transactional entries[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Merely observing that the court looked into the documents without recording reasoned findings on the contested issues of debt and default is legally insufficient and fails judicial scrutiny, necessitating a remand for proper fresh adjudication[cite: 14].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 720 of 2024 is allowed and the impugned order dated 04.04.2024 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Indore Bench) is set aside[cite: 14]. The matter is remanded back to the Adjudicating Authority to re-decide the Section 7 application after taking into consideration the contentions of both parties and recording categorical findings on the basic issues of debt and default, without expressing any opinion on the merits[cite: 14]. The parties are directed to appear before the Adjudicating Authority on 06.05.2024, and the Adjudicating Authority is requested to dispose of the application preferably within two months[cite: 14].
summary: Rahul Kumawat, representing the management of MP Agro BRK Energy Foods Limited, appealed against an NCLT Indore Bench order admitting a Section 7 CIRP application filed by Bank of India for an alleged default of Rs. 11.57 Crores[cite: 14]. In this second round of litigation, the appellant argued that the NCLT passed a cryptic order without analyzing whether default occurred, pointing out that credit balances in its cash credit accounts were sufficient to service term loan installments and that its account was protected under the RBI MSME Circular dated 07.02.2018[cite: 14]. Allowing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that simply listing documents without recording reasoned and categorical findings on the contested elements of debt and default violates the duty to pass reasoned orders[cite: 14]. The Tribunal set aside the admission order and remanded the matter back to the NCLT for fresh adjudication within two months[cite: 14].

case_title: Anil Matta vs. Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority (GNIDA) & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1147 of 2023 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1519 of 2023
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: In Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 1147 of 2023, the Appellant is Anil Matta, Resolution Professional for Primrose Infratech Private Limited (Corporate Debtor), and the Respondent is Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority (GNIDA) along with the SRA[cite: 15]. In Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 1519 of 2023, the Appellant is Atul Mittal, Resolution Professional of Zeal Developers Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor), and the Respondent is New Okhla Industrial Development Authority (NOIDA)[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: GNIDA allotted Plot No. GH-06, Sector CHI-V, Greater Noida, to a consortium, followed by the execution of a registered Lease Deed on 29.11.2011 in favor of the Corporate Debtor, Primrose Infratech Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted on outstanding lease premium and lease rent payments prior to CIRP commencement; GNIDA lodged an operational claim totaling Rs. 55,96,80,208/- with the Resolution Professional[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CP No. IB-995(ND)/2018 was admitted against Primrose Infratech on 21.12.2018[cite: 15]. The CoC approved a resolution plan, and the RP filed approval application IA No. 1489/2020[cite: 15]. GNIDA filed objection application IA No. 4869/2022 seeking rejection of the plan and service of plan copies[cite: 15]. NCLT New Delhi Court-II disposed of IA No. 4869/2022 on 24.07.2023 declaring GNIDA a Secured Operational Creditor[cite: 15]. In the companion matter, NCLT Court-II disposed of NOIDA's IA-4588/2023 on 30.08.2023 on identical lines[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered Lease Deed dated 29.11.2011, demand notices issued by GNIDA, and an affidavit dated 05.05.2023 filed by the RP admitting pre-CIRP lease rental defaults by the Corporate Debtor[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Court-II held that GNIDA holds a charge by operation of law under Sections 13 and 13-A of the UPIAD Act, 1976 and is a secured creditor under Section 3(30) of the IBC[cite: 15]. RPs appealed to the NCLAT challenging the statutory secured creditor classification and non-registration under Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 15].
legal_issues: (i) Whether Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority (GNIDA) and NOIDA qualify as 'Secured Operational Creditors' under Section 3(30) of the IBC by virtue of the statutory charge created over leased property under Section 13-A of the Uttar Pradesh Industrial Area Development Act, 1976[cite: 15]; (ii) Whether the statutory charge created by operation of law under Section 13-A of the UPIAD Act, 1976 is rendered unenforceable against a Corporate Debtor during CIRP due to non-registration of charge with the Registrar of Companies under Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013, or by virtue of the non-obstante overriding effect of Section 238 of the IBC[cite: 15].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A statutory authority possessing an automatic first charge over immovable property by operation of a state enactment for unpaid lease rentals or development dues qualifies as a 'secured creditor' under Section 3(30) of the IBC, and such statutory charge does not require registration under Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013 to be enforceable in corporate insolvency proceedings[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 13-A of the Uttar Pradesh Industrial Area Development Act, 1976 expressly mandates that any amount payable to the Authority under Section 13 constitutes a charge over the property[cite: 15]. In line with the Supreme Court's ruling in Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority vs. Prabhjit Singh Soni and State Tax Officer vs. Rainbow Papers, a charge created by virtue of law operates ipso facto upon default and is neither inconsistent with Section 238 of the IBC nor circumscribed by Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013, as registration applies to consensual charges created by the company itself rather than statutory charges arising by operation of plenary legislation[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified from the RP's own affidavit dated 05.05.2023 that the Corporate Debtor defaulted on lease rentals prior to CIRP initiation, which established an immediate statutory default under Section 13 and triggered the charge under Section 13-A of the UPIAD Act, 1976[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: GNIDA and NOIDA are Secured Operational Creditors by operation of law; hence, the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in declaring GNIDA as a Secured Creditor whose interests must be appropriately accounted for under Section 30(2) of the IBC[cite: 15].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1147 of 2023 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1519 of 2023 are dismissed, upholding the order dated 24.07.2023 passed in I.A. No. 4869 of 2022 and the order dated 30.08.2023 passed in I.A. No. 4588 of 2023 by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT New Delhi Bench Court-II)[cite: 15].
summary: The Resolution Professionals of Primrose Infratech Pvt. Ltd. and Zeal Developers Pvt. Ltd. appealed against NCLT New Delhi orders holding Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority (GNIDA) and New Okhla Industrial Development Authority (NOIDA) to be Secured Operational Creditors in respect of outstanding lease rentals[cite: 15]. The Appellants contended that Section 13-A of the UPIAD Act was enacted post-lease, charges were unregistered under Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013, and IBC Section 238 overrode state law[cite: 15]. Dismissing both appeals, the NCLAT Principal Bench relied on the Supreme Court's ruling in GNIDA vs. Prabhjit Singh Soni to hold that Section 13-A of the 1976 Act creates an automatic statutory charge over the property for unpaid dues by operation of law[cite: 15]. The Tribunal affirmed that non-registration under Section 77 of the Companies Act does not dilute a statutory charge, and the authorities must be treated as secured creditors under Section 3(30) of the IBC[cite: 15].

case_title: Hemant Shantilal Shah & Anr. vs. Care Office Equipment Ltd. & Ors.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Hemant Shantilal Shah and Heena Hemant Shah (Personal Guarantors and Suspended Management of Care Office Equipment Ltd.)[cite: 16]. Respondent No. 1 is Care Office Equipment Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 16]. Respondent No. 2 is Vikash Gautamchand Jain (Resolution Professional)[cite: 16]. Respondents Nos. 3 and 4 are Kamlesh Dhirajlal Shah and Firoz Pirbhai Sama[cite: 16]. Respondent No. 5 is Sudeep Sampatmal Dasani (Successful Resolution Applicant / SRA)[cite: 16]. Respondents Nos. 6 to 9 are Committee of Creditors (CoC) members: Bank of India (56.82%), State Bank of India (26.37%), Canara Bank (16.50%), and American Express (0.31%)[cite: 16]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Care Office Equipment Ltd. was admitted into CIRP on 29.05.2019 upon a Section 9 application[cite: 16]. During the process, Sudeep Dasani submitted an EOI and subsequent resolution plan along with persons acting in concert (PAC - Tulsiani brothers) and an SPV (Coral Minechem Pvt Ltd)[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Valuation reports revealed an average Fair Value of Rs. 13.06 Crores and Liquidation Value of Rs. 9.96 Crores[cite: 16]. The resolution plan approved by the CoC provided an outlay of approximately Rs. 10 Crores, which the Appellants contested as undervalued compared to their self-estimated asset worth of Rs. 78 Crores (including uncollected disputed receivables from Dell valued at Rs. 40.69 Crores)[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 29.05.2019[cite: 16]. Form G was republished on 12.12.2019[cite: 16]. CoC approved the resolution plan with 99.69% voting share on 26.02.2020 in its 8th meeting[cite: 16]. The Letter of Intent was issued on 11.05.2020[cite: 16]. The RP filed plan approval application IA No. 358 of 2020 in June 2020[cite: 16]. After NCLT ordered disclosure of valuation reports on 30.03.2022 and CoC reaffirmed the plan's viability on 02.08.2022, NCLT Ahmedabad allowed IA No. 358 of 2020 on 20.12.2022[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered valuation reports from two valuers; Minutes of 6th (03.02.2020), 7th (13.02.2020), and 8th (26.02.2020) CoC meetings; Section 29A eligibility undertakings and certificates; and Clauses 3(4), 7, and 12 of the resolution plan expressly providing that personal guarantees remain enforceable by Financial Creditors and extinguishing guarantor subrogation rights[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed IA No. 434 of 2020 objecting to the resolution plan[cite: 16]. NCLT Ahmedabad Bench Court-II approved the resolution plan via IA No. 358 of 2020 on 20.12.2022[cite: 16]. Appellants challenged the order before the Gujarat High Court (CA No. 26669 of 2022), which relegated them to the NCLAT, leading to Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 26 of 2023[cite: 16].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a resolution plan can validly extinguish the statutory subrogation rights of personal guarantors while simultaneously preserving the right of Financial Creditors to independently enforce personal guarantees for unpaid debt shortfalls[cite: 16]; (ii) Whether the Resolution Professional and CoC committed material irregularity by omitting to appoint a third registered valuer under Regulation 35(1)(b) of the CIRP Regulations and by excluding uncollected, litigated receivables from the valuation metrics[cite: 16]; (iii) Whether introducing associate co-applicants or an SPV for plan implementation after the initial individual EOI submission vitiates the approval process under Section 29A and Section 30(2) of the IBC[cite: 16].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A resolution plan approved by the Committee of Creditors in its commercial wisdom may legitimately preserve the independent rights of financial creditors to enforce personal guarantees against promoters/guarantors while extinguishing the guarantors' right of subrogation against the corporate debtor, as an involuntary discharge of the principal debtor in insolvency does not absolve personal guarantors from independent guarantee contracts[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 read with Section 30(2) of the IBC and the Supreme Court precedent in Lalit Kumar Jain v. Union of India, the release of a corporate debtor under an approved plan does not release personal guarantors[cite: 16]. Under Regulation 35(1)(b) of the CIRP Regulations, appointment of a third valuer is not mandatory but discretionary, resting on significant divergence or a specific proposal from the CoC[cite: 16]. Further, Section 29A compliance is satisfied if all entities and persons acting in concert forming part of the prospective resolution applicant group are vetted and furnish statutory eligibility undertakings prior to final CoC approval[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the CoC specifically considered the two valuation reports and affirmatively resolved not to appoint a third valuer, that the Appellants received copies of the valuation reports pursuant to confidentiality undertakings, that Section 29A undertakings were furnished for all associates, and that unrecovered litigated receivables (e.g. against Dell) were contingent assets properly excluded from baseline liquidation valuation[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The resolution plan complied with all mandatory parameters under Section 30(2) and CIRP Regulations 36 to 39, the commercial wisdom of the 99.69% CoC majority is non-justiciable, and the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in approving the plan[cite: 16].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 26 of 2023 is dismissed with no grounds to interfere with the impugned order dated 20.12.2022 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Ahmedabad Bench, Court-II) in I.A. No. 358 of 2020[cite: 16]. Parties are directed to bear their own costs[cite: 16].
summary: Hemant Shantilal Shah and Heena Hemant Shah, personal guarantors and suspended directors of Care Office Equipment Ltd., appealed against an NCLT Ahmedabad order approving the resolution plan submitted by Sudeep Dasani and his associates with a 99.69% CoC voting majority[cite: 16]. The appellants alleged gross undervaluation, failure to appoint a third valuer under Regulation 35(1)(b), unlawful inclusion of co-applicants post-EOI, and illegality in extinguishing their subrogation rights while allowing lenders to pursue their personal guarantees[cite: 16]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that the decision not to appoint a third valuer and the exclusion of contingent receivables fell squarely within the CoC's commercial wisdom[cite: 16]. Relying on Lalit Kumar Jain v. UOI, the Tribunal affirmed that resolution plans can validly preserve lenders' remedies against personal guarantors without affording them subrogation recourse against the resolved corporate debtor[cite: 16].

case_title: Adisri Commercial Pvt. Ltd. vs. Reserve Bank of India & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1074 of 2023 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1075 of 2023 & I.A. No. 4628 of 2023
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Adisri Commercial Pvt. Ltd. (Shareholder of Corporate Debtors SIFL and SEFL)[cite: 17]. Respondent No. 1 is the Reserve Bank of India (RBI - Appropriate Financial Sector Regulator)[cite: 17]. Respondent No. 2 is Mr. Rajneesh Sharma (Administrator of SIFL and SEFL)[cite: 17]. Other respondents include the Committee of Creditors (CoC) and National Asset Reconstruction Company Limited (NARCL - Successful Resolution Applicant / SRA)[cite: 17]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Srei Infrastructure Finance Limited (SIFL) and Srei Equipment Finance Limited (SEFL) were non-banking financial service providers registered with the RBI[cite: 17]. On 01.10.2021, RBI superseded their Boards of Directors under Section 45-IE of the RBI Act due to severe financial deterioration, non-compliance with CRAR/NOF norms, and bank borrowing defaults, appointing Rajneesh Sharma as Administrator[cite: 17]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total borrowings of SIFL stood at Rs. 11,746 Crores with defaults across 12 lenders aggregating Rs. 3,566 Crores as on 30.06.2021[cite: 17]. In particular, UCO Bank reported a continuing working capital default of Rs. 165,56,30,967.99 (Principal: Rs. 150 Crores, Interest: Rs. 15,56,30,967.99) with earliest default dates cited as 01.11.2020 (interest) and 13.02.2021 (principal)[cite: 17]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: RBI superseded the Boards on 01.10.2021 (Writ Petition challenging this was dismissed by Bombay High Court on 07.10.2021)[cite: 17]. RBI initiated CIRP under Section 227 via CP (IB) Nos. 294/KB/2021 and 295/KB/2021; NCLT Kolkata admitted the petitions on 08.10.2021[cite: 17]. Appellant's statutory appeals challenging admission were rejected for unexcused re-filing delay of 321 days on 21.12.2022, affirmed by the Supreme Court on 30.01.2023[cite: 17]. Appellant then filed recall applications IA Nos. 389/KB/2023 and 391/KB/2023 on 14.02.2023 (after 17 months), which NCLT Kolkata dismissed on 11.08.2023[cite: 17]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RBI supersession order dated 01.10.2021[cite: 17]; UCO Bank default certificate and recall notices[cite: 17]; Administrator's unconditional Form-2 written consent dated 08.10.2021[cite: 17]; unapproved Business Transfer Agreement dated 16.08.2019[cite: 17]; and records of NARCL's approved and implemented resolution plan[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissed the recall applications on 11.08.2023 holding they were impermissible review petitions in disguise[cite: 17]. The shareholder appealed to NCLAT via Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 1074 and 1075 of 2023 alleging Section 10A bar and natural justice violations[cite: 17].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction to recall a CIRP admission order passed under Section 227 of the IBC on substantive grounds such as the statutory bar under Section 10A or alleged absence of default, after the applicant's statutory appeals challenging the admission have been dismissed up to the Supreme Court[cite: 17]; (ii) Whether the statutory bar under Section 10A of the IBC applies to insolvency proceedings initiated by the Reserve Bank of India under Section 227 read with the FSP Rules, 2019 against financial service providers[cite: 17]; (iii) What constitutes the legal threshold and scope of the inherent power of recall under Rule 11 of NCLAT Rules versus an impermissible review of a judgment on merits[cite: 17].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal possesses inherent jurisdiction to recall a judgment only where a fundamental procedural defect has occurred (such as lack of service on a necessary party) or where the order was procured through fraud played on the court; the power of recall cannot be converted into an impermissible rehearing or review on merits to re-adjudicate substantive issues that have already attained finality[cite: 17]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 227 of the IBC constitutes an overarching non-obstante framework governing the insolvency and liquidation of financial service providers initiated by a sectoral regulator[cite: 17]. Once the Board of Directors of an FSP is superseded under Section 45-IE of the RBI Act, 1934, the entity is legally represented exclusively by the appointed Administrator, and hearing the Administrator satisfies all requirements of natural justice without any statutory mandate to issue notice to individual equity shareholders[cite: 17]. Section 420(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 is strictly confined to rectifying apparent clerical errors and cannot be used as a second appeal in disguise[cite: 17]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the Administrator was personally present and gave unconditional consent at the admission hearing, that continuous systemic defaults across 12 lenders were established by the regulator, that the Appellant's prior substantive appeals were dismissed up to the Supreme Court, and that the NARCL resolution plan was already approved and implemented[cite: 17]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The recall applications filed 17 months after admission were impermissible review petitions on merits; no procedural irregularity or fraud was established, and the Adjudicating Authority committed no legal error in rejecting the applications[cite: 17].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1074 of 2023 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1075 of 2023 are dismissed with no order as to costs, affirming the common order dated 11.08.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Kolkata Bench) in IA (IB) No. 391/KB/2023 and IA (IB) No. 389/KB/2023[cite: 17]. Pending Interlocutory Application I.A. No. 4628 of 2023 is closed[cite: 17].
summary: Adisri Commercial Pvt. Ltd., a shareholder of Srei Infrastructure Finance Ltd. (SIFL) and Srei Equipment Finance Ltd. (SEFL), appealed against an NCLT Kolkata order rejecting its applications to recall the CIRP admission orders dated 08.10.2021 initiated by the Reserve Bank of India under Section 227 of the IBC[cite: 17]. The appellant argued that the admission violated natural justice, that default occurred during the Section 10A prohibited period, and that assets had been transferred under a slump exchange[cite: 17]. Dismissing both appeals, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that the power of recall under inherent powers is strictly limited to procedural infirmities or fraud, and cannot be invoked as an impermissible review on merits, especially after the appellant's statutory appeals against admission had already been dismissed up to the Supreme Court[cite: 17]. The Tribunal affirmed that representation by the RBI-appointed Administrator satisfied natural justice and that the recall applications were abusive attempts to derail an approved, implemented resolution plan[cite: 17].

case_title: SRV Techno Engineering Pvt. Ltd. vs. Purvanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain, Technical Members Naresh Salecha and Indevar Pandey)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is SRV Techno Engineering Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor)[cite: 18]. The Respondent is Purvanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. (Corporate Debtor - a state government electricity distribution company in eastern Uttar Pradesh)[cite: 18]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor awarded two contracts/tenders to Appellant for system improvement, strengthening, and augmentation works to reduce AT&C losses and enhance power supply: Kopaganj Project (LOI dated 03.03.2016 / contract dated 21.03.2016 with revised BOQ of Rs. 7,37,93,117/-) and Ghosi Project (LOI dated 27.04.2016 / contract dated 10.05.2016 with revised BOQ of Rs. 6,72,24,729/-)[cite: 18]. Both revised BOQs were approved by the Managing Director, Director (Technical), and Superintending Engineer of Respondent, and a Work Completion Certificate was issued on 23.12.2017 confirming successful completion[cite: 18]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Across both projects, Appellant raised total invoices of Rs. 14,10,38,063/- against which payments of Rs. 12,33,48,156/- (or Rs. 11,81,08,663/- net) were received, leaving an admitted principal default amount of Rs. 1,76,89,875/-[cite: 18]. Appellant originally claimed Rs. 4,43,42,607/- inclusive of interest without stating default date, which was subsequently corrected via MA No. 02/2023 fixing default date as 24.04.2018 (the date of last payment received)[cite: 18]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Work completion certificate was issued on 23.12.2017[cite: 18]. Last partial payment made on 24.04.2018[cite: 18]. Demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC was hand-delivered on 03.09.2019 and dispatched via registered post on 12.09.2019[cite: 18]. Respondent sent no Section 8 reply[cite: 18]. Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 486/ALD/2019 was filed on 26.11.2019[cite: 18]. Later, Appellant initiated MSME arbitration on 16.06.2022, securing an award of Rs. 1,73,84,846/- on 04.01.2023[cite: 18]. NCLT dismissed Section 9 on 12.10.2023[cite: 18]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved LOIs, contracts, internal file notings showing approvals by MD and Chief Engineers, revised BOQ communications dated 11.01.2017, work completion certificate dated 23.12.2017 for Rs. 14.10 Crores, accounts confirmation letter dated 03.10.2017, Section 8 demand notices, and MSME arbitral award dated 04.01.2023[cite: 18]. 6.
