PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Allahabad Bench dismissed CP (IB) No. 486/ALD/2019 on 12.10.2023, ruling that because procedural defects regarding default date and quantum were cured on 03.03.2023 (via MA No. 02/2023), the petition was deemed filed on 03.03.2023, by which time the 04.01.2023 MSME award constituted a pre-existing dispute, and further held the claim unmaintainable due to internal committee non-approval and recovery nature[cite: 18]. Operational Creditor appealed to NCLAT via Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1651 of 2023[cite: 18].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the date of filing of a Section 9 petition shifts to the date on which curative amendments/clarifications (regarding default date and reconciled default quantum) are placed on record, or whether amendments relate back to the original date of petition institution[cite: 18]; (ii) Whether initiating proceedings or securing an arbitral award under Section 18 of the MSMED Act, 2006 during the pendency of a Section 9 petition constitutes a 'pre-existing dispute' under Section 5(6) and Section 8/9 of the IBC[cite: 18]; (iii) Whether a public sector corporate debtor can evade operational debt liabilities under the guise of the doctrine of indoor management by asserting that works executed and signed by its Managing Director and Superintending Engineer lacked formal sanction from an internal tender committee[cite: 18].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Curative amendments and supplementary pleadings rectifying procedural defects, omissions of default dates, or accounting reconciliations in an insolvency petition relate back to the original date of institution of the application; subsequent recourse by an operational creditor to statutory recovery forums (such as MSME facilitation/arbitration) after instituting an IBC application does not retroactively create a 'pre-existing dispute' under the IBC[cite: 18]. Furthermore, internal administrative approval lapses within a corporate debtor cannot impair third-party operational rights under the doctrine of indoor management[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9(5)(ii) proviso mandates that before rejecting an application for incompleteness, the Adjudicating Authority must grant 7 days to rectify defects; such corrections are curative and do not alter the foundational filing date (26.11.2019)[cite: 18]. Under Section 5(6) read with Sections 8 and 9 of the IBC, a 'pre-existing dispute' must exist prior to the receipt of the Section 8 demand notice[cite: 18]. A supplier's statutory claim under Section 17/18 of the MSMED Act, 2006 to recover undisputed dues is distinct in context and does not constitute a defense of pre-existing dispute on the part of the corporate debtor[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the signed work completion certificates, official letters dated 11.01.2017 approving revised BOQs bearing the Managing Director's signature, and undisputed execution of works[cite: 18]. The Corporate Debtor failed to reply to the Section 8 demand notice within 10 days and raised no dispute prior to its delivery[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 9 petition was instituted on 26.11.2019, prior to any MSME reference; no pre-existing dispute existed prior to the Section 8 demand notice; and the Corporate Debtor's defense based on internal committee sanction was barred by the doctrine of indoor management, rendering the NCLT's dismissal perverse and unsustainable[cite: 18].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1651 of 2023 is allowed, and the impugned order dated 12.10.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Allahabad Bench, Prayagraj) in CP (IB) No. 486/ALD/2019 is set aside with no order as to costs[cite: 18]. Interlocutory Applications I.A. Nos. 5952, 5954, and 5955 of 2023 are closed[cite: 18].
summary: SRV Techno Engineering Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Allahabad order dismissing its Section 9 CIRP petition against Purvanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. for unpaid electrical contract dues of Rs. 1.76 Crores[cite: 18]. The NCLT had held that because the default date and reconciled amount were corrected via miscellaneous application in 2023, the petition was deemed filed in 2023, making an intervening MSME arbitration award of January 2023 a pre-existing dispute[cite: 18]. Setting aside the dismissal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that curative amendments relate back to the original institution date (26.11.2019) and cannot be defeated by procedural technicalities[cite: 18]. The Tribunal ruled that seeking relief under the MSMED Act does not constitute a pre-existing dispute under the IBC and that a PSU cannot dispute completed, certified works under the guise of internal committee non-approval due to the doctrine of indoor management[cite: 18].

case_title: JC Flowers Asset Reconstruction Private Limited (substituted for Yes Bank Limited) vs. Laxmi Oil and Vanaspati Private Limited
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1052 of 2022 & I.A. No. 4514 of 2022
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain, Technical Members Naresh Salecha and Indevar Pandey)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Original Appellant/Financial Creditor is Yes Bank Limited, substituted by JC Flowers Asset Reconstruction Private Limited via assignment agreement dated 16.12.2022[cite: 19]. The Respondent is Laxmi Oil and Vanaspati Private Limited (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 19]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Yes Bank sanctioned a secured cash credit facility of Rs. 10 Crores on 26.03.2017 (Master Facility Agreement dated 29.03.2017), enhanced to Rs. 20 Crores on 15.02.2018 (Supplementary Agreement and Hypothecation Deed dated 21.02.2018), secured by mortgage over residential land and continuing personal guarantees[cite: 19]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: As on 28.02.2020, the cash credit account had an outstanding balance of Rs. 19,99,98,214.94 (within the sanctioned Rs. 20 Crore limit)[cite: 19]. On 01.03.2020 (value date 29.02.2020), monthly interest of Rs. 27,93,039/- was debited, resulting in an overdrawn balance of Rs. 20,27,91,254.42[cite: 19]. In Part IV of Form 1, the Financial Creditor claimed a total default of Rs. 25,99,34,488.25 as on 06.09.2021, specifying 28.02.2020 as the date of default, 20.07.2020 as the date of NPA, and 27.08.2020 as the loan recall notice date[cite: 19]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Corporate Debtor was declared NPA on 20.07.2020 for non-submission of monthly stock statements since January 2020[cite: 19]. Yes Bank issued a loan recall notice on 27.08.2020 and invoked personal guarantees on 07.09.2020[cite: 19]. Yes Bank filed Section 7 application CP (IB) No. 05/ALD/2022 before NCLT Allahabad, which was dismissed on 13.06.2022[cite: 19]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Facility agreements, bank statements showing interest capitalization on 01.03.2020, the loan recall notice dated 27.08.2020 basing acceleration explicitly on non-submission of stock statements, and RBI Covid-19 Regulatory Framework Circulars dated 27.03.2020 and 23.05.2020 providing debt moratoria from 01.03.2020 to 31.08.2020[cite: 19]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Allahabad Bench dismissed CP (IB) No. 05/ALD/2022 on 13.06.2022, holding that default could not be reckoned as 28.02.2020 and that the loan recall dated 27.08.2020 fell squarely within the prohibited Section 10A period[cite: 19]. The Financial Creditor appealed to NCLAT via Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1052 of 2022[cite: 19].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the date of default for unpaid monthly interest can be reckoned as 28.02.2020 when, under the lender's accounting system, interest becomes due on the last day of the month but becomes payable only on the 1st day of the succeeding month (01.03.2020)[cite: 19]; (ii) Whether debt payments falling payable on 01.03.2020 are shielded from default by the RBI Regulatory Package Moratorium circulars dated 27.03.2020 and 23.05.2020[cite: 19]; (iii) Whether a Section 7 CIRP application is barred under Section 10A of the IBC where an account is declared NPA on 20.07.2020 and accelerated via a loan recall notice dated 27.08.2020 during the statutory suspension window[cite: 19].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 3(12) of the IBC, a default occurs only when an obligation becomes both 'due and payable' and remains unpaid in praesenti; where interest becomes payable on the first day of the following month, no actionable default exists prior to that payable date[cite: 19]. If the date the debt becomes payable falls within an RBI regulatory moratorium or if acceleration and NPA declaration take place between 25.03.2020 and 24.03.2021, the bar under Section 10A of the IBC applies unconditionally to preclude the institution of CIRP[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 10A contains a non-obstante clause creating a total statutory prohibition on initiating CIRP for defaults occurring during the notified Covid-19 period[cite: 19]. The definition of default under Section 3(12) requires both 'due' and 'payable' conditions to be conjunctively satisfied[cite: 19]. When an installment falls payable on 01.03.2020, it is protected by the RBI Moratorium Circulars, and cannot be antedated to 28.02.2020 to bypass Section 10A[cite: 19]. Furthermore, non-submission of stock statements does not constitute a financial payment default under Section 3(12)[cite: 19]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the statement of accounts, finding the account balance on 28.02.2020 was Rs. 19.99 Crores (within the Rs. 20 Crore limit) and only exceeded the limit upon interest application on 01.03.2020[cite: 19]. The RBI circular granted a moratorium covering payments due from 01.03.2020 onwards, and the bank's loan recall notice dated 27.08.2020 fell squarely within the Section 10A window[cite: 19]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The alleged default of 28.02.2020 was untenable in law and fact, the payment payable on 01.03.2020 was covered by the RBI moratorium, and subsequent NPA/recall actions fell inside the Section 10A prohibited period; hence, the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in dismissing the Section 7 petition[cite: 19].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1052 of 2022 is dismissed with no order as to costs, affirming the order dated 13.06.2022 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Allahabad Bench, Prayagraj) in CP (IB) No. 05/ALD/2022[cite: 19]. All pending Interlocutory Applications are closed, preserving liberty for the Appellant to pursue other ordinary legal remedies for debt recovery[cite: 19].
summary: JC Flowers ARC (substituted for Yes Bank Ltd.) appealed against an NCLT Allahabad order dismissing its Section 7 CIRP application against Laxmi Oil and Vanaspati Pvt. Ltd. for default on a Rs. 20 Crore cash credit facility[cite: 19]. The lender claimed the date of default was 28.02.2020 for unserviced February interest, seeking to escape the Section 10A bar[cite: 19]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that under the bank's own system, interest was payable on 01.03.2020, and default under Section 3(12) requires debt to be both due and payable[cite: 19]. Because the payment due on 01.03.2020 was protected by the RBI Covid-19 regulatory moratorium, and the subsequent NPA declaration (20.07.2020) and loan recall notice (27.08.2020) occurred during the statutory suspension period, the petition was completely barred under Section 10A of the IBC[cite: 19].

case_title: Arunkumar Jayantilal Muchhala vs. Awaita Properties Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 121 of 2023 & I.A. No. 4828 of 2023
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Arunkumar Jayantilal Muchhala (Ex-Director of Tarapur Textiles Park Limited, Corporate Debtor)[cite: 20]. Respondent No. 1 is Awaita Properties Pvt. Ltd. (Financial Creditor)[cite: 20]. Respondent No. 2 is Tarapur Textiles Park Limited represented through its IRP/RP CA Prashant Jain[cite: 20]. PNB International Ltd. is an Intervenor in IA No. 4828/2023[cite: 20]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: On 01.01.2014, Respondent No. 1 disbursed an amount of Rs. 5,00,00,000/- (Rs. 5 Crores) via RTGS bank transfer to the Corporate Debtor to meet working capital requirements repayable on demand with interest claimed at 15% per annum[cite: 20]. The Corporate Debtor recorded this amount in its balance sheet under 'Long Term Borrowings - Unsecured loan from Related Parties', while the Appellant claimed the amount was an interest-free part-payment deposit under an unexecuted draft MOU with SKIL Infrastructure Limited for developing 'Boisar Project Land'[cite: 20]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Respondent No. 1 claimed an outstanding financial debt default of Rs. 8,56,30,137/- (inclusive of interest at 15% p.a.) as of the petition filing date, asserting default occurred upon non-payment following demand[cite: 20]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Respondent No. 1 issued a demand notice on 20.02.2018 demanding repayment of the Rs. 5 Crore loan with 15% interest, which the Corporate Debtor replied to on 26.02.2018 denying the loan[cite: 20]. A legal notice was sent on 30.05.2018, followed by the filing of Section 7 petition C.P. No. 4076/IBC/MB/2018 on 24.10.2018[cite: 20]. NCLT Mumbai admitted the petition on 06.12.2022[cite: 20]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RTGS bank transfer details and bank certification dated 01.01.2014 verifying disbursal of Rs. 5 Crores from Respondent No. 1 to the Corporate Debtor[cite: 20]; Corporate Debtor's audited balance sheet recording the debt under 'Long Term Borrowings - Unsecured loan from Related Parties'[cite: 20]; demand notice dated 20.02.2018[cite: 20]; and an unexecuted draft MOU dated October 2013 between the Corporate Debtor and SKIL Infrastructure Ltd., to which Respondent No. 1 was not a party[cite: 20]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-III admitted C.P. No. 4076/IBC/MB/2018 under Section 7 on 06.12.2022 after giving the Corporate Debtor an opportunity to produce ledger books, which it failed to do[cite: 20]. The Ex-Director appealed via Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 121 of 2023[cite: 20].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a formal written loan agreement is a mandatory statutory prerequisite under Section 5(8) and Section 7 of the IBC to establish the existence of a 'financial debt' where actual disbursal of funds is proven via bank certificates and acknowledged as long-term borrowings in the Corporate Debtor's balance sheets[cite: 20]; (ii) Whether the disbursal of funds to meet working capital requirements qualifies as a transaction having the commercial effect of a borrowing under Section 5(8)(f) possessing the element of 'time value of money', even in the absence of a written interest covenant[cite: 20]; (iii) Whether an unexecuted draft MOU between the Corporate Debtor and a distinct third-party entity (SKIL) can bind the Financial Creditor or alter the character of a direct monetary disbursal into an interest-free project advance[cite: 20].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The IBC does not prescribe any mandatory requirement for a formal written agreement to establish a financial debt; where unconditional disbursal of funds is verified through banking channels and the corporate debtor records the liability under long-term borrowings in its books of accounts, the transaction constitutes a financial debt disbursed against consideration for the time value of money, enabling the creditor to invoke Section 7 upon default[cite: 20]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) of the IBC is an expansive, inclusive definition, with Section 5(8)(f) serving as a residuary catch-all provision covering transactions having the commercial effect of a borrowing[cite: 20]. Consideration for the 'time value of money' does not strictly require payment of interest or an immediate return of cash, but encompasses loans provided to finance business operations or enhance economic prospects, and does not exclude interest-free advances as settled in Orator Marketing[cite: 20]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified incontrovertible RTGS bank records showing direct credit of Rs. 5 Crores to the Corporate Debtor, balance sheet acknowledgments classifying the sum as 'Long Term Borrowings - Unsecured loan from Related Parties', and the failure of the Corporate Debtor to produce its ledger accounts to rebut the loan nature, while disregarding the unexecuted draft MOU involving a separate legal entity (SKIL)[cite: 20]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The disbursal was a commercial financial debt disbursed against the time value of money, which remained unpaid upon demand; thus, debt and default exceeding the statutory threshold were fully proven and the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in admitting the Section 7 petition[cite: 20].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 121 of 2023 is dismissed with no order as to costs, affirming the order dated 06.12.2022 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai Bench, Court-III) in C.P. No. 4076/IBC/MB/2018[cite: 20]. The Resolution Professional is directed to proceed with the CIRP process in accordance with law, and I.A. No. 4828 of 2023 is disposed of[cite: 20].
summary: Arunkumar Jayantilal Muchhala, Ex-Director of Tarapur Textiles Park Limited, appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 7 CIRP application filed by Awaita Properties Pvt. Ltd. for default on an outstanding debt of Rs. 8.56 Crores[cite: 20]. The appellant contended that the Rs. 5 Crore transfer in 2014 was an interest-free advance under an unexecuted joint venture draft MOU with SKIL Infrastructure Ltd., arguing that in the absence of a written loan agreement, no financial debt existed[cite: 20]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that a formal written loan agreement is not mandatory under the IBC to prove financial debt when the disbursal of money is conclusively evidenced by RTGS bank records and acknowledged in the corporate debtor's balance sheet under long-term borrowings[cite: 20]. The Tribunal held that the unexecuted draft MOU with an independent entity was non-binding, and that the working capital funding carried the commercial effect of borrowing with time value of money[cite: 20].

case_title: AAA Insolvency Professionals LLP vs. Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain, Technical Members Naresh Salecha and Indevar Pandey)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is AAA Insolvency Professionals LLP (Proposed Liquidator / Insolvency Professional Entity)[cite: 21]. Respondent No. 1 is Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. (SCC Member)[cite: 21]. Respondent No. 2 is Mavent Restructuring Services LLP through Liquidator Ravinder Kumar Goyal (Appointed Liquidator)[cite: 21]. Nitin Jain was the erstwhile Liquidator of PSL Limited (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 21]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was admitted to CIRP under Section 10 of the IBC on 15.02.2019[cite: 21]. CIRP having failed, NCLT ordered liquidation on 11.09.2020 and appointed Nitin Jain as Liquidator to conduct sale as a going concern[cite: 21]. ED initiated PMLA investigations and provisionally attached assets on 02.12.2021 (partially stayed/regulated by Delhi High Court orders allowing sale of unattached assets)[cite: 21]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; appeal arises out of an interlocutory application regarding replacement and appointment of liquidator during ongoing liquidation[cite: 21]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: In the 28th SCC meeting on 24.07.2023, the erstwhile liquidator cited personal difficulties and proposed appointing an IPE[cite: 21]. SCC passed a resolution with 81.4% voting share recommending the appointment of Appellant (AAA Insolvency Professionals LLP) as Liquidator[cite: 21]. The erstwhile liquidator filed IA No. 1230/AHM/2023 under Regulation 31A(11) of the Liquidation Process Regulations for his replacement[cite: 21]. NCLT Ahmedabad partly allowed the application on 12.01.2024 by replacing the liquidator but appointing Respondent No. 2 instead of Appellant[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Minutes of the 28th SCC meeting dated 24.07.2023[cite: 21]; IA No. 1230/AHM/2023 which omitted the mandatory Form AA written consent schedule[cite: 21]; an unsubmitted letter dated 29.08.2023 claiming consent[cite: 21]; and non-filing of Form IP1 on the IBBI web portal within three days as mandated by IBBI Circular No. IBBI/CIRP/023/2019 dated 14.08.2019[cite: 21]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench rejected the appointment of Appellant on 12.01.2024 due to failure to submit written consent in Form AA Schedule II and ineligibility under Regulation 3, appointing Respondent No. 2 as Liquidator[cite: 21]. The proposed IPE appealed to NCLAT via Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 153 of 2024[cite: 21].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a proposed/prospective liquidator entity has the locus standi as an 'aggrieved person' under Section 61 of the IBC to appeal an order of the Adjudicating Authority rejecting its appointment[cite: 21]; (ii) Whether obtaining and annexing the written consent of the proposed liquidator in Form AA of Schedule II prior to filing an application under Regulation 31A(11) of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 is a mandatory statutory prerequisite or a curable technical defect[cite: 21]; (iii) Whether the Adjudicating Authority possesses the inherent jurisdiction under Sections 33 and 34 of the IBC to appoint an independent liquidator other than the entity recommended by the Stakeholders' Consultation Committee[cite: 21].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A proposed or prospective liquidator holds no vested or inherent legal right to be appointed, and therefore lacks locus standi as an 'aggrieved person' under Section 61 of the IBC to challenge an order declining its appointment[cite: 21]. Furthermore, obtaining and submitting the prior written consent of a proposed liquidator in Form AA of Schedule II is a mandatory statutory condition precedent under Regulation 31A(11) of the Liquidation Process Regulations, the omission of which cannot be excused as a mere curable defect[cite: 21]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 31A(11) of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 requires the consultation committee to file an application 'after obtaining the written consent of the proposed liquidator in Form AA of the Schedule II'[cite: 21]. Under IBBI Circular dated 14.08.2019, Form IP1 confirming consent must be uploaded on the IBBI portal within three days of execution[cite: 21]. Sections 33 and 34 of the IBC empower the Adjudicating Authority to supervise the liquidation estate and remove or appoint a liquidator where statutory preconditions are violated or where circumstances warrant the appointment of an independent professional[cite: 21]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that no written consent in Form AA was placed before the SCC during the 28th meeting or annexed to IA No. 1230/AHM/2023, and the Appellant failed to upload Form IP1 on the IBBI portal within three days of the alleged 29.08.2023 consent, demonstrating that valid statutory consent was never executed or submitted in accordance with law[cite: 21]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant lacked locus standi to maintain the appeal and violated the mandatory statutory requirements of Regulation 31A(11); consequently, the Adjudicating Authority acted within its jurisdiction in rejecting Appellant and appointing Respondent No. 2 as Liquidator[cite: 21].
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 153 of 2024 is dismissed with no order as to costs, affirming the order dated 12.01.2024 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Ahmedabad Bench) in I.A. No. 1230/AHM/2023 in C.P. (IB)/37/AHM/2017[cite: 21]. All pending Interlocutory Applications are closed[cite: 21].
summary: AAA Insolvency Professionals LLP appealed against an NCLT Ahmedabad order which partly allowed an application to replace the liquidator of PSL Limited but appointed Mavent Restructuring Services LLP (Respondent No. 2) instead of the Appellant, despite an 81.4% vote by the SCC in the Appellant's favor[cite: 21]. The NCLT had rejected the Appellant's appointment due to failure to submit mandatory written consent in Form AA under Regulation 31A(11) of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016[cite: 21]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that a proposed liquidator has no inherent right of appointment and lacks locus standi as an aggrieved person under Section 61 of the IBC[cite: 21]. The Tribunal affirmed that submitting Form AA prior to filing the replacement application and uploading Form IP1 on the IBBI portal are mandatory prerequisites, and that the NCLT retains full jurisdiction under Sections 33 and 34 to appoint an independent liquidator[cite: 21].

case_title: Shri Prem Prakash Bansal vs. IDBI Bank Limited & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain, Technical Members Naresh Salecha and Indevar Pandey)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Shri Prem Prakash Bansal, Ex-Director and majority shareholder of M/s B.P. Bansal Agritech Private Limited (Corporate Debtor / Corporate Guarantor)[cite: 22]. Respondent No. 1 is IDBI Bank Limited (Lead Financial Creditor of the Consortium)[cite: 22]. Respondent No. 2 is Shri Keyur Shah (Interim Resolution Professional)[cite: 22]. The Principal Borrower is M/s B.P. Food Products Private Limited[cite: 22]. The Intervenors are consortium members State Bank of India, Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited, and UVARC (assignee of RBL Bank Limited)[cite: 22]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Between 20.03.2014 and 13.04.2017, the Consortium of Lenders granted credit facilities aggregating to Rs. 181.29 Crores to the Principal Borrower[cite: 22]. To secure these facilities, an Inter Se Agreement and a Security Trustee Agreement were executed on 10.06.2016 appointing IDBI Trusteeship Services Limited as Security Trustee for the lenders' benefit, alongside a Deed of Guarantee dated 10.06.2016 executed by the Corporate Debtor in favor of the Security Trustee[cite: 22]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Principal Borrower's loan accounts were classified as NPA on 29.10.2017 (default date 31.07.2017)[cite: 22]. In the Section 7 petition, Respondent No. 1 claimed a total default of Rs. 49,50,91,461/- (Rs. 48,16,75,872/- under fund-based facilities and Rs. 1,34,15,589/- under bank guarantees)[cite: 22]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Respondent No. 1 issued a loan recall notice to the Principal Borrower on 21.03.2018 and invoked the Corporate Debtor's guarantee on 04.04.2018[cite: 22]. The Principal Borrower was admitted to CIRP under Section 9 on 08.08.2018 (a resolution plan was later approved on 26.05.2020 paying Rs. 18.58 Crores to IDBI Bank while expressly preserving rights against guarantors)[cite: 22]. Respondent No. 1 filed Section 7 petition TP 12 of 2019 [CP (IB) 10 of 2019] on 16.11.2018, which NCLT Indore admitted on 01.12.2022[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Facility agreements, Inter Se Agreement dated 10.06.2016, Security Trustee Agreement dated 10.06.2016, Deed of Guarantee dated 10.06.2016, recall notice dated 21.03.2018, guarantee invocation notice dated 04.04.2018, audited balance sheets showing paid-up capital and free reserves of Rs. 6.80 Crores against Rs. 181.29 Crores guarantee exposure, and intervention applications filed by SBI, Kotak, and UVARC confirming consent[cite: 22]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Corporate Debtor's shareholders previously filed IA No. 01/2021 before NCLT to declare the guarantee void under Section 186 of the Companies Act, which was dismissed on 07.01.2022 and upheld by NCLAT on 30.03.2022[cite: 22]. NCLT Indore Bench admitted Section 7 on 01.12.2022, prompting the Ex-Director to appeal via Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1541 of 2022[cite: 22].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a corporate guarantee executed by a company in excess of statutory limits without requisite approvals under Section 186 of the Companies Act, 2013 is rendered void ab initio, absolving the Corporate Guarantor of liability in Section 7 insolvency proceedings[cite: 22]; (ii) Whether a member bank of a lender consortium has privity of contract and locus standi to independently invoke a corporate guarantee and file a Section 7 CIRP petition where the guarantee was formally executed in favor of a Security Trustee acting for the consortium's benefit[cite: 22]; (iii) Whether CIRP admission against a Corporate Guarantor is barred where a resolution plan has already been approved for the Principal Borrower that expressly preserves lenders' claims against third-party guarantors[cite: 22].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Non-compliance with internal statutory limits or procedural approval requirements under Section 186 of the Companies Act, 2013 by a company issuing a corporate guarantee does not render the guarantee void or unenforceable against third-party institutional lenders; at most, it exposes the defaulting company and officers to penal consequences under Section 186(13), and a closely held entity cannot plead its own legal infraction to unjustly enrich itself and escape financial debt obligations[cite: 22]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: When a contract of guarantee and security trustee agreement is executed for the express benefit of a consortium of lenders, the lenders are direct beneficiaries of the trust and are not strangers to the contract; they are legally entitled to enforce equitable rights under Section 7 of the IBC without requiring the formal execution of proceedings solely by the security trustee[cite: 22]. Furthermore, under Section 128 of the Contract Act and settled IBC jurisprudence, the liability of a corporate guarantor is co-extensive and coterminous with that of the principal debtor, and approval of a resolution plan for the principal borrower does not extinguish the independent contractual liability of guarantors where lenders' remedies were expressly reserved[cite: 22]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the Corporate Debtor and Principal Borrower were family-owned entities sharing common promoter control, that the guarantee was signed by the Appellant following a board resolution, that the lead lender issued a formal guarantee invocation notice on 04.04.2018 upon the borrower's default, and that all consortium members intervened to affirm and support the Section 7 CIRP proceedings[cite: 22]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Deed of Guarantee was valid and enforceable, privity existed between the consortium lender and the Corporate Guarantor through the trust arrangement, and the debt and default exceeding the threshold were conclusively established; thus, the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in admitting the Corporate Debtor into CIRP[cite: 22].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1541 of 2022 is dismissed with no order as to costs, affirming the order dated 01.12.2022 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Indore Bench) in TP 12 of 2019 [CP (IB) 10 of 2019][cite: 22]. The interim order staying the formation of the Committee of Creditors is discharged, and all connected pending Interlocutory Applications are closed[cite: 22].
summary: Prem Prakash Bansal, Ex-Director of M/s B.P. Bansal Agritech Private Limited, appealed against an NCLT Indore order admitting a Section 7 CIRP application filed by IDBI Bank for a financial default exceeding Rs. 49 Crores under a corporate guarantee securing loans extended to the principal borrower, M/s B.P. Food Products Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 22]. The appellant contended that the guarantee was void under Section 186 of the Companies Act, 2013 due to lack of statutory limits, and that IDBI Bank lacked privity of contract as the guarantee was executed in favor of a Security Trustee[cite: 22]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that non-compliance with Section 186 only attracts statutory penalties under Section 186(13) and cannot be weaponized by common family promoters to evade debt liabilities[cite: 22]. The Tribunal ruled that consortium lenders, as direct beneficiaries of the security trust, possess full standing to enforce the guarantee and trigger Section 7 CIRP against the corporate guarantor[cite: 22].

case_title: Namdeo Hindurao Patil vs. Virendra Kumar Jain, Liquidator, Warana Dairy and Agro Industries Limited & Ors.
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 858 of 2023 & I.A. No. 2925 of 2024
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain, Technical Members Naresh Salecha and Indevar Pandey)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Namdeo Hindurao Patil, Suspended Director and Prospective Resolution Applicant of Warana Dairy and Agro Industries Limited (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 23]. Respondent No. 1 is Virendra Kumar Jain (Liquidator of Corporate Debtor)[cite: 23]. Respondents Nos. 2 to 5 are Committee of Creditors (CoC) members: IDBI Bank Limited (35.66% voting share), Punjab National Bank (International) Limited, London (30.71%), Shri Warana Mahila Sahakari Panth Sanstha Limited (23.87%), and Amrut Sevak Sah Pat Sanstha Limited (9.76%)[cite: 23]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed credit facilities, including a loan of Rs. 67 Crores from IDBI Bank Limited[cite: 23]. Following non-repayment, PNB International Limited initiated CIRP under Section 7 of the IBC in CP (IB) 477/C-IV/MB/2020, which was admitted on 16.09.2021[cite: 23]. In the CIRP, Form G was re-issued on 19.02.2022, pursuant to which the Appellant submitted a resolution plan on 12.05.2022[cite: 23]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose from the misutilisation and non-repayment of the Rs. 67 Crore loan facility granted by IDBI Bank[cite: 23]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: IDBI Bank issued a wilful defaulter show-cause notice on 24.01.2020 and declared the Appellant a wilful defaulter on 19.07.2021, confirmed by the Review Committee on 04.10.2021[cite: 23]. Appellant submitted his resolution plan on 12.05.2022[cite: 23]. Bombay High Court permitted withdrawal of Appellant's Writ Petition on 24.08.2022[cite: 23]. A Kolhapur Civil Judge granted a temporary conditional injunction on 19.09.2022 until defendants filed their say[cite: 23]. IDBI Bank filed its reply on 03.10.2022[cite: 23]. In the 21st CoC meeting on 06.10.2022-07.10.2022, the CoC voted with a 66.37% majority to treat Appellant as ineligible under Section 29A(b) and resolved to liquidate the Corporate Debtor[cite: 23]. Appellant's civil suit was dismissed on 19.12.2022, and his first appeal was dismissed by the District Judge on 01.04.2023[cite: 23]. NCLT Mumbai allowed liquidation application IA No. 2972/2022 and rejected Appellant's IA No. 464/2023 on 19.04.2023[cite: 23]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Wilful defaulter orders dated 19.07.2021 and 04.10.2021 under RBI Master Circular dated 01.07.2015; resolution plan submission dated 12.05.2022; minutes of the 17th, 18th, 19th, 20th, and 21st CoC meetings; orders in Regular Civil Suit No. 710/2022 and Regular Civil Appeal No. 4/2023[cite: 23]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Resolution Professional filed IA No. 2972/2022 for liquidation of the Corporate Debtor, and the Appellant filed IA No. 464/2023 challenging his Section 29A disqualification[cite: 23]. NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-IV allowed liquidation and dismissed Appellant's application on 19.04.2023[cite: 23]. The suspended director appealed to NCLAT via Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 858 of 2023[cite: 23].
legal_issues: (i) What constitutes the relevant cut-off date for assessing the eligibility or disqualification of a Resolution Applicant under Section 29A of the IBC[cite: 23]; (ii) Whether a conditional, interim status quo/injunction order obtained from a civil court after the date of plan submission can cure or wipe out a preexisting disqualification as a wilful defaulter under Section 29A(b) of the IBC[cite: 23]; (iii) Whether MSME promoters exempted under Section 240A of the IBC are entitled to an exemption from the wilful defaulter disqualification under Section 29A(b) of the IBC[cite: 23].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory eligibility of a Resolution Applicant under Section 29A of the IBC must be determined strictly with reference to the date of submission of the resolution plan; a person who stands declared as a wilful defaulter under RBI guidelines on that cut-off date is disqualified under Section 29A(b), and subsequent interim conditional orders from a civil court cannot retroactively confer eligibility[cite: 23]. Furthermore, Section 240A exemptions for MSMEs apply strictly to Section 29A clauses (c) and (h), and do not extend to wilful defaulters under clause (b)[cite: 23]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 29A was enacted to prevent persons who contributed to the downfall of a corporate debtor from regaining control[cite: 23]. Section 240A(1) contains a specific, limited non-obstante clause providing that only clauses (c) and (h) of Section 29A do not apply to an MSME resolution applicant[cite: 23]. Parliament deliberately retained Section 29A(b) for MSMEs to ensure that wilful defaulters remain barred from regaining corporate control[cite: 23]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the Appellant was declared a wilful defaulter on 19.07.2021 and 04.10.2021, whereas the resolution plan was submitted on 12.05.2022, on which date no judicial stay existed in favor of the Appellant[cite: 23]. The ad-interim civil injunction obtained subsequently on 19.09.2022 was conditional until the filing of a reply, and stood vacated when IDBI Bank filed its reply on 03.10.2022, prior to the suit's dismissal on 19.12.2022[cite: 23]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant was statutorily ineligible to submit a resolution plan on the date of submission under Section 29A(b), the CoC acted within its commercial wisdom in voting with a 66.37% majority to liquidate the Corporate Debtor, and the Adjudicating Authority committed no legal error in ordering liquidation[cite: 23].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 858 of 2023 is dismissed with no order as to costs, affirming the order dated 19.04.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai Bench, Court-IV) in I.A./2972/2022 and I.A./464/2023 in CP (IB) 477/C-IV/MB/2020[cite: 23]. Connected Interlocutory Application I.A. No. 2925 of 2024 is closed[cite: 23].
summary: Namdeo Hindurao Patil, Suspended Director of Warana Dairy and Agro Industries Limited, appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order approving the Corporate Debtor's liquidation and rejecting his application to consider his resolution plan[cite: 23]. The CoC had disqualified the appellant under Section 29A(b) of the IBC because he was declared a wilful defaulter by IDBI Bank in 2021[cite: 23]. The appellant argued that he held an ad-interim civil court injunction and was entitled to an MSME exemption under Section 240A[cite: 23]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that eligibility under Section 29A is determined strictly on the date of resolution plan submission (12.05.2022), when no judicial stay existed[cite: 23]. The Tribunal affirmed that Section 240A exempts MSMEs only from clauses (c) and (h) of Section 29A, not from the wilful defaulter disqualification under clause (b), upholding the CoC's decision to liquidate[cite: 23].

case_title: Vistra ITCL (India) Limited & Ors. vs. IIFL Home Finance Ltd. & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1590 of 2023 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1592 of 2023 & I.A. No. 5957 of 2023
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan, Technical Members Barun Mitra and Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Vistra ITCL (India) Limited, Pratiti Trading Private Limited, and Gajendra Investment Limited (Financial Creditors of the Corporate Debtor)[cite: 24]. Respondent No. 1 in Comp. App. 1590/2023 is IIFL Home Finance Ltd. (IIHFL); Respondent No. 1 in Comp. App. 1592/2023 is Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Ltd. (ARCIL, assignee of IIFL Finance Ltd.)[cite: 24]. Respondent No. 2 in both appeals is Satra Properties (India) Ltd. (Corporate Debtor / SPIL) represented by RP Vaishali Arun Patrikar[cite: 24]. Satra Property Developers Pvt. Ltd. (SPDPL) is a group entity/mortgagor[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: IIHFL sanctioned loans of Rs. 20 Crores on 28.03.2015 and Rs. 5.21 Crores on 27.07.2018 to SPIL; IIFL extended loan facilities of Rs. 60 Crores on 17.11.2015 and Rs. 40 Crores on 29.09.2016 to SPIL[cite: 24]. Defaults occurred, leading IIFL to file Section 7 applications (CP IB Nos. 175/2019 and 176/2019) against SPDPL and SPIL[cite: 24]. On 09.09.2019, parties executed Consent Terms and an Amendment Agreement acknowledging debts, prescribing repayment schedules, and requiring SPDPL to mortgage 2,00,000 sq. ft. of carpet area in the project 'Satra Hills' as additional security[cite: 24]. A registered Deed of Security was executed on 20.03.2020[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: As acknowledged in the Consent Terms and Amendment Agreement dated 09.09.2019, SPIL had an outstanding financial debt of Rs. 148,68,19,504/- due to IIFL and Rs. 22,80,76,772/- due to IIHFL as of 31.08.2019 plus 16% interest p.a.[cite: 24]. In CIRP, IIHFL filed Form C claiming Rs. 25,62,25,566/-, and IIFL filed Form C claiming Rs. 185,54,92,575/-[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced against SPIL on 03.08.2020 and against SPDPL on 10.08.2020[cite: 24]. The RP rejected the claims of IIHFL and IIFL on 15.09.2020[cite: 24]. IIHFL and IIFL filed IA No. 1686/2020 and IA No. 1687/2020 respectively before NCLT Mumbai[cite: 24]. NCLT allowed IA 1686/2020 on 22.11.2023 and allowed IA 1687/2020 on 05.12.2023, directing admission of their financial claims[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Facility agreements, Consent Terms dated 09.09.2019, Amendment Agreement dated 09.09.2019 (Clause 2.1-2.10 reserving liberty to file fresh Section 7 applications), registered Deed of Security dated 20.03.2020 (Clauses E, F, G, 4.1, 5.2, 5.3, 11.1), and RP rejection emails dated 15.09.2020[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-I allowed IA No. 1686/2020 on 22.11.2023 and IA No. 1687/2020 on 05.12.2023, ruling that the 2020 Deed of Security was executed purely as additional security and did not extinguish SPIL's underlying debt[cite: 24]. Competing financial creditors appealed via Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1590 and 1592 of 2023[cite: 24].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a registered Deed of Security executed by a group mortgagor creating a mortgage over project area as additional security operates as a novation under Section 62 of the Indian Contract Act or third-party discharge under Section 41, extinguishing the Corporate Debtor's liability for underlying financial debts[cite: 24]; (ii) Whether recitals in a security indenture indicating that the mortgaged property is sufficient to discharge secured debts and that the borrower shall stand discharged upon execution relieve the borrower of financial debt when the mortgage remains unliquidated and actual repayment is never realized[cite: 24].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An instrument executed to create additional continuing security in furtherance of preexisting settlement terms does not operate as a novation or extinguishment of the primary debtor's underlying financial obligations unless the debt is actually discharged through full satisfaction or realization of the security; recitals anticipating debt discharge upon full performance cannot be construed to relieve the borrower when the security remains unrealized and repayment obligations remain unperformed[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) of the IBC defines financial debt to include any disbursal against consideration for the time value of money[cite: 24]. Sections 41 and 62 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 do not apply where the parties execute a collateral security instrument that expressly preserves underlying financing documents and incorporates terms that the security is continuing, in addition to, and without prejudice to existing remedies upon default[cite: 24]. A clause contemplating future discharge upon the premise of security sufficiency cannot override substantive covenants reserving the right of financial creditors to pursue statutory IBC remedies[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the Consent Terms, Amendment Agreement, and Deed of Security dated 20.03.2020 harmoniously, finding that Clauses E, F, 4.1, 5.2, and 5.3 established that the mortgage of 2,00,000 sq. ft. FSI was purely an additional continuing security; no payments were realized from the mortgaged property due to intervening CIRP, and SPIL's primary financial debt remained subsisting and unliquidated[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor (SPIL) was never discharged from its financial debts under the loan agreements and Consent Terms, and the Adjudicating Authority correctly directed the RP to admit the claims of IIHFL and IIFL as Financial Debt[cite: 24].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1590 of 2023 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1592 of 2023 are dismissed, affirming the orders dated 22.11.2023 (in I.A. No. 1686/2020) and 05.12.2023 (in I.A. No. 1687/2020) passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai Bench-I)[cite: 24]. Connected Interlocutory Application I.A. No. 5957 of 2023 is closed with no order as to costs[cite: 24].
summary: Vistra ITCL (India) Ltd. and co-appellants, financial creditors of Satra Properties (India) Ltd. (SPIL), appealed against NCLT Mumbai orders directing the Resolution Professional to admit the claims of IIFL Home Finance Ltd. (Rs. 25.62 Crores) and ARCIL/IIFL Finance Ltd. (Rs. 185.54 Crores) as Financial Debt[cite: 24]. The appellants argued that under Clause G of a registered Deed of Security dated 20.03.2020 executed by group company SPDPL, SPIL was fully discharged from its debt obligations pursuant to Sections 41 and 62 of the Indian Contract Act[cite: 24]. Dismissing both appeals, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that the Deed of Security was executed solely to provide additional continuing security and did not novate the underlying loan agreements or extinguish SPIL's liability[cite: 24]. Because no repayment was ever realized from the mortgaged property, SPIL's financial debt subsisted, rendering the claims legally admissible in CIRP[cite: 24].

case_title: Pradeep P. Agarwal vs. Indiabulls Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Pradeep P. Agarwal, Suspended Director of Phulchand Exports Private Limited (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 25]. Respondent No. 1 is Indiabulls Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. (Financial Creditor/Assignee)[cite: 25]. Respondent No. 2 is Phulchand Exports Private Limited through Interim Resolution Professional Ms. Savita Agarwal[cite: 25]. The original lender was Indiabulls Housing Finance Limited (IHFL)[cite: 25]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: IHFL sanctioned five loan facilities to the Corporate Debtor between 2014 and 2018, secured by deposit of title deeds of immovable property owned by Shri Prateek Agarwal[cite: 25]. IHFL assigned the credit facilities along with underlying securities to Respondent No. 1 via a registered Assignment Agreement dated 30.09.2019[cite: 25]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in debt repayments led IHFL to issue Section 13(2) SARFAESI notices in April-May 2019 and an e-auction notice on 27.08.2019[cite: 25]. Respondent No. 1 filed Section 7 application CP (IB)-769(MB)/2022 claiming financial default[cite: 25]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The property owner challenged SARFAESI actions in SA No. 116 of 2019 before DRT-I, Mumbai[cite: 25]. In CIRP proceedings, NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-III (Shri H.V. Subba Rao and Ms. Madhu Sinha) heard CP (IB)-769(MB)/2022 and deferment application IA No. 2889/2022, reserving orders on 26.06.2023[cite: 25]. On 18.08.2023, one member was transferred to Guwahati, and Court-III was reconstituted[cite: 25]. On 05.10.2023, DRT-I Mumbai quashed the Section 13(2) demand notice and set aside the asset sale[cite: 25]. Corporate Debtor filed IA No. 5177/2023 in November 2023 for de-reserving and rehearing, in which reconstituted Court-III heard arguments and reserved orders on 04.03.2024[cite: 25]. On 22.03.2024 (approx. 9 months post-reservation), the earlier Special Bench pronounced an order admitting Section 7 and disposing of IA No. 2889/2022 as infructuous[cite: 25]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: DRT-I Mumbai judgment dated 05.10.2023 in SA No. 116/2019 setting aside the Section 13(2) default demand notice; orders of reconstituted Court-III dated 25.01.2024 and 04.03.2024 reserving orders in IA No. 5177/2023; and administrative circulars/orders issued by the President, NCLT dated 25.09.2023 and 28.11.2023 regarding bench reconstitution and reserved matters[cite: 25]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Special Bench of NCLT Mumbai admitted Section 7 on 22.03.2024 despite being apprised that an application to bring on record subsequent DRT findings (IA No. 5177/2023) had been heard and reserved by the regular reconstituted Bench on 04.03.2024[cite: 25]. The suspended director appealed to NCLAT via Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 607 of 2024[cite: 25].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an Adjudicating Authority (Special Bench) can validly pronounce an order admitting a Section 7 CIRP petition nearly nine months after reserving judgment, without awaiting orders in a pending interlocutory application (IA No. 5177/2023) seeking rehearing based on subsequent material developments (quashing of Section 13(2) default notice by DRT) that was heard and reserved by the regular reconstituted Bench[cite: 25]; (ii) Whether administrative circulars issued by the President of NCLT regulating the constitution of Special Benches operate as a fetter on judicial discretion, preventing a bench from considering subsequent events that have a fundamental bearing on the existence of default under Section 7[cite: 25].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While administrative orders and circulars issued by the President of a Tribunal regulate the administrative listing and reconstitution of benches for pronouncement of reserved orders, they do not fetter judicial discretion; where an interlocutory application bringing on record crucial subsequent events that have a fundamental impact on the core issue of default is pending and reserved for orders before a regular bench, pronouncing a long-reserved main petition without awaiting the decision on such subsequent events constitutes a procedural and judicial error warranting remand[cite: 25]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 16 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 empowers the President to regulate tribunal sittings, and Rule 150(1) envisions expeditious pronouncement of orders[cite: 25]. Under Rule 32, parties are entitled to file interlocutory applications regarding changed circumstances[cite: 25]. An appeal is a continuation of the original proceedings under Section 96 of the CPC, and an appellate tribunal is duty-bound to take note of supervening factual and legal developments that shorten litigation or promote substantial justice, ensuring both sides are fairly heard before imposing insolvency[cite: 25]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the Section 7 petition had remained reserved from 26.06.2023 to 22.03.2024 (nearly nine months); that the DRT by order dated 05.10.2023 had quashed the primary Section 13(2) notice alleging default; and that regular Court-III had already heard and reserved orders on IA No. 5177/2023 on 04.03.2024 to determine whether rehearing was necessary[cite: 25]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Special Bench ought to have deferred pronouncement to await the decision in IA No. 5177/2023; proceeding to admit the Corporate Debtor into CIRP without taking cognizance of the reserved interlocutory application caused grave procedural prejudice, requiring the admission order to be set aside and remanded for fresh hearing[cite: 25].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 607 of 2024 is allowed, and the impugned order dated 22.03.2024 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai Bench, Court-III) is set aside[cite: 25]. Company Petition CP (IB)-769(MB)/2022 along with IA No. 2889 of 2022 and IA No. 5177 of 2023 are revived before the regular Court-III of NCLT Mumbai Bench for fresh consideration and disposal after hearing both parties, with a request to decide the matters expeditiously[cite: 25]. No order as to costs[cite: 25].
summary: Pradeep P. Agarwal, Suspended Director of Phulchand Exports Pvt. Ltd., appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order dated 22.03.2024 admitting a Section 7 CIRP application filed by Indiabulls Asset Reconstruction Co. Ltd.[cite: 25]. The order was pronounced by a Special Bench nearly nine months after reserving judgment on 26.06.2023, ignoring that the regular reconstituted bench had heard and reserved orders on 04.03.2024 in IA No. 5177/2023, which sought rehearing based on a subsequent DRT order quashing the Section 13(2) SARFAESI default notice[cite: 25]. Allowing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that administrative bench-reconstitution guidelines do not circumscribe judicial discretion and that the tribunal committed a procedural error by rushing to admit the company into CIRP without awaiting orders on the impact of the supervening DRT judgment[cite: 25]. The Tribunal set aside the admission order and remanded the company petition and connected applications back to the regular NCLT Mumbai Bench for fresh consideration[cite: 25].

case_title: Ashok Dattatray Atre & Ors. vs. State Bank of India & Ors.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Ashok Dattatray Atre, Ajit Ulhas Apte, Haridas Narayan Wadghule, and Chintamani Shridhar Vaidya (Promoters/Founders and Successful Resolution Applicants / SRA)[cite: 27]. Respondent No. 1 is State Bank of India (sole 100% CoC member / Financial Creditor)[cite: 27]. Respondent No. 2 is Mr. Vijendra Kumar Jain (Liquidator / Monitoring Committee Chairman)[cite: 27]. Respondent No. 3 is Mr. Avil Jerome Menezes[cite: 27]. The Corporate Debtor is M/s Transparent Energy Systems Pvt. Ltd. (a registered MSME)[cite: 27]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was admitted into CIRP in C.P. (IB)/3448/MB/2018[cite: 27]. The Appellants submitted a resolution plan offering Rs. 1,972.02 Lakhs payable across six tranches over a three-year period (16.04.2021 to 16.04.2024)[cite: 27]. Sources of funding included recoveries from pending commercial litigations (envisaged at Rs. 1,285 Lakhs across entities such as Lloyd Steel, GAIL, and Simon India) and alternate funding mechanisms under Clause 5.1.2.12 (including equity infusion, fresh debt, and sale of the factory at Shirwal as a last resort)[cite: 27]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The SRA paid the first three tranches totaling Rs. 692.27 Lakhs in full[cite: 27]. SRA defaulted on the fourth tranche of Rs. 91.41 Lakhs due on 15.04.2023, while the fifth tranche of Rs. 274.23 Lakhs fell due in October 2023 and the sixth tranche of Rs. 914.10 Lakhs was scheduled for April 2024[cite: 27]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The resolution plan was approved by NCLT Mumbai on 16.04.2021[cite: 27]. Anticipating shortfalls in litigation recoveries due to Covid-19 disruptions, SRA filed IA No. 483 of 2023 in February 2023 seeking an extension of payment timelines[cite: 27]. Following the default in April 2023, SBI filed IA No. 4034 of 2023 in August 2023 seeking liquidation under Section 33[cite: 27]. On 09.11.2023, an arbitral award of Rs. 102 Lakhs was rendered in favor of the Corporate Debtor against Lloyd Steel[cite: 27]. NCLT Mumbai dismissed IA No. 483 of 2023 and allowed liquidation application IA No. 4034 of 2023 on 04.01.2024[cite: 27]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved resolution plan dated 16.04.2021; payment records showing timely discharge of first three tranches (Rs. 692.27 Lakhs); arbitral award dated 09.11.2023 granting Rs. 102 Lakhs; de-freezing order for Rs. 28.50 Lakhs in HDFC bank account; Letter of Intent dated 25.02.2024 from Tooltech Components Pvt. Ltd. to acquire the Shirwal Factory for Rs. 6 Crores; and SRA offer letter dated 26.02.2024 submitted to SBI[cite: 27]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-I allowed SBI's liquidation application IA No. 4034 of 2023 and dismissed SRA's extension application IA No. 483 of 2023 on 04.01.2024, holding that extending plan timelines amounted to an impermissible plan modification without CoC consent[cite: 27]. The SRA appealed to NCLAT via Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 221 and 222 of 2024[cite: 27].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal possesses the statutory jurisdiction under the IBC to grant an extension of time to a Successful Resolution Applicant for completing installment payments under an approved resolution plan without such extension being treated as an impermissible modification or withdrawal prohibited by the Supreme Court ruling in Ebix Singapore[cite: 27]; (ii) Whether the Adjudicating Authority can exercise its jurisdiction to extend payment timelines only if the Committee of Creditors affirmatively assents to the extension[cite: 27]; (iii) Whether an order of liquidation should be passed against an MSME corporate debtor where the SRA has paid significant early tranches and identified viable alternate funding options expressly contemplated in the approved plan (such as sale of non-core assets)[cite: 27].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application filed by a Successful Resolution Applicant seeking an extension of timelines to discharge financial commitments under an approved resolution plan does not constitute an impermissible modification or withdrawal of the plan under the doctrine of Ebix Singapore; the Adjudicating Authority and Appellate Tribunal possess requisite equitable and statutory jurisdiction to extend implementation timelines in appropriate cases to advance the primary IBC objective of revival and avoid premature liquidation of viable corporate entities[cite: 27]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While the commercial terms of an approved plan are binding and cannot be unilaterally modified under Sections 30 and 31, granting an extension of time for payment is an implementation facilitating mechanism and does not alter the substantive plan value or distribution structure[cite: 27]. Furthermore, the exercise of judicial discretion by the Adjudicating Authority to extend implementation timelines is not dependent upon the mandatory concurrence or veto of the Committee of Creditors[cite: 27]. In a corporate resolution involving MSMEs, financial creditors have a collaborative duty to cooperate in implementing alternate funding covenants (such as asset sales) expressly embedded in the plan before forcing the entity into Section 33 liquidation[cite: 27]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the SRA had paid Rs. 692.27 Lakhs (three full tranches), secured an arbitral award for Rs. 102 Lakhs, received a firm Letter of Intent to sell the Shirwal Factory for Rs. 6 Crores as expressly permitted by Clause 5.1.2.12 of the plan, and showed genuine bona fide intent to pay all remaining liabilities with interest[cite: 27]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in rejecting the extension application on the assumption that it lacked jurisdiction without CoC concurrence and erred in ordering liquidation; the SRA is entitled to an extension of time to sell the Shirwal Factory and complete payment of all outstanding tranches along with prevalent bank interest[cite: 27].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 221 & 222 of 2024 are allowed with parties bearing their own costs[cite: 27]. The order of the Adjudicating Authority dated 04.01.2024 passed in IA No. 4034 of 2023 ordering liquidation of the Corporate Debtor is set aside[cite: 27]. IA No. 483 of 2023 is allowed as follows: (a) Time for payment of the fourth and fifth tranches is extended till 15.04.2024; (b) SRA is permitted to sell the Shirwal Factory under Clause 5.1.2.12 of the plan, and SBI shall issue the requisite Letter of Intent with entire proceeds paid to SBI for the fourth, fifth, and sixth tranches; (c) Time for payment of the sixth tranche is extended up to 15.04.2025; (d) Any balance payment made after 15.04.2024 shall carry interest at the rate prevalent with SBI from 16.04.2024 till actual payment[cite: 27]. IA Nos. 2366 & 2367 of 2024 are disposed of[cite: 27].
summary: Ashok Dattatray Atre and co-promoters, Successful Resolution Applicants of MSME corporate debtor Transparent Energy Systems Pvt. Ltd., appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order dismissing their application (IA No. 483/2023) for extension of plan payment timelines and ordering liquidation upon SBI's application (IA No. 4034/2023)[cite: 27]. The SRA had paid the first three tranches totaling Rs. 692.27 Lakhs, but defaulted on the fourth tranche due to delays in pending recovery litigations and offered to sell its Shirwal Factory for Rs. 6 Crores as permitted under the plan's alternate funding clause[cite: 27]. Allowing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that extending payment timelines is not an impermissible modification of the plan under Ebix Singapore and does not require mandatory CoC consent[cite: 27]. The Tribunal set aside the liquidation order and extended the fourth and fifth tranches till 15.04.2024 and sixth tranche till 15.04.2025, directing SBI to issue an LOI for the factory sale subject to bank interest[cite: 27].

case_title: Potens Transmission & Power Pvt. Ltd. vs. Apex Buildsys Ltd. & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain, Technical Members Naresh Salecha and Indevar Pandey)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Potens Transmission & Power Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Auction Purchaser / H1 Bidder)[cite: 28]. The Respondent is Apex Buildsys Limited (Corporate Debtor in Liquidation) represented through Liquidator Gian Chand Narang[cite: 28]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP was initiated against the Corporate Debtor on 20.09.2018 upon an application by ICICI Bank under Section 7 of the IBC, and an order for liquidation was passed on 09.01.2020[cite: 28]. Following four failed e-auctions, the Liquidator conducted a 5th e-auction on 17.05.2021 for the sale of the Corporate Debtor as a going concern at a reserve price of Rs. 73 Crores[cite: 28]. The Appellant was declared the highest successful bidder (H1) with a bid of Rs. 73.01 Crores[cite: 28]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant deposited Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) of Rs. 7.30 Crores (10%) and paid an initial part-sale consideration of Rs. 10,95,25,000/- on 10.06.2021 and 11.06.2021, but defaulted in depositing the remaining 75% balance sale consideration of Rs. 54,75,75,000/- within the mandatory statutory 90-day outer timeline which expired on 01.09.2021[cite: 28]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The e-auction took place on 17.05.2021[cite: 28]. The Liquidator issued an intimation on 03.06.2021, and the parties executed a Term Sheet on 15.06.2021 fixing 01.09.2021 as the 90th-day payment deadline[cite: 28]. Appellant filed IA Nos. 3153/2021 and 4317/2021 seeking concessions and a 25-day extension[cite: 28]. On 25.04.2022, NCLT dismissed Appellant's applications and allowed the Liquidator's IA No. 5255/2021 to cancel the sale, leading the Liquidator to forfeit the EMD and part payment via email on 25.04.2022[cite: 28]. Appellant's subsequent appeals to NCLAT and the Supreme Court were dismissed/disposed of after failing to pay the balance Rs. 50 Crores by 01.06.2022 (though an additional court deposit of Rs. 5.5 Crores was refunded)[cite: 28]. The property was re-auctioned for Rs. 91 Crores[cite: 28]. On 04.10.2023, NCLT dismissed Appellant's refund application IA No. 5450/2022[cite: 28]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: E-auction process information document dated 17.05.2021 (clauses c & d); written declaration dated 29.05.2021 signed by the Appellant agreeing to forfeiture of EMD and all deposited monies upon default; Term Sheet dated 15.06.2021 (Clauses 7.2 and 7.3); forfeiture communication email dated 25.04.2022; and Supreme Court orders in Civil Appeal No. 4116 of 2022 dated 20.05.2022 and 02.06.2022[cite: 28]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 5450/2022 under Section 60(5) seeking refund of Rs. 18,25,25,000/- (EMD of Rs. 7.30 Crores + part consideration of Rs. 10.95 Crores)[cite: 28]. NCLT New Delhi dismissed the application on 04.10.2023[cite: 28]. Appellant appealed to NCLAT via Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1543 of 2023, conceding the EMD forfeiture but challenging the forfeiture of the Rs. 10.95 Crore part consideration under Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872[cite: 28].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the provisions of Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 apply to e-auctions conducted by a Liquidator under the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 so as to preclude the forfeiture of part-sale consideration paid by a defaulting auction purchaser[cite: 28]; (ii) Whether a Liquidator has the statutory authority to forfeit not only the Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) but also the part-sale consideration deposited by a successful bidder where the bidder has executed express contractual undertakings and term sheets permitting forfeiture upon non-payment of the balance consideration within the 90-day outer statutory limit under Schedule I Clause 1(12) of the Liquidation Process Regulations[cite: 28].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 has no application to public auctions conducted by a Liquidator under the statutory framework of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 and the Liquidation Process Regulations; where the e-auction terms, conditions, and bidder undertakings explicitly empower the Liquidator to forfeit all monies deposited upon failure to pay the full sale consideration within the mandatory outer limit, the Liquidator is legally entitled to forfeit both the EMD and any part-sale consideration without being relegated to proving actual damages in a civil suit[cite: 28]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Liquidations under the IBC are governed by statutory procedures under Schedule I of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016, where the 90-day outer limit for paying the full consideration under Clause 1(12) is mandatory[cite: 28]. Process documents and terms of auction framed pursuant to statutory authority are binding on participants who give unconditional undertakings[cite: 28]. The equitable principles of contract law or discretionary relief cannot be imported to defeat the time-bound mandate of the IBC, as established in Westcoast Infraprojects and Pratap Technocrats (which affirmed that the NCLT exercises no equity-based jurisdiction)[cite: 28]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that Clauses (c) and (d) of the e-auction process information document, the Appellant's signed declaration dated 29.05.2021, and Clause 7.3 of the Term Sheet dated 15.06.2021 unequivocally authorized the Liquidator to forfeit all amounts deposited till date upon payment default; and that the Appellant failed to pay the balance Rs. 54.75 Crores despite statutory and judicial extensions[cite: 28]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The forfeiture of the part consideration of Rs. 10,95,25,000/- was strictly in accordance with the statutory process document and agreed terms, Section 74 of the Contract Act was inapplicable, and the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in refusing to direct a refund[cite: 28].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1543 of 2023 is dismissed with no order as to costs, affirming the order dated 04.10.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT New Delhi) in I.A. No. 5450 of 2022 in CP (IB) No. 706/PB/2018[cite: 28].
summary: Potens Transmission & Power Pvt. Ltd., the highest bidder in an e-auction to purchase Apex Buildsys Limited as a going concern for Rs. 73.01 Crores, appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order dismissing its application for refund of Rs. 10.95 Crores paid towards part consideration[cite: 28]. The appellant conceded the forfeiture of its Rs. 7.30 Crore EMD but argued that under Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the liquidator could not forfeit part consideration without proving actual damages in a civil suit[cite: 28]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that Section 74 of the Contract Act does not apply to statutory auctions governed by Schedule I of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016[cite: 28]. Following its precedent in Westcoast Infraprojects, the Tribunal affirmed that bidders are strictly bound by the process documents, declarations, and term sheets that authorize forfeiture of all deposited amounts upon default in paying the balance consideration within the 90-day outer statutory limit[cite: 28].

case_title: Slimline Realty Private Limited & Ors. vs. Mr. Jigar Bhatt (Liquidator of RMOL Engineering and Offshore Ltd.)
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 690 of 2024 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 693, 694, 695 & 714 of 2024
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Justice Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are five corporate bond issuers: Slimline Realty Pvt. Ltd. (Comp. App. 690/2024), Avocado Realty Pvt. Ltd. (Comp. App. 693/2024), Budding Mercantile Company Pvt. Ltd. (Comp. App. 694/2024), Replenish Realty Pvt. Ltd. (Comp. App. 695/2024), and Winsome Realty Pvt. Ltd. (Comp. App. 714/2024)[cite: 1]. The Respondent is Mr. Jigar Bhatt, Liquidator of RMOL Engineering and Offshore Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 1]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: In 2013, the Corporate Debtor subscribed to Non-Convertible Unsecured Bonds issued by the five Appellant entities having an aggregate face value of Rs. 306.73 Crores, redeemable on 25.07.2019 at a 40% premium. The Corporate Debtor had no operational business, physical assets, or employees, and these bond subscriptions formed its sole asset. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellants defaulted in redeeming the Non-Convertible Unsecured Bonds on the due redemption date of 25.07.2019. The default claimed by the Liquidator across the five entities totaled Rs. 306.73 Crores plus interest; for instance, the principal default claimed against Slimline Realty Pvt. Ltd. was Rs. 53 Crores with default reckoned from 26.07.2019 along with accrued interest up to 25.09.2023. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP against RMOL commenced on 21.08.2019. Liquidation was ordered on 06.12.2021 and Respondent was appointed Liquidator. Demand notices were issued by the management, erstwhile RP, and Liquidator post-July 2019. In September 2023, without prior approval under Section 33(5), the Liquidator filed Section 7 applications against the Appellants [CP(IB) Nos. 1007, 1019, 1020, 1021, and 1022 of 2023]. On 16.01.2024, NCLT extended the liquidation period by 12 months under Regulation 44(2) in IA/65(AHM)2024. The Liquidator then filed IA/189(AHM)2024 seeking ex-post facto approval, which NCLT Ahmedabad allowed on 07.02.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Non-Convertible Unsecured Bond subscription documents of 2013 showing redemption date of 25.07.2019; demand notices issued for redemption; Stakeholders Consultation Committee (SCC) 4th meeting minutes dated 02.01.2024 where 38.76% voted for liquidation extension while IFCI abstained; and NCLT extension order dated 16.01.2024 noting pending Section 7 petitions for recovery of Rs. 306.73 Crores. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench Court-1 allowed IA/189(AHM)2024 on 07.02.2024, granting ex-post facto approval under Section 33(5) to continue the Section 7 petitions against the Appellants to maximize asset value. The Appellants appealed before NCLAT via Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 690, 693, 694, 695, and 714 of 2024 contending that Section 33(5) proviso requires mandatory prior approval, rendering unapproved filings null and incapable of post-facto cure, and alleging denial of natural justice.
legal_issues: (i) Whether the statutory requirement under the proviso to Section 33(5) of the IBC to obtain 'prior approval' of the Adjudicating Authority before the Liquidator institutes legal proceedings on behalf of the Corporate Debtor is mandatory or directory; (ii) What is the legal status and consequence of proceedings instituted by the Liquidator without obtaining prior approval under Section 33(5); (iii) Whether ex-post facto approval granted by the Adjudicating Authority can validate and regularize legal proceedings instituted by the Liquidator without prior approval; (iv) Whether the prospective respondent/adversary entity is entitled to notice and an opportunity of being heard before the Adjudicating Authority grants approval under the proviso to Section 33(5).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory requirement under the proviso to Section 33(5) of the IBC for a liquidator to obtain prior approval of the Adjudicating Authority before instituting suits or legal proceedings on behalf of the corporate debtor is mandatory; however, proceedings instituted without prior approval are merely unauthorized and incompetent rather than void ab initio, and subsequent grant of ex-post facto approval cures the procedural defect and renders the proceedings valid and competent from the date such post-facto approval is granted. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 33(5) contains an express negative injunction designed to preserve the liquidation estate and prevent wasteful litigation expenditure. The proviso operates as a strict exception requiring 'prior approval', but unlike Sections 28(4) or 25A(3), Section 33(5) provides no statutory penalty nullifying actions taken in breach. Drawing analogy from Section 171 of the Companies Act, 1913 and Section 446 of the Companies Act, 1956 interpreted in Bansidhar Shankarlal and Erach Boman Khavar, 'leave of court' and 'prior approval' serve identical supervisory functions; thus, an unapproved action remains ineffective until leave is secured, whereupon it is deemed regularized. Furthermore, the statutory scheme does not require notice or opportunity of hearing to the prospective debtor/respondent before granting approval under Section 33(5). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the unredeemed bonds aggregating Rs. 306.73 Crores constituted the Corporate Debtor's sole asset, that the Adjudicating Authority was fully apprised of the status via the liquidation extension order dated 16.01.2024, and that granting post-facto approval under IA/189(AHM)2024 was grounded on cogent reasons aimed at asset realization and value maximization. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: While the requirement of prior approval under Section 33(5) is mandatory, the Adjudicating Authority possessed jurisdiction to regularize the Section 7 petitions via ex-post facto approval without needing to hear the Appellants, rendering the order dated 07.02.2024 legal and valid.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 690, 693, 694, 695, and 714 of 2024 are dismissed with no order as to costs, affirming the order dated 07.02.2024 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Ahmedabad Bench, Court-1) in IA/189(AHM)2024.
summary: Five corporate entities, including Slimline Realty Pvt. Ltd. and Avocado Realty Pvt. Ltd., appealed against an NCLT Ahmedabad order granting ex-post facto approval to the Liquidator of RMOL Engineering and Offshore Ltd. to pursue Section 7 IBC applications against them for defaulting on Rs. 306.73 Crores worth of unredeemed bonds[cite: 1]. The Appellants contended that under Section 33(5) proviso, 'prior approval' is mandatory, unapproved filings are void ab initio, and the order violated natural justice. Dismissing the appeals, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that although prior approval under Section 33(5) is mandatory, unapproved proceedings are merely incompetent/ineffective rather than nullities. Applying principles from Section 446 of the Companies Act, 1956, the Tribunal ruled that ex-post facto approval validly cures the defect from the date of grant and does not require prior notice to the debtor entities.

case_title: Replenish Realty Pvt. Ltd. vs. Mr. Jigar Bhatt (Liquidator of RMOL Engineering and Offshore Ltd.)
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 695 of 2024 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 690, 693, 694 & 714 of 2024
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Justice Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Replenish Realty Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Bond Issuer in Comp. App. 695/2024), alongside connected appellants Slimline Realty Pvt. Ltd. (690/2024), Avocado Realty Pvt. Ltd. (693/2024), Budding Mercantile Company Pvt. Ltd. (694/2024), and Winsome Realty Pvt. Ltd. (714/2024)[cite: 2]. The Respondent is Mr. Jigar Bhatt, Liquidator of RMOL Engineering and Offshore Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 2]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: In 2013, the Corporate Debtor subscribed to Non-Convertible Unsecured Bonds issued by five private entities (including the Appellant) with an aggregate face value of Rs. 306.73 Crores, redeemable on 25.07.2019 at a 40% premium[cite: 2]. The Corporate Debtor had no business, employees, or physical assets, leaving these bonds as its sole liquidation asset[cite: 2]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant and connected bond issuers defaulted on redemption on the maturity date of 25.07.2019[cite: 2]. The Liquidator claimed a total default of Rs. 306.73 Crores plus interest across all five entities (e.g., Rs. 53 Crores principal default claimed against Slimline Realty Pvt. Ltd. reckoning from 26.07.2019 with accrued interest up to 25.09.2023)[cite: 2]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: RMOL entered CIRP on 21.08.2019, and the liquidation order was passed on 06.12.2021 (with the date also referenced as 06.01.2021 in the record)[cite: 2]. The Liquidator issued demand notices post-July 2019, and in September 2023 filed Section 7 applications without prior NCLT approval (Company Petition No. 1020/2023 against Replenish Realty Pvt. Ltd.)[cite: 2]. On 16.01.2024, NCLT extended the liquidation period by 12 months in IA/65(AHM)2024[cite: 2]. The Liquidator filed IA/189(AHM)2024 seeking ex-post facto approval, which NCLT Ahmedabad allowed on 07.02.2024[cite: 2]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Non-Convertible Unsecured Bond subscription agreements executed in 2013 showing maturity on 25.07.2019; demand notices issued by the Corporate Debtor's management, erstwhile RP, and Liquidator; minutes of the 4th SCC meeting dated 02.01.2024 (where 38.76% voted for liquidation extension and IFCI abstained); and NCLT order dated 16.01.2024 recording pending Section 7 petitions for recovery of Rs. 306.73 Crores[cite: 2]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench Court-1 allowed IA/189(AHM)2024 on 07.02.2024, granting ex-post facto approval under Section 33(5) to proceed with the Section 7 petitions[cite: 2]. Replenish Realty Pvt. Ltd. and companion issuers appealed before NCLAT via Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.)
