Nos. 690, 693, 694, 695, and 714 of 2024, arguing that prior approval is mandatory, unapproved petitions are null and void ab initio, and the order breached principles of natural justice[cite: 2].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the statutory requirement under the proviso to Section 33(5) of the IBC to obtain 'prior approval' of the Adjudicating Authority to institute legal proceedings on behalf of the Corporate Debtor is mandatory or directory[cite: 2]; (ii) What is the legal status and consequence of proceedings instituted by the Liquidator on behalf of the Corporate Debtor without obtaining prior approval under Section 33(5)[cite: 2]; (iii) Whether ex-post facto approval granted by the Adjudicating Authority cures the lack of prior approval and renders the proceedings authorized and competent[cite: 2]; (iv) Whether the entity against whom proceedings are to be instituted is entitled to notice or an opportunity of being heard prior to the grant of approval under Section 33(5)[cite: 2].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The requirement under the proviso to Section 33(5) of the IBC to obtain prior approval of the Adjudicating Authority before instituting suits or legal proceedings on behalf of a corporate debtor is mandatory; nevertheless, proceedings filed without prior approval are unauthorized and incompetent rather than void or nullities, and the subsequent grant of ex-post facto approval regularizes the proceedings, making them authorized and competent from the date ex-post facto approval is granted[cite: 2]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 33(5) opens with a prohibitive command to safeguard the liquidation estate against unauthorized depletion, and its proviso carves out an exception requiring prior approval[cite: 2]. Unlike Sections 28(4) and 25A(3), Section 33(5) does not attach statutory invalidity or voidness to non-compliance[cite: 2]. Interpreting Section 33(5) in parity with Section 171 of the Companies Act, 1913 and Section 446 of the Companies Act, 1956 as settled in Bansidhar Shankarlal and Erach Boman Khavar, 'prior approval' and 'leave of the court' fulfill identical supervisory aims to prevent vexatious litigation; hence, actions instituted without leave remain ineffective until approval is granted[cite: 2]. Furthermore, Section 33(5) does not require notice or a hearing to the prospective adversary prior to granting approval[cite: 2]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed the record showing that the unredeemed bonds worth Rs. 306.73 Crores constituted the Corporate Debtor's only asset, that the Adjudicating Authority had already evaluated the recovery proceedings during the liquidation extension on 16.01.2024, and that the order dated 07.02.2024 provided speaking commercial justification aimed at value maximization under the liquidation framework[cite: 2]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The requirement of prior approval under Section 33(5) is mandatory, but the Adjudicating Authority possessed jurisdiction to regularize the Section 7 petitions via ex-post facto approval without affording prior hearing to the debtor entities, rendering the approval order dated 07.02.2024 legally valid[cite: 2].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 695 of 2024 (along with companion Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 690, 693, 694, and 714 of 2024) is dismissed with no order as to costs, affirming the order dated 07.02.2024 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Ahmedabad Bench, Court-1) in IA/189(AHM)2024[cite: 2].
summary: Replenish Realty Pvt. Ltd. and four companion bond issuers appealed against an NCLT Ahmedabad order granting ex-post facto approval under Section 33(5) of the IBC to the Liquidator of RMOL Engineering and Offshore Ltd. to prosecute Section 7 petitions against them for defaults on Rs. 306.73 Crores of unredeemed bonds[cite: 2]. The Appellants contended that 'prior approval' under Section 33(5) proviso is mandatory, rendering unapproved petitions void ab initio, and alleged natural justice violations[cite: 2]. Dismissing the appeals, the NCLAT Principal Bench ruled that while prior approval under Section 33(5) is mandatory, proceedings instituted without it are merely incompetent rather than nullities[cite: 2]. Guided by precedents under Section 446 of the Companies Act, 1956, the Tribunal held that ex-post facto approval validly cures the procedural defect from the date of grant and does not require prior notice to the adversary[cite: 2].

case_title: Beacon Trusteeship Ltd. & Anr. vs. Jayesh Sanghrajka & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1494-1495 of 2022 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 99, 107 & 108 of 2023
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Justice Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are dissenting Secured Financial Creditors: Beacon Trusteeship Ltd. (7.44% voting share) and Dev Rishi Ventures LLP (substituted for ICICI Prudential Venture Capital Fund Real Estate Scheme I, 5.71% voting share)[cite: 4]. Respondent No. 1 is Jayesh Sanghrajka, Resolution Professional of Radius Estates and Developers Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 4]. Respondent No. 2 is Adani Goodhomes Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant / SRA)[cite: 4]. Respondent No. 3 is HDFC Bank Ltd. (lead Financial Creditor with 33.25% share, substituted for HDFC Ltd.)[cite: 4]. Respondent No. 4 is Ten BKC Flat Owners AOP Trust, and Respondent No. 7 is Rajesh Sureshchandra Sheth, Authorised Representative of Homebuyers (holding 33.41% share)[cite: 4]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor acquired redevelopment sub-contract rights over MHADA land at Bandra (Ten BKC Project) via an agreement dated 31.03.2016 executed with MIG (Bandra) Realtors and Builders Pvt. Ltd. (DB), who held principal development rights from Middle Income Group Cooperative Housing Society under an agreement dated 31.10.2010[cite: 4]. In 2018, Corporate Debtor issued Non-Convertible Debentures of Rs. 65 Crores to Beacon Trusteeship Ltd. through private placement[cite: 4]. Work stalled in March 2018, leading the Society to terminate the development agreement on 08.05.2020[cite: 4]. DB obtained an interim status quo from Bombay High Court under Section 9 of the Arbitration Act, followed by an interim arbitral award on 05.05.2021 conditionally staying termination subject to payment of society dues and Rs. 3.09 Crores monthly hardship compensation[cite: 4]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtor defaulted on its debenture liabilities and debt obligations, possessing nil funds in its bank account and having no independent assets other than precarious contractual redevelopment rights liable to terminate upon DB's default[cite: 4]. Registered valuers assessed the Corporate Debtor's project Fair Value between Rs. 3.24 Crores (TrueVal) and Rs. 6.31 Crores (Sundeep H.B. & Co.), with Liquidation Value determined between Rs. 2.47 Crores and Rs. 4.81 Crores, while the SRA's approved resolution plan committed upfront interim finance and project completion funding exceeding Rs. 450-600 Crores, alongside waiving Rs. 1,052 Crores in avoidance action proceeds to the CoC[cite: 4]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Beacon Trusteeship initiated Section 7 CIRP in November 2020 (CP (IB) No. 1390/2020), which NCLT Mumbai admitted on 30.04.2021[cite: 4]. CoC was constituted on 02.07.2021 and RP confirmed on 25.08.2021[cite: 4]. MCGM issued a circular on 22.01.2021 offering a 50% rebate on FSI premium if paid on or before 31.12.2021[cite: 4]. Form G was published on 13.10.2021[cite: 4]. SRA submitted its resolution plan alongside draft Construction Management Agreement (CMA) and Master Facility Agreement (MFA) on 17.12.2021[cite: 4]. The CoC approved the Resolution Plan and execution of the CMA/MFA with 83.93% (and 83.99%) voting share on 27.12.2021[cite: 4]. Consent terms between Society and DB were executed on 27.12.2021[cite: 4]. SRA infused Rs. 450 Crores interim finance before 31.12.2021 to secure the MCGM FSI rebate[cite: 4]. NCLT dismissed Appellants' objection applications on 02.12.2022 and formally approved the plan on 09.01.2023[cite: 4]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Development Agreement dated 31.10.2010, Assignment Agreement dated 31.03.2016, and arbitral stay award dated 05.05.2021[cite: 4]; Non-Convertible Debenture contracts[cite: 4]; registered valuation reports of Sundeep H.B. & Co. and TrueVal Advisors employing the residual method[cite: 4]; MCGM 50% FSI discount circular dated 22.01.2021[cite: 4]; minutes of the 3rd, 4th, 5th, 7th, 9th, 12th, and 13th CoC meetings confirming existing lenders' refusal to provide interim finance[cite: 4]; and SRA's additional affidavit dated 07.10.2022 waiving avoidance recovery proceeds[cite: 4]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Dissenting Financial Creditors filed IA Nos. 503, 808, 837, and 931 of 2022 challenging the plan, CMA, and valuation reports, which NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-V rejected on 02.12.2022[cite: 4]. Appellants appealed to NCLAT via Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 1494-1495 of 2022 and 99 of 2023[cite: 4]. Subsequently, NCLT approved the RP's plan approval application IA No. 573/2022 on 09.01.2023[cite: 4]. Appellants appealed that approval order via Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 107 and 108 of 2023, alleging illegal pre-approval transfer of project marketing rights under the CMA, undervaluation, discriminatory treatment (93% haircut to lenders versus 100% flat delivery to homebuyers without escalation), and denial of distribution matching their specific security interests[cite: 4].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a dissenting secured financial creditor is legally entitled under Section 30(2)(b) read with Section 53(1) of the IBC to receive distribution in a resolution plan matching the specific value of its underlying security interest[cite: 4]; (ii) Whether a resolution plan approved by the CoC is discriminatory or violates Section 30(2) when financial creditors absorb a substantial (93%) haircut while allottee homebuyers receive fully constructed residential flats without being subjected to construction cost escalation[cite: 4]; (iii) Whether interim execution of a Construction Management Agreement (CMA) and infusion of interim finance by a prospective resolution applicant prior to adjudicating authority approval invalidates the resolution plan[cite: 4]; (iv) What is the permissible scope of judicial review by Adjudicating Authorities and Appellate Tribunals over registered valuation reports accepted by the CoC[cite: 4].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 30(2)(b) of the IBC, a dissenting financial creditor is legally entitled only to an amount not less than what it would have received under Section 53(1) in the event of liquidation, and possesses no statutory right to demand distribution corresponding to the monetary value of its individual security interest; the commercial wisdom of the requisite CoC majority governing inter-se distribution among classes of creditors is non-justiciable, and valuation by registered experts cannot be second-guessed absent manifest arbitrariness[cite: 4]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2)(b) and Section 53(1)(b) govern distribution on the basis of admitted debt claims rather than security valuations, as authoritatively held in India Resurgence ARC and Essar Steel[cite: 4]. Under the Explanation to Section 5(8)(f), homebuyers are statutorily recognized as financial creditors in a distinct class, and because their commercial claim is specifically for physical residential units, providing them finished flats without price escalation while imposing haircuts on institutional lenders falls squarely within the CoC's commercial prerogative[cite: 4]. Additionally, Supreme Court directions in Vistra ITCL were passed under Article 142 of the Constitution based on exceptional facts and do not operate as binding precedent under Article 141 to compel payment according to security interest in resolution plans[cite: 4]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed the records establishing that the Corporate Debtor had zero cash and its sole asset was a precarious contractual development right facing forfeiture; that all financial creditors had expressly recorded inability to inject interim finance in the 4th and 5th CoC meetings; that the CMA was required by RFRP Clause 5.6 and saved over Rs. 100 Crores in MCGM FSI charges before 31.12.2021; that independent valuation experts applied standard residual methodology showing liquidation values under Rs. 5 Crores; and that Appellants were offered payouts fully complying with the liquidation entitlement floor under Section 30(2)(b)(ii)[cite: 4]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The resolution plan satisfies all statutory requirements under Section 30(2), the interim financing and construction management agreements were bona fide measures to preserve the going concern, and dissenting creditors cannot challenge CoC commercial wisdom or claim security value payouts; hence, the NCLT orders dated 02.12.2022 and 09.01.2023 warrant no interference[cite: 4].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1494-1495 of 2022, 99 of 2023, 107 of 2023, and 108 of 2023 are dismissed[cite: 4]. Interlocutory applications seeking substitution of HDFC Bank Ltd. in place of HDFC Ltd. and Dev Rishi Ventures LLP in place of ICICI Prudential Venture Capital Fund Real Estate Scheme I are allowed[cite: 4]. The orders dated 02.12.2022 and 09.01.2023 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-V in CP (IB) No. 1390 of 2020 are affirmed[cite: 4].
summary: Dissenting secured financial creditors Beacon Trusteeship Ltd. and Dev Rishi Ventures LLP appealed against NCLT Mumbai orders rejecting objections and approving Adani Goodhomes Pvt. Ltd.'s resolution plan for Radius Estates and Developers Pvt. Ltd. with 83.93% CoC voting support[cite: 4]. The Appellants challenged the plan for imposing a 93% haircut on secured lenders while providing full flat delivery to homebuyers without escalation, entering into a pre-approval construction management agreement, and denying payouts reflecting the value of their specific mortgaged flat units[cite: 4]. Dismissing the appeals, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that dissenting creditors are only entitled to the minimum liquidation value entitlement under Section 30(2)(b) and cannot claim distribution based on security interest value[cite: 4]. The Tribunal affirmed that homebuyers form a distinct class whose revival-focused treatment falls within the non-justiciable commercial wisdom of the CoC[cite: 4].

case_title: Dev Rishi Ventures LLP (Earlier ICICI Prudential Venture Capital Fund Real Estate Scheme I) vs. Jayesh Sanghrajka & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 99 of 2023 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1494-1495 of 2022, 107 of 2023 & 108 of 2023
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Justice Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are dissenting Secured Financial Creditors: Dev Rishi Ventures LLP (substituted for ICICI Prudential Venture Capital Fund Real Estate Scheme I, holding 5.71% voting share in Comp. App. Nos. 99 and 107 of 2023) and Beacon Trusteeship Ltd. (holding 7.44% voting share in Comp. App. Nos. 1494-1495 of 2022 and 108 of 2023)[cite: 5]. Respondent No. 1 is Jayesh Sanghrajka, Resolution Professional of Radius Estates & Developers Private Limited (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 5]. Respondent No. 2 is Adani Goodhomes Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant / SRA)[cite: 5]. Respondent No. 3 is HDFC Bank Limited (erstwhile Housing Development Finance Corporation Ltd., holding 33.25% voting share)[cite: 5]. Respondent No. 4 is Ten BKC Flat Owners AOP Trust, and Respondent No. 7 is Rajesh Sureshchandra Sheth, Authorised Representative of Homebuyers (holding 33.41% voting share)[cite: 5]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor acquired redevelopment and construction sub-contract rights in respect of 'Ten BKC' Project situated on MHADA-owned leased land at Bandra via an Agreement dated 31.03.2016 entered into with MIG (Bandra) Realtors and Builders Private Ltd. (DB), which held original development rights under a Development Agreement dated 31.10.2010 executed with Middle Income Group Cooperative Housing Society[cite: 5]. ICICI Prudential / Dev Rishi held secured financial debentures in the Corporate Debtor covering 14 unsold flats and receivables from 4 sold flats (alongside Beacon Trusteeship holding Rs. 65 Crores in NCDs secured by 15 unsold flats and receivables from 12 sold flats)[cite: 5]. Construction stalled in March 2018, and the Society terminated DB's development agreement on 08.05.2020 (stayed conditionally under an interim arbitral award dated 05.05.2021 subject to monthly hardship payments of Rs. 3.09 Crores)[cite: 5]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtor experienced acute distress, defaulting on debenture obligations and having zero balance in its bank accounts, with its sole value residing in derivative development rights vulnerable to automatic lapse upon DB's agreement termination[cite: 5]. Registered valuers evaluated the project Liquidation Value at Rs. 2.47 Crores (TrueVal) and Rs. 4.81 Crores (Sundeep H.B. & Co.), and Fair Value between Rs. 3.24 Crores and Rs. 6.31 Crores[cite: 5]. The SRA's plan proposed completion of the stalled project by infusing over Rs. 450 Crores in interim finance upfront and allocating Rs. 1,052 Crores of avoidance application recoveries to the CoC, but offered a 93% haircut on institutional financial debt while delivering finished units to homebuyers without escalation[cite: 5]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 30.04.2021 upon admission of Beacon Trusteeship's Section 7 petition [C.P. (IB) No. 1390 of 2020][cite: 5]. CoC was constituted on 02.07.2021, and RP appointed on 25.08.2021[cite: 5]. MCGM issued a 50% FSI premium concession circular on 22.01.2021 expiring 31.12.2021[cite: 5]. Form-G was issued on 13.10.2021[cite: 5]. SRA submitted its resolution plan with draft Construction Management Agreement (CMA) and Master Facility Agreement (MFA) on 17.12.2021[cite: 5]. CoC approved the plan and CMA/MFA on 27.12.2021 by 83.93% (and 83.99%) vote shares[cite: 5]. SRA deployed Rs. 450 Crores interim finance prior to 31.12.2021[cite: 5]. NCLT Mumbai Court-V dismissed Appellants' objection applications on 02.12.2022 and approved the resolution plan in IA No. 573/2022 on 09.01.2023[cite: 5]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered Development Agreement dated 31.10.2010; Tripartite/Assignment Agreement dated 31.03.2016; interim arbitral award dated 05.05.2021; NCD debenture mortgage trust deeds; valuation reports of Sundeep H.B. & Co. and TrueVal Advisors employing residual valuation methodology; MCGM 50% FSI premium rebate circular dated 22.01.2021; minutes of the 3rd, 4th, 5th, 7th, 8th, 9th, 12th, and 13th CoC meetings confirming lenders' inability to fund interim finance; and SRA affidavit dated 07.10.2022 assigning Rs. 1,052 Crores avoidance action recoveries to CoC[cite: 5]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: ICICI Prudential / Dev Rishi filed IA No. 808/2022 (alongside Beacon's IA Nos. 503, 837, and 931 of 2022) objecting to the resolution plan and valuation, which NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-V dismissed on 02.12.2022[cite: 5]. Appellants filed Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 1494-1495 of 2022 and 99 of 2023 against the objection dismissal[cite: 5]. NCLT then allowed plan approval application IA No. 573/2022 on 09.01.2023[cite: 5]. Appellants filed Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 107 and 108 of 2023 challenging plan approval, arguing that the CMA unlawfully handed marketing rights to SRA prior to approval, that lenders suffered an inequitable 93% haircut while homebuyers received flats without escalation, and that dissenting creditors must be paid as per the value of their specific security interests[cite: 5].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a dissenting secured financial creditor is entitled under Section 30(2)(b)(ii) read with Section 53(1) of the IBC to receive payment equal to the estimated market/liquidation value of its underlying security interest over specific mortgaged units[cite: 5]; (ii) Whether a resolution plan is unfair, discriminatory, or in breach of Section 30(2) when it imposes a substantial (93%) haircut on secured institutional lenders while providing 100% recovery to allottee homebuyers through handover of completed residential units without escalation charges[cite: 5]; (iii) Whether entering into a pre-approval Construction Management Agreement (CMA) and Master Facility Agreement (MFA) to commence urgent construction and capture municipal tax rebates invalidates the resolution process[cite: 5]; (iv) What constitutes the permissible scope of judicial review over expert valuation reports approved by the Committee of Creditors[cite: 5].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 30(2)(b) of the IBC, a dissenting financial creditor is entitled only to a monetary payout not less than the amount payable under Section 53(1) in the event of liquidation, and has no legal entitlement to enforce or receive distribution proportionate to the specific value of its underlying security interest; the distribution of plan proceeds across different classes of creditors and the commercial terms of project revival fall exclusively within the non-justiciable commercial wisdom of the requisite CoC majority[cite: 5]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: As held in India Resurgence ARC and Essar Steel, the reference to Section 53(1) in Section 30(2)(b) is solely a benchmark formula for calculating minimum monetary entitlement on the basis of admitted debt, not an order of priority for distributing proceeds according to individual security valuation[cite: 5]. Homebuyers constitute a distinct and recognized class of financial creditors under Explanation to Section 5(8)(f); because their investment aims at obtaining residential premises, transferring completed flats to them without price escalation while requiring institutional financiers to absorb haircuts violates no provision of the Code[cite: 5]. Furthermore, the Supreme Court decision in Vistra ITCL was rendered pursuant to extraordinary powers under Article 142 of the Constitution and does not establish a precedent under Article 141 entitling secured creditors to insist on security-interest valuations in resolution plans[cite: 5]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examined the record establishing that the Corporate Debtor was devoid of funds and possessed only precarious contractual rights liable to termination; all CoC members had formally refused interim financing; the urgent execution of the CMA and injection of Rs. 450 Crores saved more than Rs. 100 Crores in MCGM FSI charges prior to 31.12.2021; registered valuers properly applied the residual method showing project liquidation values below Rs. 5 Crores; and Appellants received payouts satisfying the minimum liquidation threshold under Section 30(2)(b)(ii)[cite: 5]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The resolution plan satisfied all mandatory parameters under Section 30(2) and CIRP Regulations 38-39, the interim construction arrangements were bona fide measures preserving the asset, and the CoC's commercial wisdom regarding distribution and haircuts is not amenable to appellate interference; thus, the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in passing the orders dated 02.12.2022 and 09.01.2023[cite: 5].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 99 of 2023, 107 of 2023, 108 of 2023, and 1494-1495 of 2022 are dismissed[cite: 5]. Applications for substituting Dev Rishi Ventures LLP in place of ICICI Prudential Venture Capital Fund Real Estate Scheme I and HDFC Bank Ltd. in place of HDFC Ltd. are allowed[cite: 5]. The orders dated 02.12.2022 and 09.01.2023 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-V in CP (IB) No. 1390 of 2020 are affirmed[cite: 5].
summary: Dev Rishi Ventures LLP (substituted for ICICI Prudential Venture Capital Fund Real Estate Scheme I) and Beacon Trusteeship Ltd. appealed against NCLT Mumbai orders dismissing objections and approving Adani Goodhomes Pvt. Ltd.'s resolution plan for Radius Estates & Developers Pvt. Ltd., approved by 83.93% CoC vote[cite: 5]. The Appellants challenged the plan for imposing a 93% haircut on secured lenders while providing 100% recovery to homebuyers through completed flats without escalation, entering into a pre-approval Construction Management Agreement, and denying payouts reflecting the value of their mortgaged units[cite: 5]. Dismissing the appeals, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that dissenting creditors are only entitled to the minimum liquidation value entitlement under Section 30(2)(b) and cannot claim distribution based on security interest value[cite: 5]. The Tribunal held that homebuyers form a distinct class whose revival-focused treatment falls within the non-justiciable commercial wisdom of the CoC[cite: 5].

case_title: Yamuna Expressway Industrial Development Authority vs. Monitoring Committee of Jaypee Infratech Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 493 of 2023 & I.A. Nos. 3017, 3703 of 2023 & 2535, 2548, 2660, 2669 of 2024
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Justice Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Yamuna Expressway Industrial Development Authority (YEIDA, formerly Taj Expressway Industrial Development Authority), a statutory authority constituted under the UP Industrial Area Development Act, 1976[cite: 6]. Respondent No. 1 is the Implementation and Monitoring Committee of Jaypee Infratech Ltd. (Corporate Debtor / JIL) acting through Secretary Anuj Jain[cite: 6]. Respondent No. 2 is Suraksha Realty Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant / SRA)[cite: 6]. Intervenors include National Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. (NARCL), Jaiprakash Associates Ltd. (JAL - erstwhile promoter/concessionaire), and various Homebuyers' Associations[cite: 6]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Under a Concession Agreement dated 07.02.2003, TEA/YEIDA granted concession rights to JAL to construct a 160-km six-lane expressway connecting Noida to Agra with toll collection rights for 36 years and transferred 6,177 acres of abutting land for commercial development[cite: 6]. The Concession Agreement was assigned to JIL on 19.10.2007[cite: 6]. Under Clauses 4.1(d) and 4.3(c), the sole land premium payable by the Concessionaire was equivalent to actual land acquisition costs plus annual lease rent[cite: 6]. Following farmers' agitations and the UP Government Order dated 29.08.2014, YEIDA required allottees to pay 64.7% additional compensation to land-owning farmers, which was upheld by the Supreme Court in Shakuntla Education (2022)[cite: 6]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: In JIL's CIRP, YEIDA lodged claims aggregating Rs. 6,111.591 Crores in Form-B, comprising Rs. 1,689 Crores towards 64.7% additional farmers' compensation and Rs. 624.6 Crores towards External Development Charges (EDC)[cite: 6]. The IRP verified and admitted only Rs. 461 Crores (Rs. 409.6 Crores for EDC and Rs. 51.4 Crores for pending works), rejecting the Rs. 1,689 Crore farmers' compensation claim because arbitration was sub-judice[cite: 6]. In the Suraksha Resolution Plan, only Rs. 10 Lakhs each was allocated to additional farmers' compensation and EDC on the basis that YEIDA was an unsecured operational creditor with Nil liquidation entitlement[cite: 6]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced against JIL on 07.08.2017 upon IDBI Bank's Section 7 petition[cite: 6]. YEIDA submitted Form-B claims on 23.08.2017 and 28.11.2017[cite: 6]. After the Supreme Court in Jaypee Kensington (24.03.2021) set aside NBCC's approved plan, Suraksha submitted a revised plan, which the CoC approved with 98.66% votes in June 2021[cite: 6]. YEIDA filed objection application IA No. 3306/PB/2021[cite: 6]. On 07.03.2023, NCLT New Delhi Special Bench approved Suraksha's plan and dismissed YEIDA's objections[cite: 6]. YEIDA appealed to NCLAT via Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 493 of 2023[cite: 6]. On 18.04.2024, Suraksha submitted a 'without prejudice' offer of Rs. 1,216 Crores towards farmers' compensation, which YEIDA contested[cite: 6]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Concession Agreement dated 07.02.2003 and assignment deed dated 19.10.2007[cite: 6]; UP Government Order dated 29.08.2014 and YEIDA Board Resolution dated 15.09.2014[cite: 6]; IRP verification letter dated 28.11.2017[cite: 6]; reconciled accounts showing revised EDC liabilities of Rs. 525.91 Crores plus future EDC of Rs. 572.89 Crores for Tappal/Agra[cite: 6]; and Suraksha's conditional settlement offer affidavit dated 18.04.2024[cite: 6]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Special Bench dismissed YEIDA's IA No. 3306/PB/2021 on 07.03.2023, relying on NOIDA v. Anand Sonbhadra to classify YEIDA as an unsecured operational creditor entitled to a token Rs. 10 Lakhs payout[cite: 6]. YEIDA appealed before NCLAT challenging paras 51-92 of the approval order, asserting statutory secured creditor status under Sections 13 and 13-A of the 1976 Act as established in Greater Noida v. Prabhjit Singh Soni[cite: 6].
legal_issues: (i) Whether YEIDA qualifies as a 'Secured Creditor' under Section 3(30) of the IBC by virtue of the statutory charge created under Section 13 read with Section 13-A of the UP Industrial Area Development Act, 1976 for its claim of Rs. 1,689 Crores towards additional farmers' compensation[cite: 6]; (ii) Whether the IRP and Adjudicating Authority erred in treating YEIDA as an ordinary unsecured operational creditor and allocating a nominal token amount of Rs. 10 Lakhs against its statutory acquisition cost claim[cite: 6]; (iii) Whether External Development Charges (EDC) constitute a statutory secured charge under Sections 13 and 13-A of the 1976 Act[cite: 6]; (iv) Whether prior consent of YEIDA is mandatory for transferring leasehold land rights to the SRA or assenting financial creditors under the resolution plan[cite: 6].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A statutory industrial authority holding an automatic charge over transferred property by operation of law under a state development enactment for unpaid land acquisition costs or premium qualifies as a secured creditor under the IBC; treating such statutory authority as an ordinary operational creditor with token liquidation-value distribution is unsustainable, and its secured claim must be accorded parity of distribution percentage comparable to other secured institutional creditors to satisfy Section 30(2) of the Code[cite: 6]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 13-A of the UP Industrial Area Development Act, 1976 creates an automatic statutory charge over property for any consideration money or default arising under Section 13[cite: 6]. Under Clauses 4.1(d) and 4.3(c) of the Concession Agreement, actual land acquisition costs constitute the foundational premium for lease transfers, making 64.7% additional farmers' compensation an integral part of statutory transfer consideration falling squarely within Section 13-A[cite: 6]. Following Greater Noida v. Prabhjit Singh Soni, non-placement of the statutory authority in the secured creditor class vitiates the resolution plan[cite: 6]. Conversely, External Development Charges (EDC) do not constitute land consideration, rent, or a fee/tax levied under the 1976 Act, and therefore do not carry a statutory charge under Section 13-A[cite: 6]. Furthermore, under Regulation 37(a) of the CIRP Regulations read with Concession Agreement Clause 4.3(d), the resolution plan merely deals with the corporate debtor's leasehold rights without creating higher ownership title, rendering YEIDA's prior consent unnecessary for leasehold restructuring[cite: 6]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the Concession Agreement explicitly cast the liability for all land acquisition costs upon the Concessionaire, which was upheld against JIL by the Supreme Court in Shakuntla Education; that deduction of Rs. 330 Crores (sub-leased parcels) and Rs. 143 Crores (Noida land) was impermissible because JIL bore primary liability under Jaypee Kensington; and that financial creditors received a 79% payout on their secured claims, establishing a definitive benchmark for YEIDA's secured claim[cite: 6]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: YEIDA is a secured creditor regarding its Rs. 1,689 Crore farmers' compensation claim and is legally entitled to a 79% recovery (Rs. 1,334.31 Crores) in parity with secured lenders[cite: 6]. Applying the Jet Aircraft precedent to avoid stalling a six-year-old CIRP impacting over 20,000 homebuyers, the NCLAT modified the plan directly by directing the SRA to pay Rs. 1,334.31 Crores over a 4-year schedule without remanding the plan back to the CoC[cite: 6].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 493 of 2023 is allowed in part: (1) The impugned order dated 07.03.2023 passed by NCLT New Delhi Special Bench in IA No. 3306/PB/2021 is set aside insofar as it dealt with YEIDA's Rs. 1,689 Crore claim for additional farmers' compensation, while the remainder of the order approving Suraksha's Resolution Plan is upheld[cite: 6]; (2) SRA (Suraksha Realty Ltd.) is directed to pay YEIDA 79% of its secured operational claim of Rs. 1,689 Crores, amounting to Rs. 1,334.31 Crores[cite: 6]; (3) The SRA shall pay Rs. 1,216 Crores as offered, and an additional Rs. 118.31 Crores, across the committed 4-year payment schedule with 10% upfront within 90 days[cite: 6]; (4) SRA shall implement the approved Resolution Plan in accordance with law, and all pending Interlocutory Applications stand disposed of with parties bearing their own costs[cite: 6].
summary: YEIDA appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order approving Suraksha Realty Ltd.'s resolution plan for Jaypee Infratech Ltd., which allocated only a token Rs. 10 Lakhs against YEIDA's Rs. 1,689 Crore claim for additional farmers' compensation and Rs. 10 Lakhs for External Development Charges (EDC)[cite: 6]. Partly allowing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that under Sections 13 and 13-A of the UP Industrial Area Development Act, 1976 and Supreme Court precedent in Prabhjit Singh Soni, land acquisition compensation constitutes lease premium carrying an automatic statutory charge, rendering YEIDA a secured creditor[cite: 6]. The Tribunal ruled that EDC does not carry a statutory charge[cite: 6]. To prevent derailment of the CIRP affecting 20,000 homebuyers, the Tribunal avoided remand and directly directed Suraksha to pay 79% of the secured claim (Rs. 1,334.31 Crores) across four years in parity with secured institutional lenders[cite: 6].

case_title: Devang Hemant Vyas & Ors. / Prag Bosimi Synthetics Ltd. vs. 3A Capital Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 115 of 2022 with Company Appeal (AT) No. 116 of 2022 & Company Appeal (AT) No. 133 of 2022
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain and Technical Member Ajai Das Mehrotra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants in Comp. App. No. 115/2022 are Devang Hemant Vyas and 5 other non-executive/independent directors of Prag Bosimi Synthetics Ltd. (the Company)[cite: 7]. The Appellant in Comp. App. No. 116/2022 is the Company itself (Prag Bosimi Synthetics Ltd.)[cite: 7]. 3A Capital Pvt. Ltd. is the Contempt Petitioner/decree holder (Appellant in cross-appeal Comp. App. No. 133/2022)[cite: 7]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Prag Bosimi Synthetics Ltd. availed consortium project finance led by IDBI and ICICI to establish a polyester yarn plant in Assam[cite: 7]. ICICI subscribed to 30,00,000 Redeemable Cumulative Convertible Preference Shares (RCCPS) and Cumulative Convertible Preference Shares (CCPS) of Rs. 100 face value each as security and for overdue interest conversion[cite: 7]. Following project distress and NPA declaration, the account underwent Corporate Debt Restructuring (CDR) where ICICI assigned its debt to Standard Chartered Bank (SCB)[cite: 7]. Later, 3A Capital purported to purchase the 30,00,000 preference shares from ICICI for Rs. 3,90,00,000/- (Rs. 0.13 per share) and demanded share transfer[cite: 7]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: 3A Capital claimed default by the Company in failing to register and transfer the 30,00,000 preference shares and non-payment of cumulative preference dividends, valuing its claim at Rs. 30,00,00,000/- plus accrued interest and damages[cite: 7]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: On 16.12.2010, the Company approved capital reduction cancelling 81,46,250 preference shares (including ICICI's 30 Lakh shares), which Gauhati High Court sanctioned on 18.12.2012 in CP No. 7/2011 (rejecting 3A Capital's intervention)[cite: 7]. ROC recorded capital reduction on 12.01.2013[cite: 7]. Meanwhile, 3A Capital filed CP No. 89/2011 under Section 111A before CLB Kolkata, which directed share transfer registration on 27.05.2016[cite: 7]. The Company's Section 10F appeal (CA No. 2/2016) was dismissed by Gauhati High Court on 12.07.2017, and SLP No. 32880/2017 was dismissed by the Supreme Court on 02.02.2018[cite: 7]. 3A Capital filed Contempt Application No. 03/2018 on 22.06.2018 before NCLT Guwahati[cite: 7]. NCLT disposed of the contempt application on 12.05.2022 awarding Rs. 5.79 Crores compensation to 3A Capital and Rs. 5 Lakhs penalty to MCA[cite: 7]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Sanction letters and CDR restructuring packages dated 15.06.2004, 21.07.2004, and 06.08.2009[cite: 7]; Gauhati High Court order dated 18.12.2012 in CP No. 7/2011 confirming share capital cancellation[cite: 7]; ROC Form 21 registration dated 12.01.2013[cite: 7]; CLB order dated 27.05.2016[cite: 7]; and orders of Gauhati High Court (12.07.2017) and Supreme Court (02.02.2018)[cite: 7]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Guwahati held on 12.05.2022 that while cancelled shares could not be reissued after 9 years, the Company was liable in contempt to pay CDR-equivalent compensation of Rs. 2,99,55,000/-, interest of Rs. 2,60,42,128/-, legal costs of Rs. 20 Lakhs, and Rs. 5 Lakhs fine to MCA[cite: 7]. The Company and Directors appealed (CA Nos. 115 & 116 of 2022) alleging lack of contempt jurisdiction over CLB orders, merger into appellate decrees, impossibility of performance, and impermissible grant of unprayed substantive monetary damages in contempt proceedings[cite: 7]. 3A Capital appealed (CA No. 133 of 2022) seeking share revival instead of monetary compensation[cite: 7].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) has statutory jurisdiction under Section 425 of the Companies Act, 2013 to initiate contempt proceedings and punish for disobedience of an order passed by the erstwhile Company Law Board (CLB)[cite: 7]; (ii) Whether a contempt application is maintainable in respect of a CLB order that was not pending transfer under Section 434(1)(a) on 01.06.2016 and had subsequently merged into appellate orders of the High Court and Supreme Court under the doctrine of merger[cite: 7]; (iii) Whether a court or tribunal exercising contempt jurisdiction can travel beyond the original decree to grant substantial monetary relief, unprayed legal costs, and administrative fines in lieu of an obligation that has become impossible to perform due to extinguishment of the subject matter[cite: 7]; (iv) Whether non-executive and independent directors can be held vicariously liable for contempt of company obligations without specific pleadings under Section 12(5) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971[cite: 7].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 425 of the Companies Act, 2013, the Tribunal and Appellate Tribunal possess contempt jurisdiction strictly and exclusively in respect of 'contempt of themselves' and have no jurisdiction to initiate contempt proceedings for alleged disobedience of orders passed by the erstwhile Company Law Board; furthermore, a contempt court cannot traverse beyond the four corners of the original direction to transform contempt proceedings into an execution forum granting substituted monetary damages, interest, or unprayed compensatory reliefs where compliance with the original direction has become legally impossible due to prior extinction of the subject matter[cite: 7]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory phrasing 'contempt of themselves' in Section 425 restricts the NCLT's contempt authority solely to violations of its own orders, congruent with powers of High Courts under the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971[cite: 7]. Under Section 434(1)(a), only proceedings pending before the CLB as on the effective date (01.06.2016) stood transferred to NCLT; an order finally disposed of by CLB prior to 01.06.2016 without pending contempt or execution proceedings cannot be instituted afresh under NCLT contempt jurisdiction[cite: 7]. Applying the doctrine of merger, an order of the CLB affirmed in appeal by the High Court and Supreme Court merges into the superior court's decree, precluding contempt of the subordinate tribunal's non-existent order[cite: 7]. Moreover, contempt jurisdiction cannot be utilized to circumvent execution defenses such as impossibility of performance, nor can independent and non-executive directors be subjected to conditional contempt sanctions absent specific averments establishing direct operational charge under Section 12(5) of the Contempt of Courts Act[cite: 7]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed the record showing that CLB disposed of CP No. 89/2011 on 27.05.2016, leaving no pending matter on 01.06.2016; that the 30 Lakh preference shares had already been cancelled and wiped out under the High Court's sanctioned capital reduction order dated 18.12.2012 registered with ROC in January 2013; that CLB's order merged into the Gauhati High Court judgment dated 12.07.2017; and that NCLT Guwahati exceeded jurisdiction by awarding unprayed monetary relief of Rs. 5.79 Crores and an administrative penalty to MCA inside a contempt proceeding[cite: 7]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The contempt application filed before the NCLT was wholly non-maintainable for lack of jurisdiction under Section 425, hit by the doctrine of merger, barred by legal impossibility of performance, and vitiated by the unlawful grant of substantive monetary damages; hence, the impugned contempt directions against the Company and its directors cannot be sustained[cite: 7].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 115 of 2022 and Company Appeal (AT) No. 116 of 2022 are allowed, and the impugned order dated 12.05.2022 passed by NCLT Guwahati Bench in Contempt Application No. 03 of 2018 is set aside[cite: 7]. Company Appeal (AT) No. 133 of 2022 filed by 3A Capital Pvt. Ltd. is dismissed, with no order as to costs[cite: 7].
summary: Prag Bosimi Synthetics Ltd. and its non-executive directors appealed against an NCLT Guwahati order passed in Contempt Application No. 03 of 2018 directing the company to pay Rs. 5.79 Crores (comprising CDR-equivalent compensation, interest, and legal costs) to 3A Capital Pvt. Ltd. and Rs. 5 Lakhs to MCA for failure to transfer 30 Lakh preference shares ordered by the erstwhile CLB in 2016[cite: 7]. Setting aside the order, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that under Section 425 of the Companies Act, 2013, NCLT has contempt jurisdiction strictly in respect of 'contempt of itself' and lacks authority to punish for disobedience of CLB orders[cite: 7]. The Tribunal ruled that the CLB order had merged into appellate High Court and Supreme Court decrees, that the cancelled shares were legally non-existent, and that contempt courts cannot travel beyond the original decree to award unprayed substituted monetary compensation[cite: 7].

case_title: Fedex Express Transportation and Supply Chain Services (India) Pvt. Ltd. vs. Zipker Online Services Pvt. Ltd.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain, Technical Members Naresh Salecha and Indevar Pandey)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Fedex Express Transportation and Supply Chain Services (India) Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor), a provider of integrated shipping, logistics, and supply chain management services[cite: 9]. The Respondent is Zipker Online Services Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 9]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor availed shipping and logistics services from the Operational Creditor, against which multiple commercial invoices were issued[cite: 9]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Operational Creditor raised invoices between 07.05.2019 and 08.10.2019 aggregating an unpaid operational default amount of Rs. 18,34,120.93/- plus interest[cite: 9]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Following non-payment of invoices, the Operational Creditor issued a statutory demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC demanding payment of Rs. 18,34,120.93/- with interest[cite: 9]. The Corporate Debtor sent no reply[cite: 9]. Prior to the initiation/admission of proceedings under Section 9, the name of the Corporate Debtor was struck off from the register of companies by the Registrar of Companies (ROC) and notified as dissolved under Section 248(5) of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 9]. NCLT New Delhi dismissed the Section 9 petition on 05.09.2023[cite: 9]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Unpaid commercial service invoices dated 07.05.2019 to 08.10.2019[cite: 9]; Section 8 statutory demand notice for Rs. 18,34,120.93/-[cite: 9]; and the official notification/gazette record of the ROC striking off the Corporate Debtor's name and dissolving it under Section 248(5) of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 9]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench dismissed the Section 9 application on 05.09.2023 on the ground that the Corporate Debtor's name had been struck off by the ROC and therefore could not be prosecuted under CIRP[cite: 9]. The Operational Creditor appealed to NCLAT under Section 61, contending based on prior 3-member bench rulings in Hemang Phophalia and Elektrans Shipping that striking off is no bar to CIRP and that admission under Section 7/9 automatically effects restoration of the company under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 9].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an application under Section 9 (or Section 7) of the IBC for initiating Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) is maintainable against a corporate debtor whose name has already been struck off and dissolved by the Registrar of Companies (ROC) under Section 248(5) of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 9]; (ii) Whether the filing or admission of an application under Section 7 or 9 of the IBC automatically restores the name of a struck-off dissolved company to the register of companies under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 without a substantive statutory appeal establishing business operations or just grounds[cite: 9]; (iii) Whether the earlier 3-member bench decisions of NCLAT in Hemang Phophalia and Elektrans Shipping laid down correct law or are per incuriam[cite: 9].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for the initiation of Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 7 or Section 9 of the IBC is maintainable solely against an existing, incorporated 'corporate debtor'; once an entity's name has been struck off and published as dissolved by the Registrar of Companies under Section 248(5) of the Companies Act, 2013, its certificate of incorporation stands cancelled and it ceases to be a corporate person or corporate debtor in the eyes of law[cite: 9]. Consequently, no CIRP application can be instituted or prosecuted against it unless its corporate existence is first formally restored by the Tribunal through an independent statutory appeal under Section 252 of the Companies Act, 2013, as there is no provision in law for 'automatic restoration' upon filing or admitting an insolvency petition[cite: 9]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 3(8) read with Section 3(7) of the IBC and Section 2(20) of the Companies Act, 2013, a 'corporate debtor' must be an incorporated company[cite: 9]. Under Section 248(5) and Section 250 of the Companies Act, 2013, publication of dissolution terminates the company's legal status and cancels its certificate of incorporation, with surviving rights confined to asset realization and liability discharge via recovery or winding up under Section 248(6)-(8)[cite: 9]. Because CIRP is designed solely for corporate revival and going-concern preservation rather than debt recovery, insolvency resolution cannot be foisted upon a legally non-existent dead shell[cite: 9]. Furthermore, Section 252(3) provides a substantive right of appeal requiring explicit pleadings and proof that the company was carrying on business, in operation, or that it is just to restore it; the concept of automatic deemed restoration upon admission under Section 7 or 9 runs counter to statutory procedure[cite: 9]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the earlier decisions in Hemang Phophalia and Elektrans Shipping and determined that they omitted to consider the statutory definitions of 'corporate person' and 'corporate debtor' under the Code and the mandatory procedural requirements of Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, thereby satisfying the legal test of being per incuriam under B. Satyanarayna Rao[cite: 9]. The record confirmed that the Corporate Debtor stood dissolved under Section 248(5) without any prior restorative order having been secured under Section 252[cite: 9]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: A dissolved entity whose name remains struck off from the register of companies cannot be subjected to CIRP under Section 9 of the Code without first obtaining an order of restoration under Section 252 of the Companies Act, 2013; hence, the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in dismissing the Section 9 petition[cite: 9].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1498 of 2023 is dismissed with no order as to costs, affirming the order dated 05.09.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT New Delhi Bench)[cite: 9]. All pending Interlocutory Applications (I.A. Nos. 5379, 5380, and 5381 of 2023) are closed[cite: 9].
summary: Fedex Express Transportation and Supply Chain Services (India) Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order dismissing its Section 9 CIRP petition against Zipker Online Services Pvt. Ltd. for default of Rs. 18.34 Lakhs on the ground that the debtor's name had been struck off and dissolved by the ROC under Section 248(5) of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 9]. Appellant relied on previous NCLAT rulings asserting that struck-off companies automatically restore under Section 252(3) upon IBC admission[cite: 9]. Dismissing the appeal, a 3-member NCLAT Bench declared Hemang Phophalia and Elektrans Shipping per incuriam, holding that a dissolved company ceases to be a 'corporate debtor' under Section 3(8) of the IBC[cite: 9]. The Tribunal ruled that CIRP cannot be initiated against a non-existent company without prior formal restoration under Section 252[cite: 9].

case_title: M/s Shri Karshni Alloys Private Limited vs. Mr. Ramakrishnan Sadasivan (Liquidator of M/s Surana Industries Limited)
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 438 of 2022 with Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 443 of 2022
bench: Chennai Bench (Technical Member Naresh Salecha on reference upon difference of opinion)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is M/s Shri Karshni Alloys Private Limited (Successful Private Sale Bidder)[cite: 10]. The Respondent is Mr. Ramakrishnan Sadasivan, Liquidator of M/s Surana Industries Limited (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 10]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was ordered into liquidation on 12.10.2018 in MA/453/2018[cite: 10]. After 13 failed public auctions for Raichur Assets (with liquidation value plummeting from Rs. 338.01 Crores in 2018 to scrap value of Rs. 50 Crores in July 2021), Appellant made a suo-moto private sale offer on 09.09.2021 of Rs. 105.21 Crores to acquire the Corporate Debtor as a going concern with certain concessions under Regulation 33(2)(d) of the Liquidation Process Regulations, 2016[cite: 10]. Stakeholders Consultation Committee (SCC) approved the offer in its 9th meeting on 15.09.2021, and NCLT Chennai confirmed the private sale in IA No. 997/CHE/2021 on 22.03.2022, directing payment within 15 days[cite: 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total sale consideration was Rs. 105.21 Crores[cite: 10]. Appellant deposited 10% commitment advance of Rs. 10.52 Crores, but failed to remit the remaining balance within 15 days[cite: 10]. Over extended periods up to 31.07.2022, Appellant paid only Rs. 37.80 Crores in piecemeal installments, defaulting on the balance amount of Rs. 67.41 Crores plus interest at 12% p.a.[cite: 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Private sale approved by NCLT on 22.03.2022 (uploaded 30.03.2022, initial deadline 15.04.2022)[cite: 10]. In 10th SCC meeting on 13.04.2022, lenders refused voluntary timeline extension[cite: 10]. Appellant filed IA(IBC)/512/CHE/2022 seeking extension till 31.05.2022[cite: 10]. On 29.06.2022, NCLT granted extension in two tranches (50% by 30.06.2022 and remaining 50% by 31.07.2022 with 12% interest), expressly stipulating that any deviation would entail forfeiture of the entire amount paid[cite: 10]. On 29.07.2022, Appellant filed IA No. 826/2022 citing apprehension of ED attachment under Section 32A and seeking time, which was withdrawn on 04.08.2022 and refiled as IA(IBC)/952(CHE)/2022[cite: 10]. On 01.08.2022, the 13th SCC meeting resolved to forfeit deposited sums pursuant to the NCLT order and re-auction assets[cite: 10]. Liquidator issued forfeiture letter on 02.08.2022[cite: 10]. NCLT dismissed IA(IBC)/952(CHE)/2022 on 10.08.2022[cite: 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Private sale bid dated 09.09.2021[cite: 10]; minutes of 9th, 10th, and 13th SCC meetings[cite: 10]; installment payment schedule showing total deposit of Rs. 37.80 Crores[cite: 10]; ED provisional attachment order dated 01.08.2022 (which excluded Raichur assets)[cite: 10]; Liquidator's forfeiture communication dated 02.08.2022[cite: 10]; and subsequent e-auction sale confirmation to Texcon Steels Ltd. on 28.11.2022 for Rs. 145.38 Crores[cite: 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai Bench directed conditional extension with forfeiture on 29.06.2022 in IA/512/2022, and dismissed the challenge to forfeiture on 10.08.2022 in IA/952/2022[cite: 10]. Appellant appealed both orders via Comp. App. (AT) (CH) (Ins) Nos. 443 of 2022 and 438 of 2022[cite: 10]. Following a split verdict between Judicial Member Justice M. Venugopal and Technical Member Shreesha Merla on 20.10.2023, the appeals were referred de-novo to Technical Member Naresh Salecha as Third Member for authoritative determination[cite: 10].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a private sale of corporate debtor assets requiring statutory concessions is governed by Regulation 33(2)(c) or Regulation 33(2)(d) of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016, and whether the general principles of Sections 73 and 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 apply to such sales[cite: 10]; (ii) Whether the Adjudicating Authority possesses statutory power under Rule 15 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 to unilaterally impose a condition of forfeiture while extending timelines for payment of sale consideration[cite: 10]; (iii) Whether forfeiture of deposited amounts constitutes unjust enrichment where the assets are subsequently sold in fresh auction at a price higher than the defaulted bidder's offer[cite: 10]; (iv) Whether the bidder is barred under the doctrine of approbation and reprobation from challenging the forfeiture condition after having availed the benefit of timeline enlargement and making subsequent part-payments under the conditional order[cite: 10].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A private sale under statutory liquidation regulations that requires judicial approval for concessions and waivers is governed exclusively by insolvency jurisprudence rather than the common law of contract under Sections 73 and 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872[cite: 10]. When granting extensions of time for deposit of balance consideration, the Adjudicating Authority possesses plenary power under Rule 15 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 to impose strict conditions of forfeiture upon further default[cite: 10]. A defaulting bidder who avails the extension and tenders subsequent installments is precluded by the doctrine of approbation and reprobation from challenging the accompanying forfeiture condition, and retention of forfeited sums does not constitute unjust enrichment even if a subsequent auction yields a higher realization[cite: 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 33(2)(d) of the Liquidation Process Regulations, 2016 governs private sales requiring prior permission of the Adjudicating Authority, particularly where special concessions are sought beyond the liquidator's statutory powers[cite: 10]. Under Rule 15 of the NCLT Rules, 2016, the Tribunal has express authority to enlarge time 'upon such terms, if any, as the justice of the case may require'[cite: 10]. Applying the Supreme Court's rulings in Kridhan Infrastructure, Authorised Officer SBI v. C. Natarajan, and Central Bank of India v. Shanmugavelu, statutory auctions and court-supervised insolvency sales exclude the operation of Section 74 of the Contract Act; forfeiture is a valid regulatory deterrent against frivolous bidding and delay, and its enforceability cannot be contingent upon whether the creditor suffered actual financial loss or subsequently fetched a higher price[cite: 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the Appellant explicitly invoked Regulation 33(2)(d) and Section 60(5) in its application for sale confirmation; that the SCC refused voluntary extensions in its 10th meeting; that NCLT granted a 33-day grace period with an explicit forfeiture warning in its 29.06.2022 order; that the Appellant accepted the benefit by paying Rs. 1.5 Crores in July 2022 without contemporaneous demur; that the ED attachment was proven not to attach to the Raichur assets; and that the total default exceeded Rs. 67 Crores on the terminal date of 31.07.2022[cite: 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The private sale was subject to Regulation 33(2)(d), the forfeiture condition was lawfully imposed under Rule 15 of NCLT Rules, the forfeiture did not constitute unjust enrichment, and the Appellant's challenge was barred by approbation and reprobation, rendering both impugned orders valid and sustainable[cite: 10].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 438 of 2022 and Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 443 of 2022 fail and are dismissed with no order as to costs[cite: 10]. All pending Interlocutory Applications are closed, resolving the reference following the split verdict[cite: 10].
summary: Shri Karshni Alloys Pvt. Ltd. appealed against NCLT Chennai orders extending payment timelines for purchasing the Raichur assets of Surana Industries Ltd. under private sale for Rs. 105.21 Crores, which stipulated forfeiture upon failure, and subsequently upholding the forfeiture of Rs. 37.80 Crores when default persisted past 31.07.2022[cite: 10]. The Appellant contended that private sale is governed by the Indian Contract Act, 1872 barring forfeiture absent actual loss, particularly since assets were re-auctioned for Rs. 145.38 Crores[cite: 10]. Following a split bench reference, the Third Member dismissed both appeals, holding that court-approved private sales under Regulation 33(2)(d) exclude Sections 73-74 of the Contract Act[cite: 10]. The Tribunal affirmed NCLT's jurisdiction under Rule 15 of NCLT Rules to mandate forfeiture and ruled that subsequent higher recovery does not constitute unjust enrichment[cite: 10].

case_title: M/s. A.P. Refinery Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. vs. Aar Kay Chemicals Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain and Technical Member Naresh Salecha)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are M/s A.P. Refinery Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant No. 1 Company), M/s Dhuri Cold Storage Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant No. 2 Company), common directors Ravi Nandan Goyal and Shiv Kumar Goyal (Appellants Nos. 3 and 4), and other promoter-allottees (Appellants Nos. 5-10)[cite: 11]. Respondents Nos. 1 to 9 are minority shareholders led by Aar Kay Chemicals Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 1 Company) and individual shareholders Achhru Ram Sharma, Pawan Kumar Singla, Vijay Kumar Goyal, Parshotam Dass Garg, and others[cite: 11]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant No. 1 Company was incorporated on 01.08.2003 for refining rice bran oil[cite: 11]. In 2009, Appellants held 88.70% equity and Respondents held 11.30%[cite: 11]. On 19.05.2010, Respondent No. 1 purchased 14,96,000 equity shares of Appellant No. 1 ('First Transfer')[cite: 11]. On 24.05.2010, these 14,96,000 shares were transferred from Respondent No. 1 to Appellant No. 2 ('Second Transfer')[cite: 11]. Later, Appellant No. 1 allotted 3,50,000 shares to Appellant No. 7 on 29.06.2011 ('Allotment No. 1') and 4,00,000 shares to Appellants Nos. 2, 3, 8, 9, and 10 on 10.10.2012 ('Allotment No. 2'), diluting Respondents' collective holding[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Respondents Nos. 1 to 9 alleged oppression and mismanagement under Sections 397/398 of the Companies Act, 1956, establishing that the Second Transfer of 14,96,000 shares and the subsequent allotments of 7,50,000 shares were fraudulent and executed without authorization or consent, reducing Respondents' shareholding from an effective majority/substantial holding to a disenfranchised 9.52%[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: In November 2012, Respondents filed CP No. 146/ND/2012[cite: 11]. NCLT Chandigarh disposed of it on 15.11.2017 directing retransfer of 14,96,000 shares to Respondent No. 1 prospectively[cite: 11]. Both parties appealed to NCLAT (CA Nos. 394/2017 & 55/2018)[cite: 11]. During the pendency on 28.11.2017, Appellants executed a 'Fresh Transfer' retransferring 14,96,000 shares back to Appellant No. 2[cite: 11]. On 16.04.2019, NCLAT set aside the Second Transfer retrospectively w.e.f. 19.05.2010, struck down both allotments of 2011/2012, and set aside all steps taken pursuant to the lower order[cite: 11]. Appellants appealed to the Supreme Court (Civil Appeal Nos. 4774-4775 of 2019) where stay was refused on 10.05.2019[cite: 11]. Respondents filed Execution Application CA No. 722/2019 under Section 424(3) in October 2019[cite: 11]. NCLT allowed execution on 03.06.2022[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Register of Members of Appellant No. 1 at Transfer Nos. 16-20, 21, 24, and 28[cite: 11]; unverified Board Resolutions dated 27.11.2017 and 28.11.2017 executed by common directors (Appellants Nos. 3 and 4)[cite: 11]; share purchase agreement dated 28.11.2017[cite: 11]; Form MGT-7 filed on 21.11.2019 showing continued non-compliance[cite: 11]; and ROC Punjab and Chandigarh compliance report dated 14.01.2020 confirming Appellants failed to restore Respondent No. 1's shareholding[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh Bench allowed CA No. 722/2019 on 03.06.2022, rejecting Appellants' defense of a subsequent 'Fresh Transfer' of 28.11.2017 and directing ROC to appoint a Gazetted Officer to enforce rectification of the Register of Members and ensure transfer of share certificates to Respondent No. 1[cite: 11]. Appellants appealed to NCLAT under Section 421 arguing that the executing court exceeded its decree by setting aside the unadjudicated fresh transfer dated 28.11.2017 and that execution was barred by the pending Supreme Court appeal[cite: 11].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an Execution Application under Section 424(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 is maintainable during the pendency of a statutory appeal before the Supreme Court in the absence of an express interim stay order under Order 41 Rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908[cite: 11]; (ii) Whether an executing court exceeds the scope of a decree when it enforces an appellate mandate directing retrospective restoration of shareholding status quo ante as of 19.05.2010 and invalidates an intervening paper re-transfer ('Fresh Transfer' dated 28.11.2017) engineered by common directors during the pendency of the appeal[cite: 11]; (iii) Whether common directors can defeat final binding orders of corporate oppression by setting up an independent transaction under a subsequent board resolution to retain control over disputed shares[cite: 11].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Order 41 Rule 5 of the CPC, the mere preferring or pendency of an appeal before an appellate court does not operate as an automatic stay of proceedings under the decree or order appealed from; an executing court has the jurisdictional competence and duty to enforce the decree unless an express stay is granted by the superior forum[cite: 11]. Furthermore, where an appellate tribunal commands absolute restoration of shareholding status quo ante to a specific historical date and invalidates all intermediate steps taken by parties pending appeal, the executing court is bound to give complete effect to the true import of the decree and must disregard subsequent collusive paper transfers engineered to circumvent the judgment[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 424(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 confers full execution powers on the Tribunal to enforce its orders as decrees of a civil court[cite: 11]. Under Order 41 Rule 5 of the CPC, an appeal does not stay execution unless expressly granted for sufficient cause[cite: 11]. A binding appellate decree under Sections 397/398 of the 1956 Act setting aside an illegal share transfer with retrospective effect from 19.05.2010 wipes out all subsequent derivative transactions[cite: 11]. Corporate entities sharing common interested directors cannot invoke Section 188 of the Companies Act, 2013 or contrived board resolutions to create a parallel 'fresh cause of action' that renders appellate adjudications nugatory[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified from the record that the Supreme Court refused interim stay on 10.05.2019 in Civil Appeal Nos. 4774-4775 of 2019[cite: 11]; that the ROC compliance report dated 14.01.2020 confirmed that Appellant No. 1 failed to reflect Respondent No. 1 as the owner of 14,96,000 shares in its statutory filings[cite: 11]; that Appellants Nos. 3 and 4 were common directors controlling the transferor, transferee, and subject companies who orchestrated the fresh transfer on 28.11.2017 within four days of the lower court's judgment[cite: 11]; and that paragraph 40(A) of NCLAT's judgment dated 16.04.2019 expressly annulled all steps taken pursuant to the lower order pending appeal[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The fresh transfer dated 28.11.2017 fell squarely within the sweep of actions set aside by NCLAT's earlier judgment restoring shareholding to 19.05.2010; the executing court acted fully within its jurisdiction to ensure compliance, and Appellants' continued disobedience justified enforcement and payment of previously imposed costs with 12% interest[cite: 11].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 102 of 2022 is dismissed with no grounds to interfere with the Execution Order dated 03.06.2022 passed by NCLT Chandigarh Bench in CA No. 722/2019[cite: 11]. Appellants are directed to comply with the directions and pay the previously awarded costs of Rs. 50,000/- each along with interest at the rate of 12% per annum from 16.04.2019 until realization, and all pending Interlocutory Applications are closed[cite: 11].
summary: Appellants, including M/s A.P. Refinery Pvt. Ltd., appealed against an NCLT Chandigarh execution order directing enforcement of an NCLAT decree dated 16.04.2019, which had retrospectively set aside an illegal transfer of 14,96,000 shares to Appellant No. 2 and restored Respondent No. 1's ownership w.e.f. 19.05.2010[cite: 11]. Appellants contended that execution was barred by a pending Supreme Court appeal and that an intervening 'fresh transfer' executed on 28.11.2017 constituted an independent transaction beyond the decree[cite: 11]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that under Order 41 Rule 5 of CPC, mere pendency of an appeal without an express stay does not bar execution[cite: 11]. The Tribunal ruled that the contrived re-transfer by common directors was a nullity designed to circumvent court orders and fell squarely within the appellate mandate setting aside all steps taken pending appeal[cite: 11].

case_title: Virigineni Anjaiah vs. Pridhvi Asset Reconstruction and Securitisation Company Ltd. & Anr.
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Member Justice M. Venugopal and Technical Member Jatindranath Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Virigineni Anjaiah, Suspended Director of M/s Sri Pavana Keerthi Hotels India Private Limited (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 13]. Respondent No. 1 is Pridhvi Asset Reconstruction and Securitisation Company Limited (PARAS / Assignee Financial Creditor)[cite: 13]. Respondent No. 2 is Shri Guntur Raghu Babu, Interim Resolution Professional (IRP)[cite: 13]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed a term loan facility of Rs. 19.28 Crores from erstwhile Andhra Bank payable in 94 monthly instalments spanning from June 2015 to March 2023, secured by personal guarantees of directors and mortgage over immovable properties[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor failed to complete its hospitality project and defaulted on principal instalments and interest servicing, leading to NPA classification on 31.10.2015[cite: 13]. Andhra Bank claimed Rs. 32,19,88,213/- in OA No. 403 of 2017 before DRT-I Hyderabad[cite: 13]. DRT allowed recovery of Rs. 25,71,79,268/- with 12% simple interest on 19.02.2019 and issued Debt Recovery Certificate DRC No. 176/2019 on 09.07.2019, which remained unpaid[cite: 13]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 31.10.2015[cite: 13]. Andhra Bank filed OA No. 403 of 2017 before DRT on 06.06.2017[cite: 13]. Debt was assigned to Respondent No. 1 vide registered Assignment Agreement dated 27.09.2017[cite: 13]. DRT issued final recovery order on 19.02.2019 and Recovery Certificate on 09.07.2019[cite: 13]. DRT Recovery Officer issued demand notice on 22.07.2020[cite: 13]. Respondent No. 1 filed Section 7 CIRP application [CP (IB) No. 153/7/HDB/2021] on 24.10.2021[cite: 13]. NCLT Hyderabad admitted the petition on 11.04.2022[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Term loan sanction letters and mortgage deeds executed with Andhra Bank[cite: 13]; Registered Assignment Agreement dated 27.09.2017 under Section 5 of SARFAESI Act[cite: 13]; DRT-I Hyderabad recovery judgment dated 19.02.2019 and Debt Recovery Certificate dated 09.07.2019[cite: 13]; DRT demand notice dated 22.07.2020[cite: 13]; OTS offer letter dated 16.01.2020 and audited balance sheets of Corporate Debtor for FY 2018-19 and 2019-20 reflecting debt acknowledgment[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad Bench admitted Respondent No. 1's Section 7 petition on 11.04.2022, holding that the assignee of a DRT recovery certificate qualifies as a Financial Creditor and the application was within the 3-year limitation under Article 137 from the certificate issuance date[cite: 13]. Suspended Director appealed to NCLAT via Comp. App. (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 224 of 2022, contending that the petition was barred by limitation 3 years post-NPA (31.10.2018), that a decree holder does not qualify as a financial creditor, and that the petition was an impermissible execution under Section 65[cite: 13].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a liability arising out of a money decree and subsequent Recovery Certificate issued by a Debt Recovery Tribunal constitutes a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC, entitling the holder to initiate CIRP as a 'financial creditor' under Section 5(7)[cite: 13]; (ii) Whether the issuance of a Debt Recovery Certificate by the DRT gives rise to a fresh cause of action providing a fresh 3-year period of limitation under Section 238A of the IBC read with Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963[cite: 13]; (iii) Whether the pendency of a set-aside application or appeal against the DRT final order/decree impairs its finality or bars the institution of a Section 7 application[cite: 13]; (iv) Whether initiating CIRP based on an unexecuted DRT recovery certificate constitutes a fraudulent or malicious proceeding for recovery under Section 65 of the IBC[cite: 13].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A liability arising out of a Debt Recovery Certificate issued by a Debt Recovery Tribunal constitutes a 'financial debt' within the meaning of Section 5(8) of the IBC, and the holder of such certificate qualifies as a 'financial creditor' under Section 5(7) of the Code; the issuance of a Recovery Certificate gives rise to a fresh cause of action and a fresh three-year limitation period under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963 to initiate CIRP, which is not impaired by the pendency of unadjudicated set-aside petitions against the decree[cite: 13]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(7) read with Section 5(8) of the IBC encompasses claims crystallized under a Recovery Certificate, as authoritatively settled by three-Judge Bench rulings of the Supreme Court in Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. v. A. Balakrishnan and Dena Bank v. C. Shivakumar Reddy, which superseded contrary NCLAT rulings[cite: 13]. Under Section 238A of the IBC and Article 137 of the Limitation Act, a fresh limitation period of three years begins from the date the Recovery Certificate is drawn[cite: 13]. Filing an application under Section 7 pursuant to an unsatisfied Recovery Certificate does not violate Section 65 or constitute an improper debt recovery suit, as the Code provides an independent statutory framework for corporate revival and insolvency resolution[cite: 13]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that DRT-I Hyderabad issued the Debt Recovery Certificate on 09.07.2019, and the Section 7 petition was filed on 24.10.2021, falling well within the three-year statutory limitation period[cite: 13]. Furthermore, the debt was continuously acknowledged in the Corporate Debtor's audited financial statements for FY 2018-19 and FY 2019-20 and through an OTS proposal dated 16.01.2020, while the pendency of an unstayed recall petition (MAIR No. 104/2021) by guarantors did not diminish the enforceability of the certificate[cite: 13]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt and default were conclusively established by the valid Recovery Certificate; the assignee asset reconstruction company was legally entitled to initiate Section 7 CIRP within three years of certificate issuance; hence, the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in admitting the Corporate Debtor into CIRP[cite: 13].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 224 of 2022 is dismissed with no order as to costs, affirming the order dated 11.04.2022 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Hyderabad Bench) in CP (IB) No. 153/7/HDB/2021[cite: 13]. All connected pending Interlocutory Applications (IA Nos. 481 & 766/2022) are closed[cite: 13].
summary: The Suspended Director of M/s Sri Pavana Keerthi Hotels India Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Hyderabad order admitting a Section 7 CIRP application filed by Pridhvi Asset Reconstruction and Securitisation Company Ltd. (PARAS) based on a DRT Recovery Certificate of Rs. 25.71 Crores[cite: 13]. The Appellant contended that the debt became NPA in October 2015, making the 2021 filing time-barred, and that a decree holder cannot initiate CIRP for debt recovery[cite: 13]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Chennai Bench relied on the Supreme Court's decisions in Kotak Mahindra Bank v. A. Balakrishnan and Dena Bank v. C. Shivakumar Reddy to hold that a Recovery Certificate crystallizes a financial debt under Section 5(8) and confers financial creditor status under Section 5(7) of the IBC[cite: 13]. The Tribunal affirmed that the certificate creates a fresh cause of action with a 3-year limitation window, making the petition timely and maintainable[cite: 13].

case_title: Commissioner of State Tax Department vs. Ramchandra Dallaram Chaudhary (Liquidator of M/s Anil Ltd.)
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 34 of 2024 & I.A. No. 105, 106, 990 of 2024
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain, Technical Members Naresh Salecha and Indevar Pandey)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is the Commissioner of State Tax Department (through the Assistant Commissioner of State Tax Unit-15, Ahmedabad, Gujarat)[cite: 14]. The Respondent is Ramchandra Dallaram Chaudhary, Liquidator of M/s Anil Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Outstanding statutory sales tax and value-added tax liabilities arose against the Corporate Debtor across 13 assessment periods spanning Assessment Years (AY) 1994-95 to 1997-98 under the Gujarat Sales Tax Act, 1969, and AY 2007-08 to 2016-17 under the Gujarat Value Added Tax Act, 2003[cite: 14]. Prior to CIRP, the department had issued revenue recovery notices under the Bombay Land Revenue Code (BLRC) between 2009 and 2012 for the 1994-1998 arrears[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant lodged cumulative tax claims aggregating Rs. 1001,72,32,359/- (consisting of an initial claim dated 03.11.2018 for Rs. 545,96,65,301/- and an additional claim dated 24.06.2020 for Rs. 455,75,67,058/-)[cite: 14]. The Liquidator admitted Rs. 42,99,15,943/- (for AY 2007-08 to 2010-11 and 2012-13) as Secured Operational Debt under Section 53(1)(b)(ii), and classified the remaining balance of Rs. 958,73,16,448/- as Unsecured Operational Debt[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 23.08.2017 with immediate Section 14 moratorium[cite: 14]. Public announcement estimated CIRP closure as 19.02.2018[cite: 14]. NCLT ordered liquidation on 25.10.2018 triggering moratorium under Section 33(5)[cite: 14]. During CIRP moratorium, the department passed assessment orders on 30.03.2018 (AY 2013-14) and 31.07.2018 (AY 2014-15), and issued an attachment order over immovable properties on 16.10.2018[cite: 14]. During liquidation moratorium, it passed assessment orders on 29.11.2019 (AY 2015-16) and 23.03.2020 (AY 2016-17)[cite: 14]. The Liquidator notified the final claim bifurcation on 22.06.2023 and 26.06.2023[cite: 14]. NCLT Ahmedabad rejected Appellant's IA No. 735/2023 on 31.10.2023[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Attachment order dated 16.10.2018[cite: 14]; assessment orders passed during moratorium (30.03.2018, 31.07.2018, 29.11.2019, 23.03.2020)[cite: 14]; Liquidator's classification letters dated 22.06.2023 and 26.06.2023[cite: 14]; and Appellant's own admission letter dated 23.06.2023 conceding that Rainbow Papers did not apply to AY 1994-98 and that assessments for AY 2014-17 were conducted during moratorium[cite: 14]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed IA No. 735/NCLT/AHM/2023 in IA No. 435/NCLT/AHM/2023 before NCLT Ahmedabad Bench seeking to declare its entire admitted claim of Rs. 1001.72 Crores as secured debt under Section 53[cite: 14]. NCLT rejected the application on 31.10.2023[cite: 14]. The Appellant appealed to NCLAT under Section 61(1) arguing that statutory tax dues create a first charge under Section 48 of the VAT Act and land revenue enactments, and that assessment orders issued after the estimated 180-day CIRP period did not violate moratorium[cite: 14].
