legal_issues: (i) Whether tax arrears assessed under the Gujarat Sales Tax Act, 1969 qualify as secured debts under the IBC in the absence of an express statutory first-charge provision analogous to Section 48 of the Gujarat Value Added Tax Act, 2003[cite: 14]; (ii) Whether assessment orders passed and property attachment orders issued during the subsistence of moratorium under Section 14 or Section 33(5) of the IBC can validly create a statutory first charge or secured creditor status under Section 3(30) and Section 53 of the Code[cite: 14]; (iii) Whether the expiration of the estimated 180-day CIRP timeline indicated in the Form-A public announcement terminates the statutory moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC[cite: 14].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A governmental tax department qualifies as a secured creditor under Section 3(30) of the IBC solely where the governing fiscal statute explicitly creates a first charge on the property of the corporate debtor by operation of law; in the absence of a specific statutory first charge, tax arrears remain unsecured operational debts under Section 53[cite: 14]. Furthermore, while statutory authorities may determine tax liabilities during insolvency, any assessment order passed or attachment created in violation of statutory moratorium under Section 14 or Section 33(5) cannot operate to create a secured charge over the assets of the corporate debtor or elevate operational claims into secured debts in liquidation[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 48 of the Gujarat Value Added Tax Act, 2003 creates a statutory first charge, bringing tax claims determined prior to CIRP within the definition of 'security interest' under Section 3(31) and 'secured creditor' under Section 3(30) as ruled in State Tax Officer v. Rainbow Papers[cite: 14]. However, the Gujarat Sales Tax Act, 1969 contains no equivalent provision creating a statutory first charge, rendering pre-VAT claims unsecured[cite: 14]. Under Section 14(1)(b) and Section 33(5) read with Sundaresh Bhatt, the imposition of moratorium creates a statutory prohibition against encumbering, attaching, or enforcing claims against the corporate debtor's assets, and the 330-day timeline under Section 12 is directory rather than an automatic termination of moratorium[cite: 14]. Consequently, assessments finalized post-moratorium cannot confer secured status under Section 53(1)(b)(ii)[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed the records establishing that pre-CIRP assessment orders (AY 2007-08 to 2012-13) amounting to Rs. 42.99 Crores were already correctly classified by the Liquidator as Secured Debt under Rainbow Papers[cite: 14]; that the Appellant's letter dated 23.06.2023 explicitly admitted that Rainbow Papers did not apply to AY 1994-98 under the 1969 Act and conceded that assessments for AY 2014-17 were conducted during the moratorium period[cite: 14]; and that attachment of corporate debtor assets on 16.10.2018 directly violated Section 14[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Liquidator properly classified the pre-moratorium VAT dues of Rs. 42.99 Crores as secured debt and the remaining Rs. 958.73 Crores (arising from sales tax lacking a first charge and assessments conducted during moratorium) as unsecured operational debt; therefore, the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in rejecting the Appellant's application[cite: 14].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 34 of 2024 is dismissed with no order as to costs, affirming the order dated 31.10.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Ahmedabad Bench) in IA No. 735/NCLT/AHM/2023[cite: 14]. All pending Interlocutory Applications (I.A. Nos. 105, 106, and 990 of 2024) are closed[cite: 14].
summary: The Commissioner of State Tax Department appealed against an NCLT Ahmedabad order upholding the Liquidator's classification of its Rs. 1001.72 Crore tax claim against M/s Anil Ltd., which admitted only Rs. 42.99 Crores as secured debt and treated Rs. 958.73 Crores as unsecured debt[cite: 14]. The Appellant contended that all tax claims held a first charge under Rainbow Papers and state revenue laws, and that assessments completed after the estimated 180-day CIRP period did not breach moratorium[cite: 14]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that Rainbow Papers applies only where the statute expressly creates a first charge, which was absent in the Gujarat Sales Tax Act, 1969[cite: 14]. The Tribunal further ruled that CIRP timelines are directory and that assessments and attachments conducted during Section 14 and Section 33(5) moratoria cannot create a secured charge under Section 53 of the IBC[cite: 14].

case_title: Assistant Commissioner of Income Tax vs. Prashant Jain (Resolution Professional of Diamond Power Infrastructure Ltd.) & Ors.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Justice Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is the Assistant Commissioner of Income Tax, Central Circle-3, Vadodara, Gujarat (Operational Creditor)[cite: 15]. Respondent No. 1 is Mr. Prashant Jain, Resolution Professional of Diamond Power Infrastructure Ltd. (Corporate Debtor / Respondent No. 3)[cite: 15]. Respondent No. 2 is M/s Gujarat State Export Corporation Ltd. (GSEC Ltd., acting in consortium with Mr. Rakesh Shah as Successful Resolution Applicant / SRA)[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Outstanding statutory income tax assessments and search-and-seizure inquiries arose against the Corporate Debtor across Assessment Years (AY) 2013-14 to 2019-20 (with additional references to AY 2009-10) involving allegations of incorrect plant valuations, cash sales, improper depreciation claims of Rs. 165.48 Crores, and non-business fund diversions exceeding Rs. 367 Crores[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant submitted an unquantified Form-B claim on 08.11.2019 asserting a likelihood of heavy tax demands, followed by a letter dated 06.06.2020 stating that while tax demands could not be crystallized, huge liabilities were anticipated[cite: 15]. Post-plan approval, the Appellant crystallized and issued demand notices for AY 2013-14 to 2019-20 on 29.06.2022, 30.06.2022, and 01.07.2022; the approved resolution plan did not allocate payments towards these uncrystallized demands beyond standard operational creditor provisions[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Corporate Debtor was admitted into CIRP on 24.08.2018 in CP (IB)/137 of 2018[cite: 15]. Notices under the Income Tax Act were issued on 25.10.2018[cite: 15]. Appellant submitted Form-B to the RP on 08.11.2019 without a quantified figure[cite: 15]. On 27.05.2020, NCLT Ahmedabad allowed IA No. 672 of 2019 permitting the department to conduct assessments for AY 2013-14 to 2019-20 and directing timely submission of claims to the RP[cite: 15]. Special audit report was received on 02.12.2021[cite: 15]. CoC approved GSEC Ltd.'s resolution plan by an 89.46% majority on 06.01.2022[cite: 15]. NCLT Ahmedabad Bench Court-I approved the resolution plan on 20.06.2022 in IA-160(AHM)/2022[cite: 15]. Appellant issued income tax demand notices subsequently on 29.06.2022, 30.06.2022, and 01.07.2022[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form-B dated 08.11.2019 stating no quantified claim sum and citing multiple pending litigations and potential disallowances[cite: 15]; NCLT order dated 27.05.2020 in IA No. 672 of 2019[cite: 15]; Special Audit Report dated 02.12.2021[cite: 15]; list of creditors published on IBBI website reflecting the department[cite: 15]; and assessment demand notices dated 29.06.2022 to 01.07.2022 issued post-approval of the plan[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench approved the resolution plan on 20.06.2022 in IA-160(AHM)/2022, holding that all past claims not factored into the plan stand extinguished under the clean-slate doctrine laid down in Ghanshyam Mishra[cite: 15]. The Income Tax Department appealed to NCLAT under Section 61, asserting that CIRP Regulation 12 is directory, that Rainbow Papers prohibits rejecting statutory revenue claims for delay, and that under Section 29 and Regulation 36(2)(h), ongoing statutory proceedings must be factored into the Information Memorandum and plan[cite: 15].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an uncrystallized, speculative intimation of potential tax liability submitted in Form-B without a determinative claim figure constitutes a valid 'claim' capable of collation and mandatory inclusion in the Information Memorandum and Resolution Plan under the IBC and CIRP Regulations[cite: 15]; (ii) Whether statutory tax claims crystallized via assessment orders and demand notices passed after the approval of a resolution plan by the CoC and Adjudicating Authority can be admitted or enforced against the Corporate Debtor and Successful Resolution Applicant[cite: 15]; (iii) Whether the ratio of State Tax Officer v. Rainbow Papers applies to exempt the Income Tax Department from CIRP claim submission timelines and elevate it to the status of a secured operational creditor[cite: 15].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Punctual adherence to statutory claim timelines is foundational to the corporate insolvency resolution process; an uncrystallized intimation of potential or anticipated liability without a firm, determined amount does not constitute a valid claim for collation by the resolution professional or incorporation into the information memorandum[cite: 15]. Under the 'clean slate' doctrine, once a resolution plan is approved by the Committee of Creditors and sanctioned by the Adjudicating Authority under Section 31(1) of the IBC, all claims not part of the resolution plan stand frozen and permanently extinguished, and no subsequent assessment orders or surprise demand notices can be foisted upon the corporate debtor or successful resolution applicant[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31(1) of the IBC binds all stakeholders, including the Central Government and local tax authorities, to the terms of the approved resolution plan[cite: 15]. As settled in Ghanshyam Mishra, Essar Steel, Jaypee Kensington, and RPS Infrastructure, the dominant statutory objective of the IBC is corporate revival, which mandates that the successful resolution applicant start on a fresh slate without being ambushed by 'hydra-headed' undecided or belated claims[cite: 15]. The 2019 amendment to Section 31 is clarificatory and confirms that unprovided government dues stand extinguished[cite: 15]. Furthermore, as clarified in Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Raman Ispat, the ruling in Rainbow Papers was confined to the express statutory first charge created under Section 48 of the Gujarat Value Added Tax Act, 2003; absent any statutory first-charge provision in the Income Tax Act, 1961, the tax department remains an operational creditor bound by CIRP collation discipline[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized Form-B dated 08.11.2019 and observed that the Appellant stated no fixed sum and characterized the liability as 'tentatively a huge demand'[cite: 15]; that the permission granted by NCLT on 27.05.2020 expressly required timely filing of crystallized claims so as not to derail CIRP timelines[cite: 15]; and that final assessment orders and demand notices were issued between 29.06.2022 and 01.07.2022, well after the CoC approved the plan on 06.01.2022 and the Adjudicating Authority confirmed it on 20.06.2022[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Income Tax Department failed to lodge a quantified and timely claim prior to plan approval; admitting belated assessment demands would undermine the clean slate principle and reopen a finalized resolution; therefore, the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in approving the resolution plan without accommodating the post-approval tax demands[cite: 15].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 977 of 2022 is dismissed with no order as to costs, affirming the order dated 20.06.2022 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Ahmedabad Bench Court-I) in IA-160(AHM)/2022 in CP (IB)/137 of 2018[cite: 15].
summary: The Assistant Commissioner of Income Tax appealed against an NCLT Ahmedabad order approving the resolution plan submitted by the GSEC Ltd. consortium for Diamond Power Infrastructure Ltd., contending that its multi-crore income tax demands for AY 2013-14 to 2019-20 were wrongly omitted from the plan[cite: 15]. The department argued that CIRP claim timelines are directory and that statutory revenue dues cannot be extinguished under the Rainbow Papers doctrine[cite: 15]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that an unquantified Form-B expressing a mere likelihood of heavy demand does not constitute a valid claim for collation[cite: 15]. Reaffirming the 'clean slate' doctrine enunciated in Ghanshyam Mishra and Essar Steel, the Tribunal ruled that tax assessment orders passed after plan approval cannot be enforced against the SRA, and that Rainbow Papers does not apply absent a statutory first charge[cite: 15].

case_title: Superintendent of Stamps & Inspector General of Registration vs. Avil Menezes (Resolution Professional of AMW Autocomponent Ltd.)
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1591 of 2023 & I.A. No. 5750 of 2023
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain, Technical Members Naresh Salecha and Indevar Pandey)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is the Superintendent of Stamps & Inspector General of Registration, Gandhinagar, Gujarat (Statutory Revenue Authority / Operational Creditor) acting through Authorized Officer Vipin Jayantilal Paneri[cite: 16]. The Respondent is Mr. Avil Menezes, Resolution Professional of AMW Autocomponent Limited (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 16]. The Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA) is M/s Steel Strips Wheels Limited[cite: 16]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Demerger of Asia Motor Works Ltd. (transferor) into AMW Motors Ltd. (transferee 1) and AMW Autocomponent Ltd. (transferee 2 / Corporate Debtor) was approved by the Gujarat High Court on 29.08.2012 in CP No. 133 of 2012[cite: 16]. The Collector of Stamps issued an opinion under Section 31 of the Gujarat Stamp Act, 1958 on 29.07.2013 determining stamp duty liabilities of Rs. 7,50,15,130/- and Rs. 5,53,64,009/- on the demerger scheme[cite: 16]. The Corporate Debtor challenged this in Special Civil Application No. 14182 of 2013 (withdrawn on 27.01.2020) and before the Chief Controlling Revenue Authority (dismissed for limitation on 20.04.2020)[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant claimed outstanding stamp duty and penalties aggregating Rs. 15,38,79,179/- (comprising basic stamp duty of Rs. 5,53,64,009/- plus 15% annual penalty and interest)[cite: 16]. The approved Resolution Plan of Steel Strips Wheels Limited provided an allocation of Rs. 2,65,00,000/- under 'Land Payments and Stamp Duty' in full discharge of statutory liabilities[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Indian Overseas Bank initiated Section 7 CIRP against the Corporate Debtor, admitted on 01.09.2020 with moratorium under Section 14[cite: 16]. IRP issued a public announcement inviting claims on 03.09.2020[cite: 16]. Appellant issued an impounding and recovery notice under Sections 33/39(1)(b) on 22.01.2021; RP informed Appellant of CIRP on 17.02.2021[cite: 16]. Appellant issued an order on 20.10.2021 creating a charge in revenue records[cite: 16]. Appellant submitted its claim in Form-F on 23.03.2023 (after an inordinate delay of ~30 months from public announcement and 18 months post-CoC approval)[cite: 16]. Appellant filed IA No. 1092/2023 on 27.09.2023[cite: 16]. NCLT Ahmedabad approved the Resolution Plan in IA No. 692(AHM)/2021 on 12.10.2023[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Gujarat High Court demerger order dated 29.08.2012[cite: 16]; Collector of Stamps adjudication order dated 29.07.2013[cite: 16]; High Court interim and withdrawal orders in SCA No. 14182 of 2013[cite: 16]; public announcement dated 03.09.2020[cite: 16]; Form-F claim submitted on 23.03.2023[cite: 16]; revenue record entry dated 10.05.2022[cite: 16]; and Clauses 1.1, 3.4.4, and 8.2 of the approved Resolution Plan[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench Court-I approved the Resolution Plan of Steel Strips Wheels Limited on 12.10.2023 via IA No. 692(AHM) of 2021, granting exemptions and extinguishing all unpaid pre-approval liabilities not factored into the plan[cite: 16]. The Appellant appealed under Section 61, contending that stamp duty is a mandatory statutory condition for clear property title, that its claim constitutes a secured charge under Rainbow Papers, and that Section 14 moratorium could not bar 2012 pre-CIRP stamp liabilities[cite: 16].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a statutory claim for stamp duty and penalties lodged 30 months after the public announcement and 18 months after CoC approval of a resolution plan can be mandated into the resolution plan[cite: 16]; (ii) Whether the statutory claim of the Stamp Authority qualifies as a 'secured debt' under Sections 3(30) and 3(31) of the IBC relying on the ratio of State Tax Officer v. Rainbow Papers[cite: 16]; (iii) Whether recovery notices and revenue charge creations initiated during the CIRP moratorium violate Section 14 of the IBC, and whether unprovided pre-CIRP statutory liabilities stand extinguished under the 'clean slate' doctrine upon approval of a resolution plan under Section 31(1)[cite: 16].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Punctual submission of claims within the statutory framework of the IBC is essential to the resolution process; an operational creditor or statutory authority cannot enforce an inordinately delayed claim filed after the Committee of Creditors has already deliberated upon and approved the resolution plan[cite: 16]. Under Section 31(1) of the IBC, once a resolution plan is approved by the Adjudicating Authority, the 'clean slate' doctrine applies, permanently extinguishing all past undecided or belated statutory claims and charges not incorporated into the plan, thereby preventing surprise liabilities from burdening the successful resolution applicant[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(1) of the IBC creates an absolute statutory bar prohibiting the continuation of proceedings, enforcement of security interests, or creation of encumbrances against the corporate debtor's assets from the insolvency commencement date[cite: 16]. The non-obstante clause in Section 238 overrides inconsistent state revenue laws, and actions taken to impound or record revenue charges during moratorium are legally ineffective[cite: 16]. The ruling in State Tax Officer v. Rainbow Papers does not apply to universal government claims but is confined to statutes containing an explicit legislative first charge[cite: 16]. As established in Essar Steel, Ghanshyam Mishra, and RPS Infrastructure, the CIRP cannot be an endless process, and unfiled or belated claims cannot pop up like a hydra head to derail a finalized resolution[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that although filing a claim in a wrong form (Form-F instead of Form-B) is directory as per Greater Noida v. Prabhjit Singh Soni, the Appellant failed to provide any plausible justification for waiting 30 months from the public announcement (and over two years from being expressly notified by the RP on 17.02.2021) to file its claim on 23.03.2023[cite: 16]. The record established that the CoC approved the plan long before the claim was submitted, and the plan consciously provided Rs. 2.65 Crores towards land and stamp dues in Clause 1.1, which fell squarely within the commercial wisdom of the CoC[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Resolution Plan satisfied all mandatory requirements under Section 30(2) and CIRP Regulations 36 to 39; the belated claim of the Stamp Authority stood lawfully extinguished beyond the allocation provided in the plan; and the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in approving the resolution plan[cite: 16].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1591 of 2023 is dismissed with no order as to costs, affirming the plan approval order dated 12.10.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Ahmedabad Bench) in IA No. 692 (AHM) of 2021 in CP (IB) No. 185 (AHM) of 2018[cite: 16]. All pending Interlocutory Applications (including I.A. No. 5750 of 2023) are closed[cite: 16].
summary: The Superintendent of Stamps & Inspector General of Registration appealed against an NCLT Ahmedabad order approving the resolution plan submitted by Steel Strips Wheels Limited for AMW Autocomponent Limited[cite: 16]. The Appellant contended that its claim of Rs. 15.38 Crores towards unpaid demerger stamp duty and penalties from 2012 was a statutory charge under Rainbow Papers and could not be extinguished or reduced to the Rs. 2.65 Crores provided in the plan[cite: 16]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that the claim was lodged after an inexcusable delay of 30 months from public announcement and 18 months post-CoC approval[cite: 16]. Reaffirming the clean slate doctrine laid down in Ghanshyam Mishra and Essar Steel, the Tribunal ruled that unprovided belated government claims stand extinguished upon plan approval under Section 31(1) of the IBC[cite: 16].

case_title: Mr. Maneesh Kumar Singh vs. State Bank of India & Ors.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Justice Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Mr. Maneesh Kumar Singh, Suspended Director and Personal Guarantor of Advantage Overseas Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 17]. Respondent No. 1 is State Bank of India (Financial Creditor)[cite: 17]. Respondent No. 2 is the Corporate Debtor represented through Respondent No. 3, Mr. Sunit Jagdishchandra Shah, Interim Resolution Professional (IRP)[cite: 17]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was extended credit facilities by State Bank of India starting with an initial facility of Rs. 10 Crores on 15.03.2013, secured by mortgage and loan-cum-hypothecation agreement dated 23.03.2013 and personal guarantees of Mr. Jijo John and Appellant[cite: 17]. Limits were enhanced to Rs. 51 Crores on 17.12.2014 and further renewed/enhanced to Rs. 6,249.50 Crores vide Letter of Arrangement dated 13.04.2016 and Supplemental Agreement dated 12.05.2016 backed by supplemental personal and corporate guarantees[cite: 17]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtor defaulted on its facilities, resulting in NPA classification on 08.08.2018[cite: 17]. Bank issued a demand notice on 07.01.2019 for Rs. 1,388,87,36,968/- as of 30.11.2018 and filed OA No. 107 of 2019 before DRT for recovery of Rs. 1,408,57,30,754/-[cite: 17]. In Part IV of Form 1 under Section 7, the total default claimed stood at Rs. 2,730,51,66,175.58/- as on 28.02.2023 with date of default specified as 08.08.2018[cite: 17]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA and defaulted on 08.08.2018[cite: 17]. Bank filed OA No. 107 of 2019 on 30.01.2019[cite: 17]. Corporate Debtor requested settlement on 11.03.2020 and 05.05.2020; Bank sanctioned an OTS of Rs. 425 Crores on 05.09.2020[cite: 17]. Corporate Debtor executed undertaking on 11.05.2021[cite: 17]. Parties filed joint application for consent decree before DRT on 25.06.2021, and DRT passed Consent Decree on 26.04.2022[cite: 17]. Corporate Debtor failed to comply with OTS payments, and SBI declared OTS failed on 02.01.2023[cite: 17]. SBI filed Section 7 petition [CP (IB) 496/MB/2023] on 13.03.2023, which NCLT Mumbai admitted on 10.11.2023[cite: 17]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan-cum-Hypothecation Agreements dated 23.03.2013 and 12.05.2016[cite: 17]; Guarantee deeds[cite: 17]; NPA classification records dated 08.08.2018[cite: 17]; OTS sanction letter dated 05.09.2020[cite: 17]; undertaking dated 11.05.2021[cite: 17]; Joint Application dated 25.06.2021 and DRT Consent Decree dated 26.04.2022[cite: 17]; failed OTS letter dated 02.01.2023[cite: 17]; and balance sheets of Corporate Debtor for years ending 31.03.2019 and 31.03.2020 acknowledging outstanding debt[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-IV admitted SBI's Section 7 petition on 10.11.2023 in CP (IB) 496/MB/2023[cite: 17]. Suspended Director appealed to NCLAT via Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1484 of 2023 arguing that default in the OTS schedule occurred on 04.03.2021 within the Section 10A bar period, that the petition was an impermissible execution of a DRT consent decree, and that claims based on the 08.08.2018 default were time-barred[cite: 17].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an application under Section 7 of the IBC is barred by Section 10A where the original default and NPA classification occurred prior to 25.03.2020 (on 08.08.2018), but an interim OTS installment schedule allegedly defaulted during the Section 10A period on 04.03.2021[cite: 17]; (ii) Whether the filing of an application under Section 7 following non-compliance with a DRT Consent Decree is maintainable or barred as an impermissible execution proceeding[cite: 17]; (iii) Whether the Section 7 application filed on 13.03.2023 was barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, in light of balance sheet acknowledgments, written OTS proposals under Section 18, and a subsequent DRT Consent Decree[cite: 17].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory bar under Section 10A of the IBC applies strictly and exclusively to defaults arising on or after 25.03.2020 and does not encompass continuous or preexisting defaults that occurred prior to 25.03.2020; an intervening one-time settlement proposal or installment lapse during the Section 10A window does not shift the foundational date of default or erase the creditor's statutory right to initiate CIRP based on the antecedent default[cite: 17]. Furthermore, written OTS compromise proposals and balance sheet entries operate as valid acknowledgments under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, and a subsequent consent decree passed by a Debt Recovery Tribunal gives rise to a fresh three-year limitation period under the IBC[cite: 17]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 10A and its Explanation expressly clarify that the suspension of CIRP does not apply to any default committed before 25.03.2020[cite: 17]. Following Raghavendra Joshi v. Axis Bank, default in adhering to OTS terms during the Section 10A period does not vitiate an application founded upon a pre-10A default (08.08.2018)[cite: 17]. Under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963, OTS settlement requests made on 11.03.2020 and 05.05.2020 renew the three-year limitation period, and as settled in Kotak Mahindra Bank v. A. Balakrishnan, a DRT decree (passed on 26.04.2022) creates a fresh cause of action with a 3-year limitation window to invoke Section 7[cite: 17]. Contractual failure to sell specific mortgaged properties does not excuse performance where the borrower undertook to meet shortfalls from general sources[cite: 17]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that Part IV of Form 1 explicitly identified the date of default as 08.08.2018, prior to the Section 10A window[cite: 17]; that the Corporate Debtor acknowledged debt in balance sheets up to 31.03.2020 and gave written OTS proposals in March and May 2020[cite: 17]; that the joint application for DRT consent decree was submitted on 25.06.2021 post-10A, and the consent decree was issued on 26.04.2022[cite: 17]; and that SBI's petition filed on 13.03.2023 was well within three years from both the Section 18 acknowledgments and the DRT decree[cite: 17]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 application was founded on a pre-10A default, was filed within statutory limitation as extended by Section 18 of the Limitation Act and the DRT Consent Decree, and was not barred by Section 10A; hence, the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in admitting the Corporate Debtor into CIRP[cite: 17].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1484 of 2023 is dismissed with no order as to costs, affirming the order dated 10.11.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV) in CP (IB) 496/MB/2023 admitting the Section 7 application[cite: 17].
summary: Mr. Maneesh Kumar Singh, Suspended Director and Personal Guarantor of Advantage Overseas Pvt. Ltd., appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 7 CIRP application filed by State Bank of India for a default of Rs. 2,730.51 Crores[cite: 17]. The Appellant contended that default in an interim OTS schedule arose on 04.03.2021, attracting the statutory bar under Section 10A, and that the petition was time-barred and constituted an impermissible execution of a DRT consent decree[cite: 17]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that Section 10A does not cover continuing defaults that commenced prior to 25.03.2020 (dated 08.08.2018)[cite: 17]. The Tribunal ruled that OTS proposals and balance sheets extended limitation under Section 18, and relying on Kotak Mahindra Bank v. A. Balakrishnan, affirmed that a DRT consent decree confers a fresh three-year limitation period[cite: 17].

case_title: Emta Coal Ltd. vs. L&T Finance Ltd. & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Justice Ashok Bhushan, Technical Members Barun Mitra and Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Emta Coal Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 18]. Respondent No. 1 is L&T Finance Ltd. (Original Financial Creditor / Assignor)[cite: 18]. Respondent No. 2 is Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. (Assignee Financial Creditor / Asset Reconstruction Company)[cite: 18]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: L&T Finance Ltd. extended financial debt facilities to the Corporate Debtor[cite: 18]. During the pendency of insolvency proceedings, L&T Finance Ltd. assigned the underlying debt together with all rights, titles, and interests to Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. via a registered Assignment Agreement dated 29.03.2022 under Section 5(1) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002[cite: 18]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: L&T Finance Ltd. claimed a total outstanding default amount of Rs. 74,99,25,691/- from the Corporate Debtor, reckoning the date of default as 15.08.2016[cite: 18]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 7 CIRP application [CP (IB) 634/KB/2020] was filed by L&T Finance Ltd. before NCLT Kolkata on 27.01.2020[cite: 18]. Debt assignment occurred during pendency on 29.03.2022[cite: 18]. Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. filed substitution application IA (IBC) 504/KB/2022[cite: 18]. Corporate Debtor filed impounding application IA (IBC) 1371/KB/2023[cite: 18]. NCLT Kolkata Bench (Court-II) allowed substitution and dismissed the impounding application by common order dated 04.04.2024[cite: 18]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered Assignment Agreement dated 29.03.2022 executed between L&T Finance Ltd. and Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. without any deficiency raised by the Registering Authority[cite: 18]; Section 7 application records asserting Rs. 74.99 Crores default[cite: 18]; and Maharashtra Government Notification dated 06.05.2002 as rescinded by subsequent Notification dated 26.08.2005[cite: 18]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench (Court-II) allowed IA (IBC) 504/KB/2022 substituting Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. as Financial Creditor in place of L&T Finance Ltd., and dismissed IA (IBC) 1371/KB/2023 filed by the Corporate Debtor seeking to impound the Assignment Agreement for alleged stamp duty deficiency under the Maharashtra Stamp Act, 1958[cite: 18]. The Corporate Debtor appealed to NCLAT under Section 61 via Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 895 & 896 of 2024[cite: 18].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an Asset Reconstruction Company is legally entitled under Section 5(2) and Section 5(5) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002 to be substituted in place of the original financial creditor in a pending Section 7 IBC application pursuant to a registered Assignment Agreement[cite: 18]; (ii) Whether an Adjudicating Authority is obligated under Section 33 and Section 35 of the Stamp Act to impound a registered Assignment Agreement relied upon for substitution on an allegation by the corporate debtor of inadequate stamping under state stamp laws[cite: 18].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Upon acquisition of financial assets by an Asset Reconstruction Company under Section 5(1) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, the statutory deeming fiction under Section 5(2) takes full effect, deeming the assignee to be the lender for all legal purposes and entitling it to step into the shoes of the assignor to prosecute pending proceedings[cite: 18]. Where an assignment deed is duly registered without objection by the registering authority, an Adjudicating Authority in summary insolvency proceedings is not required to impound the instrument for alleged stamp deficiency, as inadequate stamping is a curable defect that does not render the document void ab initio[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(1) of the SARFAESI Act commences with a non-obstante clause overriding contrary provisions in any other law or agreement[cite: 18]. Under Section 5(2), on acquisition of financial assets, all rights of the financial institution vest in the asset reconstruction company, and Section 5(4) read with Section 5(5) expressly mandates that pending legal proceedings shall not abate but shall be continued, prosecuted, and enforced by the assignee[cite: 18]. As affirmed in Pawan Kumar Manguturam Bairagra and the Supreme Court 7-Judge Bench curative ruling in Bhaskar Raju & Brothers, inadequate stamping does not invalidate an agreement or bar its prima facie recognition for substitution[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the Assignment Agreement dated 29.03.2022 was duly registered before the Registering Authority without any reference or determination of deficiency under stamp law, establishing a valid prima facie transfer of the debt of Rs. 74.99 Crores[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. was fully entitled by statutory deeming fiction under Section 5(2) of the SARFAESI Act to be substituted in the pending Section 7 application, and the dismissal of the Corporate Debtor's application for impounding was lawful and sound[cite: 18].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 895 & 896 of 2024 are dismissed with no order as to costs, affirming the order dated 04.04.2024 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Kolkata Bench, Court-II) in IA (IBC) 504/KB/2022 and IA (IBC) 1371/KB/2023 in CP (IB) 634/KB/2020[cite: 18].
summary: Emta Coal Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) appealed against an NCLT Kolkata order allowing Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. to substitute L&T Finance Ltd. in a pending Section 7 application for a default of Rs. 74.99 Crores and dismissing the Corporate Debtor's plea to impound the underlying Assignment Agreement dated 29.03.2022 for alleged stamp duty deficiency under the Maharashtra Stamp Act[cite: 18]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that under Section 5(2) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, an asset reconstruction company is deemed to be the lender for all purposes upon acquiring financial assets[cite: 18]. The Tribunal affirmed that because the agreement was duly registered without objection from registering authorities, and since inadequate stamping is a curable defect as settled by the Supreme Court in Bhaskar Raju & Brothers, the NCLT committed no error in allowing substitution and refusing impoundment[cite: 18].

case_title: M/s Delicasy Continental Pvt. Ltd. vs. Competition Commission of India
appeal_number: Competition Appeal (AT) No. 32 of 2022 & IA Nos. 2412, 2414 of 2022 & 1452 of 2023
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain and Technical Member Indevar Pandey)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is M/s Delicasy Continental Pvt. Ltd., an enterprise primarily engaged in the production and export of rice (arrayed as OP-6 before the Commission), through its Director Mr. Ankur Kumar[cite: 19]. The Respondent is the Competition Commission of India (CCI)[cite: 19]. Co-conspirators in the bidding cartel include Austere System Pvt. Ltd. (OP-5 / winning bidder, represented by Director Rahul Gajanan Teni), Yash Solutions (OP-1 / L-1 bidder in other divisions), M/s Toyfort (OP-8), and Fimo Info Solutions Pvt. Ltd. (OP-7)[cite: 19]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Department of Agriculture, Government of Uttar Pradesh floated public e-tenders for soil sample testing across several administrative divisions under the Government's Soil Health Card Scheme for FY 2017-18 and FY 2018-19, including Tender No. 2018_AGRUP_210583_1 (Moradabad) and Tender No. 2018_AGRUP_212591_1 (Bareilly), as well as 2018 tenders for Meerut and Saharanpur divisions[cite: 19]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Rather than independent competitive bidding, participating entities formed a bid-rigging cartel[cite: 19]. Austere Systems won the Meerut and Saharanpur tenders in 2018 while Appellant acted as an unlawful cover bidder[cite: 19]. CCI imposed a cease-and-desist order under Section 27(a) and levied a 5% penalty under Section 27(b) on average annual turnover, totaling Rs. 32,99,405/- on the Appellant company and Rs. 19,307/- on its Director Mr. Ankur Kumar under Section 48[cite: 19]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Commission received an information/complaint alleging tender bid-rigging on 07.08.2018[cite: 19]. Prima facie investigation was directed under Section 26(1) on 30.01.2020[cite: 19]. The Director General (DG) submitted the Investigation Report on 08.04.2021 (considered by CCI on 08.06.2021)[cite: 19]. Appellant was added as Opposite Party No. 6 on 08.06.2021[cite: 19]. CCI passed its final order under Section 27 on 04.04.2022[cite: 19]. Appellant appealed to NCLAT under Section 53B via Competition Appeal (AT) No. 32 of 2022[cite: 19]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: DG Investigation Report dated 08.04.2021[cite: 19]; sworn statements of Appellant's Directors (Mr. Ankur Kumar and Smt. Rajesh Rani) admitting absence of prior soil testing experience, lack of operational familiarity, and price-fixing in consultation with Austere Systems[cite: 19]; sworn statement of Mr. Rahul Teni (Director of Austere Systems) admitting unauthorized sub-contracting and cover arrangements[cite: 19]; three conflicting and fabricated versions of an unverified MoU between Appellant and Austere Systems created post-investigation notice[cite: 19]; fake experience certificates issued by Austere Systems to qualify Appellant[cite: 19]; and Appellant's GST registration suspiciously listing the office of the Deputy Director of Agriculture, Saharanpur as its principal place of business[cite: 19]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CCI held on 04.04.2022 that the Appellant colluded with Austere Systems to manipulate tenders for Meerut and Saharanpur in 2018 by submitting non-competitive cover bids, violating Section 3(3)(c) and 3(3)(d) read with Section 3(1), and imposed a 5% penalty on total average turnover under Section 27(b)[cite: 19]. The Appellant appealed to NCLAT under Section 53B, contending lack of agreement or meeting of minds, that past sub-contracting ties did not prove bid rigging, and that under the Supreme Court's Excel Crop Care doctrine, penalty could only be computed on 'relevant turnover' from soil testing (which was Nil)[cite: 19].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an enterprise engaged in a completely unrelated trade (rice export) that participates in public procurement tenders with fabricated experience certificates, unverified MoUs, and prices fixed in consultation with a rival bidder is guilty of collusive bid-rigging and market sharing under Section 3(3)(c) and Section 3(3)(d) read with Section 3(1) of the Competition Act, 2002[cite: 19]; (ii) Whether the 'relevant turnover' doctrine laid down by the Supreme Court in Excel Crop Care applies to mandate a zero penalty where an entity providing fraudulent cover bids in a public tender has zero prior turnover in the specialized market under investigation[cite: 19]; (iii) Whether a cover bidder playing an ancillary or secondary role in a procurement cartel is entitled to a proportionate reduction in the penalty percentage under Section 27(b) of the Act[cite: 19].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An enterprise that colludes with a competitor by submitting accommodating cover bids, utilizing fabricated qualification certificates, and coordinating price quotations to ensure the competitor's success in public tenders violates Section 3(3)(d) read with Section 3(1) of the Competition Act, 2002; the existence of an anti-competitive cartel does not require formal direct contracts and can be conclusively established through circumstantial evidence, common control, and admissions of price coordination[cite: 19]. Furthermore, where an infringing party acts as a first-time cover bidder in a public procurement cartel and possesses zero turnover in the specific product market, the doctrine of 'relevant turnover' cannot be applied pedantically to yield a nil penalty, but the enterprise's secondary supporting role warrants a mitigated penalty percentage under the principle of proportionality[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(3)(d) of the Act establishes a statutory presumption that any agreement or practice resulting in bid rigging or collusive bidding causes an appreciable adverse effect on competition[cite: 19]. As clarified in Excel Crop Care and subsequent jurisprudence, while Section 27(b) penalties must respect proportionality, adopting a pedantic interpretation of 'relevant turnover' that calculates fines exclusively from tender proceeds would frustrate the legislative deterrence of the Act by allowing entities that deliberately submit fraudulent cover bids to operate with total antitrust immunity[cite: 19]. Under Section 27(b), the Commission possesses statutory discretion to levy penalties up to 10% of turnover, and where a bidder acts solely as a passive instrument in a supporting capacity, the penalty must reflect its relative culpability compared to primary cartel leaders[cite: 19]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the sworn depositions and found that Appellant's directors had no knowledge of soil testing science, had never visited their alleged facility, and admitted that financial bids were determined in coordination with Austere Systems[cite: 19]; that three inconsistent versions of the sub-contract MoU were fabricated and emailed by Austere Systems during the investigation[cite: 19]; that fake experience certificates were generated to simulate eligibility[cite: 19]; and that only three bidders participated in the 2018 tenders[cite: 19]. The evidence established that Appellant was a captive cover bidder, and since its specialized soil testing turnover was nil, adopting total turnover for Section 27(b) was legally sound[cite: 19]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The finding of guilt under Section 3(3)(c) and 3(3)(d) read with Section 3(1) and the Section 27(a) cease-and-desist directions are fully justified, but because the Appellant performed an ancillary supporting role by providing cover bids, the penalty under Section 27(b) is proportionately reduced from 5% to 3% of its average annual turnover[cite: 19].
operative_order: Competition Appeal (AT) No. 32 of 2022 is partly allowed: (1) The order of the Competition Commission of India holding the Appellant guilty of contravening Section 3(3)(c) and Section 3(3)(d) read with Section 3(1) of the Competition Act, 2002 and issuing cease-and-desist directions under Section 27(a) is upheld[cite: 19]; (2) The penalty imposed on the Appellant under Section 27(b) of the Act is reduced from 5% to 3% of the average annual turnover for the relevant three preceding financial years[cite: 19]; and (3) All pending Interlocutory Applications (IA Nos. 2412, 2414 of 2022 and 1452 of 2023) stand disposed of with no order as to costs[cite: 19].
summary: M/s Delicasy Continental Pvt. Ltd., a rice export firm, appealed under Section 53B of the Competition Act against a CCI order holding it guilty of collusive bid-rigging under Section 3(3)(c) and 3(3)(d) read with Section 3(1) and imposing a 5% penalty on total turnover for submitting fraudulent cover bids in UP Government soil testing tenders won by Austere Systems[cite: 19]. Appellant argued that lack of explicit agreements and zero relevant turnover in soil testing precluded penalty under Excel Crop Care[cite: 19]. Partly allowing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench affirmed the finding of cartelization based on fabricated MoUs, fake experience certificates, and admitted price consultation[cite: 19]. The Tribunal held that adopting relevant turnover was inapplicable where it would grant total immunity to cover bidders, but reduced the penalty to 3% in view of Appellant's secondary supporting role[cite: 19].

case_title: Carestream Health India Private Limited vs. Seaview Mercantile LLP
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Yogesh Khanna and Technical Member Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Carestream Health India Private Limited (Operational Creditor/proposed licensee)[cite: 21]. The Respondent is Seaview Mercantile LLP (Corporate Debtor/licensor)[cite: 21]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: On 07.05.2019, the parties entered into a 'Without Prejudice' Letter of Intent (WP-LOI) for leasing Unit No. 702 in the Silver Metropolis building in Mumbai[cite: 21]. The Appellant paid a security deposit of Rs. 25,68,280/- intended as a deposit ensuring execution of a leave and license agreement[cite: 21]. Upon due diligence, Appellant claimed the premises were ineligible for IT/ITES/STPI registration under the Maharashtra IT/ITES Policy 2015, whereas Respondent maintained that the premises were compliant, that subsequent licensee Reliance Nippon obtained certification, and that Clause 28 of the LOI allowed forfeiture unless termination was grounded strictly on title defects[cite: 21]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant claimed a default of Rs. 29,31,193/- (comprising the principal security deposit refund of Rs. 25,68,280/- plus interest at 18% p.a. amounting to Rs. 3,37,248/-) due upon cancellation of the LOI[cite: 21]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The LOI was executed on 07.05.2019[cite: 21]. Appellant sought cancellation and refund via email on 04.06.2019, followed by reminders on 18.06.2019 and 27.08.2019, and a legal notice on 14.11.2019[cite: 21]. A demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC was issued on 10.02.2020[cite: 21]. The Respondent replied on 17.02.2020 disputing the claim and asserting its contractual right to forfeit the deposit alongside counterclaims for unpaid license fees[cite: 21]. The Section 9 petition [CP (IB) No. 765/IBC/MB/2020] was filed on 20.02.2020[cite: 21]. NCLT Mumbai Bench-V dismissed the petition on 24.03.2023[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: 'Without Prejudice' Letters of Intent (disputed versions Annexure A3 dated 07.05.2019 and undated Annexure A5) containing Clause 28 governing title due diligence and deposit forfeiture[cite: 21]; bank proof of Rs. 25,68,280/- deposit payment[cite: 21]; cancellation email dated 04.06.2019[cite: 21]; Section 8 Demand Notice dated 10.02.2020 and Section 8 notice reply dated 17.02.2020 raising pre-existing dispute and claiming Rs. 23.97 Lakhs occupation fee and Rs. 1.07 Crores vacancy damages[cite: 21]; and Maharashtra IT/ITES Policy documentation[cite: 21]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-V dismissed CP (IB) No. 765/IBC/MB/2020 on 24.03.2023, holding that the Appellant did not qualify as an Operational Creditor because refund of a security deposit does not arise from the provision of goods or services[cite: 21]. The Appellant appealed before NCLAT under Section 61, relying on Consolidated Construction Consortium Ltd. and Jaipur Trade Expocentre to argue that security deposits bear nexus with operational space services and qualify under Section 5(21)[cite: 21].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a claim for refund of a security deposit paid pursuant to an unconsummated Letter of Intent (LOI) for entering into a leave and license agreement constitutes an 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) of the IBC in the absence of actual provision or receipt of goods or services[cite: 21]; (ii) Whether genuine rival contentions regarding conflicting versions of an LOI, entitlement to forfeit a security deposit under contractual termination clauses, and counterclaims for licensee occupation fees constitute a 'pre-existing dispute' under Mobilox Innovations barring admission under Section 9 of the IBC[cite: 21].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A claim for refund of an advance security deposit paid under an executory Letter of Intent that is terminated prior to the execution of a definitive lease or license agreement does not constitute an 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) of the IBC where no actual goods or services were supplied to or received from the corporate debtor, and no GST was levied to impart the character of a commercial service; moreover, where the corporate debtor establishes plausible contractual grounds for deposit forfeiture and asserts counterclaims for occupation fees prior to the Section 8 demand notice, a bona fide pre-existing dispute exists, precluding initiation of CIRP under Section 9[cite: 21]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(21) of the IBC requires that an operational debt must bear a direct nexus with a 'claim in respect of the provision of goods or services'[cite: 21]. While the Supreme Court in Consolidated Construction Consortium held that the phrase 'in respect of' includes both suppliers and recipients of services, it does not cover an advance security deposit paid merely to secure execution of a future license where no underlying operational service ever commenced[cite: 21]. Unlike Jaipur Trade Expocentre where unpaid license fees attracting GST were held to be operational debts, a refundable security deposit is not an advance license fee and was not subject to GST[cite: 21]. Under Section 9(5)(ii)(d) and Mobilox Innovations, an application must be rejected if the defense raises a plausible contention of a pre-existing dispute that is not spurious, hypothetical, or illusory[cite: 21]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examined the documentary record and established that neither party rendered goods or services to the other; no GST was charged or paid on the deposit; substantial evidentiary conflicts existed regarding whether Annexure A3 or A5 constituted the operative LOI; Clause 28 restricted refunds strictly to defects in title rather than failure to procure regulatory IT/ITES status; and the Respondent had explicitly raised its contractual right to forfeit the deposit and asserted counterclaims exceeding Rs. 1.31 Crores in its Section 8 reply dated 17.02.2020 prior to the filing of the Section 9 application[cite: 21]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The claimed security deposit refund did not fall within the statutory definition of an operational debt under Section 5(21), and the proceedings were further barred by a substantial, documented pre-existing dispute regarding forfeiture; hence, the Adjudicating Authority committed no legal error in dismissing the Section 9 petition[cite: 21].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 579 of 2023 is dismissed with no order as to costs, affirming the order dated 24.03.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai Bench-V) in CP (IB) No. 765/IBC/MB/2020[cite: 21].
summary: Carestream Health India Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order dismissing its Section 9 CIRP application against Seaview Mercantile LLP for default in refunding a Rs. 25.68 Lakh security deposit paid under a Letter of Intent for leasing commercial premises[cite: 21]. Appellant terminated the LOI after finding the premises ineligible for IT/ITES certification, whereas Respondent asserted a right of forfeiture under Clause 28 and counterclaimed for occupation fees[cite: 21]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that a security deposit paid under an unconsummated LOI without actual provision or receipt of goods or services does not constitute an operational debt under Section 5(21) of the IBC[cite: 21]. The Tribunal further held that conflicting terms and rival claims over deposit forfeiture established a bona fide pre-existing dispute under Mobilox Innovations barring Section 9 proceedings[cite: 21].

case_title: Anand Sonbhadra (Resolution Professional of Shubhkamna Buildtech Pvt. Ltd.) vs. Gulshan Sethi & Anuradha Sethi
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 810 of 2021 with Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 768 of 2021
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain, Technical Members Naresh Salecha and Indevar Pandey)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Anand Sonbhadra, Resolution Professional of Shubhkamna Buildtech Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 22]. The Respondents are individual unit purchasers: Gulshan Sethi (Respondent in Comp. App. 810/2021) and Anuradha Sethi (Respondent in Comp. App. 768/2021)[cite: 22]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: In 2013-14, Respondent Gulshan Sethi booked 15 residential flats in the Corporate Debtor's 'Tec Homes' and 'Shubhkamana City' projects, paying consideration via cheques and cash, while Respondent Anuradha Sethi booked 6 flats on similar terms[cite: 22]. The Corporate Debtor subsequently defrauded the Respondents by reselling the identical units to third parties, resulting in criminal FIR No. 07/2017 and the arrest of the Corporate Debtor's directors[cite: 22]. To secure bail, the Corporate Debtor entered into a Settlement Agreement dated 14.11.2017 backed by a Board Resolution dated 06.11.2017, substituting and allotting fresh residential units to the Respondents under new agreements to sell executed on 12.01.2018 against their previously paid consideration[cite: 22]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Upon initiation of CIRP, Respondent Gulshan Sethi filed a financial debt claim of Rs. 17,72,75,157/- and Respondent Anuradha Sethi filed a claim of Rs. 3,93,74,137/- based on the original consideration and settlement entitlements, both of which were completely rejected by the Resolution Professional[cite: 22]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Corporate Debtor was admitted into CIRP on 26.11.2018[cite: 22]. Public announcements in Form-A were published on 29.11.2018 and 05.01.2019 fixing the claim submission deadline as 12.01.2019[cite: 22]. Respondents lodged their claims on 26.02.2019, followed up by email on 14.06.2019, which the RP acknowledged on 30.08.2019 before rejecting them[cite: 22]. Respondents filed IA Nos. 524/2019 and 525/2019 before the NCLT[cite: 22]. NCLT New Delhi Bench Court-IV allowed the applications on 23.07.2021[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Original 2013-14 allotment letters, payment receipts, and stamped agreements to sell[cite: 22]; Corporate Debtor's ledger accounts showing financial receipts[cite: 22]; Police FIR No. 07/2017 dated 14.11.2017 and bail settlement terms[cite: 22]; Corporate Debtor Board Resolution dated 06.11.2017 and Settlement Agreement dated 14.11.2017[cite: 22]; substitution allotment letters dated 12.01.2018[cite: 22]; and Clause 8.6(3) of the Resolution Plan governing uncollated unit buyer claims[cite: 22]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Resolution Professional rejected Respondents' claims, categorizing them as speculative investors and asserting that the 2017 settlement was void due to director disqualification by ROC[cite: 22]. NCLT New Delhi Bench Court-IV allowed Respondents' applications on 23.07.2021, directing admission of their claims under Clause 8.6(3) of the Resolution Plan[cite: 22]. The RP appealed to NCLAT under Section 61 via Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) Nos. 810 and 768 of 2021[cite: 22].
legal_issues: (i) Whether allottees who purchase multiple real estate units in bulk or enter into a settlement agreement for substitution of units following builder fraud qualify as 'allottees' and 'financial creditors' under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC, or are to be excluded as mere 'speculative investors'[cite: 22]; (ii) Whether the 'speculative investor' defense articulated in Pioneer Urban Land applies to the collation and admission of claims by the Resolution Professional or is confined strictly to the threshold stage of Section 7 petition admission[cite: 22]; (iii) Whether a settlement agreement and fresh allotment executed by directors subsequently disqualified by the ROC is valid and binding upon the Corporate Debtor under the doctrine of indoor management and Section 176 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 22].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Any allottee who disburses advance funds towards the purchase of a plot, apartment, or commercial unit in a real estate project is statutorily deemed to have disbursed money having the commercial effect of a borrowing under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC, thereby qualifying as a financial creditor; neither the IBC nor RERA draws a distinction between genuine end-use consumers and bulk or commercial purchasers for the purpose of claim admission, and the 'speculative investor' defense is restricted exclusively to assessing bona fides at the stage of Section 7 admission rather than during claim collation by the resolution professional[cite: 22]. Furthermore, under Section 176 of the Companies Act, 2013 and the doctrine of indoor management, acts done by directors towards third-party flat buyers remain valid and binding notwithstanding subsequent discoveries regarding administrative defects or disqualifications in their appointment[cite: 22]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8)(f) Explanation read with Section 2(d), 2(e), and 2(zn) of RERA, 2016 adopts an expansive definition of 'allottee' and 'apartment' that encompasses all persons acquiring units through sale or transfer without excluding multiple-unit holders[cite: 22]. As settled in Pioneer Urban Land, the statutory fiction treating real estate advances as financial debt operates across all allottees[cite: 22]. The judicial caution regarding speculative investors was formulated solely to prevent trigger-happy litigants from abusing Section 7 for coercive debt recovery, and does not disenfranchise legitimate debt claims in CIRP[cite: 22]. Under Section 176 of the Companies Act, 2013, internal management defects and ROC disqualifications cannot invalidate settlement deeds executed by acting directors with innocent third parties[cite: 22]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the continuous chain of documents establishing that Respondents made bona fide monetary disbursements to the Corporate Debtor in 2013-14, which were duly credited in the company's books of accounts[cite: 22]; that the 2017 settlement agreement and 2018 replacement allotments arose directly from a criminal police prosecution to substitute units that the builder had unlawfully resold[cite: 22]; and that the RP failed to establish any commercial agency agreement or substantiate the allegation that receipts represented broker commission[cite: 22]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Respondents are genuine financial creditors whose debts and allotments are legally enforceable; their claims are protected under Section 176 of the Companies Act and must be accommodated in the Resolution Plan pursuant to Clause 8.6(3); hence, the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in directing the admission of their claims[cite: 22].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 810 of 2021 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 768 of 2021 are dismissed with no order as to costs, affirming the order dated 23.07.2021 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench (Court No. IV) in IA Nos. 524/2019 and 525/2019 in CP (IB) No. 1059/ND/2018[cite: 22]. All connected pending Interlocutory Applications are closed[cite: 22].
summary: The Resolution Professional of Shubhkamna Buildtech Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order directing the admission of financial debt claims filed by Gulshan Sethi (Rs. 17.72 Crores) and Anuradha Sethi (Rs. 3.93 Crores) as allottees under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC[cite: 22]. The RP argued that the Respondents were speculative investors who purchased multiple units in bulk, and that their 2017 settlement agreement was invalid because the executing directors were disqualified by the ROC[cite: 22]. Dismissing both appeals, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that the IBC and RERA make no distinction between single and bulk purchasers for claim admission, and that the 'speculative investor' defense applies only to Section 7 admissions, not claim collation[cite: 22]. The Tribunal ruled that under Section 176 of the Companies Act, 2013 and the doctrine of indoor management, the settlement and allotments remained fully binding on the Corporate Debtor[cite: 22].

case_title: Sharon Hills Residents Association & Ors. vs. K. Parameswaran Nair (Resolution Professional of Samson & Sons Builders & Developers Pvt. Ltd.) & Anr.
appeal_number: Comp. App (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 192 of 2023 with Comp. App (AT) (CH) (INS) Nos. 212, 214 & 215 of 2023
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Member Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma and Technical Member Jatindranath Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are registered associations of homebuyers: Sharon Hills Residents Association (Comp. App. 192/2023), Angelwoods Apartments Allottees Association (Comp. App. 214/2023), Orchid Valley Apartment Buyers Association (Comp. App. 215/2023), and Sanctuary Apartment Owner's Association along with NOVA Castle Apartment Owner's Association (Comp. App. 212/2023)[cite: 24]. The Respondent is Mr. K. Parameswaran Nair, Resolution Professional of Samson & Sons Builders & Developers Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor advertised multiple residential projects across Thiruvananthapuram (Sharon Hills Phase I, Angelwoods, Orchid Valley, Sanctuary, and Nova Castle) and executed Sale and Construction Agreements with allottees for residential flats along with undivided land shares[cite: 24]. Homebuyers paid full consideration by 2015 and obtained possession of several units, but the Corporate Debtor failed to execute registered sale deeds[cite: 24]. Instead, between 2013 and 2016, the Corporate Debtor fraudulently mortgaged sold flats and lands to lenders, including a Rs. 15 Crore facility from Kerala Financial Corporation[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Upon loan default, the Corporate Debtor was admitted into CIRP, wherein the Resolution Professional received total creditor claims amounting to Rs. 180 Crores[cite: 24]. Homebuyers constituted 69.72% of the admitted debt, while institutional secured financial creditors held the remaining 30.28%[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 03.11.2021 with Section 14 moratorium in CP(IB)/05/KOB/2021[cite: 24]. Public notice was issued on 15.11.2021[cite: 24]. NCLT excluded 139 days on 01.07.2022, and subsequently granted three timeline extensions: 90 days from 18.09.2022 to 17.12.2022 (IA 269/2022), 60 days to 15.02.2023 (IA 475/2022), and 60 days to 16.04.2023 (IA 67/2023)[cite: 24]. Six project-wise plans were submitted, and on 16.04.2023 the CoC approved three homebuyer plans[cite: 24]. On 15.04.2023, the RP filed IA(IBC)/157/KOB/2023 under Rule 11 of NCLAT Rules seeking a further 90-day extension from 17.04.2023 to 18.07.2023 to complete the process[cite: 24]. NCLT Kochi rejected the extension and ordered liquidation on 26.04.2023[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered association certificates under the 1955 Act[cite: 24]; Sale and Construction Agreements and payment receipts[cite: 24]; RP claim collation sheet showing 69.72% homebuyer majority[cite: 24]; RP Compliance Reports dated 12.04.2023 and 16.04.2023 confirming receipt of 6 project plans and CoC voting approval[cite: 24]; and extension application IA(IBC)/157/KOB/2023[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kochi Bench rejected IA(IBC)/157/KOB/2023 on 26.04.2023, holding that the 330-day statutory ceiling under Section 12 had lapsed, repeated extensions could not be granted under the proviso to Section 12(3), and erroneously observed that no resolution plan was submitted by homebuyers, thereby ordering liquidation[cite: 24]. Homebuyer Associations appealed to NCLAT under Section 61, contending that project-wise resolution plans were approved by the CoC and that pushing a real estate debtor into liquidation would irreversibly prejudice allottees[cite: 24].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the Adjudicating Authority and Appellate Tribunal possess discretion under Rule 11 of NCLAT Rules read with Section 60(5) of the IBC to extend the CIRP timeline beyond the 330-day outer ceiling prescribed under Section 12(3) in exceptional circumstances[cite: 24]; (ii) Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in rejecting an extension application and ordering liquidation based on a factually perverse finding that no resolution plan had been submitted or approved, where project-wise resolution plans submitted by homebuyer associations were actively voted and approved by the CoC[cite: 24]; (iii) Whether liquidation should be avoided as a measure of last resort in real estate corporate insolvencies to protect the paramount interests of allottee homebuyers[cite: 24].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The 330-day timeline prescribed under Section 12 of the IBC for the completion of the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process is directory and not an inflexible, mandatory guillotine; where an insolvency resolution process has advanced to the final stage of plan submission and approval, delays are not attributable to litigant fault, and viable project-wise resolution plans are actively approved by the Committee of Creditors, the tribunal possesses inherent jurisdiction to grant an extension beyond 330 days to achieve corporate revival and prevent liquidation[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: As authoritatively laid down by the Supreme Court in Committee of Creditors of Essar Steel India Ltd. v. Satish Kumar Gupta, the word 'mandatorily' in the second proviso to Section 12(3) was struck down as arbitrary under Article 14 and an unreasonable restriction under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution[cite: 24]. Corporate resolution is the primary statutory objective of the IBC, whereas liquidation is strictly a measure of last resort[cite: 24]. In real estate developer insolvencies, shutting down the process prematurely inflicts irreparable harm upon allottee homebuyers who have invested life savings[cite: 24]. Following Flat Buyers Association Winter Hills and Whispering Tower, tribunals must exercise flexibility to grant short extensions to salvage projects[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the record and established that the Adjudicating Authority's finding that no resolution plan was submitted was contrary to evidence, as the RP's Compliance Report dated 12.04.2023 and voting minutes of 16.04.2023 confirmed that six plans were received and three homebuyer plans were approved by the CoC[cite: 24]. Furthermore, homebuyers comprised 69.72% of total claims, procedural delays arose from complex landlord negotiations and secured creditor deliberations, and the CIRP had reached the cusp of implementation[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The dismissal of the extension application and the consequential liquidation direction were unsustainable; in the interest of all stakeholders, a final extension of 90 days from 17.04.2023 was warranted to enable the Resolution Professional and CoC to conclude the process[cite: 24].
operative_order: Comp. App (AT) (CH) (INS) Nos. 192, 212, 214, and 215 of 2023 are allowed, and the impugned order dated 26.04.2023 passed by NCLT Kochi Bench in IA(IBC)/157/KOB/2023 in CP(IB)/05/KOB/2021 is quashed[cite: 24]. IA(IBC)/157/KOB/2023 is allowed and an extension of 90 days from 17.04.2023 is granted to the Resolution Professional to complete the insolvency resolution proceedings, with a strict direction that no further extensions shall be granted[cite: 24]. All connected pending Interlocutory Applications are closed with no order as to costs[cite: 24].
summary: Registered Homebuyer Associations across multiple real estate projects appealed against an NCLT Kochi order rejecting a 90-day CIRP extension application in IA(IBC)/157/KOB/2023 and directing liquidation of Samson & Sons Builders & Developers Pvt. Ltd. under Section 12 of the IBC[cite: 24]. The NCLT had reasoned that the 330-day outer ceiling had lapsed and recorded that no resolution plan was submitted[cite: 24]. Allowing the appeals, the NCLAT Chennai Bench held that the NCLT's finding was contrary to the record, which proved that six project plans were received and three were approved by the CoC[cite: 24]. Relying on Essar Steel v. Satish Kumar Gupta, the Tribunal reaffirmed that the 330-day limit is directory and granted a final 90-day extension to bring the homebuyer resolution plans to fruition[cite: 24].

case_title: Optinova AB vs. Bio-Med Health Care Products Private Ltd.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Justice Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Optinova AB, a company incorporated under the laws of Finland, through its Power of Attorney Holder Mr. Soumen Sanyal (Operational Creditor)[cite: 25]. The Respondent is Bio-Med Health Care Products Private Ltd., a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956 (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 25]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operational Creditor supplied medical tubing to the Corporate Debtor against purchase orders issued from time to time, maintaining a running statement of accounts[cite: 25]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed total outstanding operational debt of EUR 320,406/- (approx. Rs. 2.56 Crores)[cite: 25]. Corporate Debtor asserted that EUR 206,024/- was remitted to a fraudulent bank account due to a cyber fraud, EUR 2,495/- lacked invoices, but admitted an outstanding operational liability of EUR 111,887/- at the time of demand notice, of which EUR 62,222/- (or EUR 41,148/- balance) remained completely unpaid[cite: 25]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: On 14.01.2019, the Corporate Debtor lodged a police complaint with Commissioner of Police, Faridabad regarding third-party cyber fraud[cite: 25]. Operational Creditor issued a Section 8 Demand Notice on 20.02.2019 demanding Rs. 2.56 Crores[cite: 25]. Corporate Debtor replied on 01.03.2019 raising a notice of dispute citing the cyber fraud and police complaint[cite: 25]. Operational Creditor filed a Section 9 application [C.P. (IB) No. 323/Chd/HP/2019] before NCLT Chandigarh on 22.05.2019[cite: 25]. NCLT Chandigarh Bench dismissed the Section 9 petition on 08.09.2022[cite: 25]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Purchase orders, invoices, and running ledger accounts showing supplied medical tubing[cite: 25]; Axis Bank international transfer confirmation receipts showing remittance of EUR 206,024/- to Chase Bank in the USA instead of Nordea Bank[cite: 25]; spoofed phishing emails sent from fake domains <optimova.com> and <optiinova.com> instead of the official domain <optinova.com>[cite: 25]; police complaint dated 14.01.2019 filed against unknown third-party fraudsters[cite: 25]; Section 8 Demand Notice dated 20.02.2019 and reply dated 01.03.2019 acknowledging an unpaid balance of EUR 111,887/- to be paid in monthly installments of EUR 10,000/-[cite: 25]; and Respondent's reply affidavit acknowledging an admitted unpaid debt of EUR 62,222/-[cite: 25]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh Bench dismissed C.P. (IB) No. 323/Chd/HP/2019 on 08.09.2022 under Section 9(5), holding that the police complaint dated 14.01.2019 lodged prior to the Section 8 notice constituted a pre-existing dispute regarding the operational debt[cite: 25]. The Operational Creditor appealed to NCLAT under Section 61, contending that a third-party cyber fraud does not constitute an inter-se dispute between the contracting parties, and that an admitted unpaid operational debt of EUR 111,887/- exceeded the Section 4 threshold[cite: 25].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a cyber fraud perpetrated by an unknown third party resulting in payment into a fraudulent bank account, and a prior police complaint lodged against such unknown persons, constitutes a bona fide 'pre-existing dispute' inter se between the operational creditor and the corporate debtor under Section 8(2) and Section 9(5)(ii)(d) of the IBC[cite: 25]; (ii) Whether an admitted unpaid operational debt balance exceeding the statutory threshold under Section 4 warrants initiation of CIRP under Section 9, even if a portion of the total claimed amount is entangled in third-party cyber fraud[cite: 25]; (iii) Whether negligent transfer of funds into an unauthorized third-party bank account pursuant to spoofed phishing emails operates as a legal discharge of the corporate debtor's payment obligation to the operational creditor[cite: 25].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Sections 8 and 9 of the IBC read with the Mobilox doctrine, a 'pre-existing dispute' must be a genuine, bona fide dispute existing inter se between the operational creditor and the corporate debtor regarding the quality, provision, or payment of goods or services; the victimization of a corporate debtor by an unknown third-party cyber fraud and the lodging of a police complaint against unidentified perpetrators does not constitute a dispute inter se between the contracting parties, nor does it extinguish the corporate debtor's liability to discharge the operational debt directly to the creditor[cite: 25]. Where an undisputed portion of the operational debt remains due, payable, and unpaid, and exceeds the statutory threshold under Section 4, the Adjudicating Authority must admit the Section 9 application[cite: 25]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The test formulated in Mobilox Innovations v. Kirusa Software requires the tribunal to ascertain whether there is an active, plausible dispute between the operational creditor and the corporate debtor[cite: 25]. A third-party fraud complaint is outside the bilateral commercial relationship and cannot be weaponized as a spurious defense to evade statutory insolvency obligations[cite: 25]. Remittance to a wrong account based on careless reliance on spoofed domain names (<optimova.com> or <optiinova.com>) does not constitute valid payment or commercial discharge under Section 8(2)(b)[cite: 25]. Furthermore, under Manipal Media Network and S.S. Engineers, once an undisputed liability above the Section 4 threshold (EUR 111,887/- or EUR 62,222/-) remains unpaid, the mandatory conditions of Section 9(5)(i) are satisfied[cite: 25]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the police complaint dated 14.01.2019 was lodged exclusively against unknown third parties without naming or implicating the Operational Creditor as an accused[cite: 25]; that the Corporate Debtor failed to exercise due diligence by acting on unverified emails originating from unauthorized domain names differing from <optinova.com>[cite: 25]; that the Operational Creditor never received the sum of EUR 206,024/- in its legitimate accounts[cite: 25]; and that the Corporate Debtor explicitly acknowledged in its reply to the demand notice and in court affidavits an undisputed unpaid debt of EUR 111,887/- (later acknowledged at EUR 62,222/-), which comfortably exceeded the prevailing Section 4 threshold[cite: 25]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed an error in treating the third-party cyber fraud as an inter-se pre-existing dispute; the operational debt was admitted, due, and unpaid above the threshold limit, warranting the setting aside of the dismissal and granting a conditional 30-day window for payment via Demand Draft failing which CIRP commences automatically[cite: 25].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1359 of 2022 is allowed and the impugned order dated 08.09.2022 passed by NCLT Chandigarh Bench in C.P. (IB) No. 323/Chd/HP/2019 is set aside[cite: 25]. The Corporate Debtor is granted liberty to release payment of the outstanding operational debt as per mutually agreed terms by way of Demand Draft in favour of the Operational Creditor within 30 days from the uploading of the order, failing which the Corporate Debtor shall come under the rigours of CIRP upon expiry of the said 30-day period, with no order as to costs[cite: 25].
summary: Optinova AB, a Finnish manufacturer of medical tubing, appealed against an NCLT Chandigarh order dismissing its Section 9 CIRP petition against Bio-Med Health Care Products Pvt. Ltd. for default of EUR 320,406/- (Rs. 2.56 Crores)[cite: 25]. The NCLT had held that a prior police complaint lodged by the Corporate Debtor regarding an alleged cyber fraud (wherein EUR 206,024/- was remitted to a fraudulent US bank account) constituted a pre-existing dispute[cite: 25]. Setting aside the dismissal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that a police complaint against unknown third parties does not constitute a bona fide dispute inter se between the operational creditor and the corporate debtor under Mobilox Innovations[cite: 25]. The Tribunal held that remitting funds to a wrong account due to email spoofing did not discharge the liability, and because the Corporate Debtor acknowledged an undisputed balance exceeding the Section 4 threshold, the debtor was directed to pay within 30 days via Demand Draft, failing which CIRP would automatically commence[cite: 25].

case_title: Oriental Carbon & Chemicals Ltd. vs. OCCL Limited
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Yogesh Khanna and Technical Member Ajai Das Mehrotra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Oriental Carbon & Chemicals Limited (Demerged Company), a publicly listed company on NSE and BSE engaged in manufacturing chemicals and investments[cite: 26]. The Respondent is OCCL Limited (Resulting Company), a wholly owned subsidiary of the Appellant incorporated in Gujarat in 2022[cite: 26]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The parties formulated a Scheme of Arrangement of Demerger under Sections 230 to 232 of the Companies Act, 2013 to transfer and vest the chemical demerged undertaking from the Appellant to the Respondent on a going concern basis[cite: 26]. The Scheme defined 'Appointed Date' as the Effective Date or such other date as decided by the Boards of both companies, with 'Effective Date' defined as the date on which the last condition precedent under Clause 19 (regulatory approvals, shareholder/creditor sanctions, and ROC filing) was fulfilled[cite: 26]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; this is a company scheme of arrangement under corporate reorganization provisions rather than an insolvency default proceeding[cite: 26]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Demerged Company secured stock exchange no-objections under SEBI LODR Regulation 37 and approved the Scheme through requisite majorities of shareholders and creditors in company application C.A. (CAA) No. 1/NCLT/AHM/2023[cite: 26]. Petition C.P. (CAA) 22/NCLT/AHM/2023 was filed for sanction[cite: 26]. NCLT Ahmedabad Bench sanctioned the Scheme on 10.04.2024 but unilaterally altered the Appointed Date from the contractually agreed Effective Date to the date of pronouncement of its order (10.04.2024)[cite: 26]. 5.
