FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Scheme of Arrangement (Annexure A-5) defining 'Appointed Date' and Clause 19 'Conditions Precedent'[cite: 26]; Stock Exchange No-Objection letters under SEBI LODR Regulation 37[cite: 26]; Regional Director, ROC, and statutory authority reports confirming no objections or pending investigations under Sections 210-227[cite: 26]; shareholder and creditor voting approval resolutions[cite: 26]; MCA General Circular No. 09/2019[cite: 26]; and additional affidavit dated 07.03.2024[cite: 26]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench sanctioned the Scheme on 10.04.2024, but invoking Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 and relying on Sterlite Ports Ltd., altered the Appointed Date to the date of its pronouncement, holding that effective dates cannot be kept open[cite: 26]. The Demerged Company appealed to NCLAT under Section 421 challenging solely this modification as an unlawful interference with the commercial wisdom of shareholders and creditors[cite: 26].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the National Company Law Tribunal has the statutory jurisdiction or discretion under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 to unilaterally alter the 'Appointed Date' agreed upon by the amalgamating/demerging companies and approved by their shareholders and creditors[cite: 26]; (ii) Whether the company court's jurisdiction in sanctioning a scheme of arrangement is purely supervisory—akin to an umpire ensuring procedural and statutory compliance—or extends to an appellate review of the commercial terms agreed upon by stakeholders[cite: 26].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The jurisdiction of the Company Tribunal in sanctioning a scheme of arrangement under corporate law is strictly supervisory and not appellate; once all statutory requirements, procedural meetings, and regulatory compliances are satisfied, and the scheme is not contrary to law, public policy, or unconscionable, the tribunal has no jurisdiction to sit in appeal over the commercial wisdom of the shareholders and creditors who approved the scheme with their eyes open[cite: 26]. The tribunal cannot unilaterally modify the contractually agreed 'Appointed Date' absent compelling reasons, as altering the appointed date disrupts financial calculations, tax assessments, and commercial arrangements approved by stakeholders[cite: 26]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: As established by the Supreme Court in Miheer H. Mafatlal v. Mafatlal Industries Ltd. and Hindustan Lever, the company court acts like an umpire in a game of cricket to verify that parties act within statutory rules, leaving how the game is best played to the commercial judgment of the parties[cite: 26]. Under Sections 230 to 232 of the Companies Act, 2013 and MCA Circular No. 09/2019, parties are fully entitled to define the Appointed Date with reference to an event or Effective Date[cite: 26]. Following Accelyst Solutions and Shree Balaji Cinevision, any judicial modification of the Appointed Date throws financial accounting into disarray and is legally unwarranted where no stakeholder or regulator opposed the date proposed in the scheme[cite: 26]. The NCLT's reliance on Rule 11 and Sterlite Ports was misplaced because in Sterlite Ports the scheme itself conferred express discretion upon the tribunal to fix an alternate date, and even there the appellate tribunal retained the scheme's original date[cite: 26]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the record and found that the Scheme (Clause 19) explicitly linked the Appointed Date to the Effective Date upon completion of conditions precedent; that all statutory bodies, ROC, RD, stock exchanges, and 100% of voting shareholders and creditors approved the scheme as drawn; that no investigation or winding-up proceedings were pending against either company; and that the NCLT assigned no cogent, justifiable reason for overriding the agreed date[cite: 26]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT exceeded its supervisory jurisdiction by replacing the agreed Appointed Date with the date of order pronouncement; the modification is legally unsustainable, and the Appointed Date as originally stipulated in the Scheme must be restored[cite: 26].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 144 of 2024 is allowed: the impugned order dated 10.04.2024 passed by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench in CP(CAA) 22/NCLT/AHM/2023 is modified to the extent that the Appointed Date shall be the date as fixed under the Scheme (the Effective Date as defined in Clause 19) and not the date of pronouncement of the NCLT order[cite: 26]. All pending Interlocutory Applications are disposed of with no order as to costs[cite: 26].
summary: Oriental Carbon & Chemicals Ltd. appealed under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 against an NCLT Ahmedabad order sanctioning its demerger scheme with wholly owned subsidiary OCCL Ltd., challenging the tribunal's unilateral modification of the 'Appointed Date' from the contractually agreed Effective Date to the date of pronouncement of the sanction order[cite: 26]. Allowing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench relied on the Supreme Court's landmark rulings in Miheer H. Mafatlal and Hindustan Lever to hold that the tribunal's role in sanctioning schemes is strictly supervisory, acting as an umpire rather than an appellate authority over commercial wisdom[cite: 26]. The Tribunal held that altering the appointed date without cogent reasons disrupts financial calculations and restored the Appointed Date originally agreed upon by the shareholders and creditors under the Scheme[cite: 26].

case_title: Royal India Corporation Limited vs. Nandkishor Vishnupant Deshpande (Resolution Professional for Royal Refinery Pvt. Ltd.) & Ors.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain and Technical Member Ajai Das Mehrotra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Royal India Corporation Limited (RICL), a public company dealing in bullion trading[cite: 27]. Respondent No. 1 is Mr. Nandkishor Vishnupant Deshpande, Resolution Professional of Royal Refinery Private Limited (Corporate Debtor / RRPL)[cite: 27]. Respondents Nos. 2 and 3 are Mr. Vishal Choudhary and Mr. Gaurav Panwar (Suspended Directors of the Corporate Debtor)[cite: 27]. Respondent No. 4 is Mr. Manish Panwar (Statutory/Internal Auditor)[cite: 27]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was engaged in bullion trading, importing gold under advance authorization and selling gold locally and for export[cite: 27]. In May 2019, the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI) raided the Corporate Debtor and related entities, finding that RRPL was a front company run by Mr. Manoj Kumar Babulal Punamiya (promoter and substantial shareholder holding over 30% alongside his wife in Appellant RICL), who diverted duty-free gold into the domestic market and fulfilled export obligations with non-gold alloys[cite: 27]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: DRI search records revealed that as on 20.05.2019, an outstanding balance of Rs. 1,58,07,56,469/- was due from Appellant RICL to Corporate Debtor RRPL across three irregular ledger accounts[cite: 27]. Between 27.07.2019 and 27.08.2019 (post-raid and prior to CIRP admission on 13.11.2019), fictitious reverse sales of gold by RICL to RRPL were entered in books without physical inventory, reducing the payable balance on paper to Rs. 31,01,83,022/- to siphon value and defraud creditors[cite: 27]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: DRI search conducted in May 2019, ceasing operations[cite: 27]. Common DRI Show Cause Notice issued under Section 124 of Customs Act on 21.11.2019[cite: 27]. CIRP commenced against RRPL on 13.11.2019 upon a Section 9 petition by Raksha Bullion[cite: 27]. The RP filed IA No. 1266 of 2020 under Section 66 read with Section 26 of the IBC in 2020[cite: 27]. Customs penalty order passed on 04.02.2021 confirming front-company operations[cite: 27]. NCLT Mumbai Bench allowed the application on 07.01.2021, directing Appellant to refund Rs. 1,19,08,05,762/-[cite: 27]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: DRI search panchnamas and seized unaudited ledgers as of May 2019 showing Rs. 158.07 Crores due from RICL[cite: 27]; custom adjudication order dated 04.02.2021 and DRI SCN dated 21.11.2019 detailing common promoter control by Manoj Punamiya[cite: 27]; shareholding pattern showing Punamiya's 30% holding in RICL[cite: 27]; fabricated book entries dated 27.07.2019 to 27.08.2019 claiming gold sales from a jeweler to a refinery[cite: 27]; absence of physical gold bullion inventory during DRI searches and RP takeover in November 2019[cite: 27]; and admission by statutory auditor Respondent No. 4 that books of accounts were suppressed[cite: 27]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench allowed IA No. 1266 of 2020 on 07.01.2021, holding the reverse sales to be fraudulent transactions under Section 66 and directing Appellant to contribute Rs. 1,19,08,05,762/- back to the Corporate Debtor's account[cite: 27]. The Appellant appealed to NCLAT under Section 61, contending that Section 66 does not apply to third parties, that Regulation 35A was not observed, that no mens rea was established, and that legitimate sales reduced its dues to Rs. 31.01 Crores[cite: 27].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the Adjudicating Authority has statutory power under Section 66(1) of the IBC to direct 'any person'—including third-party corporate entities and related parties—to make contribution to the assets of the corporate debtor for participating in and benefiting from fraudulent trading transactions[cite: 27]; (ii) Whether establishment of criminal mens rea or dishonest intent is an indispensable prerequisite to trigger liability for fraudulent transactions under Section 66 of the Code[cite: 27]; (iii) Whether fictitious reverse book entries engineered between connected companies without physical movement of inventory to artificially reduce an admitted book liability can be avoided as fraudulent transactions under Section 66[cite: 27].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 66(1) of the IBC, where the business of a corporate debtor is carried on with intent to defraud creditors or for any fraudulent purpose, the Adjudicating Authority possesses comprehensive statutory authority to order 'any person' who was knowingly a party to such transactions to make contribution to the assets of the corporate debtor; this liability is not confined to the directors or officers of the debtor company but extends to affiliated entities, related beneficiaries, and third parties who actively participated in or benefited from the fraud[cite: 27]. Fictitious paper book entries showing reverse sales without physical inventory executed to extinguish pre-existing liabilities constitute fraudulent trading under Section 66, and civil recovery under insolvency law does not require proving subjective criminal mens rea once the objective purpose to defraud creditors is evident from the transactional records[cite: 27]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 66(1) employs the expansive phrase 'any persons who were knowingly parties to the carrying on of the business in such manner'[cite: 27]. Following NCLAT and Supreme Court rulings in Tridhaatu Kirti Developers LLP and Phoenix ARC v. Spade Financial Services, Section 66 provides an independent remedy to recover assets diverted through sham transactions[cite: 27]. Appellant's reliance on Gluckrich Capital is misplaced as that decision concerned transit anticipatory bail in criminal law and does not restrict Section 66[cite: 27]. Furthermore, Usha Ananthasubramanian dealt with Section 339 of the Companies Act, 2013 regarding independent heads of unrelated organizations, whereas here the debtor and appellant were proven front entities under common beneficial control[cite: 27]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examined the DRI search records and customs findings establishing that both companies were controlled and funded by Mr. Manoj Punamiya; that as on 20.05.2019, RICL owed Rs. 158.07 Crores to RRPL under three unusual ledgers[cite: 27]; that subsequent to DRI raids when operations were paralyzed, RICL purported to sell gold to a non-functioning refinery to bring down its liability to Rs. 31 Crores[cite: 27]; and that neither the DRI nor the RP found any physical bullion inventory or genuine commercial records supporting the alleged transactions[cite: 27]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The book entries reducing Appellant's liability from Rs. 158 Crores to Rs. 31 Crores were fraudulent devices designed to defraud the creditors of the Corporate Debtor, and the Adjudicating Authority acted within jurisdiction in directing the Appellant to contribute Rs. 119.08 Crores to the Corporate Debtor under Section 66(1)[cite: 27].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 137 of 2021 is dismissed with no order as to costs, affirming the order dated 07.01.2021 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench in IA No. 1266 of 2020 in CP (IB) No. 2556/MB/2019[cite: 27]. All pending Interlocutory Applications are closed[cite: 27].
summary: Royal India Corporation Ltd. (RICL) appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order in an application under Section 66 of the IBC directing it to contribute Rs. 119.08 Crores to the account of Corporate Debtor Royal Refinery Pvt. Ltd. (RRPL) for participating in fraudulent transactions[cite: 27]. DRI raids and customs findings established that both companies were front entities controlled by Manoj Punamiya, and that after DRI seized accounts showing RICL owed Rs. 158.07 Crores to RRPL, fictitious reverse sales of gold were entered on paper without physical inventory to reduce RICL's liability to Rs. 31 Crores[cite: 27]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that under Section 66(1) of the IBC, liability to make contribution extends to 'any person' or third party knowingly benefiting from transactions designed to defraud creditors[cite: 27]. The Tribunal affirmed that sham entries without inventory substantiate fraudulent trading, warranting full recovery[cite: 27].

case_title: Disha Choudhary (Erstwhile Managing Director of Dreamz Infra India Limited) vs. Dreamz Sneh Project Allottees Welfare Association & Anr.
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain and Technical Member Ajai Das Mehrotra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Ms. Disha Choudhary, Erstwhile Managing Director and Promoter of Dreamz Infra India Limited (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 28]. Respondent No. 1 is Dreamz Sneh Project Allottees Welfare Association (Financial Creditor / Homebuyers' Association)[cite: 28]. Respondent No. 2 is Mrs. Ramanathan Bhuvaneshwari (substituted Interim Resolution Professional)[cite: 28]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor floated multiple residential housing projects across Bengaluru in 2014, including 'Dreamz Sumadhur Project' and 'Dreamz Sneh Project' (located at Bhoganahalli Village, Bengaluru East Taluk)[cite: 28]. Corporate Debtor collected funds from allottees promising flat handovers between 2015 and 2019, but failed to complete construction[cite: 28]. Projects stalled completely, leading to criminal FIRs, civil suits, and judicial custody of Appellant and management for over three years alongside disqualification under Section 164 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 28]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor failed to complete and deliver flats or refund advances, resulting in continuous defaults to real estate allottees across its projects well exceeding the statutory financial default threshold under Section 4 of the IBC[cite: 28]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: On 20.08.2019, NCLT Bengaluru admitted Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 84/BB/2019 filed by Pratap Chandra Padhy and two homebuyers against the Corporate Debtor as a whole, wherein allottees of Dreamz Sneh Project submitted claims[cite: 28]. However, on 04.09.2020, NCLT Bengaluru passed an order confining the CIRP strictly to 'Dreamz Sumadhur Project'[cite: 28]. Left without an insolvency forum, Dreamz Sneh Project allottees formed an association and filed Section 7 application CP (IB) No. 83/BB/2021 on 19.08.2021[cite: 28]. NCLT Bengaluru admitted the petition on 15.02.2023, and modified IRP appointment on 21.02.2023 in IA No. 113/BB/2023[cite: 28]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Builder-Buyer Agreements stipulating delivery schedules between 2015 and 2019[cite: 28]; NCLT admission order dated 20.08.2019 in CP (IB) No. 84/BB/2019[cite: 28]; NCLT project-confinement order dated 04.09.2020[cite: 28]; claims filed by Dreamz Sneh allottees in the first CIRP[cite: 28]; Section 7 petition dated 19.08.2021[cite: 28]; and audited balance sheets of the Corporate Debtor reflecting debt acknowledgment under Section 18[cite: 28]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru Bench admitted Respondent No. 1's Section 7 petition on 15.02.2023 (modified on 21.02.2023), holding that flat delivery defaults spanned 2015 to 2019, that default qua a single allottee is sufficient under Manish Kumar, and that the judicial orders dated 20.08.2019 and 04.09.2020 gave rise to a fresh cause of action extending limitation[cite: 28]. The Suspended Managing Director appealed to NCLAT under Section 61, contending solely that the petition was barred by limitation under Article 137 because cause of action arose in 2016 and court orders cannot extend limitation outside Sections 18 and 19 of the Limitation Act[cite: 28].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an application under Section 7 of the IBC filed by an association of real estate allottees is barred by limitation where the original delivery default occurred in 2016, but allottees had timely lodged claims in an earlier company-wide CIRP that was subsequently confined to a single project by judicial order on 04.09.2020[cite: 28]; (ii) Whether a judicial order of an Adjudicating Authority restructuring or confining CIRP creates a fresh accrual of right and fresh cause of action for excluded allottees to initiate Section 7 proceedings under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963[cite: 28]; (iii) Whether the Supreme Court's ruling in Dena Bank v. C. Shivakumar Reddy permits limitation to be computed from the date of judicial determinations and orders in insolvency proceedings[cite: 28].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In real estate insolvencies involving multi-project corporate debtors, where allottees have actively participated and lodged claims in a company-wide CIRP which is subsequently narrowed down and confined to a single independent project by an order of the Adjudicating Authority, the passing of such judicial order gives rise to a fresh right and separate cause of action for the excluded project allottees to initiate a fresh Section 7 application; an application instituted within three years from the date of such judicial confinement order is well within the limitation period under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963 read with Section 238A of the IBC[cite: 28]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 238A of the IBC read with Article 137 of the Limitation Act, limitation is three years from the date on which the right to apply accrues[cite: 28]. As authoritatively held by the Supreme Court in Dena Bank (now Bank of Baroda) v. C. Shivakumar Reddy, the principles of limitation under the IBC are not construed with pedantic rigidity; a binding judicial order or decree creates a fresh right and accrual of cause of action entitling the creditor to initiate CIRP within three years of such order[cite: 28]. Furthermore, under Manish Kumar v. Union of India, allottees need only establish default exceeding the statutory threshold, and continuous delivery defaults spanning across 2015 to 2019 coupled with corporate balance sheet acknowledgments prevent the claim from becoming time-barred[cite: 28]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that allottee agreements provided for flat deliveries from 2015 to 2019; that allottees of Dreamz Sneh had submitted claims following the company's CIRP admission on 20.08.2019; that NCLT severed the projects on 04.09.2020 restricting CIRP to Dreamz Sumadhur; and that Respondent No. 1 filed the fresh Section 7 petition on 19.08.2021, less than one year from the 04.09.2020 order, falling comfortably within the 3-year statutory limit[cite: 28]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 application was instituted within statutory limitation computed from the accrual of the fresh cause of action on 04.09.2020 and was supported by continuous defaults, rendering the NCLT admission orders dated 15.02.2023 and 21.02.2023 fully lawful and sound[cite: 28].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 151 of 2023 is dismissed with no order as to costs, affirming the admission orders dated 15.02.2023 and 21.02.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Bengaluru Bench) in CP (IB) No. 83/BB/2021 and IA No. 113/BB/2023[cite: 28]. All pending Interlocutory Applications are closed[cite: 28].
summary: Disha Choudhary, Suspended Managing Director of Dreamz Infra India Ltd., appealed against an NCLT Bengaluru order admitting a Section 7 CIRP application filed by Dreamz Sneh Project Allottees Welfare Association, contending that the petition was barred by limitation because the project delivery defaults originated in 2016[cite: 28]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Chennai Bench held that the allottees had timely filed claims in an earlier 2019 company-wide CIRP which the NCLT subsequently restricted solely to 'Dreamz Sumadhur Project' on 04.09.2020[cite: 28]. Relying on the Supreme Court's ruling in Dena Bank v. C. Shivakumar Reddy and Manish Kumar v. UOI, the Tribunal held that the order of 04.09.2020 gave rise to a fresh cause of action, making the Section 7 petition filed on 19.08.2021 well within the three-year limitation period under Article 137[cite: 28].

case_title: Chintan Jhunjhunwala vs. Avani Towers Private Limited & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Justice Ashok Bhushan, Technical Members Barun Mitra and Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Chintan Jhunjhunwala, Suspended Director of Energy Properties Private Limited (Corporate Debtor / Landowner)[cite: 30]. Respondent No. 1 is Avani Towers Private Limited (Financial Creditor / Developer, represented by RP Jitendra Lohia in its own CIRP)[cite: 30]. Respondent No. 2 is Energy Properties Private Limited represented through IRP Mahesh Chand Gupta[cite: 30]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor owned 10.19 acres of land at Ramrajatala, Howrah (acquired in 2008 under SARFAESI)[cite: 30]. On 16.06.2008, Corporate Debtor entered into a Development Agreement with Avani Towers Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 30]. Under Clause 8.1, the developer provided an initial interest-free refundable Security Deposit of Rs. 12 Crores, but additionally agreed that any further advance up to Rs. 3 Crores (mutually enhanced to Rs. 3.5 Crores) advanced to the owner would carry interest at the agreed rate of 18% per annum compounded and payable quarterly[cite: 30]. Possession was handed over under MoAs dated 02.03.2010 and 24.06.2010, but the project failed to take off[cite: 30]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted in paying the quarterly compounded interest on the additional advance of Rs. 3.5 Crores[cite: 30]. In September 2019, the Financial Creditor filed a Section 7 application claiming a total default of Rs. 10,90,72,565/-, representing the unpaid interest accrued at 18% compounded quarterly up to 31.08.2019 (excluding the principal amount of Rs. 3.5 Crores), specifying the date of default as 01.10.2010 (and continuing quarterly thereafter)[cite: 30]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Development Agreement executed on 16.06.2008[cite: 30]. First quarterly interest default occurred on 01.10.2010[cite: 30]. Corporate Debtor deducted TDS at 18% compounded interest for FY 2010-11 to 2013-14[cite: 30]. On 31.03.2014, Corporate Debtor wrote a letter acknowledging liability but citing inability to provide interest[cite: 30]. Accounts confirmed on 01.04.2013 and acknowledged in financial statements for FY 2013-14, 2014-15, and 2017-18[cite: 30]. Section 7 application [C.P. (IB) 1711/KB/2019] was filed on 30.09.2019[cite: 30]. NCLT Kolkata Bench (Court-I) admitted the petition on 20.03.2024[cite: 30]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Development Agreement dated 16.06.2008 (specifically Clause 8.1, 8.2, 8.3, and Third Schedule Part II)[cite: 30]; Corporate Debtor's letter dated 31.03.2014 admitting 18% interest liability and developer's reply dated 05.04.2014[cite: 30]; TDS deduction certificates under the Income Tax Act[cite: 30]; and audited balance sheets of Corporate Debtor for FY 2013-14, 2014-15 (Note 4 and Note 19), and 2017-18 classifying Rs. 5.54 Crores as unsecured loan under 'Long Term Borrowings'[cite: 30]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench Court-I admitted Avani Towers' Section 7 petition on 20.03.2024, holding that the advance carried the time value of money and was a Financial Debt, and that the petition filed on 30.09.2019 was within limitation due to balance sheet acknowledgments under Section 18[cite: 30]. The Suspended Director appealed to NCLAT under Section 61, contending that the deposit was not a financial debt, that the developer held development rights estopping it from seeking refund, and that claims were barred by limitation[cite: 30].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an additional monetary advance disbursed by a developer to a landowner under a development agreement carrying an agreed interest rate of 18% per annum compounded quarterly constitutes a 'financial debt' disbursed against consideration for the time value of money having the commercial effect of a borrowing under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC[cite: 30]; (ii) Whether the classification of an advance as 'inventory' in the developer's books alters the intrinsic nature of the financial debt where the corporate debtor consistently acknowledged the transaction as an unsecured loan under 'long-term borrowings' in its balance sheets[cite: 30]; (iii) Whether continuous balance sheet acknowledgments and written requests seeking relief from interest provision extend limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 for filing a Section 7 application[cite: 30].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The determination of whether a debt constitutes a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC depends on the true commercial nature and substance of the transaction rather than mere nomenclature or unilateral accounting classifications; where an advance carrying compound interest payable quarterly is disbursed to finance a corporate debtor, the transaction possesses the commercial effect of a borrowing and embodies consideration for the time value of money, entitling the creditor to invoke Section 7 upon default of interest payments[cite: 30]. Furthermore, unequivocal balance sheet disclosures and corporate correspondence acknowledging the debt as long-term borrowings renew the statutory period of limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963[cite: 30]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC, any transaction having the commercial effect of a borrowing qualifies as financial debt[cite: 30]. Applying the Supreme Court's authoritative ruling in Global Credit Capital Limited v. Sach Marketing Pvt. Ltd., agreements must be scrutinized to ascertain their true substance; where a deposit carries a fixed return of interest without forfeiture covenants, it constitutes a borrowing against the time value of money[cite: 30]. Clause 8.1 of the Development Agreement drew a sharp distinction between the primary interest-free security deposit of Rs. 12 Crores and the additional Rs. 3.5 Crore advance carrying 18% quarterly compound interest[cite: 30]. Section 7 proceedings for defaulted interest were wholly independent of project completion, and book balance sheet acknowledgments fulfill Section 18 of the Limitation Act to defeat any limitation bar[cite: 30]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized Clause 8.1 and the Corporate Debtor's letter dated 31.03.2014, establishing that the debtor specifically admitted the 18% quarterly interest liability and requested suspension of interest provisioning due to project delays[cite: 30]. Furthermore, the Corporate Debtor deducted TDS on interest from 2010 to 2014, and its audited financial statements for FY 2013-14, 2014-15 (Note 4 & Note 19), and 2017-18 explicitly recorded the debt of Rs. 5.54 Crores as an unsecured loan from an associate under 'Long Term Borrowings', creating continuous statutory acknowledgments extending limitation to the filing date of 30.09.2019[cite: 30]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt was a financial debt, default of quarterly interest exceeding Rs. 10.90 Crores was proven, and the application was well within statutory limitation; therefore, the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in admitting the Corporate Debtor into CIRP[cite: 30].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 769 of 2024 is dismissed with no order as to costs, affirming the order dated 20.03.2024 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Kolkata Bench, Court-I) in C.P. (IB) No. 1711/KB/2019 admitting the Section 7 application[cite: 30].
summary: Chintan Jhunjhunwala, Suspended Director of Energy Properties Pvt. Ltd., appealed against an NCLT Kolkata order admitting a Section 7 CIRP application filed by Avani Towers Pvt. Ltd. for default in paying Rs. 10.90 Crores of quarterly compounded interest on an advance of Rs. 3.5 Crores under a 2008 Development Agreement[cite: 30]. Appellant argued that the advance formed part of an unrefundable security deposit, that the claim was time-barred since default occurred in 2010, and that the developer was estopped from claiming refund while holding development rights[cite: 30]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench relied on Global Credit Capital v. Sach Marketing to hold that an advance carrying 18% compound interest possesses the commercial effect of a borrowing with time value of money under Section 5(8)(f)[cite: 30]. The Tribunal held that TDS deductions and balance sheet entries under 'Long Term Borrowings' continuously renewed limitation under Section 18, rendering the admission lawful[cite: 30].

case_title: Harinder Bashista vs. Sanjib Kumar & Ors.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Justice Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Harinder Bashista, Suspended Director of M/s Vardhman Estates & Developers Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 31]. The Respondents are Sanjib Kumar and 145 other real estate allottees of 'Vardhman I Valley' project (Financial Creditors)[cite: 31]. The Resolution Professional is Mr. Abhishek Anand[cite: 31]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Greater Noida Authority allotted Plot No. 26/1 (40,470 sq. meters in Knowledge Park-III) to M/s Zestha Projects Pvt. Ltd. via Lease Deed dated 26.12.2008[cite: 31]. Zestha entered into a joint development agreement with the Corporate Debtor on 16.04.2007 to develop a commercial/residential/IT project named 'Vardhman I Valley'[cite: 31]. Allottees booked residential, office, and commercial units, paid 70% to 100% of the sale consideration, and executed Builder Buyer Agreements promising possession within 3 to 4 years alongside 12% assured returns[cite: 31]. The project was registered under UP RERA on 30.09.2017, with revised possession deadlines of 2018-19, which the developer failed to meet[cite: 31]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtor committed continuous default in failing to complete construction, procure completion certificates, or handover possession[cite: 31]. In the Section 7 petition, the allottees claimed a total financial debt default of Rs. 39,18,80,005.35/- (comprising principal advances and accrued interest)[cite: 31]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: In October 2021, 117 Financial Creditors representing 104 allotted units filed Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 674(PB)/2021[cite: 31]. On 01.08.2022, NCLT allowed impleadment of 22 allottees (IA 2524/2022) and 2 allottees (IA 2624/2022)[cite: 31]. On 07.10.2022 and 12.09.2022, NCLT permitted an amended Section 7 application and memo of parties, expanding the applicants to 146 Financial Creditors representing 122 units[cite: 31]. NCLT Principal Bench admitted the petition on 07.02.2023[cite: 31]. On 21.02.2023, NCLAT granted an interim order staying CoC constitution[cite: 31]. IRP submitted a project status report on 11.10.2023[cite: 31]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered joint agreement dated 16.04.2007; Builder Buyer Agreements; Schedule-1 and Annexure D (Part-I) identifying unit numbers and multi-unit allotments (e.g., Sahil Gupta 4 units, Sunil Gupta 6 units, Sangeeta Gupta 4 units)[cite: 31]; IRP Inspection and Surveyor Report dated 11.10.2023 proving work was 34% to 91% incomplete across all 5 towers and confirming that zero Occupancy/Completion Certificates or Fire NOCs were issued[cite: 31]; Greater Noida Authority letter dated 16.11.2021 refusing completion; and conditional 'No Dues and No Claim' certificates from certain allottees (such as Kamal Bhardwaj dated 05.03.2020)[cite: 31]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench admitted the Section 7 application on 07.02.2023, holding that the applicants crossed the statutory threshold of 100 allottees, that incomplete construction was proven by RERA reports, and that RERA decree holders and assured return buyers remain valid allottees[cite: 31]. The Suspended Director appealed to NCLAT under Section 61, contending that the petition originally represented only 99 units, that 23 commercial buyers who allegedly took possession and buyers who signed No Dues Certificates must be excluded, reducing the count below 100[cite: 31].
legal_issues: (i) How the statutory threshold of 'not less than one hundred allottees or not less than ten per cent of the total number of allottees' under the second proviso to Section 7(1) of the IBC is to be computed in real estate insolvencies where individual buyers hold multiple units or joint allotments[cite: 31]; (ii) Whether unitholders who have signed conditional 'No Dues and No Claim Certificates' or executed sub-leases in an uncompleted project lacking an Occupancy Certificate cease to be 'allottees' for the purpose of meeting the Section 7 numerical threshold[cite: 31]; (iii) Whether allottees holding RERA recovery decrees or contracts with assured return clauses are disqualified as speculative investors from initiating Section 7 CIRP[cite: 31].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: For the purpose of satisfying the numerical threshold of 100 allottees under the second proviso to Section 7(1) of the IBC, each independent allotment of an apartment or unit qualifies as an independent allotment, and joint allottees of a single apartment are reckoned as a single allottee; allottees do not lose their legal character as financial creditors or allottees merely by executing conditional 'No Dues Certificates' or accepting physical possession of commercial units where the project remains incomplete and no statutory Completion or Occupancy Certificate has been issued by the competent planning authority[cite: 31]. Furthermore, holders of RERA decrees or agreements with assured return covenants remain real estate allottees and cannot be excluded from the statutory threshold count as speculative investors[cite: 31]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7(1) second proviso read with Section 2(d) of RERA, 2016 and the Supreme Court's ruling in Manish Kumar v. Union of India establishes that the threshold requires a critical mass of 100 allottees or one-tenth of total allottees, with default required only to be proven in rem exceeding the Section 4 threshold (Rs. 1 Crore)[cite: 31]. Individual buyers allotted multiple units represent separate allottee units[cite: 31]. As held in Jones Lang Lasalle and Mukul Agarwal, an allottee who secures a RERA decree does not lose the underlying character of being an allottee, as a decree is merely an adjudication of debt quantum[cite: 31]. A 'No Dues Certificate' forgoing delay penalties does not cancel the underlying allotment contract, and in the absence of an Occupancy Certificate, unauthorized occupation cannot extinguish allottee status[cite: 31]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examined Annexure D (Part-I) and Schedule-1, establishing that the application initially represented 104 allotted units and expanded to 122 units upon impleadment of 24 allottees by NCLT on 01.08.2022, consistently exceeding the 100-allottee threshold[cite: 31]. The IRP's Surveyor Report dated 11.10.2023 proved that work was heavily pending (65% residential, 52% IT block, 91% club), external utilities were 100% pending, and zero Occupancy or Fire Certificates existed, refuting the contention that 23 units were legally handed over[cite: 31]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 application satisfied all statutory numerical thresholds and evidenced undisputed debt and default exceeding Rs. 39 Crores; therefore, the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in admitting the Corporate Debtor into CIRP, subject to excluding the litigation stay period (21.02.2023 to 31.05.2024) from the CIRP timeline[cite: 31].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 197 of 2023 is dismissed with no order as to costs, affirming the order dated 07.02.2023 passed by NCLT Principal Bench in CP (IB)-674(PB)/2021 admitting the Section 7 application[cite: 31]. The period from 21.02.2023 until 31.05.2024 is directed to be excluded from the CIRP timeline of the Corporate Debtor, and the IRP is directed to proceed with CIRP in accordance with law[cite: 31].
summary: Harinder Bashista, Suspended Director of Vardhman Estates & Developers Pvt. Ltd., appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order admitting a Section 7 CIRP application filed by 146 allottees representing 122 units in the stalled 'Vardhman I Valley' project for a default of Rs. 39.18 Crores[cite: 31]. Appellant contended that the petition failed to meet the 100-allottee threshold under Section 7(1) proviso, arguing that 23 buyers who took possession, buyers who signed 'No Dues Certificates', and assured-return investors should be excluded[cite: 31]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench relied on Manish Kumar v. UOI to hold that the applicants represented more than 100 independent units[cite: 31]. The Tribunal affirmed that without a statutory Occupancy Certificate, unitholders do not lose allottee status, and that RERA decree holders and assured return buyers remain valid financial creditors[cite: 31].

case_title: Tamil Nadu Warehousing Corporation vs. Mr. Anurag Goel, RP of Shree Ambika Sugars Ltd. & Anr.
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Member Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma and Technical Member Jatindranath Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Tamil Nadu Warehousing Corporation; Respondent No. 1 is Mr. Anurag Goel, Resolution Professional of Shree Ambika Sugars Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 2 is an entity discharged from the underlying proceedings[cite: 1, 2]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Warehousing and realization proceedings concerning the sale of stock stored by the Corporate Debtor with the Appellant corporation[cite: 2]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Monetary proceeds realized from the sale of stock were ordered to be deposited, and Respondent No. 2 was discharged on findings that the stock did not belong to them[cite: 2]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Division Bench Chennai pronounced the substantive order in open court on 09.11.2023 in IA(IBC)/540/CHE/2022; the order was uploaded on 17.11.2023; certified copy was applied for on 12.12.2023 and issued on 12.12.2023; the appeal was filed on 29.12.2023 with a 13-day delay beyond the initial 30 days (total 50 days)[cite: 1, 2, 4]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Endorsement on the certified copy showing application for copy dated 12.12.2023; court records confirming pronouncement of the substantive order on 09.11.2023 in the presence of counsel[cite: 2, 4]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai passed the substantive order on 09.11.2023; Appellant filed CA (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 158/2024 with IA No. 423/2024 (condonation of refiling delay of 44 days) and IA No. 424/2024 (condonation of 13 days delay in filing appeal)[cite: 1].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the period of limitation under Section 61(2) of the IBC begins to run from the date of substantive pronouncement in open court in the presence of counsel or from the date the order is uploaded on the website[cite: 2, 4]; (ii) Whether counsel's oral plea of being unable to properly hear the concluding part of the pronouncement excuses delay and enables exclusion under Section 12 of the Limitation Act when the certified copy was applied for after 30 days[cite: 2, 4].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Limitation for preferring an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC commences from the date the substantive order is actually pronounced in open court in the presence of counsel, not from the date of uploading or receipt of certified copy, and failure to apply for a certified copy within the initial 30 days forfeits the benefit of Section 12(2) of the Limitation Act. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) IBC mandates an outer limit of 30 days plus a discretionary 15 days; where an appeal is filed 50 days from pronouncement, the appellate tribunal has no statutory power to condone delay beyond the aggregate 45-day window[cite: 1, 2]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the substantive order was pronounced on 09.11.2023 before counsel, certified copy was applied for on 12.12.2023 (after 33 days), and the oral claim of not hearing the order was an unpleaded, unsustainable afterthought[cite: 2, 4, 5]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal was filed 50 days after pronouncement, which is beyond the non-extendable statutory period of 45 days under Section 61(2); hence, the delay application and the appeal must be rejected.
operative_order: IA No. 423/2024 (refiling delay) is allowed; IA No. 424/2024 (delay condonation in filing) is rejected; and Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 158/2024 stands dismissed as barred by limitation[cite: 1].
summary: Tamil Nadu Warehousing Corporation appealed against an NCLT Chennai order dated 09.11.2023 directing it to deposit sale proceeds realized from stock and discharging Respondent No. 2[cite: 1, 2]. The appellant filed the appeal on 29.12.2023 alongside an application seeking condonation of 13 days of delay, contending that limitation should run from 17.11.2023 (when the order was uploaded) because its counsel failed to hear the pronouncement clearly on 09.11.2023[cite: 1, 2]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Chennai Bench held that limitation runs from the date of substantive pronouncement in open court[cite: 4]. Because the certified copy was applied for after 30 days and the total gap was 50 days, the delay exceeded the maximum condonable window under Section 61(2) of the IBC[cite: 4].

case_title: Ashok Kriplani, Erstwhile RP of Dreamz Infra India Ltd. vs. Konduru Prasanth Raju, RP of Dreamz Infra India Ltd. & 17 Ors.
appeal_number: IA No. 59/2024 (Review Petition) in TA (AT) No. 79/2021 (Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 851/2020)
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Member Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma and Technical Member Jatindranath Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Applicant is Ashok Kriplani, Erstwhile Resolution Professional of Dreamz Infra India Ltd.; Respondent No. 1 is Konduru Prasanth Raju, current Resolution Professional of Dreamz Infra India Ltd., along with 17 other respondents[cite: 1]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dispute arising out of the administration, CIRP management, and replacement/resolution professional orders in the corporate insolvency of Dreamz Infra India Ltd[cite: 1]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Regulatory and procedural replacement/challenge under CIRP; no specific monetary claim metric formed the crux of the review petition. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT passed common order on 04.09.2020; NCLAT dismissed CA (AT) (Ins) No. 851/2020 (TA No. 79/2021) on 07.06.2023; Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 19.10.2023 leaving it open to file a review; Review IA No. 59/2024 was filed on 25.11.2023[cite: 1, 2]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLAT appellate judgment dated 07.06.2023; Supreme Court order dated 19.10.2023 dismissing appeal while granting liberty to seek review 'in accordance with law'[cite: 1, 2]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLAT dismissed the appeal on 07.06.2023; the Supreme Court dismissed the civil appeal on 19.10.2023 granting liberty to file review to be decided in accordance with law; Applicant filed IA No. 59/2024 invoking Article 142 of the Constitution[cite: 1, 2].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the NCLAT possesses statutory jurisdiction to entertain a substantive Review Petition under the IBC, 2016[cite: 3, 5]; (ii) Whether the Supreme Court's order leaving it open to file a review to be decided 'in accordance with law' read with Article 142 of the Constitution vests a statutory tribunal with review powers absent substantive legislative enactment[cite: 1, 2, 3].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Review is a substantive statutory creation and cannot be exercised by a court or tribunal of limited jurisdiction unless explicitly conferred by the governing statute; extraordinary powers under Article 142 of the Constitution cannot be invoked to artificially manufacture a power of review contrary to statutory silence[cite: 2, 3, 5]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Neither the IBC, 2016 nor the Companies Act, 2013 contains any provision conferring review jurisdiction upon the NCLAT; the Supreme Court's direction granting liberty to file a review to be decided 'in accordance with law' mandates adjudication under existing codified law, which does not recognize review[cite: 3, 4, 5]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examined the statutory text of the IBC, 2016 and the order of the Hon'ble Supreme Court dated 19.10.2023, observing that grant of liberty to pursue a remedy cannot expand statutory jurisdiction beyond plenary limits[cite: 2, 3, 5]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The review application is entirely devoid of statutory foundation, unmaintainable in law, and must be dismissed[cite: 5].
operative_order: IA No. 59/2024 (Review Petition) in TA No. 79/2021 (Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 851/2020) is dismissed as not maintainable[cite: 1, 5].
summary: Ashok Kriplani, erstwhile Resolution Professional of Dreamz Infra India Ltd., filed a review petition before NCLAT Chennai seeking review of its judgment dated 07.06.2023, which had dismissed his appeal against an NCLT order[cite: 1]. Following dismissal of his appeal by the Supreme Court with liberty to file a review to be decided 'in accordance with law', the applicant argued that Article 142 of the Constitution made the review maintainable[cite: 1, 2]. Dismissing the review petition, the NCLAT Chennai Bench held that the power of review is a creation of statute and is completely absent under the IBC, 2016 and Companies Act, 2013[cite: 3, 5]. The Tribunal ruled that Supreme Court liberty cannot create review jurisdiction where none exists legislatively[cite: 3, 4].

case_title: Sub Registrar Pallikonda Sub Registrar Office vs. Amier Hamsa Ali Abbas Rawther
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Member Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma and Technical Member Jatindranath Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Sub Registrar, Pallikonda Sub Registrar Office; the Respondent is Amier Hamsa Ali Abbas Rawther[cite: 1]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Contempt proceedings arising out of alleged non-compliance with NCLT Chennai registration/adjudication orders within insolvency proceedings in IBA/579/2019[cite: 1, 2]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Dispute over quantification of stamp duty and registration of instruments under Section 47A of the Indian Stamp Act, leading to contempt allegations[cite: 3]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Chennai passed an order on 08.08.2023 directing impleadment of IG Registration; on 10.05.2024, NCLT passed an order in IA(IBC)/836/2024 in Cont.P/13/2023 directing IG Registration to file a personal affidavit within two weeks explaining non-compliance[cite: 2, 4]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Impugned order dated 10.05.2024 calling for a personal affidavit from IG Registration; prior orders dated 08.08.2023 and 05.01.2024[cite: 2, 4]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In pending contempt proceedings Cont.P/13/2023, NCLT Chennai directed the IG Registration to file an explanatory affidavit on 10.05.2024; the Sub Registrar appealed against that order before NCLAT Chennai under Section 61 of the IBC read with Section 19 of the Contempt of Courts Act[cite: 2].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an interlocutory order in contempt proceedings calling for an explanatory reply affidavit constitutes an appealable order under Section 19 of the Contempt of Courts Act read with Section 61 of the IBC[cite: 2, 4]; (ii) Whether a subordinate officer (Sub Registrar) can maintain an appeal projecting the cause of a superior authority (IG Registration) who was directed to file an affidavit[cite: 3, 4].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal against a contempt order under Section 19 of the Contempt of Courts Act read with Section 425 of the Companies Act lies exclusively against an order imposing punishment; an interim order merely calling upon an authority to file an explanatory affidavit does not decide contempt or inflict punishment and is non-appealable[cite: 2, 4]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 425 of the Companies Act, 2013 and Section 19 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, appellate jurisdiction cannot be invoked prematurely against an interlocutory direction to file a reply; furthermore, contempt is personal, and a subordinate official has no locus standi to act as a shield or file an appeal on behalf of an unpenalized superior officer[cite: 1, 2, 3, 4]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed the order dated 10.05.2024 and found no summons for personal appearance or order of punishment was issued against either the Sub Registrar or the IG Registration, and stamp duty disputes must be raised under the Indian Stamp Act, not via contempt appeals[cite: 2, 3, 4]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal is premature, brought without standing, and unmaintainable under Section 61 of the IBC read with Section 19 of the Contempt of Courts Act[cite: 4, 5].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 192/2024 is dismissed as not maintainable[cite: 1, 5].
summary: The Sub Registrar, Pallikonda Sub Registrar Office appealed against an NCLT Chennai order dated 10.05.2024 in contempt proceedings Cont.P/13/2023, wherein the Tribunal directed the Inspector General of Registration, Government of Tamil Nadu, to file a personal explanatory affidavit regarding non-compliance with earlier orders[cite: 1, 2]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Chennai Bench held that under Section 425 of the Companies Act read with Section 19 of the Contempt of Courts Act and Section 61 of the IBC, an appeal lies only against an order imposing punishment, not against a direction calling for a reply[cite: 1, 2, 4]. The Tribunal also held that the Sub Registrar had no locus standi to litigate on behalf of the IG Registration[cite: 3, 4].

case_title: Mr. Ratnakar Shetty, RP, M/s Lalith Gangadhar Constructions Pvt. Ltd. vs. Sathish Kumar & Ors.
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Member Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma and Technical Member Jatindranath Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant in Comp App Nos. 101, 102, 104 & 105 of 2024 is Mr. Ratnakar Shetty, Resolution Professional of M/s Lalith Gangadhar Constructions Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); in Comp App No. 204/2024, the Appellant is India Real Estate Investment Fund; Respondents include Sathish Kumar and other creditors/CoC members[cite: 1]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Real estate development and construction operations undergoing Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under CP(IB)No.87/BB/2021 before NCLT Bengaluru[cite: 2]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Insolvency proceedings wherein multiple extension applications were filed to complete CIRP and consider pending resolution plans rather than forcing the debtor into corporate liquidation[cite: 2]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated under CP(IB)No.87/BB/2021; NCLT Bengaluru rejected repeated extension applications under Section 12(2) on 22.01.2024 (IA Nos. 835/2022, 547/2023, 601/2023, 861/2023); on 24.05.2024, NCLT directed the RP to take steps for liquidation under Section 33 within three weeks; appeals were heard on 20.06.2024[cite: 2, 4]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Filings showing that earlier Section 12 extension applications seeking 60 days remained undecided until the requested period lapsed without adjudication on merits; approved resolution plans awaiting consideration; NCLT orders dated 22.01.2024 and 24.05.2024[cite: 2, 4]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru rejected successive Section 12 extension applications on 22.01.2024 holding multiple extensions barred by Section 12(2), and later directed liquidation steps under Section 33 on 24.05.2024; the RP and an investor appealed to NCLAT Chennai[cite: 2, 3, 4].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the time limitation prescribed under Section 12 of the IBC for completion of CIRP is directory or mandatory, and whether recurring extension applications are barred where prior applications lapsed without adjudication on merits[cite: 5]; (ii) Whether an Adjudicating Authority can force a Corporate Debtor into liquidation under Section 33 when a viable resolution is achievable through a reasonable extension of time[cite: 4, 5].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory time period for CIRP completion under Section 12 of the IBC is directory in nature rather than mandatory, and Adjudicating Authorities possess the discretion to grant extensions beyond statutory limits in exceptional cases to prevent unnecessary liquidation and achieve corporate rescue[cite: 5]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12(2) read with the Supreme Court's ruling in Essar Steel establishes that liquidation must be a measure of last resort; where prior extension applications remained pending undecided until the requested period expired due to procedural delays not attributable to the applicant, subsequent applications for extension are legally maintainable and not barred by Section 12(2)[cite: 5]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examined the procedural record, finding that prior applications were not decided on merits, the delay was largely institutional/procedural, resolution plans were pending, and no bad faith was established. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in rejecting the extension applications; a further extension of 45 days is granted to complete CIRP, while the challenge to the Section 33 direction in Appeal No. 204/2024 is dismissed as premature.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) Nos. 101, 102, 104 & 105 of 2024 are allowed, the impugned orders dated 22.01.2024 are quashed, and NCLT Bengaluru is directed to grant an extension of 45 days from the date of uploading this order to complete CIRP; Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 204/2024 is dismissed as premature[cite: 1].
summary: The Resolution Professional of Lalith Gangadhar Constructions Pvt. Ltd. appealed against NCLT Bengaluru orders dated 22.01.2024 rejecting successive applications under Section 12(2) of the IBC seeking a 60-day CIRP extension, alongside an appeal by India Real Estate Investment Fund against an order dated 24.05.2024 directing steps under Section 33 for liquidation[cite: 1, 2, 4]. The NCLT had held that recurring extension applications are impermissible[cite: 2]. Allowing the RP's appeals, the NCLAT Chennai Bench relied on Essar Steel to hold that CIRP timelines under Section 12 are directory[cite: 5]. Because earlier extension applications had lapsed without adjudication on merits due to procedural delays, the Tribunal quashed the rejection orders, granted a final 45-day extension to conclude CIRP, and dismissed the liquidation appeal as premature.

case_title: Mr. Padmanabhan vs. Priya S. Anand, Liquidator of M/s RRP Housing Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 167/2024 with Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 168/2024 (IA Nos. 441, 442, 443, 444, 445, 446, 447 & 448/2024)
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Member Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma and Technical Member Jatindranath Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Mr. Padmanabhan and Mr. Thamizh, Erstwhile Directors and Shareholders of M/s RRP Housing Private Limited (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 is Priya S. Anand, Liquidator of the Corporate Debtor; Respondent No. 2 is M/s AKS Housing Development Co. Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Auction Purchaser)[cite: 2]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Real estate development projects undertaken by the Corporate Debtor involving immovable property situated at Maraimalai Nagar, Chennai, which was subjected to an auction sale under liquidation proceedings. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Following initiation of CIRP at the instance of M/s Adinath Enterprises, the Corporate Debtor was ordered into liquidation on 04.04.2019; the auction of the subject property was conducted and completed on 05.05.2022 at the reserve price, and sale proceeds were subsequently distributed by the Liquidator to satisfy admitted claims[cite: 4]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Corporate Debtor was put into liquidation on 04.04.2019; auction sale took place on 05.05.2022; Appellants filed IAs (IA Nos. 118/CHE/2023 and 129/CHE/2023) challenging the auction sale belatedly on 19.12.2022; the Liquidator notified distribution of funds via IA No. 1301 on 12.03.2024; NCLT Chennai rejected the Appellants' applications on 13.03.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Auction sale notice and newspaper publications issued in one English daily and one regional language daily; registered sale certificate issued following the auction on 05.05.2022; distribution of proceeds notified on 12.03.2024[cite: 4]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai rejected IA Nos. 118/CHE/2023 and 129/CHE/2023 on 13.03.2024, refusing to set aside the auction sale; the erstwhile directors appealed to NCLAT Chennai under Section 61 of the IBC[cite: 5].
legal_issues: (i) Whether erstwhile directors or shareholders of a corporate debtor retain locus standi to challenge an auction sale and seek setting aside of a sale certificate after liquidation proceedings have attained finality[cite: 4]; (ii) Whether an auction sale conducted at the reserve price can be reopened on belated allegations of inadequate newspaper circulation under Regulation 12(3) of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations after sale proceeds have already been distributed[cite: 4].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Erstwhile directors and shareholders of a corporate debtor cease to have actionable locus standi to reopen or challenge a concluded auction sale or sale certificate once the order of liquidation has attained finality, particularly when they failed to raise objections at the time of the sale notice and permitted the auction and distribution of liquidation proceeds to conclude without timely challenge[cite: 5]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Provisions of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 and Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 cannot be invoked belatedly by erstwhile promoters as a device to derail finalized liquidation transactions where no contemporaneous objections were lodged before the liquidator upon publication of the auction notice[cite: 4]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the liquidation order had attained finality, the auction was held on 05.05.2022 without contemporaneous objection, the applications were preferred only on 19.12.2022, and sale proceeds had already been distributed by the Liquidator to creditors. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The challenges raised by the ex-directors were barred by delay, acquiescence, and lack of standing; hence, the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in rejecting the applications and affirming the auction sale[cite: 5].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 167/2024 and Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 168/2024 are dismissed, the impugned orders dated 13.03.2024 passed by NCLT Chennai are affirmed, and all connected interlocutory applications are closed.
summary: Mr. Padmanabhan and Mr. Thamizh, erstwhile directors of RRP Housing Pvt. Ltd., appealed against NCLT Chennai orders dated 13.03.2024 rejecting their applications to set aside the auction sale of a Maraimalai Nagar property sold to AKS Housing Development Co. Pvt. Ltd. on 05.05.2022. The appellants alleged undervaluation, sale at reserve price, and defective publication under Regulation 12(3) of the Liquidation Process Regulations. Dismissing both appeals, the NCLAT Chennai Bench held that erstwhile directors lose standing to challenge auction proceedings once liquidation attains finality[cite: 5]. The Tribunal held that having failed to object contemporaneously, the appellants could not belatedly reopen completed auction sales after sale proceeds had already been distributed to creditors.

case_title: The Kerala State Electricity Board Limited vs. Shri Kumar Rajan, RP of M/s Kerala Paper Products Limited & Ors.
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Member Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma and Technical Member Jatindranath Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is The Kerala State Electricity Board Limited (represented by its Nodal Officer-Litigation, Palakkad); Respondent No. 1 is Shri Kumar Rajan, Resolution Professional of M/s Kerala Paper Products Limited (formerly Hindustan Newsprint Limited, Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 2 is the Corporate Debtor; Respondent No. 3 is M/s Kerala Industrial Infrastructure Development Corporation (KINFRA), a statutory body of the Government of Kerala (Successful Resolution Applicant)[cite: 2]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Provision and supply of electrical power and energy utility services to the paper manufacturing manufacturing facility of the Corporate Debtor, leading to unpaid electricity tariff dues[cite: 2]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational energy dues claimed by the Appellant under the Electricity Act, 2003 were purportedly not fully provided for in the Resolution Plan approved for the Corporate Debtor. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Kochi Bench approved the Resolution Plan submitted by KINFRA under Sections 30(6) and 31(1) on 29.01.2021; Government of Kerala issued GO(Ms) No.21/2021/P-ARD on 15.09.2021; Appellant filed CA (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 16/2022; joint settlement application IA No. 573/2024 was placed on 26.06.2024[cite: 2]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved Resolution Plan dated 29.01.2021; Government Order GO(Ms) No.21/2021/P-ARD dated 15.09.2021 mandating resolution of disputes between state instrumentalities via a High/Special Power Committee; Joint Compromise Application IA No. 573/2024. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kochi approved KINFRA's resolution plan on 29.01.2021; KSEBL appealed to NCLAT Chennai under Section 61 alleging violations of the Electricity Act, 2003, before jointly moving IA No. 573/2024 to refer the dispute to the state committee.
legal_issues: (i) Whether commercial and operational debt disputes arising under an approved IBC resolution plan between two statutory public sector undertakings/instrumentalities of a state government should be adjudicated before judicial tribunals or referred to an administrative High-Power Committee in terms of governing executive orders and Supreme Court precedents[cite: 3].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Legal controversies and monetary claims arising between governmental departments, ministries, or public sector undertakings ought not to be agitated before courts or tribunals, but should be resolved through conciliation by a designated High-Powered Committee to prevent avoidable and expensive public litigation[cite: 3]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Provisions of Section 31(1) and Section 61 of the IBC do not preclude public sector entities from resolving their mutual claims through specialized alternate dispute resolution mechanisms prescribed by the State Government under executive notifications fortified by Supreme Court jurisprudence[cite: 3]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal took notice of the consensus reflected in joint IA No. 573/2024 and verified that both the Appellant and Respondent No. 3 are statutory bodies of the Government of Kerala governed by GO(Ms) No.21/2021/P-ARD dated 15.09.2021. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The parties having agreed to submit their dispute to the Special Power Committee in terms of the Government Order, the appeal warrants closure with liberty to pursue resolution before the said committee.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 16/2022 and IA No. 34/2022 are disposed of in terms of IA No. 573/2024, closing the appeal and leaving it open for the parties to resolve their disputes through the Special Power Committee constituted under GO(Ms) No.21/2021/P-ARD dated 15.09.2021[cite: 3].
summary: Kerala State Electricity Board Limited appealed against an NCLT Kochi order dated 29.01.2021 approving the resolution plan submitted by Kerala Industrial Infrastructure Development Corporation (KINFRA) for Kerala Paper Products Limited, contending that its outstanding electricity dues were not fully discharged in accordance with the Electricity Act, 2003[cite: 2]. During hearing, both public sector entities filed IA No. 573/2024 expressing mutual consensus to resolve their inter-governmental dispute before the Special Power Committee pursuant to Kerala Government Order GO(Ms) No.21/2021/P-ARD. Relying on ONGC precedents discouraging litigation between state instrumentalities, the NCLAT Chennai Bench disposed of and closed the appeal, directing resolution through the designated committee[cite: 3].

case_title: Mr. Thamizh vs. Priya S. Anand, Liquidator of M/s RRP Housing Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Member Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma and Technical Member Jatindranath Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Mr. Thamizh, Erstwhile Director and Shareholder of M/s RRP Housing Private Limited (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 is Priya S. Anand, Liquidator of the Corporate Debtor; Respondent No. 2 is M/s AKS Housing Development Co. Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Auction Purchaser)[cite: 2]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Real estate development undertakings of the Corporate Debtor, involving immovable properties located at Maraimalai Nagar, Chennai, auctioned during the liquidation estate realization. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: CIRP was initiated against the Corporate Debtor by M/s Adinath Enterprises leading to a liquidation order on 04.04.2019; property was sold at the reserve price via auction on 05.05.2022 to Respondent No. 2, and liquidation proceeds were distributed to creditors[cite: 4]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidation ordered on 04.04.2019; auction sale concluded on 05.05.2022; Appellant filed IA (IBC)/129(CHE)/2023 challenging the auction sale on 19.12.2022; distribution notified on 12.03.2024; NCLT Chennai dismissed IA No. 129/2023 on 13.03.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Auction sale notification published in English and regional vernacular dailies; confirmation of auction sale dated 05.05.2022; liquidator's distribution notification dated 12.03.2024 filed via IA No. 1301[cite: 4]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai rejected IA (IBC)/129(CHE)/2023 on 13.03.2024; the erstwhile director challenged the rejection before NCLAT Chennai in CA (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 168/2024[cite: 5].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an erstwhile director or shareholder retains legal standing to challenge an auction sale and seek revocation of a sale certificate once liquidation has attained finality[cite: 4]; (ii) Whether alleged defects in newspaper circulation under Regulation 12(3) of the Liquidation Regulations can be entertained post-distribution of sale proceeds when no objections were lodged at the time of sale notice[cite: 4].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An erstwhile director or shareholder ceases to possess legal entitlement to dispute auction sales or seek the cancellation of sale certificates after liquidation proceedings have attained judicial finality and proceeds have been distributed to claimants[cite: 5]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory scheme under the IBC and Liquidation Process Regulations mandates certainty in insolvency sales; retrospective procedural challenges raised months after auction confirmation cannot reopen settled liquidation distributions[cite: 4]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the liquidation order was final, the auction sale occurred on 05.05.2022 without contemporaneous objection, the application was filed belatedly on 19.12.2022, and funds stood distributed. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal lacks legal merit as the ex-director lacks standing and acquiesced in the process, justifying dismissal of the appeal[cite: 5].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 168/2024 is dismissed, the impugned order dated 13.03.2024 passed in IA (IBC)/129(CHE)/2023 by NCLT Chennai is affirmed, and all pending IAs are closed[cite: 5].
summary: Mr. Thamizh, erstwhile director of RRP Housing Pvt. Ltd., appealed against the NCLT Chennai order dated 13.03.2024 in IA (IBC)/129(CHE)/2023 rejecting his challenge to the auction sale of corporate real estate at Maraimalai Nagar, Chennai, conducted on 05.05.2022 in favor of AKS Housing Development Co. Pvt. Ltd. The appellant claimed inadequate advertisement under Regulation 12(3) of the Liquidation Process Regulations and sale at reserve price. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Chennai Bench held that erstwhile directors have no locus standi to reopen liquidation sales after liquidation has attained finality[cite: 5]. The Tribunal affirmed that belated objections cannot be entertained once sale proceeds have been disbursed to creditors.

case_title: P. Duraiswamy & 6 Ors. vs. Coimbatore Vijay Machine Works Pvt. Ltd. & 5 Ors.
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Member Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma and Technical Member Jatindranath Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are P. Duraiswamy and 6 others (petitioners in oppression and mismanagement proceedings); the Respondents are Coimbatore Vijay Machine Works Pvt. Ltd. and 5 others. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate shareholding and management dispute in Coimbatore Vijay Machine Works Pvt. Ltd. instituted via Company Petition TCP/37/2016 under Sections 397/398 of the Companies Act, 1956. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Dispute over non-filing of statutory records and struck-off status of the company, with no quantified debt default metric involved. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Oppression petition filed in 2016; interim direction passed by NCLT on 18.06.2018 directing revival steps; NCLT Chennai passed impugned order on 31.01.2024; appeal decided on 25.06.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Orders of NCLT Chennai dated 18.06.2018 and 31.01.2024 in TCP/37/2016 calling upon the petitioner to file a company revival application under Section 252. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai kept the main oppression petition TCP/37/2016 in abeyance on 31.01.2024 and directed the petitioners to file an application under Section 252 for revival of the struck-off company; the petitioners appealed against this procedural direction to NCLAT Chennai.
legal_issues: (i) Whether an interim order of an Adjudicating Authority directing an oppression petitioner to take steps under Section 252 for company revival while keeping the main petition in abeyance is an appealable order determining substantive rights under company law[cite: 2].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An interlocutory procedural order of a tribunal that merely calls upon a party to initiate statutory revival proceedings and keeps a company petition in abeyance without adjudicating substantive rights or imposing liabilities does not constitute a determinative, appealable order[cite: 2]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 252 and appellate provisions under company law require an actual crystallization of rights or liabilities before appellate intervention can be invoked; procedural liberties granted to revive a defunct company leave all underlying contentions intact to be determined by the primary forum[cite: 2]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the impugned order dated 31.01.2024 and verified that no dispute or substantive merit was decided against the Appellants, and full liberty was retained to advance all grounds upon preferring the Section 252 application[cite: 2]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The order under challenge does not crystallize any right or liability; hence, the appellate tribunal declines to exercise jurisdiction and disposes of the appeal[cite: 2].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 32/2024 is laid to rest/dismissed with liberty to the Appellants to file an application under Section 252, and NCLT Chennai is requested to dispose of the revival application and TCP/37/2016 as expeditiously as possible[cite: 2].
summary: P. Duraiswamy and six others appealed against an NCLT Chennai order dated 31.01.2024 in TCP/37/2016 (oppression and mismanagement petition under Sections 397/398 of the Companies Act, 1956). The NCLT kept the petition in abeyance and directed the appellants to file an application under Section 252 for the revival of the struck-off company, Coimbatore Vijay Machine Works Pvt. Ltd. The appellants contended that respondents should have been directed to seek revival pursuant to an earlier 2018 direction. Declining to exercise appellate jurisdiction, the NCLAT Chennai Bench held that the impugned direction did not crystallize any substantive rights or liabilities[cite: 2]. The Tribunal closed the appeal, leaving it open to the appellants to agitate all grounds in the Section 252 proceedings[cite: 2].

case_title: Sarah Qureshi vs. GB Bakers Industries Pvt. Ltd. & 7 Ors.
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Member Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma and Technical Member Jatindranath Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Sarah Qureshi; Respondent No. 1 is GB Bakers Industries Pvt. Ltd.; Respondents Nos. 2, 3, 5 and 8 are appearing directors and shareholders, alongside Respondents 4, 6 and 7. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate dispute and internal shareholder grievance concerning company affairs, share rectification, investigation, and allegations of oppression and mismanagement under Sections 59, 213, 241, and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 in CP/5/241/HDB/2022. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Disputed intra-company management actions and shareholdings, resolved through a consensual mediated settlement without adjudication of monetary default metrics. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Hyderabad Bench passed the impugned order in CP/5/241/HDB/2022 on 19.10.2022; parties executed a Compromise Memo on 10.05.2024 following mediation; appeal heard and disposed of on 27.06.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Report of the Court-appointed Mediator; Memorandum of Compromise dated 10.05.2024 duly executed and signed by all litigating parties with signatures verified by respective counsel. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Following the order dated 19.10.2022 of NCLT Hyderabad, the Appellant preferred Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 111/2022; during appellate pendency, the dispute was referred to mediation resulting in a compromise report placed before the NCLAT on 27.06.2024.
legal_issues: (i) Whether an appellate company proceeding arising from an oppression and mismanagement petition can be finally closed and the impugned order modified in terms of a mutually executed Memorandum of Compromise and mediator's report.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where litigating shareholders and directors in corporate oppression and mismanagement proceedings arrive at an amicable settlement through mediation and execute a formal Memorandum of Compromise, appellate tribunals may accept the compromise, modify the impugned order accordingly, and bring the corporate litigation to a final close. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 241, 242, and 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 permit the appellate forum to dispose of proceedings in accordance with verified settlements that resolve private corporate disputes without prejudicing the public interest or statutory company regulation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examined the mediator's report and verified the execution and authenticity of the Memorandum of Compromise dated 10.05.2024 signed by all parties and endorsed by their respective advocates. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The settlement being voluntary, lawful, and complete, the impugned order is modified to align with the compromise terms, and the company petition and appeal are closed.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 111/2022 is laid to rest/disposed of; the underlying Company Petition CP/5/241/HDB/2022 is closed, and the impugned order dated 19.10.2022 is modified to be read in terms of the Compromise Memo dated 10.05.2024.
summary: Sarah Qureshi appealed against an NCLT Hyderabad order dated 19.10.2022 in CP/5/241/HDB/2022 involving disputes under Sections 59, 213, 241, and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 concerning GB Bakers Industries Pvt. Ltd. During appellate proceedings before the NCLAT Chennai Bench, the parties underwent mediation and submitted a signed Memorandum of Compromise dated 10.05.2024 resolving all disputes. Accepting the mediator's report and verified compromise memo, the Tribunal modified the impugned order to reflect the settlement terms and formally closed the appeal and underlying company petition.

case_title: Geometrix Laser Solutions Pvt. Ltd. vs. Dr. BVS Lakshmi & Anr.
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Member Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma and Technical Member Jatindranath Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Geometrix Laser Solutions Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 1 in the underlying company petition); Respondent No. 1 is Dr. BVS Lakshmi (Petitioner in Section 130 proceedings); Respondent No. 2 is an additional respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Shareholder and corporate governance proceedings initiated under Section 130 of the Companies Act, 2013 by Respondent No. 1 seeking appointment of an independent auditor to reopen and recast financial statements of the Appellant company for eight financial years (FY 2010-2011 to FY 2016-2017). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Dispute over alleged accounting irregularities and recasting of corporate accounts; no specific debt or default amount was in issue in this evidentiary interlocutory application. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Underlying petition CP No. 131/130/HDB/2019 filed before NCLT Hyderabad; Appellant filed IA No. 45/2023 seeking to introduce additional documents; NCLT rejected IA No. 45/2023 on 06.11.2023; appeal decided on 14.06.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Documents sought to be introduced on record comprised copies of police complaints filed before the Police Commissioner, First Information Reports (FIRs), and copies of judicial precedents[cite: 3]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad dismissed IA No. 45/2023 on 06.11.2023 under Rule 40 of NCLT Rules, 2016; the company appealed to NCLAT Chennai under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 3, 4].
