legal_issues: (i) Whether copies of police complaints, FIRs, and criminal investigative papers are admissible as additional evidence under Rule 40 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 in civil proceedings under Section 130 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 3]; (ii) Whether judicial precedents require formal introduction as evidentiary exhibits through an interlocutory application for additional documents.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Documents originating from criminal proceedings (such as police complaints and FIRs) are intended solely for penal adjudication and are inadmissible as evidence in civil or corporate proceedings; furthermore, binding judicial precedents are matters of law that can be cited during oral arguments and cannot be tendered as additional documentary evidence[cite: 3]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 40 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 confers discretionary authority on the Adjudicating Authority to regulate additional evidence; this power must be exercised on grounds of strict legal relevance to the civil issues under inquiry, and cannot be expanded by importing general CPC provisions (Order VIII or Order XIII) into summary corporate inquiries[cite: 3, 4]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed the schedule of proposed documents and observed that the criminal complaints had no legal relevance to the recasting of accounts under Section 130, while copies of judgments needed no formal proof as evidentiary exhibits[cite: 3]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT Hyderabad acted within its procedural discretion under Rule 40 in rejecting IA No. 45/2023, and the appeal is devoid of merit[cite: 4].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 113/2023 is dismissed, affirming the order dated 06.11.2023 passed by NCLT Hyderabad in IA No. 45/2023 in CP No. 131/130/HDB/2019[cite: 4].
summary: Geometrix Laser Solutions Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Hyderabad order dated 06.11.2023 rejecting its interlocutory application (IA No. 45/2023) to introduce additional documents in proceedings under Section 130 of the Companies Act, 2013 filed by Dr. BVS Lakshmi to reopen corporate accounts from 2010 to 2017. The documents sought to be introduced included police complaints, FIRs, and judicial case precedents[cite: 3]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Chennai Bench held that documents pertaining to criminal proceedings cannot be read into evidence in civil proceedings before company tribunals[cite: 3]. The Tribunal affirmed that judicial precedents do not need to be marked as exhibits and that the NCLT properly applied Rule 40 of the NCLT Rules, 2016[cite: 4].

case_title: Sandeep Jindal vs. Corporation Bank (Now Union Bank of India) & Anr.
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 973 of 2024 (IA Nos. 4333 & 4334 of 2024)
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain and Technical Member Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Sandeep Jindal, Suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor; Respondent No. 1 is Corporation Bank (now Union Bank of India, Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is an additional party[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities sanctioned by Corporation Bank (now Union Bank of India) to the Corporate Debtor, subsequently settled via a sanctioned One Time Settlement (OTS) letter dated 14.11.2023 for an aggregate sum of Rs. 8 Crores (Rs. 5 Crores payable by borrower and Rs. 3 Crores by guarantor)[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default leading to admission under Section 7 on 07.05.2024; Appellant paid Rs. 4 Crores till 18.04.2024, Rs. 1.70 Crores on 15.05.2024, and Rs. 1 Crore on 16.05.2024, subsequently satisfying the entire remaining balance under the OTS sanctioned at Rs. 8 Crores[cite: 12, 12]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application admitted by Adjudicating Authority on 07.05.2024; NCLAT stayed further steps on 16.05.2024 granting time till 31.05.2024 to make payment; Bank condoned slight delay via letter dated 11.06.2024; compromise completed and early hearing taken up on 26.06.2024[cite: 12, 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Sanctioned OTS letter dated 14.11.2023 for Rs. 8 Crores; bank extension condonation letter dated 11.06.2024 (Annexure A-2A); payment receipts confirming full remittance of the settlement amount; applications IA No. 4333 of 2024 and IA No. 4334 of 2024 under Rule 11[cite: 12, 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority admitted the Section 7 petition on 07.05.2024; Suspended Director appealed to NCLAT via Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 973 of 2024, leading to the full out-of-court settlement and closure of CIRP[cite: 12, 12].
legal_issues: (i) Whether Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) proceedings initiated under Section 7 of the IBC ought to be closed upon full discharge of debt liabilities pursuant to a mutually accepted One Time Settlement (OTS) between the Corporate Debtor and the Financial Creditor[cite: 12].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a corporate debtor fully satisfies and discharges the entire agreed debt amount under a binding One Time Settlement with the financial creditor during appellate proceedings, the continuation of the corporate insolvency resolution process becomes redundant and must be closed to prevent unnecessary corporate distress[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 read with Section 7 of the IBC empower the Appellate Tribunal to recognize commercial settlements arrived at post-admission and terminate CIRP proceedings when no outstanding default survives[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified bank statements and the respondent bank's explicit confirmation and letter dated 11.06.2024 establishing receipt of the entire Rs. 8 Crore OTS amount without surviving financial claims[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Full payment having been made in satisfaction of the OTS, nothing remains to be pursued under insolvency, warranting formal termination of the CIRP[cite: 12].
operative_order: IA No. 4334 of 2024 is allowed preponing the hearing to 26.06.2024; IA No. 4333 of 2024 is disposed of; and the CIRP proceedings initiated against the Appellant pursuant to the admission order dated 07.05.2024 under Section 7 are hereby closed[cite: 12].
summary: Sandeep Jindal, Suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor, appealed against an Adjudicating Authority order dated 07.05.2024 admitting a Section 7 CIRP application filed by Corporation Bank (now Union Bank of India)[cite: 12]. During the appellate proceedings, the appellant completed payments under an Rs. 8 Crore One Time Settlement sanctioned on 14.11.2023, which the bank acknowledged along with a delay condonation letter dated 11.06.2024[cite: 12, 12]. Moving IA Nos. 4333 and 4334 of 2024 under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016, the appellant sought early disposal on grounds of full satisfaction[cite: 12]. The NCLAT Principal Bench accepted the settlement, preponed the hearing, and formally closed the CIRP proceedings[cite: 12].

case_title: Assistant Provident Fund Commissioner vs. VBC Industries Limited through TSN Raja & 2 Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 12/2021 with Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 304/2021, TA (AT) No. 196/2021 & TA (AT) No. 197/2021
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Member Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma and Technical Member Jatindranath Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: In CA No. 12/2021, the Appellant is Assistant Provident Fund Commissioner, DO Kurnool, Andhra Pradesh; Respondent No. 1 is VBC Industries Limited represented through RP TSN Raja; Respondent No. 2 is Committee of Creditors (CoC); Respondent No. 3 is an additional party[cite: 13]. Companion appeals involve The Assistant Commissioner of Central Tax and workmen/shareholders[cite: 13]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Resolution and statutory claims in the corporate insolvency resolution process of VBC Industries Limited involving statutory dues and provident fund liabilities[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Statutory provident fund and tax dues claimed by statutory authorities against the Corporate Debtor, subject to parallel litigation. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: High Court of Telangana passed judgment in Writ Petition No. 11557/2021 on 03.04.2021; Supreme Court passed judgment in Special Leave to Appeal (C) No(s). 7768/2021 on 18.08.2023; appeal heard before NCLAT Chennai on 07.06.2024[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Delay condonation application IA No. 33/2021; judgment of the Telangana High Court dated 03.04.2021; order of the Supreme Court dated 18.08.2023 in SLP (C) No. 7768/2021[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CA (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 12/2021 was listed along with delay condonation application IA No. 33/2021 before NCLAT Chennai, where no one appeared to press the application on 07.06.2024[cite: 13].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC accompanied by an application for condonation of delay can be maintained when the appellant fails to appear and press the delay condonation application[cite: 13].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal accompanied by a delay condonation application cannot survive or be entertained on merits where the applicant fails to appear and prosecute the application for condonation of delay, entailing dismissal for want of prosecution[cite: 13]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 61 of the IBC, admission of an appeal filed beyond the statutory period is contingent upon the adjudication and allowance of the delay condonation application; rejection of the delay petition for default automatically extinguishes the appeal[cite: 13]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that counsel for respondents appeared while no representation was made on behalf of the appellant to press IA No. 33/2021[cite: 13]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The delay condonation application being rejected for want of prosecution, Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 12/2021 must be dismissed[cite: 13].
operative_order: In CA (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 12/2021, Delay Condonation Application IA No. 33/2021 is rejected for want of prosecution and the Company Appeal stands dismissed; companion appeals CA No. 304/2021, TA No. 196/2021, and TA No. 197/2021 are listed for hearing on 03.07.2024 with directions to exchange pleadings and supply the Supreme Court order dated 18.08.2023[cite: 13].
summary: The Assistant Provident Fund Commissioner, Kurnool, filed Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 12/2021 before NCLAT Chennai challenging proceedings involving VBC Industries Limited, along with delay condonation application IA No. 33/2021[cite: 13]. When the matter was called for hearing, respondents appeared through counsel, but no appearance was made on behalf of the appellant to prosecute the delay condonation plea[cite: 13]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Chennai Bench held that upon the failure of an appellant to appear and press the condonation of delay application, the application stands rejected for want of prosecution, and consequently, the appeal itself stands dismissed as unadmitted[cite: 13].

case_title: Mr. D. N. Pratap Chowdary vs. Mr. Pankaj Bhattad & Ors.
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Member Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma and Technical Member Jatindranath Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Mr. D. N. Pratap Chowdary, Suspended Director of M/s Naolin Infrastructure Private Limited (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 is Mr. Pankaj Bhattad (Interim Resolution Professional); Respondent No. 2 is M/s Mytrah Energy (India) Private Limited (Operational Creditor); Respondent No. 3 is the Corporate Debtor[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Infrastructure contract works and operational transactions between M/s Mytrah Energy (India) Pvt. Ltd. and M/s Naolin Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. resulting in an unpaid operational debt claim[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational default adjudicated under Section 9 of the IBC leading to the initiation of CIRP against the Corporate Debtor[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Hyderabad Bench passed the impugned CIRP admission order under Section 9 in CP(IB) No. 69/9/HDB/2023 on 04.06.2024; Appellant concurrently filed Writ Petition No. 15859/2024 before the High Court; appeal was argued and dismissed on 24.06.2024[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Admission order dated 04.06.2024; records of parallel Writ Petition No. 15859/2024 filed before the High Court challenging the very same NCLT order without disclosure to the Appellate Tribunal[cite: 14]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad admitted the Section 9 application on 04.06.2024; Suspended Director filed Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 210/2024 before NCLAT Chennai, while simultaneously pursuing Writ Petition No. 15859/2024 before the High Court without disclosing the parallel proceeding[cite: 14].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an appellant can simultaneously pursue parallel remedies before a High Court under Article 226 and an Appellate Tribunal under Section 61 of the IBC against the same CIRP admission order; (ii) Whether concealment of the pendency of a parallel writ petition constitutes an abuse of process justifying dismissal of the appeal[cite: 14].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A litigant cannot be permitted to pursue two simultaneous, parallel judicial remedies before different forums for the identical cause of action; concealing the invocation and pendency of an extraordinary writ remedy while arguing a statutory appeal constitutes an abuse of the process of law disentitling the party to equitable or appellate relief[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory appellate remedy under Section 61 of the IBC cannot be exercised in favor of a litigant who engages in forum shopping and material suppression of contemporaneous constitutional writ proceedings challenging the same impugned order[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the disclosure upon respondent's objection, finding that Writ Petition No. 15859/2024 was actively pending against the order dated 04.06.2024 and had been deliberately concealed by the appellant during oral arguments[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal is an abuse of process tainted by material non-disclosure, warranting summary dismissal[cite: 14].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 210 of 2024 and IA No. 571/2024 are dismissed on account of misconduct and suppression of facts[cite: 14].
summary: Mr. D. N. Pratap Chowdary, Suspended Director of Naolin Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd., appealed against an NCLT Hyderabad order dated 04.06.2024 admitting a Section 9 CIRP petition filed by Mytrah Energy (India) Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 14] During oral arguments, the respondent Operational Creditor disclosed that the appellant had simultaneously instituted Writ Petition No. 15859/2024 before the High Court challenging the identical admission order, which fact was suppressed from the Appellate Tribunal[cite: 14]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Chennai Bench held that pursuing two parallel remedies for the same cause of action while concealing the writ petition constitutes an abuse of the judicial process, disentitling the appellant from relief[cite: 14].

case_title: TP Anilkumar & Ors. vs. Indus Motor Company Private Limited & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 27/2024 with Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 28/2024 (IA Nos. 477, 478 & 479/2024)
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Member Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma and Technical Member Jatindranath Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: In CA No. 27/2024, the Appellants are TP Anilkumar & Ors.; in CA No. 28/2024, the Appellants are TP Ajithkumar & Ors. (shareholders/directors); Respondents are Indus Motor Company Private Limited & Ors.[cite: 15] 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Internal corporate governance and shareholder dispute under company petition CP No. 02/KOB/2020 pending before NCLT Kochi Bench, wherein a comprehensive forensic audit was directed into company affairs[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Dispute over corporate mismanagement and forensic examination findings; no specific monetary debt default adjudicated in this procedural timeline appeal. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company Petition filed in 2020; Interim Forensic Audit Report submitted on 02.04.2024; Final Forensic Audit Report submitted on 24.04.2024; NCLT Kochi rejected IA No. 64/KOB/2024 on 02.05.2024; NCLT took reports on record granting 1 week to file objections on 27.05.2024; appeals disposed of on 06.06.2024[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Interim Forensic Audit Report dated 02.04.2024; Final Forensic Audit Report dated 24.04.2024; NCLT Kochi orders dated 02.05.2024 and 27.05.2024[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kochi dismissed IA No. 64/KOB/2024 on 02.05.2024 seeking stay of audit and document supply as infructuous, and later granted one week on 27.05.2024 to file objections; Appellants appealed to NCLAT Chennai in CA Nos. 27 and 28 of 2024[cite: 15].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an Adjudicating Authority erred in granting an excessively constricted timeframe of one week to file objections to voluminous Interim and Final Forensic Audit Reports[cite: 15]; (ii) Whether appellate intervention is justified to balance equities by extending time to file objections while preserving expeditious trial of an old company petition[cite: 15].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In corporate adjudication where interim and final forensic audit reports carry a direct, determinative bearing on the substantive merits of a company petition, principles of natural justice and equity require that litigating parties be afforded a reasonable and fair opportunity to submit objections before reports are finalized against them[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Appellate authority under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 encompasses procedural modifications of Adjudicating Authority timelines to balance fairness with expedition, ensuring procedural deadlines do not defeat substantive defenses[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the interim and final reports were taken on record on 27.05.2024, one week was inadequate to analyze them, and the respondent consented to a peremptory two-week extension[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Granting an absolute final extension of two weeks to file objections balances equity and ends the appellate controversy, while keeping merits open for the NCLT[cite: 15].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 27/2024 is dismissed as withdrawn; Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 28/2024 is closed by modifying the order dated 27.05.2024 to grant the Appellants a peremptory two weeks from 06.06.2024 to file objections to the forensic audit reports with no further extension, and requesting NCLT Kochi to decide CP No. 02/KOB/2020 expeditiously[cite: 15].
summary: TP Anilkumar and TP Ajithkumar appealed against NCLT Kochi orders dated 02.05.2024 and 27.05.2024 in CP No. 02/KOB/2020 concerning Indus Motor Company Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 15] The NCLT had taken Interim and Final Forensic Audit Reports on record and granted the appellants only one week to submit objections, failing which further objections would be precluded[cite: 15]. In CA No. 27/2024, the appellant withdrew the appeal[cite: 15]. In CA No. 28/2024, the NCLAT Chennai Bench held that given the serious impact of forensic reports, parties must have adequate opportunity to respond[cite: 15]. By consent, the Tribunal extended the objection period by a final two weeks, barred further extensions, and closed the appeal[cite: 15].

case_title: Income Tax Department Through Deputy Commissioner of Income Tax vs. ILC Industries Ltd. & 2 Ors.
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Member Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma and Technical Member Jatindranath Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Income Tax Department Through Deputy Commissioner of Income Tax (Operational Creditor); Respondent No. 1 is ILC Industries Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondents Nos. 2 and 3 are additional parties[cite: 16]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Assessment and operational statutory income tax claims against the Corporate Debtor undergoing insolvency proceedings under CP(IB) No. 155/BB/2018 before NCLT Bengaluru[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Statutory income tax liabilities claimed against the Corporate Debtor, adversely affected by the approval or disposal orders in IA No. 12/2020[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Bengaluru passed the impugned order on 13.01.2020; Appellant received knowledge and copy on 13.02.2020; statutory 30-day appeal period expired on 14.03.2020; Supreme Court Covid-19 limitation extension began on 15.03.2020; appeal filed on 28.06.2021 (over 15 months later)[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Impugned order dated 13.01.2020; Delay Condonation Application IA No. 1207/2020 admitting knowledge date as 13.02.2020; absence of certified copy application[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru passed an order in IA No. 12/2020 on 13.01.2020; Appellant filed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 469/2021 (transferred as TA (AT) No. 194/2021) on 28.06.2021 seeking benefit of the Covid-19 limitation extension[cite: 16].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the benefit of the Supreme Court's suo motu extension of limitation due to Covid-19 applies to an appeal under Section 61(2) of the IBC where the initial 30-day limitation period had already expired prior to 15.03.2020[cite: 16]; (ii) Whether failure to apply for a certified copy within 30 days of receipt/knowledge of the impugned order forfeits entitlement to condonation under Section 61(2)[cite: 16].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The general extension of limitation granted by the Supreme Court during the Covid-19 pandemic extends solely the period of limitation and not the discretionary condonable period under a special statute; where the initial statutory limitation period expired prior to 15.03.2020, the litigant cannot seek refuge under the pandemic extension orders[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 61(1) and 61(2) of the IBC, an appeal must be preferred within 30 days, extendable by up to 15 days only upon showing sufficient cause; as held in Sagufa Ahmed, once the primary 30-day window expires prior to the pandemic freeze, the appeal cannot be revived over a year later[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the appellant's pleadings, finding that knowledge was acquired on 13.02.2020, the 30 days expired on 14.03.2020 before the apex court's order took effect on 15.03.2020, and no certified copy was ever applied for[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal is grossly time-barred and cannot be condoned under Section 61(2) of the IBC[cite: 16].
operative_order: IA No. 1207/2020 for condonation of delay is rejected, and TA (AT) No. 194/2021 (Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 469/2021) is dismissed as barred by limitation[cite: 16].
summary: The Income Tax Department appealed against an NCLT Bengaluru order dated 13.01.2020 passed in IA No. 12/2020 in CP(IB) No. 155/BB/2018 concerning ILC Industries Ltd.[cite: 16] The appellant admitted receiving knowledge of the order on 13.02.2020, meaning its 30-day period expired on 14.03.2020, but filed the appeal only on 28.06.2021, seeking refuge under the Supreme Court's Covid-19 limitation extension[cite: 16]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Chennai Bench relied on Sagufa Ahmed v. Upper Assam Plywood Products to hold that the pandemic extension only preserved unexpired limitation periods, not discretionary condonation windows that expired prior to 15.03.2020[cite: 16]. The appeal was dismissed as barred by limitation[cite: 16].

case_title: M/s Afita Constructions Pvt. Ltd. vs. Dr. G.V. Narasimha Rao & Anr.
appeal_number: IA No. 528/2024 in Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 326/2023 (IA No. 992/2023)
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Member Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma and Technical Member Jatindranath Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Applicant/Appellant is M/s Afita Constructions Pvt. Ltd. (through Managing Director Mr. Firoz Akbarali Sadikot); Respondent No. 1 is Dr. G.V. Narasimha Rao (Resolution Professional); Respondent No. 2 is Neoaska Pharma Private Limited[cite: 17]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Construction and operational claims involved in the insolvency proceedings of Neoaska Pharma Private Limited[cite: 17]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default and claim distribution metrics adjudicated in the resolution process culminating in appellate orders; no independent monetary claim metric was adjudicated in this procedural application[cite: 17]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLAT Chennai dismissed CA (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 326/2023 on 20.10.2023; Supreme Court disposed of Section 62 appeal observing liberty to file review to be decided in accordance with law; Applicant filed IA No. 528/2024 under Rule 11 of NCLAT Rules seeking recall of the order; decided on 21.06.2024[cite: 17]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLAT judgment dated 20.10.2023; Supreme Court order under Section 62 leaving review open to be decided in accordance with law; Recall application IA No. 528/2024[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Following dismissal of its appeal by NCLAT Chennai on 20.10.2023, Appellant moved the Supreme Court, which granted liberty to pursue review in accordance with law; Appellant then filed IA No. 528/2024 styling it as an application for recall under Rule 11[cite: 17].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an application for review or recall is maintainable before the NCLAT under the IBC, 2016 or Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016; (ii) Whether liberty granted by the Supreme Court to seek review 'in accordance with law' enables a party to convert a review into a recall application to re-argue an appeal de novo[cite: 17].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The power of review or substantive recall of a final judgment does not exist under the IBC, and liberty granted by an appellate court to seek review in accordance with law cannot be converted into an impermissible application for recall to obtain a de novo rehearing of an appeal already decided on merits[cite: 17]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 does not provide for review jurisdiction; hence, any review or recall filed pursuant to liberty to act 'in accordance with law' must be rejected because the governing code contains no statutory basis for such a proceeding[cite: 17]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examined the relief sought in IA No. 528/2024 and determined it was an attempt to reopen concluded issues through a disguised review/recall application[cite: 17]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Review not being contemplated under the IBC, the application cannot be maintained under Rule 11 and must be rejected[cite: 17].
operative_order: IA No. 528/2024 in Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 326/2023 is rejected[cite: 17].
summary: M/s Afita Constructions Pvt. Ltd. filed IA No. 528/2024 invoking Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 seeking recall of an NCLAT Chennai judgment dated 20.10.2023 passed in CA (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 326/2023[cite: 17]. The applicant had challenged the judgment before the Supreme Court under Section 62 of the IBC, where the Court left it open to file a review to be decided 'in accordance with law'[cite: 17]. Dismissing the application, the NCLAT Chennai Bench held that the IBC does not statutorily provide for review, and liberty to file a review in accordance with law cannot be converted into a recall petition to re-argue the appeal de novo[cite: 17].

case_title: M/s Bhagyanagar Hotel Pvt Ltd. vs. Krishna Mohan Gollamudi, Liquidator of M/s. Sai Nath Estates Pvt. Ltd.
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Member Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma and Technical Member Jatindranath Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is M/s Bhagyanagar Hotel Pvt Ltd.; the Respondent is Mr. Krishna Mohan Gollamudi, Liquidator of M/s Sai Nath Estates Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 18]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operation of a running hotel on commercial premises owned by the Corporate Debtor undergoing liquidation proceedings[cite: 18]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Liquidation estate asset recovery and possession proceedings; no specific monetary claim metric formed the subject matter of the miscellaneous applications[cite: 18]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLAT Chennai finally adjudicated CA (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 13/2024 on 29.04.2024; Supreme Court dismissed Civil Appeal No. 6332/2024 on 17.05.2024 granting liberty to seek time to close the hotel; Appellant filed IA Nos. 471, 472, and 473/2024; decided on 05.06.2024[cite: 18]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLAT judgment dated 29.04.2024; Supreme Court order dated 17.05.2024 in Civil Appeal No. 6332/2024; formal undertaking by appellant's counsel to vacate premises within three months[cite: 18]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: After the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal against the NCLAT judgment on 17.05.2024 while allowing liberty to seek time to close operations, Appellant filed IA No. 471/2024 to reopen the appeal afresh, IA No. 472/2024 for 3 months to vacate, and IA No. 473/2024 for stay[cite: 18].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an appellate tribunal can entertain an application to reopen and rehear an appeal on merits after the judgment has been affirmed and the appeal dismissed by the Supreme Court[cite: 18]; (ii) Whether a tenant/occupant of a corporate debtor's liquidation asset may be granted time to vacate based on an undertaking given pursuant to Supreme Court liberty[cite: 18].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal possesses no legal jurisdiction to reopen or rehear an appeal on merits once its final judgment has been tested before and affirmed by the Supreme Court; any application seeking to reopen proceedings that have attained finality before the apex court is fundamentally misconceived[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Liberty granted by the Supreme Court to seek limited time to vacate or wind down commercial operations from an insolvency estate must be strictly exercised within the four corners of the apex court's directions and cannot be converted into a backdoor attempt to relitigate substantive rights[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the Supreme Court order dated 17.05.2024 dismissing the Civil Appeal and the unconditional undertaking given by the appellant's counsel to hand over peaceful possession within three months[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Reopening of the appeal is rejected; three months' time is granted to vacate the premises upon an undertaking, with no further extension permitted[cite: 18].
operative_order: IA No. 471/2024 (reopening of appeal) is dismissed; IA No. 472/2024 is disposed of recording the Appellant's undertaking to vacate the hotel premises positively within 3 months from 05.06.2024 with no further extensions; and IA No. 473/2024 is closed without separate orders[cite: 18].
summary: M/s Bhagyanagar Hotel Pvt. Ltd. filed applications before NCLAT Chennai following the dismissal of its Civil Appeal No. 6332/2024 by the Supreme Court on 17.05.2024[cite: 18]. In IA No. 471/2024, the appellant sought to reopen the company appeal to be heard afresh on merits, while in IA No. 472/2024 it prayed for three months' time to vacate the premises of Sai Nath Estates Pvt. Ltd. (in liquidation)[cite: 18]. Dismissing the plea to reopen the appeal as misconceived, the NCLAT Chennai Bench held that proceedings affirmed by the Supreme Court cannot be reheard[cite: 18]. Operating on the Supreme Court's liberty, the Tribunal granted a final three-month period to vacate the premises based on the appellant's undertaking[cite: 18].

case_title: Hackbridge Hewittic and Easun Ltd. vs. State Bank of India
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Member Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma and Technical Member Jatindranath Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Hackbridge Hewittic and Easun Ltd. (Corporate Debtor / Respondent in Company Petition); the Respondent is State Bank of India (Financial Creditor)[cite: 19]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial credit facilities availed by the Corporate Debtor from State Bank of India, leading to insolvency proceedings under Company Petition No. IBA/1178/2019[cite: 19]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Financial debt default forming the foundation of the Section 7 petition IBA/1178/2019; no specific monetary figures were adjudicated in this procedural pleading appeal[cite: 19]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Insolvency petition IBA/1178/2019 instituted before NCLT; NCLT passed impugned order on 24.07.2023 declining leave to file supplementary counter affidavit; NCLAT decided appeal on 05.06.2024[cite: 19]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Principal Counter Affidavit previously filed; Supplementary Counter Affidavit tendered by the Corporate Debtor; NCLT impugned order dated 24.07.2023[cite: 19]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT rejected the Corporate Debtor's request to place a supplementary counter affidavit on record on 24.07.2023 in the absence of prior leave and on grounds of conflict with initial pleadings; the Corporate Debtor appealed to NCLAT Chennai[cite: 19].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an Adjudicating Authority can evaluate the evidentiary veracity and substantive admissibility of a supplementary counter affidavit at the threshold stage of deciding whether to grant leave to take it on record[cite: 19]; (ii) Whether a litigating respondent in an insolvency proceeding should be permitted reasonable freedom to formulate and exchange pleadings without premature judicial restriction[cite: 19].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority adjudicating upon an issue should not prematurely restrain a party from exchanging their pleadings, nor should it evaluate the veracity, merits, or evidentiary admissibility of supplementary pleadings at the preliminary threshold of granting leave to take them on record[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Procedural regulations, including Rule 52 of the NCLT Rules, 2016, must be administered to facilitate complete presentation of rival cases; taking a supplementary pleading on record does not amount to an acceptance of its merits or propriety, which remain entirely open to be argued at final hearing[cite: 19]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal observed that the NCLT rejected the supplementary counter affidavit based on perceived inconsistencies with earlier pleadings without reserving that evaluation for the final hearing[cite: 19]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The impugned order declining leave is quashed; leave to place the supplementary counter affidavit on record is granted, while prayer to withdraw the initial counter affidavit is denied[cite: 19].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 360/2023 is allowed partly for Relief No. 1 by quashing the order dated 24.07.2023 and granting leave to place the supplementary counter affidavit on record in IBA/1178/2019 before NCLT, while Relief No. 2 regarding withdrawal of the initial counter affidavit is denied[cite: 19].
summary: Hackbridge Hewittic and Easun Ltd. appealed against an NCLT order dated 24.07.2023 passed in IBA/1178/2019, whereby the Adjudicating Authority declined to take its supplementary counter affidavit on record for lack of prior leave and alleged conflict with its original counter affidavit under Rule 52 of the NCLT Rules[cite: 19]. Setting aside the order, the NCLAT Chennai Bench held that an Adjudicating Authority should not restrict a party from exchanging pleadings or pre-judge the veracity and substantive merits of an affidavit at the threshold stage of placing it on record[cite: 19]. The Tribunal granted leave to file the supplementary counter affidavit while keeping all substantive arguments open for final determination by the NCLT[cite: 19].

case_title: Alfa Chemo Plast Pvt. Ltd. vs. U Foam Pvt. Ltd.
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Member Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma and Technical Member Jatindranath Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Alfa Chemo Plast Pvt. Ltd. (Aggrieved Creditor / Applicant); the Respondent is U Foam Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 20]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Insolvency resolution process of U Foam Pvt. Ltd. under CP (IB) No. 698/10/HDB/2018 culminating in the submission and approval of a resolution plan under Section 30(6) of the IBC[cite: 20]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational or financial claims dealt with under the approved resolution plan in IA No. 2/2021[cite: 20]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Hyderabad approved the resolution plan on 12.08.2021; Appellant e-filed appeal on 25.04.2022; defects notified by Registry on 25.04.2022; refiling done on 11.02.2024 after a 644-day delay; initial filing delay was 218 days, leaving 89 days delay even after excluding the Covid-19 limitation moratorium; appeal decided on 11.06.2024[cite: 20]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registry defect endorsement dated 25.04.2022; delay calculation showing 644 days in refiling and 89 days in filing beyond statutory/Covid limits; delay applications IA Nos. 453 and 454 of 2024[cite: 20]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad approved the resolution plan on 12.08.2021; Appellant e-filed CA (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 171/2024 on 25.04.2022 with defects, which were refiled only on 11.02.2024 alongside delay applications[cite: 20].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an unexplained inordinate delay of 644 days in refiling an appeal after curing defects can be condoned; (ii) Whether the NCLAT has jurisdiction under the proviso to Section 61(2) of the IBC to condone an initial filing delay of 89 days that persists beyond the permissible statutory 15-day condonable period and the Covid-19 exclusion period[cite: 20].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Litigants must exercise due diligence in prosecuting legal remedies; an unexplained, inordinate delay in refiling an appeal cannot be casually condoned, and an appellate tribunal lacks statutory jurisdiction to condone a filing delay exceeding the outer limit of 15 days prescribed under the proviso to Section 61(2) of the IBC[cite: 20]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) mandates that appeals must be filed within 30 days, with a strict maximum discretionary condonation period of 15 days; where an appeal remains delayed by 89 days even after granting the full benefit of the Supreme Court Covid-19 limitation exclusion, the delay falls outside the statutory boundary and the tribunal is legally powerless to condone it[cite: 20]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examined the defect records and delay applications, finding that defects notified on 25.04.2022 were refiled after 644 days without plausible reason, and net filing delay stood at 89 days[cite: 20]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Applications for condonation of refiling and filing delay lack legal merit and must be rejected, entailing dismissal of the appeal[cite: 20].
operative_order: IA No. 454/2024 (refiling delay of 644 days) and IA No. 453/2024 (filing delay of 89 days) are dismissed; consequently, Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 171/2024 is dismissed as time-barred, and all connected IAs are closed[cite: 20].
summary: Alfa Chemo Plast Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Hyderabad order dated 12.08.2021 approving the resolution plan of U Foam Pvt. Ltd. in CP (IB) No. 698/10/HDB/2018[cite: 20]. The appeal was e-filed on 25.04.2022, defects were communicated the same day, but refiling took place only on 11.02.2024 after an unexplained delay of 644 days[cite: 20]. Furthermore, even after excluding the Supreme Court Covid-19 limitation moratorium, an initial filing delay of 89 days remained[cite: 20]. Rejecting both delay condonation applications, the NCLAT Chennai Bench held that the refiling delay was completely unjustified and that the filing delay of 89 days far exceeded the strict 15-day limit condonable under Section 61(2) of the IBC, dismissing the appeal as barred by limitation[cite: 20].

case_title: Sandeep Jindal vs. Corporation Bank (Now Union Bank of India) & Anr.
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 973 of 2024 (IA Nos. 4333 & 4334 of 2024)
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain and Technical Member Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Sandeep Jindal, Suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor; Respondent No. 1 is Corporation Bank (now Union Bank of India, Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is an additional party[cite: 21]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities sanctioned by Corporation Bank (now Union Bank of India) to the Corporate Debtor, subsequently settled via a sanctioned One Time Settlement (OTS) letter dated 14.11.2023 for an aggregate sum of Rs. 8 Crores (Rs. 5 Crores payable by borrower and Rs. 3 Crores by guarantor)[cite: 21]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default leading to admission under Section 7 on 07.05.2024; Appellant paid Rs. 4 Crores till 18.04.2024, Rs. 1.70 Crores on 15.05.2024, and Rs. 1 Crore on 16.05.2024, subsequently satisfying the entire remaining balance under the OTS sanctioned at Rs. 8 Crores[cite: 21]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application admitted by Adjudicating Authority on 07.05.2024; NCLAT stayed further steps on 16.05.2024 granting time till 31.05.2024 to make payment; Bank condoned slight delay via letter dated 11.06.2024; compromise completed and early hearing taken up on 26.06.2024[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Sanctioned OTS letter dated 14.11.2023 for Rs. 8 Crores; bank extension condonation letter dated 11.06.2024 (Annexure A-2A); payment receipts confirming full remittance of the settlement amount; applications IA No. 4333 of 2024 and IA No. 4334 of 2024 under Rule 11[cite: 21]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority admitted the Section 7 petition on 07.05.2024; Suspended Director appealed to NCLAT via Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 973 of 2024, leading to the full out-of-court settlement and closure of CIRP[cite: 21].
legal_issues: (i) Whether Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) proceedings initiated under Section 7 of the IBC ought to be closed upon full discharge of debt liabilities pursuant to a mutually accepted One Time Settlement (OTS) between the Corporate Debtor and the Financial Creditor[cite: 21].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a corporate debtor fully satisfies and discharges the entire agreed debt amount under a binding One Time Settlement with the financial creditor during appellate proceedings, the continuation of the corporate insolvency resolution process becomes redundant and must be closed to prevent unnecessary corporate distress[cite: 21]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 read with Section 7 of the IBC empower the Appellate Tribunal to recognize commercial settlements arrived at post-admission and terminate CIRP proceedings when no outstanding default survives[cite: 21]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified bank statements and the respondent bank's explicit confirmation and letter dated 11.06.2024 establishing receipt of the entire Rs. 8 Crore OTS amount without surviving financial claims[cite: 21]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Full payment having been made in satisfaction of the OTS, nothing remains to be pursued under insolvency, warranting formal termination of the CIRP[cite: 21].
operative_order: IA No. 4334 of 2024 is allowed preponing the hearing to 26.06.2024; IA No. 4333 of 2024 is disposed of; and the CIRP proceedings initiated against the Appellant pursuant to the admission order dated 07.05.2024 under Section 7 are hereby closed[cite: 21].
summary: Sandeep Jindal, Suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor, appealed against an Adjudicating Authority order dated 07.05.2024 admitting a Section 7 CIRP application filed by Corporation Bank (now Union Bank of India)[cite: 21]. During the appellate proceedings, the appellant completed payments under an Rs. 8 Crore One Time Settlement sanctioned on 14.11.2023, which the bank acknowledged along with a delay condonation letter dated 11.06.2024[cite: 21]. Moving IA Nos. 4333 and 4334 of 2024 under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016, the appellant sought early disposal on grounds of full satisfaction[cite: 21]. The NCLAT Principal Bench accepted the settlement, preponed the hearing, and formally closed the CIRP proceedings[cite: 21].

case_title: Assistant Provident Fund Commissioner vs. VBC Industries Limited through TSN Raja & 2 Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 12/2021 with Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 304/2021, TA (AT) No. 196/2021 & TA (AT) No. 197/2021
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Member Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma and Technical Member Jatindranath Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: In CA No. 12/2021, the Appellant is Assistant Provident Fund Commissioner, DO Kurnool, Andhra Pradesh; Respondent No. 1 is VBC Industries Limited represented through RP TSN Raja; Respondent No. 2 is Committee of Creditors (CoC); Respondent No. 3 is an additional party[cite: 22]. Companion appeals involve The Assistant Commissioner of Central Tax and workmen/shareholders[cite: 22]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Resolution and statutory claims in the corporate insolvency resolution process of VBC Industries Limited involving statutory dues and provident fund liabilities[cite: 22]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Statutory provident fund and tax dues claimed by statutory authorities against the Corporate Debtor, subject to parallel litigation. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: High Court of Telangana passed judgment in Writ Petition No. 11557/2021 on 03.04.2021; Supreme Court passed judgment in Special Leave to Appeal (C) No(s). 7768/2021 on 18.08.2023; appeal heard before NCLAT Chennai on 07.06.2024[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Delay condonation application IA No. 33/2021; judgment of the Telangana High Court dated 03.04.2021; order of the Supreme Court dated 18.08.2023 in SLP (C) No. 7768/2021[cite: 22]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CA (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 12/2021 was listed along with delay condonation application IA No. 33/2021 before NCLAT Chennai, where no one appeared to press the application on 07.06.2024[cite: 22].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC accompanied by an application for condonation of delay can be maintained when the appellant fails to appear and press the delay condonation application[cite: 22].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal accompanied by a delay condonation application cannot survive or be entertained on merits where the applicant fails to appear and prosecute the application for condonation of delay, entailing dismissal for want of prosecution[cite: 22]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 61 of the IBC, admission of an appeal filed beyond the statutory period is contingent upon the adjudication and allowance of the delay condonation application; rejection of the delay petition for default automatically extinguishes the appeal[cite: 22]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that counsel for respondents appeared while no representation was made on behalf of the appellant to press IA No. 33/2021[cite: 22]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The delay condonation application being rejected for want of prosecution, Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 12/2021 must be dismissed[cite: 22].
operative_order: In CA (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 12/2021, Delay Condonation Application IA No. 33/2021 is rejected for want of prosecution and the Company Appeal stands dismissed; companion appeals CA No. 304/2021, TA No. 196/2021, and TA No. 197/2021 are listed for hearing on 03.07.2024 with directions to exchange pleadings and supply the Supreme Court order dated 18.08.2023[cite: 22].
summary: The Assistant Provident Fund Commissioner, Kurnool, filed Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 12/2021 before NCLAT Chennai challenging proceedings involving VBC Industries Limited, along with delay condonation application IA No. 33/2021[cite: 22]. When the matter was called for hearing, respondents appeared through counsel, but no appearance was made on behalf of the appellant to prosecute the delay condonation plea[cite: 22]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Chennai Bench held that upon the failure of an appellant to appear and press the condonation of delay application, the application stands rejected for want of prosecution, and consequently, the appeal itself stands dismissed as unadmitted[cite: 22].

case_title: Mr. D. N. Pratap Chowdary vs. Mr. Pankaj Bhattad & Ors.
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Member Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma and Technical Member Jatindranath Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Mr. D. N. Pratap Chowdary, Suspended Director of M/s Naolin Infrastructure Private Limited (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 is Mr. Pankaj Bhattad (Interim Resolution Professional); Respondent No. 2 is M/s Mytrah Energy (India) Private Limited (Operational Creditor); Respondent No. 3 is the Corporate Debtor[cite: 23]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Infrastructure contract works and operational transactions between M/s Mytrah Energy (India) Pvt. Ltd. and M/s Naolin Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. resulting in an unpaid operational debt claim[cite: 23]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational default adjudicated under Section 9 of the IBC leading to the initiation of CIRP against the Corporate Debtor[cite: 23]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Hyderabad Bench passed the impugned CIRP admission order under Section 9 in CP(IB) No. 69/9/HDB/2023 on 04.06.2024; Appellant concurrently filed Writ Petition No. 15859/2024 before the High Court; appeal was argued and dismissed on 24.06.2024[cite: 23]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Admission order dated 04.06.2024; records of parallel Writ Petition No. 15859/2024 filed before the High Court challenging the very same NCLT order without disclosure to the Appellate Tribunal[cite: 23]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad admitted the Section 9 application on 04.06.2024; Suspended Director filed Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 210/2024 before NCLAT Chennai, while simultaneously pursuing Writ Petition No. 15859/2024 before the High Court without disclosing the parallel proceeding[cite: 23].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an appellant can simultaneously pursue parallel remedies before a High Court under Article 226 and an Appellate Tribunal under Section 61 of the IBC against the same CIRP admission order; (ii) Whether concealment of the pendency of a parallel writ petition constitutes an abuse of process justifying dismissal of the appeal[cite: 23].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A litigant cannot be permitted to pursue two simultaneous, parallel judicial remedies before different forums for the identical cause of action; concealing the invocation and pendency of an extraordinary writ remedy while arguing a statutory appeal constitutes an abuse of the process of law disentitling the party to equitable or appellate relief[cite: 23]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory appellate remedy under Section 61 of the IBC cannot be exercised in favor of a litigant who engages in forum shopping and material suppression of contemporaneous constitutional writ proceedings challenging the same impugned order[cite: 23]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the disclosure upon respondent's objection, finding that Writ Petition No. 15859/2024 was actively pending against the order dated 04.06.2024 and had been deliberately concealed by the appellant during oral arguments[cite: 23]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal is an abuse of process tainted by material non-disclosure, warranting summary dismissal[cite: 23].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 210 of 2024 and IA No. 571/2024 are dismissed on account of misconduct and suppression of facts[cite: 23].
summary: Mr. D. N. Pratap Chowdary, Suspended Director of Naolin Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd., appealed against an NCLT Hyderabad order dated 04.06.2024 admitting a Section 9 CIRP petition filed by Mytrah Energy (India) Pvt. Ltd[cite: 23]. During oral arguments, the respondent Operational Creditor disclosed that the appellant had simultaneously instituted Writ Petition No. 15859/2024 before the High Court challenging the identical admission order, which fact was suppressed from the Appellate Tribunal[cite: 23]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Chennai Bench held that pursuing two parallel remedies for the same cause of action while concealing the writ petition constitutes an abuse of the judicial process, disentitling the appellant from relief[cite: 23].

case_title: Crown Business Park Tower A Buyers Association vs. Atul Kumar Kansal & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 431 of 2023 with Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 432, 433 & 434 of 2023
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Crown Business Park Tower A Buyers Association (Comp. App. 431/2023), Amarjit Singh, Suspended Director of Crown Realtech Pvt. Ltd. (Comp. App. 432 & 433/2023), and Cimco Projects Ltd., a PRA that failed to submit a plan (Comp. App. 434/2023). Respondent No. 1 is Atul Kumar Kansal, RP of Crown Realtech Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 3, 3]. Respondent No. 3 is Crown Abacus IT Park Association, an association of 225 allottees (Successful Resolution Applicant / SRA). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was developing a commercial/IT real estate project launched in 2007. Section 7 CIRP was initiated on 06.12.2019 on a petition by homebuyer Mohan Agarwal. Real estate allottees constituted 95.82% of the CoC voting share. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Admitted homebuyer claims totaled Rs. 155.97 Crores. SRA submitted a resolution plan outlay of Rs. 155.11 Crores, which the CoC approved in its 8th meeting on 05.12.2020 with a 96.38% vote share. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 06.12.2019. CoC was constituted on 03.01.2020. Last date for submitting resolution plans was extended to 30.09.2020, on which date only SRA submitted a plan. CoC approved the plan on 05.12.2020. RP filed approval IA No. 5687/2020 on 11.12.2020. NCLT Principal Bench approved the plan on 21.02.2023 while dismissing Amarjit Singh's objection IA No. 5006/2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Minutes of CoC meetings (specifically the 2nd and 3rd meetings revising RFRP criteria for associations registered prior to 03.01.2020 and reducing PBG to Rs. 5 Lakhs), Form G publications, Information Memorandum and Addendum dated 20.08.2020, and the approved Resolution Plan. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench approved SRA's resolution plan on 21.02.2023 in IA No. 5687/2020 and deferred pending claim IAs. Appellants appealed to NCLAT alleging discriminatory RFRP eligibility criteria, mismatch in saleable area (1,00,000 sq. ft. vs 83,944 sq. ft.), illegality in monetizing car parks, and denial of hearing.
legal_issues: (i) Whether fixing distinct eligibility criteria and reduced Performance Bank Guarantee thresholds under Section 25(2)(h) and Regulation 36A for an association of homebuyers constitutes hostile discrimination against other PRAs; (ii) Whether fixing the CoC constitution date (03.01.2020) as the registration cut-off date for eligible allottee associations is arbitrary; (iii) Whether a resolution plan is invalidated by the lack of absolute certainty regarding saleable inventory when the Adjudicating Authority defers unresolved homebuyer claim applications and the SRA undertakes to absorb resulting liabilities; (iv) Whether monetizing multi-level covered car parking spaces in a commercial real estate resolution plan violates Section 2(n) of the RERA Act, 2016.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 25(2)(h) of the IBC and Regulation 36A(4), the CoC possesses the commercial discretion to prescribe distinct, rational eligibility criteria for different categories of prospective resolution applicants, and extending relaxed net worth/PBG criteria to an association of homebuyers who have already funded the project does not constitute impermissible discrimination. Furthermore, the lack of complete inventory certainty does not vitiate a resolution plan where the SRA is an allottees' association that voluntarily assumes the commercial risk and gives an unconditional undertaking to honor liabilities arising from deferred claim adjudications. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 2(n)(iii) of the RERA Act, 2016 defines common areas to include only 'open parking areas'; covered, multi-level parking constructed at substantial capital expenditure in commercial/IT projects does not constitute non-alienable common area under RERA and can be legitimately allocated to generate plan funding. In line with K. Sashidhar and Jaypee Kensington, the commercial wisdom of a 96.38% CoC majority dominated by allottees cannot be judicially reviewed absent non-compliance with Section 30(2). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the CoC was constituted on 03.01.2020, establishing a valid rational nexus for the cut-off date; Cimco Projects failed to submit a plan despite extensions; and available project space (2,49,171 sq. ft.) adequately cushioned the 1,00,000 sq. ft. inventory projection against pending claims. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The resolution plan was legally compliant under Section 30(2) and approved in accordance with the commercial wisdom of the CoC; the NCLT order approving the plan was sound, subject to SRA honoring subsequent claim adjudications.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 432, 433, and 434 of 2023 are dismissed, and all interim orders stand vacated. Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 431 of 2023 is disposed of by upholding the NCLT approval order dated 21.02.2023, subject to the direction that the SRA shall give effect to all claims accepted in pending applications in the same manner as other real estate allottees under the plan, and the Adjudicating Authority is directed to dispose of pending applications expeditiously. Parties shall bear their own costs.
summary: Appellants comprising an excluded buyers association, suspended management, and an interested bidder challenged an NCLT Principal Bench order approving the resolution plan of Crown Realtech Pvt. Ltd. submitted by Crown Abacus IT Park Association (homebuyers association) with 96.38% CoC voting. The appellants alleged discriminatory RFRP criteria, arbitrary cut-off dates, inventory discrepancies, and unlawful sale of parking spaces. Dismissing the appeals, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that the CoC is legally empowered under Regulation 36A to frame rational distinct criteria for allottee associations, and that covered multi-level parking is not non-alienable common area under RERA Section 2(n). The Tribunal upheld the plan subject to the SRA honoring subsequent claim determinations.

case_title: Deepak Sakharam Kulkarni & Connected Matters vs. Manoj Kumar Agarwal, RP of D.S. Kulkarni Developers Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 63 of 2024 with Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 1142, 1307, 1308, 1223, 1226, 1660, 1050, 1051, 1361, 1385 of 2023
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants include Promoters (Deepak & Shirish Kulkarni), Group Entities (DS Kulkarni & Co., DSK Global Education), Homebuyers (allottees of Anandghan and Madhukosh projects), and Operational Creditors/Employees. Respondent No. 1 is Manoj Kumar Agarwal, RP of D.S. Kulkarni Developers Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). Respondents Nos. 2-4 comprise the Consortium SRA (Ashdan Properties, Classic Promoters, and Atul Builders). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was a major real estate company undergoing CIRP initiated by Bank of Maharashtra under Section 7 on 26.09.2019. CIRP yielded a resolution plan approved by the CoC on 13.08.2021 with an 83.37% vote share. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose on bank credit facilities exceeding statutory thresholds; SRA's approved resolution plan provided an outlay of Rs. 826.30 Crores (with Rs. 30 Crores upfront and deferred balance) against claims exceeding Rs. 1,900 Crores. Payout to operational creditors was 0.368% and employees 0.97%. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 26.09.2019. NCLT excluded time via orders dated 11.01.2022 and 20.06.2022 extending CIRP to cover the CoC plan approval on 13.08.2021. RP filed approval IA No. 1950/2021 on 24.08.2021. NCLT Mumbai approved the plan on 23.06.2023, subsequently dismissing homebuyers' pending claim IAs as infructuous on 01.08.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered sale deeds dated 07.06.2002 for 41R land at Bavdhan; 99-year Lease Deed dated 24.09.2008 in favor of DSK Global; registered tripartite agreements dated 30.06.2017; allotment letters dated April 2017; bank ledgers; MahaRERA order dated 05.02.2018; and registered valuation reports. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-I approved the resolution plan on 23.06.2023 in IA No. 1950/2021 and rejected homebuyer claim applications on 01.08.2023. Eleven connected appeals were filed before the NCLAT.
legal_issues: (i) Whether a resolution plan can validly extinguish third-party property rights by confiscating land owned by a partnership firm or cancelling a 99-year lease and appropriating college buildings without statutory termination and compensation under Section 18(1)(f) and Section 30(2)(e) of the IBC; (ii) Whether the RP and SRA can reject homebuyer claims supported by genuine pre-CIRP allotment letters and registered tripartite agreements on the ground that payments were credited to group entities rather than the corporate debtor's bank accounts; (iii) Whether approved resolution plans can be challenged on low valuation or meagre payouts to operational creditors (0.368%) and employees (0.97%) absent violation of Section 30(2)(b).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 18(1)(f) and its Explanation, the asset pool of a corporate debtor in CIRP cannot include assets owned by third parties or subsidiaries; a resolution plan cannot be utilized as a device to expropriate third-party land or unilaterally extinguish long-term leasehold and building rights without adhering to due process of law under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, as such clauses violate Section 30(2)(e) of the IBC. Furthermore, genuine pre-CIRP allotment letters acknowledging payment bind the corporate debtor and qualify purchasers as allottees under Section 5(8)(f). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18(1)(f) Explanation expressly excludes third-party assets held under contractual arrangements. An un-terminated 99-year lease cannot be extinguished by resolution plan fiat without paying contractual building construction costs. Under Section 5(8)(f), consideration acknowledged by the corporate debtor for apartment allotments constitutes an amount raised under a real estate transaction having the commercial effect of borrowing. Regarding operational payouts, commercial wisdom of the CoC governs distribution under Section 30(2)(b) unless the liquidation threshold is breached. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified registered 2002 sale deeds establishing separate title over 41R Bavdhan land, registered 99-year lease covenants requiring construction compensation, bank ledgers verifying payments for homebuyer apartments, and valuation compliance under Regulations 27 and 35. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Offending clauses expropriating DSK Global's building and DSK & Co.'s 41R land were severed and deleted; homebuyer claims were directed to be admitted and provided units under the plan; operational and promoter challenges were dismissed.
operative_order: Company Appeal Nos. 63/2024, 1142/2023, 1223/2023, and 1226/2023 are dismissed. Appeal No. 1307/2023 is partly allowed, modifying Appendix-IV Item No. 10 to exclude 0H41R land of DSK & Co.. Appeal No. 1308/2023 is partly allowed, deleting Clauses 13.4, 13.5, and 13.6 of the plan to preserve DSK Global's lease/building rights. Appeal Nos. 1361, 1385, 1660, 1050, and 1051 of 2023 are allowed, directing the RP and SRA to admit the appellants as homebuyers and allot them units as per the plan. The NCLT approval order dated 23.06.2023 is upheld as modified. Parties shall bear their own costs.
summary: Multiple stakeholders appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order approving the resolution plan for D.S. Kulkarni Developers Ltd. submitted by a consortium led by Ashdan Properties. Appellants included promoters alleging undervaluation, group entities challenging expropriation of their separate land and 99-year leasehold college buildings, homebuyers whose claims were rejected due to payments routed via group firms, and operational creditors receiving 0.368%. Partly allowing the appeals, the NCLAT Principal Bench severed and deleted plan clauses unlawfully extinguishing third-party lease and land titles under Section 18(1)(f) and Section 30(2)(e) of the IBC. The Tribunal ordered the admission of all bona fide homebuyers who held pre-CIRP allotment letters and directed the SRA to provide them units under the plan.

case_title: State Bank of India vs. Abhijeet Ferrotech Limited
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is State Bank of India (Financial Creditor, incorporating the erstwhile State Bank of Travancore). The Respondent is Abhijeet Ferrotech Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: State Bank of Travancore sanctioned working capital credit facilities of Rs. 99 Crores on 17.03.2012, renewed on 08.04.2013. A Master Restructuring Agreement (MRA) was executed under CDR on 28.09.2013, with reconstituted limits of Rs. 89.46 Crores sanctioned on 14.02.2014 and further enhanced to Rs. 126.20 Crores on 28.12.2015. CDR subsequently failed in December 2015. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The account slipped into NPA on 30.09.2016 w.e.f. 31.03.2013. SBI issued a loan recall notice on 25.11.2016. In Part-IV of Form 1, the Financial Creditor claimed an outstanding default of Rs. 144,70,88,690/- as of 19.07.2021, specifying 30.09.2016 as the date of default. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NPA occurred on 30.09.2016. Loan recall notice was issued on 25.11.2016. SARFAESI notice was issued on 17.02.2017. SBI filed recovery OA No. 742/2018 (TA No. 179/2020) under Section 19 of the RDDBFI Act on 11.09.2018. Corporate Debtor submitted an OTS proposal on 07.07.2021 offering Rs. 21.29 Crores. Section 7 petition TP (IBC) No. 02/CB/2022 was filed on 01.08.2021. DRT-II Kolkata dismissed Section 19 on 17.06.2022. DRAT set aside the dismissal on 19.03.2024, which the Calcutta High Court stayed on 30.04.2024. NCLT Cuttack rejected the Section 7 petition on 21.03.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Credit sanction letters (2012-2015); Master Restructuring Agreement; NPA certificate; Section 13(2) notice; DRT pleadings; and the Corporate Debtor's written OTS proposal dated 07.07.2021 acknowledging outstanding liabilities. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Cuttack Bench rejected SBI's Section 7 application on 21.03.2023, holding that the petition was barred under Section 10 CPC and issue estoppel by virtue of DRT-II Kolkata's order dated 17.06.2022. SBI appealed to NCLAT via Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 690 of 2023.
legal_issues: (i) Whether an application under Section 7 of the IBC is barred under Section 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 or principles of issue estoppel/res judicata by virtue of an order passed by the Debts Recovery Tribunal under Section 19 of the Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993; (ii) Whether the overriding effect of Section 238 of the IBC mandates that insolvency proceedings must proceed independently of recovery or debt determination proceedings pending before civil courts or debt recovery tribunals.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for initiating CIRP under Section 7 of the IBC is an independent proceeding in rem aimed at corporate resuscitation and value maximization, rather than a debt recovery proceeding; neither Section 10 of the CPC nor the doctrine of issue estoppel/res judicata arising from debt recovery proceedings under Section 19 of the RDDBFI Act can operate as a bar to entertaining and deciding a Section 7 petition on its own merits. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238 of the IBC contains an overriding non-obstante clause that explicitly supersedes inconsistent provisions in any other enactment. As affirmed by the Supreme Court in Innoventive Industries, Swiss Ribbons, and A. Navinchandra Steels, proceedings under Section 7 are independent and cannot be subordinated to civil recovery actions or stayed under Section 10 CPC. The Adjudicating Authority is strictly confined to verifying whether a financial debt exceeding the statutory threshold is due and in default under Section 7(5), taking into account acknowledgments such as written OTS proposals. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed the Section 7 petition and found that the default of Rs. 144.70 Crores and date of default (30.09.2016) were duly supported by sanction letters, NPA certificates, and a clear acknowledgment of debt in the Corporate Debtor's OTS proposal dated 07.07.2021; the NCLT committed an error of law in treating the DRT dismissal as an insurmountable bar. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed a fundamental legal error in applying Section 10 CPC and dismissing the Section 7 petition based on DRT proceedings; the order was set aside and the petition revived for fresh consideration.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 690 of 2023 is allowed; the impugned order dated 21.03.2023 passed by NCLT Cuttack Bench is set aside. The Company Petition TP (IBC) No. 02/CB/2022 is revived before the Adjudicating Authority to be considered afresh on merits in accordance with law. Parties shall bear their own costs.
summary: State Bank of India appealed against an NCLT Cuttack order rejecting its Section 7 CIRP petition against Abhijeet Ferrotech Ltd. for a default of Rs. 144.70 Crores[cite: 5]. The NCLT had rejected the petition by invoking Section 10 of the CPC and issue estoppel, holding that the proceeding was barred due to a DRT-II Kolkata order dismissing the bank's Section 19 recovery application. Setting aside the dismissal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that Section 7 constitutes an independent proceeding in rem for corporate revival that cannot be stayed or barred by DRT recovery proceedings. Relying on Section 238, the Tribunal ruled that Section 10 CPC is inapplicable and revived the petition before NCLT for fresh adjudication.

case_title: State Bank of India vs. India Power Corporation Ltd.
appeal_number: IA No. 158/2024 in Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 53 of 2024
bench: Chennai Bench (Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma, Member (Judicial), Third Member on Reference)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is State Bank of India (Financial Creditor acting through its Stressed Assets Management Branch, Hyderabad)[cite: 6]. The Respondent is India Power Corporation Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 6]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: State Bank of India initiated insolvency proceedings against India Power Corporation Ltd. under Section 7 of the IBC read with Rule 4 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Rules, 2016 and Section 60(2) of the Code before NCLT Hyderabad[cite: 6]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Financial Creditor claimed default under financial debt facilities, which was contested and rejected by the Adjudicating Authority[cite: 6]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Hyderabad dismissed the Section 7 petition in CP (IB) No. 205/7/HDB/2021 on 30.10.2023[cite: 6]. A free copy of the order was supplied to the parties under Rule 50 of the NCLT Rules on 14.11.2023[cite: 6]. The Financial Creditor did not apply for a certified copy upon payment of fees under Section 76 of the Evidence Act prior to the expiry of the statutory 30-day limitation period[cite: 6]. The appeal was subsequently filed before NCLAT Chennai accompanied by IA No. 158/2024 seeking condonation of 3 days of delay beyond 30 days[cite: 6]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Order sheet of NCLT Hyderabad dated 30.10.2023, free copy dispatch endorsement dated 14.11.2023, and IA No. 158/2024 seeking condonation of 3 days of delay[cite: 6]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 53 of 2024, a two-member bench of NCLAT Chennai differed in opinion on 01.05.2024 regarding whether a free copy under Rule 50 satisfies Rule 22(2) of the NCLAT Rules[cite: 6]. Member (Judicial) held that a certified copy obtained on demand and fee payment is mandatory, while Member (Technical) held that a free copy under Rule 50 qualifies as a certified copy[cite: 6]. The matter was referred by the Chairperson to a Third Member[cite: 6].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a copy of an order provided by the Registry of the NCLT free of cost under Rule 50 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 qualifies as a 'Certified Copy' for the purpose of Rule 22(2) of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 and Section 76 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 to sustain an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC[cite: 6]; (ii) Whether applying for a certified copy on payment of legal fees is mandatory to claim exclusion of time under Section 12(2) of the Limitation Act, 1963[cite: 6].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A 'free copy' supplied by the Registry of the Adjudicating Authority as an administrative intimation under Rule 50 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 does not constitute a 'Certified Copy' within the meaning of Rule 22(2) of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 read with Rule 2(9) of the NCLT Rules and Section 76 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872; to maintain an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC and claim exclusion of time under Section 12(2) of the Limitation Act, an appellant must make an application on demand accompanied by the prescribed legal fees prior to the expiry of the limitation period[cite: 6]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 22(2) of the NCLAT Rules mandates presentation of an appeal with a certified copy[cite: 6]. Under Section 2(9) of the NCLT Rules and Section 76 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, a certified copy requires two conjunctive statutory ingredients: an express 'demand' by the applicant and 'payment of legal fees'[cite: 6]. Rule 50 of the NCLT Rules merely casts an administrative duty on the Registry to provide a free copy for intimation purposes, which is conceptually distinct from a certified copy made available on cost under the Schedule of Fees[cite: 6]. As established in V. Nagarajan and Munagala Roja Harsha Vardhini, the right to a free copy does not dispense with the statutory obligation to apply for a certified copy to compute limitation[cite: 6]. Under the doctrine of binding precedent (Chandra Prakash), a three-member bench ruling holds binding primacy over a two-member bench[cite: 6]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the Appellant did not apply for a certified copy with prescribed fees under Section 76 of the Evidence Act before the expiry of the 30-day statutory limitation period following the pronouncement on 30.10.2023, relying solely on a free copy provided on 14.11.2023[cite: 6]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Third Member concurred with the Member (Judicial), holding that a free copy under Rule 50 cannot substitute for a certified copy under Rule 22(2) of the NCLAT Rules, and answered the reference accordingly[cite: 6].
operative_order: The reference is answered in agreement with the Member (Judicial), holding that a free copy provided under Rule 50 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 cannot be treated as a Certified Copy under Rule 22(2) of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 read with Section 76 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872[cite: 6]. Let the records be placed before the regular bench for consequential disposal of IA No. 158/2024 and Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 53 of 2024[cite: 6].
summary: In an appeal by State Bank of India against an NCLT Hyderabad order dismissing its Section 7 IBC petition, a split verdict arose on whether a free copy provided under Rule 50 of the NCLT Rules satisfies the certified copy requirement under Rule 22(2) of the NCLAT Rules[cite: 6]. On reference to the Third Member, Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma concurred with the Member (Judicial), holding that a free copy is merely an administrative intimation and cannot substitute for a certified copy under Section 76 of the Indian Evidence Act, which strictly requires an application on demand and payment of prescribed fees[cite: 6]. Following V. Nagarajan, an appellant cannot claim limitation benefits without applying for a certified copy[cite: 6].

case_title: Everlike Real Estate & Developers Pvt. Ltd. vs. Mohit Goyal, RP of Aadi Best Consortium Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain, Technical Members Naresh Salecha and Indevar Pandey)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Everlike Real Estate & Developers Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 7]. Respondent No. 1 is Mohit Goyal, Resolution Professional of Aadi Best Consortium Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 7]. Respondent No. 2 is Skael Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant / SRA)[cite: 7]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: In 2014, the Corporate Debtor approached the Appellant to sell commercial units in a project at Plot No. RC 1/2, Vaishali-1, Ghaziabad, U.P.[cite: 7]. The parties executed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) on 24.05.2016 for an aggregate commercial area of 25,000 sq. ft. for a total consideration of Rs. 12.50 Crores, containing assured rental returns of Rs. 15 Lakhs per month or 18% per annum interest upon default[cite: 7]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant paid Rs. 10 Crores by cheques between 2014 and 2016[cite: 7]. The Corporate Debtor defaulted on possession and assured returns, leading the Appellant to file a criminal FIR on 04.06.2022[cite: 7]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP was admitted under Section 9 on 31.03.2022[cite: 7]. Public announcement was made inviting claims by 15.04.2022[cite: 7]. The Appellant submitted Form CA on 20.04.2022, which the RP admitted as a financial debt in a class[cite: 7]. CoC approved Respondent No. 2's resolution plan with 100% votes on 18.08.2023[cite: 7]. Appellant filed IA No. 114 of 2023 on 03.11.2023 seeking re-categorization from Category 4 to Category 2[cite: 7]. NCLT New Delhi Bench-II dismissed the IA and approved the resolution plan on 05.04.2024[cite: 7]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: MOU dated 24.05.2016 mentioning 25,000 sq. ft. without specifying unit numbers, floors, or demarcated space, alongside unproduced Annexure-I; proof of Rs. 10 Crore payments; approved Resolution Plan Chapter 8; and e-mail correspondence dated 16.08.2023 and 13.09.2023[cite: 7]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-II approved the resolution plan in IA No. 6676/2023 and rejected Appellant's IA No. 114/2023 on 05.04.2024, holding that the MOU was not a valid Builder Buyer Agreement (BBA)[cite: 7]. Appellant appealed to NCLAT under Section 61[cite: 7].
