legal_issues: (i) Whether a Memorandum of Understanding specifying an undemarcated area of commercial space with guaranteed rental returns/interest constitutes a valid Builder Buyer Agreement or Agreement for Sale under Section 2(c)/(e) of the RERA Act, 2016 and Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC[cite: 7]; (ii) Whether the Resolution Applicant and CoC can validly classify homebuyers/allottees into separate sub-categories based on the existence of a valid BBA and provide differential payouts (40% vs 5%)[cite: 7]; (iii) Whether an individual allottee has locus to challenge an approved resolution plan after the class of creditors has approved it by majority under Section 25A(3A) of the IBC[cite: 7].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC and Section 2(d)/(e) of the RERA Act, 2016, an allottee must hold an agreement pertaining to a separate and self-contained identifiable unit to be treated on par with standard homebuyers holding a valid Builder Buyer Agreement; a prospective resolution applicant and the Committee of Creditors acting within their commercial wisdom are legally entitled to classify creditors into distinct, rational sub-categories and provide differential payouts based on whether allottees possess valid BBAs or merely unallocated MOUs[cite: 7]. Furthermore, an individual financial creditor in a class is legally bound by the democratic majority vote of that class and lacks independent locus to challenge the approved plan[cite: 7]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 2(e) of the RERA Act defines an apartment as a 'separate and self-contained part of any immovable property'[cite: 7]. An MOU that fails to identify specific units, floors, or boundaries lacks the statutory character of a BBA[cite: 7]. In line with Essar Steel and Jaypee Kensington, the commercial wisdom of the CoC extends to differential distribution among different classes or sub-classes of creditors[cite: 7]. Under Section 25A(3A), once an authorized representative casts a vote reflecting the majority of the class, all individual constituent allottees are bound[cite: 7]. Under Fervent Synergies, an initial admission of a claim by the RP creates no promissory estoppel against the Resolution Applicant's categorization in the plan[cite: 7]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the MOU dated 24.05.2016 and verified that it omitted specific shop/unit numbers, failed to produce the referenced Annexure-I, and contained unusual commercial return covenants (Rs. 15 Lakhs monthly rent / 18% interest), confirming that the Appellant did not hold a valid BBA[cite: 7]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The classification of the Appellant under Category 4 (cancelled units without valid BBA) receiving 5% payout was rational, lawful, and within the commercial wisdom of the 100% CoC; the NCLT committed no error in approving the plan and dismissing the application[cite: 7].
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 978 of 2024 is dismissed with no order as to costs[cite: 7]. All connected Interlocutory Applications are closed[cite: 7].
summary: Everlike Real Estate & Developers Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order approving the resolution plan of Aadi Best Consortium Pvt. Ltd. submitted by Skael Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. and dismissing its IA seeking reclassification from Category 4 (units without valid BBA, receiving 5% payout) to Category 2 (pending possession, receiving 40% refund)[cite: 7]. The Appellant had paid Rs. 10 Crores under an MOU for 25,000 sq. ft. of commercial space[cite: 7]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that an MOU lacking demarcated, self-contained unit details cannot be equated with a valid BBA under RERA Section 2(e)[cite: 7]. Relying on Essar Steel and Jaypee Kensington, the Tribunal ruled that the CoC possesses commercial wisdom to provide differential treatments to sub-classes of creditors, and an individual allottee is bound by the majority vote of the class[cite: 7].

case_title: Anuj Bajpai, Liquidator of Shirt Company (India) Pvt. Ltd. vs. Employee Provident Fund Organisation & Ors.
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1141 of 2023 & I.A. No. 3979 of 2023
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain, Technical Members Naresh Salecha and Indevar Pandey)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Anuj Bajpai, Liquidator of Shirt Company (India) Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 10]. Respondent No. 1 is the Employee Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO), Regional Office Coimbatore[cite: 10]. Respondents Nos. 2 & 3 are the Recovery Officer and Enforcement Officer of EPFO[cite: 10]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was admitted into CIRP on 26.02.2020 and ordered into liquidation on 22.12.2021[cite: 10]. The Corporate Debtor had failed to maintain separate funds for provident fund and pension fund liabilities[cite: 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: EPFO lodged a total statutory claim of Rs. 1,24,86,750/- comprising: Section 7A contribution (Rs. 34,47,599/-); Section 7Q interest (Rs. 28,64,318/-); Section 14B damages (Rs. 61,38,551/-); and provisional costs/charges (Rs. 36,282/-)[cite: 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 26.02.2020[cite: 10]. Liquidation was ordered on 22.12.2021[cite: 10]. On 20.06.2022, EPFO issued sale proclamations and attached company assets[cite: 10]. Liquidator filed IA No. 2229 of 2022 challenging attachment and seeking to subject claims to Section 53 waterfall[cite: 10]. On 13.12.2022, NCLT directed the Liquidator to create a fixed deposit of Rs. 1,24,86,750/- to secure EPF dues and release asset attachments for e-auction[cite: 10]. Auction took place on 15.12.2022[cite: 10]. NCLT Mumbai partly allowed IA No. 2229/2022 on 30.06.2023, discharging attachments as the entire claim was secured in FD[cite: 10]. Liquidator appealed to NCLAT[cite: 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: EPFO statutory assessment orders under Sections 7A, 7Q, and 14B; Fixed Deposit receipt of Rs. 1,24,86,750/- (SBI A/c No. 41518465189); and e-Auction notices[cite: 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV partly allowed IA No. 2229/2022 on 30.06.2023, halting separate recovery proceedings and lifting attachments because the full Rs. 1.24 Crore claim was secured by fixed deposit[cite: 10]. The Liquidator appealed, arguing that interest and damages are statutory penalties that fall under the Section 53 waterfall rather than Section 36(4)[cite: 10].
legal_issues: (i) Whether provident fund dues, including interest under Section 7Q and damages under Section 14B of the EPF Act, 1952, are excluded from the liquidation estate under Section 36(4)(a)(iii) of the IBC or are subject to the waterfall distribution mechanism under Section 53[cite: 10]; (ii) Whether the phrase 'any amount due from an employer' under Section 11(2) of the EPF Act is confined strictly to employee contributions under Section 7A[cite: 10].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: By virtue of Section 36(4)(a)(iii) of the IBC, all sums due to any workman or employee from the provident fund, pension fund, and gratuity fund are explicitly excluded from the liquidation estate assets and cannot be used for recovery in liquidation; such dues, including interest under Section 7Q and damages under Section 14B of the EPF Act, 1952, must be paid in priority and in full outside the liquidation waterfall mechanism of Section 53 of the IBC[cite: 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 36(4)(a)(iii) of the IBC creates an express statutory carve-out for provident fund and pension dues, shielding them from the corporate debtor's liquidation estate[cite: 10]. Under Section 11(2) of the EPF Act, 1952, 'any amount due from an employer' operates as a first charge on assets[cite: 10]. As authoritatively held by the Supreme Court in Maharashtra State Cooperative Bank, the expression 'any amount due from an employer' cannot be given a restrictive interpretation limited to Section 7A contributions, but encompasses statutory interest under Section 7Q and damages under Section 14B as an extended liability arising from default[cite: 10]. Following Moser Baer, Sunil Kumar Jain, and Jet Aircraft Maintenance Engineers, workmen provident fund dues do not form part of the liquidation assets and must be paid in full outside Section 53[cite: 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the claim of Rs. 1,24,86,750/- assessed by EPFO under Sections 7A, 7Q, and 14B of the EPF Act constituted statutory dues arising from employer default, which were fully secured in an earmarked fixed deposit pursuant to NCLT directions[cite: 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no legal error in treating the entire EPFO claim of Rs. 1.24 Crores as protected under Section 36(4) outside the Section 53 waterfall; the appeal was devoid of merit[cite: 10].
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1141 of 2023 is dismissed with no order as to costs[cite: 10]. All connected Interlocutory Applications are closed[cite: 10].
summary: The Liquidator of Shirt Company (India) Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order holding that the entire claim of Rs. 1.24 Crores filed by the EPFO (comprising Section 7A contributions, Section 7Q interest, and Section 14B damages) was protected outside the liquidation estate by an earmarked fixed deposit[cite: 10]. The Liquidator contended that only Section 7A contributions are excluded under Section 36(4)(a)(iii) of the IBC, while interest and damages must fall within the Section 53 waterfall[cite: 10]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench relied on Maharashtra State Cooperative Bank and Moser Baer to hold that 'any amount due from an employer' under Section 11(2) of the EPF Act includes interest and damages as integral parts of provident fund dues[cite: 10]. The Tribunal affirmed that all EPF dues stand excluded from the liquidation estate and must be paid in priority without waiting for Section 53 waterfall distribution[cite: 10].

case_title: Seeta Shah vs. ICICI Bank Limited
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Seeta Shah, Suspended Director of Ushdev Engitech Limited (Corporate Debtor / Corporate Guarantor)[cite: 11]. The Respondent is ICICI Bank Limited (Financial Creditor)[cite: 11]. Ushdev International Limited (UIL) is the Principal Borrower[cite: 11]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: ICICI Bank extended credit facilities of Rs. 100 Crores to UIL under two bilateral non-fund based facilities of Rs. 50 Crores each vide credit letters dated 24.12.2014 and 14.10.2015[cite: 11]. Corporate Debtor executed a Deed of Guarantee on 10.08.2016 securing the facilities[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Principal Borrower defaulted and was declared NPA in December 2016[cite: 11]. ICICI Bank invoked the Corporate Guarantee on 16.10.2017 demanding payment within 5 days[cite: 11]. As of guarantee invocation, debt due was over Rs. 230 Crores, and total admitted financial debt reached Rs. 294,51,35,655/-[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced against UIL on 14.05.2018[cite: 11]. NCLT approved UIL's resolution plan on 03.02.2022, erroneously observing that excluded securities were extinguished[cite: 11]. On 11.03.2022, NCLAT allowed appeals by CoC and ICICI Bank, deleting directions extinguishing excluded securities[cite: 11]. ICICI Bank filed Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 119 of 2021 against the Corporate Guarantor[cite: 11]. NCLT Mumbai Court-V admitted the Section 7 petition on 26.04.2023[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Credit agreement letters (2014-2015); Deed of Guarantee dated 10.08.2016 (including Clause 33); invocation notice dated 16.10.2017; UIL resolution plan clauses defining Excluded Securities; and NCLAT judgment dated 11.03.2022[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-V admitted ICICI Bank's Section 7 petition on 26.04.2023[cite: 11]. Suspended Director appealed to NCLAT arguing the guarantee was extinguished under Section 134 of the Contract Act and Clause 33 of the guarantee due to plan approval of the principal borrower[cite: 11].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the approval of a resolution plan in respect of a Principal Borrower under Section 31 of the IBC operates as an automatic release or discharge of a Corporate Guarantor under Section 134 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 where the plan expressly preserves third-party guarantees as 'Excluded Securities'[cite: 11]; (ii) Whether converting unpaid debt into non-convertible redeemable preference shares under an approved plan reduces the debt of the principal borrower below the threshold of Rs. 218 Crores under Clause 33 of the guarantee to render it unenforceable[cite: 11].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The approval of a resolution plan under Section 31 of the IBC in respect of a principal borrower does not ipso facto discharge or extinguish the independent liabilities of a corporate or personal guarantor; an involuntary discharge or scaling down of the principal debtor's liability occurring by operation of insolvency law does not absolve the surety under Section 134 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, particularly where the approved resolution plan expressly reserves the right of financial creditors to enforce third-party guarantees[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 128 of the Contract Act, the liability of a guarantor is coextensive with that of the principal debtor[cite: 11]. Section 134 applies strictly where a creditor voluntarily discharges or releases a debtor by contract; a discharge occurring by operation of law under bankruptcy or insolvency statutes does not absolve the surety, as established by the Supreme Court in Maharashtra State Electricity Board and Lalit Kumar Jain v. Union of India[cite: 11]. Under Section 31(1) of the IBC, an approved plan binds the guarantor while preserving lenders' remedies against third parties[cite: 11]. Furthermore, converting debt into non-convertible redeemable preference shares lacking voting/dividend rights is merely a restructured form of indebtedness and does not constitute cash satisfaction or reduction of debt below contractual fall-off thresholds[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the NCLAT judgment dated 11.03.2022 had already set aside directions extinguishing excluded securities and conclusively held the 10.08.2016 guarantee enforceable, and that the principal debt exceeded Rs. 230 Crores at invocation and Rs. 294 Crores at petition filing, defeating any reliance on Clause 33[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Guarantee remained valid, active, and enforceable; Section 134 of the Contract Act was inapplicable, and the Adjudicating Authority properly admitted the Section 7 petition[cite: 11].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 574 of 2023 is dismissed with no order as to costs, upholding the order dated 26.04.2023 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench, Court-V in C.P. (IB) No. 119 of 2021[cite: 11].
summary: Seeta Shah, Suspended Director of Ushdev Engitech Ltd. (Corporate Guarantor), appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 7 CIRP application filed by ICICI Bank for unpaid dues exceeding Rs. 230 Crores[cite: 11]. The Appellant contended that the debt of Principal Borrower Ushdev International Ltd. was resolved under an approved resolution plan with balance debt converted into preference shares, discharging the guarantor under Section 134 of the Contract Act and Clause 33 of the guarantee[cite: 11]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that under Lalit Kumar Jain, an involuntary discharge of the principal borrower by operation of insolvency law does not absolve the guarantor[cite: 11]. The Tribunal affirmed that the guarantee was expressly preserved as an Excluded Security, preference shares did not wipe out the debt, and the Section 7 admission was sound[cite: 11].

case_title: H.E. Captain Ameet K Agarwal vs. Gannon Dunkerley and Company Limited & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain and Technical Member Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is H.E. Captain Ameet K Agarwal, Suspended Director of Sangeeta Aviation Services Private Limited (Corporate Debtor). Respondent No. 1 is Gannon Dunkerley and Company Limited (Financial Creditor / Decree Holder). Respondent No. 2 is Mr. Bijendra Kumar Jha, Resolution Professional[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: At the request of the Corporate Debtor, the Financial Creditor extended short-term financing by disbursing two payments of Rs. 50,00,000/- each on 22.03.2017 and 31.05.2017, totaling Rs. 1,00,00,000/-, secured by two bills of exchange and corresponding post-dated cheques[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The two cheques (Nos. 026411 and 026428) deposited on 15.05.2018 were dishonored on 16.05.2018 due to 'Exceeds arrangement'[cite: 12]. Following non-payment, the Financial Creditor instituted a commercial summary suit before the Bombay High Court[cite: 12]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Cheques dishonored on 16.05.2018[cite: 12]. The Bombay High Court passed a commercial decree on 09.01.2019 in Summary Suit No. 714 of 2018 awarding Rs. 1,21,71,243/- with 12% annual interest[cite: 12]. Section 7 application (CP No. 3073/IBC/MB/2019) was filed in July 2019[cite: 12]. NCLT Mumbai Bench-III admitted the Section 7 petition on 10.08.2021[cite: 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank statements showing disbursals of Rs. 50 Lakhs each on 22.03.2017 and 31.05.2017; two dishonored bills of exchange and cheques; and the Bombay High Court decree dated 09.01.2019[cite: 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai admitted Gannon Dunkerley's Section 7 petition on 10.08.2021[cite: 12]. Suspended Director appealed to NCLAT under Section 61, contending that a money decree does not qualify as a financial debt and lacked a formal loan agreement[cite: 12].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a money decree awarded by a High Court in a commercial summary suit based on dishonored bills of exchange and underlying financial disbursals qualifies as a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC, entitling the decree-holder to maintain an application under Section 7[cite: 12].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A money decree passed by a competent court or tribunal in favor of a financial creditor based on an underlying transaction involving monetary disbursal against consideration for the time value of money gives rise to a financial debt and creates a fresh cause of action enabling the decree-holder to maintain a petition under Section 7 of the IBC[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) defines financial debt as a debt disbursed against consideration for the time value of money[cite: 12]. As clarified by the Supreme Court in Orator Marketing, the stipulation of interest is not a condition precedent to qualify as a financial debt, and interest-free or commercial debt obligations fall within its scope[cite: 12]. Furthermore, following Urgo Capital and Dena Bank, a decree-holder is explicitly recognized as a creditor competent to trigger Section 7[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified bank records showing direct disbursals of Rs. 1 Crore in 2017, the issuance of bills of exchange and dishonored cheques, and the Bombay High Court decree dated 09.01.2019 awarding principal and 12% interest[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The underlying transaction and ensuing decree established a valid financial debt and default, making Gannon Dunkerley a financial creditor entitled to initiate CIRP[cite: 12].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 719 of 2021 is dismissed, upholding the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 10.08.2021 admitting the Section 7 application and initiating CIRP against Sangeeta Aviation Services Private Limited[cite: 12]. Respondent No. 1 is entitled to proceed as a financial creditor under Section 7, and IA No. 5680 of 2023 is disposed of[cite: 12].
summary: H.E. Captain Ameet K Agarwal, Suspended Director of Sangeeta Aviation Services Pvt. Ltd., appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 7 CIRP petition filed by Gannon Dunkerley & Co. Ltd[cite: 12]. The appellant argued that a High Court money decree based on a summary suit does not constitute a financial debt under Section 5(8) of the IBC in the absence of a formal loan agreement[cite: 12]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that underlying financial disbursals, bills of exchange, and a subsequent court decree collectively establish a valid financial debt[cite: 12]. Relying on Urgo Capital and Dena Bank, the Tribunal affirmed that a decree-holder can maintain a Section 7 petition[cite: 12].

case_title: Madhukar Shetty vs. Bank of Baroda & Ors.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Members Barun Mitra and Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Madhukar Shetty, Ex-Director of Genesis Resorts Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). Respondent No. 1 is Bank of Baroda (Financial Creditor). Respondent No. 2 is Vijay Pitamber Lulla, Resolution Professional. Respondent No. 3 is the Committee of Creditors (CoC) represented by Bank of Baroda. Finquest Solutions Pvt. Ltd. is the Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA)[cite: 13]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed credit facilities of Rs. 149.05 Crores from Bank of Baroda between 2012 and 2014 to construct a hotel in Vile Parle, Mumbai[cite: 13]. Restructuring was permitted on 18.02.2015, but defaults persisted[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Account classified as NPA on 30.11.2016[cite: 13]. Bank of Baroda initiated Section 7 CIRP for a total debt of Rs. 231.09 Crores (Principal: Rs. 149.05 Crores; Interest: Rs. 82.04 Crores)[cite: 13]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 petition admitted on 11.12.2019[cite: 13]. Form G published on 28.01.2020[cite: 13]. Registered valuers appointed in 1st CoC meeting on 10.01.2020 submitted reports in July–October 2020 (average liquidation value: Rs. 83.52 Crores; fair value: Rs. 118.88 Crores)[cite: 13]. CoC approved Finquest Solutions' resolution plan with a 100% vote share in its 10th meeting[cite: 13]. RP filed plan approval IA No. 1177/2021 on 05.04.2021[cite: 13]. Ex-Director filed objection IA No. 1768/2021[cite: 13]. NCLT Mumbai approved the resolution plan on 20.12.2023[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Valuation reports dated 09.07.2020, 08.09.2020, and 09.10.2020; Mazars India LLP independent due diligence report on SRA eligibility; Minutes of 1st, 8th, 9th, and 10th CoC meetings[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-I approved the resolution plan in IA No. 1177/2021 and dismissed ex-Director's IA No. 1768/2021 on 20.12.2023[cite: 13]. Ex-Director appealed to NCLAT alleging undervaluation and SRA ineligibility due to SEBI proceedings[cite: 13].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the valuation exercise conducted by registered valuers under CIRP Regulations 27 and 35 is vitiated by ignoring pre-CIRP valuations or balance sheet figures; (ii) Whether the Successful Resolution Applicant was ineligible under Section 29A(f) of the IBC due to historical SEBI penalty proceedings against its promoters[cite: 13].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Valuation conducted during CIRP in strict compliance with Regulations 27 and 35 by IBBI-registered valuers forms a valid basis for CoC commercial decisions, and pre-CIRP historical valuations are irrelevant; furthermore, SRA eligibility under Section 29A(f) is determined as of the plan submission date, and past regulatory penalties set aside or stayed by appellate tribunals do not constitute disqualification[cite: 13]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulations 27 and 35 mandate independent valuation by registered valuers post-CIRP admission[cite: 13]. In line with M.K. Rajagopalan and Ngaitlang Dhar, once the CoC is satisfied with valuation reports and approves a plan by requisite majority, the Adjudicating Authority and Appellate Tribunal cannot substitute their judgment for the commercial wisdom of the CoC or entertain speculative challenges to asset valuation[cite: 13]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that three independent registered valuers submitted reports in 2020 establishing liquidation and fair values, that an independent agency (Mazars) vetted SRA eligibility, and that SEBI orders against promoters were stayed or set aside by the Securities Appellate Tribunal[cite: 13]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The valuation process was immaculate, the SRA was fully eligible under Section 29A, and the resolution plan was validly approved by a 100% CoC majority[cite: 13].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 739-740 of 2024 are dismissed, upholding the order dated 20.12.2023 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench-I in IA-1177/2021 and IA-1768/2021 approving the resolution plan[cite: 13]. Parties to bear their own costs[cite: 13].
summary: Madhukar Shetty, Ex-Director of Genesis Resorts Pvt. Ltd., appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order approving the resolution plan submitted by Finquest Solutions Pvt. Ltd. with a 100% CoC vote share[cite: 13]. The appellant alleged severe undervaluation compared to 2015/2019 bank valuations and balance sheets, and claimed the SRA was ineligible under Section 29A due to SEBI proceedings against its promoters[cite: 13]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that post-CIRP valuation under Regulations 27 and 35 by registered valuers is legally binding and pre-CIRP valuations are irrelevant[cite: 13]. The Tribunal also noted that SEBI orders against the promoters had been set aside by the Securities Appellate Tribunal, making the SRA fully eligible, and upheld the commercial wisdom of the CoC[cite: 13].

case_title: Bhuvan Madan, IRP of Indrajit Power Private Limited vs. Nominated Authority, Ministry of Coal & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Bhuvan Madan, Interim Resolution Professional (IRP) of Indrajit Power Private Limited (Corporate Debtor). Respondent No. 1 is the Nominated Authority, Ministry of Coal, Government of India. Respondent No. 2 is Indian Bank (erstwhile Allahabad Bank)[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: On 16.03.2015, a Coal Mine Development and Production Agreement (CMDPA) was executed between the President of India (via Nominated Authority) and the Corporate Debtor, backed by a Performance Bank Guarantee (PBG) issued by Indian Bank[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Nominated Authority issued show cause notices on 01.06.2022 and 05.06.2022 for failing to achieve scheduled production for FY 2018-19 to 2022-23[cite: 14]. Scrutiny Committee recommended PBG appropriation on 27/28.07.2023[cite: 14]. Nominated Authority passed a formal Appropriation Order on 27.10.2023 to invoke Rs. 7,38,37,440/- from PBG Part 2[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CMDPA executed on 16.03.2015[cite: 14]. Appropriation Order passed on 27.10.2023[cite: 14]. Delhi High Court WP No. 1416/2023 challenging committee minutes was withdrawn on 03.11.2023[cite: 14]. CIRP commenced against the Corporate Debtor on 01.02.2024[cite: 14]. Nominated Authority issued dispute notice disposal order on 28.03.2024 and called upon Indian Bank to encash Rs. 7.38 Crores on 05.04.2024 and 10.04.2024[cite: 14]. IRP filed IA No. 1710/2024 before NCLT Mumbai, which dismissed it on 29.04.2024[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CMDPA dated 16.03.2015; Show cause notices; Scrutiny Committee minutes; Nominated Authority Appropriation Order dated 27.10.2023; Delhi High Court order dated 03.11.2023; and bank invocation letters dated 05.04.2024 and 10.04.2024[cite: 14]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-IV dismissed I.A. No. 1710/2024 on 29.04.2024, holding that Section 14 of the IBC does not bar the encashment of performance bank guarantees during moratorium[cite: 14]. IRP appealed to NCLAT under Section 61[cite: 14].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the imposition of a moratorium under Section 14(1)(a) of the IBC prohibits the beneficiary from invoking and encashing an unconditional Performance Bank Guarantee furnished by a corporate debtor[cite: 14].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 14(3)(b) of the IBC read with the 2018 amendment, the moratorium under Section 14 does not apply to a surety in a contract of guarantee or performance bank guarantees furnished by a corporate debtor, and beneficiaries are legally entitled to invoke and encash unconditional bank guarantees even during the pendency of CIRP[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(31) proviso expressly excludes performance guarantees from the definition of 'security interest'. Furthermore, Section 14(3)(b) explicitly exempts contracts of guarantee from the moratorium[cite: 14]. As expounded in V. Ramakrishnan, Bharat Aluminium Co., and Standard Chartered Bank, a bank guarantee is an independent contract between the issuing bank and the beneficiary, and its encashment does not deplete the corporate debtor's own assets but shifts liability to the surety[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that a formal Appropriation Order was validly passed by the Nominated Authority on 27.10.2023 prior to the CIRP commencement date of 01.02.2024, and that the bank guarantee was unconditional and irrevocable[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The moratorium under Section 14 does not bar the encashment of a performance bank guarantee, and the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in refusing to grant an injunction[cite: 14].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 989 of 2024 is dismissed, upholding the order dated 29.04.2024 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-IV in IA No. 1710 (MB) 2024[cite: 14]. Parties to bear their own costs[cite: 14].
summary: Bhuvan Madan, IRP of Indrajit Power Pvt. Ltd., appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order dismissing his interlocutory application seeking to restrain the Ministry of Coal (Nominated Authority) from encashing a Performance Bank Guarantee (PBG) of Rs. 7.38 Crores[cite: 14]. The appellant argued that the invocation letters issued in April 2024 post-CIRP commencement violated the Section 14 moratorium[cite: 14]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that under Section 14(3)(b) of the IBC and Supreme Court precedents like V. Ramakrishnan, performance bank guarantees are exempt from moratorium[cite: 14]. The Tribunal affirmed that a bank guarantee is an independent contract, and its encashment by the Nominated Authority pursuant to a pre-CIRP appropriation order is fully lawful[cite: 14].

case_title: Sangita Arora vs. IFCI Limited & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Ms. Sangita Arora, Personal Guarantor of Supertech Limited (Corporate Debtor). Respondent No. 1 is IFCI Limited (Financial Creditor). Respondent No. 2 is Reetesh Kumar Agarwal, Resolution Professional[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: IFCI advanced a Rupee Term Loan of Rs. 150 Crores and a Corporate Loan of Rs. 100 Crores to Supertech Limited. The Appellant executed a Deed of Personal Guarantee securing the Rupee Term Loan[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Supertech Limited defaulted on loan repayments, prompting IFCI to recall both loans and issue a demand notice to the Personal Guarantor[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: IFCI e-filed an application under Section 95(1) against the Appellant on 02.06.2021, receiving e-filing number 07101020/7186/2021, and registered on 09.08.2021[cite: 15]. PNB Housing Finance Ltd. (PNBHFL) filed a subsequent Section 95 application against the Appellant on 24.07.2021, which was registered earlier on 02.08.2021[cite: 15]. NCLT New Delhi Bench-VI passed an order on 01.05.2024 in IFCI's application appointing the RP under Section 99[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Section 95 application e-filed by IFCI on 02.06.2021 with electronic filing records; Deed of Personal Guarantee; loan recall notices; and NCLT order dated 01.05.2024[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-VI appointed an RP under Section 99 on 01.05.2024 upon IFCI's Section 95 application[cite: 15]. Personal Guarantor appealed to NCLAT under Section 61, contending that PNBHFL's application was registered earlier on 02.08.2021, which triggered interim moratorium under Section 96 to bar subsequent orders[cite: 15].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the date of 'filing' of an application under Section 95 of the IBC for triggering interim moratorium under Section 96 is the date of electronic presentation and e-filing or the subsequent date on which the Registry numbers and registers the application[cite: 15].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under the statutory scheme of the NCLT Rules, 2016 and Section 96 of the IBC, an application under Section 95 is deemed 'filed' on the exact date it is successfully presented and e-filed in electronic form at the Registry and accorded an electronic filing number, and interim moratorium triggers immediately from that e-filing date; subsequent administrative numbering and registration by the Registry are ministerial acts that do not alter the foundational filing date[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 2(14) of the NCLT Rules defines 'filed' as filing in the office of the Registry, which, under Rule 10(2), includes electronic filing[cite: 15]. As established in the Three-Member Bench ruling of Krishan Kumar Basia, postponing filing until formal numbering would introduce fatal uncertainty regarding interim moratorium enforcement under Section 96[cite: 15]. Procedural omissions or defects that are subsequently cured relate back to the initial presentation date, as affirmed by the Supreme Court in Vidyawati Gupta[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that IFCI e-filed its complete Section 95 application on 02.06.2021 (obtaining e-filing number 07101020/7186/2021), which predated PNBHFL's e-filing of 24.07.2021, notwithstanding that PNBHFL's application was administratively registered on 02.08.2021 prior to IFCI's registration on 09.08.2021[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: IFCI's application was first in time based on e-filing date; interim moratorium commenced on 02.06.2021, and the NCLT acted completely within jurisdiction in appointing the RP[cite: 15].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1102 of 2024 is dismissed, upholding the order dated 01.05.2024 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench-VI in C.P. (IB) No. 427/ND/2021 appointing the Resolution Professional under Section 99[cite: 15]. No order as to costs[cite: 15].
summary: Ms. Sangita Arora, Personal Guarantor of Supertech Ltd., appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order appointing a Resolution Professional under Section 99 on a Section 95 application filed by IFCI Ltd.[cite: 15]. The appellant argued that another creditor, PNBHFL, had its application registered earlier on 02.08.2021 (whereas IFCI's application was registered on 09.08.2021), triggering an interim moratorium that allegedly ousted IFCI's petition[cite: 15]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench relied on the Three-Member Bench precedent in Krishan Kumar Basia to hold that 'filing' under Section 96 occurs on the date of electronic presentation (02.06.2021 for IFCI) rather than the date of administrative numbering[cite: 15]. The Tribunal affirmed that IFCI's petition was first in time and the appointment of the RP was valid[cite: 15].

case_title: Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI) vs. Sambandh Finserve Private Limited
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Yogesh Khanna and Technical Member Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI) (Financial Creditor). The Respondent is Sambandh Finserve Private Limited (Corporate Debtor, an NBFC whose license was canceled by RBI, with an Administrator appointed on 04.11.2020)[cite: 16]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: SIDBI sanctioned two term loans of Rs. 20 Crores and Rs. 30 Crores via Letters of Intent dated 21.02.2019 and 23.10.2019, executed loan agreements and deeds of hypothecation, and disbursed Rs. 50 Crores in total (Rs. 20 Crores on 28.02.2019; Rs. 30 Crores in two tranches of Rs. 15 Crores on 14.11.2019 and 17.01.2020)[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Repayable in 36 monthly installments due on the 10th of each month. Respondent defaulted post-November 2020. Account classified as NPA on 15.12.2020. Outstanding amount as of 05.09.2022 stood at Rs. 35,65,60,488/-[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account classified as NPA on 15.12.2020[cite: 16]. SIDBI filed initial Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 42/CB/2022 on 14.09.2022, which NCLT Cuttack dismissed on 22.11.2022 under Section 10A[cite: 16]. NCLAT dismissed SIDBI's appeal (Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 28/2023) on 12.01.2023 with liberty to file a fresh application[cite: 16]. SIDBI filed fresh Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 27/CB/2023 citing default date as 10.07.2021[cite: 16]. NCLT Cuttack dismissed the fresh petition on 08.05.2023[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Letters of Intent, Loan Agreements, Deeds of Hypothecation, ROC charge registrations, statements of account, and the Corporate Debtor's categorical counter affidavit admitting debt and default post-September 2020[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Cuttack Bench dismissed SIDBI's fresh Section 7 petition on 08.05.2023, holding that a second petition for the same debt was not maintainable following the dismissal of CP No. 42/CB/2022 and that changing the default date violated Section 10A[cite: 16]. SIDBI appealed to NCLAT[cite: 16].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a financial creditor is barred from filing a fresh Section 7 application with a modified or subsequent date of default occurring outside the Section 10A suspension period after an earlier petition citing an NPA date within the 10A window was dismissed with liberty; (ii) Whether each successive monthly installment default under a term loan agreement constitutes a fresh, independent cause of action[cite: 16].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Non-payment of successive monthly installments under a term loan agreement constitutes separate and independent events of default, each giving rise to a fresh cause of action; where an initial insolvency petition is dismissed under Section 10A due to an NPA date falling within the prohibited window, a financial creditor is fully entitled to file a fresh application based on subsequent installment defaults occurring outside the Section 10A period, as supported by liberty granted by an appellate tribunal[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 10A bars the filing of applications for defaults occurring strictly between 25.03.2020 and 24.03.2021, but it does not extinguish the underlying debt or bar actions for fresh defaults arising thereafter, as affirmed in NuFuture Digital (India) Ltd. and Kotak Mahindra Bank v. Anuj Kumar[cite: 16]. Furthermore, following Dena Bank and Abhijeet Infrastructure, pleadings regarding dates of default in Form-1 can be amended or updated to reflect continuing defaults[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified from statements of account and the Corporate Debtor's unequivocal counter affidavit that installment defaults continued post-25.03.2021, culminating in a default exceeding the Rs. 1 Crore threshold by 10.07.2021[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The fresh petition was based on independent post-10A defaults, was fully maintainable pursuant to NCLAT's liberty order, and met all thresholds under Section 7[cite: 16].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 784 of 2023 is allowed; the impugned order dated 08.05.2023 passed by NCLT Cuttack Bench is set aside[cite: 16]. The Section 7 application filed by SIDBI is admitted against Sambandh Finserve Private Limited, and the Adjudicating Authority is directed to take up the matter within 10 days to initiate CIRP proceedings in accordance with the IBC[cite: 16]. No order as to costs[cite: 16].
summary: SIDBI appealed against an NCLT Cuttack order dismissing its fresh Section 7 CIRP petition against Sambandh Finserve Pvt. Ltd. for a default of Rs. 35.65 Crores[cite: 16]. The NCLT had dismissed the petition, holding that a second petition for the same debt was barred because an earlier petition had been rejected under Section 10A and the default date could not be shifted[cite: 16]. Allowing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that each successive monthly installment default constitutes a fresh, independent cause of action occurring outside the Section 10A suspension period[cite: 16]. Relying on NuFuture Digital and Dena Bank, the Tribunal ruled that fresh petitions based on post-10A defaults are fully maintainable, especially when filed with liberty from the Appellate Tribunal, and admitted the petition for CIRP initiation[cite: 16].

case_title: M/s. Toyfort vs. Competition Commission of India
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain, Technical Members Naresh Salecha and Indevar Pandey)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is M/s. Toyfort, a sole proprietorship concern owned by Suresh Kumar Gupta engaged in the sale of toys and stationery[cite: 17]. The Respondent is the Competition Commission of India (CCI)[cite: 17]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Department of Agriculture, Government of Uttar Pradesh, invited e-tenders for soil sample testing in various divisions (specifically Moradabad and Bareilly in 2018, and Meerut and Jhansi in 2017)[cite: 17]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The CCI alleged bid-rigging and cartelization in soil testing tenders, leading to an investigation by the Director General (DG) and subsequent penalty imposition[cite: 17]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A general complaint was received by CCI on 07.08.2018[cite: 17]. CCI passed a prima facie order under Section 26(1) on 30.01.2020 directing DG investigation[cite: 17]. DG submitted the investigation report on 08.04.2021[cite: 17]. CCI issued notice and heard the parties, passing the final penalty order under Section 27[cite: 17]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Statements of Suresh Kumar Gupta (Proprietor of Toyfort) and Rahul Teni (Director of Austere Systems); common shareholding (Suresh Gupta and son Piyush Gupta held 30% in Austere Systems); EMD of Toyfort submitted from the bank account of Shikhir Gupta (Director of rival bidder Fimo Info Solutions); shared registered address between Toyfort and Fimo Info Solutions; and a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) dated 19.02.2018 between Toyfort and Austere Systems[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CCI held Toyfort and other opposite parties in contravention of Sections 3(3)(c) and 3(3)(d) read with Section 3(1) of the Competition Act, imposing a penalty of 5% of average annual turnover[cite: 17]. Toyfort appealed to NCLAT under Section 53B via Competition Appeal (AT) No. 34 of 2022[cite: 17].
legal_issues: (i) Whether M/s. Toyfort indulged in bid-rigging and collusive bidding in contravention of Sections 3(3)(c) and 3(3)(d) read with Section 3(1) of the Competition Act, 2002 in respect of the 2017 soil testing tenders for Meerut and Jhansi divisions[cite: 17]; (ii) Whether the monetary penalty imposed by the Commission at 5% of average turnover was legally sustainable and proportional[cite: 17].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Sections 3(3)(c) and 3(3)(d) read with Section 3(1) of the Competition Act, 2002, submission of bids by related entities and non-qualified concerns without independent intent to compete, but solely to create a façade of competition and support a winning bidder, constitutes illegal bid-rigging and cartelization. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 27(b) empowers the CCI to impose monetary penalties up to 10% of turnover, and where relevant turnover from an illegal tender is nil, the total turnover of the enterprise can be utilized for penalty computation to avoid regulatory arbitrage and achieve statutory deterrence, as established in Excel Crop Care. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized sworn statements under oath, shared shareholdings (30% in Austere Systems), common registered addresses, and financial transactions (EMD paid by a rival director), concluding that Toyfort acted as a cover bidder for Austere Systems without possessing any soil-testing experience or infrastructure. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The finding of guilt under Section 3(3)(c) and (d) and the cease-and-desist order under Section 27(a) were legally sound and upheld, but the penalty under Section 27(b) was modified and reduced from 5% to 3% of average annual turnover to account for the appellant's supporting/cover role in the cartel[cite: 17].
operative_order: Competition Appeal (AT) No. 34 of 2022 is partly allowed; the Competition Commission of India's order holding M/s. Toyfort guilty under Section 3(3)(c) and 3(3)(d) read with Section 3(1) and the cease-and-desist order under Section 27(a) are upheld, while the penalty under Section 27(b) is reduced from 5% to 3% of the average annual turnover for the last three years[cite: 17]. All pending IAs are disposed of[cite: 17].
summary: M/s. Toyfort, a sole proprietorship engaged in toy sales, appealed against a Competition Commission of India (CCI) order finding it guilty of bid-rigging and cartelization in 2017 soil testing tenders for Meerut and Jhansi divisions invited by the UP Department of Agriculture[cite: 17]. The CCI had imposed a penalty of 5% of average annual turnover[cite: 17]. Dismissing the challenge to liability, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that Toyfort, along with related entities Austere Systems and Fimo Info Solutions, acted in concert as cover bidders to create a façade of competition without possessing any technical experience or infrastructure[cite: 17]. Upholding the guilt and cease-and-desist directions, the Tribunal partially allowed the appeal by reducing the monetary penalty to 3% of average annual turnover[cite: 17].

case_title: HTC Impex Pvt. Ltd. vs. Santipara Tea Company Ltd.
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1547 of 2022 & I.A. No. 4948 of 2022
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain and Technical Member Ajai Das Mehrotra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is HTC Impex Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor). The Respondent is Santipara Tea Company Ltd. (Corporate Debtor, owner of Demdima Tea Estate). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Pursuant to purchase orders placed in 2012 for agrochemicals, insecticides, herbicides, and pesticides, the Appellant supplied goods and raised invoices upon delivery. Last supply was made on 15.05.2012. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: First default occurred 90 days post first invoice raised on 31.01.2012. Last on-account part payment was made by the Corporate Debtor on 05.08.2014 for Rs. 20,000/-. Claimed outstanding stood at Rs. 7,24,530/- with 14% p.a. interest, allegedly confirmed via letter dated 09.03.2015. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Last payment made on 05.08.2014 (or account confirmation on 09.03.2015). Winding-up petition (CP No. 161 of 2016) filed before Calcutta High Court on 19.02.2016, disposed of on 29.03.2016 granting liberty to take steps in accordance with law due to a Central Government notification dated 28.01.2016 under Section 16E of the Tea Act, 1953 taking over management. Section 9 application filed in January 2020 (CP No. 166/KB/2020). NCLT Kolkata dismissed Section 9 as time-barred on 21.09.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Invoices, ledger accounts, on-account payment receipt dated 05.08.2014, account confirmation letter dated 09.03.2015, Calcutta High Court order dated 29.03.2016, and Ministry of Commerce notification dated 28.01.2016. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata dismissed CP No. 166/KB/2020 on 21.09.2022 on grounds of limitation. Operational Creditor appealed to NCLAT under Section 61, claiming time was excluded during the pendency of high court winding-up proceedings and Supreme Court litigation concerning Duncans Industries. emulation.
legal_issues: (i) Whether the period of limitation for filing an application under Section 9 of the IBC stands extended or arrested during the pendency of a winding-up petition disposed of under the Tea Act, 1953, or by virtue of a third-party judgment of the Supreme Court in Duncans Industries.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, an application under Section 9 of the IBC must be filed within three years from the date when the right to sue accrues (such as the date of last part payment or account confirmation), and limitation is neither arrested nor extended by the disposal of a prior winding-up petition where statutory consent was omitted, nor by third-party litigation to which the parties were not privy. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The three-year limitation period is absolute. A winding-up petition disposed of on the technical ground that Central Government consent under the Tea Act, 1953 was required does not keep the cause of action alive indefinitely when the creditor fails to pursue statutory remedies or seek such consent. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the last payment occurred on 05.08.2014 (or account confirmation on 09.03.2015), meaning the three-year limitation period expired by March 2018, rendering a Section 9 petition filed in January 2020 hopelessly time-barred. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 9 application was barred by limitation, and the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in dismissing it.
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1547 of 2022 & I.A. No. 4948 of 2022 are dismissed, upholding the order dated 21.09.2022 passed by NCLT Kolkata dismissing CP No. 166/KB/2020. No costs.
summary: HTC Impex Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Kolkata order dismissing its Section 9 IBC application against Santipara Tea Company Ltd. for an operational debt of Rs. 7.24 Lakhs on the ground of limitation. The appellant argued that limitation was suspended during earlier winding-up proceedings before the Calcutta High Court and subsequent Supreme Court litigation involving Duncans Industries. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that the last payment occurred in August 2014 (or March 2015), making a 2020 petition time-barred, and that third-party judgments or unprosecuted winding-up liberty cannot extend limitation.

case_title: Yarn Sales Corporation vs. Punjab State Power Corporation Ltd. & Anr.
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 292 of 2024 & I.A. No. 981, 982 of 2024
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain and Technical Member Indevar Pandey)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Yarn Sales Corporation (represented by partner Rajesh Kumar, Successful Auction Purchaser). Respondent No. 1 is Punjab State Power Corporation Ltd. (PSPCL, distribution licensee). Respondent No. 2 is the Liquidator of Gian Chand & Sons Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was admitted into liquidation on 05.09.2019. Liquidator invited claims, and PSPCL submitted a claim of Rs. 34,59,859/- for past electricity dues for account no. 3002810493 at the company's building in Ludhiana, which the Liquidator admitted. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Connection was disconnected due to non-payment of pre-CIRP electricity dues. Outstanding raised by PSPCL totaled Rs. 70,17,865/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Corporate Debtor admitted to liquidation on 05.09.2019. E-auction took place on 18.02.2022. Appellant purchased land and building for Rs. 4.30 Crores. Sale certificate was issued on 22.03.2022 'on as is where is, as is what is, whatever there is and no recourse basis', stipulating that past, present, and future statutory liabilities including electricity dues should be borne by the successful bidder. Appellant applied for a fresh 99KW electricity connection on 12.05.2022. PSPCL demanded clearance of Rs. 70.17 Lakhs on 20.05.2022. NCLT Chandigarh dismissed Appellant's IA No. 962/2022 on 01.12.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Sale certificate dated 22.03.2022 containing 'as is where is' clauses; PSPCL demand letter dated 20.05.2022 for Rs. 70,17,865/-; and liquidation claim records. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh dismissed IA No. 962/2022 on 01.12.2023, holding that since the asset was purchased on an 'as is where is' basis with explicit terms making the auction purchaser liable for past electricity dues, the demand was valid. Auction purchaser appealed to NCLAT under Section 60(5)[cite: 19].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a distribution licensee can insist upon the payment of pre-CIRP/pre-liquidation electricity arrears of the corporate debtor as a precondition for granting a fresh electricity connection to a successful auction purchaser who acquired assets on an 'as is where is' basis under the IBC[cite: 19].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 238 of the IBC, the provisions of the Code override all other laws including the Electricity Act, 2003; consequently, a distribution licensee cannot insist on the payment of pre-CIRP or pre-liquidation electricity arrears of the corporate debtor as a condition for granting a fresh electricity connection to a successful auction purchaser, notwithstanding any 'as is where is' or liability-shifting clauses inserted in the e-auction sale certificate. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238 gives overriding effect to the IBC over the Electricity Act (as settled by the Supreme Court in Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam v. Raman Ispat and Tata Power Western Odisha). Once claims are submitted and dealt with in liquidation, unpaid arrears stand extinguished under the 'clean slate' principle, and contractual terms in a sale certificate cannot override statutory mandates. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that PSPCL had submitted its claim in the liquidation process, that the property was purchased in liquidation, and that PSPCL was conditioning a new connection on past arrears. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in upholding the electricity dues demand; the clean slate principle shields the auction purchaser from past liabilities, and a fresh connection must be granted upon complying with regular formalities excluding past dues[cite: 19].
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 292 of 2024 is allowed; the impugned order dated 01.12.2023 passed by NCLT Chandigarh in IA No. 962 of 2022 is set aside[cite: 19]. Respondent No. 1 is directed to grant a fresh electricity connection to the Appellant after taking all necessary regular charges, excluding the outstanding pre-CIRP/pre-liquidation dues of the Corporate Debtor which stand extinguished[cite: 19].
summary: Yarn Sales Corporation, a successful auction purchaser of land and building in the liquidation of Gian Chand & Sons Pvt. Ltd., appealed against an NCLT Chandigarh order dismissing its application against PSPCL[cite: 19]. The NCLT had held that because the property was sold on an 'as is where is' basis and the sale certificate explicitly stated that past electricity dues must be borne by the bidder, PSPCL could lawfully condition a new connection on the payment of Rs. 70.17 Lakhs in past arrears[cite: 19]. Allowing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench relied on Tata Power Western Odisha and Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam to hold that under Section 238 of the IBC, the clean slate principle overrides any 'as is where is' clauses in sale certificates[cite: 19]. The Tribunal ruled that past electricity dues stand extinguished in liquidation and ordered PSPCL to grant a fresh connection without demanding pre-CIRP arrears[cite: 19].

case_title: Sanskriti Allottee Welfare Association (Reg.) & Ors. vs. Gaurav Katiyar, RP of Earthcon Universal Infratech Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan, Technical Members Barun Mitra and Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Sanskriti Allottee Welfare Association and individual homebuyers of the 'Sanskriti' residential project developed by the Corporate Debtor, Earthcon Universal Infratech Pvt. Ltd. Respondent No. 1 is Gaurav Katiyar, Resolution Professional (RP). Respondent No. 2 is Noida Power Company Limited (NPCL, electricity supplier)[cite: 20]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was developing housing projects 'Sanskriti' and 'CASA' in Greater Noida West. Section 7 CIRP was admitted in 2019. Homebuyers received possession between February 2018 and January 2020. NPCL provided a single-point temporary commercial electricity connection for construction, which also powered resident apartments without separate connections. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: At CIRP commencement, homebuyers paid maintenance at Re. 1/- per sq. ft. plus GST, while an accumulated unpaid electricity bill of Rs. 70 Lakhs (escalating to over Rs. 99 Lakhs and subsequently Rs. 1.58–1.69 Crores) was owed to NPCL. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated in 2019. 12th CoC meeting held on 21.01.2022 resolved to increase maintenance charges from Re. 1/- to Rs. 2/- per sq. ft. plus GST to absorb common area electricity costs. RP notified residents on 28.01.2022. Homebuyers filed IA No. 1146/2022. NCLT passed interim orders on 14.03.2022 directing residents to pay pending maintenance/electricity charges while restraining disconnection. RP filed IA No. 3234/2023 seeking modification to permit disconnection. NCLT New Delhi passed the impugned order on 14.06.2023 dismissing IA 1146/2022 as infructuous and allowing IA 3234/2023 with liberty to take coercive steps for non-payment[cite: 20]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CoC 3rd, 12th, and 15th meeting minutes; NPCL electricity bills and disconnection notices; RP communications dated 23.06.2021, 04.02.2022, and 21.02.2022; and NCLT orders dated 14.03.2022 and 14.06.2023[cite: 20]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-III dismissed homebuyer IA No. 1146/2022 as infructuous and allowed RP's IA No. 3234/2023 on 14.06.2023, granting liberty to enforce maintenance and common area electricity collections through coercive measures[cite: 20]. Homebuyers appealed to NCLAT under Section 61[cite: 20].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the Committee of Creditors and Resolution Professional are legally empowered during CIRP to increase monthly maintenance charges to absorb common area electricity dues owed to a utility supplier; (ii) Whether electricity charges incurred to maintain a real estate project as a going concern constitute CIRP costs that exempt residents from paying current maintenance and electricity dues during moratorium under Section 14[cite: 20].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 14(2) and (2A) read with the Explanation to Section 14(1) of the IBC, while essential supplies like electricity must be continued during CIRP to preserve corporate value, beneficiaries and residents enjoying such services are legally obligated to pay current dues arising from their consumption; neither the moratorium nor Regulations 31/32 exempt residents from paying current maintenance and common area electricity charges, and the CoC in its commercial wisdom is fully competent to upwardly revise maintenance fees to cover actual utility outlays. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(2A) and the Explanation to Section 14(1) introduced by the 2020 Amendment clarify that essential supplies are protected only subject to the condition that current dues are regularly paid. Following Shailesh Verma, non-payment of current consumption charges entitles suppliers and resolution professionals to suspend services or enforce collections. Under RERA Section 11(4)(d), the promoter/RP must provide essential services on reasonable charges. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that CoC 3rd, 12th, and 15th meeting minutes established a shortfall of Re. 1/- per sq. ft. in covering common area power consumption (28,000 units monthly), that the CoC approved the hike to Rs. 2/- per sq. ft. with over 80% majority, and that resident defaults had escalated arrears to over Rs. 1.68 Crores. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC acted within its commercial competence, the RP committed no procedural impropriety, and residents are bound to pay current maintenance and electricity charges, validating the NCLT's coercive collection liberty[cite: 20].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 878 of 2023 is dismissed, upholding the order dated 14.06.2023 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench-III in IA No. 1146/2022 and IA No. 3234/2023[cite: 20]. No order as to costs[cite: 20].
summary: Sanskriti Allottee Welfare Association and individual homebuyers appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order that dismissed their application challenging a CoC decision to double maintenance charges from Re. 1/- to Rs. 2/- per sq. ft. and allowed the RP's application granting liberty to take coercive steps (including electricity disconnection) against residents defaulting on maintenance and common area power dues[cite: 20]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that under Section 14(2A) and the Explanation to Section 14(1) of the IBC (as interpreted in Shailesh Verma), essential supplies like electricity must be paid for currently, and residents cannot shelter behind moratorium to avoid paying common area power costs[cite: 20]. The Tribunal upheld the CoC's commercial decision and the NCLT's order[cite: 20].

case_title: Jaldhara Properties and Trading Pvt. Ltd. vs. Prashant Jain, RP of Sudal Industries Ltd. & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 707 of 2023 with Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1420 of 2023
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain, Technical Members Naresh Salecha and Indevar Pandey)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Jaldhara Properties and Trading Pvt. Ltd. (unsecured financial creditor). Respondent No. 1 is Sudal Industries Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). Respondent No. 2 is Prashant Jain, Resolution Professional / RP for PPIRP[cite: 21]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant filed an application under Section 7 of the IBC on 09.12.2020 before NCLT Mumbai as an unsecured financial creditor claiming Rs. 9,63,75,010/-, registered as CP (IB) No. 63/MB-IV/2021[cite: 21]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose on financial debt owed by the Corporate Debtor to the Appellant[cite: 21]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application filed on 09.12.2020[cite: 21]. The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Act, 2021 (Act No. 26 of 2021) introducing Chapter III-A (Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process / PPIRP) and Section 11A received presidential assent on 11.08.2021 and became enforceable retrospectively w.e.f. 04.04.2021[cite: 21]. Corporate Debtor filed an application under Section 54C for PPIRP initiation on 04.09.2022 (CP (PP) No. 01/MB-IV/2022)[cite: 21]. NCLT Mumbai admitted the Section 54C application on 20.04.2023[cite: 21]. RP filed IA No. 3021/2023 on 13.07.2023 for base resolution plan approval under Section 54K(15), which NCLT approved on 10.08.2023[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Section 7 petition dated 09.12.2020; Section 54C PPIRP application dated 04.09.2022; base resolution plan approval application IA No. 3021/2023; and NCLT orders dated 20.04.2023 and 10.08.2023[cite: 21]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai prioritized and admitted the Corporate Debtor's subsequent Section 54C PPIRP application on 20.04.2023 and approved the base plan on 10.08.2023 while refusing to consider the Appellant's prior Section 7 petition[cite: 21]. Jaldhara Properties filed two appeals under Section 61 (Comp. App. 707/2023 against PPIRP admission and Comp. App. 1420/2023 against plan approval)[cite: 21].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an application for Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (PPIRP) filed under Section 54C can be given priority of consideration and decision over and above a pending Section 7 application filed prior to the commencement of the Amendment Act, 2021, in light of the bar under Section 11A(4) of the IBC[cite: 21].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 11A(4) of the IBC (inserted by the Amendment Act, 2021 w.e.f. 04.04.2021), the statutory provisions governing the priority and disposal of PPIRP applications under Section 54C vis-à-vis Section 7, 9, or 10 applications do not apply where a Section 7, 9, or 10 application was already filed and pending as of 04.04.2021; consequently, an Adjudicating Authority commits a patent illegality by giving precedence to a subsequent Section 54C PPIRP application over a pre-existing, pending Section 7 petition. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 11A regulates precedence between Section 54C and Section 7/9/10 applications, but sub-section (4) explicitly carves out an exception, excluding its operation where a Section 7/9/10 application was pending as on 04.04.2021[cite: 21]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that Jaldhara's Section 7 petition was instituted on 09.12.2020 (prior to the 04.04.2021 amendment), whereas the Corporate Debtor's Section 54C application was filed much later on 04.09.2022[cite: 21]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Section 11A(4) squarely applied, barring the NCLT from prioritizing the PPIRP application over the pending Section 7 petition; both the PPIRP admission and subsequent plan approval orders were patently illegal and set aside[cite: 21].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 707 of 2023 and Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1420 of 2023 are allowed[cite: 21]. The impugned order dated 20.04.2023 initiating PPIRP and the impugned order dated 10.08.2023 approving the base resolution plan in IA No. 3021 of 2023 are set aside[cite: 21]. No costs[cite: 21].
summary: Jaldhara Properties and Trading Pvt. Ltd. appealed against two NCLT Mumbai orders: one initiating Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (PPIRP) under Section 54C upon the Corporate Debtor's application, and another approving the base resolution plan[cite: 21]. The appellant had filed a Section 7 petition on 09.12.2020, which the NCLT sidelined in favor of the Corporate Debtor's subsequent September 2022 PPIRP application[cite: 21]. Allowing both appeals, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that under Section 11A(4) of the IBC (inserted by the 2021 Amendment w.e.f. 04.04.2021), priority rules do not apply where a Section 7 application was already pending prior to 04.04.2021[cite: 21]. The Tribunal ruled that the NCLT committed a patent error by prioritizing the PPIRP application, setting aside both the PPIRP initiation and the plan approval[cite: 21].

case_title: M/s Agroha Paper Industries Private Limited vs. Bank of Maharashtra
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is M/s Agroha Paper Industries Private Limited (Corporate Debtor / Corporate Applicant, represented by Director Chetan Agarwal). The Respondent is Bank of Maharashtra (Financial Creditor)[cite: 22]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed a loan facility from Bank of Maharashtra, which suffered financial distress and business losses triggered by the Covid-19 pandemic, leading to a default in loan repayment[cite: 22]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Bank of Maharashtra classified the Corporate Debtor's account as NPA on 28.10.2018 and issued a demand notice under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act on 11.01.2019[cite: 22]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 28.10.2018[cite: 22]. SARFAESI notice issued on 11.01.2019[cite: 22]. Corporate Debtor filed a Section 10 application on 04.08.2022 seeking initiation of CIRP against itself[cite: 22]. Bank took physical possession under Section 14 of SARFAESI on 24.05.2022 and auctioned properties[cite: 22]. NCLT Allahabad dismissed the Section 10 application on 22.08.2023[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan account NPA classification records; SARFAESI notices under Section 13(2) and 13(4); physical possession order under Section 14 dated 24.05.2022; and e-auction records[cite: 22]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Allahabad Bench dismissed the Corporate Debtor's Section 10 application on 22.08.2023, holding that the application lacked bona fides and was filed to pre-empt advanced SARFAESI recovery proceedings initiated by the Bank[cite: 22]. Corporate Debtor appealed to NCLAT under Section 61[cite: 22].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an Adjudicating Authority is bound to admit a complete application filed under Section 10 of the IBC by a corporate applicant once debt and default are established and Section 11 disqualifications are absent, or whether it can reject the application for lack of bona fides and as an abuse of process to pre-empt advanced SARFAESI recovery proceedings[cite: 22].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While Section 10 of the IBC enables a corporate applicant to initiate CIRP for its own insolvency resolution, an Adjudicating Authority is not a rubber stamp and is fully empowered to dismiss a Section 10 petition where the corporate applicant comes with unclean hands and attempts to abuse the judicial process as a dilatory logjam to frustrate advanced, pre-existing SARFAESI recovery proceedings initiated by a financial creditor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Although Unigreen Global and Leo Duct establish that complete Section 10 applications meeting Section 11 parameters are generally admitted, those rulings do not preclude an Adjudicating Authority from weeding out petitions lacking bona fides where a corporate debtor attempts to weaponize the moratorium to evade wilful defaulter identification and derail lawful asset auctions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that SARFAESI proceedings (Section 13(2) notice in Jan 2019, physical possession in May 2022) heavily preceded the Section 10 filing of August 2022, and that the promoters engaged in duplicity by dodging wilful defaulter hearings while attempting selective settlements. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 10 application lacked bona fides, constituted an abuse of process aimed at stalling bank recovery, and was correctly dismissed by the Adjudicating Authority[cite: 22].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1342 of 2023 is dismissed, upholding the impugned order dated 22.08.2023 passed by NCLT Allahabad Bench in CP (IB) No. 72/ALD/2022[cite: 22]. No costs[cite: 22].
summary: M/s Agroha Paper Industries Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Allahabad order dismissing its Section 10 corporate applicant CIRP petition against itself[cite: 22]. The NCLT had dismissed the application, holding that the corporate debtor approached the tribunal with unclean hands to pre-empt advanced SARFAESI recovery proceedings initiated by Bank of Maharashtra after the account turned NPA in October 2018[cite: 22]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that while Section 10 facilitates insolvency resolution, it cannot be weaponized as an abuse of process to frustrate lawful recovery actions when corporate promoters dodge wilful defaulter proceedings[cite: 22]. The Tribunal upheld the dismissal[cite: 22].

case_title: Rita Malhotra & Anr. vs. Orris Infrastructure Private Limited
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Rita Malhotra and Bina Chopra (Financial Creditors / Allottees). The Respondent is Orris Infrastructure Private Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was developing a commercial complex known as 'Floreal Tower' in Gurgaon. Corporate Debtor entered into an agreement/MOU with the Appellants on 24.04.2010 for commercial space allotment accompanied by a Monthly Assured Return (MAR) plan. Appellants paid the entire consideration of Rs. 29.98 Lakhs. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Clauses 2, 4, 5, and 6 of the MOU stipulated MAR payments for 36 months post-building completion or until office leasing, whichever was earlier. Corporate Debtor obtained an Occupancy Certificate on 16.08.2017. MAR payments were made up to June 2019. Default occurred when subsequent MAR payments and post-dated cheques under 2018/2019 settlement deeds were dishonored. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: MOU executed on 24.04.2010. Space Buyers Agreement executed on 26.04.2010. Occupancy Certificate issued on 16.08.2017. Initial Section 7 petition filed on 01.06.2018, withdrawn post-settlement. Second Section 7 petition filed and disposed of on 07.07.2019 with liberty to revive. Petition revived upon default. IBC Section 7 amended by Act 1 of 2020 w.e.f. 28.12.2019 introducing real estate allottee thresholds (100 allottees or 10%). NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi dismissed the Section 7 petition on 19.09.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: MOU dated 24.04.2010; Space Buyers Agreement dated 26.04.2010; Occupancy Certificate dated 16.08.2017; Settlement Deeds dated 09.07.2018 and 06.03.2019; and uncashed demand drafts. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench dismissed the Appellants' Section 7 petition on 19.09.2023, holding it non-maintainable for failing to meet the statutory threshold of 100 allottees or 10% under the second proviso to Section 7(1). Appellants appealed to NCLAT under Section 61[cite: 25].
legal_issues: (i) Whether investors under an assured return investment scheme linked to a commercial real estate allotment fall outside the definition of 'allottees under a real estate project' to evade the mandatory threshold requirements introduced by the second proviso to Section 7(1) of the IBC (Amendment Act 1 of 2020)[cite: 25].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Commercial space or unit allottees enrolled in an assured return scheme linked to a real estate project fall squarely within the definition of 'allottees' under the RERA Act and Explanation (ii) to Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC, and cannot bypass the mandatory threshold requirement of joining jointly with not less than 100 allottees or 10% of total allottees under the second proviso to Section 7(1) when initiating insolvency proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The second proviso to Section 7(1) read with Explanation (ii) to Section 5(8)(f) and RERA Section 2(d) encompasses all unit purchasers in a real estate project. Following Vishal Chelani and Rahul Gyanchandani, an allottee seeking remedies or assured returns does not lose the statutory status of a homebuyer/allottee, and artificial classifications attempting to segregate assured return investors from allottees are invalid. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the Appellants purchased commercial unit space in Floreal Tower (totaling 504 units, with 366 under assured returns), and filed a Section 7 petition individually without meeting the 100-allottee or 10% threshold. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellants retained the legal status of allottees, and their individual petition was barred for non-compliance with the second proviso to Section 7(1), validating the NCLT's dismissal[cite: 25].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 484 of 2024 is dismissed, upholding the order dated 19.09.2023 passed by NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi in CP (IB) No. 234(PB)/2019[cite: 25]. No costs[cite: 25].
summary: Rita Malhotra and Bina Chopra appealed against an NCLT Principal Bench order dismissing their Section 7 CIRP petition against Orris Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd[cite: 25]. The appellants had invested Rs. 29.98 Lakhs in commercial space at Floreal Tower under an MOU providing Monthly Assured Returns (MAR)[cite: 25]. The NCLT had dismissed the petition because it failed to meet the statutory threshold under the second proviso to Section 7(1) of the IBC (requiring 100 allottees or 10%)[cite: 25]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that assured return investors in commercial real estate projects remain 'allottees' under RERA and IBC Section 5(8)(f), as affirmed in Vishal Chelani and Rahul Gyanchandani[cite: 25]. The Tribunal ruled that the petition was rightly dismissed for failing to meet the mandatory threshold[cite: 25].

case_title: Inkel Limited vs. Shaji Mathew & Anr.
appeal_number: TA (AT) No. 258/2021 & Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 83 of 2021
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Member Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma and Technical Member Jatindranatha Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Inkel Limited (holding company holding 65% shares in the Corporate Debtor). Respondent No. 1 is Shaji Mathew (Operational Creditor). Respondent No. 2 is Seguro Foundations and Structures Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor and subsidiary of Inkel). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operational Creditor Shaji Mathew filed an application under Section 9 of the IBC before NCLT Kochi to initiate CIRP against Seguro Foundations and Structures Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 2). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose on operational dues owed by the subsidiary Corporate Debtor. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 9 petition (IBA/30/KOB/2020) filed by Operational Creditor. Operational Creditor filed IA No. 187/KOB/2020 seeking impleadment of Inkel Ltd. as an additional corporate debtor. NCLT Kochi allowed IA 187/2020 and passed the impugned impleadment order on 26.11.2020 without issuing a pre-impleadment notice to Inkel Ltd. Notice of impleadment served on Inkel Ltd. on 03.12.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Annual returns and directors' reports for FY 2018 and 2019 showing Inkel's 65% shareholding and managerial control; Share Purchase Agreement dated 08.11.2017; Share Subscription Agreement dated 16.11.2017; and NCLT Kochi order dated 26.11.2020. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kochi Bench allowed IA No. 187/KOB/2020 on 26.11.2020 ex parte, directing the impleadment of Inkel Ltd. as an additional corporate debtor based on its 65% shareholding and control. Inkel Ltd. appealed to NCLAT under Section 61, claiming violation of natural justice for lack of pre-impleadment notice.
legal_issues: (i) Whether an Adjudicating Authority is mandatorily required to issue a pre-impleadment show-cause notice to a third party before passing an order under Section 60(5) read with Order 1 Rule 10 CPC to implead them as a necessary or proper party to CIRP proceedings; (ii) Whether a holding company holding 65% shares and exercising managerial control can be impleaded as an additional corporate debtor in Section 9 insolvency proceedings against its subsidiary.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Order 1 Rule 10 of the CPC and NCLT procedural rules, issuing a pre-impleadment notice to a person proposed to be added as a party is not mandatory; a court or tribunal possesses the judicial discretion to implead a necessary or proper party first and thereafter issue notice for effective adjudication, leaving it open to the impleaded party to raise objections or seek striking out post-impleadment. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Order 1 Rule 10(2) empowers the tribunal to add parties at any stage. Following Delhi High Court precedent in Star Light Credit v. Robin Gupta and Walchandnagar Industries, insisting on pre-impleadment show cause notices is a contradiction in terms, as courts determine necessity first and issue notice subsequently. 3.
