EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that Inkel Ltd. held 65% shares in Seguro Foundations, exercised active operational and managerial control over its affairs, and that the impugned order explicitly granted Inkel Ltd. an opportunity to file a counter-affidavit post-impleadment. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The ex-parte impleadment order without prior notice violated no rules of natural justice, as post-impleadment notice and hearing adequately protected the appellant's rights.
operative_order: TA (AT) No. 258/2021 & Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 83/2021 are dismissed, upholding the impugned order dated 26.11.2020 passed by NCLT Kochi Bench in IA No. 187/KOB/2020 in IBA/30/KOB/2020[cite: 23].
summary: Inkel Limited, a holding company owning 65% shares in subsidiary Seguro Foundations and Structures Pvt. Ltd., appealed against an NCLT Kochi order that impleaded Inkel as an additional corporate debtor in Section 9 CIRP proceedings initiated by Operational Creditor Shaji Mathew[cite: 23]. The appellant argued that the impleadment order was passed ex parte without prior notice, violating natural justice[cite: 23]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Chennai Bench held that under Order 1 Rule 10 of the CPC (as explained in Star Light Credit and Walchandnagar Industries), a pre-impleadment show-cause notice is not mandatory[cite: 23]. The Tribunal ruled that tribunals have judicial discretion to add necessary parties first and issue notice subsequently for defense, and upheld the impleadment[cite: 23].

case_title: Fortune Land Holdings LLP vs. SPG Macrocosm Limited
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Fortune Land Holdings LLP (Financial Creditor). The Respondent is SPG Macrocosm Limited (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: In October 2018, the Corporate Debtor approached the Appellant for a loan of Rs. 70,00,000/-. A Loan Agreement was executed on 01.10.2018 for disbursal repayable within 36 months with 15% annual interest. An unsecured demand promissory note was executed as security. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Loan disbursed via RTGS: Rs. 15 Lakhs and Rs. 20 Lakhs on 09.10.2018, and Rs. 35 Lakhs on 10.01.2018 (totaling Rs. 70 Lakhs). Corporate Debtor defaulted on repayments starting from October 2021. Demand notices issued on 05.10.2021, 05.01.2022, 02.04.2022, 01.07.2022, and legal notice on 31.12.2022. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan agreement executed on 01.10.2018. Disbursals made in October 2018 and January 2018. Defaults began in October 2021. Appellant filed Section 7 petition (C.P. No. 23/MP/2023) before NCLT Indore. NeSL authenticated record of default (Form D) issued on 22.08.2023. NCLT Indore dismissed the Section 7 petition on 29.02.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan Agreement dated 01.10.2018; Unsecured Demand Promissory Note dated 01.10.2018; RTGS payment receipts; N.R. Panchal & Co. independent audit report / balance sheet reflecting the loan under Non-Current Liabilities; and NeSL Record of Default (Form D) authenticated on 22.08.2023[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Indore Bench dismissed Fortune Land Holdings' Section 7 petition on 29.02.2024, holding that the unsecured promissory note was insufficiently stamped under Schedule I Article 49(b) of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, and that the loan was a business loan rather than a financial debt. Appellant appealed to NCLAT under Section 61[cite: 24].
legal_issues: (i) Whether minor stamping deficiencies in a collateral promissory note render a Section 7 financial debt application inadmissible when primary evidence of debt and default (loan agreement, balance sheet, and NeSL record of default) is conclusively established; (ii) Whether a corporate loan carrying 15% interest constitutes a financial debt under Section 5(8) of the IBC[cite: 24].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 7 of the IBC, once the existence of a financial debt and default is conclusively established through primary evidence such as a registered loan agreement, independent audit reports reflecting non-current liabilities, and authenticated records of default from an information utility (NeSL), minor evidentiary or stamping deficiencies in a collateral promissory note cannot be used by an Adjudicating Authority to dismiss the petition. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Following the Supreme Court's seven-judge bench ruling in In Re: Interplay Between Arbitration Agreements and the Indian Stamp Act, unstamped or inadequately stamped instruments are curable defects that do not render underlying obligations void or unenforceable. Furthermore, a loan advanced for corporate purposes with stipulated interest constitutes a financial debt under Section 5(8) of the IBC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified the Loan Agreement dated 01.10.2018 reflecting Rs. 70 Lakhs principal and 15% interest, N.R. Panchal & Co.'s audit report reflecting the liability, and NeSL Form D Record of Default authenticated on 22.08.2023. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Debt and default were overwhelmingly proven by documentary evidence, and stamping issues regarding the promissory note could not defeat substantive insolvency proceedings; the dismissal order was set aside and CIRP admitted[cite: 24].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 621 of 2024 is allowed; the impugned order dated 29.02.2024 passed by NCLT Indore Bench is set aside[cite: 24]. The Section 7 application filed by the Appellant is admitted against SPG Macrocosm Limited, and the Adjudicating Authority is directed to take up the matter within 10 days to initiate CIRP proceedings in accordance with the IBC[cite: 24]. Each party shall bear its own costs[cite: 24].
summary: Fortune Land Holdings LLP appealed against an NCLT Indore order dismissing its Section 7 CIRP petition against SPG Macrocosm Ltd[cite: 24]. The appellant had advanced a loan of Rs. 70 Lakhs at 15% interest vide a Loan Agreement dated 01.10.2018[cite: 24]. The NCLT had dismissed the petition, holding that the collateral promissory note was insufficiently stamped under the Indian Stamp Act and that the loan was a general business loan[cite: 24]. Allowing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that primary evidence including the loan agreement, independent audit balance sheets, and NeSL Record of Default conclusively established debt and default[cite: 24]. Relying on the Supreme Court's seven-judge bench ruling on stamping, the Tribunal ruled that stamping defects in collateral notes are curable and cannot defeat substantive IBC proceedings, admitting the petition for CIRP initiation[cite: 24].

case_title: Rita Malhotra & Anr. vs. Orris Infrastructure Private Limited
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Rita Malhotra and Bina Chopra (Financial Creditors / Allottees). The Respondent is Orris Infrastructure Private Limited (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 25]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was developing a commercial complex known as 'Floreal Tower' in Gurgaon. Corporate Debtor entered into an agreement/MOU with the Appellants on 24.04.2010 for commercial space allotment accompanied by a Monthly Assured Return (MAR) plan. Appellants paid the entire consideration of Rs. 29.98 Lakhs. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Clauses 2, 4, 5, and 6 of the MOU stipulated MAR payments for 36 months post-building completion or until office leasing, whichever was earlier. Corporate Debtor obtained an Occupancy Certificate on 16.08.2017. MAR payments were made up to June 2019. Default occurred when subsequent MAR payments and post-dated cheques under 2018/2019 settlement deeds were dishonored. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: MOU executed on 24.04.2010. Space Buyers Agreement executed on 26.04.2010. Occupancy Certificate issued on 16.08.2017. Initial Section 7 petition filed on 01.06.2018, withdrawn post-settlement. Second Section 7 petition filed and disposed of on 07.07.2019 with liberty to revive. Petition revived upon default. IBC Section 7 amended by Act 1 of 2020 w.e.f. 28.12.2019 introducing real estate allottee thresholds (100 allottees or 10%). NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi dismissed the Section 7 petition on 19.09.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: MOU dated 24.04.2010; Space Buyers Agreement dated 26.04.2010; Occupancy Certificate dated 16.08.2017; Settlement Deeds dated 09.07.2018 and 06.03.2019; and uncashed demand drafts. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench dismissed the Appellants' Section 7 petition on 19.09.2023, holding it non-maintainable for failing to meet the statutory threshold of 100 allottees or 10% under the second proviso to Section 7(1). Appellants appealed to NCLAT under Section 61[cite: 25].
legal_issues: (i) Whether investors under an assured return investment scheme linked to a commercial real estate allotment fall outside the definition of 'allottees under a real estate project' to evade the mandatory threshold requirements introduced by the second proviso to Section 7(1) of the IBC (Amendment Act 1 of 2020)[cite: 25].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Commercial space or unit allottees enrolled in an assured return scheme linked to a real estate project fall squarely within the definition of 'allottees' under the RERA Act and Explanation (ii) to Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC, and cannot bypass the mandatory threshold requirement of joining jointly with not less than 100 allottees or 10% of total allottees under the second proviso to Section 7(1) when initiating insolvency proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The second proviso to Section 7(1) read with Explanation (ii) to Section 5(8)(f) and RERA Section 2(d) encompasses all unit purchasers in a real estate project. Following Vishal Chelani and Rahul Gyanchandani, an allottee seeking remedies or assured returns does not lose the statutory status of a homebuyer/allottee, and artificial classifications attempting to segregate assured return investors from allottees are invalid. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the Appellants purchased commercial unit space in Floreal Tower (totaling 504 units, with 366 under assured returns), and filed a Section 7 petition individually without meeting the 100-allottee or 10% threshold. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellants retained the legal status of allottees, and their individual petition was barred for non-compliance with the second proviso to Section 7(1), validating the NCLT's dismissal[cite: 25].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 484 of 2024 is dismissed, upholding the order dated 19.09.2023 passed by NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi in CP (IB) No. 234(PB)/2019[cite: 25]. No costs[cite: 25].
summary: Rita Malhotra and Bina Chopra appealed against an NCLT Principal Bench order dismissing their Section 7 CIRP petition against Orris Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd[cite: 25]. The appellants had invested Rs. 29.98 Lakhs in commercial space at Floreal Tower under an MOU providing Monthly Assured Returns (MAR)[cite: 25]. The NCLT had dismissed the petition because it failed to meet the statutory threshold under the second proviso to Section 7(1) of the IBC (requiring 100 allottees or 10%)[cite: 25]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that assured return investors in commercial real estate projects remain 'allottees' under RERA and IBC Section 5(8)(f), as affirmed in Vishal Chelani and Rahul Gyanchandani[cite: 25]. The Tribunal ruled that the petition was rightly dismissed for failing to meet the mandatory threshold[cite: 25].

case_title: UniCredit S.P.A. vs. IR Exports Private Limited
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Members Barun Mitra and Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is UniCredit S.P.A. (European Commercial Bank acting as Operational Creditor / Assignee). The Respondent is IR Exports Private Limited (formerly known as JR Apparel & Accessories Pvt. Ltd. / Corporate Debtor)[cite: 26]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: On 20.03.2017, the Corporate Debtor entered into a sales contract with Durst Phototechnik AG (Supplier) to purchase an industrial inkjet printer (Alpha 190-D) for Euro 535,780.00[cite: 26]. Corporate Debtor made a down payment of Euro 135,780.00 and issued six promissory notes dated 11.05.2017 totaling Euro 421,000.00 (comprising Euro 400,000 balance machine cost and Euro 21,000 special financing interest at 3% p.a.) maturing between 18.11.2017 and 18.05.2020[cite: 26]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Supplier issued invoice no. 21706064 dated 15.05.2017 for Euro 535,780.00[cite: 26]. Machine was delivered late on 28.08.2017 (agreed delivery: 15.04.2017)[cite: 26]. Corporate Debtor paid only the first promissory note of Euro 72,666.67 on 20.12.2017 and defaulted on subsequent installments[cite: 26]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Machine delivered on 28.08.2017 with acceptance certificate[cite: 26]. Supplier assigned receivables and endorsed promissory notes to UniCredit via Cash Discount Agreement on 23.08.2017[cite: 26]. First installment paid on 20.12.2017[cite: 26]. Operational Creditor issued Section 8 demand notice on 19.05.2021[cite: 26]. Section 9 petition filed before NCLT Chandigarh[cite: 26]. NCLT Chandigarh dismissed the Section 9 petition on 06.07.2023[cite: 26]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Sales contract dated 20.03.2017; proforma and tax invoices; bill of lading dated 18.05.2017; acceptance certificate dated 28.08.2017; promissory notes; Cash Discount Agreement dated 23.08.2017; and email communications between Corporate Debtor and Supplier spanning September 2017 to March 2018 documenting performance defects, test runs, and requests to take back the machine[cite: 26]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh Bench dismissed UniCredit's Section 9 application on 06.07.2023, holding that the Corporate Debtor raised a bona fide pre-existing dispute regarding machine defects, improper service of the demand notice, and the presence of an arbitration clause[cite: 26]. Operational Creditor appealed to NCLAT under Section 61[cite: 26].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the Corporate Debtor's email communications documenting severe performance defects, machine idling, and requests for machine return prior to the service of the Section 8 demand notice constitute a genuine 'pre-existing dispute' under Section 9(5)(2)(d) of the IBC; (ii) Whether the presence of an acceptance certificate executed upon delivery precludes the corporate debtor from raising performance-based pre-existing disputes[cite: 26].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 9(5)(2)(d) of the IBC, an Adjudicating Authority must reject a Section 9 application if a genuine, plausible pre-existing dispute regarding product quality, performance defects, or breach of contract existed between the parties prior to the receipt of the Section 8 demand notice; the standard of a pre-existing dispute does not require proof of ultimate success, but merely the existence of a real, non-illusory contention. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Following Mobilox Innovations and Innoventive Industries, once a plausible pre-existing dispute is substantiated by contemporaneous documentation such as emails and repair logs, the operational creditor falls outside the summary purview of Section 9. Acceptance certificates do not estop a corporate buyer from raising genuine performance grievances if equipment fails subsequent to initial delivery. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized email trails from September 2017 to March 2018 (including communications on 11.09.2017, 25.09.2017, 05.10.2017, 07.11.2017, and technical report by expert Mr. Mario on 07.03.2018) establishing that the inkjet printer suffered from persistent recipe, ink-bleeding, and temperature issues, and that the machine remained non-functional and idle. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: A genuine and bona fide pre-existing dispute existed prior to the service of the demand notice, and the NCLT committed no error in dismissing the Section 9 petition[cite: 26].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1330 of 2023 is dismissed, upholding the impugned order dated 06.07.2023 passed by NCLT Chandigarh Bench in CP (IB) No. 236/CHD/HRY/2021[cite: 26]. No orders as to costs[cite: 26].
summary: UniCredit S.P.A., an Italian commercial bank acting as assignee of an operational debt, appealed against an NCLT Chandigarh order dismissing its Section 9 CIRP petition against IR Exports Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 26] The debt arose from unpaid promissory notes for an industrial inkjet printer supplied by Durst Phototechnik AG[cite: 26]. The NCLT had dismissed the petition based on pre-existing performance defects and improper notice service[cite: 26]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that contemporaneous emails exchanged between September 2017 and March 2018 demonstrated a genuine pre-existing dispute regarding machine malfunctions, ink bleeding, and requests to take back the equipment[cite: 26]. Relying on Mobilox Innovations, the Tribunal ruled that plausible pre-existing disputes bar Section 9 proceedings and upheld the dismissal[cite: 26].

case_title: Tulip Star Hotels Ltd. & Anr. vs. Anish Niranjan Nanavaty & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1127 of 2024 with Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 1129 of 2024
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Tulip Star Hotels Ltd. & Anr. (Shareholder / Promoter and Suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor, V Hotels Ltd.). Respondent No. 1 is Anish Niranjan Nanavaty, Resolution Professional. Respondent No. 2 is Macrotech Developers Ltd. (MDL / Successful Resolution Applicant). Respondent No. 4 is Pegasus Asset Reconstruction Company Pvt. Ltd. (secured financial creditor). Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Ltd. (ARCIL) is another secured financial creditor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP against V Hotels Ltd. commenced on an application by ARCIL. RP appointed registered valuers (average fair value: Rs. 1074.27 Crores; average liquidation value: Rs. 758.35 Crores). Two secured financial creditors (ARCIL and Pegasus) submitted claims admitted at Rs. 1546.1 Crores and Rs. 521.80 Crores respectively. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose on secured loan facilities extended by financial creditors, culminating in CIRP admission. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Information Memorandum and addendum published on 01.08.2022. CoC approved MDL's resolution plan with a 100% vote share on 26.06.2023. NCLT previously passed order on 21.07.2023 upholding ARCIL's interest calculation at 22%, which NCLAT set aside on 21.11.2023 in Comp. App. (Ins.) Nos. 1114-1115/2023, reducing ARCIL's interest rate to 14.85% and directing claim redetermination. Pegasus wrote to RP on 27.11.2023 seeking redetermination of its claim on identical terms. SRA submitted an Addendum on 09.12.2023 confirming no change in financial outlay (Rs. 888.69 Crores payable to secured creditors). CoC approved the Addendum with 97.34% votes in its 32nd meeting on 13.12.2023. Supreme Court dismissed promoter appeals against NCLAT's 14.85% interest ruling on 10.05.2024. NCLT Mumbai Court-II approved the resolution plan and addendum on 26.04.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Valuation reports; claims records; NCLAT judgment dated 21.11.2023; Pegasus email dated 27.11.2023; SRA Addendum dated 09.12.2023; CoC 32nd meeting minutes dated 13.01.2023; and Supreme Court order dated 10.05.2024. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Court-II dismissed promoter IA No. 111/2024 (challenging Addendum), allowed RP's IA No. 5606/2023 (redetermining Pegasus's claim), and allowed IA No. 2830/2023 (approving the Resolution Plan) on 26.04.2024[cite: 28]. Promoters appealed to NCLAT via Comp. App. 1127 and 1129 of 2024[cite: 28].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the redetermination of one secured financial creditor's claim (ARCIL) pursuant to an appellate order invalidates an approved resolution plan or necessitates recalculation without a corresponding inter se claim redetermination of another secured financial creditor (Pegasus); (ii) Whether a promoter/shareholder with nil payout under a resolution plan has locus to challenge inter se claim adjustments among secured financial creditors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The redetermination of a financial creditor's claim pursuant to an appellate order does not invalidate an approved resolution plan or its financial outlay if the total financial proposal remains unchanged; where a co-secured financial creditor voluntarily requests a parallel claim redetermination on identical terms, and the CoC approves an addendum by requisite majority with pro-rata inter se distribution, such adjustments affect only inter se creditors and provide no ground for a nil-payout shareholder/promoter to challenge plan approval. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Following K. Sashidhar, Essar Steel, and the Supreme Court's clarificatory order dated 10.05.2024 in this very matter, re-working or verification of claims following interest rate modifications has no impact on the overall resolution plan implementation, affecting solely inter se distribution among a similar class of creditors. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that Pegasus explicitly requested claim redetermination at 14.05% on 27.11.2023, that the SRA's Addendum confirmed the total secured payout remained pegged at Rs. 888.69 Crores, and that the CoC approved the pro-rata distribution ratio (65.91:34.09) with 97.34% votes. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The redetermination was legally regular, the CoC acted within its commercial wisdom, the plan met Section 30(2) parameters, and the appeals lacked merit.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1127 of 2024 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1129 of 2024 are dismissed, upholding the orders dated 26.04.2024 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench, Court-II in IA No. 111 of 2024, IA No. 5606 of 2023, and IA No. 2830 of 2023 approving the resolution plan and addendum[cite: 28]. No order as to costs[cite: 28].
summary: Promoters and shareholders of V Hotels Ltd. appealed against two NCLT Mumbai orders approving the resolution plan submitted by Macrotech Developers Ltd. (MDL) with 100% CoC voting, approving an addendum, and redetermining secured creditor claims[cite: 28]. The appellants argued that once NCLAT reduced ARCIL's interest rate to 14.85%, Pegasus's claim should also have been formally redetermined prior to plan approval, and that the addendum altered financial terms[cite: 28]. Dismissing the appeals, the NCLAT Principal Bench noted that Pegasus had voluntarily sought parallel redetermination, the SRA's addendum confirmed no change to the total secured payout of Rs. 888.69 Crores, and the Supreme Court had already clarified that interest redeterminations affect only inter se creditor distribution without impacting plan implementation[cite: 28]. The Tribunal upheld the plan approval and dismissed the appeals[cite: 28].

case_title: National Highways Authority of India vs. IVRCL Chengapalli Tollways Limited & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins.) No. 62 of 2024 & IA No. 626 of 2024
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Member Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma and Technical Member Jatindranath Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) represented through DGM (T) & Project Director[cite: 8]. Respondent No. 1 is IVRCL Chengapalli Tollways Limited (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 8]. Respondent No. 2 is the Resolution Professional[cite: 8]. Respondent No. 3 is the Committee of Creditors / other respondents[cite: 8]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: On 25.03.2010, NHAI and Respondent No. 1 entered into a concession agreement for a BOT road project involving six-laning of Chengapalli to Coimbatore Bypass and four-laning of Coimbatore Bypass to TN/Kerala Border (NH-47), under which Respondent No. 1 was required to pay an escalating annual premium[cite: 8]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Respondent No. 1 defaulted on premium payments; NHAI deferred Rs. 303.01 crores of premium vide supplementary agreement dated 15.12.2016, later withdrawing the deferment on 25.03.2021 due to non-compliance[cite: 8]. Appellant submitted a total claim of Rs. 431.70 Crores (later revised to Rs. 444.90 Crores), of which the RP admitted Rs. 400.02 Crores[cite: 8]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced against Respondent No. 1 on 20.04.2022[cite: 8]. NCLT Hyderabad approved the resolution plan under Section 31(1) on 01.05.2023[cite: 8]. E-filing of the company appeal by NHAI was done on 15.01.2024 (a delay of 229 days beyond the 30-day statutory period expiring on 31.05.2023)[cite: 8]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Concession agreement dated 25.03.2010; supplementary agreement dated 15.12.2016; NHAI withdrawal letter dated 25.03.2021; Form F claim submissions; and NCLT plan approval order dated 01.05.2023[cite: 8]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad approved the resolution plan on 01.05.2023 in CP (IB) No. 28/7/HDB/2022[cite: 8]. NHAI filed Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins.) No. 62 of 2024 along with IA No. 626 of 2024 for condonation of delay of 229 days, contending that Section 32 appeals have no prescribed limitation period[cite: 8].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an appeal filed under Section 32 read with Section 61(3) of the IBC against an order approving a resolution plan is subject to the limitation period and 15-day outer condonation limit prescribed under Section 61(2) of the IBC[cite: 8]; (ii) Whether the NCLAT can invoke its inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 to excuse an inordinate delay of 229 days beyond the statutory condonable limit[cite: 8].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal against a resolution plan approval order under Section 32 of the IBC, though governed in manner and grounds by Section 61(3), cannot be read in isolation from the self-contained limitation framework of Section 61(1) and 61(2); consequently, every appeal must be filed within 30 days, extendable by a maximum of 15 days upon sufficient cause, and neither the Appellate Tribunal nor the courts possess jurisdiction to condone delays beyond this 45-day outer limit[cite: 8]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61 commences with a non-obstante clause and applies to all appeals under Part II of the Code; Section 32 merely delineates the grounds of challenge and does not create an independent appellate regime untethered from statutory limitation[cite: 8]. Inherent powers under Rule 11 of NCLAT Rules (analogous to Section 151 CPC) are complementary and cannot be invoked to override express statutory limitations or create rights not contemplated by the parent statute[cite: 8]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the impugned order was passed on 01.05.2023, limitation expired on 31.05.2023, and the appeal was e-filed on 15.01.2024, resulting in an un-condonable delay of 229 days[cite: 8]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal is hopelessly barred by limitation under Section 61(2) of the IBC, and the delay cannot be condoned under Rule 11 or on grounds of alleged fraud or delayed knowledge[cite: 8].
operative_order: IA No. 626 of 2024 seeking condonation of delay is rejected, and consequently Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins.) No. 62 of 2024 stands dismissed as barred by limitation, with no order as to costs[cite: 8].
summary: The National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) appealed against an NCLT Hyderabad order dated 01.05.2023 approving the resolution plan for IVRCL Chengapalli Tollways Ltd[cite: 8]. NHAI filed its appeal with a delay of 229 days, arguing that Section 32 of the IBC prescribes no limitation period for challenging resolution plans[cite: 8]. Dismissing the appeal and rejecting the delay condonation application, the NCLAT Chennai Bench held that Section 32 must be read harmoniously with Section 61, making the 30-day limitation period and 15-day condonable extension under Section 61(2) fully applicable[cite: 8]. Citing Supreme Court rulings in V. Nagarajan and Kalpraj Dharamshi, the Tribunal reiterated that the IBC is a special, time-bound code, and the Tribunal has no inherent power under Rule 11 to condone delays beyond the statutory outer limit of 45 days[cite: 8].

case_title: Nikhil Jain & Ors. vs. Anil Goel, Liquidator of Birla Cotsyn (India) Ltd. & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Yogesh Khanna and Technical Member Ajai Das Mehrotra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant No. 1 is Nikhil Jain (Acquirer/Investor)[cite: 9]. Appellants Nos. 2 and 3 are Rohtsoffe International Pvt. Ltd. and Wendt Finance Pvt. Ltd. (Acquirer entities represented by Director Nikhil Jain)[cite: 9]. Respondent No. 1 is Anil Goel, Liquidator of Birla Cotsyn (India) Ltd[cite: 9]. Respondent No. 2 is Bombay Stock Exchange Ltd. (BSE)[cite: 9]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Birla Cotsyn (India) Ltd. was pushed into liquidation under Chapter III of the IBC, during which the Liquidator invited and pursued a Scheme of Arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Regulation 2-B of the Liquidation Process Regulations for the revival of the Corporate Debtor, backed by the Appellants as successful scheme proponents offering Rs. 52.3 Crores[cite: 9]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (company liquidation and revival scheme proceeding)[cite: 9]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: First motion of the Scheme of Arrangement was approved by NCLT Mumbai[cite: 9]. NCLT passed the impugned order on 04.04.2024 directing the Liquidator to obtain a prior No-Objection Certificate (NOC) from BSE under Regulation 37 of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015[cite: 9]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Scheme of Arrangement proposal submitted by the Liquidator; notice issued to BSE under Section 230(5) of the Companies Act received by BSE on 16.05.2023; and NCLT order dated 02.05.2023 permitting the Scheme to proceed[cite: 9]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Liquidator filed CP (CAA)/189(MB)/2023 before NCLT Mumbai for approval of the Scheme[cite: 9]. NCLT Mumbai passed an order on 04.04.2024 holding that prior NOC from BSE under Regulation 37 of LODR was mandatory[cite: 9]. Appellants challenged the order before NCLAT via Company Appeal (AT) No. 148 of 2024[cite: 9].
legal_issues: (i) Whether Regulation 37(1) and (2) of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 requiring a prior No-Objection Certificate (NOC) from stock exchanges applies to a Scheme of Arrangement filed by a Liquidator under Section 230 of the Companies Act read with Regulation 2-B of the Liquidation Process Regulations[cite: 9]; (ii) Alternatively, whether the exemption provided under Regulation 37(7) of LODR for restructuring proposals under Section 31 of the IBC applies mutatis mutandis to a scheme for revival of a company in liquidation under Regulation 2-B read with Section 230 of the Companies Act[cite: 9].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 230(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, a liquidator is treated as a separate and distinct category of applicant from the 'company' or 'listed entity'; consequently, obligations imposed on a 'listed entity' under Regulation 37(1) and (2) of SEBI (LODR) Regulations—such as obtaining a prior NOC from stock exchanges before filing a scheme—do not apply to a scheme of arrangement filed by a liquidator for a company undergoing liquidation[cite: 9]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applying purposive interpretation under the doctrine of dynamic statutory construction (Shailesh Dhairyawan v. Mohan Balkrishna), revival schemes under Section 230 in liquidation operate in a similar continuum to resolution plans under Section 31 of the IBC; hence, the exemption from prior stock exchange NOC under Regulation 37(7) of LODR applies equally to liquidation revival schemes to prevent civil death of companies and avoid conflict with the non-obstante overriding effect of Section 238 of the IBC[cite: 9]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examined Section 230(1) and (5) of the Companies Act, Regulations 5, 11, and 37 of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, and established Supreme Court precedents (Arun Kumar Jagatramka, Meghal Homes, S.C. Sekaran), finding that notice to stock exchanges under Section 230(5) was duly served, and that demanding a prior NOC in liquidation would create an absurd, onerous burden inconsistent with the Code's single-window resolution framework[cite: 9]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Prior NOC from stock exchanges under Regulation 37(1) and (2) of LODR is not required for schemes of arrangement submitted by liquidators for companies in liquidation, and the Adjudicating Authority erred in stalling the proceedings[cite: 9].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 148 of 2024 is allowed, the impugned order dated 04.04.2024 is set aside, and the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai) is directed to proceed with hearing the scheme on merits without insisting on a prior NOC from stock exchanges and dispose of the same within four weeks[cite: 9].
summary: Nikhil Jain and other acquirers appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order dated 04.04.2024 which held that a prior No-Objection Certificate (NOC) from the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) under Regulation 37 of SEBI (LODR) Regulations was mandatory for a Scheme of Arrangement filed by the Liquidator of Birla Cotsyn (India) Ltd under Section 230 of the Companies Act[cite: 9]. Allowing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that Regulation 37 applies only to a 'listed entity' acting voluntarily, whereas Section 230(1) treats a liquidator as a distinct entity[cite: 9]. Citing Supreme Court rulings in Arun Kumar Jagatramka and the clean slate theory, the Tribunal ruled that revival schemes in liquidation operate in the same continuum as Section 31 resolution plans, meaning the Regulation 37(7) exemption from prior stock exchange NOC applies equally to liquidator-led schemes[cite: 9]. The Tribunal set aside the impugned order and directed the NCLT to decide the scheme within four weeks[cite: 9].

case_title: Deepak Kishan Chhabria & Anr. vs. Orbit Electricals Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant No. 1 is Deepak Kishan Chhabria (son of Kishan P. Chhabria)[cite: 10]. Appellant No. 2 is Vini Deepak Chhabria (wife of Deepak)[cite: 10]. Respondent No. 1 is Orbit Electricals Pvt. Ltd[cite: 10]. Respondent No. 2 is Prakash Pralhad Chhabria (son of Pralhad)[cite: 10]. Respondents Nos. 3 and 4 are Independent Directors[cite: 10]. Respondent No. 5 is Aruna Katara[cite: 10]. Respondent No. 6 is Kishan P. Chhabria[cite: 10]. Respondent No. 7 is Priya Chhabria[cite: 10]. Respondent No. 8 is Vijay Kishan Chhabria[cite: 10]. Respondent No. 9 is Meena D'Sa (Sr. VP - Finance)[cite: 10]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Establishment of Finolex Cables Limited (FCL, 1974) and Finolex Industries Limited (FIL, 1981) by brothers Pralhad and Kishan P. Chhabria, followed by a 2011 amalgamation of 14 investment companies into Orbit Electricals Pvt. Ltd. resulting in a share ratio of 88.10% to Pralhad and 7.30% to Kishan[cite: 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (corporate governance, share transfer, and oppression/mismanagement dispute under Sections 241/242)[cite: 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: MoU executed between FCL and FIL on 11.10.2011; Pralhad Trust created on 12.03.2012; Pralhad gifted shares to Prakash and Aruna on 15.03.2012; Pralhad executed WILL on 15.10.2014; Pralhad executed Gift Deed and transfer of 100,300 shares to Prakash on 28.03.2016; Board meeting held on 31.03.2016; Pralhad died on 05.05.2016; Company Petition No. 47 of 2016 filed on 16.11.2016; EOGM requisitioned by Prakash on 18.03.2019; EOGM notice issued on 09.04.2019; MA No. 1449/2019 filed on 12.04.2019; EOGM held on 03.05.2019; NCLT dismissed MA No. 1449/2019 on 31.12.2019[cite: 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Articles of Association (AoA) of Orbit; Trust Deed dated 12.03.2012; WILL dated 15.10.2014; Gift Deed and Share Transfer Form dated 28.03.2016 for 100,300 shares; Board minutes dated 31.03.2016 and 21.06.2016; EOGM notice dated 09.04.2019; Scrutinizer's Report dated 03.05.2019; and FCL AGM Scrutinizer's Report dated 13.10.2023[cite: 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed CP No. 47 of 2016 before NCLT Mumbai under Sections 241-242 alleging oppression and mismanagement. During pendency, Appellants filed MA No. 1449/2019 challenging the EOGM notice and proposed amendments to Articles 59 and 60. NCLT Mumbai dismissed MA No. 1449/2019 on 31.12.2019, leading to Company Appeal (AT) No. 64 of 2020[cite: 10].
legal_issues: (i) Whether amendments made to Articles 59 and 60 of the Articles of Association of Orbit Electricals in 2014 constitute 'entrenched articles' under Section 5(3) and (4) of the Companies Act, 2013 requiring unanimous agreement by all members for subsequent alteration[cite: 10]; (ii) Whether the amendment of Article 59 and deletion of Article 60 passed by a special majority (91.74%) at the EOGM on 03.05.2019 is legally valid under Section 14 of the Companies Act[cite: 10]; (iii) Whether a corporate representative appointed under Section 113 of the Companies Act is bound to vote in accordance with the instructions of the allotting company's Board of Directors[cite: 10].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 5(4) of the Companies Act, 2013, provisions for entrenchment in a private company's articles can only be made either upon formation or by an amendment agreed to by all the members of the company; where an amendment is passed at a general meeting where not all members are present or consenting, it cannot be deemed an entrenched article, and subsequent alterations are validly governed by a special resolution under Section 14[cite: 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 113(2) of the Companies Act establishes that an authorized corporate representative acts as an agent of the body corporate and is legally bound to exercise voting rights in strict conformity with the directions of the board of directors of the representing company[cite: 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the minutes of the AGM dated 30.09.2014, showing that only 4 out of 13 members were present when Articles 59 and 60 were adopted, precluding them from attaining entrenched status, and examined the EOGM Scrutinizer's Report dated 03.05.2019, confirming that special resolutions to amend Article 59 and delete Article 60 passed with a 91.74% majority[cite: 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no error in dismissing MA No. 1449/2019, as the EOGM dated 03.05.2019 validly amended the non-entrenched articles by special resolution, and the company's representative at FCL was legally bound by Orbit's board directions[cite: 10].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 64 of 2020 is dismissed, the impugned order dated 31.12.2019 in MA No. 1449/2019 is affirmed, the FCL AGM voting results of 29.09.2023 remain undisturbed, and NCLT Mumbai is requested to expedite final disposal of CP No. 47 of 2016 preferably within six months, with parties bearing their own costs[cite: 10].
summary: Deepak Chhabria and his wife appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order dated 31.12.2019 dismissing their miscellaneous application (MA No. 1449/2019) which sought to restrain an EOGM of Orbit Electricals Pvt. Ltd. called to amend Article 59 and delete Article 60 of its Articles of Association[cite: 10]. The appellants argued that the articles were 'entrenched' under Section 5(4) of the 2013 Act and required unanimous consent, and challenged the board's authority to direct voting in FCL[cite: 10]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that the 2014 resolution was passed by only 4 members, failing the statutory requirement of unanimity needed for entrenchment[cite: 10]. The Tribunal ruled that the EOGM dated 03.05.2019 validly amended the articles by special resolution (91.74% majority), that corporate representatives under Section 113 are bound by board instructions, and directed the NCLT to expedite the pending main oppression petition within six months[cite: 10].

case_title: Vikash Gautamchand Jain, RP of Kethos Tiles Pvt. Ltd. vs. Vikash Gautamchand Jain & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1173 of 2024 & No. 1323 of 2024
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 1173 of 2024 is Vikash Gautamchand Jain, Resolution Professional (RP) of Kethos Tiles Private Limited[cite: 12]. The Appellant in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 1323 of 2024 is Kritish Patel, Promoter of Kethos Tiles Private Limited (Corporate Debtor / MSME)[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Kethos Tiles Pvt. Ltd., an eligible Micro, Small & Medium Enterprise (MSME), filed an application under Section 54C of the IBC to initiate Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (PPIRP)[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default on debt obligations of the MSME corporate debtor leading to PPIRP admission. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Adjudicating Authority admitted the Section 54C application and initiated PPIRP on 04.01.2024[cite: 12]. Public announcement made on 06.01.2024[cite: 12]. 3rd CoC meeting held on 30.04.2024 (and continued/resolved on 02.05.2024), wherein CoC noted that the 120-day PPIRP period was expiring on 03.05.2024 and passed a resolution with 91.75% voting share to seek a 60-day extension[cite: 12]. RP filed an extension application, which the NCLT rejected on 06.06.2024, terminating the PPIRP[cite: 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Section 54C application; public announcement dated 06.01.2024; revised base resolution plan under consideration; minutes of the 3rd CoC meeting dated 30.04.2024; and e-voting results dated 02.05.2024[cite: 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench (Court-I) rejected the RP's extension application (IA No. 769/AHM/2024) via order dated 06.06.2024, holding that Section 54D(3) mandates termination if no plan is approved within 120 days and that Section 12 extension principles do not apply to PPIRP[cite: 12]. RP and Promoter appealed to NCLAT via Company Appeals Nos. 1173 and 1323 of 2024[cite: 12].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the 120-day timeline prescribed under Section 54D(1) of the IBC for completion of Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (PPIRP) is strictly mandatory, resulting in automatic termination, or whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction to grant an extension of time on sufficient cause and on the strength of a CoC resolution[cite: 12].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The 120-day timeline prescribed under Section 54D(1) of the IBC for completing the Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (PPIRP) is directory rather than mandatory; the statute does not provide for automatic termination upon expiry of 120 days, and the Adjudicating Authority retains the judicial discretion to extend the time period for reasonable grounds upon an application filed pursuant to a requisite CoC resolution. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Provisions containing timelines for insolvency resolution (such as Section 7/9/10 provisos, Section 12, and Regulation 35A) use the word 'shall' but have consistently been construed by the Supreme Court (e.g., Surendra Trading Co., Essar Steel) as directory to serve the ultimate objective of value maximization and corporate revival rather than driving a viable company into liquidation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the CoC, in its 3rd meeting with a 91.75% majority vote, resolved to seek a 60-day extension because a revised base resolution plan was actively under consideration. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in holding that it lacked jurisdiction to extend the PPIRP period beyond 120 days, and the rejection of the extension application was legally unsustainable[cite: 12].
operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 1173 and 1323 of 2024 are allowed, the impugned order dated 06.06.2024 passed by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench in IA No. 769/AHM/2024 is set aside, IA No. 769/AHM/2024 is allowed, and the PPIRP period is extended by 60 days from the date of the judgment[cite: 12].
summary: Vikash Gautamchand Jain (RP of Kethos Tiles Pvt. Ltd.) and Kritish Patel (Promoter) appealed against an NCLT Ahmedabad order dated 06.06.2024 which rejected an application for a 60-day extension of the Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (PPIRP) and terminated the proceedings[cite: 12]. The NCLT had held that under Section 54D(3), proceedings must terminate if a plan is not approved within 120 days. Allowing the appeals, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that Section 54D timelines are directory, not mandatory, and do not trigger automatic termination[cite: 12]. Citing Supreme Court precedents on statutory interpretation and timelines (such as Essar Steel and Surendra Trading Co.), the Tribunal ruled that the Adjudicating Authority has discretionary power to extend PPIRP timelines on sufficient cause backed by a CoC resolution, setting aside the termination and granting a 60-day extension[cite: 12].

case_title: Vantage Point Asset Management Pte. Ltd. vs. Gaurav Misra, Resolution Professional of Alchemist Infra Realty Ltd.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan, Technical Members Barun Mitra and Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Vantage Point Asset Management Pte. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant / SRA, represented through attorney Ashok Kacker / Vikash Kumar). The Respondent is Gaurav Misra, Resolution Professional of Alchemist Infra Realty Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 13]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP commenced against Alchemist Infra Realty Ltd. on 08.10.2021[cite: 13]. Appellant submitted a resolution plan proposing corporate revival and monetization of land banks, which required the vacation of attachments levied by the Directorate of Enforcement (ED) and other authorities[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (resolution plan approval and statutory immunity dispute under Section 32A)[cite: 13]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 08.10.2021[cite: 13]. CoC approved the Appellant's resolution plan with 100% vote share on 18.10.2023[cite: 13]. Letter of Intent issued on 20.10.2023[cite: 13]. RP filed IA No. 01/2024 for plan approval[cite: 13]. NCLT New Delhi Bench (Court-II) approved the resolution plan on 04.07.2024 while refusing in paragraph 60 to lift ED attachments under PMLA[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resolution plan documents; Form-H compliance certificate; CoC approval minutes dated 18.10.2023; and PMLA attachment orders issued by the Directorate of Enforcement[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench (Court-II) approved the resolution plan in IA No. 01/2024 on 04.07.2024 but inserted adverse observations in paragraph 60 refusing to release properties attached by the ED under PMLA, relegating the SRA to separate proceedings[cite: 13]. SRA appealed to NCLAT via Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1495 of 2024 challenging paragraph 60[cite: 13].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an Adjudicating Authority, while approving a resolution plan under Section 31 of the IBC, has the power and legal mandate under Section 32A to order the release and lifting of property attachments levied by the Directorate of Enforcement (ED) under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA) for offences committed prior to the commencement of CIRP[cite: 13].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 32A of the IBC, once a resolution plan resulting in a change of management (excluding erstwhile promoters or related parties) is approved by the Adjudicating Authority, a statutory shield (an 'impregnable wall') is erected that completely extinguishes the criminal liability of the corporate debtor and bars any action—including attachment, seizure, retention, or confiscation—against the properties of the corporate debtor under any law such as the PMLA in relation to offences committed prior to CIRP. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 32A(2) read with its Explanation clarifies that 'an action against the property of the corporate debtor' encompasses PMLA attachments. As held by the Supreme Court in Manish Kumar v. Union of India and the Bombay High Court in Shiv Charan v. PMLA Adjudicating Authority, the NCLT is fully empowered under Section 60(5) and Section 32A to direct the ED to lift prior attachments on properties covered under an approved resolution plan. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the CoC approved the plan with 100% vote share, that the SRA was completely independent of the erstwhile management (satisfying Section 29A/32A criteria), and that the attached properties were integrated into the resolution plan for monetization and revival. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed a patent error in paragraph 60 by refusing to extend the statutory immunity of Section 32A to uplift ED attachments, and the SRA is fully entitled to the release of attached properties[cite: 13].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1495 of 2024 is allowed, the findings and observations recorded in paragraph 60 of the impugned order dated 04.07.2024 denying the benefit of Section 32A are set aside, and it is ordered that the protection of Section 32A extends to lifting the attachments made by the Enforcement Directorate over the assets of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 13].
summary: Vantage Point Asset Management Pte. Ltd., the Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA) for Alchemist Infra Realty Ltd., appealed against part of an NCLT New Delhi order dated 04.07.2024 which approved the resolution plan but refused in paragraph 60 to lift property attachments levied by the Directorate of Enforcement (ED) under the PMLA[cite: 13]. Allowing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that under Section 32A of the IBC and the Supreme Court's ruling in Manish Kumar v. Union of India, approval of a resolution plan with a change in management erects an impregnable wall granting complete immunity to the corporate debtor's property from PMLA attachments for pre-CIRP offences[cite: 13]. Citing the Bombay High Court ruling in Shiv Charan, the Tribunal ruled that the NCLT is fully empowered to direct the ED to release attachments on plan-covered properties, setting aside paragraph 60[cite: 13].

case_title: Wind World (India) Limited vs. Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency Limited & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Wind World (India) Limited (Corporate Debtor, represented by Resolution Professional Shailen Shah). Respondent No. 1 is Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency Limited (IREDA - Financial Creditor). Respondent No. 2 is Wind World (India) Infrastructure Private Limited (Subsidiary of Corporate Debtor / WWIIPL, formerly Enercon India Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd.)[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Respondent No. 2 constructed substations and power switchyards ('the Facility') to pool power from wind energy projects. Vide a Facility Agreement dated 28.12.2007 (modified up to 2016), Respondent No. 2 handed over the Facility to the Corporate Debtor to use, operate, and maintain in exchange for facility usage charges. Respondent No. 2 subsequently borrowed two loan facilities of Rs. 90 Crores each from IREDA (Respondent No. 1), creating a hypothecation charge over the substations/assets on 05.07.2012 and 19.12.2013, alongside a Conditional Deed of Assignment dated 23.12.2013 assigning all rights to IREDA. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted on paying facility usage charges to its subsidiary (Respondent No. 2) exceeding Rs. 170 Crores, disabling Respondent No. 2 from servicing its loans with IREDA and triggering an event of default. IREDA classified Respondent No. 2's account as NPA on 31.03.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Facility Agreement executed on 28.12.2007. CIRP commenced against the Corporate Debtor (holding company) on 20.02.2018 under Section 7. IREDA issued SARFAESI notices under Section 13(2) against the subsidiary on 12.05.2021 and 13.06.2021. IREDA issued an Expression of Interest (EoI) on 25.04.2022 seeking new operation and maintenance contractors for the Facility. Corporate Debtor filed IA No. 422/2022 before NCLT Ahmedabad, which was dismissed on 28.11.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Facility Agreement dated 28.12.2007; Facility Usage Agreement dated 12.08.2013; Loan Agreements and Hypothecation Deeds dated 05.07.2012 and 19.12.2013; Conditional Deed of Assignment dated 23.12.2013; SARFAESI notices; and EOI notice dated 25.04.2022. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Corporate Debtor filed IA No. 422 of 2022 before NCLT Ahmedabad Bench (Court-1) challenging IREDA's EOI notice dated 25.04.2022 as violative of Section 14 moratorium. NCLT Ahmedabad dismissed IA No. 422/2022 on 28.11.2022, holding that the Corporate Debtor did not own the facility and only held operational rights. Corporate Debtor appealed to NCLAT via Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 175 of 2023[cite: 14].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the issuance of an Expression of Interest (EoI) by a secured financial creditor of a subsidiary company to appoint a new operation and maintenance contractor for a facility operated by the holding company corporate debtor violates the moratorium under Section 14(1)(d) of the IBC[cite: 14].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 14(1)(d) of the IBC prohibits the recovery of any property by an owner or lessor where such property is occupied by or in the possession of the corporate debtor; however, where a corporate debtor is merely appointed as an operating and maintenance contractor under an agreement explicitly stating that ownership remains solely with a third party (or subsidiary), the corporate debtor is neither an owner/lessor nor in legal 'occupation/possession' of the property in the statutory sense, and lenders enforcing security interests against the actual owner are not barred by Section 14(1)(d). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Following the Supreme Court's ruling in Rajendra K. Bhutta v. MHADA, 'occupation' under Section 14(1)(d) requires actual legal possession and beneficial user, and cannot be stretched to protect a defaulting operating contractor that fails to pay facility usage charges to the asset-owning subsidiary. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examined Clause 2.1 and Clause 2.2(d) of the Facility Agreements, establishing that ownership of the switchyards/substations remained exclusively with Respondent No. 2 (WWIIPL), and that the Corporate Debtor merely held contractual operating rights while defaulting on Rs. 170 Crores in facility charges. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor was neither the owner nor in statutory occupation/possession of the facility under Section 14(1)(d), and IREDA was fully entitled to initiate SARFAESI measures and invite EoIs against the defaulting subsidiary[cite: 14].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 175 of 2023 is dismissed, upholding the order dated 28.11.2022 passed by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench in IA No. 422/2022 in CP (IB) No. 14 of 2018[cite: 14]. No orders as to costs[cite: 14].
summary: Wind World (India) Ltd. (Corporate Debtor, through its RP) appealed against an NCLT Ahmedabad order dated 28.11.2022 dismissing its application (IA No. 422/2022) which challenged an Expression of Interest (EoI) notice issued by IREDA (Financial Creditor)[cite: 14]. IREDA had issued the EoI to appoint a new operation and maintenance contractor for power switchyards/substations owned by the corporate debtor's subsidiary (WWIIPL), against which IREDA initiated SARFAESI proceedings[cite: 14]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that under the Facility Agreements, ownership of the switchyards remained solely with the subsidiary, and the corporate debtor merely held operating rights while defaulting on Rs. 170 Crores in facility charges[cite: 14]. Citing Rajendra K. Bhutta, the Tribunal ruled that Section 14(1)(d) moratorium does not apply because the corporate debtor was not in statutory 'occupation or possession' of the facility, upholding the Adjudicating Authority's dismissal[cite: 14].

case_title: Col. Ashish Khanna, SM (Retd.) vs. Delhi Gymkhana Club Limited & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Col. Ashish Khanna, SM (Retd.), former Secretary of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 15]. Respondent No. 1 is Delhi Gymkhana Club Limited[cite: 15]. Respondent No. 2 is the Union of India, Ministry of Corporate Affairs[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Employment contract dated 12.04.2018 appointing the Appellant as Secretary-cum-CEO of Delhi Gymkhana Club Limited for a fixed tenure of three years[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (service and company management dispute)[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Appellant's appointment commenced on 12.04.2018 and concluded on 11.04.2021[cite: 15]. Show cause notice issued by the General Committee on 27.07.2020; services terminated on 04.08.2020[cite: 15]. NCLT passed interim orders on 26.06.2020 and 01.04.2022[cite: 15]. NCLT dismissed CA-409/2020 on 25.03.2021. NCLAT dismissed CA No. 48 of 2021 on 15.04.2021[cite: 15]. Supreme Court disposed of Civil Appeal No. 2856 of 2021 on 13.12.2021 (clarified on 11.03.2022)[cite: 15]. NCLT passed the impugned order on 05.04.2024 adjourning applications CA-88/2023 and CA-34/2024 to 03.10.2024[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appointment letter dated 12.04.2018, Show Cause Notice dated 27.07.2020, termination email dated 04.08.2020, NCLT and NCLAT orders, and an email sent by the Appellant to the Registrar of NCLT on 16.02.2024[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Union of India filed CP No. 71/241-242/PB/2020 under Section 241 of the Companies Act[cite: 15]. Appellant filed CA No. 409/2020 seeking protection under Section 218 and reinstatement, which NCLT dismissed on 25.03.2021[cite: 15]. Subsequent appeals to NCLAT and the Supreme Court were disposed of[cite: 15]. Appellant later filed CA-88/2023 and CA-34/2024, which NCLT adjourned to 03.10.2024 vide order dated 05.04.2024, leading to the present appeal[cite: 15].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an employee whose 3-year fixed employment tenure has elapsed can invoke Section 218 of the Companies Act, 2013 to claim reinstatement or protection during the pendency of a Section 241 company petition[cite: 15]; (ii) Whether the Adjudicating Authority committed a legal error or violated Rule 150 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 by adjourning applications CA-88/2023 and CA-34/2024 in light of the Appellant's conduct and unseemly emails sent to the Registry[cite: 15].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 218 of the Companies Act, 2013 provides protection to employees against discharge, suspension, or punishment during ongoing investigations or oppression-mismanagement proceedings, but it does not apply to revive an employment contract whose fixed statutory tenure has fully elapsed by efflux of time[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 150(1) of the NCLT Rules, 2016 requiring the pronouncement of orders within 30 days is directory rather than mandatory, and an order cannot be rendered void solely on the ground of a delayed delivery[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed the appointment letter dated 12.04.2018, previous judicial findings of the NCLT, NCLAT, and Supreme Court confirming that the Appellant's 3-year term had elapsed, and the emails containing scurrilous allegations sent by the Appellant to the Registry[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the Appellant's fixed tenure of employment had expired and his earlier claims under Section 218 were conclusively adjudicated and rejected up to the Supreme Court, subsequent applications seeking identical reliefs were a re-agitation of settled issues, and the Adjudicating Authority rightly exercised control over its proceedings by adjourning the matter[cite: 15].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 224 of 2024 is dismissed with no order as to costs, upholding the order dated 05.04.2024 passed by the National Company Law Tribunal, New Delhi, Principal Bench[cite: 15].
summary: Col. Ashish Khanna (Retd.), former Secretary of Delhi Gymkhana Club Ltd., appealed against an NCLT order dated 05.04.2024 which adjourned his applications (CA-88/2023 and CA-34/2024) seeking protection under Section 218 of the Companies Act and re-appointment[cite: 15]. The appellant argued that the NCLT violated NCLT Rules and failed to comply with earlier NCLAT directions for early disposal[cite: 15]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that the appellant's 3-year tenure had expired in April 2021, a fact affirmed by the Supreme Court, rendering Section 218 protection inapplicable[cite: 15]. The Tribunal strongly deprecated the appellant's conduct in sending intemperate emails to the Registry and upheld the NCLT's decision to adjourn the matters[cite: 15].

case_title: Mitsubishi Heavy Industries Limited vs. Punj Lloyd Limited & Ors.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Mitsubishi Heavy Industries Limited (Beneficiary/Employer)[cite: 16]. Respondent No. 1 is Punj Lloyd Limited (Corporate Debtor/Contractor) represented through Ashwini Mehra, Liquidator[cite: 16]. Respondent No. 2 is State Bank of India (Issuing Bank)[cite: 16]. Respondents Nos. 3, 4, and 5 are IDBI Bank Limited, United Bank of India, and Central Bank of India (Counter-Guarantors)[cite: 16]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: In 2014, Indian Oil LNG Pvt. Ltd. (IOLPL) awarded a tender for constructing Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) tanks in Ennore/Chennai to the Appellant, who on 15.09.2015 subcontracted parts of the work to Respondent No. 1 for a contract price requiring an unconditional and irrevocable Performance Bank Guarantee (PBG) of Rs. 47,72,34,933/- issued by State Bank of India[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Agreed mechanical completion date was 23.03.2018; mechanical completion certificate was issued with a delayed date of 31.01.2019 (a delay of over 10 months)[cite: 16]. On 26.08.2019, serious leakages were detected in the LNG tanks during the Defects Liability Period, which Respondent No. 1 refused to inspect or repair, prompting the Appellant to invoke the PBG for the full amount of Rs. 47,72,34,933/- on 30.10.2019[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced against Respondent No. 1 on 08.03.2019[cite: 16]. PBG invoked on 30.10.2019[cite: 16]. RP filed IA No. 2478/2019 on 13.11.2019 seeking restraint, and Adjudicating Authority granted an interim stay on the same day under Section 14[cite: 16]. NCLAT delivered its judgment in C&C Construction on 26.07.2021[cite: 16]. Adjudicating Authority ordered liquidation of the Corporate Debtor as a going concern on 27.05.2022[cite: 16]. Adjudicating Authority allowed RP's application via the impugned order dated 30.10.2023[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Subcontract dated 15.09.2015 containing clause 6.4.1.4 for an unconditional and irrevocable PBG; Performance Bank Guarantee No. 0480314BG0000756 issued by SBI; mechanical completion certificate dated 31.01.2019; emails dated 26.08.2019 regarding tank leakage; and invocation letter dated 30.10.2019[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed IA No. 2478/2019 (re-numbered as IA No. 4393/PB/2023) before NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi, seeking to restrain encashment of the PBG[cite: 16]. NCLT allowed the application on 30.10.2023, holding that the PBG was not unconditional and that fault/losses were unproven[cite: 16]. Appellant appealed to NCLAT via Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1479 of 2023[cite: 16].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC bars the beneficiary from invoking and encashing an unconditional and irrevocable Performance Bank Guarantee issued in connection with a corporate debtor's contract[cite: 16]; (ii) Whether an Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction under the IBC to examine underlying contractual disputes, fault attribution, or quantification of claims to restrain the invocation of an unconditional bank guarantee[cite: 16].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 3(31) and Section 14(3)(b) of the IBC, a performance bank guarantee and surety contracts to a corporate debtor are expressly excluded from the scope of a moratorium; an unconditional and irrevocable bank guarantee constitutes an independent contract between the bank and the beneficiary, and its encashment cannot be restrained on account of pending underlying contractual disputes or corporate insolvency/liquidation[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(31) explicitly states that 'security interest' shall not include a performance guarantee, and Section 14(3)(b) provides that moratorium provisions do not apply to a surety in a contract of guarantee to a corporate debtor[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal inspected the text of Bank Guarantee No. 0480314BG0000756, which explicitly recorded that the bank 'unconditionally and irrevocably guarantees... to pay to MHI on its first written demand, without any right of set off, counter claim or dispute whatsoever', establishing that the PBG was absolute and unconditional[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed a fundamental error in holding that the PBG was conditional and in restraining its encashment during liquidation, as the settled legal position permits unfettered invocation of unconditional bank guarantees absent established egregious fraud or irretrievable injustice[cite: 16].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1479 of 2023 is allowed, the impugned order dated 30.10.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority in IA No. 2478/2019 (re-numbered as IA No. 4393/2023) is set aside, and the IA is dismissed with parties bearing their own costs[cite: 16].
summary: Mitsubishi Heavy Industries Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Principal Bench order restraining the encashment of a Performance Bank Guarantee (PBG) of Rs. 47.72 Crores issued by State Bank of India in respect of LNG tank construction contracts executed with Punj Lloyd Ltd. (now in liquidation)[cite: 16]. The NCLT had held that the PBG was not unconditional and that the beneficiary had failed to prove fault or quantify losses[cite: 16]. Allowing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that under Section 3(31) and Section 14(3)(b) of the IBC, performance bank guarantees are outside the purview of a moratorium[cite: 16]. Reaffirming Supreme Court precedents such as Standard Chartered Bank and Himadri Chemicals, the Tribunal ruled that an unconditional bank guarantee is an independent contract that must be honoured on demand irrespective of underlying disputes or the corporate debtor's liquidation status, setting aside the restraint order[cite: 16].

case_title: M/s Yash Solutions & Ors. vs. Competition Commission of India
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain and Technical Member Indevar Pandey)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant No. 1 is M/s Yash Solutions (Unit of Yash Ornaments Pvt. Ltd.)[cite: 17]. Appellant No. 2 is M/s Chaitanya Business Outsourcing Pvt. Ltd[cite: 17]. Appellant No. 3 is Mr. Praveen Kumar Agarwal (Managing Director of Yash Solutions)[cite: 17]. Appellant No. 4 is Mr. Nitish Agarwal (Director of Chaitanya Business Outsourcing and CEO of Yash Solutions)[cite: 17]. The Respondent is the Competition Commission of India (CCI)[cite: 17]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Tenders invited by the Department of Agriculture, Government of Uttar Pradesh, for soil sample testing across various divisions (specifically e-tenders for Moradabad and Bareilly in 2018, and multiple divisions in 2017 and 2018)[cite: 17]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (anti-competitive cartelization and bid-rigging proceeding under the Competition Act, 2002)[cite: 17]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Complaint filed on 07.08.2018[cite: 17]. CCI passed Section 26(1) investigation order on 30.01.2020[cite: 17]. Director General (DG) submitted investigation report on 08.04.2021[cite: 17]. CCI passed final penalty order under Section 27 on 04.04.2022[cite: 17]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bidding documents, audit reports, experience certificates, term deposit receipts, common IP addresses used for e-bid submissions, matching login IDs (acs.yopl@gmail.com), identical commercial invoices for ICP-OES machines and lab consumables from Thermo Fisher and Today Tech Scientific Solutions, call data records (CDR), and statements of proprietors/directors on oath[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CCI initiated investigation upon a complaint; DG investigated 9 tenders and submitted a report implicating 9 opposite parties and their key personnel[cite: 17]. CCI issued notice, heard parties, and passed final order on 04.04.2022 finding contravention of Section 3(3)(c) and 3(3)(d) read with Section 3(1), imposing penalties of 5% on average turnover of enterprises and average income of individuals[cite: 17]. Appellants appealed to NCLAT via Competition Appeal (AT) No. 38 of 2022[cite: 17].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the Appellants engaged in bid-rigging, collusive bidding, and market sharing in respect of soil testing tenders floated by the Department of Agriculture, Government of Uttar Pradesh in 2017 and 2018, in contravention of Sections 3(3)(c) and 3(3)(d) read with Section 3(1) of the Competition Act, 2002[cite: 17]; (ii) Whether the penalty imposed by the CCI at 5% of the total average turnover (instead of relevant turnover of the infringing product) is legally sustainable for first-time MSME bidders whose direct revenue from the specific tender business was minimal or zero[cite: 17].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In cartelization and bid-rigging cases where direct evidence is rare, circumstantial evidence, common IP addresses, identical invoice details, fabricated experience certificates, and practical cooperation substituting competition are sufficient to establish contravention under Section 3(3) of the Competition Act, 2002, for which a probabilistic standard of proof applies[cite: 17]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 3(3) clauses (a) to (d), agreements are statutorily presumed to have an appreciable adverse effect on competition (AAEC), obviating the need for a separate inquiry under Section 19(3)[cite: 17]. Furthermore, where contravening enterprises are first-time or multi-product/service entities whose specific turnover from the unlawful cartel activity is negligible or zero, restricting penalty strictly to relevant turnover would allow cartelists to walk free with zero penalty, defeating the deterrent objective of Section 27(b) and the proportionality doctrine in Excel Crop Care[cite: 17]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized sworn statements, common IP logs from NIC, matching invoice serial numbers, and admissions by key personnel (Praveen Kumar Agarwal, Nitish Agarwal, and Naresh Kumar Sharma) establishing that Yash Solutions orchestrated cover bids and supplied fabricated certificates and machinery invoices to sister/rival concerns (Satish Kumar, Siddhi Vinayak, Saraswati Sales, and Chaitanya Business Outsourcing)[cite: 17]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellants acted as the masterminds of an elaborate bid-rigging cartel in public procurement tenders, and the CCI's findings of contravention and imposition of 5% penalty on average annual turnover are fully justified and unassailable[cite: 17].
operative_order: Competition Appeal (AT) No. 38 of 2022 is dismissed, upholding the final order dated 04.04.2022 passed by the Competition Commission of India in Suo Motu Case No. 1 of 2020, and pending interlocutory applications are disposed of[cite: 17].
summary: M/s Yash Solutions, M/s Chaitanya Business Outsourcing, and their directors appealed against a CCI order dated 04.04.2022 which penalized them for cartelization and bid-rigging in soil testing tenders issued by the Department of Agriculture, Government of Uttar Pradesh, in 2017 and 2018[cite: 17]. The CCI had imposed a penalty of 5% of average turnover after finding that Yash Solutions orchestrated cover bids, used common IP addresses, and provided fake experience certificates and machinery invoices to sister and rival entities[cite: 17]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that circumstantial evidence, common IP logs, and admissions conclusively proved collusive bidding under Section 3(3) of the Competition Act[cite: 17]. The Tribunal upheld the CCI's calculation of penalties, ruling that restricting penalties to relevant turnover would allow entities with zero tender revenue to escape unpunished, frustrating the deterrent intent of the law[cite: 17].

case_title: Srigopal Choudhary vs. Srei Equipment Finance Limited
appeal_number: I.A. No. 2256 of 2024 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 626 of 2024
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan, Technical Members Barun Mitra and Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Srigopal Choudhary (former Resolution Professional of M/s Ortel Communication Limited)[cite: 18]. The Respondent is Srei Equipment Finance Limited (Financial Creditor with a 53.45% vote share)[cite: 18]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) commenced against the Corporate Debtor (M/s Ortel Communication Limited) on 27.11.2018, and the Appellant was confirmed as Resolution Professional (RP) on 01.02.2019[cite: 18]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (resolution professional removal and procedural limitation dispute)[cite: 18]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Adjudicating Authority passed the order removing the Appellant as RP on 07.06.2023[cite: 18]. Appellant filed IA No. 3216/2023 for recall under Rule 49 of NCLT Rules, which was dismissed on 12.12.2023[cite: 18]. Appeal against recall dismissal (Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1690 of 2023) was dismissed by NCLAT on 03.01.2024[cite: 18]. Present appeal against the main order of 07.06.2023 was e-filed on 12.01.2024 with a delay of 209 days[cite: 18]. Supreme Court dismissed the subsequent Civil Appeal No. 2602 of 2024 on 05.03.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLT order dated 07.06.2023 removing the RP; recall application IA No. 3216/2023; NCLT order dated 12.12.2023; and NCLAT judgment dated 03.01.2024[cite: 18]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Court III removed the Appellant as RP via order dated 07.06.2023[cite: 18]. Appellant unsuccessfully pursued a recall application and a subsequent appeal before NCLAT[cite: 18]. Finally, Appellant filed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 626 of 2024 along with IA No. 2256 of 2024 seeking condonation of 209 days of delay by excluding the time spent prosecuting the recall application under Section 14 of the Limitation Act[cite: 18].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an appellant is entitled to the exclusion of time under Section 14 of the Limitation Act, 1963 for the period spent prosecuting a recall application before the Adjudicating Authority when the prior proceeding was adjudicated and disposed of on merits rather than dismissed due to a defect of jurisdiction or other cause of a like nature[cite: 18].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: To invoke Section 14 of the Limitation Act for the exclusion of time, all mandatory conditions must be satisfied, crucially including the requirement that the failure or dismissal of the prior proceeding was due to a 'defect of jurisdiction or other cause of a like nature' resulting in the court's inability to entertain it; where a prior application is fully entertained, heard, and disposed of on merits, Section 14 has no application[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 requires that the prior forum be 'unable to entertain' the proceeding due to jurisdictional infirmities, which does not cover a situation where a litigant pursues a substantive recall application (such as under Rule 49 of NCLT Rules) that is fully heard and decided on merits[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that IA No. 3216/2023 was entertained by the NCLT, evaluated on its merits, and rejected on 12.12.2023 because the applicant failed to show sufficient cause for non-appearance, establishing that the prior proceeding did not fail due to a defect of jurisdiction[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the essential conditions of Section 14 of the Limitation Act were not satisfied, the time spent pursuing the recall application cannot be excluded, rendering the 209-day delay in filing the appeal beyond the condonable outer limit[cite: 18].
operative_order: IA No. 2256 of 2024 for condonation of delay is rejected, and consequently Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 626 of 2024 stands dismissed as barred by limitation, with no order as to costs[cite: 18].
summary: Srigopal Choudhary, former Resolution Professional of M/s Ortel Communication Limited, appealed against an NCLT order dated 07.06.2023 removing him as RP, with a delay of 209 days[cite: 18]. The appellant sought exclusion of the period from 08.06.2023 to 03.01.2024 under Section 14 of the Limitation Act, claiming he was bona fide prosecuting a recall application (IA No. 3216/2023) and a subsequent appeal[cite: 18]. Dismissing the delay condonation application, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that Section 14 is inapplicable because the recall application was fully entertained, heard, and decided on merits by the NCLT rather than dismissed for lack of jurisdiction or technical defect[cite: 18]. The Tribunal ruled the appeal time-barred[cite: 18].

case_title: Mr. Byju Raveendran vs. Think & Learn Private Limited & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins.) No. 262 of 2024 & IA Nos. 699, 700 & 727 of 2024
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain and Technical Member Jatindranath Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Byju Raveendran (Suspended Director, Promoter & Shareholder of Think & Learn Private Limited). Respondent No. 1 is Think & Learn Private Limited (Corporate Debtor, represented by IRP Pankaj Srivastava). Respondent No. 2 is The Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI - Operational Creditor). Intervenor / Applicant in IA No. 727 of 2024 is GLAS Trust Company LLC (USA, administrative and collateral agent for US lenders under a USD 1.2 Billion credit agreement)[cite: 19]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: BCCI filed CP (IB) No. 149/BB/2023 on 23.09.2023 under Section 9 of the IBC against Think & Learn Pvt. Ltd. for an operational debt of Rs. 1,58,90,92,400/- arising from sponsorship and branding agreements[cite: 19]. Separately, GLAS Trust Company LLC filed CP (IB) No. 55/BB/2024 under Section 7 on 22.01.2024 as financial creditor based on a parent guarantee for a USD 1.2 Billion term loan extended to Byju's Alpha, Inc[cite: 19]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by Corporate Debtor on operational dues owed to BCCI amounting to Rs. 158.90 Crores[cite: 19]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Bengaluru Bench admitted BCCI's Section 9 petition on 16.07.2024, imposed a moratorium, and appointed Pankaj Srivastava as IRP[cite: 19].
