On the same day, NCLT disposed of GLAS Trust's Section 7 petition granting liberty to file claims before the IRP[cite: 19]. Byju Raveendran filed Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins.) No. 262 of 2024 on 30.07.2024[cite: 19]. Riju Raveendran (ex-promoter/brother) transferred the first settlement installment of Rs. 50 Crores on 30.07.2024 via RTGS, offering to clear the entire Rs. 158 Crore BCCI debt through personal funds[cite: 19]. NCLAT approved the settlement and closed CIRP on 02.08.2024[cite: 19]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: BCCI Section 9 petition; NCLT admission order dated 16.07.2024; RTGS transfer UTR No. ICICR52024073000412272 for Rs. 50 Crores dated 30.07.2024; undertakings and affidavits of Riju Raveendran dated 01.08.2024 detailing personal fund generation through historical share sales (2015-2022) and tax compliance; Form-C claim filed by GLAS Trust on 25.07.2024; and US Delaware Bankruptcy Court order dated 18.03.2024[cite: 19]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru admitted BCCI's Section 9 petition on 16.07.2024[cite: 19]. Suspended director appealed to NCLAT Chennai Bench[cite: 19]. During preliminary hearings on 30.07.2024 and 31.07.2024, the appellant reported a settlement with BCCI backed by personal fund undertakings from Riju Raveendran[cite: 19]. GLAS Trust intervened (IA 727/2024), opposing the settlement as preferential/tainted round-tripping linked to US litigation[cite: 19]. NCLAT heard parties on 30-31 July and 01-02 August 2024, accepting the settlement under Rule 11[cite: 19].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the NCLAT can exercise its inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 to approve a pre-CoC settlement between a corporate debtor and an operational creditor and set aside an admission order under Section 9, notwithstanding objections from intervening financial creditors alleging preferential payments or tainted funds[cite: 19].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a settlement is reached between a corporate debtor and a petitioning creditor before the constitution of the Committee of Creditors (CoC), the Appellate Tribunal is fully empowered under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 (read in light of Swiss Ribbons, Abhishek Singh, and Kamal K. Singh) to set aside the admission order and close the CIRP, provided the settlement is bona fide and the source of funds is accounted for, leaving other creditors free to pursue independent legal remedies for their claims[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12A and Regulation 30A govern post-admission withdrawals involving CoC approval, but where the CoC is not yet constituted, parties can approach the tribunal directly under Rule 11 to record settlements and prevent unnecessary corporate disruption, as the first hour of justice is the hour of compromise[cite: 19]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed affidavits and undertakings showing that the settlement amount (Rs. 158 Crores) was paid by ex-promoter Riju Raveendran out of personal funds accumulated from historical share sales (2015-2022) on which income tax was paid in India, noting that the intervening US lenders failed to produce concrete evidence of tainted round-tripping while their creditor rights remained safeguarded[cite: 19]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The pre-CoC settlement between the suspended management and BCCI is genuine and lawful, warranting the invocation of Rule 11 to set aside the CIRP admission order, subject to automatic revival in case of payment default[cite: 19].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins.) No. 262 of 2024 is disposed of; the settlement between the parties is approved and taken on record; the NCLT admission order dated 16.07.2024 in CP (IB) No. 149/BB/2023 is set aside, and the CIRP against Think & Learn Private Limited is closed, with the caveat that default in the remaining undertaking payments shall automatically revive the admission order[cite: 19].
summary: Byju Raveendran (suspended director of Think & Learn Pvt. Ltd.) appealed against an NCLT Bengaluru order dated 16.07.2024 admitting a Section 9 CIRP petition filed by BCCI for a default of Rs. 158.90 Crores[cite: 19]. During appellate hearings, the appellant reported a full settlement with BCCI funded by ex-promoter Riju Raveendran[cite: 19]. GLAS Trust Company LLC (US lenders' agent) intervened, alleging that the settlement funds were tainted round-tripping from a disputed USD 1.2 Billion loan and violated US bankruptcy injunctions[cite: 19]. Allowing the appeal and exercising inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, the NCLAT Chennai Bench approved the pre-CoC settlement[cite: 19]. The Tribunal held that Riju Raveendran established that the funds came from personal, tax-paid Indian share sales, and that intervening creditors' rights were protected under the IBC framework, setting aside the CIRP admission subject to strict compliance with the payment undertaking[cite: 19].

case_title: Venus Petrochemicals (Bombay) Private Limited & Ors. vs. Sunil M. Thakkar & Ors.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain, Technical Members Naresh Salecha and Indevar Pandey)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant No. 1 is Venus Petrochemicals (Bombay) Private Limited (Corporate Debtor). Appellant No. 2 is Atul M. Thakkar (Ex-Director). Appellant No. 3 is Anand A. Thakkar (Director / son of Atul). Respondent No. 1 is Sunil M. Thakkar (Shareholder / brother of Atul). Respondent No. 2 is Lopa S. Thakkar (Shareholder / wife of Sunil). Respondent No. 3 is Yashesh A. Thakkar (Director / son of Sunil). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was incorporated on 21.06.1995, engaged in chemical solvents and specialty chemicals, with equity shareholding held equally in a 50:50 ratio between the Atul Thakkar family and the Sunil Thakkar family. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (family-controlled company oppression, mismanagement, and deadlock dispute under Sections 241 and 242). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company successfully operated without dispute from 1995 to 2015 under joint directorship of Atul and Sunil. Disputes erupted in December 2015 when Atul inducted his son Anand onto the board using a casting vote. Respondents filed Company Petition No. 12/MB/2019 before NCLT Mumbai under Sections 241-242 in November 2018. NCLT Mumbai passed final judgment on 01.04.2022. NCLAT appointed an interim administrator on 19.10.2022, discharged on 23.01.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Board minutes from December 2015, January 2016, September 2016, and July 2017 recording induction of family members; use of chairman's casting vote; cessation of Sunil's remuneration in April 2016; financial investments in a loss-making Dubai subsidiary (Venus Petrochemicals Middle East DMCC); and statutory director disqualification records under Section 166(4). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Sunil Thakkar and family filed CP No. 12/MB/2019 before NCLT Mumbai under Sections 241 and 242 alleging oppression and mismanagement. NCLT Mumbai allowed the petition on 01.04.2022, curtailing the chairman's casting vote, mandating equal board representation, and requiring joint bank account signatures. Appellants challenged the order before NCLAT via Comp. App. (AT) No. 65 of 2022.
legal_issues: (i) Whether the unilateral induction of family members to the board of directors by the chairman using a casting vote in a 50:50 family-controlled company (quasi-partnership) constitutes 'oppression and mismanagement' under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013; (ii) Whether the Adjudicating Authority is legally empowered under Section 242 to strip a chairman of his casting vote, mandate equal board representation, and require joint bank signatures to resolve an oppressive deadlock.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A closely held family company with equal 50:50 shareholding operating on mutual trust and confidence constitutes a 'quasi-partnership' (Ebrahimi v. Westbourne Galleries; TCS v. Cyrus Investments); where a dominant faction misuses a chairman's casting vote not in good faith for corporate benefit, but to unilaterally alter board composition, oust the 50% co-promoter, and arrogate management control, it amounts to 'oppression and mismanagement' under Section 241, empowering the Tribunal under Section 242 to restructure board governance, eliminate casting votes, and mandate joint signatories. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 242 grants wide equitable powers to regulate company conduct and cure prejudice to members; while appointment of directors is generally internal management, exercising a casting vote to permanently tilt corporate balance in a 50:50 deadlock destroys legitimate expectations of equal management participation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed board resolutions from 2015 to 2019, showing that Atul Thakkar used his casting vote exclusively to induct his son Anand and block Sunil's sons, while abruptly terminating Sunil's remuneration in April 2016 and funding loss-making foreign subsidiaries against co-shareholder dissent. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellants engaged in oppressive conduct that paralyzed corporate governance and destroyed the quasi-partnership foundation, validating the NCLT's remedial directions.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 65 of 2022 is dismissed, upholding the Impugned Order dated 01.04.2022 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench in C.P. No. 12/MB/2019, with no order as to costs and pending IAs closed.
summary: Venus Petrochemicals (Bombay) Pvt. Ltd. and its directors appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order dated 01.04.2022 which held them guilty of oppression and mismanagement under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act. The dispute arose in a 50:50 family-controlled chemical business where Atul Thakkar used his casting vote as chairman to induct his son to the board and block the co-promoter Sunil Thakkar's family, while stopping Sunil's remuneration. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that the company operated as a quasi-partnership where mutual trust and equal management participation were foundational. Citing supreme court jurisprudence on quasi-partnerships and oppression, the Tribunal ruled that misusing a casting vote to seize unilateral control is oppressive, affirming the NCLT's directions to eliminate casting votes, enforce equal board representation, and mandate joint bank signatories.

case_title: Axis Bank Limited vs. Naren Sheth & Anr.
appeal_number: I.A. No. 4166 of 2024 in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1164 of 2024
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Yogesh Khanna and Technical Member Ajai Das Mehrotra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Axis Bank Limited (Financial Creditor). Respondent No. 1 is Naren Sheth. Respondent No. 2 is the other respondent / corporate debtor representative[cite: 21]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial debt owed by the corporate debtor to Axis Bank Limited, leading to NCLT proceedings. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default on banking credit facilities. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT passed the impugned order on 05.04.2024[cite: 21]. Appellant applied for a certified copy on 08.04.2024 (Application No. D-0005 / D4005)[cite: 21]. Registry issued a certified copy on 15.04.2024 (marked as a free certified true copy)[cite: 21]. Axis Bank filed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1164 of 2024 along with IA No. 4166 of 2024 for condonation of a 15-day delay[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLT order dated 05.04.2024; certified copy application receipt dated 08.04.2024 bearing Application No. D-0005; and copy issued on 15.04.2024[cite: 21]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Axis Bank filed an appeal against the NCLT order dated 05.04.2024 with a 15-day delay[cite: 21]. Respondent No. 1 objected to the delay condonation application (IA 4166/2024), arguing that no fee was paid for obtaining the certified copy (making it a 'free copy' under Rule 50 which cannot save limitation per SBI v. India Power Corp), and that limitation commenced directly on the date of pronouncement without excluding the date of order[cite: 21].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the date of pronouncement of an order is to be excluded when computing the 30-day limitation period under Section 61(2) of the IBC pursuant to Section 12 of the Limitation Act and Rule 3 of NCLAT Rules[cite: 21]; (ii) Whether an application for a certified copy submitted on 08.04.2024 and issued by the Registry bearing an application number constitutes a valid certified copy for limitation purposes, and whether a delay of 15 days is condonable[cite: 21].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When computing limitation for filing an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC, the date of pronouncement of the order must be excluded pursuant to Section 12(1) of the Limitation Act (applied via Section 238A) and Rule 3 of the NCLAT Rules[cite: 21]. Furthermore, where an appellant formally applies for a certified copy within limitation and receives a copy bearing the Registry's application number and issuance date, it constitutes a valid certified copy sufficient to remove confusion regarding free copies[cite: 21]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238A of the IBC makes Sections 4 to 24 of the Limitation Act applicable to NCLAT proceedings as far as may be applicable; Section 12(2) and Rule 3 explicitly mandate the exclusion of the date of judgment[cite: 21]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the impugned order was passed on 05.04.2024, that Axis Bank applied for a certified copy on 08.04.2024 (App. No. D-0005) and received it on 15.04.2024, and that excluding the date of pronouncement brought the filing well within the condonable 15-day extension period[cite: 21]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The computation of limitation correctly excludes the date of pronouncement, the certified copy was properly applied for, and the 15-day delay is fully condonable upon sufficient cause[cite: 21].
operative_order: IA No. 4166 of 2024 for condonation of delay is allowed, the 15-day delay is condoned, and the main appeal is directed to be listed for hearing on 21.11.2024[cite: 21].
summary: Axis Bank Limited filed an application (IA No. 4166 of 2024) seeking condonation of a 15-day delay in filing Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1164 of 2024 against an NCLT order dated 05.04.2024[cite: 21]. Respondent No. 1 objected, arguing that limitation began strictly on the date of order without day-exclusion and that the annexed copy was an invalid free copy under Rule 50[cite: 21]. Allowing the delay condonation application, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that under Section 238A of the IBC, Section 12 of the Limitation Act, and Rule 3 of the NCLAT Rules, the date of pronouncement must be excluded from computation[cite: 21]. The Tribunal also held that a copy obtained via a formal application bearing a Registry application number constitutes a valid certified copy, and condoned the 15-day delay[cite: 21].

case_title: Vinod Kumar Agarwal & Anr. vs. State Bank of India & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1245 of 2023 & No. 1247 of 2023
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain and Technical Member Indevar Pandey)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants in the two appeals are Vinod Kumar Agarwal and Prahalad Kumar Agarwal (Personal Guarantors)[cite: 22]. Respondent No. 1 is State Bank of India (Financial Creditor). Respondent No. 2 is Shikhar Chand Jain (IRP / Resolution Professional)[cite: 22]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Vandana Vidhyut Limited (Principal Borrower) secured credit facilities from a consortium of six banks (led by PNB, including SBI), which was guaranteed by the Appellants via a Deed of Guarantee executed on 27.10.2010[cite: 22]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Principal borrower defaulted on loan repayment; account classified as NPA; principal borrower admitted into CIRP on 26.04.2021 before NCLT Mumbai and subsequently driven into liquidation[cite: 22]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Deed of Guarantee executed on 27.10.2010[cite: 22]. Consortium issued SARFAESI notice under Section 13(2) on 26.05.2016 allowing 60 days (expiring 24.07.2016)[cite: 22]. Personal guarantors signed balance sheet acknowledging debt on 01.09.2017[cite: 22]. State Bank of India filed an application under Section 95 of the IBC against the personal guarantors on 02.12.2021[cite: 22]. Rule 7(1) / Section 95 demand notice issued on 21.06.2021 allowing 14 days (expiring 05.07.2021)[cite: 22]. NCLT Cuttack Bench admitted the Section 95 application on 31.07.2023[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Deed of Guarantee dated 27.10.2010; SARFAESI Section 13(2) notice dated 26.05.2016; audited balance sheet signed by appellants on 01.09.2017 acknowledging debt; Section 95 demand notice dated 21.06.2021; and NCLT admission order dated 31.07.2023[cite: 22]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: State Bank of India filed applications under Section 95 of the IBC on 02.12.2021 against personal guarantors Vinod Kumar Agarwal and Prahalad Kumar Agarwal[cite: 22]. NCLT Cuttack Bench admitted the applications on 31.07.2023, holding that the limitation period started from the expiry of the 21.06.2021 demand notice (05.07.2021), making the petition within time[cite: 22]. Personal guarantors appealed to NCLAT via Company Appeals Nos. 1245 and 1247 of 2023[cite: 22].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an application filed under Section 95 of the IBC against a personal guarantor is barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act when calculated from the initial SARFAESI notice date (24.07.2016), or whether a fresh limitation period is triggered by an intervening debt acknowledgement in a balance sheet (01.09.2017) and protected by Supreme Court Covid-19 limitation extensions[cite: 22].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Article 137 of the Limitation Act read with Section 18, where a personal guarantor acknowledges debt liability in a balance sheet signed by them, a fresh period of limitation of three years is computed from the date of such signing; furthermore, where the resulting limitation expiry falls within the protective window of the Supreme Court's Suo Motu COVID-19 extension orders (extending limitation up to 01.03.2022 plus 90 days), an insolvency application filed under Section 95 remains well within limitation[cite: 22]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 of the Limitation Act applies to debt acknowledgements in financial statements (Asset Recovery Corp. v. Bishal Jaiswal), restarting the limitation clock for personal guarantee obligations independent of when a SARFAESI notice was issued[cite: 22]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal inspected the financial balance sheet signed by the appellants on 01.09.2017 acknowledging liability, calculated a fresh 3-year limitation expiring on 31.08.2020, and noted that this date was fully shielded by the Supreme Court's Suo Motu COVID-19 limitation extension orders, rendering the Section 12.2021 filing timely[cite: 22]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 95 application was not barred by limitation, and the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in admitting the insolvency petition against the personal guarantors[cite: 22].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1245 of 2023 and Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1247 of 2023 are dismissed, upholding the common order dated 31.07.2023 passed by NCLT Cuttack Bench admitting the Section 95 applications, with no order as to costs[cite: 22].
summary: Vinod Kumar Agarwal and Prahalad Kumar Agarwal (personal guarantors for Vandana Vidhyut Ltd.) appealed against an NCLT Cuttack order dated 31.07.2023 admitting Section 95 insolvency applications filed by State Bank of India[cite: 22]. The appellants argued that the petitions were time-barred under Article 137, counting from the date of default in July 2016 following a SARFAESI notice[cite: 22]. Dismissing the appeals, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that even if default occurred in 2016, the appellants signed a balance sheet on 01.09.2017 acknowledging the debt, which triggered a fresh 3-year limitation period expiring on 31.08.2020[cite: 22]. Citing the Supreme Court's Bishal Jaiswal ruling on balance sheet acknowledgements and Suo Motu COVID-19 limitation extensions, the Tribunal ruled that the December 2021 filing was well within time, affirming the admission order[cite: 22].

case_title: Kritish Patel, Promoter of Kethos Tiles Pvt. Ltd. vs. Vikash Gautamchand Jain, RP & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1173 of 2024 & No. 1323 of 2024
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 1173 of 2024 is Vikash Gautamchand Jain, Resolution Professional (RP) of Kethos Tiles Private Limited[cite: 23]. The Appellant in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 1323 of 2024 is Kritish Patel, Promoter of Kethos Tiles Private Limited (Corporate Debtor / MSME)[cite: 23]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Kethos Tiles Pvt. Ltd., an eligible Micro, Small & Medium Enterprise (MSME), filed an application under Section 54C of the IBC to initiate Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (PPIRP)[cite: 23]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default on debt obligations of the MSME corporate debtor leading to PPIRP admission. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Adjudicating Authority admitted the Section 54C application and initiated PPIRP on 04.01.2024[cite: 23]. Public announcement made on 06.01.2024[cite: 23]. 3rd CoC meeting held on 30.04.2024 (and continued/resolved on 02.05.2024), wherein CoC noted that the 120-day PPIRP period was expiring on 03.05.2024 and passed a resolution with 91.75% voting share to seek a 60-day extension[cite: 23]. RP filed an extension application, which the NCLT rejected on 06.06.2024, terminating the PPIRP[cite: 23]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Section 54C application; public announcement dated 06.01.2024; revised base resolution plan under consideration; minutes of the 3rd CoC meeting dated 30.04.2024; and e-voting results dated 02.05.2024[cite: 23]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench (Court-I) rejected the RP's extension application (IA No. 769/AHM/2024) via order dated 06.06.2024, holding that Section 54D(3) mandates termination if no plan is approved within 120 days and that Section 12 extension principles do not apply to PPIRP[cite: 23]. RP and Promoter appealed to NCLAT via Company Appeals Nos. 1173 and 1323 of 2024[cite: 23].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the 120-day timeline prescribed under Section 54D(1) of the IBC for completion of Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (PPIRP) is strictly mandatory, resulting in automatic termination, or whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction to grant an extension of time on sufficient cause and on the strength of a CoC resolution[cite: 23].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The 120-day timeline prescribed under Section 54D(1) of the IBC for completing the Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (PPIRP) is directory rather than mandatory; the statute does not provide for automatic termination upon expiry of 120 days, and the Adjudicating Authority retains the judicial discretion to extend the time period for reasonable grounds upon an application filed pursuant to a requisite CoC resolution[cite: 23]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Provisions containing timelines for insolvency resolution (such as Section 7/9/10 provisos, Section 12, and Regulation 35A) use the word 'shall' but have consistently been construed by the Supreme Court (e.g., Surendra Trading Co., Essar Steel) as directory to serve the ultimate objective of value maximization and corporate revival rather than driving a viable company into liquidation[cite: 23]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the CoC, in its 3rd meeting with a 91.75% majority vote, resolved to seek a 60-day extension because a revised base resolution plan was actively under consideration[cite: 23]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in holding that it lacked jurisdiction to extend the PPIRP period beyond 120 days, and the rejection of the extension application was legally unsustainable[cite: 23].
operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 1173 and 1323 of 2024 are allowed, the impugned order dated 06.06.2024 passed by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench in IA No. 769/AHM/2024 is set aside, IA No. 769/AHM/2024 is allowed, and the PPIRP period is extended by 60 days from the date of the judgment[cite: 23].
summary: Vikash Gautamchand Jain (RP of Kethos Tiles Pvt. Ltd.) and Kritish Patel (Promoter) appealed against an NCLT Ahmedabad order dated 06.06.2024 which rejected an application for a 60-day extension of the Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (PPIRP) and terminated the proceedings[cite: 23]. The NCLT had held that under Section 54D(3), proceedings must terminate if a plan is not approved within 120 days[cite: 23]. Allowing the appeals, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that Section 54D timelines are directory, not mandatory, and do not trigger automatic termination[cite: 23]. Citing Supreme Court precedents on statutory interpretation and timelines (such as Essar Steel and Surendra Trading Co.), the Tribunal ruled that the Adjudicating Authority has discretionary power to extend PPIRP timelines on sufficient cause backed by a CoC resolution, setting aside the termination and granting a 60-day extension[cite: 23].

case_title: Khushbu Dye Chem Private Limited vs. Chemical Suppliers India Private Limited
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan, Technical Members Barun Mitra and Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Khushbu Dye Chem Private Limited (Operational Creditor). The Respondent is Chemical Suppliers India Private Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant supplied chemicals (Isopropyl Alcohol, Toluene, Methyl Methacrylate, etc.) worth Rs. 1,82,54,891/- against seven invoices under purchase orders, with payment terms of 70 days. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Principal claim of Rs. 1,82,54,891/- plus claimed interest of Rs. 42,72,193/-. Demand notice issued on 24.06.2022. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice dated 24.06.2022. Section 9 petition (C.P. (IB)-892(ND)/2022) filed before NCLT New Delhi. NCLT dismissed the petition on 17.01.2024. NCLAT decided the appeal on 06.08.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Seven supply invoices; demand notice dated 24.06.2022; replies and rejoinders dated July 2022; six dishonored cheques with 'payment stopped by drawer' remark; police complaints; credit and debit notes; emails regarding unlifted IPA material; and GST returns. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Court-III dismissed the Section 9 application on 17.01.2024, holding that the debt amount fell below the Rs. 1 Crore threshold under Section 4 and that pre-existing disputes existed. Operational Creditor appealed to NCLAT via Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 664 of 2024.
legal_issues: (i) Whether the operational debt amount after accounting for legitimate adjustments and excluding unilateral interest falls below the minimum threshold value of Rs. 1 Crore under Section 4 of the IBC; (ii) Whether there existed pre-existing disputes between the parties regarding the invoices and transactions prior to the issuance of the demand notice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Unilateral stipulations of interest without a binding agreement cannot be added to inflate an operational debt to meet the statutory threshold, and interest cannot be claimed as an operational debt under Section 5(21) of the Code (SS Polymers v. Kanodia Technoplast); furthermore, where legitimate ledger adjustments and valid pre-existing disputes bring the enforceable principal claim below the statutory threshold of Rs. 1 Crore under Section 4, a Section 9 application is not maintainable. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(21) defines 'operational debt' without including interest (unlike 'financial debt' under Section 5(8)), and unilateral invoices containing interest terms without corporate debtor consent do not crystallize into operational debt. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal analyzed invoices, ledger deductions, payments of Rs. 20,71,000/-, disputed debit notes, and pre-existing correspondence regarding unlifted materials (IPA supplies), finding that the enforceable debt fell below Rs. 1 Crore and genuine pre-existing disputes existed. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT committed no error in dismissing the Section 9 petition, as the established operational debt was below the statutory threshold and pre-existing disputes were duly made out.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 664 of 2024 is dismissed, upholding the order dated 17.01.2024 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench, Court-III in C.P. (IB)-892(ND)/2022, with parties bearing their own costs.
summary: Khushbu Dye Chem Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor) appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order dismissing its Section 9 CIRP petition against Chemical Suppliers India Pvt. Ltd. for unpaid chemical supply dues. The NCLT had held that after adjustments and excluding unauthorized interest, the claim fell below the Rs. 1 Crore threshold under Section 4, and that pre-existing disputes existed. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that unilateral interest cannot be added to inflate operational debt under Section 5(21), and that valid adjustments and pre-existing disputes regarding unlifted material fully justified the dismissal.

case_title: Infrastructure Leasing and Financial Services Ltd. & Anr. vs. Sadbhav Engineering Limited & Anr.
appeal_number: Interlocutory Application Nos. 1288, 2006 and 3262 of 2024 in Company Appeal (AT) No. 346 of 2018
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Applicants are Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services Ltd. (IL&FS) and Jharkhand Road Projects Implementation Company Ltd. (JRPICL). Respondents / Award Holders are Sadbhav Engineering Ltd. & GKC Projects Ltd. Intervenor is Edelweiss Alternative Asset Advisors Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Arbitration proceedings between JRPICL (IL&FS group company) and Sadbhav Engineering resulting in arbitral awards dated 06.08.2020 and 28.03.2023. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: NCLAT interim order dated 15.10.2018 stayed institution/continuation of suits or recovery actions against IL&FS and its 348 group companies. Order dated 11.01.2019 permitted arbitrations to continue but directed awards to be kept in sealed covers. Order dated 26.05.2022 directed opening of sealed covers. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Interim stay on 15.10.2018; Resolution framework approved on 12.03.2020; Award opened in 2022; Sadbhav filed execution petition (Execution Case No. 12 & 13 of 2023) at Ranchi Civil Court. IA 1288/2024 filed by IL&FS; NCLAT passed order on 28.08.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Arbitral awards dated 06.08.2020 and 28.03.2023; NCLAT orders dated 15.10.2018, 11.01.2019, 12.03.2020, and 26.05.2022; Section 34 petition before Delhi HC; and Ranchi execution petitions. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: IL&FS and JRPICL filed IA No. 1288 of 2024 seeking clarification of the 26.05.2022 order and permanent restraint against Sadbhav and GKC Projects from executing arbitral awards. Sadbhav filed IA No. 3262 of 2024 opposing the restraint. NCLAT heard applications and delivered judgment on 28.08.2024.
legal_issues: (i) Whether the order dated 26.05.2022 permitting the opening of arbitral awards from sealed covers automatically lifted the general interim stay/moratorium granted on 15.10.2018 against execution and recovery actions against IL&FS group entities; (ii) Whether the interim stay operating since 2018 should be allowed to continue indefinitely or whether a show-cause notice should be issued for its prospective vacation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An order directing the opening of an arbitral award from a sealed cover (such as the order dated 26.05.2022) does not implicitly modify, lift, or vacate a general interim stay/injunction protecting a corporate group (IL&FS) from execution and recovery proceedings; however, such comprehensive interim protections cannot be permitted to operate indefinitely without a time limit, and the tribunal may issue notice to show cause why the interim stay should not cease after a reasonable date. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Inherent powers under NCLAT proceedings to regulate debt resolution frameworks and corporate rehabilitation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Tribunal reviewed the exact wording of the 26.05.2022 order, confirming it only modified paragraph 2 of the 11.01.2019 order (regarding sealed covers) without touching the broad 15.10.2018 stay, but noted that over five years had elapsed since the stay was instituted. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Clarified that the 26.05.2022 order did not permit award enforcement, but directed IL&FS to show cause why the 15.10.2018 interim protection should not expire as of 15.10.2024.
operative_order: IA No. 1288 of 2024 is allowed in part, clarifying that the order dated 26.05.2022 did not permit award enforcement; IL&FS and group entities are directed to show cause by 14.10.2024 why the interim order dated 15.10.2018 should not cease to operate with effect from 15.10.2024.
summary: IL&FS and JRPICL filed interlocutory applications seeking clarification of the NCLAT's 26.05.2022 order and an order restraining Sadbhav Engineering and GKC Projects from executing arbitral awards. The NCLAT Principal Bench clarified that the 2022 order merely allowed opening arbitral awards from sealed covers and did not lift the general interim stay granted on 15.10.2018 against execution actions. However, noting that over five years had passed, the Tribunal directed IL&FS to show cause why the interim protection should not expire on 15.10.2024.

case_title: Sanjeev Mahajan vs. Indian Bank (Erstwhile Allahabad Bank) & Ors.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan, Technical Members Barun Mitra and Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Sanjeev Mahajan (Shareholder and Promoter of Corporate Debtor, M/s Nimitaya Hotel & Resorts Pvt. Ltd.). Respondent No. 1 is Indian Bank (Erstwhile Allahabad Bank). Respondent No. 2 is the Resolution Professional. Respondent No. 3 is Nehru Place Hotels and Real Estates Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant / SRA)[cite: 33]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed financial facilities from Indian Bank, leading to Section 7 CIRP admission vide order dated 24.12.2021 in CP (IB) No. 1913/2019[cite: 33]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default on credit facilities extended by Indian Bank. Resolution Plan of SRA approved for Rs. 120.01 Crores[cite: 33]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP admitted on 24.12.2021[cite: 33]. NCLAT permitted Section 12A settlement proposal via order dated 04.07.2022[cite: 33]. Appellant submitted a revised settlement offer of Rs. 100 Crores on 25.11.2022[cite: 33]. CoC deliberated proposals in 13th and 14th meetings (held on 26.11.2022 and 07.12.2022) and approved SRA's plan of Rs. 120.01 Crores with 100% vote share while rejecting the appellant's offer on 08.01.2023[cite: 33]. CIRP 330-day period expired on 28.01.2023[cite: 33]. Appellant sent subsequent offers (e.g., Rs. 118.26 Crores on 21.03.2023 and Rs. 120 Crores on 10.10.2023), which the Bank declined on 05.05.2023[cite: 33]. Appellant filed IA No. 2594 of 2023, which NCLT dismissed[cite: 33]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal on 20.08.2024[cite: 33]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Section 7 admission order; NCLAT judgments dated 04.07.2022 and 21.11.2022; minutes of 13th, 14th, 15th, and 16th CoC meetings; settlement proposal dated 25.11.2022; and Bank's rejection email dated 05.05.2023[cite: 33]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Court V, New Delhi, rejected the Appellant's IA No. 2594 of 2023 via order dated 03.07.2024, which sought to compel the Bank to negotiate a subsequent Section 12A settlement proposal of Rs. 118.26 Crores submitted post-CoC approval of the resolution plan[cite: 33]. Appellant appealed to NCLAT via Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1440 of 2024[cite: 33].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a promoter/shareholder can compel a sole financial creditor/CoC member to negotiate and accept a Section 12A settlement proposal submitted after the CoC has already evaluated, compared, and rejected it in favour of a higher-value resolution plan approved by a 100% voting majority[cite: 33].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While Section 12A permits settlement and withdrawal of CIRP applications with requisite CoC approval, neither the statute nor judicial precedent grants a promoter an indefeasible right to submit endless, unsolicited settlement proposals after the Committee of Creditors has, in its commercial wisdom, properly considered, compared, and rejected a prior settlement offer and approved a higher-value resolution plan with 100% vote share. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12A and Regulation 30A provide mechanisms for settlement, but the commercial wisdom of the CoC in evaluating the viability, value, and collateral release implications of competing offers (such as guarantee extinguishment) is non-justiciable unless patently arbitrary. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the minutes of the 13th, 14th, 15th, and 16th CoC meetings, confirming that the Appellant's initial Rs. 100 Crore offer (which sought complete release of personal guarantees) was thoroughly debated, compared against the SRA's Rs. 120.01 Crore plan, and rejected by a 100% CoC vote on 08.01.2023. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC's rejection of the settlement proposal was thoroughly considered and non-arbitrary, and post-approval attempts by the promoter to submit increased offers cannot override the approved resolution plan.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1440 of 2024 is dismissed, upholding the order dated 03.07.2024 passed by NCLT New Delhi, Court V in IA No. 2594/2023 in CP (IB) No. 1913/ND/2019, with no order as to costs[cite: 33].
summary: Sanjeev Mahajan, promoter of M/s Nimitaya Hotel & Resorts Pvt. Ltd., appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order dated 03.07.2024 dismissing his application (IA No. 2594/2023) which sought to compel Indian Bank to negotiate a post-approval Section 12A settlement proposal of Rs. 118.26 Crores[cite: 33]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that the appellant's initial settlement offer of Rs. 100 Crores (which conditioned release of personal guarantees) had been duly considered, compared against a higher resolution plan of Rs. 120.01 Crores, and rejected by a 100% CoC vote on 08.01.2023[cite: 33]. The Tribunal ruled that promoters have no right to submit endless revised offers after CoC plan approval, affirming the Adjudicating Authority's dismissal[cite: 33].

case_title: Mr. Paresh Parekh & Anr. vs. Alchemist Asset Reconstruction Co. Ltd. & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1204 of 2024 & No. 1205 of 2024
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan, Technical Members Barun Mitra and Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Mr. Paresh Parekh and Mr. Manish Patel (Personal Guarantors of Corporate Debtor, Sort India Enviro Solutions Ltd. / SIESL). Respondent No. 1 is Alchemist Asset Reconstruction Company Limited (Financial Creditor / Assignee). Respondent No. 2 is Mr. B.L. Chakravarti (Resolution Professional)[cite: 34]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sort India Enviro Solutions Ltd. entered into working capital and term loan agreements with RBL Bank Ltd. on 28.11.2015 for credit facilities up to Rs. 32.30 Crores, secured by deeds of guarantee executed by the Appellants and a Put Option Agreement dated 12.11.2016 with Agnus Capital LLP[cite: 34]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate debtor defaulted, and its loan account was classified as NPA on 31.05.2018[cite: 34]. Corporate debtor admitted into CIRP on 23.09.2020[cite: 34]. Statutory demand notice issued to personal guarantors on 14.07.2020 for Rs. 32.25 Crores[cite: 34]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan agreements executed on 28.11.2015 and 17.10.2016; Put Option Agreement on 12.11.2016; NPA on 31.05.2018; Debt assigned by RBL Bank to Alchemist ARC via Assignment Agreement on 28.06.2018[cite: 34]. Alchemist ARC filed Section 95 petitions on 09.10.2020 in CP (IB) Nos. 360 and 361/NCLT/AHM/2020[cite: 34]. RP submitted Section 99 report recommending admission on 13.10.2021[cite: 34]. NCLT Ahmedabad Bench-II admitted the Section 95 petitions on 30.04.2024[cite: 34]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreements; deeds of guarantee dated 28.11.2015 and 17.10.2016; Put Option Agreement dated 12.11.2016; Assignment Agreement dated 28.06.2018; NeSL records; and RP report under Section 99[cite: 34]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Alchemist ARC filed Section 95 petitions against personal guarantors Paresh Parekh and Manish Patel[cite: 34]. NCLT Ahmedabad Bench-II admitted the petitions on 30.04.2024 after considering the RP's Section 99 report[cite: 34]. Personal guarantors appealed to NCLAT via Company Appeals Nos. 1204 and 1205 of 2024[cite: 34].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a financial creditor holding a personal guarantee is legally precluded from invoking the deed of guarantee and initiating insolvency proceedings under Section 95 of the IBC without first exhausting remedies under a collateral Put Option Agreement with a third party[cite: 34]; (ii) Whether a personal guarantor has the locus standi to challenge a registered debt assignment agreement executed between the original lender and an Asset Reconstruction Company under Section 5 of the SARFAESI Act[cite: 34]; (iii) Whether technical hurdles or connectivity glitches during virtual hearings before the Adjudicating Authority resulted in a violation of natural justice[cite: 34].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act, the liability of a surety is coextensive with that of the principal debtor unless otherwise provided by contract; a creditor holding an unconditional and irrevocable deed of guarantee is entitled to invoke the guarantee and initiate personal insolvency under Section 95 of the IBC without exhausting alternate collateral remedies (such as a Put Option Agreement), and an assignment of debt executed under Section 5 of the SARFAESI Act vests all lender rights in the assignee company, depriving guarantors of any locus to challenge the assignment[cite: 34]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(2) of the SARFAESI Act creates a legal fiction whereby an Asset Reconstruction Company acquiring financial assets is deemed to be the lender, vesting all rights of the original financial institution in the ARC. Furthermore, time-bound IBC proceedings under Section 95/99 do not vitiate a hearing where an appellant is afforded an opportunity to submit written submissions[cite: 34]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal inspected the Term Loan Agreement (Clause 14), Assignment Agreement, Deed of Guarantee (Clauses 2, 14, 31, 32), and the Put Option Agreement, finding that the guarantee was absolute and unconditional, that the assignment complied with SARFAESI provisions, and that the RP's Section 99 report correctly verified un-discharged debt and default[cite: 34]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The personal guarantors' obligations were absolute, coextensive, and independent of the Put Option Agreement, and the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in admitting the Section 95 applications[cite: 34].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 1204 and 1205 of 2024 are dismissed, upholding the common order dated 30.04.2024 passed by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench-II admitting the Section 95 petitions against the personal guarantors, with no order as to costs[cite: 34].
summary: Mr. Paresh Parekh and Mr. Manish Patel (personal guarantors for Sort India Enviro Solutions Ltd.) appealed against NCLT Ahmedabad orders dated 30.04.2024 admitting Section 95 insolvency applications filed by Alchemist Asset Reconstruction Co[cite: 34]. The appellants argued that Alchemist was barred from invoking the personal guarantees because it had not first exercised its rights under a collateral Put Option Agreement with Agnus Capital, and challenged the validity of the debt assignment[cite: 34]. Dismissing the appeals, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that a deed of guarantee is an independent, unconditional contract whose liability is coextensive under Section 128 of the Contract Act, and lenders are not required to exhaust alternate securities first[cite: 34]. The Tribunal ruled that the debt assignment under Section 5 of the SARFAESI Act was valid, giving the appellants no locus to object, and affirmed the personal insolvency admission[cite: 34].

case_title: Gulshan Kumar Ahuja vs. Monika Garg (Sole Proprietor, Aggarwal Enterprises) & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain and Technical Member Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Gulshan Kumar Ahuja (Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor, M/s Ahuja Cotspin Pvt. Limited). Respondent No. 1 is Monika Garg (Sole Proprietor of Aggarwal Enterprises - Operational Creditor). Respondent No. 2 is Ms. Priya Bhushan Sharma (Interim Resolution Professional / IRP)[cite: 29]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operational Creditor supplied raw cotton to the Corporate Debtor, raising various invoices between 13.08.2018 and 16.09.2018[cite: 29]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt comprising principal and claimed interest totaling Rs. 1,91,51,792/- (Principal: Rs. 1,69,37,569/-; Interest: Rs. 22,14,223/-)[cite: 29]. Demand notice issued under Section 8 on 27.05.2019[cite: 29]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Invoices raised between August and September 2018[cite: 29]. DGGI GST intelligence raids conducted on corporate debtor factories on 15.02.2019 and 25.02.2019[cite: 29]. Section 8 demand notice issued on 27.05.2019 (received 31.05.2019)[cite: 29]. Corporate debtor replied on 08.06.2019[cite: 29]. Section 9 petition filed by Operational Creditor on 15.11.2019[cite: 29]. NCLT Chandigarh Bench admitted the Section 9 petition on 12.06.2024[cite: 29]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Supply invoices; DGGI raid and search records; electronic credit ledger deposits; Punjab & Haryana High Court CWP No. 21444 of 2019 filings; Section 8 demand notice dated 27.05.2019; reply dated 08.06.2019; and GSTR returns of the operational creditor[cite: 29]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Monika Garg filed CP (IB) 657/CHD/PB/2019 under Section 9 of the IBC before NCLT Chandigarh Bench[cite: 29]. Corporate debtor contested the petition alleging pre-existing disputes relating to bogus GST invoices and DGGI investigations[cite: 29]. NCLT Chandigarh admitted the Section 9 application on 12.06.2024[cite: 29]. Suspended director appealed to NCLAT via Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1202 of 2024[cite: 29].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an ongoing investigation, raid, or writ petition involving the Directorate General of GST Intelligence (DGGI) regarding alleged bogus invoices and tax compliance constitutes a 'pre-existing dispute' between an operational creditor and a corporate debtor sufficient to bar the initiation of CIRP under Section 9 of the IBC[cite: 29]; (ii) Whether the principal operational debt exceeded the statutory threshold[cite: 29].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: For a pre-existing dispute to bar the admission of a Section 9 application under the IBC, there must be a genuine, real, and pre-existing dispute directly between the operational creditor and the corporate debtor concerning the operational debt or invoices prior to the demand notice (Mobilox Innovations v. Kirusa Software); external regulatory investigations, tax audits, or writ proceedings initiated by the Directorate General of GST Intelligence (DGGI) against a corporate debtor regarding tax compliance do not constitute a pre-existing dispute between the contracting commercial parties, especially where the operational creditor is not a party to those tax proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8 and Section 9 require notice of a dispute relating to the unpaid operational debt between the parties, and generalized tax evasion probes or third-party investigations cannot be weaponized as a substitute for a genuine inter partes commercial dispute. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the operational creditor filed all GSTR returns, that DGGI had initiated no legal proceedings against the operational creditor, and that the operational creditor was not a party to the corporate debtor's writ petition before the Punjab & Haryana High Court, leaving the underlying operational debt undisputed and exceeding the statutory threshold. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The corporate debtor failed to demonstrate a genuine pre-existing dispute between the commercial parties, and the Adjudicating Authority correctly admitted the Section 9 application[cite: 29].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1202 of 2024 is dismissed, upholding the order dated 12.06.2024 passed by NCLT Chandigarh Bench in C.P. (IB) 657/CHD/PB/2019 admitting the Section 9 application, with no order as to costs and pending IAs closed[cite: 29].
summary: Gulshan Kumar Ahuja (suspended director of Ahuja Cotspin Pvt. Ltd.) appealed against an NCLT Chandigarh order dated 12.06.2024 admitting a Section 9 CIRP petition filed by Monika Garg (proprietor of Aggarwal Enterprises) for unpaid cotton supply dues[cite: 29]. The appellant argued that a pre-existing dispute existed because DGGI intelligence officers raided the factory in February 2019 over suspected bogus GST invoices and instructed the company to halt payments[cite: 29]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that tax investigations and writ petitions involving DGGI (to which the operational creditor was not even a party) do not constitute a genuine pre-existing commercial dispute between the trading parties[cite: 29]. Citing Mobilox Innovations, the Tribunal ruled that the debt and default were clearly established and undisputed between the parties, affirming the CIRP admission[cite: 29].

case_title: Dheeraj Wadhawan vs. Union Bank of India & Anr. (with Kapil Wadhawan vs. Union Bank of India & Anr.)
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 863 of 2024 & No. 1135 of 2024
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Dheeraj Wadhawan and Kapil Wadhawan (Personal Guarantors of Corporate Debtor, Dewan Housing Finance Corporation Limited / DHFL)[cite: 38]. Respondent No. 1 is Union Bank of India (Financial Creditor)[cite: 38]. Respondent No. 2 is the Resolution Professional[cite: 38]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: DHFL availed credit facilities comprising Rs. 450 Crores in term loans and Rs. 450 Crores in working capital, secured by a joint deed of personal guarantee executed by the Appellants on 22.06.2019 and four Security Trustee Agreements (STA) executed between 2012 and 2015[cite: 38]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default on credit facilities by DHFL; RBI initiated CIRP against DHFL on 03.12.2019 in CP (IB) No. 4258/MB/2019, where UBI's claim of Rs. 35,17,30,39,020/- was admitted[cite: 38]. UBI invoked personal guarantees on 10.09.2020 and issued demand notices on 07.10.2020 for a default amount of Rs. 3,958,30,48,963.71/-[cite: 38]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Guarantee executed on 22.06.2019; UBI invoked guarantees on 10.09.2020 and served notice on 07.10.2020[cite: 38]. Section 95 applications filed by UBI in December 2020 (CP (IB) No. 4/MB/2021 and CP (IB) No. 5/MB/2021)[cite: 38]. NCLT directed RP report on 01.02.2022 (affirmed by NCLAT on 16.03.2022 and Supreme Court on 02.09.2022)[cite: 38]. NCLT Mumbai admitted Section 95 petitions on 20.03.2024 and 02.04.2024[cite: 38]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Joint deed of guarantee dated 22.06.2019; Security Trustee Agreements; guarantee invocation letter dated 10.09.2020; demand notice dated 07.10.2020; and Section 95 applications[cite: 38]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai admitted Section 95 applications filed by UBI against personal guarantors Dheeraj Wadhawan and Kapil Wadhawan on 20.03.2024 and 02.04.2024 respectively[cite: 38]. Personal guarantors appealed to NCLAT via Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) Nos. 863 and 1135 of 2024[cite: 38].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an individual financial creditor belonging to a consortium can independently maintain and prosecute an application under Section 95 of the IBC against a personal guarantor without joining all other consortium members or acting through the security trustee, in light of Clause 43 of the Deed of Guarantee and Clause 8.5 of the Security Trustee Agreement[cite: 38]; (ii) Whether grounds of maintainability omitted during the first round of litigation (reaching up to the Supreme Court) can be raised in a second round[cite: 38].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 95(1) of the IBC, a financial creditor may apply either by itself, jointly with other creditors, or through a resolution professional to initiate insolvency against a personal guarantor; where a deed of guarantee (Clause 43) explicitly entitles individual banks to proceed against guarantors without exhausting remedies against the borrower or other security, and where the Security Trustee Agreement (Clause 8.5) allows banks to perform obligations independently, an individual consortium bank can validly maintain a Section 95 petition without requiring collective action or prior consent from all lenders[cite: 38]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 95(1) is disjunctive ('either by himself, or jointly with other creditors'), granting an individual creditor statutory standing to trigger personal insolvency[cite: 38]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized Clause 43 of the Deed of Guarantee and Clause 8.5 of the STA, confirming that bank enforcement rights were concurrent with those of the security trustee, and noted that no other consortium members objected to the individual filing[cite: 38]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The individual bank possessed full legal competence to initiate Section 95 proceedings, and the appeals lacked merit[cite: 38].
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) Nos. 863 of 2024 and 1135 of 2024 are dismissed, upholding the Adjudicating Authority's orders admitting the Section 95 applications against the personal guarantors, with no order as to costs[cite: 38].
summary: Dheeraj Wadhawan and Kapil Wadhawan (personal guarantors for DHFL) appealed against NCLT Mumbai orders admitting Section 95 insolvency applications filed individually by Union Bank of India (UBI)[cite: 38]. The appellants argued that as UBI was part of a banking consortium, an insolvency petition under Section 95 could only be maintained collectively by all banks or through the security trustee, citing Clause 43 of the guarantee deed and Clause 8.5 of the Security Trustee Agreement[cite: 38]. Dismissing the appeals, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that Section 95(1) explicitly allows a creditor to apply individually or jointly[cite: 38]. Citing express clauses in the guarantee deed permitting individual bank enforcement without exhausting remedies, the Tribunal ruled that individual lenders have concurrent standing, affirming the personal insolvency admission[cite: 38].

case_title: Indiabulls Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. vs. Pawan Kapoor
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Yogesh Khanna)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Indiabulls Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. (Financial Creditor / Secured Creditor). The Respondent is Pawan Kapoor (Personal Guarantor)[cite: 39]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Mortgage of subject property belonging to the Respondent to secure credit facilities extended to the corporate debtor[cite: 39]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default on loan facilities leading to SARFAESI enforcement and personal insolvency proceedings[cite: 39]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Appellant took symbolic possession under Section 13(4) of the SARFAESI Act on 20.06.2019[cite: 39]. District Magistrate, Gautam Budh Nagar passed a possession order on 16.03.2020[cite: 39]. Section 95 application filed against the personal guarantor on 07.01.2021[cite: 39]. NCLT New Delhi initiated personal insolvency and interim moratorium under Section 96 on 03.02.2021[cite: 39]. Tehsildar took actual physical possession of the mortgaged property on 27.01.2021 (after the interim moratorium commenced on 07.01.2021)[cite: 39]. NCLT passed an order on 25.02.2021 directing restoration of possession to the IRP[cite: 39]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: SARFAESI Section 13(4) notice dated 20.06.2019; DM possession order dated 16.03.2020; Section 95 filing date (07.01.2021); NCLT interim moratorium order dated 03.02.2021; and physical possession record dated 27.01.2021[cite: 39]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Court IV passed an order on 25.02.2021 in IA No. 1009/2021 directing that physical possession of the subject mortgaged property taken on 27.01.2021 be forthwith restored to the IRP following the commencement of the interim moratorium under Section 96 on 07.01.2021[cite: 39]. Indiabulls ARC appealed to NCLAT via Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 192 of 2021[cite: 39].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an interim moratorium under Section 96 of the IBC stays ongoing SARFAESI enforcement proceedings and requires the restoration of physical possession taken after the filing of a Section 95 application[cite: 39]; (ii) Whether taking symbolic or physical possession of a mortgaged property prior to the admission of a Section 95 application vests title in the secured creditor so as to exclude the property from Section 96 interim moratorium[cite: 39].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 96(1) of the IBC, the submission of an application under Section 95 triggers an interim moratorium on the date of the application in relation to 'all the debts', staying any legal action or proceeding pending in respect of any debt; unlike corporate insolvency where Section 14 moratorium operates upon an adjudicating authority's order, Section 96 interim moratorium operates automatically upon filing, insulating all debts and related security interests and prohibiting the continuation of SARFAESI enforcement or physical dispossession after the application date (Dilip B. Jiwrajka v. Union of India; Sanjay Dhingra v. IDBI Bank)[cite: 39]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 96 focuses on the 'debt' rather than the 'debtor', staying all recovery actions concerning personal guarantees and mortgaged assets once a Section 95 application is filed[cite: 39]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the Section 95 application was filed on 07.01.2021 (triggering the interim moratorium), whereas actual physical possession by the Tehsildar occurred later on 27.01.2021[cite: 39]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because physical possession was taken after the interim moratorium commenced on 07.01.2021, the SARFAESI action was legally stayed, and the NCLT correctly ordered the restoration of possession to the IRP[cite: 39].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 192 of 2021 is dismissed, upholding the order dated 25.02.2021 passed by NCLT New Delhi directing restoration of possession of the subject property to the IRP, with observations that the secured creditor cannot proceed further under the SARFAESI Act until the moratorium is lifted[cite: 39].
summary: Indiabulls Asset Reconstruction Co. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order dated 25.02.2021 which directed the immediate restoration of physical possession of a mortgaged property to the Interim Resolution Professional (IRP)[cite: 39]. Indiabulls argued that because it took symbolic possession in June 2019 and obtained a District Magistrate order in March 2020 (prior to the Section 95 filing in January 2021), it held a vested right not affected by the interim moratorium[cite: 39]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that under Section 96 of the IBC (as interpreted by the Supreme Court in Dilip B. Jiwrajka and Delhi High Court in Sanjay Dhingra), filing a Section 95 application automatically triggers an interim moratorium in relation to 'all the debts' on the date of filing[cite: 39]. The Tribunal ruled that because physical possession was executed on 27.01.2021 (after the Section 95 filing on 07.01.2021), the SARFAESI proceedings were stayed, affirming the restoration order[cite: 39].

case_title: Gujarat Industrial Development Corporation vs. Zaveri & Co. Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain and Technical Member Naresh Salecha)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Gujarat Industrial Development Corporation (GIDC - a statutory government corporation). Respondent No. 1 is Zaveri & Co. Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant / SRA). Respondent No. 2 is Rakesh Kumar Agarwal (Resolution Professional / RP). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: GIDC executed a 99-year lease deed on 21.02.2008 with Gujarat Hydrocarbon & Power SEZ Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) for land admeasuring 296-47-81 Hectares in Vilayat Industrial Estate, Bharuch, for setting up a SEZ, in consideration of Rs. 51,97,50,000/-. GIDC permitted mortgage creation in favour of financial creditor SREI Infrastructure Finance Ltd. via letter dated 04.01.2011. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate debtor failed to submit construction plans or utilize land, leading to GIDC show cause notices (11.03.2011 and 20.12.2018) and eviction proceedings under the Gujarat Public Premises Act, 1972. Corporate debtor admitted to CIRP on 18.11.2020. GIDC filed a claim in Form B for Rs. 1,80,62,53,182/- (non-utilization penalty, conversion fees, revenue charges), of which SRA allocated only Rs. 6,14,49,685/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 18.11.2020. GIDC filed IA No. 136 of 2022 under Section 60(5) challenging the resolution plan. NCLT approved the resolution plan via order dated 19.09.2023 in IA No. 4585 of 2021, after IA No. 136 of 2022 was purportedly withdrawn on 13.09.2023. GIDC appealed to NCLAT. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Lease deed dated 21.02.2008; rectification deed dated 11.02.2011; mortgage permission letter dated 04.01.2011; GIDC claim submissions; NCLT orders dated 13.09.2023 and 19.09.2023; and vakalatnama records. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: GIDC filed IA No. 136 of 2022 challenging plan approval and seeking remand. On 13.09.2023, counsel Prerna Mohapatra (appearing for advocate Aastha Mehta) withdrew IA 136/2022. Subsequently, NCLT approved the resolution plan on 19.09.2023 in IA 4585/2021. GIDC appealed, claiming unauthorized withdrawal without client instruction. NCLAT allowed the refiling/filing delays, set aside the withdrawal and plan approval orders, and remanded IA 136/2022 for fresh disposal.
legal_issues: (i) Whether a lawyer has the implied or ostensible authority to make binding concessions or withdraw a substantive application (such as IA 136/2022) without express, written instructions from the client, and whether an order passed on the basis of unauthorized withdrawal is legally sustainable[cite: 40].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: According to accepted notions of professional responsibility and Supreme Court precedent (Himalayan Coop. Group Housing Society v. Balwan Singh), a lawyer must follow client instructions rather than substitute judgment, and possesses no implied or ostensible authority to compromise, settle, or unconditionally withdraw a substantive claim or application without express, specific authorization; admissions or withdrawals made without client instruction do not bind the principal, and courts cannot rely on them to conclude legal rights. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(5) and NCLAT procedural powers to correct judicial proceedings vitiated by unauthorized counsel actions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that GIDC was a government corporation, that no written or oral instructions were given to advocate Aastha Mehta (or colleague Prerna Mohapatra) to withdraw IA 136/2022, and that the application was actively being pursued to protect valuable state land and a massive statutory claim. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The withdrawal of IA No. 136 of 2022 was unauthorized and vitiated, requiring the setting aside of both the withdrawal order and the consequential resolution plan approval, with remand for fresh adjudication[cite: 40].
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 1648 and 1649 of 2023 are allowed, the orders dated 13.09.2023 (permitting withdrawal of IA 136/2022) and 19.09.2023 (approving the resolution plan in IA 4585/2021) are set aside, IA No. 136 of 2022 is restored to the file of the Adjudicating Authority, and parties are directed to appear before NCLT on 09.09.2024 for fresh adjudication[cite: 40].
summary: Gujarat Industrial Development Corporation (GIDC) appealed against two NCLT orders: one permitting the withdrawal of GIDC's intervention application (IA 136/2022) challenging a resolution plan, and another approving the resolution plan for Gujarat Hydrocarbon & Power SEZ Ltd[cite: 40]. GIDC argued that its advocate abruptly and without authorization withdrew IA 136/2022, which sought to protect GIDC's land title and massive statutory claims[cite: 40]. Allowing the appeals, the NCLAT Principal Bench relied on the Supreme Court's ruling in Himalayan Coop. Group Housing Society, holding that lawyers have no implied authority to withdraw substantive claims without express client instructions[cite: 40]. The Tribunal set aside the unauthorized withdrawal order and the consequential plan approval order, restoring IA 136/2022 for fresh consideration before the NCLT[cite: 40].

case_title: Khushbu Dye Chem Private Limited vs. Chemical Suppliers India Private Limited
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan, Technical Members Barun Mitra and Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Khushbu Dye Chem Private Limited (Operational Creditor)[cite: 33]. The Respondent is Chemical Suppliers India Private Limited (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 33]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant supplied chemicals (Isopropyl Alcohol, Toluene, Methyl Methacrylate, etc.) worth Rs. 1,82,54,891/- against seven invoices under purchase orders, with payment terms of 70 days[cite: 33]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Principal claim of Rs. 1,82,54,891/- plus claimed interest of Rs. 42,72,193/-[cite: 33]. Demand notice issued on 24.06.2022[cite: 33]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice dated 24.06.2022[cite: 33]. Section 9 petition (C.P. (IB)-892(ND)/2022) filed before NCLT New Delhi[cite: 33]. NCLT dismissed the petition on 17.01.2024[cite: 33]. NCLAT decided the appeal on 06.08.2024[cite: 33]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Seven supply invoices; demand notice dated 24.06.2022; replies and rejoinders dated July 2022; six dishonored cheques with 'payment stopped by drawer' remark; police complaints; credit and debit notes; emails regarding unlifted IPA material; and GST returns[cite: 33]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Court-III dismissed the Section 9 application on 17.01.2024, holding that the debt amount fell below the Rs. 1 Crore threshold under Section 4 and that pre-existing disputes existed[cite: 33]. Operational Creditor appealed to NCLAT via Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 664 of 2024[cite: 33].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the operational debt amount after accounting for legitimate adjustments and excluding unilateral interest falls below the minimum threshold value of Rs. 1 Crore under Section 4 of the IBC[cite: 33]; (ii) Whether there existed pre-existing disputes between the parties regarding the invoices and transactions prior to the issuance of the demand notice[cite: 33].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Unilateral stipulations of interest without a binding agreement cannot be added to inflate an operational debt to meet the statutory threshold, and interest cannot be claimed as an operational debt under Section 5(21) of the Code (SS Polymers v. Kanodia Technoplast); furthermore, where legitimate ledger adjustments and valid pre-existing disputes bring the enforceable principal claim below the statutory threshold of Rs. 1 Crore under Section 4, a Section 9 application is not maintainable[cite: 33]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(21) defines 'operational debt' without including interest (unlike 'financial debt' under Section 5(8)), and unilateral invoices containing interest terms without corporate debtor consent do not crystallize into operational debt[cite: 33]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal analyzed invoices, ledger deductions, payments of Rs. 20,71,000/-, disputed debit notes, and pre-existing correspondence regarding unlifted materials (IPA supplies), finding that the enforceable debt fell below Rs. 1 Crore and genuine pre-existing disputes existed[cite: 33]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT committed no error in dismissing the Section 9 petition, as the established operational debt was below the statutory threshold and pre-existing disputes were duly made out[cite: 33].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 664 of 2024 is dismissed, upholding the order dated 17.01.2024 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench, Court-III in C.P. (IB)-892(ND)/2022, with parties bearing their own costs[cite: 33].
summary: Khushbu Dye Chem Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor) appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order dismissing its Section 9 CIRP petition against Chemical Suppliers India Pvt. Ltd. for unpaid chemical supply dues[cite: 33]. The NCLT had held that after adjustments and excluding unauthorized interest, the claim fell below the Rs. 1 Crore threshold under Section 4, and that pre-existing disputes existed[cite: 33]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that unilateral interest cannot be added to inflate operational debt under Section 5(21), and that valid adjustments and pre-existing disputes regarding unlifted material fully justified the dismissal[cite: 33].

case_title: Infrastructure Leasing and Financial Services Ltd. & Anr. vs. Sadbhav Engineering Limited & Anr.
appeal_number: Interlocutory Application Nos. 1288, 2006 and 3262 of 2024 in Company Appeal (AT) No. 346 of 2018
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Applicants are Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services Ltd. (IL&FS) and Jharkhand Road Projects Implementation Company Ltd. (JRPICL). Respondents / Award Holders are Sadbhav Engineering Ltd. & GKC Projects Ltd. Intervenor is Edelweiss Alternative Asset Advisors Limited[cite: 35]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Arbitration proceedings between JRPICL (IL&FS group company) and Sadbhav Engineering resulting in arbitral awards dated 06.08.2020 and 28.03.2023[cite: 35]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: NCLAT interim order dated 15.10.2018 stayed institution/continuation of suits or recovery actions against IL&FS and its 348 group companies[cite: 35]. Order dated 11.01.2019 permitted arbitrations to continue but directed awards to be kept in sealed covers[cite: 35]. Order dated 26.05.2022 directed opening of sealed covers[cite: 35]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Interim stay on 15.10.2018; Resolution framework approved on 12.03.2020; Award opened in 2022; Sadbhav filed execution petition (Execution Case No. 12 & 13 of 2023) at Ranchi Civil Court[cite: 35]. IA 1288/2024 filed by IL&FS; NCLAT passed order on 28.08.2024[cite: 35]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Arbitral awards dated 06.08.2020 and 28.03.2023; NCLAT orders dated 15.10.2018, 11.01.2019, 12.03.2020, and 26.05.2022; Section 34 petition before Delhi HC; and Ranchi execution petitions[cite: 35]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: IL&FS and JRPICL filed IA No. 1288 of 2024 seeking clarification of the 26.05.2022 order and permanent restraint against Sadbhav and GKC Projects from executing arbitral awards[cite: 35]. Sadbhav filed IA No. 3262 of 2024 opposing the restraint[cite: 35]. NCLAT heard applications and delivered judgment on 28.08.2024[cite: 35].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the order dated 26.05.2022 permitting the opening of arbitral awards from sealed covers automatically lifted the general interim stay/moratorium granted on 15.10.2018 against execution and recovery actions against IL&FS group entities[cite: 35]; (ii) Whether the interim stay operating since 2018 should be allowed to continue indefinitely or whether a show-cause notice should be issued for its prospective vacation[cite: 35].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An order directing the opening of an arbitral award from a sealed cover (such as the order dated 26.05.2022) does not implicitly modify, lift, or vacate a general interim stay/injunction protecting a corporate group (IL&FS) from execution and recovery proceedings; however, such comprehensive interim protections cannot be permitted to operate indefinitely without a time limit, and the tribunal may issue notice to show cause why the interim stay should not cease after a reasonable date[cite: 35]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Inherent powers under NCLAT proceedings to regulate debt resolution frameworks and corporate rehabilitation[cite: 35]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Tribunal reviewed the exact wording of the 26.05.2022 order, confirming it only modified paragraph 2 of the 11.01.2019 order (regarding sealed covers) without touching the broad 15.10.2018 stay, but noted that over five years had elapsed since the stay was instituted[cite: 35]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Clarified that the 26.05.2022 order did not permit award enforcement, but directed IL&FS to show cause why the 15.10.2018 interim protection should not expire as of 15.10.2024[cite: 35].
operative_order: IA No. 1288 of 2024 is allowed in part, clarifying that the order dated 26.05.2022 did not permit award enforcement; IL&FS and group entities are directed to show cause by 14.10.2024 why the interim order dated 15.10.2018 should not cease to operate with effect from 15.10.2024[cite: 35].
summary: IL&FS and JRPICL filed interlocutory applications seeking clarification of the NCLAT's 26.05.2022 order and an order restraining Sadbhav Engineering and GKC Projects from executing arbitral awards[cite: 35]. The NCLAT Principal Bench clarified that the 2022 order merely allowed opening arbitral awards from sealed covers and did not lift the general interim stay granted on 15.10.2018 against execution actions[cite: 35]. However, noting that over five years had passed, the Tribunal directed IL&FS to show cause why the interim protection should not expire on 15.10.2024[cite: 35].

case_title: Lords Social Welfare Association (Home Buyers Association) vs. New Okhla Industrial Development Authority & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 506 of 2024 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 554 of 2024
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan, Technical Members Barun Mitra and Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 506 of 2024 is Lords Social Welfare Association (Home Buyers Association / Successful Resolution Applicant), and in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 554 of 2024 is the Committee of Creditors of Kindle Developers Private Limited[cite: 1]. Respondent No. 1 is New Okhla Industrial Development Authority (NOIDA)[cite: 1]. Respondent No. 2 is Mr. Kashi Viswanathan Sivaraman (Resolution Professional of Kindle Developers Pvt. Ltd.)[cite: 1]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: NOIDA executed a Lease Deed dated 24.10.2011 (corrected vide Correction Deed dated 19.10.2012) in favor of Kindle Developers Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) allotting commercial/sports city Plot No. SC-01/D1, Sector 79, Noida, admeasuring 40,000 sq. mtr., on a total premium of Rs. 120.75 Crores, payable in installments with 11% interest[cite: 1]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted on installment and lease rent payments; NOIDA issued notice dated 27.01.2015 and subsequently cancelled the lease deed on 13.08.2015 due to non-payment[cite: 1]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Lease cancelled on 13.08.2015[cite: 1]. Corporate Debtor filed a restoration application on 14.06.2016[cite: 1]. CIRP commenced on 09.03.2018[cite: 1]. NOIDA filed IA No. 1592 of 2019 on 02.12.2019 seeking exclusion of the plot[cite: 1]. CoC approved the resolution plan on 04.12.2019[cite: 1]. NCLT rejected restoration on 10.11.2020 and allowed NOIDA's exclusion application via order dated 11.01.2024[cite: 1]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Lease Deed dated 24.10.2011; Correction Deed dated 19.10.2012; Cancellation letter dated 13.08.2015; Corporate Debtor's restoration request dated 14.06.2016; NOIDA's rejection letter dated 10.10.2020; and balance sheets reflecting Rs. 170.21 Crores collected from homebuyers[cite: 1]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai/New Delhi Bench-II allowed IA No. 1592 of 2019 on 11.01.2024, excluding Plot No. SC-01/D1 from the resolution plan[cite: 1]. CoC and Homebuyers Association appealed to NCLAT via Company Appeals Nos. 506 and 554 of 2024[cite: 1].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a lease cancelled prior to the commencement of CIRP can be deemed to subsist under Section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 as a tenancy holding over due to continuous possession or a pending restoration application[cite: 1]; (ii) Whether an industrial development authority's cancellation of a plot lease prior to insolvency strips the corporate debtor of possessory rights, excluding the land from the CIRP asset pool[cite: 1].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a tenancy by holding over requires either the acceptance of post-determination rent by the lessor or an express/implied assent to the lessee's continued possession; mere continued physical possession without rent acceptance or landlord assent reduces the status of the former lessee to that of a tenant at sufferance, which creates no new tenancy[cite: 1]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 of the IBC and moratorium protections do not apply to property that ceased to be an asset of the corporate debtor long before the initiation of CIRP[cite: 1]. A statutory authority's right to resume possession upon breach under Section 14 of the UP Industrial Area Development Act, 1976 operates independently of corporate insolvency[cite: 1]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that NOIDA never accepted lease rent post-13.08.2015, never gave written or implied assent to continuation, and expressly rejected the Corporate Debtor's belated restoration application on 10.11.2020[cite: 1]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The lease stood validly terminated on 13.08.2015, the plot did not form part of the corporate debtor's assets, Section 116 of the TOPA did not apply, and the Adjudicating Authority correctly directed the exclusion of the plot from the resolution plan, warranting liquidation under Section 33(1)[cite: 1].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 506 and 554 of 2024 are dismissed, upholding the order dated 11.01.2024 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench-II in IA No. 1592 of 2019[cite: 1]. I.A. No. 1664 of 2019 for plan approval is rejected as infructuous, and the Corporate Debtor is ordered into liquidation under Section 33(1) of the IBC, with Mr. Vikram Bajaj appointed as Liquidator[cite: 1]. NOIDA is permitted to seek early disposal of Allahabad High Court Writ Petition (C) No. 26400 of 2023 and take possession of the assets in accordance with law[cite: 1].
