legal_issues: (i) Whether a counterparty to a PPA can validly terminate the contract and claim termination compensation during the ongoing CIRP moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC[cite: 18]; (ii) Whether a Resolution Professional is legally obligated to collate and admit claims arising from post-CIRP events of default and contract terminations[cite: 18].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a corporate debtor is admitted into CIRP and moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC is declared, counterparties are barred from terminating essential contracts or permits on grounds of pre-existing operational defaults, and any claims arising from post-CIRP contract terminations cannot be entertained or collated by the Resolution Professional as claims against the corporate debtor[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 13 of the CIRP Regulations restricts the Resolution Professional to verifying claims existing as on the CIRP commencement date; claims arising from post-CIRP breaches or termination actions taken during moratorium are legally impermissible[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that CIRP commenced on 05.12.2018, that GUVNL issued its termination notice on 25.11.2019 (well after moratorium initiation), filed its claim with an 849-day delay on 01.07.2021, and sought compensation arising directly from that post-CIRP termination[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The post-CIRP termination of the PPA during moratorium was legally void under Section 14, the resulting compensation claim did not exist on the CIRP date, and the Adjudicating Authority correctly upheld the RP's rejection[cite: 18].
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 1183 of 2024 along with interlocutory applications is dismissed with no order as to costs, upholding the order dated 25.04.2024 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, New Delhi, Court III) in IA-1241/2023[cite: 18].
summary: Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Limited (GUVNL) appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order dismissing its application (IA-1241/2023) which sought to admit a claim of Rs. 3.36 Crores towards termination compensation under a Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) with Adel Landmarks Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 18]. GUVNL argued that the corporate debtor defaulted by failing to supply power since March 2015 and that it validly terminated the PPA on 25.11.2019[cite: 18]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that GUVNL's termination notice was issued on 25.11.2019, which was during the ongoing CIRP moratorium (commenced 05.12.2018), in direct violation of Section 14 of the IBC[cite: 18]. The Tribunal affirmed that the Resolution Professional is statutorily mandated under Regulation 13 to verify claims existing as on the CIRP date, and cannot entertain claims arising from post-CIRP contract terminations[cite: 18]. The appeal was dismissed[cite: 18].

case_title: Mr. Manish Jaju (RP of CAN Enterprises Pvt. Ltd.) vs. Malharshanti Enterprises & Ors. (with connected appeals)
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 545 of 2023 with Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 598 of 2023 & Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 600 of 2023
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain, Technical Members Naresh Salecha and Indevar Pandey)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant in Appeal No. 545 of 2023 is Mr. Manish Jaju (Resolution Professional of CAN Enterprises Pvt. Ltd.). Appellant in Appeal No. 598 of 2023 is Paton Constructions Pvt. Ltd. (Unsecured Financial Creditor). Appellants in Appeal No. 600 of 2023 are Naresh Sevantilal Shah and Charu Naresh Shah (Suspended Directors of Corporate Debtor). Respondent No. 1 in all appeals is Malharshanti Enterprises (Operational Creditor)[cite: 19]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Construction and development work carried out by Malharshanti Enterprises for CAN Enterprises Pvt. Ltd., culminating in unpaid operational debt default[cite: 19]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational creditor's claim originally admitted at Rs. 1,95,01,079/- by erstwhile IRP. Paton Constructions claimed Rs. 1,05,877/- based on an unsecured loan of Rs. 1 Lakh advanced on 06.09.2019 (the day after oral arguments concluded in Section 9 proceedings). Suspended director Naresh Shah claimed Rs. 1,77,24,370/-[cite: 19]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 9 application admitted on 27.01.2020. NCLAT upheld admission on 19.01.2021 in Appeal No. 415 of 2020. Supreme Court dismissed suspended director's SLP as withdrawn on 10.03.2021. RP Manish Jaju rejected operational creditor's claim on 02.12.2020. NCLT Mumbai allowed operational creditor's IA No. 47 of 2021 on 16.02.2023[cite: 19]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Section 8 demand notice dated 02.12.2017; arbitration notice dated 10.04.2018; loan agreement dated 20.08.2019 with Paton Constructions for Rs. 50 Lakhs (only Rs. 1 Lakh disbursed); forensic audit report by Mr. Amarjit Chopra; and CoC minutes replacing IRP and moving Section 12A withdrawal[cite: 19]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-III allowed operational creditor's IA No. 47 of 2021 on 16.02.2023, setting aside the RP's rejection of claims, castigating the RP's conduct, and directing claim admission[cite: 19]. RP, financial creditor, and suspended directors filed three separate appeals[cite: 19].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a Resolution Professional is legally empowered to reject in toto an operational creditor's claim that was judicially adjudicated and admitted upon the initiation of CIRP, and subsequently confirmed by appellate tribunals; (ii) Whether a miniscule loan advanced immediately after the conclusion of arguments in a Section 9 petition can be used to engineer a sole-member CoC to derail CIRP via Section 12A withdrawal; (iii) Whether a Resolution Professional has the locus standi to file an appeal in a personal capacity challenging an NCLT order setting aside claim rejections[cite: 19].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Resolution Professional has no adjudicatory power to reject claims that have been formally examined and admitted upon the judicial admission of a winding-up or insolvency petition, nor does an RP possess personal locus standi to challenge NCLT claim-admission orders on merits; an RP must maintain strict neutrality, and collusive attempts by promoters and newly inducted micro-creditors to create a single-member CoC to execute a back-door Section 12A exit are illegal and constitute gross misconduct[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 admission orders carry finality regarding debt and default, and subsequent claim verification by an RP cannot overturn concurrent judicial findings upheld up to the Supreme Court[cite: 19]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the chronology, noting that Paton Constructions advanced a mere Rs. 1 Lakh on 06.09.2019 (immediately after Section 9 arguments concluded) to become the sole CoC member, promptly replaced the IRP, and moved to close CIRP while rejecting the Rs. 1.95 Crore admitted operational claim[cite: 19]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The RP exceeded his statutory authority in collusion with the suspended directors and financial creditor to manipulate CoC constitution, the Adjudicating Authority correctly set aside the claim rejections, and all three appeals are frivolous and devoid of merit[cite: 19].
operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 545, 598, and 600 of 2023 are dismissed[cite: 19]. In Appeal No. 545 of 2023, the appellant RP is saddled with a cost of Rs. 10 Lakhs to be paid to the Prime Minister's National Relief Fund within four weeks, and the Chairman of IBBI is directed to investigate the conduct and professional misconduct of the RP[cite: 19].
surge_summary: Three connected appeals were filed by the Resolution Professional (Manish Jaju), a micro-financial creditor (Paton Constructions), and the suspended directors (Naresh Shah & Charu Shah) against an NCLT Mumbai order dated 16.02.2023 which set aside the RP's rejection of Malharshanti Enterprises' operational claim[cite: 19]. The appellants argued that pre-existing disputes and lack of documentation justified rejecting the claim and upholding a Section 12A withdrawal application moved by Paton Constructions as the sole CoC member[cite: 19]. Dismissing all three appeals, the NCLAT bench strongly denounced the collusive actions of the RP, suspended directors, and Paton Constructions (which advanced a mere Rs. 1 Lakh immediately after Section 9 arguments concluded solely to engineer a sole-member CoC)[cite: 19]. The Tribunal held that an RP has no power to overturn claims admitted upon judicial insolvency admission, lacks personal locus to appeal claim-admission orders on merits, and must maintain neutrality[cite: 19]. The Tribunal upheld the NCLT order, imposed a Rs. 10 Lakh personal cost on the RP, and directed the IBBI to investigate his professional misconduct[cite: 19].

case_title: Commercial Tax Department, Government of Madhya Pradesh vs. Mrs. Teena Saraswat Pandey & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain, Technical Members Naresh Salecha and Indevar Pandey)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is the Commercial Tax Department, Government of Madhya Pradesh. Respondent No. 1 is Mrs. Teena Saraswat Pandey (Resolution Professional / Liquidator). Respondent No. 2 is Agarwal Real City Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant / SRA)[cite: 21]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Chandraudai Automobiles Pvt. Ltd. initiated Section 9 CIRP against Rajpal Abhikaran Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). SRA submitted a resolution plan offering Rs. 22.61 Crores against total admitted claims of Rs. 113.94 Crores[cite: 21]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Secured financial creditors admitted at Rs. 23.02 Crores (proposed Rs. 19.11 Crores); unsecured financial creditors at Rs. 76.01 Crores (proposed Rs. 3.20 Crores); operational creditors at Rs. 14.91 Crores (proposed NIL)[cite: 21]. Appellant's statutory tax claim amounted to Rs. 12,61,57,345/-, submitted on Form B as an unsecured operational creditor[cite: 21]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 9 petition admitted on 26.03.2021[cite: 21]. CoC approved resolution plan with 90.41% votes on 17.12.2021[cite: 21]. Adjudicating Authority approved the resolution plan via order dated 25.08.2022[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form B tax claim dated 29.07.2021 (with 'NA' against retention of title); CoC voting records (90.41% approval); liquidation valuation report of Rs. 18.39 Crores; and resolution plan allocation tables[cite: 21]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Indore Bench approved the resolution plan on 25.08.2022. Commercial Tax Department appealed to NCLAT via Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1265 of 2022[cite: 21].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a statutory tax department claiming a first charge under Section 33 of the Madhya Pradesh Value Added Tax Act, 2002 (MPVAT Act) is entitled to be treated as a 'secured creditor' with priority over secured financial creditors in a resolution plan, akin to the ruling in Rainbow Papers[cite: 21]; (ii) Whether Section 33 of the MPVAT Act, being expressly subject to Section 530 of the Companies Act, 1956 (subordinate to Section 529A worker and secured creditor dues), is pari materia with Section 48 of the Gujarat Value Added Tax Act, 2003[cite: 21].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A statutory first charge created under state tax enactments does not automatically elevate a tax department to a secured financial creditor under the IBC if the governing state statute is expressly made subject to company liquidation priority provisions (such as Section 530 and Section 529A of the Companies Act), and if the department submitted its claim as an unsecured operational creditor on Form B[cite: 21]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 33 of the MPVAT Act differs fundamentally from Section 48 of the GVAT Act (which was interpreted in Rainbow Papers) because Section 33 explicitly incorporates the proviso 'subject to the provisions of Section 530 of the Companies Act, 1956', which in turn subordinates tax revenues to workmen's dues and secured creditors under Section 529A[cite: 21]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized Form B filed by the appellant, noting that it submitted its claim as an unsecured operational creditor without claiming security interest, and verified that Section 33 of the MPVAT Act is pari materia with Section 37 of the MVAT Act (previously distinguished in Zicom Saas) rather than Section 48 of the GVAT Act[cite: 21]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellant's tax dues do not enjoy secured status under the MPVAT Act due to statutory subordination to secured creditors and workmen under Section 529A, and the resolution plan validly allocated NIL to operational creditors based on liquidation value[cite: 21].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1265 of 2022 along with interlocutory applications is dismissed with no order as to costs, upholding the order dated 25.08.2022 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, Indore Bench) approving the resolution plan[cite: 21].
summary: The Commercial Tax Department of Madhya Pradesh appealed against an NCLT Indore order approving the resolution plan of Rajpal Abhikaran Pvt. Ltd., contending that its statutory tax claim of Rs. 12.61 Crores should be treated as a secured debt with first charge priority under Section 33 of the MPVAT Act, relying on the Supreme Court's ruling in Rainbow Papers[cite: 21]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that Rainbow Papers is distinguishable because Section 33 of the MPVAT Act is expressly made subject to Section 530 of the Companies Act (subordinate to Section 529A secured creditors and workmen), whereas Section 48 of the GVAT Act lacked such a subordination proviso[cite: 21]. The Tribunal affirmed that the appellant submitted its claim as an unsecured operational creditor on Form B, that the MPVAT provision is pari materia with the MVAT Act considered in Zicom Saas, and that the resolution plan's NIL allocation to operational creditors in liquidation waterfall is legally sound[cite: 21].

case_title: Kisanrao Kashiprasad Borele vs. Ajay Gupta, Erstwhile Resolution Professional & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Yogesh Khanna and Technical Member Ajai Das Mehrotra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Kisanrao Kashiprasad Borele (Sole member of CoC / Financial Creditor). Respondent No. 1 is Ajay Gupta (Erstwhile Resolution Professional). Respondent No. 2 is the Liquidator[cite: 22]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 22]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: 330-day outer CIRP period expired on 06.06.2024 without a fully approved resolution plan[cite: 22]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: 330 days expired on 06.06.2024[cite: 22]. Resolution professional filed an application under Section 60(5) for a 90-day CIRP extension[cite: 22]. NCLT dismissed the extension application and ordered liquidation under Section 33(1)(a) on 14.08.2024[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: EOI submitted by the sole CoC member pending consideration with the resolution professional; and statements from both the resolution professional and liquidator consenting to the extension[cite: 22]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT dismissed the CIRP extension application and ordered liquidation on 14.08.2024. The sole CoC member appealed to NCLAT via Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1732 of 2024[cite: 22].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the outer time limit of 330 days for completion of CIRP is strictly mandatory or can be extended in exceptional cases where delays are attributable to judicial processes and a resolution applicant's EOI is actively pending consideration[cite: 22]; (ii) Whether liquidation should be ordered when a sole financial creditor/CoC member seeks an extension to evaluate a pending resolution plan[cite: 22].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In terms of the Supreme Court's ruling in Essar Steel, the word 'mandatorily' in the second proviso to Section 12(3) of the IBC is struck down as manifestly arbitrary, meaning that 330 days is ordinarily the outer limit, but in exceptional cases where only a short period is left, fault cannot be ascribed to the litigant, and revival is in the interest of stakeholders, the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal may extend time beyond 330 days[cite: 22]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12(3) timelines must be balanced with the primary objective of the IBC, which is the resolution and revival of the corporate debtor rather than automatic driving into liquidation[cite: 22]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the sole CoC member submitted an EOI that was actively pending consideration with the resolution professional, and that both the liquidator and resolution professional consented to the extension subject to cost and fee adjustments[cite: 22]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the sole financial creditor supported revival and an EOI was pending, it is an exceptional case warranting a 60-day extension of the CIRP, setting aside the liquidation order[cite: 22].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1732 of 2024 is allowed, setting aside the impugned order dated 14.08.2024, and extending the time for completion of the CIRP process by 60 days from the date of the order[cite: 22]. Pending applications are closed[cite: 22].
summary: Kisanrao Kashiprasad Borele, sole member of the CoC, appealed against an NCLT order dated 14.08.2024 which dismissed an application for a 90-day CIRP extension and directed the liquidation of the corporate debtor because the 330-day period expired on 06.06.2024[cite: 22]. Allowing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench noted that the appellant's EOI was pending consideration and that both the resolution professional and liquidator consented to the extension[cite: 22]. Relying on the Supreme Court's judgment in Essar Steel (which struck down the word 'mandatorily' in Section 12(3)), the Tribunal held that in exceptional cases where revival serves stakeholders best, time can be extended beyond 330 days[cite: 22]. The Tribunal set aside the liquidation order and granted a 60-day extension to complete the CIRP[cite: 22].

case_title: Debabrata Das vs. State Bank of India & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain and Technical Member Ajai Das Mehrotra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Debabrata Das (Suspended Director of Dynametic Overseas Pvt. Ltd., Corporate Debtor). Respondent No. 1 is State Bank of India (Financial Creditor). Respondent No. 2 is the IRP[cite: 23]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: State Bank of India advanced credit facilities to Dynametic Overseas Pvt. Ltd., which subsequently defaulted[cite: 23]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Loan account classified as NPA on 05.08.2013[cite: 23]. Total debt claimed and admitted was Rs. 1,48,36,62,808.65[cite: 23]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 05.08.2013[cite: 23]. Section 7 application filed on 24.03.2021 (or 04.03.2021)[cite: 23]. NCLT admitted Section 7 on 12.09.2022[cite: 23]. Financial creditor filed IA No. 455 of 2023 on 11.01.2023 to bring on record balance sheets for FY 2014-2015, 2015-2016, and 2017-2018[cite: 23]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreements; NPA declaration dated 05.08.2013; disputed NEFT entry dated 06.06.2016; and statutory balance sheets of the corporate debtor for FY 2014-2015, 2015-2016, 2017-2018, and 2018-2019 acknowledging debt[cite: 23]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT admitted SBI's Section 7 petition on 12.09.2022. Suspended director appealed to NCLAT via Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1349 of 2022[cite: 23]. During appeal, SBI filed IA No. 455 of 2023 to produce balance sheets establishing written acknowledgement under Section 18 of the Limitation Act[cite: 23].
legal_issues: (i) Whether balance sheets acknowledging debt can be introduced and taken on record for the first time at the appellate stage to extend limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act[cite: 23]; (ii) Whether an application under Section 7 filed on 24.03.2021 is barred by limitation when the NPA date was 05.08.2013[cite: 23].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, a fresh period of limitation is computed from the date when an acknowledgement of liability in writing is signed by the corporate debtor; as settled by the Supreme Court in Dena Bank and Axis Bank v. Naren Sheth, statutory balance sheets acknowledging debt can be introduced and accepted as additional documents even at the appellate stage to save a petition from being time-barred[cite: 23]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 applications are governed by Article 137 of the Limitation Act (three years from right to sue), which is extendable under Sections 18 and 19 through written acknowledgements or part payments[cite: 23]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed IA No. 455 of 2023, noting that the corporate debtor's signed balance sheets for FY 2014-2015, 2015-2016, 2017-2018, and 2018-2019 unequivocally acknowledged the financial debt, thereby continuously extending the limitation period prior to the March 2021 filing date[cite: 23]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The additional balance sheets establish continuous written acknowledgement under Section 18, rendering the Section 7 petition well within limitation[cite: 23].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1349 of 2022 is dismissed, and IA No. 455 of 2023 is allowed, taking the corporate debtor's statutory balance sheets on record[cite: 23]. The order dated 12.09.2022 admitting Section 7 is upheld[cite: 23].
summary: Debabrata Das, suspended director of Dynametic Overseas Pvt. Ltd., appealed against an NCLT order dated 12.09.2022 admitting a Section 7 CIRP petition filed by State Bank of India for a default of Rs. 148.36 Crores (NPA date: 05.08.2013)[cite: 23]. The appellant argued that the petition filed on 24.03.2021 was time-barred and disputed a 2016 NEFT entry relied upon by the NCLT[cite: 23]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench allowed SBI's interlocutory application (IA No. 455 of 2023) to bring on record the corporate debtor's statutory balance sheets for FY 2014-2015, 2015-2016, 2017-2018, and 2018-2019[cite: 23]. Relying on the Supreme Court's rulings in Dena Bank and Axis Bank v. Naren Sheth, the Tribunal held that balance sheets acknowledging debt can be accepted at the appellate stage under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, successfully extending limitation and rendering the Section 7 petition fully maintainable[cite: 23].

case_title: Atlantic Spinning And Weaving Mills Limited vs. The Special Land Acquisition Officer & Ors.
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Member Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma and Technical Member Jatindranath Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Atlantic Spinning and Weaving Mills Limited, represented by its Liquidator, Ms. Sujata Chattopadhyay. Respondents Nos. 1 to 6 are private contesting entities/individuals. Respondent No. 7 is the Special Land Acquisition Officer and Competent Authority, NHAI, Bengaluru[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Liquidation proceedings of Atlantic Spinning and Weaving Mills Limited[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (Interlocutory appeal arising from an NCLT order disposing of a miscellaneous liquidation application)[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Hyderabad Bench rendered the impugned order on 21.03.2024 in IA (IBC) No. 512 of 2021[cite: 24]. Company appeal filed before NCLAT Chennai Bench[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLT order dated 21.03.2024 disposing of IA (IBC) No. 512 of 2021 by noting that certain reliefs sought were already adjudicated in a prior disposed-of application (IA No. 452/2022) and granting liberty to file a fresh application for remaining reliefs[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad Bench disposed of IA (IBC) No. 512 of 2021 on 21.03.2024. The liquidator appealed to NCLAT Chennai Bench via Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 293 of 2024[cite: 24].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an order disposing of an interlocutory application by noting that certain reliefs were already granted in a prior proceeding and granting liberty to file a fresh application for remaining unaddressed reliefs constitutes an appealable 'decision' or 'order' on merits under Section 61 of the IBC[cite: 24].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An interlocutory order or procedural ruling that does not express a definite judicial opinion or adjudicate competing rights on merits, but merely disposes of an application because the issues overlap with prior proceedings while granting liberty to file a fresh application for remaining reliefs, does not constitute an appealable 'decision' or 'order' under Section 61 of the IBC[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The term 'order' under Section 61 of the IBC must be construed in the context of an adjudication that attaches finality to a lis or affects substantive rights on merits, rather than procedural dispositions[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed the impugned order, confirming that the NCLT merely observed that some reliefs sought in IA 512/2021 were already adjudicated in IA 452/2022 and left it open for the liquidator to seek remaining reliefs afresh[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellant's rights were not prejudiced and no final adjudication on merits was rendered, making the appeal under Section 61 legally not maintainable[cite: 24].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 293 of 2024 is dismissed as not maintainable, with a clarification that if the appellant files an appropriate application within two weeks in compliance with the impugned order, the NCLT is requested to decide it within one month[cite: 24]. Interlocutory applications IA Nos. 769 and 770 of 2024 are disposed of/closed[cite: 24].
summary: Atlantic Spinning and Weaving Mills Ltd., through its liquidator, appealed against an NCLT Hyderabad Bench order dated 21.03.2024 passed in IA (IBC) No. 512 of 2021[cite: 24]. The NCLT had disposed of the application by noting that several reliefs sought were identical to those already adjudicated in a prior application (IA No. 452/2022), while granting liberty to file a fresh application for any remaining unaddressed reliefs[cite: 24]. Dismissing the appeal as not maintainable, the NCLAT Chennai Bench held, citing Supreme Court precedents on the definition of 'decision' and 'order', that an administrative or procedural disposal which does not adjudicate rights on merits or affect substantive claims, but grants liberty to re-file for remaining reliefs, is not appealable under Section 61 of the IBC[cite: 24]. The Tribunal granted a expedited timeline for filing a fresh application before the NCLT[cite: 24].

case_title: Preet Mohinder Kohli vs. Harbir Automobile Private Limited
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Sh. Preet Mohinder Kohli (Operational Creditor / Lessor and assignee of co-owners Surinder Kohli and Neeru Kohli). The Respondent is Harbir Automobile Private Limited (Corporate Debtor / Lessee)[cite: 25]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Leased commercial premises situated at Industrial Shed No. 41, Industrial Area, Phase-II, Chandigarh, to the corporate debtor vide lease agreements dated 20.01.2016 and 11.09.2016 at a monthly rent of Rs. 8,00,000/-[cite: 25]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational creditor claimed a total default of Rs. 1,45,77,438/- plus 24% p.a. interest up to June 2021, combining personal dues and assigned debts from brother and wife[cite: 25]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8 issued on 10.06.2021; replied to on 22.06.2021[cite: 25]. Corporate debtor offered vacation of premises on 10.10.2020. Police complaints filed in Dec 2020 and Jan 2021. Physical possession handed over before police authorities on 24.08.2021[cite: 25]. NCLT Chandigarh dismissed Section 9 petition on 01.03.2024[cite: 25]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Lease agreements; Section 8 demand notice and reply; police complaints dated 04.12.2020 and 21.01.2021; compromise/possession handover letter dated 24.08.2021; GST authorities' letter dated 26.06.2023 confirming cancellation and forged invoices; and ledger statements reflecting advance rent, security deposits, and TDS deductions[cite: 25]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Chandigarh Bench) dismissed CP(IB) No. 203/CHD/CHD/2021 under Section 9 on 01.03.2024, holding that there existed a bona fide pre-existing dispute between the parties[cite: 25]. Operational Creditor appealed to NCLAT[cite: 25].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a Section 9 application filed by an operational creditor is barred by the existence of a bona fide pre-existing dispute regarding rent liability, GST compliance, and lease termination/possession handover[cite: 25]; (ii) Whether multiple assigned operational debts can be clubbed together to meet the Rs. 1 Crore threshold under Section 4 of the IBC[cite: 25].

case_title: Mr. Jagdishchandra Mansukhani vs. STCI Finance Limited
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan, Technical Members Barun Mitra and Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Mr. Jagdishchandra Mansukhani (Personal Guarantor). Respondent No. 1 is STCI Finance Limited (Financial Creditor). Respondent No. 2 is Mr. Rajendra R. Agrawal (Resolution Professional)[cite: 26]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: STCI Finance sanctioned a corporate short-term loan of Rs. 10 Crores to Man Tubinox Ltd. (Borrower No. 1) and Man Infraprojects Ltd. (Borrower No. 2) under a Loan Agreement dated 01.12.2015. The appellant executed a Deed of Guarantee on 01.12.2015[cite: 26]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Borrowers committed default; financial creditor issued a recall notice on 17.01.2017 for Rs. 8,52,72,832/- and a SARFAESI Section 13(2) notice on 01.06.2017 demanding Rs. 7,38,80,553/-[cite: 26]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Guarantee invoked via SARFAESI notice on 01.06.2017. Appellant wrote acknowledgement letter seeking time on 12.06.2017. Section 95 application filed by STCI Finance on 30.09.2021. Adjudicating Authority appointed RP on 19.04.2022 and admitted Section 95 application under Section 100 on 07.06.2024[cite: 26]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreement dated 01.12.2015; Deed of Guarantee dated 01.12.2015; SARFAESI notice dated 01.06.2017; Appellant's written reply letter dated 12.06.2017 requesting time till 31.07.2017; and Supreme Court Suo Motu limitation extension orders[cite: 26]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench IV admitted STCI Finance's Section 95 application against the personal guarantor under Section 100 of the IBC on 07.06.2024. legal_issues: (i) Whether a letter written by a personal guarantor in response to a SARFAESI notice requesting time to settle constitutes a valid acknowledgement of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act to extend the limitation period[cite: 26]; (ii) Whether a Section 95 application filed on 30.09.2021 against a personal guarantor is barred by limitation when the guarantee was invoked on 01.06.2017[cite: 26].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, an acknowledgement of liability in writing signed by the party against whom a right is claimed before the expiration of the prescribed period starts a fresh period of limitation; as established by the Supreme Court in Laxmi Pat Surana and Laxmiratan Cotton Mills, acknowledgement of debt by a guarantor or borrower extends limitation, and such correspondence must be construed liberally to ascertain the existence of a subsisting jural relationship[cite: 26]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 95 applications against personal guarantors are governed by Article 137 of the Limitation Act, subject to extension under Section 18 and Supreme Court Suo Motu COVID-19 limitation exclusions[cite: 26]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the appellant's letter dated 12.06.2017 written in response to the 01.06.2017 SARFAESI notice, wherein he acknowledged the debt, stated that borrowers were in advanced lender discussions, and requested an extension till 31.07.2017[cite: 26]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The letter dated 12.06.2017 constituted a valid written acknowledgement under Section 18, extending the limitation period to 11.06.2020, which, when combined with the Supreme Court's COVID-19 Suo Motu limitation exclusions, rendered the September 2021 filing fully within time[cite: 26].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1439 of 2024 is dismissed with no order as to costs, upholding the order dated 07.06.2024 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai Bench IV) in I.A. No. 969/2023 in C.P. (IB) No. 1264/MB/2021[cite: 26].
summary: Mr. Jagdishchandra Mansukhani (Personal Guarantor) appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order dated 07.06.2024 admitting a Section 95 insolvency application filed by STCI Finance Limited[cite: 26]. case_title: Kisanrao Kashiprasad Borele vs. Ajay Gupta, Erstwhile Resolution Professional & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Yogesh Khanna and Technical Member Ajai Das Mehrotra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Kisanrao Kashiprasad Borele (Sole member of CoC / Financial Creditor). Respondent No. 1 is Ajay Gupta (Erstwhile Resolution Professional). Respondent No. 2 is the Liquidator[cite: 22]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 22]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: 330-day outer CIRP period expired on 06.06.2024 without a fully approved resolution plan[cite: 22]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: 330 days expired on 06.06.2024[cite: 22]. Resolution professional filed an application under Section 60(5) for a 90-day CIRP extension[cite: 22]. NCLT dismissed the extension application and ordered liquidation under Section 33(1)(a) on 14.08.2024[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: EOI submitted by the sole CoC member pending consideration with the resolution professional; and statements from both the resolution professional and liquidator consenting to the extension[cite: 22]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT dismissed the CIRP extension application and ordered liquidation on 14.08.2024. The sole CoC member appealed to NCLAT via Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1732 of 2024[cite: 22].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the outer time limit of 330 days for completion of CIRP is strictly mandatory or can be extended in exceptional cases where delays are attributable to judicial processes and a resolution applicant's EOI is actively pending consideration[cite: 22]; (ii) Whether liquidation should be ordered when a sole financial creditor/CoC member seeks an extension to evaluate a pending resolution plan[cite: 22].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In terms of the Supreme Court's ruling in Essar Steel, the word 'mandatorily' in the second proviso to Section 12(3) of the IBC is struck down as manifestly arbitrary, meaning that 330 days is ordinarily the outer limit, but in exceptional cases where only a short period is left, fault cannot be ascribed to the litigant, and revival is in the interest of stakeholders, the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal may extend time beyond 330 days[cite: 22]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12(3) timelines must be balanced with the primary objective of the IBC, which is the resolution and revival of the corporate debtor rather than automatic driving into liquidation[cite: 22]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the sole CoC member submitted an EOI that was actively pending consideration with the resolution professional, and that both the liquidator and resolution professional consented to the extension subject to cost and fee adjustments[cite: 22]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the sole financial creditor supported revival and an EOI was pending, it is an exceptional case warranting a 60-day extension of the CIRP, setting aside the liquidation order[cite: 22].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1732 of 2024 is allowed, setting aside the impugned order dated 14.08.2024, and extending the time for completion of the CIRP process by 60 days from the date of the order[cite: 22]. Pending applications are closed[cite: 22].
summary: Kisanrao Kashiprasad Borele, sole member of the CoC, appealed against an NCLT order dated 14.08.2024 which dismissed an application for a 90-day CIRP extension and directed the liquidation of the corporate debtor because the 330-day period expired on 06.06.2024[cite: 22]. Relying on the Supreme Court's judgment in Essar Steel (which struck down the word 'mandatorily' in Section 12(3)), the Tribunal held that in exceptional cases where revival serves stakeholders best, time can be extended beyond 330 days[cite: 22]. The Tribunal set aside the liquidation order and granted a 60-day extension to complete the CIRP[cite: 22].

case_title: Debabrata Das vs. State Bank of India & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain and Technical Member Ajai Das Mehrotra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Debabrata Das (Suspended Director of Dynametic Overseas Pvt. Ltd., Corporate Debtor). Respondent No. 1 is State Bank of India (Financial Creditor). Respondent No. 2 is the IRP[cite: 23]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: State Bank of India advanced credit facilities to Dynametic Overseas Pvt. Ltd., which subsequently defaulted[cite: 23]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Loan account classified as NPA on 05.08.2013[cite: 23]. Total debt claimed and admitted was Rs. 1,48,36,62,808.65[cite: 23]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 05.08.2013[cite: 23]. Section 7 application filed on 24.03.2021 (or 04.03.2021)[cite: 23]. NCLT admitted Section 7 on 12.09.2022[cite: 23]. Financial creditor filed IA No. 455 of 2023 on 11.01.2023 to bring on record balance sheets for FY 2014-2015, 2015-2016, and 2017-2018[cite: 23]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreements; NPA declaration dated 05.08.2013; disputed NEFT entry dated 06.06.2016; and statutory balance sheets of the corporate debtor for FY 2014-2015, 2015-2016, 2017-2018, and 2018-2019 acknowledging debt[cite: 23]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT admitted SBI's Section 7 petition on 12.09.2022. Suspended director appealed to NCLAT via Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1349 of 2022[cite: 23]. During appeal, SBI filed IA No. 455 of 2023 to produce balance sheets establishing written acknowledgement under Section 18 of the Limitation Act[cite: 23].
legal_issues: (i) Whether balance sheets acknowledging debt can be introduced and taken on record for the first time at the appellate stage to extend limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act[cite: 23]; (ii) Whether an application under Section 7 filed on 24.03.2021 is barred by limitation when the NPA date was 05.08.2013[cite: 23].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, a fresh period of limitation is computed from the date when an acknowledgement of liability in writing is signed by the corporate debtor; as settled by the Supreme Court in Dena Bank and Axis Bank v. Naren Sheth, statutory balance sheets acknowledging debt can be introduced and accepted as additional documents even at the appellate stage to save a petition from being time-barred[cite: 23]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 applications are governed by Article 137 of the Limitation Act (three years from right to sue), which is extendable under Sections 18 and 19 through written acknowledgements or part payments[cite: 23]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed IA No. 455 of 2023, noting that the corporate debtor's signed balance sheets for FY 2014-2015, 2015-2016, 2017-2018, and 2018-2019 unequivocally acknowledged the financial debt, thereby continuously extending the limitation period prior to the March 2021 filing date[cite: 23]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The additional balance sheets establish continuous written acknowledgement under Section 18, rendering the Section 7 petition well within limitation[cite: 23].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1349 of 2022 is dismissed, and IA No. 455 of 2023 is allowed, taking the corporate debtor's statutory balance sheets on record[cite: 23]. The order dated 12.09.2022 admitting Section 7 is upheld[cite: 23].
summary: Debabrata Das, suspended director of Dynametic Overseas Pvt. Ltd., appealed against an NCLT order dated 12.09.2022 admitting a Section 7 CIRP petition filed by State Bank of India for a default of Rs. 148.36 Crores (NPA date: 05.08.2013)[cite: 23]. The appellant argued that the petition filed on 24.03.2021 was time-barred and disputed a 2016 NEFT entry relied upon by the NCLT[cite: 23]. Relying on the Supreme Court's rulings in Dena Bank and Axis Bank v. Naren Sheth, the Tribunal held that balance sheets acknowledging debt can be accepted at the appellate stage under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, successfully extending limitation and rendering the Section 7 petition fully maintainable[cite: 23].

case_title: Atlantic Spinning And Weaving Mills Limited vs. The Special Land Acquisition Officer & Ors.
bench: Chennai Bench (Judicial Member Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma and Technical Member Jatindranath Swain)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Atlantic Spinning and Weaving Mills Limited, represented by its Liquidator, Ms. Sujata Chattopadhyay. Respondents Nos. 1 to 6 are private contesting entities/individuals. Respondent No. 7 is the Special Land Acquisition Officer and Competent Authority, NHAI, Bengaluru[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Liquidation proceedings of Atlantic Spinning and Weaving Mills Limited[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (Interlocutory appeal arising from an NCLT order disposing of a miscellaneous liquidation application)[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Hyderabad Bench rendered the impugned order on 21.03.2024 in IA (IBC) No. 512 of 2021[cite: 24]. Company appeal filed before NCLAT Chennai Bench[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLT order dated 21.03.2024 disposing of IA (IBC) No. 512 of 2021 by noting that certain reliefs sought were already adjudicated in a prior disposed-of application (IA No. 452/2022) and granting liberty to file a fresh application for remaining reliefs[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad Bench disposed of IA (IBC) No. 512 of 2021 on 21.03.2024. The liquidator appealed to NCLAT Chennai Bench via Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 293 of 2024[cite: 24].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an order disposing of an interlocutory application by noting that certain reliefs were already granted in a prior proceeding and granting liberty to file a fresh application for remaining unaddressed reliefs constitutes an appealable 'decision' or 'order' on merits under Section 61 of the IBC[cite: 24].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An interlocutory order or procedural ruling that does not express a definite judicial opinion or adjudicate competing rights on merits, but merely disposes of an application because the issues overlap with prior proceedings while granting liberty to file a fresh application for remaining reliefs, does not constitute an appealable 'decision' or 'order' under Section 61 of the IBC[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The term 'order' under Section 61 of the IBC must be construed in the context of an adjudication that attaches finality to a lis or affects substantive rights on merits, rather than procedural dispositions[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed the impugned order, confirming that the NCLT merely observed that some reliefs sought in IA 512/2021 were already adjudicated in IA 452/2022 and left it open for the liquidator to seek remaining reliefs afresh[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellant's rights were not prejudiced and no final adjudication on merits was rendered, making the appeal under Section 61 legally not maintainable[cite: 24].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 293 of 2024 is dismissed as not maintainable, with a clarification that if the appellant files an appropriate application within two weeks in compliance with the impugned order, the NCLT is requested to decide it within one month[cite: 24]. Interlocutory applications IA Nos. 769 and 770 of 2024 are disposed of/closed[cite: 24].

Dismissing the appeal as not maintainable, the NCLAT Chennai Bench held, citing Supreme Court precedents on the definition of 'decision' and 'order', that an administrative or procedural disposal which does not adjudicate rights on merits or affect substantive claims, but grants liberty to re-file for remaining reliefs, is not appealable under Section 61 of the IBC[cite: 24]. The Tribunal granted a expedited timeline for filing a fresh application before the NCLT[cite: 24].

NCLT Mumbai dismissed Section 9 petition via order dated 22.05.2024[cite: 27]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered L&L Agreement dated 04.05.2017; demand notices dated 16.11.2018 and 06.02.2019; COVID-19 license fee reduction correspondence; undertakings dated 29.08.2021 and 10.03.2023; and email vacation notice dated 27.03.2023[cite: 27]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai Bench) dismissed CP (IB)/483/MB/2023 under Section 9 on 22.05.2024, holding that excluding Section 10A dues, unsupported interest, and unestablished reimbursements brought the claim below the Rs. 1 Crore threshold[cite: 27]. Operational Creditor appealed to NCLAT[cite: 27].
legal_issues: (i) Whether license fee defaults occurring between 25.03.2020 and 25.03.2021 are protected under Section 10A of the IBC and must be excluded from the default computation[cite: 27]; (ii) Whether interest claimed at 18% p.a. without an express contractual interest clause in the leave and license agreement can be included to meet the Rs. 1 Crore statutory threshold under Section 4 of the IBC[cite: 27]; (iii) Whether unsubstantiated expense reimbursements and inflated claims can maintain a Section 9 application[cite: 27].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 10A of the IBC, no application for CIRP can be filed for any default arising during the prohibited COVID-19 relief window, and such protected amounts must be excluded; furthermore, interest cannot be added to a debt to cross the statutory threshold unless an express contractual agreement providing for interest exists between the parties[cite: 27]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 10A protects corporate debtors from insolvency filings for defaults during the pandemic period, and temporary COVID-19 rent modifications do not extinguish this statutory protection; Section 4 mandates a strict Rs. 1 Crore threshold of proved operational debt[cite: 27]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the L&L Agreement, finding no clause for 18% interest (disallowing Rs. 1,66,56,022/-), noted that Rs. 69,30,442/- fell squarely within the Section 10A prohibited period, and verified that unproven debit notes for expense reimbursements (Rs. 47,01,629/-) were unsubstantiated, leaving an actual default of Rs. 35,02,857/-[cite: 27]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The recalculated valid default of Rs. 35,02,857/- fell far below the mandatory Rs. 1 Crore threshold under Section 4 of the IBC, rendering the Section 9 petition not maintainable[cite: 27].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1409 of 2024 along with IA No. 5117 of 2024 is dismissed with no orders as to costs, affirming the order dated May 22, 2024 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, New Mumbai Bench) in CP (IB)/483/MB/2023[cite: 27].
summary: Samrat Restaurant (Operational Creditor) appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order dismissing its Section 9 CIRP application against Brewcrafts Microbrewing Pvt. Ltd. for an alleged default of Rs. 5.22 Crores under a leave and license agreement[cite: 27]. The appellant argued that subsequent settlement letters shifted the default date outside Section 10A and that 18% interest was payable[cite: 27]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that the NCLT correctly excluded license fees falling due during the Section 10A prohibited period (Rs. 69.30 Lakhs), disallowed uncontracted interest (Rs. 1.66 Crores), and rejected unsubstantiated utility reimbursements (Rs. 47.01 Lakhs)[cite: 27]. The Tribunal affirmed that the actual enforceable default was only Rs. 35.02 Lakhs, which is well below the Rs. 1 Crore statutory threshold under Section 4, and upheld the dismissal[cite: 27].

case_title: Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Limited vs. Mr. Udayraj Patwardhan (Resolution Professional of Adel Landmarks Private Limited)
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain, Technical Members Naresh Salecha and Indevar Pandey)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Limited (GUVNL - State Government Undertaking for bulk power purchase)[cite: 28]. The Respondent is Mr. Udayraj Patwardhan (Resolution Professional of Adel Landmarks Private Limited, Corporate Debtor)[cite: 28]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: GUVNL entered into a Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) dated 29.05.2007 (supplemented on 13.01.2014) with the corporate debtor for purchasing wind power from its renewable energy project in Gujarat[cite: 28]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate debtor ceased power supply from March 2015, constituting an O&M default under the PPA. GUVNL issued a default notice on 15.06.2019 and a termination notice on 25.11.2019, claiming termination compensation of Rs. 3,36,09,886/-[cite: 28]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated against corporate debtor on 05.12.2018 with moratorium under Section 14[cite: 28]. PPA termination notice issued on 25.11.2019 (during CIRP)[cite: 28]. GUVNL filed Form B claims on 01.07.2021 (849 days delay)[cite: 28]. CoC approved a resolution plan on 15.09.2022[cite: 28]. NCLT New Delhi dismissed GUVNL's claim application (IA-1241/2023) on 25.04.2024[cite: 28]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: PPA dated 29.05.2007; default notice dated 15.06.2019; termination notice dated 25.11.2019; GUCER petition filed on 04.07.2020 (subsequently withdrawn); Form B claim dated 01.07.2021; and RP's rejection letters dated 13.01.2022 and 26.09.2022[cite: 28]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Court III dismissed GUVNL's IA-1241/2023 on 25.04.2024, holding that claims arising from post-CIRP termination of a PPA during moratorium cannot be verified or admitted by the Resolution Professional[cite: 28]. GUVNL appealed to NCLAT[cite: 28].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a counterparty to a PPA can validly terminate the contract and claim termination compensation during the ongoing CIRP moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC[cite: 28]; (ii) Whether a Resolution Professional is legally obligated to collate and admit claims arising from post-CIRP events of default and contract terminations[cite: 28].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a corporate debtor is admitted into CIRP and moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC is declared, counterparties are barred from terminating essential contracts or permits on grounds of pre-existing operational defaults, and any claims arising from post-CIRP contract terminations cannot be entertained or collated by the Resolution Professional as claims against the corporate debtor[cite: 28]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 13 of the CIRP Regulations restricts the Resolution Professional to verifying claims existing as on the CIRP commencement date; claims arising from post-CIRP breaches or termination actions taken during moratorium are legally impermissible[cite: 28]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that CIRP commenced on 05.12.2018, that GUVNL issued its termination notice on 25.11.2019 (well after moratorium initiation), filed its claim with an 849-day delay on 01.07.2021, and sought compensation arising directly from that post-CIRP termination[cite: 28]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The post-CIRP termination of the PPA during moratorium was legally void under Section 14, the resulting compensation claim did not exist on the CIRP date, and the Adjudicating Authority correctly upheld the RP's rejection[cite: 28].
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 1183 of 2024 along with interlocutory applications is dismissed with no order as to costs, upholding the order dated 25.04.2024 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, New Delhi, Court III) in IA-1241/2023[cite: 28].
summary: Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Limited (GUVNL) appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order dismissing its application (IA-1241/2023) which sought to admit a claim of Rs. 3.36 Crores towards termination compensation under a Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) with Adel Landmarks Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 28]. GUVNL argued that the corporate debtor defaulted by failing to supply power since March 2015 and that it validly terminated the PPA on 25.11.2019[cite: 28]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that GUVNL's termination notice was issued on 25.11.2019, which was during the ongoing CIRP moratorium (commenced 05.12.2018), in direct violation of Section 14 of the IBC[cite: 28]. The Tribunal affirmed that the Resolution Professional is statutorily mandated under Regulation 13 to verify claims existing as on the CIRP date, and cannot entertain claims arising from post-CIRP contract terminations[cite: 28]. The appeal was dismissed[cite: 28].

case_title: Mr. Manish Jaju (RP of CAN Enterprises Pvt. Ltd.) vs. Malharshanti Enterprises & Ors. (with connected appeals)
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 545 of 2023 with Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 598 of 2023 & Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 600 of 2023
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain, Technical Members Naresh Salecha and Indevar Pandey)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant in Appeal No. 545 of 2023 is Mr. Manish Jaju (Resolution Professional of CAN Enterprises Pvt. Ltd.). Appellant in Appeal No. 598 of 2023 is Paton Constructions Pvt. Ltd. (Unsecured Financial Creditor). Appellants in Appeal No. 600 of 2023 are Naresh Sevantilal Shah and Charu Naresh Shah (Suspended Directors of Corporate Debtor). Respondent No. 1 in all appeals is Malharshanti Enterprises (Operational Creditor)[cite: 29]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Construction and development work carried out by Malharshanti Enterprises for CAN Enterprises Pvt. Ltd., culminating in unpaid operational debt default[cite: 29]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational creditor's claim originally admitted at Rs. 1,95,01,079/- by erstwhile IRP. Paton Constructions claimed Rs. 1,05,877/- based on an unsecured loan of Rs. 1 Lakh advanced on 06.09.2019 (the day after oral arguments concluded in Section 9 proceedings). Suspended director Naresh Shah claimed Rs. 1,77,24,370/-[cite: 29]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 9 application admitted on 27.01.2020. NCLAT upheld admission on 19.01.2021 in Appeal No. 415 of 2020. Supreme Court dismissed suspended director's SLP as withdrawn on 10.03.2021. RP Manish Jaju rejected operational creditor's claim on 02.12.2020. NCLT Mumbai allowed operational creditor's IA No. 47 of 2021 on 16.02.2023[cite: 29]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Section 8 demand notice dated 02.12.2017; arbitration notice dated 10.04.2018; loan agreement dated 20.08.2019 with Paton Constructions for Rs. 50 Lakhs (only Rs. 1 Lakh disbursed); forensic audit report by Mr. Amarjit Chopra; and CoC minutes replacing IRP and moving Section 12A withdrawal[cite: 29]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-III allowed operational creditor's IA No. 47 of 2021 on 16.02.2023, setting aside the RP's rejection of claims, castigating the RP's conduct, and directing claim admission[cite: 29]. RP, financial creditor, and suspended directors filed three separate appeals[cite: 29].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a Resolution Professional is legally empowered to reject in toto an operational creditor's claim that was judicially adjudicated and admitted upon the initiation of CIRP, and subsequently confirmed by appellate tribunals; (ii) Whether a miniscule loan advanced immediately after the conclusion of arguments in a Section 9 petition can be used to engineer a sole-member CoC to derail CIRP via Section 12A withdrawal; (iii) Whether a Resolution Professional has the locus standi to file an appeal in a personal capacity challenging an NCLT order setting aside claim rejections[cite: 29].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Resolution Professional has no adjudicatory power to reject claims that have been formally examined and admitted upon the judicial admission of a winding-up or insolvency petition, nor does an RP possess personal locus standi to challenge NCLT claim-admission orders on merits; an RP must maintain strict neutrality, and collusive attempts by promoters and newly inducted micro-creditors to create a single-member CoC to execute a back-door Section 12A exit are illegal and constitute gross misconduct[cite: 29]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 admission orders carry finality regarding debt and default, and subsequent claim verification by an RP cannot overturn concurrent judicial findings upheld up to the Supreme Court[cite: 29]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the chronology, noting that Paton Constructions advanced a mere Rs. 1 Lakh on 06.09.2019 (immediately after Section 9 arguments concluded) to become the sole CoC member, promptly replaced the IRP, and moved to close CIRP while rejecting the Rs. 1.95 Crore admitted operational claim[cite: 29]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The RP exceeded his statutory authority in collusion with the suspended directors and financial creditor to manipulate CoC constitution, the Adjudicating Authority correctly set aside the claim rejections, and all three appeals are frivolous and devoid of merit[cite: 29].
operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 545, 598, and 600 of 2023 are dismissed[cite: 29]. In Appeal No. 545 of 2023, the appellant RP is saddled with a cost of Rs. 10 Lakhs to be paid to the Prime Minister's National Relief Fund within four weeks, and the Chairman of IBBI is directed to investigate the conduct and professional misconduct of the RP[cite: 29].
summary: Three connected appeals were filed by the Resolution Professional (Manish Jaju), a micro-financial creditor (Paton Constructions), and the suspended directors (Naresh Shah & Charu Shah) against an NCLT Mumbai order dated 16.02.2023 which set aside the RP's rejection of Malharshanti Enterprises' operational claim[cite: 29]. The appellants argued that pre-existing disputes and lack of documentation justified rejecting the claim and upholding a Section 12A withdrawal application moved by Paton Constructions as the sole CoC member[cite: 29]. Dismissing all three appeals, the NCLAT bench strongly denounced the collusive actions of the RP, suspended directors, and Paton Constructions (which advanced a mere Rs. 1 Lakh immediately after Section 9 arguments concluded solely to engineer a sole-member CoC)[cite: 29]. The Tribunal held that an RP has no power to overturn claims admitted upon judicial insolvency admission, lacks personal locus to appeal claim-admission orders on merits, and must maintain neutrality[cite: 29]. The Tribunal upheld the NCLT order, imposed a Rs. 10 Lakh personal cost on the RP, and directed the IBBI to investigate his professional misconduct[cite: 29].

case_title: Commercial Tax Department, Government of Madhya Pradesh vs. Mrs. Teena Saraswat Pandey & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain, Technical Members Naresh Salecha and Indevar Pandey)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is the Commercial Tax Department, Government of Madhya Pradesh. Respondent No. 1 is Mrs. Teena Saraswat Pandey (Resolution Professional / Liquidator)[cite: 31]. Respondent No. 2 is Agarwal Real City Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant / SRA)[cite: 31]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Chandraudai Automobiles Pvt. Ltd. initiated Section 9 CIRP against Rajpal Abhikaran Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). SRA submitted a resolution plan offering Rs. 22.61 Crores against total admitted claims of Rs. 113.94 Crores[cite: 31]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Secured financial creditors admitted at Rs. 23.02 Crores (proposed Rs. 19.11 Crores); unsecured financial creditors at Rs. 76.01 Crores (proposed Rs. 3.20 Crores); operational creditors at Rs. 14.91 Crores (proposed NIL)[cite: 31]. Appellant's statutory tax claim amounted to Rs. 12,61,57,345/-, submitted on Form B as an unsecured operational creditor[cite: 31]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 9 petition admitted on 26.03.2021[cite: 31]. CoC approved resolution plan with 90.41% votes on 17.12.2021[cite: 31]. Adjudicating Authority approved the resolution plan via order dated 25.08.2022[cite: 31]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form B tax claim dated 29.07.2021 (with 'NA' against retention of title); CoC voting records (90.41% approval); liquidation valuation report of Rs. 18.39 Crores; and resolution plan allocation tables[cite: 31]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Indore Bench approved the resolution plan on 25.08.2022. Commercial Tax Department appealed to NCLAT via Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1265 of 2022[cite: 31].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a statutory tax department claiming a first charge under Section 33 of the Madhya Pradesh Value Added Tax Act, 2002 (MPVAT Act) is entitled to be treated as a 'secured creditor' with priority over secured financial creditors in a resolution plan, akin to the ruling in Rainbow Papers[cite: 31]; (ii) Whether Section 33 of the MPVAT Act, being expressly subject to Section 530 of the Companies Act, 1956 (subordinate to Section 529A worker and secured creditor dues), is pari materia with Section 48 of the Gujarat Value Added Tax Act, 2003[cite: 31].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A statutory first charge created under state tax enactments does not automatically elevate a tax department to a secured financial creditor under the IBC if the governing state statute is expressly made subject to company liquidation priority provisions (such as Section 530 and Section 529A of the Companies Act), and if the department submitted its claim as an unsecured operational creditor on Form B[cite: 31]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 33 of the MPVAT Act differs fundamentally from Section 48 of the GVAT Act (which was interpreted in Rainbow Papers) because Section 33 explicitly incorporates the proviso 'subject to the provisions of Section 530 of the Companies Act, 1956', which in turn subordinates tax revenues to workmen's dues and secured creditors under Section 529A[cite: 31]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized Form B filed by the appellant, noting that it submitted its claim as an unsecured operational creditor without claiming security interest, and verified that Section 33 of the MPVAT Act is pari materia with Section 37 of the MVAT Act (previously distinguished in Zicom Saas) rather than Section 48 of the GVAT Act[cite: 31]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellant's tax dues do not enjoy secured status under the MPVAT Act due to statutory subordination to secured creditors and workmen under Section 529A, and the resolution plan validly allocated NIL to operational creditors based on liquidation value[cite: 31].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1265 of 2022 along with interlocutory applications is dismissed with no order as to costs, upholding the order dated 25.08.2022 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, Indore Bench) approving the resolution plan[cite: 31].
summary: The Commercial Tax Department of Madhya Pradesh appealed against an NCLT Indore order approving the resolution plan of Rajpal Abhikaran Pvt. Ltd., contending that its statutory tax claim of Rs. 12.61 Crores should be treated as a secured debt with first charge priority under Section 33 of the MPVAT Act, relying on the Supreme Court's ruling in Rainbow Papers[cite: 31]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that Rainbow Papers is distinguishable because Section 33 of the MPVAT Act is expressly made subject to Section 530 of the Companies Act (subordinate to Section 529A secured creditors and workmen), whereas Section 48 of the GVAT Act lacked such a subordination proviso[cite: 31]. The Tribunal affirmed that the appellant submitted its claim as an unsecured operational creditor on Form B, that the MPVAT provision is pari materia with the MVAT Act considered in Zicom Saas, and that the resolution plan's NIL allocation to operational creditors in liquidation waterfall is legally sound[cite: 31].

case_title: Atlas Equifin Pvt Ltd vs. Jackie Kakubhai Shroff and Others
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Yogesh Khanna and Technical Member Ajai Das Mehrotra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Atlas Equifin Pvt Ltd (Majority Shareholder / Company). Respondent No. 1 is Jackie Kakubhai Shroff (Minority Shareholder owning 10% equity share capital). Respondents Nos. 2 and 7 are other co-respondents[cite: 32]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate governance dispute and management deadlocks within a private limited company[cite: 32]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (Company law appeal under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 arising from an oppression and mismanagement petition)[cite: 32]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Transfer Company Petition No. 57 of 2014 filed before NCLT Mumbai Bench[cite: 32]. NCLT passed final judgment and order on 10.02.2023 directing the company to purchase the shares of the petitioner[cite: 32]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Company petition pleadings; shareholding distribution (majority 90%, minority 10%); Article 5 of Articles of Association restricting share transfers; and NCLT order dated 10.02.2023 appointing CA Sujal Shah as Valuer[cite: 32]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench disposed of Transfer CP No. 57 of 2014 on 10.02.2023 by ordering the purchase of the minority shareholder's shares under Section 242(2)(b) and appointing a valuer[cite: 32]. The company appealed to NCLAT via Company Appeal (AT) No. 46 of 2023[cite: 32].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the Tribunal can direct a company or majority shareholders to purchase the shares of a minority shareholder under Section 242(2)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013 without first recording a definitive positive finding of 'oppression and mismanagement'[cite: 32]; (ii) Whether the existence of an irretrievable deadlock, bitterness, or a quasi-partnership breakdown empowers the Tribunal to grant exit reliefs to end matters complained of[cite: 32].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 242(1) and 242(2)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013, the Tribunal possesses wide equitable powers to make such orders as it thinks fit to bring to an end the matters complained of; even in the absence of established mala fides or formal oppression, the Tribunal can direct a share buyout to resolve management deadlocks, boardroom incompatibilities, and corporate bitterness, thereby doing substantial justice between the parties[cite: 32]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 242(2)(b) is not strictly dependent on proof of prior oppression if an equitable exit mechanism is necessary to prevent operational paralysis in a closely held private company[cite: 32]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the private company structure where Article 5 barred open-market share transfers, the extreme loggerheads between majority and minority shareholders, and the failure of prior settlement proposals, establishing an irreconcilable deadlock[cite: 32]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT committed no legal error in directing a share purchase to end the corporate deadlock and bitterness, and the appellant's challenge fails[cite: 32].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 46 of 2023 is dismissed with no orders as to costs, affirming the judgment and order dated 10.02.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (National Company Law Tribunal, Mumbai Bench) in Transfer Company Petition No. 57 of 2014[cite: 32].
summary: Atlas Equifin Pvt Ltd appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order directing the company to purchase the 10% equity shares held by minority shareholder Jackie Kakubhai Shroff pursuant to Section 242(2)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 32]. The appellant contended that the NCLT erred by ordering a share purchase without recording any specific findings of oppression and mismanagement[cite: 32]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held, relying on Supreme Court precedents including M.S.D.C. Radharamanan and Mistry's case, that the Tribunal has wide equitable powers under Section 242 to order a buyout and provide an exit mechanism to resolve management deadlocks and corporate bitterness, even if formal oppression is not proven[cite: 32]. The Tribunal affirmed the appointment of the valuer and dismissed the appeal[cite: 32].
