ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 242(1) and 242(2)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013, the Tribunal possesses wide equitable powers to make such orders as it thinks fit to bring to an end the matters complained of; even in the absence of established mala fides or formal oppression, the Tribunal can direct a share buyout to resolve management deadlocks, boardroom incompatibilities, and corporate bitterness, thereby doing substantial justice between the parties[cite: 32]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 242(2)(b) is not strictly dependent on proof of prior oppression if an equitable exit mechanism is necessary to prevent operational paralysis in a closely held private company[cite: 32]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the private company structure where Article 5 barred open-market share transfers, the extreme loggerheads between majority and minority shareholders, and the failure of prior settlement proposals, establishing an irreconcilable deadlock[cite: 32]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT committed no legal error in directing a share purchase to end the corporate deadlock and bitterness, and the appellant's challenge fails[cite: 32].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 46 of 2023 is dismissed with no orders as to costs, affirming the judgment and order dated 10.02.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (National Company Law Tribunal, Mumbai Bench) in Transfer Company Petition No. 57 of 2014[cite: 32].
summary: Atlas Equifin Pvt Ltd appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order directing the company to purchase the 10% equity shares held by minority shareholder Jackie Kakubhai Shroff pursuant to Section 242(2)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 32]. The appellant contended that the NCLT erred by ordering a share purchase without recording any specific findings of oppression and mismanagement[cite: 32]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held, relying on Supreme Court precedents including M.S.D.C. Radharamanan and Mistry's case, that the Tribunal has wide equitable powers under Section 242 to order a buyout and provide an exit mechanism to resolve management deadlocks and corporate bitterness, even if formal oppression is not proven[cite: 32]. The Tribunal affirmed the appointment of the valuer and dismissed the appeal[cite: 32].

case_title: Imdadali M. Momin & Ors. vs. Pellucid Lifesciences Private Limited
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain, Technical Members Naresh Salecha and Indevar Pandey)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are six financial creditors/former promoters (Imdadali M. Momin and five others). Respondent is Pellucid Lifesciences Private Limited (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 33]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was incorporated on 30.08.2013 with Appellant No. 1 as promoter director. Between 2013 and 2022, appellants advanced cumulative unsecured loans totaling Rs. 1,25,44,997.25 to the corporate debtor[cite: 33]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellants claimed a default of Rs. 1,25,44,997.25 with 12% interest, citing the date of default as 30.11.2022. During proceedings, the corporate debtor made partial repayments totaling Rs. 99,07,375.48 via RTGS on 16.01.2024[cite: 33]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 demand notice served on 15.11.2022; default claimed on 30.11.2022[cite: 33]. Section 7 application filed on 07.03.2023[cite: 33]. Corporate debtor paid Rs. 99 Lakhs during pendency on 16.01.2024[cite: 33]. NCLT Ahmedabad Bench rejected the Section 7 petition via order dated 25.04.2024[cite: 33]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Section 7 demand notice; corporate debtor ledger accounts; income tax TDS certificates for FY 2021-2022 reflecting interest deductions for appellants 1 and 3; and corporate debtor's bank payment proofs for Rs. 99,07,375.48[cite: 33]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Ahmedabad Bench) rejected CP (IB) No. 74 (AHM) of 2023 on 25.04.2024, holding that the debt lacked loan terms and that insolvency proceedings cannot be used for debt recovery[cite: 33]. Financial creditors appealed to NCLAT[cite: 33].
legal_issues: (i) Whether unsecured advances extended by promoters/family members without any formal loan agreement, tenure, repayment schedule, or fixed interest rate qualify as a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC[cite: 33]; (ii) Whether insolvency proceedings under Section 7 can be maintained solely for the recovery of disputed interest after the corporate debtor has repaid the principal and admitted interest[cite: 33].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A debt qualifies as a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC only if there is a disbursement against consideration for the time value of money, supported by ascertainable commercial terms such as a repayment schedule and interest frequency; unsecured advances lacking formal loan agreements or interest stipulations, resembling promoter equity investments, do not constitute financial debt, and the IBC cannot be utilized as a forum for recovering disputed interest[cite: 33]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(11), 3(12), and 5(8) require demonstrable default on an established financial debt[cite: 33]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that no formal loan agreement existed, interest had never been demanded prior to notice, Appellant No. 1 was a promoter director removed from the board following a family dispute, and the corporate debtor had paid Rs. 99,07,375.48 covering principal and TDS-backed interest[cite: 33]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The advances were in the nature of promoter investments rather than financial debt, the principal and verified interest stood fully repaid, and the Section 7 petition was rightly rejected as an abuse of process for debt recovery[cite: 33].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1145 of 2024 is dismissed with no order as to costs, upholding the order dated 25.04.2024 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, Ahmedabad Bench) in CP (IB) No. 74 (AHM) of 2023[cite: 33].
summary: Imdadali M. Momin and five other family members/former promoters appealed against an NCLT Ahmedabad order rejecting their Section 7 CIRP application against Pellucid Lifesciences Pvt. Ltd. for an alleged default of Rs. 1.25 Crores[cite: 33]. The appellants argued that advances made since 2013 constituted financial debt and that TDS deductions proved interest liability[cite: 33]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that in the absence of a written loan agreement, tenure, or repayment terms, advances made by promoters at inception constitute equity investments rather than financial debt[cite: 33]. The Tribunal noted that the corporate debtor had already paid Rs. 99.07 Lakhs during proceedings, covering the principal and TDS-backed interest, and affirmed that the IBC is a resolution mechanism rather than a forum for recovering disputed interest[cite: 33].

case_title: Commercial Tax Department, Government of Madhya Pradesh vs. Mrs. Teena Saraswat Pandey & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain, Technical Members Naresh Salecha and Indevar Pandey)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is the Commercial Tax Department, Government of Madhya Pradesh. Respondent No. 1 is Mrs. Teena Saraswat Pandey (Resolution Professional / Liquidator). Respondent No. 2 is Agarwal Real City Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant / SRA)[cite: 34]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Chandraudai Automobiles Pvt. Ltd. initiated Section 9 CIRP against Rajpal Abhikaran Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). SRA submitted a resolution plan offering Rs. 22.61 Crores against total admitted claims of Rs. 113.94 Crores[cite: 34]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Secured financial creditors admitted at Rs. 23.02 Crores (proposed Rs. 19.11 Crores); unsecured financial creditors at Rs. 76.01 Crores (proposed Rs. 3.20 Crores); operational creditors at Rs. 14.91 Crores (proposed NIL)[cite: 34]. Appellant's statutory tax claim amounted to Rs. 12,61,57,345/-, submitted on Form B as an unsecured operational creditor[cite: 34]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 9 petition admitted on 26.03.2021[cite: 34]. CoC approved resolution plan with 90.41% votes on 17.12.2021[cite: 34]. Adjudicating Authority approved the resolution plan via order dated 25.08.2022[cite: 34]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form B tax claim dated 29.07.2021 (with 'NA' against retention of title); CoC voting records (90.41% approval); liquidation valuation report of Rs. 18.39 Crores; and resolution plan allocation tables[cite: 34]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Indore Bench approved the resolution plan on 25.08.2022. Commercial Tax Department appealed to NCLAT via Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1265 of 2022[cite: 34].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a statutory tax department claiming a first charge under Section 33 of the Madhya Pradesh Value Added Tax Act, 2002 (MPVAT Act) is entitled to be treated as a 'secured creditor' with priority over secured financial creditors in a resolution plan, akin to the ruling in Rainbow Papers[cite: 34]; (ii) Whether Section 33 of the MPVAT Act, being expressly subject to Section 530 of the Companies Act, 1956 (subordinate to Section 529A worker and secured creditor dues), is pari materia with Section 48 of the Gujarat Value Added Tax Act, 2003[cite: 34].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A statutory first charge created under state tax enactments does not automatically elevate a tax department to a secured financial creditor under the IBC if the governing state statute is expressly made subject to company liquidation priority provisions (such as Section 530 and Section 529A of the Companies Act), and if the department submitted its claim as an unsecured operational creditor on Form B[cite: 34]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 33 of the MPVAT Act differs fundamentally from Section 48 of the GVAT Act (which was interpreted in Rainbow Papers) because Section 33 explicitly incorporates the proviso 'subject to the provisions of Section 530 of the Companies Act, 1956', which in turn subordinates tax revenues to workmen's dues and secured creditors under Section 529A[cite: 34]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized Form B filed by the appellant, noting that it submitted its claim as an unsecured operational creditor without claiming security interest, and verified that Section 33 of the MPVAT Act is pari materia with Section 37 of the MVAT Act (previously distinguished in Zicom Saas) rather than Section 48 of the GVAT Act[cite: 34]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellant's tax dues do not enjoy secured status under the MPVAT Act due to statutory subordination to secured creditors and workmen under Section 529A, and the resolution plan validly allocated NIL to operational creditors based on liquidation value[cite: 34].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1265 of 2022 along with interlocutory applications is dismissed with no order as to costs, upholding the order dated 25.08.2022 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, Indore Bench) approving the resolution plan[cite: 34].
summary: The Commercial Tax Department of Madhya Pradesh appealed against an NCLT Indore order approving the resolution plan of Rajpal Abhikaran Pvt. Ltd., contending that its statutory tax claim of Rs. 12.61 Crores should be treated as a secured debt with first charge priority under Section 33 of the MPVAT Act, relying on the Supreme Court's ruling in Rainbow Papers[cite: 34]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that Rainbow Papers is distinguishable because Section 33 of the MPVAT Act is expressly made subject to Section 530 of the Companies Act (subordinate to Section 529A secured creditors and workmen), whereas Section 48 of the GVAT Act lacked such a subordination proviso[cite: 34]. The Tribunal affirmed that the appellant submitted its claim as an unsecured operational creditor on Form B, that the MPVAT provision is pari materia with the MVAT Act considered in Zicom Saas, and that the resolution plan's NIL allocation to operational creditors in liquidation waterfall is legally sound[cite: 34].

case_title: Arunkumar Jayantilal Muchhala vs. Awaita Properties Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
appeal_number: I.A. No. 4373 of 2024 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 121 of 2023
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Applicant/Appellant is Arunkumar Jayantilal Muchhala (Ex-Director of Tarapur Textiles Park Limited, Corporate Debtor). Respondent No. 1 is Awaita Properties Pvt. Ltd. (Financial Creditor). Respondent No. 2 is Tarapur Textiles Park Limited through its IRP/RP CA Prashant Jain[cite: 35]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: On 01.01.2014, Respondent No. 1 disbursed Rs. 5 Crores to the Corporate Debtor repayable on demand with 15% p.a. interest, recorded as unsecured long-term borrowings in the balance sheet[cite: 35]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred on 15.03.2016 upon non-payment following demand. Total default claimed was Rs. 8,56,30,137/- as of September 2018[cite: 35]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Disbursal on 01.01.2014; default on 15.03.2016; Section 7 petition filed on 24.10.2018; NCLT admitted Section 7 on 06.12.2022; NCLAT dismissed appeal on 02.04.2024; Supreme Court dismissed Civil Appeal No. 5531 of 2024 as withdrawn with liberty to review on 06.05.2024; recall application filed under Rule 11[cite: 35]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RTGS bank transfer records for Rs. 5 Crores; balance sheet entries; demand letters dated 20.02.2018 and 30.05.2018; and Form-1 Part IV particulars[cite: 35]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai admitted Section 7 on 06.12.2022. NCLAT dismissed the appeal (CA No. 121 of 2023) on 02.04.2024. Supreme Court permitted withdrawal with liberty to seek review on limitation on 06.05.2024. Appellant filed IA No. 4373 of 2024 under Rule 11 for recall/review[cite: 35].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an application for recall of an appellate judgment is maintainable under Rule 11 of NCLAT Rules when the Supreme Court granted liberty to file a review limited to the question of limitation[cite: 35]; (ii) Whether a Section 7 petition for a demand loan is governed by Article 21 (running from disbursal) or residuary Article 137 (running from date of default) of the Limitation Act[cite: 35].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Power of recall under Rule 11 is distinct from review and is strictly exercisable only for procedural errors (such as lack of service or fraud); however, in exceptional circumstances and pursuant to Supreme Court liberty, courts may entertain review arguments on limitation to prevent miscarriage of justice, while adhering to settled law that Section 7 applications are governed by Article 137 with limitation running from the date of default[cite: 35]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(12) defines default as non-payment when due; for demand loans, the right to sue and limitation under Article 137 accrue from the date of default following a demand, rather than Article 21 from the date of disbursal[cite: 35]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that while disbursal occurred on 01.01.2014, the debt was repayable on demand, default occurred on 15.03.2016 upon unfulfilled assurance of payment, and the petition was filed on 24.10.2018 (within the 3-year limitation window)[cite: 35]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The recall/review application is devoid of merit as the Section 7 petition was instituted well within three years from the date of default under Article 137[cite: 35].
operative_order: I.A. No. 4373 of 2024 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 121 of 2023 is dismissed with no order as to costs, affirming that the underlying Section 7 petition was filed within limitation[cite: 35].
summary: Arunkumar Jayantilal Muchhala, Ex-Director of Tarapur Textiles Park Ltd., filed an interlocutory application (IA No. 4373 of 2024) under Rule 11 of NCLAT Rules seeking recall/review of the NCLAT judgment dated 02.04.2024, pursuant to liberty granted by the Supreme Court on 06.05.2024 in Civil Appeal No. 5531 of 2024, on the sole ground that the Section 7 petition was barred by limitation[cite: 35]. Dismissing the application, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that although recall is strictly confined to procedural errors, the bench entertained the limitation review in deference to the Supreme Court's liberty[cite: 35]. The Tribunal reaffirmed that Section 7 applications are governed by the residuary Article 137 of the Limitation Act, with limitation running from the date of default (15.03.2016) rather than the date of disbursal (01.01.2014)[cite: 35]. Because the petition was filed on 24.10.2018 (within three years of default), the petition was fully within limitation, and the recall application was dismissed[cite: 35].

case_title: Times Innovative Media Limited vs. Pawan Kumar Aggarwal (Liquidator) & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Times Innovative Media Limited (Operational Creditor). Respondent No. 1 is Pawan Kumar Aggarwal (Liquidator of Brand Connect Communications [India] Pvt. Ltd.). Respondent No. 2 is the ex-Director/Shareholder of the Corporate Debtor (Unsecured Financial Creditor)[cite: 36]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate insolvency resolution process against Brand Connect Communications (India) Pvt. Ltd. commenced on 27.03.2018, followed by a liquidation order dated 28.01.2019[cite: 36]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: In liquidation, Appellant's operational claim was admitted at Rs. 2,57,24,248/- (or Rs. 2,57,51,620/-), and Respondent No. 2's unsecured financial claim was admitted at Rs. 50,56,051/- (originating from loans advanced in 2011-2012)[cite: 36]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 27.03.2018; liquidation ordered on 28.01.2019; Stakeholders' Consultation Committee met on 07.06.2019; Liquidator communicated rejection of operational creditor priority on 03.09.2021; Adjudicating Authority dismissed IA No. 2382 of 2021 on 24.04.2024[cite: 36]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Claim admission records; Stakeholders' Consultation Committee meeting minutes dated 07.06.2019; and Liquidator's rejection order dated 03.09.2021[cite: 36]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai Bench, Court-II) dismissed IA No. 2382 of 2021 on 24.04.2024, holding that Section 53 of the IBC does not distinguish between unrelated and related party unsecured financial creditors in the liquidation waterfall[cite: 36]. Operational Creditor appealed to NCLAT[cite: 36].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an unsecured financial creditor who is a related party or ex-director of the corporate debtor ranks lower in the liquidation waterfall than an unrelated operational creditor under Section 53 of the IBC[cite: 36]; (ii) Whether Section 53(1) of the IBC permits differential treatment or subordination of related party unsecured financial debts to equity or operational dues[cite: 36].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under the waterfall mechanism in Section 53(1) of the IBC, financial debts owed to unsecured creditors (ranking under Clause [d]) enjoy statutory priority over operational debts and remaining dues (ranking under Clause [f]), and Section 53 makes no distinction between unrelated unsecured financial creditors and related party unsecured financial creditors[cite: 36]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Related party restrictions under Section 21 (CoC voting) and Section 29A (resolution applicant eligibility) apply during CIRP and do not alter the statutory distribution priority in liquidation under Section 53[cite: 36]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that Respondent No. 2 resigned as director on 01.10.2013 (more than 5 years prior to CIRP), that Respondent No. 2's financial claim was duly admitted as an unsecured financial debt without challenge, and that Section 53 explicitly places unsecured financial debts above operational debts[cite: 36]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The liquidator and Adjudicating Authority correctly applied Section 53 waterfall priorities, and related party status does not subordinate an admitted unsecured financial debt below operational claims[cite: 36].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1139 of 2024 is dismissed with no order as to costs, affirming the order dated 24.04.2024 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, Court-II, Mumbai Bench) in IA No. 2382 of 2021 in C.P. (IB) No. 220/MB/2017[cite: 36].
summary: Times Innovative Media Ltd. (Operational Creditor) appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order dismissing its interlocutory application (IA No. 2382 of 2021) which challenged the liquidator's decision to accord distribution priority under Section 53 of the IBC to Respondent No. 2 (an ex-director and unsecured financial creditor) over the appellant[cite: 36]. The appellant argued that a related party unsecured creditor should be treated as an equity shareholder under Section 53(1)(h) or subordinated below operational creditors[cite: 36]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that Section 53 of the IBC does not draw any distinction between related and unrelated unsecured financial creditors, and that unsecured financial debt (ranking under Clause [d]) inherently ranks above operational debt (ranking under Clause [f])[cite: 36]. The Tribunal affirmed that related party disabilities under Sections 21 and 29A do not rewrite the liquidation distribution waterfall, and upheld the dismissal[cite: 36].

case_title: Kochar Sung Up Acrylic Limited & Anr. vs. Sunny Kochar & Ors.
bench: Chennai Bench (Sitting at Principal Bench) (Judicial Member Justice Yogesh Khanna and Technical Member Ajai Das Mehrotra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant No. 1 is Kochar Sung Up Acrylic Ltd. Appellant No. 2 is Pushpdeep Kochar. Respondent No. 1 is Sunny Kochar (Original Petitioner alleging oppression and mismanagement)[cite: 37]. Respondents Nos. 2 and 3 are co-respondents[cite: 37]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Inter-se family management dispute and corporate governance issues within Kochar Sung Up Acrylic Ltd.[cite: 37]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (Company law petition alleging oppression and mismanagement under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013)[cite: 37]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company Petition CP No. 24(CH)/2024 filed by Respondent No. 1[cite: 37]. Hearing held on 10.05.2024[cite: 37]. NCLT recorded a bench note on 07.06.2024 granting leave to amend[cite: 37]. Respondent No. 1 filed CA No. 147 of 2024 directly placing on record an extensive amended petition, which NCLT allowed via order dated 21.08.2024[cite: 37]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Original Company Petition; bench notes of NCLT dated 10.05.2024 and 07.06.2024; CA No. 147 of 2024; comparative chart showing substantial additions of new interim/final reliefs, a new respondent (ROC Chandigarh), new petitioner contributions, and numerous statutory non-compliance grounds[cite: 37]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh Bench II allowed CA No. 147 of 2024 on 21.08.2024, taking the redrafted amended petition on record based on the 07.06.2024 order[cite: 37]. Appellants challenged both the 07.06.2024 and 21.08.2024 orders via Company Appeals (AT) Nos. 276 and 277 of 2024[cite: 37].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an applicant in a company petition can introduce substantial amendments, new causes of action, additional parties, and extensive new final reliefs without filing a formal amendment application detailing the proposed changes and securing a proper opportunity for the opposite party to respond[cite: 37]; (ii) Whether NCLT can permit wholesale redrafting of a petition under the guise of an amendment without adhering to Order VI Rule 17 of the CPC and principles of natural justice[cite: 37].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While tribunals are not strictly bound by the CPC, fundamental principles of natural justice and orderly pleading require that any substantial amendment introducing new causes of action, new parties, or extensive additional reliefs must be sought via a formal application disclosing the proposed changes, and the opposite party must be afforded a proper opportunity of hearing and filing a written response[cite: 37]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 424 of the Companies Act, 2013 does not dispense with the basic tenets of natural justice or permit tribunals to allow sweeping redrafts of petitions on mere asking without formal applications or procedural safeguards[cite: 37]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed the comparative chart of pleadings, finding that the amended petition introduced 14 new final reliefs, 9 new interim reliefs, impleaded the Registrar of Companies as a new respondent, set up a new factual case regarding the petitioner's role, and raised numerous fresh statutory violation grounds without prior notice or opportunity to rebut[cite: 37]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's orders permitting the wholesale redrafting of the petition without a proper amendment application or opportunity for the appellants to object violated natural justice and settled legal precedents, necessitating a complete set-aside and fresh procedural compliance[cite: 37].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) Nos. 276 and 277 of 2024 are allowed, setting aside the impugned orders dated 07.06.2024 and 21.08.2024 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Chandigarh Bench II) in CA No. 147/2024 in CP No. 24(CH)/2024[cite: 37]. The respondent is granted liberty to file a formal amendment application inclusive of proposed amendments, providing the appellants an opportunity to respond, for fresh adjudication by the NCLT in accordance with law[cite: 37].
summary: Kochar Sung Up Acrylic Ltd. and its director appealed against NCLT Chandigarh orders permitting Sunny Kochar to bring on record a heavily redrafted amended petition in a company oppression and mismanagement proceeding without filing a formal amendment application[cite: 37]. The appellants argued that the amended petition introduced entirely new causes of action, additional parties, 14 new final reliefs, and numerous fresh statutory non-compliance grounds in violation of Order VI Rule 17 of the CPC and natural justice[cite: 37]. Allowing both appeals, the NCLAT bench held that substantial amendments cannot be introduced on a mere oral request or erroneous docket notes without a structured application and an opportunity for the opposing party to file a rebuttal[cite: 37]. The Tribunal set aside the impugned orders and directed the petitioner to file a proper amendment application for fresh consideration by the NCLT[cite: 37].

case_title: Amit Narang vs. Aditya Birla Finance Limited & Anr.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan, Technical Members Barun Mitra and Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Amit Narang, Suspended Director of Narang Developers Private Limited (Corporate Debtor / Co-Borrower)[cite: 38]. Respondent No. 1 is Aditya Birla Finance Limited (Financial Creditor / NBFC)[cite: 38]. Respondent No. 2 is Narang Developers Private Limited through its Interim Resolution Professional[cite: 38]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Respondent No. 1 sanctioned loan facilities aggregating Rs. 11.50 Crores wherein the Corporate Debtor acted as a Co-Borrower, pursuant to Sanction letters dated 19.09.2016 and 04.12.2018, Facility Agreement dated 29.09.2016, Supplementary Facility Agreement dated 07.12.2018, and an Indenture of Mortgage executed on 17.10.2016[cite: 38]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Loan accounts were classified as Non-Performing Assets (NPA) on 16.06.2019[cite: 38]. Financial Creditor issued a Demand Notice under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act on 05.07.2019[cite: 38]. Following part payments of Rs. 30 Lakhs and Rs. 70 Lakhs and a failed restructuring proposal to clear dues by 15.03.2020, the claimed date of default was set as 15.03.2020[cite: 38]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 16.06.2019[cite: 38]. SARFAESI notice issued on 05.07.2019[cite: 38]. Corporate debtor offered to clear dues by 15.03.2020[cite: 38]. Part payment made on 01.05.2021[cite: 38]. Acknowledgement email sent on 11.05.2022[cite: 38]. Section 7 petition filed in 2023 and admitted by NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV on 28.03.2024[cite: 38]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Sanction letters, facility agreements, Indenture of Mortgage dated 17.10.2016 signed by the Corporate Debtor, Demand Promissory Notes, restructuring letters dated 10.02.2020 and 20.02.2020, part payment receipt dated 01.05.2021, and acknowledgement email dated 11.05.2022[cite: 38]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV admitted Aditya Birla Finance's Section 7 petition on 28.03.2024, initiating CIRP against Narang Developers Pvt. Ltd[cite: 38]. Suspended Director appealed to NCLAT via Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 684 of 2024[cite: 38].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a co-borrower who has not received direct disbursement of funds into its own account can be treated as a 'financial debtor' under Section 5(8) of the IBC[cite: 38]; (ii) Whether an application under Section 7 is barred by limitation or hit by Section 10A where default is claimed as 15.03.2020 but followed by subsequent part payments and written acknowledgements of debt[cite: 38].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The liability of a co-borrower is joint and several with the principal borrower, and a financial creditor is fully entitled to initiate CIRP proceedings under Section 7 against a co-borrower who executes loan documents, demand promissory notes, and guarantees repayment[cite: 38]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8)(a) encompasses interest-bearing loan facilities extended under common loan agreements[cite: 38]. Under Section 18 of the Limitation Act and established precedents, part payment or an unequivocal written acknowledgement of debt extends the limitation period afresh[cite: 38]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the Corporate Debtor signed the loan application, sanction letters, facility agreements, demand promissory notes, and mortgage confirmation as a co-borrower, and subsequently acknowledged the debt in writing on 11.05.2022 and made part payments on 01.05.2021[cite: 38]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor was a valid co-borrower with co-extensive liabilities, the petition was neither barred by limitation nor hit by Section 10A due to intervening acknowledgements and part payments, and the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in admitting the Section 7 application[cite: 38].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 684 of 2024 is dismissed with no order as to costs, upholding the order dated 28.03.2024 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, Mumbai Bench-IV) in C.P. (IB) No. 1142 (MB) of 2023[cite: 38].
summary: Amit Narang, Suspended Director of Narang Developers Pvt. Ltd., appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 7 CIRP application filed by Aditya Birla Finance Ltd. for default on a Rs. 11.50 Crore loan facility[cite: 38]. The appellant argued that funds were disbursed to other entities (Csango and Pacific Link) and not directly to the corporate debtor, making it merely a co-borrower without repayment obligations, and that the petition was barred by limitation and Section 10A[cite: 38]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that a co-borrower's liability is joint, several, and co-extensive with the primary borrower[cite: 38]. The Tribunal ruled that the interest-bearing loan constituted a financial debt under Section 5(8)(a), and that the limitation period stood extended afresh due to a part payment on 01.05.2021 and an explicit written acknowledgement of debt on 11.05.2022, thereby rendering the petition maintainable[cite: 38].

case_title: Yogesh Kelkar & Ors. vs. Resolution Professional of Anudan Properties Private Limited & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 751 of 2023 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 717 of 2023
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants in CA No. 751 of 2023 are 31 home buyers of Anudan Properties Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor), and in CA No. 717 of 2023 are partnership construction firms[cite: 39]. Respondent No. 1 is the Resolution Professional[cite: 39]. Respondent No. 2 is LICHFL Trustee Company Private Limited (Secured Financial Creditor / CoC sole/dominant member with 76.35% vote share)[cite: 39]. Respondent No. 3 is KGK Realty (India) Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant / SRA)[cite: 39]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor launched a residential-cum-commercial construction project named 'Silver Spring' alongside rehabilitating 457 slum dwellers under a Slum Rehabilitation Scheme, funded by LICHFL to the tune of Rs. 79.90 Crores[cite: 39]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor failed to complete the project, leading to default and LICHFL initiating Section 7 insolvency proceedings[cite: 39]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 15.03.2021[cite: 39]. RP published Form-G five times; resolution plans were voted on in the 17th CoC meeting ending 24.04.2022, where KGK Realty's plan was approved[cite: 39]. Adjudicating Authority granted a 32-day CIRP extension and approved KGK Realty's resolution plan via order dated 29.03.2023[cite: 39]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form-G publication records; 17th CoC meeting minutes recording comparative evaluation and voting results; resolution plan submitted by KGK Realty; and homebuyer objection applications (IA Nos. 1569, 2055, and 2214 of 2022)[cite: 39]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV approved KGK Realty's resolution plan via order dated 29.03.2023 in IA No. 1575 of 2022[cite: 39]. Homebuyers and construction firms appealed to NCLAT via Company Appeals Nos. 751 and 717 of 2023[cite: 39].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the commercial wisdom of a dominant or single-member Committee of Creditors in approving a resolution plan is justiciable and amenable to judicial review on grounds of fairness to minority stakeholders[cite: 39]; (ii) Whether a resolution plan can create differential or variable additional payment structures for homebuyers based on initial booking rates without violating the equitable framework of the IBC[cite: 39].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in approving a resolution plan with the requisite statutory majority is paramount, non-justiciable, and immune from judicial interference by adjudicating authorities so long as the plan satisfies the mandatory thresholds under Section 30(2) of the IBC[cite: 39]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31(1) restricts the Adjudicating Authority's judicial review to ensuring that the approved resolution plan complies with Section 30(2); neither the NCLT nor the NCLAT can sit in appeal over the commercial business decisions or valuation assessments made by the CoC[cite: 39]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified from 17th CoC meeting minutes that all three PRAs were given equal opportunity, structured evaluation matrices were applied, extensive negotiations were conducted, and the SRA's plan passed with a 76.35% majority vote[cite: 39]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC exercised its commercial wisdom in a legally sound manner, the plan met all compliance requirements under Section 30(2), and minority homebuyer dissatisfaction cannot override a validly approved resolution plan[cite: 39].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 751 and 717 of 2023 are dismissed with no order as to costs, upholding the order dated 29.03.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai Bench) in I.A. No. 1575 (MB)/2022 approving the resolution plan[cite: 39].
summary: Yogesh Kelkar and other home buyers, alongside two construction firms, appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order approving the resolution plan submitted by KGK Realty (India) Pvt. Ltd. for Anudan Properties Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 39]. The appellants contended that the CoC, dominated by LICHFL with 76.35% voting power, acted arbitrarily, ignored a superior plan submitted by Aanya Real Estate, and imposed unfair additional construction costs on homebuyers[cite: 39]. Dismissing both appeals, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that the commercial wisdom of the CoC in evaluating and approving a resolution plan is supreme and non-justiciable[cite: 39]. The Tribunal ruled that the CoC followed due process through 17 meetings and multiple Form-G evaluations, that the SRA's plan met all statutory parameters under Section 30(2), and that individual stakeholder dissatisfaction cannot vitiate a collective business decision[cite: 39].

case_title: Era Labourer Union of SIDCUL vs. Apex Buildsys Ltd.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan, Technical Members Barun Mitra and Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Era Labourer Union of SIDCUL, Pant Nagar, through its secretary (representing workmen)[cite: 40]. The Respondent is Apex Buildsys Ltd. (Corporate Debtor, represented by Liquidator)[cite: 40]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor operated a manufacturing factory at Pant Nagar, Uttarakhand, which suspended production in February 2017[cite: 40]. On 20.06.2017, the corporate debtor issued transfer letters to workmen, followed by a lockout declaration and a permanent closure notice on 31.07.2017 under the UP Industrial Disputes Act, 1947[cite: 40]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational claims for wages and dues submitted by the workmen union; liquidator admitted claims to the extent of Rs. 1,09,70,698.27 out of Rs. 11,42,92,579/- claimed[cite: 40]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Lockout/closure notice issued on 31.07.2017[cite: 40]. Uttarakhand High Court disposed of writ petitions on 27.04.2019[cite: 40]. CIRP commenced on 20.08.2018[cite: 40]. Liquidation ordered on 09.01.2020[cite: 40]. Appellant filed IA No. 2545 of 2021 on 04.06.2021[cite: 40]. NCLT Court-V, New Delhi dismissed IA No. 2545 of 2021 on 02.04.2024[cite: 40]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Transfer letter dated 20.06.2017; closure notice dated 31.07.2017; Uttarakhand Labour Department order dated 02.02.2018; High Court judgment dated 27.04.2019; Supreme Court order dated 13.11.2019; and liquidator's claim admission statements[cite: 40]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority (NCLT New Delhi, Court-V) dismissed IA No. 2545 of 2021 on 02.04.2024, holding that it lacked jurisdiction to adjudicate the validity of an industrial closure notice issued under the UP Industrial Disputes Act prior to CIRP[cite: 40]. Workmen union appealed to NCLAT[cite: 40].
legal_issues: (i) Whether the Adjudicating Authority under Section 60(5)(c) of the IBC possesses residuary jurisdiction to entertain a challenge to an industrial lockout or permanent closure notice issued under a state labor enactment prior to the commencement of CIRP[cite: 40]; (ii) Whether a liquidator is bound by prior interim correspondence when adjudicating operational workman claims during liquidation[cite: 40].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The residuary jurisdiction of the Adjudicating Authority under Section 60(5)(c) of the IBC is confined to questions of law or fact arising out of or in relation to insolvency resolution proceedings; it cannot be invoked to adjudicate independent public law disputes, labor disputes, or the validity of industrial closures executed under specialized state labor enactments prior to insolvency[cite: 40]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(5)(c) cannot be stretched to cover matters entirely dehors the insolvency proceedings; industrial disputes regarding lockouts or permanent closures under the UP Industrial Disputes Act must be agitated before appropriate labor forums rather than the NCLT[cite: 40]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the permanent closure and transfer notices were issued on 31.07.2017 (more than a year before the August 2018 CIRP commencement), and that the liquidator had already examined and partially admitted the workmen's financial claims to the tune of Rs. 1.09 Crores[cite: 40]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The validity of the pre-CIRP closure notice falls outside the realm of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority correctly declined jurisdiction, and post-closure wage claims were rightly excluded by the liquidator as the plant remained lawfully closed[cite: 40].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1572 of 2024 is dismissed with no order as to costs, upholding the order dated 02.04.2024 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, Court V, New Delhi) in IA No. 2545 of 2021 in CP (IB) No. 706 (PB) of 2018[cite: 40].
summary: Era Labourer Union of SIDCUL appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order dismissing its interlocutory application (IA No. 2545 of 2021) which sought to declare a pre-CIRP factory lockout and permanent closure notice dated 31.07.2017 illegal and to claim consequential wages[cite: 40]. The appellant argued that high court and supreme court liberty orders mandated the NCLT to adjudicate the closure validity[cite: 40]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that the NCLT lacks residuary jurisdiction under Section 60(5)(c) of the IBC to adjudicate pre-insolvency industrial disputes and closures governed by state labor statutes like the UP Industrial Disputes Act[cite: 40]. The Tribunal affirmed that the liquidator correctly admitted legitimate pre-closure claims while excluding post-closure wages for a non-operational factory, and upheld the dismissal[cite: 40].

case_title: Adesh Kumar Gupta & Ors. vs. Liberty Shoes Limited & Ors.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Judicial Member Justice Yogesh Khanna and Technical Member Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Adesh Kumar Gupta (CEO, Executive Director & Shareholder holding 0.56%, along with five supporting entities/shareholders, aggregating a total promoter holding of 5.83%) and related corporate entities[cite: 41]. Respondent No. 1 is Liberty Shoes Limited (Public Listed Company)[cite: 41]. Respondents Nos. 2 to 23 are executive directors, independent directors, KMPs, and major shareholders[cite: 41]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Family management disputes and corporate governance friction among three founding promoter groups (PD Group, DP Group, and Bansal Group) of Liberty Shoes Limited[cite: 41]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (Company law appeal arising from a petition alleging oppression, mismanagement, and illegal removal from directorship)[cite: 41]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Special notice for removal of Appellant No. 1 circulated by a shareholder on 02.09.2023 for inclusion in the AGM agenda[cite: 41]. Appellants filed CP No. 99/CHD/HRY/2023 along with a waiver application under Section 244 on 21.09.2023[cite: 41]. NCLT Chandigarh Bench declined to stay the AGM on 27.09.2023[cite: 41]. AGM held on 30.09.2023, resulting in the overwhelming shareholder removal of Appellant No. 1 as Director/Executive Director[cite: 41]. NCLT dismissed the waiver application via Impugned Order dated 20.11.2023[cite: 41]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Board emails complaining of related party transactions and fund governance; E&Y family settlement consultation records; statutory special notices under Section 169; Delhi High Court injunction order dated 14.08.2023 regarding defamatory communications; and AGM voting results of 30.09.2023[cite: 41]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh Bench dismissed CA No. 179 of 2023 seeking a waiver under Section 244(1)(b) on 20.11.2023, holding that the petition was predominantly a directorial grievance[cite: 41]. Appellants appealed to NCLAT via Company Appeal (AT) No. 238 of 2023[cite: 41].
legal_issues: (i) Whether minority shareholders holding less than the statutory 10% threshold (holding 5.83%) are entitled to a waiver under the proviso to Section 244(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 to file an oppression and mismanagement petition when their primary grievance centers around the removal of a key executive director[cite: 41]; (ii) Whether a 'directorial complaint' regarding removal from executive directorship can form a valid basis for invoking Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 41].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Mere removal or termination of a director or executive chairman does not constitute oppressive or prejudicial conduct under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013; a petition whose primary causa proxima or gravamen is a directorial dispute cannot trigger the just and equitable clause for oppression and mismanagement[cite: 41]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The power to grant waiver under the proviso to Section 244(1) is discretionary and judicial, requiring the Tribunal to assess whether the petition genuinely pertains to systemic oppression and mismanagement rather than masking personal directorial grievances[cite: 41]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examined the pleadings and timing, finding that the company petition was filed on 21.09.2023 as a direct retaliatory measure against a pending September 2023 special notice for removal from directorship, and that shareholders overwhelmingly voted to remove Appellant No. 1 at the AGM on 30.09.2023[cite: 41]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The grievance was fundamentally a personal directorial dispute rather than an act of systemic oppression affecting minority shareholders, and the Adjudicating Authority committed no legal error in refusing to grant a waiver under Section 244[cite: 41].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 238 of 2023 along with pending interlocutory applications is dismissed with no orders as to costs, upholding the order dated 20 November 2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Chandigarh Bench) in CA No. 179/2023 in CP No. 99/CHD/HRY/2023[cite: 41].
summary: Adesh Kumar Gupta and other minority shareholder entities (holding 5.83% aggregate shareholding) appealed against an NCLT Chandigarh order dismissing their application for a waiver under Section 244(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 41]. The appellants argued that exceptional circumstances existed due to promoter deadlocks and that they had highlighted severe corporate governance breaches, related party transactions, and insider trading[cite: 41]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that the appellants' petition was overwhelmingly padded with historical grievances whose true causa proxima was the lawful removal of Appellant No. 1 from his executive directorship by an overwhelming majority of shareholders at the AGM on 30.09.2023[cite: 41]. Relying on the Supreme Court's ruling in Tata Consultancy Services vs. Cyrus Investments, the Tribunal affirmed that directorial disputes cannot be projected as oppression and mismanagement under Section 241, and upheld the denial of the waiver[cite: 41].

case_title: Committee of Creditors of Kindle Developers Private Limited & Anr. vs. New Okhla Industrial Development Authority & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 506 of 2024 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 554 of 2024
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan, Technical Members Barun Mitra and Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 506 of 2024 is Lords Social Welfare Association (Home Buyers Association / Successful Resolution Applicant), and in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 554 of 2024 is the Committee of Creditors of Kindle Developers Private Limited[cite: 42]. Respondent No. 1 is New Okhla Industrial Development Authority (NOIDA)[cite: 42]. Respondent No. 2 is Mr. Kashi Viswanathan Sivaraman (Resolution Professional of Kindle Developers Pvt. Ltd.)[cite: 42]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: NOIDA executed a Lease Deed dated 24.10.2011 (corrected vide Correction Deed dated 19.10.2012) in favor of Kindle Developers Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) allotting commercial/sports city Plot No. SC-01/D1, Sector 79, Noida, admeasuring 40,000 sq. mtr., on a total premium of Rs. 120.75 Crores, payable in installments with 11% interest[cite: 42]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted on installment and lease rent payments; NOIDA issued notice dated 27.01.2015 and subsequently cancelled the lease deed on 13.08.2015 due to non-payment[cite: 42]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Lease cancelled on 13.08.2015[cite: 42]. Corporate Debtor filed a restoration application on 14.06.2016[cite: 42]. CIRP commenced on 09.03.2018[cite: 42]. NOIDA filed IA No. 1592 of 2019 on 02.12.2019 seeking exclusion of the plot[cite: 42]. CoC approved the resolution plan on 04.12.2019[cite: 42]. NCLT rejected restoration on 10.11.2020 and allowed NOIDA's exclusion application via order dated 11.01.2024[cite: 42]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Lease Deed dated 24.10.2011; Correction Deed dated 19.10.2012; Cancellation letter dated 13.08.2015; Corporate Debtor's restoration request dated 14.06.2016; NOIDA's rejection letter dated 10.10.2020; and balance sheets reflecting Rs. 170.21 Crores collected from homebuyers[cite: 42]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-II allowed IA No. 1592 of 2019 on 11.01.2024, excluding Plot No. SC-01/D1 from the resolution plan[cite: 42]. CoC and Homebuyers Association appealed to NCLAT via Company Appeals Nos. 506 and 554 of 2024[cite: 42].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a lease cancelled prior to the commencement of CIRP can be deemed to subsist under Section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 as a tenancy holding over due to continuous possession or a pending restoration application[cite: 42]; (ii) Whether an industrial development authority's cancellation of a plot lease prior to insolvency strips the corporate debtor of possessory rights, excluding the land from the CIRP asset pool[cite: 42].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a tenancy by holding over requires either the acceptance of post-determination rent by the lessor or an express/implied assent to the lessee's continued possession; mere continued physical possession without rent acceptance or landlord assent reduces the status of the former lessee to that of a tenant at sufferance, which creates no new tenancy[cite: 42]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 of the IBC and moratorium protections do not apply to property that ceased to be an asset of the corporate debtor long before the initiation of CIRP[cite: 42]. A statutory authority's right to resume possession upon breach under Section 14 of the UP Industrial Area Development Act, 1976 operates independently of corporate insolvency[cite: 42]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that NOIDA never accepted lease rent post-13.08.2015, never gave written or implied assent to continuation, and expressly rejected the Corporate Debtor's belated restoration application on 10.11.2020[cite: 42]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The lease stood validly terminated on 13.08.2015, the plot did not form part of the corporate debtor's assets, Section 116 of the TOPA did not apply, and the Adjudicating Authority correctly directed the exclusion of the plot from the resolution plan, warranting liquidation under Section 33(1)[cite: 42].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 506 and 554 of 2024 are dismissed, upholding the order dated 11.01.2024 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench-II in IA No. 1592 of 2019[cite: 42]. I.A. No. 1664 of 2019 for plan approval is rejected as infructuous, and the Corporate Debtor is ordered into liquidation under Section 33(1) of the IBC, with Mr. Vikram Bajaj appointed as Liquidator[cite: 42]. NOIDA is permitted to seek early disposal of Allahabad High Court Writ Petition (C) No. 26400 of 2023 and take possession of the assets in accordance with law[cite: 42].
summary: Lords Social Welfare Association (Homebuyers Association) and the Committee of Creditors appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order excluding Plot No. SC-01/D1, Sector 79, Noida, from the resolution plan of Kindle Developers Pvt. Ltd[cite: 42]. The appellants argued that the lease was not validly cancelled, that the corporate debtor was a tenant holding over under Section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act, and that homebuyers were kept in the dark[cite: 42]. Dismissing both appeals, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that the lease was lawfully cancelled by NOIDA on 13.08.2015 (prior to the 2018 CIRP commencement), that filing a belated restoration application does not revive a terminated lease, and that Section 116 of TOPA is inapplicable without landlord assent or rent acceptance[cite: 42]. The Tribunal affirmed the exclusion of the land, rejected the resolution plan application, ordered the liquidation of the corporate debtor under Section 33(1), and appointed Mr. Vikram Bajaj as Liquidator[cite: 42].

case_title: Sandeep Mittal & Ravi Mittal vs. M/s ASREC (India) Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 37 of 2024 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 573 of 2024
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan, Technical Members Barun Mitra and Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Sandeep Mittal and Ravi Mittal (Suspended Directors/Promoters of Corporate Debtor, M/s Shree Industries Ltd. / erstwhile Rama Finance Ltd.)[cite: 44]. Respondent No. 1 is M/s ASREC (India) Ltd. (Financial Creditor / Assignee of Bank of Baroda)[cite: 44]. Respondent No. 3 is Mr. Gaurav Singhal (Interim Resolution Professional / Resolution Professional)[cite: 44]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Gujarat State Financial Corporation (GSFC), Gujarat Industrial Investment Corporation (GIIC), Bank of Baroda, and Dena Bank advanced term loans to M/s Ganpati Pulp and Paper Ltd. (GPPL)[cite: 44]. Following default, GSFC took possession under Section 29 of the SFC Act, 1951 and auctioned GPPL's assets[cite: 44]. M/s Rama Finance Ltd. (now Shree Industries Ltd. / Corporate Debtor) offered Rs. 3.88 Crores, accepted via Agreement dated 27.11.1990, requiring Rs. 50 Lakhs down payment and the balance Rs. 3.38 Crores payable in 20 quarterly installments with 16% interest, secured by a guarantee deed dated 12.12.1990[cite: 44]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: ASREC (India) Ltd. claimed an outstanding debt of Rs. 92,35,21,674.03 as of 30.06.2022, alleging default from 01.04.2017[cite: 44]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Agreement executed on 27.11.1990[cite: 44]. Bank of Baroda assigned its debt to ASREC on 29.03.2011[cite: 44]. Gujarat High Court disposed of LPA No. 2480 of 2010 on 26.07.2021[cite: 44]. ASREC filed Section 7 application [IB-40(ND)/2023] on 23.11.2022[cite: 44]. NCLT New Delhi admitted Section 7 on 13.12.2023[cite: 44]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Sale acceptance letter dated 07.11.1990; Sale Agreement dated 27.11.1990; Deed of Guarantee dated 12.12.1990; GSFC inter-institutional letter dated 17.10.2000; and corporate debtor's settlement proposal letter dated 04.03.2021[cite: 44]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Court-III admitted ASREC's Section 7 petition on 13.12.2023, holding the transaction constituted a financial debt[cite: 44]. Suspended directors appealed to NCLAT[cite: 44].
legal_issues: (i) Whether an agreement for the purchase of assets under Section 29 of the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951 involving deferred payment of the purchase price constitutes a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC or a pure sale-purchase transaction[cite: 44]; (ii) Whether 'disbursement' of money against the consideration for the time value of money is a sine qua non for a debt to qualify as a financial debt under the IBC[cite: 44].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The true nature of a transaction must be determined from the contemporaneous documents reflecting the agreement; an agreement for the purchase of assets where the balance purchase price is payable in installments does not constitute a loan or financial debt under Section 5(8) of the IBC, as no money is disbursed by the vendor/creditor to the purchaser against consideration for the time value of money[cite: 44]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 5(8) of the IBC, 'financial debt' requires the actual disbursement of money against consideration for the time value of money, as reaffirmed in Pioneer Urban and Global Credit Capital; disbursal of property or unpaid purchase price in an asset sale does not satisfy the statutory test of a financial debt[cite: 44]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the letter dated 07.11.1990, Agreement dated 27.11.1990, and Deed of Guarantee dated 12.12.1990, finding they were exclusively part of an auction sale of GPPL's assets where the Corporate Debtor was a purchaser paying purchase price installments, not a borrower receiving a loan[cite: 44]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The transaction was purely a sale of assets and the claim represented unpaid purchase price rather than a financial debt; hence, the Section 7 petition was completely not maintainable and the admission order was illegal[cite: 44].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 37 and 573 of 2024 are allowed, setting aside the order dated 13.12.2023 passed by NCLT New Delhi Court-III in (IB)-40(ND)/2023[cite: 44]. Section 7 application filed by Respondent No. 1 is dismissed with costs assessed at Rs. 1,00,000/- to be paid to the Appellant in Appeal No. 37 of 2024 within one month[cite: 44].
summary: Sandeep Mittal and Ravi Mittal, suspended directors of Shree Industries Ltd. (erstwhile Rama Finance Ltd.), appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order admitting a Section 7 CIRP application filed by ASREC (India) Ltd. for an alleged default of Rs. 92.35 Crores[cite: 44]. The appellants contended that the underlying 1990 transaction was a sale agreement for purchasing the assets of an ailing company (GPPL) under Section 29 of the SFC Act, and not a loan or financial debt[cite: 44]. Allowing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that contemporaneous documents (sale notice, agreement, and guarantee deed) conclusively established a sale-purchase transaction of assets with deferred payment of purchase price, lacking any monetary disbursement for time value of money[cite: 44]. The Tribunal ruled that unpaid purchase consideration cannot be converted into a financial debt, set aside the admission order, and dismissed the Section 7 petition with costs[cite: 44].

case_title: Saratvam Creators vs. Sudhir Constructions Infraspace Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan, Technical Members Barun Mitra and Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Saratvam Creators (claimed Unsecured Financial Creditor / EPC Contractor)[cite: 45]. Respondent No. 1 is Sudhir Construction Infraspace Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 45]. Respondent No. 6 is the Bank of Maharashtra (Secured Financial Creditor)[cite: 45]. Respondent No. 7 is the Suspended Director[cite: 45]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was awarded a HAM Road Project by PWD and formed an SPV (Sudhir Constructions Infraspace [Shegaon Palkhi Road] Pvt. Ltd.)[cite: 45]. On 18.06.2022, the SPV entered into a back-to-back execution agreement with the Appellant as EPC Contractor[cite: 45]. Subsequently, on 05.08.2022 (after service of a Section 7 advance notice by Bank of Maharashtra on 04.07.2022), the SPV, Corporate Debtor, and Appellant executed a Loan Agreement for Rs. 195 Crores and a Deed of Guarantee-cum-Indemnity[cite: 45]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Bank of Maharashtra's secured claim was admitted for Rs. 160.95 Crores[cite: 45]. Appellant claimed Rs. 195,28,11,699/- as an unsecured financial creditor based on the guarantee, while actual disbursement claimed in Form-C was only Rs. 19,43,13,000/-[cite: 45]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Bank of Maharashtra served Section 7 advance copy on 04.07.2022[cite: 45]. Loan agreement and guarantee executed on 05.08.2022[cite: 45]. CIRP commenced on 03.03.2023 on an application by a third creditor for Rs. 1.25 Crores[cite: 45]. IRP constituted CoC on 27.03.2023 admitting Appellant's claim in toto (39.16% vote share) and Bank of Maharashtra (32.28%)[cite: 45]. Bank of Maharashtra filed IA No. 2142 of 2023 on 10.04.2023 objecting to CoC constitution[cite: 45]. NCLT Mumbai allowed IA No. 2142 of 2023 on 02.08.2024[cite: 45]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: EPC contract dated 18.06.2022; Loan agreement dated 05.08.2022; Deed of Guarantee-cum-Indemnity dated 05.08.2022; Form-C claim filing showing actual disbursement of Rs. 19.43 Crores; and Escrow account statements showing Rs. 19.73 Lakhs/Crores paid back to the Appellant[cite: 45]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-V allowed Bank of Maharashtra's IA No. 2142 of 2023 on 02.08.2024, directing the RP to reconstitute the CoC by excluding unsecured financial creditors and ordering a forensic audit[cite: 45]. Appellant appealed to NCLAT[cite: 45].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a party that executes an EPC contract for a project SPV and subsequently enters into a guarantee agreement with the corporate debtor after receiving notice of a Section 7 petition qualifies as an 'unsecured financial creditor' entitled to sit on the CoC[cite: 45]; (ii) Whether total disbursement of the sanctioned loan amount is a prerequisite for admitting a financial debt claim under a guarantee, and whether the creation of such debt post-notice is vitiated by malafides[cite: 45].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under the IBC, a financial debt requires a legally valid liability or obligation in respect of a claim that is due, supported by actual disbursement against the consideration for the time value of money; a guarantor's liability cannot exceed that of the principal borrower, and claims manufactured post-receipt of a Section 7 insolvency petition notice solely to dilute a secured lender's voting share are legally untenable[cite: 45]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 8(2) of the CIRP Regulations requires financial debt to be substantiated by financial contracts supported by financial statements or records evidencing that amounts committed under a facility have been drawn by the corporate debtor[cite: 45]. A guarantor is liable only to the extent of actual dues and default of the principal borrower[cite: 45]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized Form-C, noting that while the loan agreement was for Rs. 195 Crores, actual disbursement claimed was only Rs. 19.43 Crores, and escrow account records proved that the Appellant actually received back more than Rs. 19.73 Crores from the project escrow account, extinguishing any sustainable debt[cite: 45]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The admission of the inflated Rs. 195 Crore claim by the RP was patently unsustainable, the documents were executed after receiving notice of insolvency to manipulate CoC voting share, and the Adjudicating Authority correctly ordered the reconstitution of the CoC and a forensic audit[cite: 45].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1664 of 2024 is dismissed, upholding the order dated 02.08.2024 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-V in IA No. 2142 of 2023[cite: 45]. Liberty is granted to the parties to file fresh applications before the Adjudicating Authority regarding the 'related party' status and the Appellant's claim as a financial/secured creditor based upon the outcome of the ordered transaction audit report[cite: 45].
summary: Saratvam Creators appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order directing the reconstitution of the CoC of Sudhir Constructions Infraspace Pvt. Ltd. by excluding unsecured financial creditors and ordering a forensic audit upon an application by the Bank of Maharashtra[cite: 45]. The appellant argued that it was a valid unsecured financial creditor holding a Rs. 195 Crore guarantee[cite: 45]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that the loan and guarantee agreements were suspiciously executed on 05.08.2022 immediately after receiving an advance copy of a Section 7 petition on 04.07.2022, that actual disbursement was only Rs. 19.43 Crores, and that project escrow records showed the appellant had already received back more than that amount[cite: 45]. The Tribunal affirmed the Adjudicating Authority's order ousting the appellant from the CoC due to manipulated claims, while granting liberty to seek reconsideration upon receipt of the forensic transaction audit report[cite: 45].

case_title: Department of State Tax Through The Dy. Commr. of State Tax vs. Cicil Biochem Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1332 of 2024 & I.A. No. 4394, 4835 of 2024
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Arun Baroka)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is the Department of State Tax, Government of Maharashtra, through the Deputy Commissioner of State Tax[cite: 46]. Respondent No. 1 is Cicil Biochem Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) and Respondent No. 2 is the Resolution Professional[cite: 46]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of Cicil Biochem Pvt. Ltd., wherein a Resolution Plan was submitted and placed before the Adjudicating Authority for approval via IA No. 906 of 2021[cite: 46]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant's statutory tax claim was admitted in the CIRP for an amount of Rs. 83,83,04,408/- (Rs. 83.83 Crores), against which the approved resolution plan allocated a payout of only 0.13%[cite: 46]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Adjudicating Authority allowed IA No. 906 of 2021 approving the Resolution Plan vide order dated 19.10.2023[cite: 46]. The Appellant filed an appeal with a 15-day delay, which was condoned via IA No. 4835 of 2024 on 19.09.2024[cite: 46]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Admitted claim records of the Department of State Tax amounting to Rs. 83,83,04,408/-; terms of the Resolution Plan allocating a 0.13% recovery; and the statutory text of Section 37 of the Maharashtra Value Added Tax Act, 2002[cite: 46]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority approved the Resolution Plan on 19.10.2023[cite: 46]. The Department of State Tax appealed to the NCLAT challenging its treatment as an operational creditor and the 0.13% allocation, asserting secured creditor status under Rainbow Papers[cite: 46].
legal_issues: (i) Whether a state tax authority is entitled to be treated as a 'secured creditor' under Section 30(2)(b) and Section 53 of the IBC by virtue of the first charge provision under Section 37 of the Maharashtra Value Added Tax Act, 2002 (MVAT Act), relying on the Supreme Court's ruling in Rainbow Papers[cite: 46]; (ii) Whether Section 37 of the MVAT Act is distinguishable from Section 48 of the Gujarat Value Added Tax Act, 2003 due to being expressly subject to central enactments[cite: 46].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A statutory first charge created under a state tax enactment does not elevate the tax authority to the status of a secured creditor under the IBC if the state provision is expressly made subject to the creation of first charge under Central Acts; in such cases, the waterfall priority under Section 53 of the IBC prevails, and the tax department is legitimately treated as an operational creditor whose allocation under a resolution plan complies with Section 30(2)(b)[cite: 46]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Unlike Section 48 of the GVAT Act (considered in Rainbow Papers), Section 37 of the MVAT Act explicitly employs the qualifying phrase 'subject to any provision regarding creation of first charge in any Central Act for the time being in force', thereby subordinating state tax claims to the priority waterfall in Section 53 of the IBC as established in Department of State Tax v. Zicom Saas Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 46]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified the statutory wording of Section 37 of the MVAT Act and applied its binding coordinate bench precedent in Zicom Saas Pvt. Ltd. to conclude that the statutory charge was subordinate to the IBC framework[cite: 46]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Rainbow Papers is inapplicable to Section 37 of the MVAT Act; the Appellant was rightly treated as an operational creditor, and the 0.13% distribution under the approved Resolution Plan violates neither Section 30(2)(b) nor any other provision of the IBC[cite: 46].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1332 of 2024 is dismissed, affirming the order dated 19.10.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority in IA No. 906 of 2021 approving the Resolution Plan[cite: 46]. Delay of 15 days is condoned and pending IAs are closed[cite: 46].
summary: The Department of State Tax, Maharashtra, appealed against an NCLT order dated 19.10.2023 approving the Resolution Plan of Cicil Biochem Pvt. Ltd., wherein its admitted statutory claim of Rs. 83.83 Crores was allocated only 0.13%[cite: 46]. Relying on the Supreme Court's ruling in State Tax Officer v. Rainbow Papers Limited, the appellant argued that Section 37 of the MVAT Act created a first charge on the debtor's properties, entitling it to be treated as a secured creditor[cite: 46]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench followed its earlier precedent in Department of State Tax v. Zicom Saas Pvt. Ltd., holding that Section 37 of the MVAT Act is expressly made subject to Central Acts, unlike Section 48 of the GVAT Act[cite: 46]. The Tribunal affirmed that the waterfall mechanism under Section 53 of the IBC overrides the state charge, the appellant was properly categorized as an operational creditor, and the plan approval was lawful[cite: 46].
